Suggestive Inquiry: Summaries

Master Lexicon and Concordance

Terms, persons, works and voices of A Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery (1850), drawn only from the book. Quotes are verbatim; references point to chapter paragraphs (¶) and footnotes (n). Refs beginning APP are the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer.

Conventions. Headwords start with a capital letter; inside a headword, a word is capitalised only where the book itself mostly capitalises it. A leading “the” is dropped unless it belongs to a title or the term needs it. Spelling follows the book’s majority use (Sulphur, center); other spellings and word forms found in the text are listed after the kind. A note in italics after the kind tells homonyms apart. “Identified with” lists only identities the text itself asserts; “See also” links related entries editorially (shared names or forms, or a compound and its head word) and asserts no identity.

1 Corinth.

treatise

A scriptural passage (cap. 3, v. 7) Atwood cites in support of the point that it is God who gives the increase.

Cited by Atwood, with the reference cap. 3, v. 7 given in the footnote, in support of the point that the increase comes from God: “neither he that watereth, but God, that giveth the increase” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n32].

References: IV.1 n32, IV.1 ¶40

1 Kings

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: King

References: II.3 n40

A

A. Kircher

person · Kircher, Kircheri

Cited for alchemy’s antiquity, for a Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies, and for a transmutation story.

Atwood cites A. Kircher (Oedipus Aegyptiacus; de Lapide Philos. Dissert.) in support of alchemy’s antiquity, and as the source of the Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n2; I.1 ¶7]. His Mundus Subterraneus supplies an explicit transmutation story [I.1 ¶77].

References: I.1 n2, I.1 n29, I.1 ¶3, I.1 ¶7, I.1 ¶77

Abbot Panorimitanus

person

An abbot Atwood cites as having praised the Hermetic Art and the wisdom of Arnold.

Cited by Atwood as one who praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold’s wisdom [I.1 ¶43].

References: I.1 ¶43

Abbot Reginald

person

Named as the addressee of Aquinas’ Thesaurus Alchimiae.

Mentioned only as the person to whom Aquinas’ Thesaurus Alchimiae is addressed [I.1 ¶42; I.1 n49; I.1 n51].

References: I.1 n49, I.1 n51, I.1 ¶42

Ablative reasoning

term

In a view attributed to Plato, the defective reasoning by negation through which Matter is apprehended, describing it only by what it is not.

A quoted view (Plato): Matter can be apprehended, but only by a reasoning that proceeds by negation, describing it by what it is not: “Matter is indeed to be apprehended, and that by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53].

References: III.2 ¶53

Abraham

person

Cited through the Sepher Jezirah (Liber de Creatione) as an example of the wisely simple, and elsewhere for travelling with his asses.

Atwood cites the Sepher Jezirah (Liber de Creatione, Authore Abraham, cap. 1), presenting Abraham as an example of the wisely simple who subdued the will to the Law of Wisdom, and closing with a Latin injunction: “Intellige in scientia et sepias intellignetia” [II.3 ¶55; II.3 n61; II.3 ¶56; II.3 n62] (our rendering, roughly: understand in knowledge and be wise in understanding). Elsewhere he is mentioned, by way of illustration, as one who constantly travelled with his asses [III.2 ¶64].

References: II.3 n61, II.3 n62, II.3 ¶55, II.3 ¶56, III.2 ¶64

Abraham the Jew

person

Mentioned as the one who indicated the fire and the furnace to Flamel.

Mentioned by Atwood as the one who indicated the fire and furnace to Flamel [III.1 ¶37].

See also: Jew

References: III.1 ¶37

Abram den Dior

person

Cited for reference only.

References: III.2 n28

Absolute ground

term

The ultimate foundation of knowledge; philosophers dispute its conditions and difficulty, but, Atwood says, none deny that it is possible.

Atwood’s term for the ultimate ground of knowledge. She notes that “philosophers have disputed about the conditions and difficulty of the Absolute ground” [II.1 ¶33]; the record adds that none deny its possibility.

References: II.1 ¶33

Absolute Identity

term · Identity

What the hypostasis bounding abstract reason proves to be when met by the inquiring light within; prior to all duality of consciousness.

In Atwood’s account, the hypostasis that bounds abstract reason, when met by the inquiring light within, proves to be Absolute Identity, “which, before all duality of consciousness, is the fortitude and life of all” [III.2 ¶31]. She also speaks of the “incomprehensible nature of the objective contact in Identity” [III.2 ¶33].

See also: Identity, True Identity of nature

References: III.2 ¶31, III.2 ¶33

Abyss of being

term

In a quoted account, the abyss where the parts of the world lay mingled and formless before the spirit’s breath agitated the mass.

From a passage attributed to the metropolitan of Memphis: before the spirit’s breath agitated the mass, the parts of the world “lay mingled and inform, brooding overwhelmed in the Abyss of Being” [III.3 ¶46].

See also: Being

References: III.3 ¶46

Abysse

term · Abyss

That which is without ground, fathomless or void (Boehme); for Atwood also the Kabalists’ name for the Matter, called by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.

Quoting Boehme, the text defines it: “the Abysse, that is without ground, or fathomless or void” [III.2 ¶16]; in the same place the One Thing is spoken of as “the first divine manifestation out of the abyss” [III.2 ¶16]. Atwood elsewhere uses the word for the Matter as the Kabalists name it: “that Abyss of the Kabalists, styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60], so Abyss = Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite.

Identified with: without ground, fathomless, void [III.2 ¶16]; Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite [III.2 ¶60]

References: III.2 ¶16, III.2 ¶60

Acetum

term

A name connected with dissolution, identified by Atwood with the vitriolic solvent; in Hermes and the Master, ‘our Acetum’ with which the soul or sulphurous Form is mingled.

Atwood names it alongside the solvent: something “becomes their vitriolic solvent and most sharp acetum” [I.2 ¶40]; the reader takes it as a name of the dissolving stage, which is an inference. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the watery soul is mingled with it to obtain the sulphurous Form: “to mingle the same with our Acetum” [I.3 ¶27]; the same words recur in a passage quoted from the Master [IV.2 ¶14]. In neither quoted passage is the Acetum itself explained.

Identified with: vitriolic solvent [I.2 ¶40]

References: I.2 ¶40, I.3 ¶27, IV.2 ¶14

Actives and passives

term · actives, passives

Paired principles that, by action and reaction, raise one another successively until spiritual ability is complete.

Atwood describes the work as “raising successively actives by passives, and, vice versa, passives by actives” [IV.1 ¶41], continuing until spiritual ability is complete. Compare agent and patient.

References: IV.1 ¶41

Acts of Parliament and Pope’s Bulls

collective voice · acts of Parliament, Pope’s Bull’s

Legal measures Atwood cites to illustrate the suppression of transmutation, which only drove its pursuit into secrecy.

Cited by Atwood to illustrate the legal suppression of transmutation, which in her account only drove the pursuit into secrecy [I.1 ¶55; I.1 n61].

References: I.1 n61, I.1 ¶55

Adamic soil

term

A mystical soil whose glories the prophet describes, spoken of with the winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles.

Atwood speaks of “that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], whose glories the prophet describes, in a context of winds, clouds, snow and wooden receptacles. The text as recorded gives no further plain meaning.

References: III.2 ¶12

Adaptation

term · adaptations

In the Smaragdine Table of Hermes, the manner by which all things arose from the One Thing.

A term of the Smaragdine Table (Hermes, quoted): “so all things arose from this one thing by adaptation” [I.1 ¶9], and “Hence were all wonderful adaptations of which this is the manner.” [I.1 ¶9]. A second rendering of the Table reads “so all things proceeded from this One Thing by adaptation” [IV.2 ¶44].

References: I.1 ¶9, IV.2 ¶44

Adept

term · adepts, true adepts, adeptest

A true master of the Art, one who has accomplished it, sharply distinguished by Atwood from pretenders; in quoted authorities, the initiate whom the Lord illuminates and seals.

Atwood’s usual word for a genuine, accomplished master of the Art. The adepts are those who truly understood Geber: “They who have really understood Geber, his adept compeers” [I.1 ¶33]. They are rare and set against pretenders: “The true adepts have been rare exceptions in the world” [I.1 ¶41]; “Many usurped the title of the adepts, who had no knowledge even of the preliminaries of the Art” [I.1 ¶53]; “the pretenders to the Art were in latter times far more numerous than the true adepts” [I.1 ¶86] (said with reference to Sendivogius). The public could not tell them apart, so “even the true adepts — for the public knew not to distinguish — suffered equal cruelty” [I.1 ¶66]. She applies the title to individuals: Ripley “though reputed a good adept” [I.1 ¶64]; “Henry Khunrath, a pious and learned adeptest” [I.1 ¶70].

On their writing: “the adepts appear to have a directly contrary aim” [I.1 ¶82], their writing deliberately obscuring, being “so very abstruse and envious in their disguises” [IV.1 ¶18]; they caution against excitation [IV.1 ¶18]. “Aristotle is much blamed by Adepts in general” [I.1 ¶16], and of the Bononian Enigma “the adepts claim it as having exclusive reference to the occult material of their art” [I.1 ¶20]. A cited speaker says “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17]; Eirenaeus (quoted) says “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26]. “Verily, says the adept” introduces a cited speaker [III.1 ¶8], where the word is also used of those who call the fire of life Antimony.

In quoted patristic passages the adept is the initiate: Clemens Alexandrinus, “he sets his seal upon the adept whom he illuminates with his beams” [II.2 ¶5]; the Bishop of Alexandria, “He sets his seal upon the Adepts” [IV.2 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood ties the word to discovery: “The seeker, however, in this point of relation, is the adept, the discoverer, the finder.” [APP ¶23] — the seeker at the point where the Golden Fleece appears.

Identified with: the seeker [APP ¶23]

See also: Adepts (cited voice), Experimental adeptist, French adept, Modern adept, More modern class of adepts, Mysterious adeptest, No less experienced adept, No less subtle than experienced adept, Sage

References: I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶20, I.1 ¶33, I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶53, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70, I.1 ¶82, I.1 ¶86, II.2 ¶5, III.1 ¶8, IV.1 ¶17, IV.1 ¶18, IV.2 ¶16, IV.3 ¶26, APP ¶23

Adepts

collective voice — cited voice · the adept, the wise, the wise Adept, the wise Adepts

The anonymous ‘adept’ or ‘adepts’ whose sayings Atwood cites throughout, almost always in support and sometimes explicitly endorsed, on the matter, the fire, the stages of the work and its spiritual end.

Atwood frequently quotes an unnamed ‘adept’, sometimes identified only by a footnoted work (Rosarium, Lumen de Lumine, Filium Ariadne, Introitus Apertus, Mercury’s Caducean Rod, Maieri Symbola Aureae Mensae, Fama et Confessionis, R.C.), and the adepts collectively. The voice is used in support, and she sometimes endorses it explicitly [III.1 ¶64; III.1 ¶66]. The adept also backs her condemnation of fraudulent books [I.1 ¶53].

The matter and gold. “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44; I.2 n43]; “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63; I.3 n70]. The subject is despised: “It is what the world cares not for, as the adept says, but disesteems it” [II.2 ¶18]. The adepts teach that all things derive from one Spirit, gold nearest it [I.2 ¶48]; purified sulphur as seed and mercury as earth of the wise [I.3 n29; I.3 n30]; the Matter’s birth is “singular and not without a miracle” [III.3 ¶62]; “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n7].

Fire and process. “men neither see nor do they believe there is any other fire but the common fire” [I.3 n41]; the three fires “should be quickly lighted” with a Fourth supervening [IV.2 ¶11; IV.2 n2]; “O happy gate of Blackness!” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n44]; the Seed of Spirit is “a decompounded ens, extremely heavy, shining through the darkness like a fiery star” [II.3 ¶30]; “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41] (extent of quotation unclear); “Open the compound creature; look up the elements; divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; on renewal of the powder, “if the process fails in any stage, an addition of the same will renew it” [II.1 ¶25]; Nature alone cannot enter the True Light: “she has no hands” [III.2 ¶61; III.2 n45]; the Orient Animal is stripped “not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. Also cited: the sign of returning colours and the white elixir, “now our king hath triumphed over the miseries of death” [I.3 n22]; a reading of ‘dust of the earth’ [I.3 n51]; the Preparing Spirit and cleansing of the Argent vive [IV.1 ¶10]; the guide [II.3 n37]; the Light becoming visible, “Lux manifeste et visibilis ad oculum” [III.3 ¶10], and “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North!”, glossed by Atwood as the Light arising out of the crucifixion of cerebral life [III.3 ¶15]; the purified substance’s endless transformations [III.2 ¶22; III.2 n22]; the loadstone, Salt, Pole and Fire and the union of agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30; IV.2 n19]; nature’s ordinary manifestation contradicting her perfect law [I.2 ¶18; I.2 ¶20]; imaginative impressures lingering in a place [III.4 ¶42].

Spiritual end. The Corner Stone is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise” [III.1 ¶66]; “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18; IV.2 n16], which Atwood completes and extends; the adepts’ maxim “they who sow in tears shall reap in joy” she expands into the sacrifice of Self-Will [III.3 ¶20]; they say “Natus est jam Elias Artista” [IV.2 ¶12] (our rendering: Elias the Artist is now born) and concealed the three operations [IV.2 ¶3]; with Plutarch they witness to the fable’s meaning [IV.2 ¶7]; God “has always revealed them to his elected children” [IV.4 ¶25]. Their analysis of man’s life as a pure fire in an ethereal vapour is reported ‘as they profess’ yet presented by Atwood as shown [IV.4 ¶4].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Adepts call the Art “Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29], and reducing their ground to physical science is dismissed as twaddle [APP ¶30].

Wise and adepts. Atwood endorses their declarations that none attain the Art without right intention and God’s blessing and that the pursuit is dangerous to the ill-informed: “As the adepts indeed foretold, their records have proved like a curious two-edged instrument” [III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶16].

Wise Adept. Cited by Atwood: when Pluto’s Palace is exposed with Minerva’s Artifice, or Vulcan stands with her at the Altar, “the Association is ominous” [IV.1 ¶34].

Wise Adepts. Atwood, with approval, says their enigmas, fables, parables and maxims all tend to one discovery and are to be studied with the Key [IV.4 ¶32].

See also: Adept, Sage, The Wise

References: I.1 ¶53, I.2 n43, I.2 ¶18, I.2 ¶20, I.2 ¶44, I.2 ¶48, I.3 n22, I.3 n29, I.3 n30, I.3 n41, I.3 n51, I.3 n63, I.3 n70, II.1 ¶25, II.2 n16, II.2 ¶18, II.3 n37, II.3 n44, II.3 ¶30, II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶41, II.3 ¶52, III.1 ¶64, III.1 ¶66, III.2 n22, III.2 n45, III.2 ¶22, III.2 ¶61, III.3 n7, III.3 ¶10, III.3 ¶15, III.3 ¶17, III.3 ¶20, III.3 ¶62, III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶42, IV.1 ¶10, IV.1 ¶34, IV.2 n16, IV.2 n19, IV.2 n2, IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 ¶12, IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 ¶3, IV.2 ¶30, IV.2 ¶7, IV.4 ¶25, IV.4 ¶32, IV.4 ¶4, APP ¶29, APP ¶30

Adfar

person

A solitary adept of Alexandria, named as the master of Morienus.

Named by Atwood as a solitary adept of Alexandria and Morienus’s master [I.1 ¶35].

References: I.1 ¶35

Adoration

term

Bound up with sacrifice and prayer; its three terms contain all the Divine measures, and its end is where rational inquiry rests and true love is found.

Atwood connects adoration with sacrifice and the advantages of prayer. She speaks of “these three terms of adoration, in which, according to the authorities, all the Divine measures are contained” [III.4 ¶25]; these reconcile the warring elements of life and give three supernal benefits. “And thus the end of all adoration is attained” [III.4 ¶26] — the point at which rational inquiry rests and true love is found.

References: III.4 ¶25, III.4 ¶26

Adrop

term

In Khunrath, the starting matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed; called Saturn, the lead of the Wise.

From Khunrath (quoted): the matter of the first act, whose bonds of coagulation are relaxed, called “our heart of Saturn” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives its identity: “Adrop (which in its proper tongue is called Saturn, i.e., the lead of the Wise)” [IV.1 ¶36]; so Adrop = Saturn = lead of the Wise.

Identified with: Saturn [IV.1 ¶36]; lead of the Wise [IV.1 ¶36]

References: IV.1 ¶36

Adventitious image and central form

term · adventitious image, central form

The externally generated form imposed on a body, to be constricted, set against the body’s inner central form, to be developed into life and act.

Atwood contrasts two forms in a body: “the adventitious or externally generated image may be constricted utterly, and the central form contrariwise developed into life and act” [I.2 ¶20]. The work, on this account, suppresses the outward image and brings forth the inner form.

See also: Form

References: I.2 ¶20

Adytum

term

The temple’s interior sanctuary, entered by the Aspirant after leaving the statues behind; an image of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within.

Atwood uses the image of “the Aspirant entering into the interior to behold the Adytum, leaves behind him all the statues in the temple” [III.2 ¶66], as a figure of the mind entertaining the simple Unity of Light within. She also speaks of approaching “to the gate of the first Adytum” [III.3 ¶3], whose vestibule is where the Tears of Isis are contemplated.

References: III.2 ¶66, III.3 ¶3

Adytum of life

term

In Proclus, the soul’s innermost recess, where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.

Quoted from Proclus: the soul withdraws “into her interior recesses and into the Adytum of Life” [II.4 ¶29], where with closed eye she perceives the genus of the gods.

See also: Life

References: II.4 ¶29

Aelia Laelia Crispis

person

A riddling inscription, unattributed in the text, describing a thing that is none of the opposites yet all, cited after the claim that the Matter is one Identity.

An unattributed riddling inscription cited after Atwood’s claim that the Matter is one Identity; it describes something that is none of the opposites yet all, nowhere in particular yet everywhere: “No male, nor female, nor hermaphrodite,” [III.3 ¶66].

References: III.3 ¶66

Aeneid

treatise

Book 6 of the Aeneid, cited for its descent to the shades, which Atwood reads as an illustration of stages of the work and of the Epopteia of Universal Nature.

Atwood quotes Book 6 in Latin to illustrate the inner journey. The apparitions: “Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum” [II.3 ¶21; II.3 n16] (ours: here, trembling with sudden fear, he seizes his sword), as Aeneas draws on bodiless shades until warned. The place of shades: “Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae” [II.3 ¶26; II.3 n28] (ours: this is the place of shades, of sleep and drowsy night). The courage required: “Nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.” [II.3 n37] (ours: now, Aeneas, there is need of courage, now of a firm heart). Aeneas meeting his father in Elysium receives the Epopteia of Universal Nature, spirit and mind pervading the whole: “Spiritus intus alit” [II.4 ¶21; II.4 ¶22; II.4 n14] (ours: a spirit within nourishes).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), where the author is not named, the drawn sword illustrates the light of reason confronting and dispersing the images in the vital chaos: “Strictamqu Aeneas aciem venientibus offert” [APP ¶165] (ours: Aeneas offers the drawn blade to those coming); Aeneas, the Golden Bough, Tartarus and Elysium are read as stages of the work [APP ¶166; APP ¶168; APP ¶171].

References: II.3 n16, II.3 n28, II.3 n37, II.3 n39, II.3 ¶21, II.3 ¶26, II.4 n14, II.4 ¶21, II.4 ¶22, APP ¶165, APP ¶166, APP ¶168, APP ¶171

Aerial moisture

term

The incombustible moisture in which, according to the Alchemists, the thick fire of life is imprisoned; unpurified, it is Hades.

A view of the Alchemists that Atwood endorses: the life is “a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture” [II.3 ¶29]. Unpurified, this moisture is Hades [II.3 ¶29].

References: II.3 ¶29

Aesculapius

person

Named as Hippocrates’ paternal ancestor, honoured with Hercules, a demigod among the Greeks and, for Atwood, modern Mesmerism’s only just pride.

Atwood names him as Hippocrates’ paternal ancestor, honoured together with Hercules, a demigod only among the Greeks, and the only just pride of modern Mesmerism [IV.3 ¶32; IV.3 ¶34; IV.3 ¶36].

References: IV.3 ¶32, IV.3 ¶34, IV.3 ¶36

Afflatus

term

The imparted spirit whose reception gives wisdom by awakening a consciousness related to the universal.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the wisdom imparted by the reception of the Afflatus” [APP ¶41]; its reception awakens a consciousness related to the universal.

References: APP ¶41

Agent

term · agents

The spirit, which vivifies and holds together the particles of the matter and is superior to the body in operation; paired with the patient.

Atwood calls the spirit “the agent, because it vivifies and holds the particles of the matter together” [I.3 n37], superior to the body in operation. Elsewhere she warns “lest the sin of the agent be multiplied in the patient” [IV.3 ¶56], where the agent is not further defined. See agent and patient.

See also: Spiritual agent and spiritual patient

References: I.3 n37, IV.3 ¶56

Agent and patient

term · patients and agents, patient, patients

The active and receptive parties of the work, which act and react on one another progressively and, after Hermetic dissolution, are one identity.

Atwood: after Hermetic dissolution “the agent and the patient are one identity” [I.2 ¶48]. The work is progressive action and reaction between them: “The whole work is an action of agent on patient, and the reaction of patient, advancing, on agent.” [APP ¶111] (Appendix, Table Talk, later layer). The work may be protracted “by the indisposition of patients, as by the ignorance of agents” [IV.1 ¶17], terms not further defined there. Compare actives / passives.

See also: Patient, Spiritual agent and spiritual patient

References: I.2 ¶48, IV.1 ¶17, APP ¶111

Agrippa

person · Cornelius Agrippa

Cornelius Agrippa, Trithemius’ pupil, author of the Occult Philosophy and the Vanity of the Sciences, cited by Atwood throughout as a witness to self-knowledge, secrecy and the inward Operator.

Listed as Trithemius’ pupil among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his three books of Occult Philosophy and his Vanity of the Sciences (De Vanitate Scientiarum) for the oath of secrecy and the singleness of the subject — “I could tell many tings of this art, if I had not sworn to keep silence” [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n70] — and argues that the Vanity is a consummation, not a recantation. From the Vanity she also takes the account of Alexander the Great’s death by the venom of the waters of the Styx, paralleling Vaughan’s [I.1 ¶74, I.1 n94]; knowledge by entering into oneself, with oblivion as impediment: “entering not either into the schools of other philosophers, but into yourself, ye shall know all things” [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n13]; and the praise of the ‘asinine condition’ of the disciple of Wisdom, which she applies to the Philosophic Subject: “There is no creature, concludes the panegyrist, that is so able to receive divinity as an ass” [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

From the Occult Philosophy (Book 3): the soul freed from the senses comprehends all; man is image of God and microcosm — “Whosoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself” [II.1 ¶9, II.1 n4]; and the pure mind laid asleep and brought into its divine nature, which Atwood endorses as alluding to Alchemy: “in us, I say, is the Operator of miracles” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n26]. She says the work expounds diffusely that imaginative impressions linger and pollute the ether of a place [III.4 ¶42].

Other uses: Scripture is no longer read “under the Bark of the Law” [III.3 ¶59]; Scripture is obscure and mystical yet significant (“Clausum est Armarium”) [IV.3 ¶46]; the two natures to be joined (“Pinge duos Angues”) [III.1 ¶50]; within Vaughan’s lessons, a heavenly life as condition of communion with superiors [III.4 ¶44]; and his mature conviction that “to know Nothing was the most happy life” [IV.4 ¶27].

Atwood also qualifies him: he knew the First Preparation but not the Solution of the Salt, as his practice at Malines shows, and confessed he could not increase the transmutative virtue [IV.1 ¶36].

See also: Disciple of Cornelius Agrippa (not named)

References: I.1 n70, I.1 n94, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶74, II.1 n26, II.1 n4, II.1 ¶26, II.1 ¶9, II.3 n19, II.3 ¶24, II.4 n13, II.4 n31, II.4 ¶19, III.1 n29, III.1 ¶50, III.2 n47, III.2 ¶64, III.3 ¶59, III.4 ¶42, III.4 ¶44, IV.1 ¶36, IV.3 ¶46, IV.4 ¶27

Aimantique

term

Name a cited French source (Mystere de la Croix) gives to the work of repeated cooking until rainbow colours and heavy drops appear.

Quoted from the French source Mystere de la Croix: the work of repeated cooking, continued until the rainbow colours and heavy drops appear, is so named — “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶18]. The word renders as ‘magnetic’ (our translation; by: ours). The text here does not itself link it to Atwood’s ‘magnetic series’ [III.3 ¶10].

References: III.3 ¶18

Ain

term

In Reuchlin, as quoted, the Hebrew name of the Absolute Essence while retracted in darkness and at rest — ‘nothing as respects us’.

Quoted from Reuchlin: Ain names the Absolute Essence while it is retracted in darkness and at rest, and is glossed by the text itself as “Ain, i.e., to say, Nihil quoad nos; nothing or no entity as respects us” [III.2 ¶10]. It is called nothing not absolutely but relative to us, because “we, being affected with inability in the conception, do judge and imagine of those things which do not appear immediately as if they were not at all” [III.2 ¶10]. Asserted identity: Ain = Nihil quoad nos [III.2 ¶10].

Identified with: Nihil quoad nos [III.2 ¶10]

References: III.2 ¶10

Aladdin

person

Figure invoked as an image of works that vanish before celestial light.

Invoked as an illustration: such works vanish before celestial light like “Aladdin’s rapid castle” [II.3 ¶36].

References: II.3 ¶36

Alain de l’Isle

person · Alani Philosophi, Alanai de Insulis

Alain de l’Isle, author of the Dicta de Lapide and a commentary on Merlin’s Prophecies, said to have obtained the Elixir; cited as a case of editors suppressing alchemical testimony.

Atwood cites him (as Alani Philosophi, Alanai de Insulis) for his Dicta de Lapide and his commentary on the Prophecies of Merlin (Prophetia Anglicana Merlini, Francf. 1608). He is said to have obtained the Elixir, and serves as an example of editors suppressing alchemical testimony [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n53, I.1 n54].

References: I.1 n53, I.1 n54, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45

Albertus Magnus

person · Albert, Albertus, Albertus Mangus, A. Magnus, Alberti mag.

Albertus Magnus, a practising alchemist by Atwood’s proofs, cited for the first matter, perfect solution as the first rule, the vessel, and man as seat of the highest mineral virtue.

Atwood offers proof that Albert was a practising alchemist who described the first matter and commended alchemy as the best means of inquiry, and an example of renunciation of worldly advantage; she cites De Mineralibus, Libellus de Alchemia, Concordanditia Philosophorum de Lapide, Secretum Secretorum and the Breve Compendium: “De transmutatione horum corporum metallicorum et mutatione unius in aliud non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶41, I.1 n45, I.1 n46]. He is named with Lully as revering Geber [I.1 ¶32].

First matter: the mercury of the wise is “a watery element, cold and moist, a permanent water” [I.2 ¶29, I.2 n27]; he agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. From the book of Minerals: the highest mineral virtue is in man — “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all, burns more than all glorious in him erect” [II.1 ¶12]; and from De Minerabilis, all things may be reduced to gold: “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold, is found in the ultimate alchemical analysis of every existing thing” [III.2 n38].

Solution: “The beginning of the work, says Albertus Magnus, is a perfect solution” — dissolve and recongeal, fix and volatilize [II.3 n2]; “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution”, washing the occult Arcanum (‘our brass’) until pure [II.2 ¶16, II.2 n15]; “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass”, purified by successive dissolution and coagulation [IV.1 ¶4, IV.1 n2].

Vessel: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]; Norton’s verse says “And this sheweth best Albertus Magnus, In his Boke De Mineralibus” on the right figure of vessels [III.4 ¶31].

In quoted verse: Ripley names “Albert, Raymond and Arnolde” as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62]; Norton names “Albertus Magnus, the Black Freere” as lacking understanding of multiplying the Red Stone [I.1 ¶60].

References: I.1 n45, I.1 n46, I.1 ¶32, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶60, I.2 n27, I.2 ¶29, II.1 ¶12, II.1 ¶8, II.2 n15, II.2 ¶16, II.3 n2, III.1 n30, III.1 ¶62, III.2 n38, III.2 ¶60, III.4 ¶31, IV.1 n2, IV.1 ¶4

collective voice — Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights, Auroras, Keys, Guides and the like · Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides

Atwood’s list of generic alchemical book titles, all pointing to the Royal Road once it is found but useless to most modern readers.

Atwood lists these generic titles of alchemical books — Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides — to show that all direct to the Royal Road once it is found, yet are useless to most modern readers [III.4 ¶15].

References: III.4 ¶15

Alchemical solution

term

Atwood’s later definition: the throwing down of the walls of the harmony-ensphered life, accompanied with noise.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The throwing down of the Walls of this is harmony-ensphered life is the Alchemical solution” [APP ¶50]; it is accompanied with noise. Asserted identity: Alchemical solution = the throwing down of the Walls [APP ¶50].

Identified with: throwing down of the Walls [APP ¶50]

See also: Solution

References: APP ¶50

Alchemists

collective voice · the older masters, the Alchemists aforesaid

The Alchemists as a collective voice Atwood draws on for the Matter, solution, the unclean Instrument, the threefold Law’s periods, and the stirring of Motion.

Atwood treats the Alchemists as a body of witness, generally supporting her reading:

  • They recommend observing nature for analogy [I.3 n27].
  • Their condemnation of the defiled vulgar Matter, and its preparation into the Mercury of the Philosophers, she links to the purification of the Spirit [II.2 ¶16]; their description of the subject — “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” — fits the Common Soul [II.2 ¶18]; their Matter is the Passive Nature: “the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].
  • They supply the term dissolve for the trance change (“it ought to be dissolved”), and Black Saturn, the mineral tree, the doves [II.3 n2, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶18].
  • Life is a fire imprisoned in aerial moisture (“Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi”); they warn of horrors and phantoms [II.3 ¶29].
  • Their saying that there is “nothing of an unclean nature that enters into the composition of the Stone, except One thing” Atwood endorses, explaining at length that the unclean Instrument is necessary because the philosophers are obscure about it [III.1 ¶61].
  • They name the three periods of the threefold Law: “called by the Alchemists, for certain accurate reason, Altitude, Latitude and Profundity” [III.3 ¶72].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): their Vulcan is decoded as Motion [APP ¶129]; and the older masters’ “when Vulcan appears in the same altar with Minerva the conjunction is ominous” marks the point of passivity at which the Artist must stir up the Motion, which Atwood glosses as the stirred Wisdom-life being taken by self-will [APP ¶82].

See also: Alchemists and Greek physicians, Ancient physiologists and alchemists, Modern Alchemists, Old Alchemists

References: I.3 n27, II.2 ¶16, II.2 ¶18, II.3 n2, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶18, II.3 ¶29, III.1 ¶61, III.2 ¶60, III.3 ¶72, APP ¶129, APP ¶82

Alchemists and Greek physicians

collective voice

Joint witnesses asserting an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena.

Cited in support: the Alchemists and Greek physicians assert an immutable Being pre-existent to sensibles, provable in intellect and confirmed in phenomena [IV.4 ¶13].

See also: Alchemists

References: IV.4 ¶13

Alchemy

term · Alchemical, Alchimia, Alchimica, Alchimiam, Alchimiae, Alkimy, Holy Alkimy, holi Alkimy

The Hermetic art: in Atwood’s account an antique sacred science of vital chemistry, fermenting and purifying the human spirit by its own Light into regenerated life and relation with God.

The early account (main text). Atwood calls it the Hermetic art, to be considered “an antique arifice coeval, for aught we know to the contrary, with the universe itself” [I.1 ¶3]; Egypt’s Sacred Art, of which “This Emerald Table, unique and authentic as it may be regarded, is all that remains to us from Egypt of her Sacred Art” [I.1 ¶10], with its practical method in the Tractatus Aureus. She suggests it was “perhaps” stigmatized as a Black Art partly from the word Chemia [I.1 ¶5]. Now preserved in archives and despised, it is either “the acme of human folly, or contrariwise, as the recondite perfection of wisdom and causal science” [I.1 ¶76]; “the world has learned to despise alchemy, confounding the genuine doctrine with their sophistical and vile productions” [I.1 ¶53].

It concerns transmutation of metals: per Albert, “non est physici determinare, sed artis quae est Alchimica”, and he “recommends alchemy as the best and most easy means of rational investigation” [I.1 ¶39]. It has nothing to do with modern chemistry: “No modern art or chemistry, notwithstanding all its surreptitious claims, has any thing in common to do with Alchemy, beyond the borrowed terms” [II.1 ¶5]; it requires the vital force, and philosophers sought it “not so much out of covetousness for gold or silver, but for the knowledge’s sake” [II.1 ¶10]. In it “the nature of things is altogether altered and ultimately reversed” and Final Causes are manifest [III.4 ¶9]. God grants it to few; its records hold the inner sense aloof from the literal, and “the Art will probably continue concealed though many ages still” [III.4 ¶16].

Norton (quoted) calls it “most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶52], holy because found only by grace: “Called this science Holy Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10]. Further verse in the same discussion affirms: “Yet is this science of Alkimy full trew;” [III.4 ¶14].

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood defines it directly: “Alchemy is an universal art of vital chemistry” [APP ¶6] that ferments, purifies and dissolves the human spirit into new life; “Alchemy is a process of fermenting the vital Spirit in and by its own Light.” [APP ¶27]; “Alchemy is the art of fermenting the human vital spirit” to purify and finally dissolve it, so the principle is reconstructed through regeneration [APP ¶68]. “Alchemy goes beyond nature”, taking her up and advancing her beyond her created state [APP ¶155]. It brings man into relationship with God.

Asserted identities: = Divine Chemistry, “the transmutation of Life” [APP ¶25]; = Holy Alchemy, “called by the Adepts Holy Alchemy” [APP ¶29]; = philosophy: “Alchemy is philosophy; it is the philosophy, the seeking of The Sophia in the mind.” [APP ¶183], fully understood only by those working the process.

Identified with: Divine Chemistry [APP ¶25]; Holy Alchemy [APP ¶29]; Philosophy [APP ¶183]; most profounde philosophye [I.1 ¶52]

References: I.1 ¶10, I.1 ¶3, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶5, I.1 ¶52, I.1 ¶53, I.1 ¶76, II.1 ¶10, II.1 ¶5, III.4 ¶10, III.4 ¶14, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶9, APP ¶155, APP ¶183, APP ¶25, APP ¶27, APP ¶29, APP ¶6, APP ¶68

Anaxagoras

person · Anaxagorus

Called by Atwood one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School; cited for Intellect as separating principle, the ignited Stone as inner Sun, and as an alchemist.

Atwood calls him ‘one of the earliest of the Greek hermetic School’ and cites his lost works as preserved by Simplicius (via Taylor’s note to Aristotle’s Metaphysics) for Intellect’s efficient, separating operation: “Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing” [III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶22, III.1 n27]. What he describes as past, internal philosophers describe as present; his “it begins from that which is small to exercise its comprehending power” she applies to starting with a small portion [III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶32]. He “calls it Intellect”, naming the One Thing in consciousness [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶35]; matter is the progeny of mind [III.2 ¶40].

His ‘ignited Stone’ Atwood identifies with the inner Sun, saying he was discredited through the error that he meant the visible sun [II.3 ¶54]; he identifies the central earth with the Salt of Saturn (“hands loftily”) [II.3 ¶41].

Celebrated as an alchemist, author of the boke of Conversions Naturall, praised by Norton as the plainest writer; his metaphysics agrees with Aristotle’s [I.1 ¶14, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16]. Within the Ordinal he is cited for “Nemo prima fronte reperitur discretus” [IV.1 ¶26].

References: I.1 ¶14, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16, II.3 ¶41, II.3 ¶54, III.1 n27, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶22, III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶32, III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶35, III.2 ¶40, IV.1 ¶26

Ancients

collective voice

Atwood’s most frequent group authority, cited throughout as support for the reality, experimental basis and discipline of the Hermetic wisdom and the Mysteries.

Atwood cites “the ancients” almost always as support for her own positions:

  • Reality and experience. They assert higher realities known through both intellect and experiment [I.2 ¶49]. For them the truth is the same experience in everyone, “one and the same in all, where difference is merged in objective union” [II.2 ¶13]. They held that the worst evil is not seeing one’s own evil, and they gave warnings about how the Spirit is to be handled [II.2 ¶14].
  • Preparing the mind. They warn against passive dreaming in the phantasy. Before contemplation, they require the mind to be cleared and made passive [II.2 ¶22]. They insisted on ways of removing the barriers to the Divine Light. Their Wisdom was gained by discipline, and it goes beyond reason without contradicting it [IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶17].
  • Life and Being. They held this life to be a lessening of existence [III.2 ¶50]. The “wise ancients” compared a state of Being that verges on annihilation to darkness for the eye [III.2 ¶54].
  • Figures of the union. Atwood reads the pairs Peleus and Thetis, Earth and Heaven, Bacchus and Ariadne, and Jason and Medea as their prefigurations of the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the marriage, by the ancients so many times prefigured” [III.3 ¶15].
  • The Mysteries. They are her authority for treating the Mysteries as real inductions. They found their whole philosophy in the vital experiment, and she weighs their philosophy against Physical science [IV.4 ¶5, IV.4 ¶9, IV.4 ¶13].

References: I.2 ¶49, II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14, II.2 ¶22, III.2 ¶50, III.2 ¶54, III.3 ¶15, IV.4 ¶13, IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶17, IV.4 ¶5, IV.4 ¶9
