Antimonial spirit

term

The Alchemists’ Antimonial Spirit, rectified by Art and balanced between attraction and repulsion. It alone withstands life’s drift toward dissolution.

This is the Alchemists’ term, cited via Bohme. Their “Antimonial Spirit rectified by Art” [II.1 ¶20] is described as balanced between attraction and repulsion. It is the only thing that resists life’s drift toward dissolution.

See also: Spirit

References: II.1 ¶20

Antimony

term

The adepts’ name for the matter of the tincture and for the fire of life. It is not the ordinary mineral, and Basil Valentine calls its preparation the key of Alchemy.

Antimony appears only in quoted voices, mostly Basil Valentine’s. Atwood adds a gloss of her own.

  • Not the common substance. For the adept and Basil Valentine, Antimony names the matter of the tincture. The “oil of this antimony” is “not made of crude melted antimony, such as the apothecaries and merchants sell”, but is drawn from “the true mineral” [II.1 ¶25].
  • Fire of life. The Paracelsians speak of “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts” [III.1 ¶10]. Identity: = fire of life.
  • Key of Alchemy. Basil Valentine says “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”. It is matured with the corporeal fire of the microcosm [III.1 ¶37]. Identity: = stone of Fire: “our stone of Fire (which is Antimony)” [III.1 ¶37].
  • Fixed medicine. “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases and eradicates them”, but only after all its venomous impurity has been removed [IV.1 ¶40]. Atwood explains this removal as the purging of self-will and other vices from the operator’s mind. This reading is hers, and it ties the substance to the operator’s own purification.

Identified with: Fire of life [III.1 ¶10]; Stone of Fire [III.1 ¶37]

References: II.1 ¶25, III.1 ¶10, III.1 ¶37, IV.1 ¶40

Antimony of the wise

term

Named by Atwood among the dark presences at the conjunction. The text does not define it.

Atwood names it among the dark presences at the conjunction: “Night, Saturn and the Antimony of the Wise will be present” [III.3 ¶13]. The record does not define it. Compare Antimony.

See also: The Wise

References: III.3 ¶13

Antiquity

person

Cited as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall.

Atwood names Antiquity as the source of the well-known image of the Brazen Wall [IV.1 ¶4].

References: IV.1 ¶4

Aornus

term · Aornum

Atwood’s name for the cave-like place of descent, which she reads as the heavy, inelastic nether air bordering on the chaos of matter.

Atwood describes this place of descent as having air “destitute of elasticity, Aornus, heavy like that of an enclosed cave, and vast” [II.3 ¶18]. She reads it as the heavy lower air bordering on the chaos of matter. The text supports only this physical description. Any further role in the work would be inference.

References: II.3 ¶18

Apollo

person

Invoked by Atwood to show how deeply the truth is hidden: enough to puzzle even Apollo.

Atwood says the truth is so wrapped up that it “might puzzle Apollo himself to explicate the whole Enigma” [IV.4 ¶2]. She uses Apollo only as a figure of speech.

See also: Argo and Apollo (classical allusion)

References: IV.4 ¶2

Apollonius

person

Quoted through Vaughan on the Brahmans, whose way of dwelling illustrates the philosophers’ habitation.

Atwood quotes Apollonius through Vaughan: “I have seen, says Apollonius, the Brahmans of India dwelling on the earth and not on the earth” [II.4 ¶11]. She uses this as an illustration of the philosophers’ habitation.

References: II.4 ¶11

Apollonius Rhodius

person

Cited in footnotes, in the Argonautics and Fawkes’s translation, as a parallel to the terror caused by Achilles’ armour.

Two footnotes cite Apollonius Rhodius (Argonaut., Lib. 2; Fawkes’ Apollonius Rhodius Argonautics, Book 1) as a reference or parallel for the terror caused by Achilles’ armour: “So the gloomy god/Stood mute with fearto see the golden rode” [III.1 n32, III.1 n35].

References: III.1 n32, III.1 n35

Apostle

collective voice

The Apostle’s scriptural words, which Atwood cites repeatedly to support the nearness of being, transformation, resurrection and the spiritual purification of the operator.

Atwood cites the Apostle as scriptural support, always with approval:

  • Nearness of being (Act 17:27, 28): “He is not far off from every one of us; for in Him we live, and move, and have our being” [II.1 ¶26, II.1 n24].
  • Light to light. His “and from glory to glory” supports Agrippa’s “light to light” [II.4 ¶19].
  • Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15). This answers how what is destroyed can increase. It covers the law of resurrection, the natural body followed by the spiritual body, and leaven: “that which is sown is not the body that shall be, but mere grain” [III.3 ¶23, III.3 n13, III.3 ¶24, III.3 n17].
  • The veil lifted. When one turns to the Lord or the Spirit, the veil over the reading of Moses is lifted, “the veil shall be taken away”, and those who behold are transformed [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n38].
  • Spiritual warfare (2 Corinth. 10:4, 5). The purification of the operator is spiritual, not carnal: “the weapons of this warfare are not carnal, as the Apostle teaches” [IV.1 ¶40, IV.1 n33].
  • Trial by Fire (1 Corinth. 3:11-17). The one foundation, man as the Temple of God, and “the Fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is” are tied to Atwood’s call to press on to Divine Perfection [IV.1 ¶46, IV.1 n41].

References: II.1 n24, II.1 ¶26, II.4 ¶19, III.3 n13, III.3 n17, III.3 n38, III.3 ¶23, III.3 ¶24, III.3 ¶59, IV.1 n33, IV.1 n41, IV.1 ¶40, IV.1 ¶46

Apotheosis

term

Atwood’s term for the final stage of the church’s mysteries, which was kept most secret.

Atwood mentions the church’s mysteries, “especially those that relate to the final apotheosis”, as the part kept most secret [II.2 ¶5]. The record does not explain it further.

References: II.2 ¶5

Apuleius

person

Author whose accounts of initiation into the mysteries of Isis Atwood uses repeatedly to illustrate the inner light, the goddess (Universal Nature) and the soul’s liberation.

Atwood cites Apuleius chiefly as a witness of initiation. From On the God of Socrates she takes the inner light experienced when separated from the body: “this knowledge sometimes shines forth with a most rapid coruscation like a bright and clear light in the most profound darkness” [II.3 ¶50, II.3 n54]; his ‘midnight Sun’ she identifies with the ignited Stone [II.3 ¶54]. The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) likewise uses the midnight sun seen when initiated by Isis to illustrate the coruscation of released light [APP ¶126].

From the Metamorphoses, book 11, she draws: the bough connected with the Mercurial caduceus in the procession of Isis initiates [II.3 ¶11, II.3 n6]; the appearance of the goddess (Isis/nature) in the Eleusian Fane and her mandates to the initiate — “Moved by thy prayers, O Lucius! Behold, I am come!” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶17, II.4 n9]; Lucius’ praise of the goddess, which Atwood applies to the Universal Nature — “Thou rollest the heavens round the steady poles, dost illuminate the sun, govern the world, and tread on the dark realms of Tartarus.” [II.4 ¶18, II.4 n10]; and Lucius’ rosy crown and shedding of the beast’s hide as images of the soul’s liberation [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n11].

He is listed with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Julian among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27]; he is called to witness by Agrippa [II.1 ¶26]; and Reuchlin’s passage cites him to excuse an obscure phrase: “you must pardon, as Apuleius says, the strange expression” [III.2 ¶24]. In I.1 ¶11 he appears as the hypothetical forger of the prophecy, a theory Atwood rejects.

References: I.1 ¶11, I.1 ¶27, II.1 ¶26, II.3 n54, II.3 n6, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶50, II.3 ¶54, II.4 n10, II.4 n11, II.4 n31, II.4 n9, II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶17, II.4 ¶18, II.4 ¶19, III.2 ¶24, APP ¶126

Apuleius of Megara

person

Author of the Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass, cited for being turned into an ass before admission to the mysteries of Isis.

Atwood cites the Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass of Apuleius of Megara to illustrate that he was turned into an ass before his admission to the mysteries of Isis [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

References: III.2 n47, III.2 ¶64

Aquarium Sapientum

treatise · Aquarium Sepientum

Treatise in the Mus. Herm. cited for verses on the regeneration (union, dissolution, reunion of spirit, soul and body) and for the triune universal essence.

Atwood quotes translated verses from the Aquarium Sapientum (in Mus. Herm., ‘The Enigma’): spirit, soul and body in one seat, then dissolution, then reunion in the last heat — “The Spirit is given to the body for a time,” [III.1 ¶51, III.1 ¶52, III.1 n57]. She endorses this as ‘the constant doctrine and rule of the regeneration’.

Under the spelling Aquarium Sepientum (Mus. Herm., p. 112) it is cited after the birth of Horus to illustrate the triune and fivefold divine-human essence: “Triuna universalis essentia, quae Jehovah appellatur” [IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 n3].

See also: Author of the Aquarium Sapientum

References: I.3 n37, II.2 n16, III.1 n57, III.1 ¶51, III.1 ¶52, IV.2 n3, IV.2 ¶11

Aquaster

term

Apparently a region that consciousness must pass through, clear and rational, before entering the Fire World; the text does not define it further.

Atwood speaks of consciousness passing “clear and rational from out the Aquaster, enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]; a quoted adept likewise speaks of “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41]. The context suggests a middle region traversed before the Fire World, but the text gives no definition.

References: II.3 ¶16, II.3 ¶41

Aquinas

person

Confessed adept whose alchemical treatises Atwood cites for transmutation, deliberate obscurity, secrecy and the sufficiency of Mercury, while criticizing his ‘false panegyrists’.

Atwood cites Aquinas (Thesaurus Alchimiae, addressed to brother Reinaldo; Meteorum, lib. iv; De Esse et Essentia; Secreta Alchimiae) as a confessed adept affirming transmutation — “Metalla transmutari possunt unum in aliud” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 n49] — and for his deliberate obscurity and warnings to keep the secret from worldly seekers, which she takes to point to the art’s higher theosophical purpose [I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶42, I.1 n50, I.1 n51]. She criticizes his ‘false panegyrists’.

From the Roasrium Abbrev. (Tract. iii and v) she takes the doctrine that Mercury alone suffices, being the root of gold and silver and working itself: “It is Mercury alone which perfects in our work” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n13].

References: I.1 n49, I.1 n50, I.1 n51, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶42, I.2 n13, I.2 ¶11, I.3 n15

Arabian

collective voice — Aristotele Arabus in the Rosarium

An Arabian authority (given in the Rosarium as Aristotele Arabus) cited on the Stone: nothing is added, separation only removes superfluities.

Via the Rosarium (Aristotele Arabus), ‘the Arabian’ supports the claim that nothing is added in the work: “to which we add nothing different or extract, only in the separation removing superfluities” [I.2 ¶43, I.2 n42]. His ‘subtle phrase’ on the Stone known and proven is also cited: “Sumatur lais in capitulis notus” [III.2 ¶7].

See also: Arabians

References: I.2 n42, I.2 ¶43, III.2 ¶7

Arabian Caraha

term

Apparently a place or vessel in which the two serpents, tied in a love knot, are shut up; the text does not explain it.

In a passage from Cornelius Agrippa’s ‘ingenious disciple’, the two serpents are to be bound and enclosed: “tie them in a love knot and shut them up in the Arabian Caraha” [III.1 ¶50]. The context suggests a vessel or enclosure, but the text gives no explanation.

References: III.1 ¶50

Arabian Elixir

term

In Vaughan’s account, the philosophers’ medicine reduced by bodily fermentation to a portable dust.

Quoting Vaughan, Atwood records that the philosophers reduced their medicine by bodily fermentation to a dust: “they reduced their medicine to a dust, and this dust is the Arabian Elixir” [IV.3 ¶22] — so the Arabian Elixir = this dust. Unlike the medicine itself it was portable: “This Elixir the philosophers could carry about them” [IV.3 ¶22].

Identified with: dust (the reduced medicine) [IV.3 ¶22]

See also: Elixir

References: IV.3 ¶22

Arabian Nights

treatise

Cited to characterize the ‘entertaining’ style of the Christian philosophers’ promises.

Atwood invokes the Arabian Nights to illustrate the ‘entertaining’ style of the Christian philosophers’ promises [II.3 ¶34].

References: II.3 ¶34

Arabians

collective voice

Group voice cited for a name of the Matter: Flower of White Salt.

The Arabians are cited for a name of the Matter: “Flos Salis Albi” (Flower of White Salt) [III.2 ¶8].

See also: Arabian (Aristotele Arabus in the Rosarium)

References: III.2 ¶8

Arcadia

treatise

Cited within a Vaughan passage to show that the work does not occupy the operator’s attention.

In a passage from Vaughan, the Arcadia illustrates that the work does not occupy the attention: “a lady may read the Arcadia” [III.4 ¶38].

References: III.4 ¶38

Arcanum

term · Arcana, great Arcanum, occult Arcanum

The secret of the work: the ‘great Arcanum’ possessed when the tincture rises from the black, identified by Albertus with ‘our brass’, and wholly revealed to Eirenaeus.

The term appears mostly in quoted voices. A ‘more modern experimentalist’ says that when the masculine tincture rises from the black “he will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53]. Albertus (spelled ‘Mangus’) identifies the ‘occult Arcanum’ with ‘our brass’, to be washed until pure: “Take, says Albertus Mangus, the occult Arcanum, which is our brass, and wash it that it may be pure and clean” [II.2 ¶16]. Urbigeranus and other Adepts make the Theory of their Arcanum the medium by which the Royal Diadem is extracted; without it dissolution is impossible: “it will be entirely impossible to accomplish without the Theory of their Arcanum” [IV.1 ¶7].

Atwood herself uses it for the whole secret of the work, revealed to Eirenaeus in two and a half years: “the whole Arcanum was revealed to him” [IV.1 ¶17]. In the plural, Eirenaeus speaks of the Chaos “in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43] — the secrets present potentially, not yet actually.

Identified with: our brass [II.2 ¶16]

References: I.3 n53, II.2 ¶16, IV.1 ¶17, IV.1 ¶43, IV.1 ¶7

Arcanum Ignis Aquae

treatise

Work supplying the epigraph of IV.1, setting the theme that the arts are bought by labor.

The chapter epigraph of IV.1 comes from Arcanum Ignis Aquae (Resp. 6): “Dii sudoribus vendunt Artes” [IV.1 ¶1] — the gods sell the arts for sweat (translation ours), setting the theme of labor.

References: IV.1 ¶1

Arcanum Liquaris Alkahest

treatise

Work cited for a Latin statement on transmuting the salt of blood by urinous ferment.

Atwood cites the Arcanum Liquaris Alkahest (Resp. 876, 78) in Latin on transmuting the salt of blood: “sanquinis salem per urinaceum fermentum sic transmutari debere” [II.1 ¶21, II.1 n18] — that the salt of blood ought thus to be transmuted by a urinous ferment (translation ours).

See also: Alkahest

References: II.1 n18, II.1 ¶21

Archaeus

term

Paracelsus’ term, which Atwood sets beside the solar plexus as the workshop of the Celestial life, in which the Light lies hidden until drawn out.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the term in apposition to the solar plexus: “the solar plexus, the Archaeus of Paracelsus, is its workshop” [APP ¶32] — the workshop of the Celestial life; so Archaeus = solar plexus there. In the main text she speaks of “the Light, so long hidden and enshrined in the Archaeus” [III.3 ¶71], drawn out by artificial heat and exhalation. Van Helmont, quoted, gives the Archaeus a ‘sky’ in which ideas from the soul’s starry heaven and the spirit of the seven bowels are read: “For in the sky of our Archaeus, aspectual Ideas are deciphered” [III.2 ¶17]. The text does not define the term further.

Identified with: solar plexus [APP ¶32]

References: III.2 ¶17, III.3 ¶71, APP ¶32

Archetypal Law of light

term

The order in which all things are causally ranged as originally distributed, seen ‘as in a glass’ by one who has the Principle.

Atwood speaks of “the great Archetypal Law of Light, in which are all things causally ranged” [III.3 ¶39]: the order of things as originally distributed, which the one who possesses the Principle beholds ‘as in a glass’. See also Archetype, whose creative mind orders all things by this Law.

See also: Light

References: III.3 ¶39

Archetypal light

term

The original Light before which the understanding stands to perfect its new-born attributes; perceived, it burns up prior images and is identified with Truth.

In the main text, Atwood describes “the understanding vehicle now standing in open presence before its Archetypal Light” [II.4 ¶16], by which it perfects its new-born attributes. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says that this light, once perceived, burns up all prior images, perceives itself alone, “transmuting all that is not combustible into itself” [APP ¶106]; it is both objective and subjective and is identified with Truth: “for it is objective and subjective both; it is Truth” [APP ¶106].

Identified with: Truth [APP ¶106]

See also: Light

References: II.4 ¶16, APP ¶106

Archetypal Wisdom

term

The hidden essence of the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason is only an embryo image.

Atwood speaks of “that Archetypal Wisdom which the ancients celebrated as the occult essence of that Law” [II.1 ¶35] — the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason gives only an embryo image. Archetypal Wisdom = the occult essence of the Intellectual Law.

Identified with: occult essence of the Intellectual Law [II.1 ¶35]

See also: Wisdom

References: II.1 ¶35

Archetype

term · Archetypes, Archetypal Form, Archetypal mind

The original of which the self and natural things are images; the creative mind ordering all things causally and the end of the soul’s progression.

For Atwood the Archetype is the original of which the self is an image and the end of the soul’s progression; it is the creative mind whose Law of Light orders all things causally, “where the Archetype shadows the intellectual spheres” [III.3 ¶39], and in which things are “that which is in the Archetypal mind creatively efficient” [III.3 n27]. In the plural, the Archetypes are the originals of things beheld in nature, which do not truly resemble them: “If indeed things beheld in nature were such as the Archetypes, whence they are derived” [III.2 ¶61]; one established in Intellect is “able through it, as an image, to behold the Archetype” [III.2 ¶66].

In Hermes’ account, Poemander asks: “hast thou seen that Archetypal Form, which was before the interminated and infinite beginning?” [III.3 ¶56] — the pattern in which God’s Will and Counsel beheld the beautiful world and which it imitated in making this world.

References: III.2 ¶61, III.2 ¶66, III.3 n27, III.3 ¶39, III.3 ¶56

Archytas

person — the Pythagorean

Pythagorean whose fragments Atwood cites on Wisdom as contemplation of first Principles and on right method of investigation as the key to discovery.

From a fragment given by Taylor in his Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagorus, Archytas supports Atwood’s account of Wisdom, which contemplates the whole and discovers the Principles of Being, leading to a vision of Divinity: “he will have conjoined ends with beginnings” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n34]. He also supports her stress on method — mankind has not known how to investigate: “If you investigate rightly, says Archytas, discovery will be easy for you” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 ¶53].

References: II.1 n34, II.1 ¶37, II.1 ¶52, II.1 ¶53

Argent vive

term · Argent vives, our Argent vive, argentums vivum nostrum

The philosophic Mercury, the subject of the Art: a water of another nature, a stone and no stone, gold essential but unripe, cleansed and coagulated by its own sulfur.

The term comes almost entirely in quoted voices. Lully calls it a water of another nature: “argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18]; in it the conversion of natures is carried out: “the method of conversion in our Argent vive is the reduction of natures to their first root” [I.2 ¶25]. Arnold: “it is a stone and no stone, in which the whole Art consists, spirit, soul and body” [I.2 ¶29] — volatile, clear, One Thing.

It is identified with the philosophic Mercury (Hermes and the Scholiast): “for that is Mercury which is spoken of concerning the residual earth” [I.3 ¶9]; “this argent vive, then, which is the residuum of the philosophic earth after the separation” [I.3 n9]. Hermes requires two to be mortified together — “it behooves us to mortify two Argent vives together” [I.3 ¶32]; “the Argent vive of Auripigment and the Oriental Argent vive of magnesia” [III.1 ¶43] — not further explained. Eirenaeus: “For Argent Vive is gold essential Only unripe” [III.1 ¶69], which prepared by art gives the secret menstrual.

The Adept, with Atwood, describes its course: “this Argent vive was at first gross, unclean, fugitive, being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” [IV.1 ¶10]; cleansed by Art and coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white, it becomes subtle and penetrative, resolving mineral bodies; “this Argent vive, which is decocted linearly, is generated pontically” [IV.1 ¶11]. In Geber’s definition it is the volatile: “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]. In Eirenaeus’ projection verse, “Then upon Argent vive cast this with care.” [IV.3 ¶25] — apparently in the place of the ‘mercury purged and purified’ of ¶20, though the text does not state this. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” [IV.2 ¶35], unexplained.

Identified with: aqua alterius naturae (water of another nature) [I.2 ¶18]; Mercury [I.3 ¶9]; residuum of the philosophic earth [I.3 n9]; gold essential, only unripe [III.1 ¶69]; the volatile [IV.3 ¶9]

References: I.2 ¶18, I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶29, I.3 n9, I.3 ¶32, I.3 ¶9, III.1 ¶43, III.1 ¶69, IV.1 ¶10, IV.1 ¶11, IV.2 ¶35, IV.3 ¶25, IV.3 ¶9

Argo and Apollo

collective voice — classical allusion · Argo, Apollo

Classical allusion used to say the philosophic vessels ‘speak for themselves’.

Atwood illustrates that the philosophic vessels speak for themselves: they, “like the planks of Argo, on occasion, are still oracular” [III.4 ¶32].

See also: Apollo

References: III.4 ¶32

Aristiteles

person

Cited for reference only.

References: II.2 n18

Aristophanes

person

Author whose chorus of the Initiated Atwood cites for the privileged light of those who perform acts of piety and justice.

From In Ramis, Act 1, Atwood cites the chorus to illustrate the privileged light of the initiated, who perform acts of piety and justice: “The sun shines but for us, exclaims the chorus of the Initiated in Aristophanes” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 n7].

References: II.4 n7, II.4 ¶16

Aristotle

person · the Stagyrite

Authority (the Stagyrite) cited widely on Wisdom, Intellect, Matter and reduction of metals; Atwood qualifies charges of envy against him but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.

Norton and the adepts criticize Aristotle for envy and veiling; Atwood qualifies this, cites his works (epistles to Alexander on the Philosophers’ stone, Secreta Secretorum, book of Meteors) as evidence of hidden knowledge, yet declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher without more evidence [I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, I.1 n22]. Through Ripley’s verse the Book of Meteors concurs that metals are not transmutable unless reduced to their beginning [I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶6, I.2 n6]; he is cited (n38) for metals reducible to water [III.2 n38].

On Wisdom and Intellect: Wisdom is the highest science, drawn from what is universal in oneself [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n30], the true being of Intellect, small in bulk but surpassing in energy [II.1 n31]; mystical exercises bring the understanding into contact with its cause, and intellect is identical with the intelligible — “True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n32; cf. II.1 ¶44]. He compares Universals to colors needing the sun and calls human reason ‘intellect in capacity’ [II.1 ¶34]; his ‘passive intellect’ names the Mundane Spirit first revealed in humanity [II.2 ¶17]; “That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified” [III.1 ¶23, III.1 n30]. The self-perceiving final object “is good, according to the words of the Stagyrite, and the end of spiritual generation” [IV.2 ¶8].

On Matter, ‘the logician’: “I mean, he says, by Matter, that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity” [III.2 ¶53, III.2 n42]. His triple distinction of heaven [III.2 ¶33, III.2 n32] and his ‘perfect world’, read as the ethereal [III.2 ¶38]; his abstruse diction illustrates concealment; his criticisms of predecessors — “Parmenides appears to have touched upon the One according to Reason; but Melissus, according to Matter” [III.2 ¶38] — are said to aim at the letter, not the spirit, though he is also blamed for making away with his brethren ‘after the manner of the Ottomans’ [III.2 ¶36]; his logic is praised in its original intent, later degraded [III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶41, III.2 ¶42, III.2 n37]. From the Ethics: “Ab actionibus procedit speculatio” [IV.1 ¶18]; one deliberates about means, not ends, analyzing back to the first Cause as in a diagram [IV.1 ¶30, IV.1 n25]. ‘The Aristotle’ is cited for the change of the corruptible into incorruption: “Behold I show you a mystery, says the Aristotle, we shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed” [III.3 ¶27, III.3 n18].

References: I.1 n22, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, I.2 n6, I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶6, II.1 n30, II.1 n31, II.1 n32, II.1 ¶34, II.1 ¶37, II.1 ¶44, II.2 ¶17, III.1 n30, III.1 ¶23, III.2 n32, III.2 n37, III.2 n38, III.2 n42, III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶36, III.2 ¶38, III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶41, III.2 ¶42, III.2 ¶53, III.3 n18, III.3 ¶27, IV.1 n25, IV.1 ¶18, IV.1 ¶30, IV.2 n1, IV.2 ¶7, IV.2 ¶8

Arkite Mysteries

term

Ancient rites which, Atwood says, refer to the physical secret of regeneration, the god dead and revived being principal in them.

Atwood states that “the Arkite Mysteries have reference to the physical secret of the regeneration” [III.3 ¶69]; the god dead and revived is principal in them.

Arkite Mysteries. Cited by Atwood in support of the claim that these mysteries refer to the physical secret of regeneration [III.3 ¶69]. See the term entry Arkite Mysteries.

See also: Mysteries

References: III.3 ¶69

Armed magnet

term

Something rectified by Power and Motive ‘by an infallible rule’; the text does not explain it.

Atwood speaks of Power and Motive that “rectifies the Armed Magnet by an infallible rule” [IV.1 ¶33]. The expression is not explained.

See also: Magnet

References: IV.1 ¶33

Arndt

person

Mystic named in the Appendix as the one who recognizes the depth of the Psalms.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Arndt is named as the one Mystic who recognizes the depth of the Psalms [APP ¶97].

References: APP ¶97

Arnold

person · Arnoldi, Arnold di Villa Nova, Arnold di Villanova, Arnolde, Arnolde of the New Towne, Arnboldi

Confessed adept whose Speculum and Rosarium Atwood cites constantly: reduction to first root, the matter as stone and no stone, dissolution of the Stone in its own mercury.

Atwood ranks Arnold di Villa Nova as a confessed adept whose skill, including projections with transmuting powder, is attested by contemporaries [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶43]; he possibly convinced Lully by exhibiting transmutation [I.1 ¶48], though Lully did not receive the mystery from him [IV.1 ¶36]. His Speculum gives the basis of the whole theory: “there abides in nature a certain pure matter” [I.2 ¶2]; species are indestructible — “Species non transmutari sed individual specierum” [I.2 ¶5, I.2 n3, I.2 n4] — so the subject must be freed by artificial reduction.

His precept “Converte elementa et quod quaeris invenies” [I.2 ¶22] means reduction of natures to their first root [I.2 ¶25]; Atwood glosses “Convert the elements, says Arnold, and you shall have what you desire” as separating and rejoining in harmonious proportion [I.3 n23]. The matter is a stone and no stone: “Ii is a stone and no stone, spirit, soul, and body” [I.3 n5, I.3 n13, I.3 n17], following whatever is done to it [cf. I.2 ¶29, I.2 n30]. From the Rosarium: “The work of philosophers, says Arnold, is to dissolve the Stone in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7, IV.1 n6], to first Matter; the operator needs “three requisites, viz., subtlety of mind, manual skill, and a free will for the operation” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n19].

With Hermes he witnesses that the art must be entrusted by one to another [II.1 ¶25]; verse (versifier not named) cites the Rosary of ‘Arnolde of the New Towne’ for the claim that none can operate alone: “There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging.” [I.3 n17]. He is also cited for the same testimony [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n100], as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25], with Albert and Raymond in Ripley’s verse as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62], with Lully and Artephius as agreeing with the Lucerna Salis on whitening [III.2 ¶5], and within the Ordinal, where the Art belongs to great men so poor men should beware, and the operator should be patient and gentle: “Esto longanimus et suavis” [IV.1 ¶12].

References: I.1 n100, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶43, I.1 ¶48, I.1 ¶76, I.2 n18, I.2 n22, I.2 n3, I.2 n30, I.2 n4, I.2 ¶2, I.2 ¶22, I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶29, I.2 ¶5, I.3 n13, I.3 n17, I.3 n23, I.3 n5, II.1 ¶25, III.1 n2, III.1 n25, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶62, III.1 ¶8, III.2 ¶5, III.4 n19, III.4 ¶20, IV.1 n6, IV.1 ¶12, IV.1 ¶36, IV.1 ¶7

Aromal essences

term · aromal emanations

The addressee’s term for what Nature wraps herself in to realize her imaginings (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the term as the addressee’s own (‘what you call’): “She wraps herself about with what you call aromal essences, aromal emanations” [APP ¶122] — Nature clothing herself to realize her imaginings.

See also: Essence

References: APP ¶122

Art mechanical

term

In Norton’s Ordinal, handicraft, the work of the hands, called Art mechanical; what the Gross Work consists of.

A term from Norton’s Ordinal, quoted by Atwood: handicraft, “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]. The record says the Gross Work consists of this handicraft. It is equated there with handie crafte.

Identified with: handie crafte [IV.1 ¶28]

References: IV.1 ¶28

Art of Alchemy

term

The Art Atwood calls holy above all arts for aiding devout minds; a remedy of imperfect souls offering means of assimilation, though not itself the cause of salvation.

Atwood writes that “The Art of Alchemy is of all Arts distinguished as holt” [IV.4 ¶25] (the spelling is the book’s), because it aids devout minds. She adds that “the Art is said to be a remedy of imperfect souls, and offers the means of assimilation” [IV.4 ¶25]. She also holds that the Art is not itself the cause of salvation [IV.4 ¶25].

See also: Alchemy, Hermetic art

References: IV.4 ¶25

Art of life

term

The ultimate Art, which Atwood says she will not fully expose and which is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.

Atwood speaks of discovering, “by a theoretic conduct, the ultimate Art of Life” [IV.2 ¶3]. She does not fully expose this Art; it is to be discovered by a theoretic conduct.

See also: Life

References: IV.2 ¶3

Art of vital administration

term

A concealed practical art which, with the vessel, the ancients are said to have hidden; Atwood names it without explaining it.

Atwood mentions “the concealed vessel or art of vital administration” [II.1 ¶8] among the things the ancients hid. The text does not explain it here; the “or” may present the vessel and the art as alternative names for one concealed thing, or as two things named together; the text does not decide.

References: II.1 ¶8

Art of Vulcan

term

The art said by unnamed others to have been first practised in Egypt by Cham, from whom some derive both the name and the art of alchemy.

Reporting what others say (not her own claim), Atwood records that in Egypt “it was there that the art of Vulcan was first practiced by Cham, one of the sons of the Patriarch” [I.1 ¶5]; some derive both the name and the art of alchemy from Cham.

See also: Vulcan

References: I.1 ¶5

Art of Wisdom

term

Atwood’s name for the Art as long called holy, with nothing impure or impious in it.

Atwood writes: “These is nothing impure, or of itself impious, in this Art of Wisdom, long distinguished as holy.” [IV.4 ¶24] (wording as in the book). Compare Art of Alchemy, called holy in the next paragraph [IV.4 ¶25].

See also: Hermetic art, Wisdom

References: IV.4 ¶24

Artephius

person · Artefius, Atrephius, Artefii

Author of a celebrated treatise on the philosophers’ stone whom Atwood quotes at length on long life, secrecy and the non-literal, cabalistic sense of the art.

Atwood quotes Artephius at length from his celebrated treatise on the philosophers’ stone (given in a note as Artefii Antiquissimi Philosophi de Arte Occulta atque Lapide Philosophorum Liber secretus) on long life by the quintessence. He says he publishes everything but one point: “I except one thing only, which it is not lawful that I should write, because it can be revealed truly only by God, or by a master” [I.1 ¶27; I.1 ¶36; I.1 n42]. She treats him as a link in alchemy’s history as it passed from Asia to Europe [I.1 ¶37].

She cites him with approval to show that the art is cabalistic and must not be read literally: “he that takes the philosophers’ saying according to the outward sense and signification has already lost the clue to Ariadne” [I.1 ¶84; I.1 n108]. Under the spelling Atrephius (Liber Secretissimus Artefii) he supports her description of the subject: “a white fume, in substance like to pure silver” [I.2 ¶29; I.2 n28].

With Arnold and Lully he is said to agree with the Lucerna Salis description of whitening, as cited earlier “in the Theory” [III.2 ¶5]. As Artefius he is named, with Trevisan and Flammel, among “the sincerest” who passed over the Preparation of Mercury in silence [IV.3 ¶7].

References: I.1 n108, I.1 n42, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶37, I.1 ¶84, I.2 n28, I.2 ¶29, III.2 ¶5, IV.3 ¶7

Artificial destruction

term

In Geber, a dissolution according to the course of nature; men’s ignorance of it made them think gold-making impossible.

Quoted from Geber: “the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47]. Because men did not know of this dissolution, they thought gold-making impossible.

References: II.1 ¶47

Artificial method

term

The method of the Art, which Atwood says Palingenius divulges in a few lines of verse.

Atwood introduces verses of Palingenius as one who “divulges the artificial method in the few following lines” [III.1 ¶26]. The phrase apparently means the method of the Art itself.

References: III.1 ¶26

Artist

term

The practitioner of the Art, who begins, ends and repeats the experiment, but who, according to the theosophist Atwood quotes, cannot do the work and only prepares the way and the matter.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes the practitioner: “as the Artist begins, ends, and repeats the mysterious experiment” [APP ¶17].

A theosophist she quotes sets limits on the human operator: “the Artist is not to attempt it — he cannot do it” [IV.3 ¶38]. The Artist only prepares the way and the matter, and must have understanding and faith [IV.3 ¶38]. The two records differ in emphasis: the Artist as active experimenter, and the Artist as one who cannot do the work alone.

See also: Wise artist

References: IV.3 ¶38, APP ¶17

Ascelpius Trallianus

person

An authority (spelled thus in the book) cited for deriving Wisdom from clearness and light.

Cited in support of deriving Wisdom from clearness and light: “it is a certain clearness, as being that which renders all things conspicuous” [II.4 ¶26].

References: II.4 ¶26

Ascendant

term

In Norton, the astrological ascendant, which should be direct and fiery and, with its Lord, made fortunate for the operation; a common sign suits the work’s many repetitions.

Quoted from Norton: the operation calls for what “Is a direct and Fiery ascendant” [IV.2 ¶34]. The ascendant and its Lord are to be made fortunate. A common sign suits the many repetitions of the work [IV.2 ¶34].

References: IV.2 ¶34

Asclepian prophecy

treatise

The prophecy of Egypt’s fall in the Asclepian Dialogue; Atwood sees the decline after 640 as something like its fulfilment, only worse than predicted.

Atwood treats the decline after 640 as something like the fulfilment of the Asclepian prophecy, but worse than it predicted [I.1 ¶30]. See Asclepius for the prophecy itself.

References: I.1 ¶30

Asclepius

treatise · Asclepian Dialogues, Asclepian Dialogue, Asclepias

The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes, a theosophic Hermetic book; Atwood defends as authentic its prophecy of Egypt’s fall and cites it on the magicians’ original divine power.

Atwood describes the Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes as a theosophic Hermetic book. It is the source of the prophecy of Egypt’s fall: “Oh, Egypt! Egypt! Fables alone shall remain of thy religion” [I.1 ¶7; I.1 ¶10; I.1 n11]. She defends the prophecy as authentic.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she cites the Dialogue, “so called, the 2 nd Book of Hermes, ch. 9”, to support her view that the magicians first drew their power from the Divine Source and later fell into debasement and idolatry [APP ¶5]. See also Asclepian prophecy.

References: I.1 n11, I.1 ¶10, I.1 ¶7, APP ¶5

Ashes

term

In Khunrath, what the impure body becomes when consumed and blackened; of great worth, the diadem of the body, holding our pigmy.

Quoted from Khunrath: the impure body, consumed and blackened, becomes ashes, and these are of great worth: “in them lies our pigmy, conquering and subduing giants” [IV.1 ¶36]. He identifies them with the diadem of the body: “they are the diadem of thy body” [IV.1 ¶36].

Identified with: the diadem of thy body [IV.1 ¶36]

References: IV.1 ¶36

Ashmole

person · Elias Ashmole

Compiler of the Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum, praised by Atwood and cited on secrecy, practical experience, incredulity, the Kelly story and a verse Tablet of Philosophy.

Atwood praises Elias Ashmole’s collection, the Theatrum Chemicum Britanicum (London 1652). She cites his preface to show secrecy and the need for practical experience, and also cites him on incredulity as a punishment: “I know enough to hold my tongue, but not enough to speak” [I.1 ¶62; I.1 ¶64; I.1 n66].

Ashmole tells the warming-pan story and judges Kelly more profuse than a sober philosopher should be [I.1 ¶66].

From the Theatrum (p. 336, Experience and Philosophy) she quotes a verse Tablet erected by Philosophy to Experience: “Blessed be thou, Experience!” [III.3 ¶75; III.3 ¶76; III.3 n49]. It speaks of the One Thing, the first Material Mother and the Three Powers in one seat, which the text at III.3 ¶77 glosses as Sulphur, Mercury and Salt.

References: I.1 n21, I.1 n66, I.1 ¶62, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶66, III.3 n49, III.3 ¶75, III.3 ¶76, III.4 n23, III.4 n8

Assent

term

In Synesius, the soul’s consent to its purification; without it the soul lacks every purifying machine, assent being the greatest pledge of reconciliation.

Quoted from Synesius: “the soul is deprived of every purifying machine because destitute of assent, which is the greatest pledge of reconciliation” [II.2 ¶13]. The context suggests assent means the soul’s own consent to being purified.

References: II.2 ¶13

Astral birth

term

In Boehme, what the new man looks into, equated with the geniture; not further explained.

Quoted from Boehme: the new man looks into “the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16], which equates it with geniture. The text gives no further explanation.

Identified with: geniture [III.2 ¶16]

References: III.2 ¶16

Astral fire

term

A fire said to conquer all things and assimilate them to itself; Paracelsus places it in the tincture, and Eudoxus says the Stone is an Astral Fire.

Two quoted authorities use the term. Paracelsus speaks of the fire in the tincture: “an astral fire which conquers all things and changes them into a nature like itself” [I.1 ¶76].

Eudoxus identifies the Stone with it: “Our stone is an Astral Fire” [IV.3 ¶16]. He says it sympathizes with Natural Fire and grows, like a Salamander, in Elementary Fire [IV.3 ¶16].

Identified with: Our stone [IV.3 ¶16]

See also: Fire

References: I.1 ¶76, IV.3 ¶16

Astrum solis

term

Atwood’s name for the internal spiritual Sun gotten and conceived through the work, which she identifies with a series of traditional images.

In her own voice Atwood gives a chain of identities: “This is the true Astrum Solis gotten and conceived, the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52]. So it is the internal spiritual Sun, the Perpetual Motion of the Wise and the Saturnian Salt.

She goes on: “And this we take to be that midnight Sun of Apuleius, the ignited Stone of Anaxagoras” [II.3 ¶54]; and “This is the triumphal Chariot of Antimony, the Armed Magnet of Helvetius turned swiftly about the current axle of life, which is the Wheel of Fire signalized in Ezekiel” [II.3 ¶54].

The records show it as what the work produces within: something gotten and conceived. Every equation here is Atwood’s own.

Identified with: internal spiritual Sun; Perpetual Motion of the Wise; Saturnian Salt [II.3 ¶52]; midnight Sun of Apuleius; ignited Stone of Anaxagoras [II.3 ¶54]; Chariot of Antimony; Armed Magnet of Helvetius; Wheel of Fire [II.3 ¶54]

References: II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54

Atalanta Fugiens

treatise

An emblem book whose Latin verses Atwood cites in notes to illustrate the one bird as vulture and crow, the egg analogy and the reddening of the whitened water.

Atwood quotes Latin verses from Atalanta Fugiens in her notes as illustrations, not as arguments.

  • Emblema xliii shows that the vulture and the crow are one: “Montis in excelso consistit vertice vultur,” [I.3 n12] (ours: On the lofty summit of a mountain stands a vulture).
  • Epigramma 8 illustrates the egg analogy: “Est avis in mundo sublimior omnibus, ovum” [I.3 n26] (ours: There is a bird in the world loftier than all, an egg…).
  • Emb. xli illustrates the reddening of the whitened water: “Adonis ab apro occuditur, cui Venus occurens tinxit rosas sanquine” [I.3 n54] (ours: Adonis is slain by a boar; Venus, running to him, dyed the roses with blood).

The translations are ours, not the book’s.

References: I.3 n12, I.3 n26, I.3 n54

Athanor

term

The philosophic furnace in which the matter is decocted with continual fire; Hermes’ furnace with a glass, the sealed furnace of the Second Operation, less important than the internal Fire.

A Scholiast calls it “the philosophic furnace called Athanor” [I.3 n57], in which the matter is decocted with continual fire.

Atwood refers to “that Athanor of Hermes before mentioned, or furnace having a glass to it” [II.4 ¶15], “that singular fundamental of his small new world”. She uses it as a comparison for how the Image of Universal Nature is revealed in Elysian intellection.

Eirenaeus subordinates the outer fire to the inner: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. Khunrath names “one theosophic cabalistically sealed furnace of Athanor” [IV.1 ¶36] for the Second Operation.

Identified with: philosophic furnace [I.3 n57]; furnace having a glass to it [II.4 ¶15]

References: I.3 n57, II.4 ¶15, III.1 ¶14, IV.1 ¶36

Athenagoras

person

Author of Du Parfait Amour, which Atwood says shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes; named among the authors of extant treatises on the stone.

Atwood says Athenagoras’s Du Parfait Amour shows practical knowledge of the art it allegorizes [I.1 ¶29]. She names him with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Zosimus and Archelaus as authors of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

References: I.1 n34, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶29

Augurellus

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.2 n48

Aura

term

In Vaughan, the material efflux of the soul, which differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.

Quoted from Vaughan: “the aura or material efflux of the soul” [III.3 ¶27]. It differs from the aerial spirit in constitution only, not in nature.

Identified with: material efflux of the soul [III.3 ¶27]

References: III.3 ¶27

Aurific light

term

The gold-making light of the ferment, into whose substance the ferment transmutes everything.

Atwood says the ferment “transmutes all into the substance of its own Aurific Light” [III.1 ¶24].

See also: Light

References: III.1 ¶24

Aurific principle

term

In Albertus Magnus, the gold-making principle, identified with fire in the life of all things and strongest in man.

Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “fire, which is the true aurific principle in the life of all” [II.1 ¶12]. This equates the aurific principle with fire, and the record adds that it is strongest in man.

Identified with: Fire [II.1 ¶12]

See also: Principles

References: II.1 ¶12

Aurific seed

term

A living gold-producing seed, the Light that springs from reason’s conscious alliance with the higher Cause; the true form of gold, which the covetous spirit cannot quicken.

Atwood says the seed must be quickened in life, unlike dead metal. The covetous spirit fails at this: “it cannot quicken the aurific seed in life” [III.4 ¶11]. The seed is not further explained in that passage.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she calls it the Light springing from reason’s conscious alliance with the higher Cause, which “is the Divine aurific seed and true form of gold.” [APP ¶152]. She also identifies it with the Golden Bough: “That was the Golden Bough which Aeneas carried” [APP ¶152].

Identified with: True form of gold [APP ¶152]; Golden Bough [APP ¶152]

See also: Seed

References: III.4 ¶11, APP ¶152

Aurific substance of life

term

The gold-making substance of life, which the will should return to its source and live there rather than possess.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the will fails “for want of returning the aurific substance of life into its source and living there” [APP ¶159]. On her account the will should return this substance to its source, not possess it.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶159

Aurified

term

Atwood’s gloss: illuminated, by contrariation of its Form.

Atwood glosses the word herself: “aurified — that is, illuminated by contrariation of its Form” [III.2 n38]. Aurified therefore means illuminated (stated).

Identified with: illuminated [III.2 n38]

References: III.2 n38

Auripigment

term · auripigments

A kind of sulphur, drawn dry from the fountain by the crowned king; Atwood takes it as the multiplicative virtue of the philosophers’ stone and a name for the luminous vital principle.

In the Hermetic passage quoted, the crowned king is described as “drawing from thence the Auripigment dry, without moisture” [I.3 ¶18]. The Hermetic Master’s version repeats this: “drawing from thence the Auripigment, dry without moisture” [III.3 ¶17], without defining it.

The same quoted Hermetic material names it among sulphurs: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It also identifies the fat of the brain with it: “and of the brain, which too is auripigment” [I.3 ¶20].

Atwood reads it as “that auripigment of philosophers which is the multiplicative virtue of their stone” [I.3 n22]. According to the readers’ record she also treats it as a name for the luminous vital principle (no quote given).

Identified with: Sulphur [I.3 ¶20]; multiplicative virtue of their stone [I.3 n22]; fat of the brain [I.3 ¶20]

References: I.3 n22, I.3 ¶18, I.3 ¶20, III.3 ¶17

Author of Antiquity Unveiled

collective voice

Writer of L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, cited by Atwood critically for treating the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men.

Atwood cites the author of L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, etc. only to criticize him: he saw the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men, a view Atwood rejects [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n4].

References: II.2 n4, II.2 ¶4

Author of the Aquarium Sapientum

collective voice · the excellent author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone, the pious author of the Aquarium, author of the Aquarium

The author of the Aquarium Sapientum, or Water Stone, cited by Atwood for the spirit-soul-body cycle and for the warning that pride or covetousness makes the art vanish.

Atwood cites this author from the Aquarium Sapientum (in the Musaeum Hermeticum) for a Latin enigma illustrating the separation, putrefaction and reunion of spirit, soul and body: “Spiritus ipse datur pro tempore corpori” [I.3 n21] (our rendering: the spirit itself is given to the body for a time). Elsewhere, as “the pious author of the Aquarium”, he supports her point that pride or covetousness after possession makes the art disappear: “this art will vanish from under thy hands” [III.4 ¶7; III.4 n4]. Atwood endorses this warning.

See also: Aquarium Sapientum

References: I.3 n21, III.4 n4, III.4 ¶7

Author of the Filum Ariadne

collective voice

Writer of Le Filet d’Aridane, cited in support of the point that the dissolution needs hands, which Nature lacks.

Cited (work: Le Filet d’Aridane) in support of Atwood’s point that the dissolution requires hands, which Nature lacks: “Nature cannot of herself enter into the dissolution” [IV.1 ¶5; IV.1 n3]. Atwood endorses the citation.

References: IV.1 n3, IV.1 ¶5

Author of the Lucerna Salis

collective voice · the author of Lucerna Salis

Writer of the Lucerna Salis (cited in Digby’s translation), repeatedly used by Atwood in support of points on the white work, prayer and labour, the gold of the Wise, and fermentation.

Atwood cites the Lucerna Salis (footnoted as Digby’s translation / Digby’s Lucerna Salis) several times, always in support:

  • White work: on the whitening of the matter, with the advice “Govern your fire with a great deal of care” [III.2 ¶5; III.2 ¶6; III.2 n7].
  • Study, prayer and labour: study, meditation and prayer are needed; God grants the art only through instruction and labour, and without prayer obstructs or spoils it: “He does not either grant it immediately to any person, but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n21]. Also cited for many passages to the same effect as Ricardus [III.4 n16].
  • Gold of the Wise: from the Latin verse Aurum Sapientum, the gold of the Wise as pure water, its dissolution and reunion into One inseparable Thing; it declares “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold” [III.3 ¶32; III.3 n22].
  • Fermentation and multiplication (cap. 8): fermenting with pure gold or silver before projection, purifying the metals, and tenfold multiplication by dissolving and coagulating; “one drachm of gold is sufficient for the fermentation in the red” [IV.3 ¶24; IV.3 n5].

See also: Lucerna Salis Phil.

References: III.2 n7, III.2 ¶5, III.2 ¶6, III.3 n22, III.3 ¶32, III.4 n16, III.4 n21, III.4 ¶20, IV.3 n5, IV.3 ¶24

Author of the Lumen de Lumine

collective voice

Writer of the Lumen de Lumine, cited from its chapter on Matter in support of Atwood’s account of Tenebrae activae beneath sense and imagination.

Cited from the chapter on Matter in Lumen de Lumine in support of Atwood’s account of the Tenebrae activae lying beneath sense and imagination, described as “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13; III.2 n13].

See also: Lumen de Lumine

References: III.2 n13, III.2 ¶13

Author of the Rosarium

collective voice · the wise author of the Rosarium, Author of the Rosary

Writer of the Rosarium, cited by Atwood in support of solution, dissolution and patient repetition, and among testimonies to inexhaustible abundance she says are not literally true.

Atwood cites the Rosarium (Rosar. Abbrev., Tract ii, De Lapide, in Thet. Chem., vol iii) in support of Solution as the first preparation: subjects of species must be reduced to first matter, with an analogy from glass-making [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n2].

It also supports dissolution, the earthy body of sense made to flow: “Corpora qui vult purgare oportet fluxa facere” [II.3 n2] (ours: whoever would purge bodies must make them fluid).

The “wise author of the Rosarium” (cap. 3) is cited for grinding, cooking and repeating without weariness: “Tere, coque, et reitera, et non te taedeat” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n7].

As “Author of the Rosary” he is cited for an inexhaustible abundance won by industry, patience and one’s own labour, in a passage that continues with Eirenaeus and is footnoted to Introitus Apertus cap. 35; Atwood then says this testimony is not literally true [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7].

See also: Monk in his Rosary

References: I.2 n2, I.2 ¶5, II.3 n2, IV.1 n7, IV.1 ¶7, IV.3 n7, IV.3 ¶26

Author of the Tractatus Aureus

collective voice — anonymous · the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus

The unnamed author of the Tractatus Aureus, cited as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), this author of the Tractatus Aureus (Museum Hermeticum, edit. 1649, p. 45) is cited with approval as having carefully prepared the magic Key that opens the door into the Hermetic garden [APP ¶100].

See also: Tractatus Aureus

References: APP ¶100

Author of The Triumph

collective voice · our author of The Triumph, The Triumph

The author of The Triumph, cited for listing the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone.

This author is cited for a list of the fixed principles: the Elements, the Three Principles, white and citrine Mercury, and fixed Sulphur as the Stone. The list begins: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6].

References: IV.2 ¶6

Authorities

collective voice

Unnamed authorities cited in support of the claim that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures.

Cited, unnamed, in support of the statement that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures [III.4 ¶25].

References: III.4 ¶25

Authorities in Norton

collective voice — Philosophers, Astrologers, Auctors · Philosophers, Astrologers, Auctors

Authorities cited within Norton’s verse on working ‘within locks nyne’ and on the importance of a fitting place.

These authorities speak inside Norton’s verse, which Atwood quotes: “Philosophers said, by their engine, How it should be wrought within locks nyne” [III.4 ¶41]. The passage also stresses how much a fitting place matters for the work.

See also: Norton, Philosopher (unnamed voice), Philosophers

Avarice

Avicenna

person · Avicen

Reputed practitioner of transmutation, cited by Atwood on species and the Matter and named among masters who wrote obscurely.

Atwood lists works attributed to him (de Tinctura Metallorum, Porta Elementa, de Mineralibus) and calls him a reputed practitioner of transmutation and magic whose writings are neither lucid nor numerous [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n40]. He is cited, by reference only, as concurring on species [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n5], and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

In Norton’s verse “Avicen” is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the Ordinal his Porta is cited for balanced feeding of the matter: “Comedas ut bibas, et bibas ut comeda;” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: eat as you drink, and drink as you eat).

Azoth

term

Name for the Universal Mercury and the Stone’s active principle, which with fire suffices for the work, reducing bodies to First Matter and reanimating them.

Khunrath (quoted) identifies it: “Azoth, viz., the Universal Mercury” — “which alone with its internal and external fire is sufficient for thee”, transforming itself by fire into what it will, and visible and tangible [I.1 ¶81]. Elsewhere Khunrath presents it as something to be touched and seen, sufficient with internal and external fire for the Stone: “thou shalt see Azoth! The Universal!” [III.3 ¶9].

The Latin formula “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” is given as Hermes’ saying via Norton, without explanation [IV.2 ¶13] (ours: fire and Azoth suffice for thee). In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood repeats it as sufficient for the freed spirit: “ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [APP ¶131].

In IV.3 a cited voice (“continues he”) makes it the Stone’s active principle: “Azoth of our Stone, continues he, reduces bodies to their First Matter and reanimates them with the Universal Form” [IV.3 ¶28]. The vivific Ens is so named because it adheres to bodies, drawing its like into itself by supernatural magnetism: “the Hermetic philosophers have given it the name of azoth, which adheres to bodies” [IV.3 ¶29].

Asserted identities: = Universal Mercury [I.1 ¶81]; = The Universal [III.3 ¶9]; = vivific Ens [IV.3 ¶29].

Identified with: Universal Mercury [I.1 ¶81]; Universal [III.3 ¶9]; Vivific ens [IV.3 ¶29]

References: I.1 ¶81, III.3 ¶9, IV.2 ¶13, IV.3 ¶28, IV.3 ¶29, APP ¶131

Bacon

person

Named among masters who celebrated the Head Stone and wrote obscurely; his dictum on man as Nature’s servant is accepted by Atwood only for outward seeking.

In Norton’s verse Bacon is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. He is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21], and as having observed the Organon becoming worse than useless [III.2 ¶42].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood uses his lucid style to show that clear language seems mystical when turned to the a priori ground [APP ¶111]. She accepts his dictum “Man is the servant and interpreter of Nature” only for outward seeking and qualifies it: turned within, man can be Nature’s revealer and master [APP ¶120].

References: I.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶21, III.2 ¶42, APP ¶111, APP ¶120

person

Bards and hallowed sages of Asia Minor

collective voice

Ancient sages contrasted with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun under which moderns remain blind.

Atwood contrasts them with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun, while moderns remain blind [IV.4 ¶28].

References: IV.4 ¶28

Basil Valentine

person · B. Valentine, Basil, the Monk Basil, the Benedict Valentine

Adept called “the monk”, praised by Atwood as the star of his century and among her most-cited authorities on First Matter, Antimony, extraction, and experience before practice.

Atwood praises Basil Valentine as the star of the fifteenth century, credited with a new method for the Red Elixir, and assesses editions and translations of his works (Chimische Schriften, Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, Stone of Fire, Twelve Keys) [I.1 ¶59; I.1 ¶61; I.1 n65]. He is listed among genuine seekers against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49], among adepts warning against practice before full understanding, though “Basil’s” receipts also misled literal readers [I.1 ¶86], and as agreeing concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

First Matter. From De Prima Materia: it is like no particular thing, indescribable without experience, one yet three, a third thing: “Corpus anima spiritus in duobus existit” [I.2 ¶31; I.2 ¶32; I.2 ¶42; I.2 n33] (ours: body, soul, spirit exist in two). All metals have one root containing mercury, salt and sulfur: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11; II.1 n8]. His Stone of Fire allegory of flight, fall and mountain Atwood reads as displaying the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis; it names what “is the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19; III.2 ¶20; III.2 n20].

Antimony and extraction. The true tincture is not common antimony; “how that extraction should be made, is a principal secret in which the whole art of Alchemy consists” [II.1 ¶25]. “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”, done with the microcosm’s corporeal fire [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n42]. Antimony must be freed of venom, which Atwood glosses as purging self-will from the mind; separation is by Fire, Vulcan the sole master: “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n34].

Experience. “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” — advice Atwood calls excellent; his celestial part, separating pure from impure by spiritual reason, leads into her turn to spiritual reason [III.1 ¶13; III.1 n10; III.1 n14; III.1 n15]. “more is learned by once seeing the work done, than can be taught by the writing of many pages” [IV.1 ¶2; IV.1 n1]. The winged Matter must be bound and accustomed to flight gradually, lest like Icarus it fly too near the Sun: “permit it not to fly suddenly” [IV.1 ¶15; IV.1 n15].

He also teaches that exterior spirits are intelligent and deceive the unwary, being “endowed with senses and understanding, know Arts, and have in themselves an occult operative life” [II.3 ¶23; II.3 n18]. In the Appendix (later layer) his Keys are called the best illustration of the Art as a fermentative process [APP ¶29].

References: I.1 n36, I.1 n65, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶49, I.1 ¶59, I.1 ¶61, I.1 ¶86, I.2 n33, I.2 ¶31, I.2 ¶32, I.2 ¶42, I.3 n23, I.3 n66, II.1 n8, II.1 ¶11, II.1 ¶25, II.3 n18, II.3 ¶23, III.1 n10, III.1 n14, III.1 n15, III.1 n42, III.1 n8, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶37, III.2 n20, III.2 ¶19, III.2 ¶20, III.2 ¶60, III.4 n24, IV.1 n1, IV.1 n15, IV.1 n34, IV.1 ¶15, IV.1 ¶2, IV.1 ¶40, APP ¶29

Blood

term

Read variously by quoted authorities: in Roger Bacon’s phrase the understanding; in verse from Theat. Chem. Brit. the principal matter of all that increases; in Boehme the fire-and-water union whose warmth is life.

The records give three quoted readings, not reconciled:

  • Jacob Boehme: the red fire-form and the thin water-form, “both of which contracting together into one, are converted into Blood”; “the original in the blood, viz., fire, which is its warmth, is life”, and from that warmth the Thin Water of Life proceeds [III.3 ¶24].

Blood of the Lion

term · Lion’s Blood, Lyons Blood, blood of the Greene Lyon

It is the King’s only food, given after he rises from the dead: “And tis as strange that thys Kings food, Can be nothing but thys Lyons Blood;” [III.1 ¶65]; and it is worked with Luna or Sol to prepare the ferments [III.1 ¶65]. Asserted identity: = a right good secret [III.1 ¶65]. A reader noted that the same passage may also call it the King’s Father and Mother; this is uncertain.

Body

In quoted authorities, the hard, dry or dead part of the matter that imprisons the spirit or fire and must be dissolved, rotted and glorified.

Three quoted voices use the term:

  • Eirenaeus: the hard, dry body in which the fire is imprisoned, rotted by ‘our water’: “which in the hard and dry body is imprisoned” [III.1 ¶14]. A gloss in the passage (whose voice is unclear) makes it the ethereal body: “by rotting the moles of the body (i.e., of the ethereal body)” [III.1 ¶14].
  • Eudoxus: what remains after the Water is distilled off: “the Body remains in the bottom of the vessel, like a dead, black, and dredgy earth” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is not to be despised, and must be wholly dissolved and glorified. He names it Adam: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
  • The Scholiast (reported by Atwood): “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” [I.3 n38], glossed as “the bodies (i.e., the sensible and vegetable media of life)” [I.3 n38], which must be dissolved into their radical source.

Boehme

person · Behmen, Jacob Boehme, Bohme, Jacob Bhemen

Writer Atwood treats as the plainest experiential exponent of the mystery, cited throughout for the Tincture, the Three Principles and divine manifestation, though she judges him theosophical rather than intellectual.

Atwood calls Jacob Boehme the plainest exponent of the mystery from experience, with explicit pointers to the physical basis of magic and the material of the stone, citing the Aurora, Three Principles, Mysterium Magnum, Tree of Life, Turned Eye and Epistles [I.1 ¶68; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n77]. She qualifies this: his revelation is theosophical, not intellectual [I.1 ¶70]. His writings alarmed alchemists by applying alchemy openly to human life [II.1 ¶9].

The Work. From the Tract. Aur., Epistles and Forty Questions she takes the white and red stages and the concealment under the Seal of God: “the Work is easy and simple, but the wisdom therein is great and the greatest mystery” [II.1 ¶24; II.1 n20]. Forty Questions 17 gives the core operation, Sol and Luna brought through death at the cross and reconceived: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48; III.1 n53]; Atwood says it comprehends ‘the end and beginning of the Sacred Art’. The Three Principles supplies the Antimonial Spirit and the Invisible Mercury: “the agent in the preparation of this spirit, continues Bohme, is the Invisible Mercury” [II.1 ¶20], and the disorder of arterial blood [II.1 ¶21; II.1 n17]; the Generation of the Three Principles gives the creation of a cloud condensed into water: “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. His account of the Tincture, which “is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16], is endorsed as agreeing with the ancient Kabalah [III.2 ¶17]; the Turned Eye gives ‘modern testimony’ of his illumination: “the gate was opened to me” [III.2 ¶16]. The operator must first “seek God’s love and grace, and resign up themselves to become wholly one with that” [III.1 ¶39]; Atwood qualifies that the divine cannot exactly be given into possession [III.1 ¶40]. On contrition and the Tincture: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24]. He is among Adepts comparing the work to the Creed [IV.3 ¶27].

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): he knew the mystery by experienced in-seeing whereby he became it [APP ¶117]; the deepest writer on ontological subjects, less scientific than the Platonists but more descriptive, awakening, suggestive [APP ¶62]; his three primary forms and doctrine of the Absolute Will read as expressions of conscious experience of the creative mystery [APP ¶65]; surpassing the Neo-Platonists on the Life Center [APP ¶122]. His Law of Divine Manifestation, the order the Hermetic Work imitates: “An Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to introduce the No Thing into Something, that the Will might feel and find and behold itself” [APP ¶73]; cited for the Sulphur, Salt and Mercury nomenclature [APP ¶81]; ‘in the Experience’ of the uncreated beyond the metaphysicians, though they surpassed him in scientific intuition [APP ¶96]. Also: the Third Principle as medium of perceiving the First, “the sidereal and elementary birth” [APP ¶27]; the Three-fold Life on will begetting a being out of its own image [APP ¶36]; his Mercurius, or spirit of the Sound, for the harmony freed from the lower life [APP ¶49]; Signatura Rerum on knowing things in their roots on entering the Signature, “through the principle in the sound with the voice” [APP ¶63]; with de St Martin, source of ‘the Crown’, and contrasted with Engelbrecht as penetrating surfaces, his body swallowed up with Light [APP ¶104; APP ¶105]; the bitterness of self-life from which nature shields us, “the bitter anguish of the driving wheel of existence” [APP ¶154].

References: I.1 n77, I.1 ¶68, I.1 ¶70, II.1 n16, II.1 n17, II.1 n20, II.1 n23, II.1 ¶20, II.1 ¶21, II.1 ¶24, II.1 ¶25, II.1 ¶9, III.1 n43, III.1 n53, III.1 ¶39, III.1 ¶40, III.1 ¶48, III.1 ¶49, III.2 n15, III.2 n16, III.2 n17, III.2 ¶15, III.2 ¶16, III.2 ¶17, III.3 n16, III.3 ¶24, IV.3 ¶27, APP ¶104, APP ¶105, APP ¶117, APP ¶122, APP ¶154, APP ¶27, APP ¶36, APP ¶49, APP ¶62, APP ¶63, APP ¶65, APP ¶73, APP ¶81, APP ¶96

Book of Jezirah

treatise

Book whose first chapter Atwood compares with the building of Solomon’s Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.

Atwood quotes chapter 1, “with the Fiery Letters of the Law, He engraved the empty, and the void, and the obscure mind” [IV.2 ¶33; IV.2 n21], and compares it with the building of Solomon’s Temple and the threefold completion of the Stone.

References: IV.2 n21, IV.2 ¶33

Book of Revelation

treatise · Revel., the Revelation, the Apocalypse, Revelation of St.John

The Book of Revelation, which Atwood cites for the competent minister, the Stone with a new name, the white splendour, Wisdom’s fruits and the marriage of man and God.

Atwood cites Revel. 3:7 for the qualifications of the competent minister: “he that hath the Key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n17]. Chapters 2–3 support the promises of material fruits with Wisdom: “To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the Tree of Life” [IV.3 n22]; the passages at [IV.3 ¶41–45] apparently come from these chapters (the footnote numbering is unclear). Chapters 1:14 and 2:17 illustrate the white appearance of the primeval splendour (the White Stone, the Son of Man): “whose hair was like wool, and white as snow” [III.2 ¶4; III.2 n5]. She also invokes the Stone of the Apocalypse and the Stone with the new name [II.3 ¶52, ¶54]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) the Book of Revelation is said to hint at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79].

See also: Bible, Revelation

References: II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54, III.2 n5, III.2 ¶4, IV.3 n17, IV.3 n20, IV.3 n22, IV.3 ¶39, IV.3 ¶41, IV.3 ¶42, IV.3 ¶43, IV.3 ¶44, IV.3 ¶45, APP ¶79

Book of Wisdom

treatise

Book Atwood praises in the Appendix as the best description of Wisdom as man’s exemplar.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood calls it the best description of Wisdom as man’s exemplar [APP ¶90]. Cited together with the Poemander, chapter 11, verse 22 illustrates the whole world held before the divine vision, as before one who has the Principle: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

See also: Wisdom

References: III.3 n26, III.3 ¶39, APP ¶90

Books of our fathers

collective voice

Old sources whose unguents made from fats, hair and similar things are rejected in the passage citing them.

Cited critically: the unguents made from fats, hair and the like, “which are written in the books of our fathers” [I.3 ¶53], are rejected.

References: I.3 ¶53

Boorhaave

person · Boerhaave

Modern authority who lauds the Isaacs and, with Homberg and Boyle, held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.

Atwood cites Boorhaave for the Isaacs’ reputation: he lauds them and seems acquainted with occult science [I.1 ¶58]. With Homberg and Boyle he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

References: I.1 ¶58, I.2 ¶14, I.2 ¶15

Botri

term

Atwood’s gloss: the Philosopher’s Stone, made from the Citrine extracted from the Red.

Atwood glosses the term in a footnote: “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52], made from the Citrine extracted from the Red. Asserted identity: = Philosopher’s Stone.

Identified with: Stone [I.3 n52]

References: I.3 n52

Boyle

person

Modern figure rumoured to have known Philalethes, and named among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, though without proof.

Boyle is rumoured, uncertainly, to have been intimate with Philalethes [I.1 ¶73]. With Homberg and Boerhaave he is among moderns who held with the alchemists a universal Ether, “this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand” [I.2 ¶14], but Atwood notes they lacked proof [I.2 ¶15].

References: I.1 ¶73, I.2 ¶14, I.2 ¶15

Brass

term · our brass, Fixed Brass

A veiled name in quoted authorities: for Hermes the Art of the permanent water; for Albertus the occult Nature to be washed, dissolved and fixed.

Hermes (quoted): “the Art of this permanent water is our brass” [I.3 ¶43]; Democritus draws out the ‘Fixed Brass’ bodily: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily, writes our Abderite” [I.3 n53].

Albertus (quoted) uses it for the occult Nature: “Take the occult Nature, which is our Brass” [IV.1 ¶4], which is to be washed pure and clean, then dissolved, distilled, sublimed, calcined and fixed.

Asserted identities: = Art of this permanent water [I.3 ¶43]; = occult Nature [IV.1 ¶4]. See also body of brass, Brazen Body.

Identified with: Art of this permanent water [I.3 ¶43]; occult Nature [IV.1 ¶4]

See also: Fixed brass

References: I.3 n53, I.3 ¶43, IV.1 ¶4

Brazen body

term

In Hermes as quoted, the body to be burned with exceeding great fire, exemplified by Democritus drawing out the ‘Fixed Brass’.

Quoted from Hermes: “Burn then the Brazen Body with an exceeding great fire” [I.3 ¶42]. Democritus, exemplifying this juncture, draws out the ‘Fixed Brass’ and works it on the coals [I.3 ¶42].

See also: Body

References: I.3 ¶42

Brazen wall

term

Atwood’s image of the barrier surrounding ‘our Heaven’ that must be scaled and passed before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.

Atwood: “this is that Brazen Wall celebrated by Antiquity, which surrounds our Heaven and must be scaled” [IV.1 ¶4]. It must be passed through before the equilibriate felicity of Being within is discerned.

References: IV.1 ¶4

Brethren

term

Atwood’s gloss: the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit, finally gathered into accord with its first source.

Atwood glosses the term: “by the brethren, the inferior degrees of illumination in the spirit” [I.3 n50], which are finally gathered into accord with the spirit’s first source.

See also: Brethren (group voice)

References: I.3 n50

Brethren

collective voice — group voice

A group voice whose phrase names the only builders who ‘erect structures in the air’.

The phrase of the Brethren for the only builders who ‘erect structures in the air’: “Master mason, of Grand Architects” [IV.2 ¶14].

See also: Brethren

References: IV.2 ¶14

Brethren of the Rosy Cross

collective voice · brotherhood of the Rosy Cross, fraternity of the Rosy Cross, Rosy Cross

A fraternity which Atwood says agreed about the Matter and found it experimentally; she quotes their letter and the Matter’s speeches.

Atwood says the Christian brotherhood of the Rosy Cross agreed concerning the Matter, searched Nature experimentally, found it and used it [III.2 ¶60]. A letter circulated under their name gives an allegory of the initiatory passage (mountain, beasts, night, guide, courage): “There is a mountain situated in the midst of the earth or center of the world” [II.3 ¶31; II.3 ¶32]. From the Latin original of the Fraternity, as given in Vaughan’s Coelum Terrae, she quotes speeches of the Matter as Goddess (First Matter, Eagle and Lion, five gates) and as Dragon or Mercury: “I am a Goddess for beauty and extraction” [III.3 ¶62; III.3 n45].

See also: Cross, Rosicrucian Fraternity

References: II.3 ¶31, II.3 ¶32, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n45, III.3 ¶62, III.3 ¶63, III.3 ¶64

Buba

term

In Hermes as quoted, that to which the son is to be joined, called Jupiter and a hidden secret.

Quoted from Hermes: “join the son to Buba, which is Jupiter and a hidden secret” [I.3 ¶37]. Asserted identity: = Jupiter.

Identified with: Jupiter [I.3 ¶37]

References: I.3 ¶37

Bysse

term

Boehme’s word, glossed in the quoted passage itself as the ground or original foundation.

Quoted from Boehme, who glosses it: “the Bysse, or ground or original foundation” [III.2 ¶16]. Asserted identity: = ground or original foundation.

Identified with: ground or original foundation [III.2 ¶16]

References: III.2 ¶16

C

Cabalistic

term

Said of Lully’s mind and of the art itself: veiled, full of mysteries, not to be understood according to the letter.

Atwood says one must “possess the key of his cabalistic mind” [I.1 ¶48] to understand Lully’s obscure alchemical works. Artephius (quoted) applies it to the art: “For is not our art cabalistic” [I.1 ¶84], full of mysteries, not taught openly, not to be understood according to the letter.

See also: Kabalah

References: I.1 ¶48, I.1 ¶84

Cabalistic method

term

Atwood’s name for a practice of the time of concealing truth by displacing order, inverting and dispersing repetitions.

Atwood blames the displacement of verses from their original order on “the mischievous cabalistic method in vogue at that time” [I.1 ¶64], and traces to it the artifices used to hide the truth, such as inversion of order and dispersed repetition: “A variety of artifices according to the cabalistic method” [I.1 ¶82].

References: I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶82

Cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience

collective voice

Ancient sources whose reported view grounds man’s rank in a Divine Reason and latent Faculty of Wisdom; Atwood says it was once proved but is now beyond evidence.

Atwood reports their view that man’s rank rests on a Divine Reason and a latent Faculty of Wisdom: “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32]. She says this was once proved but is now beyond present evidence [II.1 ¶32].

See also: Experience, Kabalah

References: II.1 ¶32

Calcinations

term · calcination, calcine

One of the preparations the vulgar Matter undergoes; Synesius makes calcination a name of the single operation, the same as extracting soul, spirit or body.

Quoted from Synesius, calcination is one of the names of the single operation: “to extract the soul, or the spirit, or the body, is nothing else than the aforesaid calcinations” [III.3 ¶60], and these names are used “in regard they signify the operation of Venus” [III.3 ¶60]. Atwood herself lists calcinations among the preparations the vulgar Matter passes through before it becomes the Mercury of the Philosophers: “Hence all those preparations, solutions, calcinations, etc.” [II.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she places it as a step before a reunion into permanent form: “after calcinations there is a reunion” [III.2 ¶64]. The text does not define the operation further.

Identified with: extraction of the soul, spirit or body [III.3 ¶60]; operation of Venus [III.3 ¶60]

References: II.2 ¶16, III.2 ¶64, III.3 ¶60

Calid

person

A king, initiated and converted, cited as author of the Liber Secretorum and as one of the Mahomedan princes agreed concerning the Matter.

Atwood cites Calid as a king who was initiated and converted and who wrote treatises, among them the Liber Secretorum, or Secret of Secrets [I.1 ¶35]. Later she counts him among “the Mahomedan princes” who agree concerning the Matter, using him as supporting testimony [III.2 ¶60].

References: I.1 ¶35, III.2 ¶60

Caligo divina

term

Dionysius’s name for the primordial cloud, obscure and humanly incomprehensible though visible; called Tenebrae activae by the author of the Lumen de Lumine.

A quoted term: Dionysius’s name for the primordial cloud, of which it is said “it is obscure and humanly incomprehensible, though visible indeed” and “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13].
