It is identified with the Kabalists’ term: “The author of the Lumen de Lumine calls it, from the Kabalists, Tenebrae activae” [III.2 ¶13], described as beneath all sense and imagination.

Identified with: Tenebrae activae [III.2 ¶13]

References: III.2 ¶13

Callimachus

person

Author whose Hymn to Minerva and Hymn to Apollo Atwood quotes on the purity Divinity requires.

Atwood quotes Callimachus’s Hymn to Minerva in support of the point that Divinity rejects anything mixed: “All mixture of her pure and simple oil” [III.2 ¶64; III.2 ¶65; III.2 n48]. She quotes the Hymn to Apollo (in Dodd’s version) to illustrate the coming of the God of Light and the purity required to behold him: “Apollo’s eyes endure None but the good, the perfect, and the pure.” [IV.2 ¶37; IV.2 ¶38; IV.2 n26]. In both cases she uses him approvingly as illustration.

References: III.2 n48, III.2 ¶64, III.2 ¶65, IV.2 n26, IV.2 ¶37, IV.2 ¶38

Calx

term

Where the conflux of the water below and the ether above takes place, and from which the physical Tetractys springs.

Atwood says the meeting of the water below and the ether above happens in a Calx: “the conflux of these two is in a Calx” [III.3 ¶72]; from it the physical Tetractys springs. The term is not further defined.

References: III.3 ¶72

Cambar

term

In a saying of Hermes, that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame, and is corrupted in the heat of the boiling fire.

A quoted term from Hermes: that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame — “that which in the heat of the boiling fire is corrupted is Cambar” [I.3 ¶42]. Not further explained.

References: I.3 ¶42

Camden

person

Author of Antiquities, cited as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins.

Atwood cites Camden’s Antiquities in support, as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins [I.1 ¶47].

References: I.1 ¶47

Capricornus 214

person

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n34

Caput mortuum

term

The ashes in which the principle of body is preserved and from which the whole life is restored; also an epithet of the Matter.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “what they call the ashes or Caput Mortuum” [APP ¶26] as where the principle of body is preserved; from that one principle the whole life is restored. She reports that Khunrath has other names for it: “Khunrath call it ‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’” [APP ¶26], and tentatively adds “I think he refers to it under the term Duanach” [APP ¶26].

In the main text, quoting Synesius and the New Light, caput mortuum is one of the epithets of the Matter: “O our caput mortuum, or dead head, or foeces of our sea!” [I.2 ¶33].

Identified with: Ashes [APP ¶26]; our pigmy / diadem of the body (Khunrath) [APP ¶26]; Duanach (Khunrath; tentative) [APP ¶26]; dead head; foeces of our sea [I.2 ¶33]

References: I.2 ¶33, APP ¶26

Catholic art of reason

term

Atwood’s hedged name for Reason investigating her First Source.

Atwood names the process she has described, with the hedge ‘it would seem’, “the Catholic Art of Reason investigating her First Source” [IV.2 ¶21].

See also: Reason

References: IV.2 ¶21

Catholic effect of life

term

What the Hermetic experiment arrives at, passing from either extreme of mind and matter, where external and internal worlds blend.

Atwood says the Hermetic experiment, “as passing from whither extreme of Mind and matter, to prove them, it arrives at the Catholic Effect of Life” [IV.4 ¶11]; there the external and internal worlds blend.

See also: Life

References: IV.4 ¶11

Catholic embryo

term

For some modern Kabalists, the universal germ before birth, seen as a nebulous cloud; a concentration of Divinity that gives birth to the primitive Ether.

A view Atwood reports from some modern Kabalists: the universal germ before its birth appears as a cloud — “This nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo before its birth” [III.2 ¶13] — an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity, giving birth to the primitive Ether.

References: III.2 ¶13

Catholic germ

term

‘That which is sown’ in man: it contains all things and must die before it is quickened.

Atwood glosses ‘that which is sown’ in man: “that which is sown (viz., the catholic germ of his existence” [I.3 n8]. It contains all things and must die before it is quickened.

Identified with: that which is sown [I.3 n8]

References: I.3 n8

Catholic nature

term

The universal nature that is the subject of the Art: precious when exalted, defiled and despised in the common world.

Atwood: “The same catholic nature, which in its preternatural exaltation appears so very precious” [I.3 n40] is, in the common world, defiled and despised. The context presents it as the subject of the Art.

References: I.3 n40

Catholic torch

term

Something miraculously kindled that kindles the Light of Universal Nature, acting through the three kingdoms and rejoicing most in the Mind of Man.

Atwood: “The catholic torch, miraculously kindled, kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]; it acts through the three kingdoms by voluntary assimilation and rejoices most in the Mind of Man. The text does not identify it further.

References: IV.4 ¶32

Causal center

term

In the Table Talk, where the individual light of life is lodged, driving adhering evil to the extremities and freeing the threefold life to ascend.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of the time “when the individual light of life is lodged in its causal center” [APP ¶150]: adhering evil is then precipitated to the extremities and the threefold life is freed to ascend.

See also: Center

References: APP ¶150

Causal discovery

term

Knowledge of cause, the only thing that fulfils the Idea of Truth, superior to the exhibition of phenomena.

Atwood holds that “neither can anything short of the Causal Discovery fulfill the Idea of Truth” [IV.4 ¶13]; it ranks above the mere exhibition of phenomena, the only doubt being whether it is possible. The adjacent passage speaks of knowledge “leading out from the Causal Fountain into natural effect” [IV.4 ¶12]. See also Causal Knowledge.

References: IV.4 ¶12, IV.4 ¶13

Causal fountain

term

The source of all things and of Wisdom, from which riches come and whose emanative splendour the true gods are.

Atwood speaks of “riches as from the Causal fountain of all things” [II.4 ¶19], and of the true gods “as an emanative splendour from the Causal Fountain, make manifest in energy its Intellectual Law” [II.4 ¶29]. It is also the source of Wisdom, to be approached by prayer as one applies to a master of an art: “the Causal Fountain for Wisdom, which is His alone and voluntarily to bestow” [III.4 ¶20].

See also: Fountain

References: II.4 ¶19, II.4 ¶29, III.4 ¶20

Causal knowledge

term

Knowledge of causes, the worthiest part of knowledge, without which external science leaves us no wiser; withheld from the unworthy.

Atwood insists the unworthy be kept from it, lest they handle ‘the powerful machine of nature’ for selfish ends: “these are unfit to be admitted to the Causal Knowledge” [I.3 n10]. Without it external science leaves us no wiser: “what would we be wiser without the Causal knowledge of these things?” [IV.4 ¶29]; and “For the discovery of the Causal Nature is doubtless of all parts of knowledge the worthiest to be sought after” [IV.4 ¶32]. See also Causal Discovery.

References: I.3 n10, IV.4 ¶29, IV.4 ¶32

Causal light

term

The light within a person, which the Art draws forth, fixes and brings to manifestation; nature’s Causal Light reached through the Understanding.

Atwood identifies it with what is within: “That which is within, viz., the causal light, must be drawn forth by art and fixed” [I.3 n8]. The Art aims to “bring the Causal light to manifestation” [II.1 ¶17], and to recover “the Ancient Experiment of nature into her Causal Light” [III.4 ¶2]. It is reached by rational permeation, “by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20]. The goal includes knowing the First Truth experimentally and being able “to revolve the Causal Light in permanence of intellection” [IV.4 ¶22]. Beyond the identification with ‘that which is within’, the text does not define it.

Identified with: that which is within [I.3 n8]

See also: Light

References: I.3 n8, II.1 ¶17, III.4 ¶2, IV.1 ¶20, IV.4 ¶22

Causal nature

term

In Hermes (Asclepius), something man can both find and effect.

Quoting Hermes in the Asclepius: “man should be able not only to find the Causal Nature but to effect it” [III.1 ¶21]. Atwood also calls its discovery the worthiest part of knowledge [IV.4 ¶32] (see Causal Knowledge).

References: III.1 ¶21

Causal source

term

The goal of the ancients’ method of ascent, surveyed more or less immediately after gradual assimilation.

Atwood describes the ancients’ ascent as proceeding by gradual assimilation “to a survey more or less immediate of the Causal Source” [III.2 ¶33].

See also: Identic source

References: III.2 ¶33

Causal truth

term

The truth of causes, as opposed to remote effects, beheld in the apperceptive vision granted to those proved and reproved.

Atwood contrasts it with remote effects, speaking of those “who have never glanced even in imagination toward the Causal Truth” [II.1 ¶49]; it is drawn from a deep well. It is what is beheld when Light meets Light, by those proved and reproved “previous to being admitted to the apperceptive vision of the Causal Truth which they describe” [III.2 ¶28].

See also: Truth

References: II.1 ¶49, III.2 ¶28

Causes

term · Cause

Four causes — essence, matter, origin of motion, and end — which in the Art pass into one another; cause is not mere antecedence in time.

Atwood names four causes: essence (the principle, ‘First Why’); matter or subject; that whence motion begins; and “That for the sake of which the inquiry subsists, and the Good which is the end of regeneration” [IV.2 ¶7]. In the Art the First becomes efficient in the Third and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶7]. She rejects attempts to “reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence or juxtaposition in time” [IV.4 ¶15], citing the testimony of instinct, and says this science “exhibits all things in their constructive Causes” [IV.4 ¶22].

References: IV.2 ¶7, IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶22

Cave of Mercury

term

A place to be entered with prudent motive, from which the mineral radix of the Art is carried away; by Hermetic interpretation, Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life.

Atwood gives the Hermetic interpretation: “the Cave of Mercury, which, according to the Hermetic interpretation, is Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life” [III.1 ¶19]. It is to be entered with a prudent motive, and the mineral radix of the Art is carried away from it [III.1 ¶19].

Identified with: Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life [III.1 ¶19]

See also: Mercury

References: III.1 ¶19

Celestial elements

term

The prior Elements of Life the ancients actually investigated, as opposed to the common elements or abstractions.

Atwood says the ancients investigated not the common elements or abstractions but “the prior Elements of Life; which some, openly distinguishing, call the Celestial Elements” [III.2 ¶36].

Identified with: prior Elements of Life [III.2 ¶36]

See also: Elements

References: III.2 ¶36

Celestial life

term · Celestial

In the Table Talk, the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, representing the Vegetable Kingdom and seated in the epigastric region.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The Celestial is the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, and represents the Vegetable Kingdom.” [APP ¶32]. It resides in the epigastric region, its workshop the solar plexus; it is identified with the medial life, through which the third life must be born [APP ¶32]. Compare celestial medial life.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶32

Celestial light

term

In Boehme, the light in which the Tincture is, containing a substance like water which is no water.

Quoting Boehme, the Tincture is in the Celestial Light: “And there is in the Celestial Light, continues the same author, a Substance like water which yet is no water” [III.2 ¶16].

See also: Light

References: III.2 ¶16

Celestial medial life

term · first medial life

The intermediate life preceding the heroic work, which must be cut off, shut up and buried; until it dissolves the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved.

Atwood speaks of “the celestial medial life which, in the order of divine rites, precedes the heroic work” [III.1 ¶26]. It must be cut off in its prime, shut up and buried; until “this dissolution of the first medial life” [III.1 ¶28] takes place, the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved. Compare Celestial life, which the Table Talk identifies with the medial life [APP ¶32].

See also: Life

References: III.1 ¶26, III.1 ¶28

Celestial Ploughshare

term

Image of the incessant, repeated purifying labour that clears the wasted field of human life.

Atwood’s image for the repeated purifying labour of the work, which serves “to clear the wasted field of human life, and harrow it for a more congenial growth” [IV.1 ¶9].

References: IV.1 ¶9

Celestial prototype

term

In Rabbi Ben Jochai, the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinguished from apparent man.

Atwood says the Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” [II.1 ¶40]. Quoting Rabbi Ben Jochai, it is the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinct from apparent man: “on that form in man, which is the Celestial Prototype” [II.1 ¶42]; “no form, no world, could exist before the human prototype” [II.1 ¶42].

Identified with: that form in man [II.1 ¶42]

References: II.1 ¶40, II.1 ¶42

Celsus

person

A cited figure whose ladder Atwood uses as an image of ascending knowledge and identifies with the magnetic chain.

Atwood invokes “Celsus’ ladder” as an image of ascending knowledge [I.1 ¶64]. Later she identifies the magnetic chain with “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54]. The book gives nothing else about Celsus.

References: I.1 ¶64, III.2 ¶54

Center

term · true center

In the Table Talk, the center of substantial life which every creature seeks, which each person can find in himself at moments.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “the center of the substantial life which every creature is seeking” [APP ¶113]. She holds that “Every one can find in himself at moments the true center” [APP ¶115], apparently through deep thought, and that the same revelation is given to all who enter it [APP ¶115].

See also: Center and circumference, Centers and circumferences

References: APP ¶113, APP ¶115

Center and circumference

term · center, circumference, centers

Atwood’s paired terms for the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, and the circumference, where being’s equilibrium is broken for manifestation.

Atwood sets the universal centre, from which the sensible world is an outbirth, against the circumference, where “the equilibrium of being is broken everywhere at the circumference for manifestation” [II.4 ¶50]. In the illumination she describes, the light spreads outward, “diffusing itself from the freed center outwardly center outwardly until it moved the dark circumference of sense itself” [II.4 ¶54]. The context suggests the work frees the centre so that its light reaches and moves the outer, sensible life. See also centers and circumferences; circulation.

See also: Center, Centers and circumferences, Circumference

References: II.4 ¶50, II.4 ¶54

Centers and circumferences

term · centers, circumferences

Paired terms Atwood uses in warning that the centers must not be stirred before the circumferences can conceive them.

Atwood warns against acting “lest the centers should be stirred up before the circumferences are ready to conceive them” [IV.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the pair further here; compare center / circumference.

See also: Center, Center and circumference, Circumference

References: IV.1 ¶13

Central efficient

term

That with which the Aqua Philosophica, once conjoined in consciousness, becomes all-powerful.

In a footnote Atwood says of the Aqua Philosophica that “being conjoined in consciousness with the central Efficient, it becomes all-powerful” [I.3 n36]. The term is not further defined.

See also: Efficient

References: I.3 n36

Central fire

term

A fire within the will or nature: in the Table Talk, Lucifer’s stirring of it burned up the ether; in Vaughan, it stands opposed to the moist natures.

Two voices use the term. Quoting Vaughan, the text says that when heat is excessive the moist natures “will stand up against the central fire, and the central fire against them” [III.4 ¶44], producing a division in the Chaos. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of Lucifer’s fall as “the stirring up of the central fire in his will” [APP ¶133], which inflamed the vehicle of his life and burned up the ether. Both passages apparently treat the central fire as dangerous when wrongly roused.

See also: Fire

References: III.4 ¶44, APP ¶133

Central force

term

The inner force of the Universal Spirit, which repeated operations draw wholly out until it acts forcibly at the circumference.

Atwood describes repeated operations upon the Universal Spirit continued “until the central force, wholly drawn out, acts forcibly at the circumference” [IV.3 ¶29]. Compare center / circumference.

References: IV.3 ¶29

Central magnet

term

That whose whole voluntary force alone can arrest the imaginative flux of freed vitality and compel it to repose.

Atwood says that to arrest the imaginative flux of the freed vitality “it need the whole voluntary force of the central magnet” [III.2 ¶24], and that “this alone, which is its proper reason, can compel it to repose” [III.2 ¶24]. The central magnet is thus apparently equated with “its proper reason”, though the referent of “its” is unclear from the passage.

Identified with: its proper reason [III.2 ¶24]

See also: Magnet

References: III.2 ¶24

Central Salt of nature

term

In the Moorish philosopher’s words, something man may draw to himself in abundance; not further defined.

Quoting the Moorish philosopher, the text speaks of one “who is able to draw to himself the Central Salt of nature in abundance” [II.1 ¶9]. The term is not explained.

References: II.1 ¶9

Central source

term

The goal towards which consciousness is translated, beneath the sensible medium, by obscuration.

Atwood speaks of the need “to translate the consciousness underneath this medium by obscuration, towards the Central Source” [II.3 ¶5]. The context suggests the Central Source is the inward origin reached by withdrawing consciousness beneath the sensible medium.

References: II.3 ¶5

Chaldaic Oracles

treatise · Oracula Chaldaeorum, Oracula Chaldeor, the Chaldaic oracle

A collection of oracles Atwood cites for Latin verse on the life-bearing fire and, in the Table Talk, for the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested.

Atwood cites the Oracula Chaldeor for Latin verse on “Vitifer Ignis” and a Centre [IV.1 ¶35]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she uses the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the soul as the place where the law of Light is manifested: “There is room for the image also in the circumlucid place. Every way to the unfashioned soul stretch the reins of fire” [APP ¶96]. Elsewhere in the Table Talk they are only referred to for comparison on the solution (‘Article Hecate, etc.’) [APP ¶50]. See also the Chaldaic oracle.

Chaldaic oracle. Atwood cites the Chaldaic oracle often, always in support:

  • That there are pure demons and that the products of evil matter are useful: “Natura suadet esse demonas puros, et malae materiae germina utilia et bona” [II.3 ¶24] (our translation: nature persuades that there are pure demons, and that the germs of evil matter are useful and good).
  • That the practitioner should not heed apparitions: “he apply not his mind to it, nor esteem the voice proceeding thence to be true” [II.3 ¶20].
  • On the guide and the promised light: “the mortal, approaching the fire, will have a light from divinity” [II.3 n37].
  • In what she calls ‘operative language’, on fire, the intellectual pattern and the Presters of Intellectual Fire: “O how the world hath Intellectual guides inflexible!” [II.4 ¶31].
  • As pursuing the same Art of Reason she describes (Monad, Duad, Triad, the Matrix and the Prester of Fire): “For the mind of the Father said that all things be cut into Three” [IV.2 ¶21].

See also Chaldaic Oracles.

See also: Oracles

References: II.3 n15, II.3 n25, II.3 n37, II.3 ¶20, II.3 ¶24, II.4 n24, II.4 ¶31, II.4 ¶32, II.4 ¶33, II.4 ¶34, II.4 ¶35, IV.1 n27, IV.1 ¶35, IV.2 n18, IV.2 ¶21, IV.2 ¶22, IV.2 ¶23, IV.2 ¶29, APP ¶50, APP ¶96

Chalybs

term · Chalybes

A quoted term glossed as ‘steel’: the means of extracting ‘our sea water’ and, in Cosmopolite, the partner that conceives with gold.

Quoted voices only. In the passage citing Synesius and the New Light, the text speaks of “our chalybs, or steel” [I.2 ¶33], the means by which ‘our sea water’ is extracted; it is otherwise unexplained. In Cosmopolite (quoted via Eudoxus), after gold couples with ‘it’, “the Chalybes conceives and begets a son more glorious than the Father” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not say what the chalybs plainly is, beyond the gloss ‘steel’.

Identified with: Steel [I.2 ¶33]

References: I.2 ¶33, IV.3 ¶10

Chamelion

term

In Eirenaeus, the product of the Dragon–Lodestone conjunction and purgations: ‘our Chaos’, containing all the Arcana in virtue, not yet in act.

Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus), the text says that after the conjunction of the Dragon and the Lodestone and the purgations, “Hence comes the Chamelion which is our Chaos, in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43]. So the Chamelion is identified with Chaos [IV.1 ¶43].

Identified with: Chaos [IV.1 ¶43]

References: IV.1 ¶43

Chaos

term

The primeval thing, named by several voices; in Atwood it holds the two Principles, which may be dissevered if the internal agent wakes too soon and are to be united to a new Life.

Several voices use the term:

  • Khunrath (quoted): when the process is done rightly, “the new Chaos of the Universal Nature” appears unfolded and separated [III.3 ¶9].
  • Ovid (quoted): “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” [III.3 ¶45] (our translation: the ancients called me Chaos, for I am a thing of old). In the same paragraph the metropolitan of Memphis gives an account in which the ‘primeval parent’, moved by the breath of Erebus, brought forth Hyle and Eros.
  • Vaughan (quoted): when moist natures and central fire are set against each other, “there will be a terrible division in the Chaos” [III.4 ¶44].
  • Atwood: if the internal agent wakes too soon there may be “a disseveration in the Chaos, and the two Principles stand up one against the other” [IV.1 ¶15].
  • Uncertain voice: “Learn to unite the Principles of our Chaos to a new Life” [IV.2 ¶18], to be regenerated by Water and the Spirit.

The records differ: Khunrath speaks of the Chaos appearing unfolded and separated in the right process, while Vaughan and Atwood warn of a premature division of its Principles. Eirenaeus identifies the Chamelion with ‘our Chaos’ [IV.1 ¶43].

References: III.3 ¶45, III.3 ¶9, III.4 ¶44, IV.1 ¶15, IV.2 ¶18

Charity

term · charitable

In Vaughan, the nurse of Faith: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.

Quoting Vaughan, the text says “as God is the Father, so Charity is the nurse of Faith” [III.4 ¶44]: charitable works yield hope of heaven, and hope leads to belief.

References: III.4 ¶44

Charlotte Bronte

person

Mentioned in the Table Talk as being Jupiter and Lune, and as one who ought to have reworked her sister’s book.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Charlotte Bronte is said to be Jupiter and Lune and to have ought to rework her sister’s book [APP ¶175].

References: APP ¶175

Charnocke

person

Author of the Breviary of Philosophy, whom Atwood cites on the nested vessels, instructing the potter, and the value of a faithful servant.

Atwood cites Charnocke’s Breviary of Philosophy in illustration. From chap. 1, on the nested vessels and the need to instruct the potter: “One within another, it is a pretty feate, The Third without them to guide up the heate” [III.4 ¶33]. From chap. 3 (‘Idem’), on the trouble with indifferent assistants and the worth of a faithful servant [III.4 ¶34–35].

References: III.4 n29, III.4 n30, III.4 ¶33, III.4 ¶34, III.4 ¶35

Chaucer

person

Cited for the tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman, which Atwood uses to illustrate the boastings and beliefs of ignorance.

Atwood cites Chaucer’s tale of the Chanon’s Yeoman as illustrating the boastings and beliefs of ignorance about the art [I.1 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶64, I.3 n17

Cheiron

collective voice — Latin verse, unattributed

Unattributed Latin verse on Cheiron, teacher of Achilles, whom Atwood reads as Power and Motive in alliance educating the Heroic Fire.

Atwood quotes unattributed Latin verse: “Ille pius Cheiron justissimus omnes Inter Nubigenas et Magni Doctor Achillis.” [IV.1 ¶32] (our translation: that pious Cheiron, most just among all the Cloud-born, and teacher of great Achilles). She identifies Cheiron as Power and Motive in alliance, educating the Heroic Fire [IV.1 ¶33]; this reading is hers.

References: IV.1 ¶32, IV.1 ¶33

Chemia

term · Chemeia, Chimia, Chemiae

An old name of Egypt (Cham), from the blackness of its soil according to Plutarch; also a name for the art, which the adept calls too narrow.

Reporting Plutarch, the text calls Egypt the art’s “mother land, Cham; for so, during a long period, according to Plutarch, was Egypt denominated, or Chemia” [I.1 ¶5], named from the blackness of her soil. Thus Chemia = Egypt = Cham [I.1 ¶5]. Further, “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated, and other black matters” [I.1 ¶5]. Others derive both name and art from Cham [I.1 ¶5]. A footnote cites Suidas: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” [I.1 n8] (our translation: Chimia is the making of gold and silver). Quoting an adept, the text rejects those “who pin also the narrow name of Chemia on a science ancient and infinite” [I.2 ¶8].

Identified with: Egypt [I.1 ¶5]; Cham [I.1 ¶5]

References: I.1 n8, I.1 ¶5, I.2 ¶8

Chemistry

term · chemical, chemists

Atwood’s word for the art in its historical record: chemical books burned, the chemists’ divine water, Roman knowledge shown by the lamps.

Atwood uses ‘chemical’ and ‘chemists’ of the art itself in her historical survey: books teaching how to make gold and silver were condemned, so that “every chemical book was to be seized and burned together in the public market-place” [I.1 ¶18]; she mentions “a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20] and Roman knowledge of the art shown by the lamps [I.1 ¶20].

References: I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶20

Chimaeras

term

In the Table Talk, fantastic forms the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it; all must be destroyed.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes fantastic forms that the imaginative spirit makes in the ether when the seeking light enters it, and says “These Chimaeras have all to be destroyed” [APP ¶171]. The context suggests these are illusory images to be cleared away in the inward work.

References: APP ¶171

Chloric ether

term

A murky enveloping medium through whose circumference the intellect penetrates to reach the lapsed soul; not further explained.

Atwood speaks of the intellect penetrating “the murky circumference of the chloric ether” [II.3 ¶11] to reach the lapsed soul. The term is not further explained.

See also: Ether

References: II.3 ¶11

Chronicle

collective voice

An unnamed chronicle Atwood cites for the lasting visibility in Paris, as late as 1740, of Flamel’s charities and symbols of the art.

Atwood cites a chronicle in support of the lasting evidence of Flamel in Paris as late as 1740: “the evidence of his charitable deeds remained and the symbols of the art” [I.1 ¶58].

References: I.1 ¶58

Chronicon Magnum Belgicum

treatise

A chronicle Atwood cites for its praise of Albert at his death.

Atwood cites the Chronicon Magnum Belgicum for its praise of Albert at his death: “magnus in magia, major in philosophia, maximus in theologia” [I.1 ¶41] (our translation: great in magic, greater in philosophy, greatest in theology).

References: I.1 n48, I.1 ¶41

Chrysopaea

treatise

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n38

Cicero

person

Cited from De Nat. Deor. on the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things, and from De Legibus on the Initia as a beginning of a life of reason.

Atwood cites Cicero, De Nat. Deor., lib. ii, in support of the ether as an igneous nature begetting all things: “coelestis alstissima aethereaque natura” [I.2 ¶16] (our translation: the celestial, highest and ethereal nature). She also cites De Legibus, lib. 2, cap. 14, in support of the Initia as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue and of the hope of immortality [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n6]. She uses him with approval.

References: I.2 n15, I.2 ¶16, II.2 n6, II.2 ¶4

Circulation

term · circulations, ultimate circulation, rotary circulation

The movement of being and, in the work, the rising and falling of the life-principles between heaven and earth by which they are rectified and exalted; the Stone is completed in three.

Atwood uses circulation in two related senses. Of being as a whole: “And all things in that ultimate circulation are diaphanous” [II.4 ¶50], whereas “But in the sensible world the circulation of things is altogether different” [II.4 ¶50], since there it is broken at the circumference (compare center / circumference). The Vital Spirit ascends and descends in ‘successive circulations’ [II.4 ¶50].

In the practical work, circulation is the upward and downward movement of the life-principles between heaven and earth, which rectifies and exalts them: the operator proceeds “by carrying the circulation upward through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20]; the matter is “Thus exalted by a rotary circulation” [IV.2 ¶32]; and the Stone is “completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33].

See also: Three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)

References: II.4 ¶50, IV.2 ¶20, IV.2 ¶32, IV.2 ¶33

Circulatory confine

term

What encloses the hidden Reason; it must undergo resolution before the Reason can awaken.

Atwood says the hidden Reason cannot awaken “without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. The term is not further defined.

References: II.4 ¶39

Circulatory medium

term

The medium by which the hypostatic unit is multiplied throughout life; not further defined.

Atwood says the hypostatic unit is multiplied “by the circulatory medium throughout life” [IV.2 ¶37]. The term is not further defined.

See also: Medium

References: IV.2 ¶37

Circumference

term

Nature’s outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, as opposed to the root.

Atwood uses circumference for nature’s outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, in contrast to the root: “For nature at the circumference subsists in this way” [III.4 ¶8].

See also: Center and circumference, Centers and circumferences

References: III.4 ¶8

Circumferential life

term · circumferential manifestations

The outward life of the spirit, terrified at first by the new light and contrasted with its ‘central whole’.

In Atwood’s notes, the circumferential life is the outward life of the spirit. The new light at first “causes a terrification of the whole circumferential life” [I.3 n69]. It is set against a central whole, into which the spirit is spoken of as “converting her circumferential manifestations into their central whole conditionedly” [I.3 n65]. The context suggests the outward manifestations are to be drawn back into the centre.

See also: Life

References: I.3 n65, I.3 n69

Citrine

term

In a passage quoted from Hermes, a stage or substance extracted out of the Red, from which Botri is made.

In the passage quoted from Hermes, Citrine is extracted out of the Red, and Botri is made from it: “if it be citrine and nothing else know it will be thy Wisdom” [I.3 ¶41]. The text does not explain it further.

References: I.3 ¶41

Citrine Mercury

term

According to Flammel, as reported through Eudoxus, the Mercury used for the Imbibition of the Red.

Eudoxus reports Flammel as saying that “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not explain it further.

See also: Mercury

References: IV.3 ¶10

Clairvoyant life

term

In the Appendix, the intermediate state through which present life is led into the third life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood describes the clairvoyant life as the intermediate state through which present life passes into the third life: “this present life may be led through the clairvoyant life into it” [APP ¶2]. Compare common trance, in which the third life is not known.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶2

Clarified hypostasis

term · hypostasis

Atwood’s term for the purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light.

Atwood speaks of a purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light: “this clarified hypostasis (shall we not believe in it?), is the stage of all Forms” [III.2 ¶26]. Elsewhere in the same chapter she uses hypostasis for the ground that bounds abstract reason; met by the inner light, that ground is the Absolute Identity [III.2 ¶31]. The text does not say that these two uses name the same thing, so both readings are open.

See also: Hypostasis

References: III.2 ¶26

Claudian

person

Author of De Raptu Prosepinae, which Atwood quotes to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis.

Atwood quotes Claudian’s work (spelled de Paptu Proserpineae / De Raptu Prosepinae in the text) to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis: “Jam furor humanus nostro de pectore sensus Expluit” [II.3 ¶15; II.3 ¶19; II.3 n11; II.3 n14]. She uses him as supporting illustration.

References: II.3 n11, II.3 n14, II.3 ¶15, II.3 ¶19

Clemens Alexandrinus

person · the Bishop of Alexandria

Writer Atwood cites for the books of Hermes and as a witness that the Mysteries were sacred and continued in Christianity.

Atwood cites Clemens Alexandrinus as naming in detail the books attributed to Hermes [I.1 ¶7]. She uses him in support of her view of the Mysteries. He called them blessed: “O mysteries truly sacred, O pure light!” He also describes the Greater Mysteries as unveiling nature, with the Lord as hierophant [II.2 ¶3; II.2 ¶5; II.2 n9]. In Part IV, “the Bishop of Alexandria” is cited, with a footnote naming Clemens Alexandrinus, for the view that the Mysteries continued in Christianity, the Lord illuminating the Adepts: “It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.” [IV.2 ¶16; IV.2 n12]. The link to the footnote depends on reading the marker (2) as n12.

References: I.1 ¶7, II.2 n9, II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶5, IV.2 n12, IV.2 ¶16

Cleopatra

person

Cited to illustrate the art’s revival in Egypt, through her earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to her.

Atwood mentions Cleopatra when describing the art’s revival in Egypt. She cites the earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to Cleopatra, including Ars auri faciendi [I.1 ¶18; I.1 n25].

References: I.1 n25, I.1 ¶18

Clerke

term · Clearke

In the poem The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the learned person who will find truth in the work, as against the ‘lay’.

In the quoted poem The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the Clerke is the learned person who will find truth in the work: “For surely if thow be a Clerke, Thow wilt finde trewth in thys werke:” [III.1 ¶65]. The lay are told to keep counsel and leave off. The narrator says he is “noe Clerke” in science, yet he has laboured in the work.

References: III.1 ¶65

Clue of life

term

Something the depraved ‘entangled’ and climbed by into self-sufficiency; not explained in the text.

Atwood says the depraved climbed into self-sufficiency “basely entangling the clue of life” [III.4 ¶4]. The text does not explain the expression further.

See also: Life

References: III.4 ¶4

Co-nascent spirit

term

A spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose on seeing the Divine Nature; the vision in Hades is allied to it.

Atwood describes a spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose when they see the Divine Nature: “For to this spirit the vision in Hades is allied” [II.4 ¶19].

See also: Spirit

References: II.4 ¶19

Coacervation

term

The error of treating the Identity of Being as heaped up or compounded instead of uncompounded.

Atwood warns that “the Identity of every Being is something uncompounded, and that the mind should not fall into the error of coacervation” [III.2 ¶52]. Coacervation is thus the error of treating that Identity as heaped up or compounded. Compare compounded.

References: III.2 ¶52

Coagulation

term · coagulated

Fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution; Albertus says the cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur.

In the passage quoted from Albertus, coagulation is fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution: “a successive dissolution and coagulation to make the fixed volatile, and volatile fixed” [IV.1 ¶4]. The cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur. Synesius lists coagulate among the names of the one operation of coction (see coction).

References: IV.1 ¶4

Coal

term · extinct coal, live coal

In a passage from Hermes, a coal whose life is fire; extinct, it becomes a dead body and is returned to the water for thirty days.

In the passage quoted from Hermes: “The life of the coal is fire, which being extinct, becomes a dead body” [I.3 n22]. The extinct coal is returned to the water for thirty days. The text gives no plain meaning.

References: I.3 n22

Coction

term · decoction, decoct, decocted, decoctio

The cooking or maturing of the matter; Synesius says all the named operations are only names for this single operation.

Coction is the cooking, digesting or maturing of the matter.

  • Atwood speaks of the elixir obtained “through superior skill and coction in the vegetal life” [I.2 ¶46].
  • Basil Valentine calls it the boiling and maturing of the stone of Fire with the corporeal fire of the microcosm: “let no man wonder at this coction” [III.1 ¶37].
  • During the severation, Atwood writes, “a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. The waters decoct the sensual dominant, and the dragons are decocted in their own venom.
  • Synesius describes a gentle, gradual and long cooking, “the coction of this water”. He treats it as the single operation: dissolve, calcine, tinge, whiten, renew, bathe, wash, coagulate, imbibe, fix, grind, dry and distill “are all one, and signify no more than to decoct nature until such time as she be perfected” [III.3 ¶60].
  • Decoction, Atwood reports, is what Hermes calls the first part of the work: “the former Hermes calls decoction, which dissolving the matter discharges also its impurities by a proper rule” [I.3 n7]. It reduces the matter until it is close to annihilation and free of every outward form.
  • Zachary treats the cooking as continuing until it is complete: “donec decoctio compleatur” (ours: until the decoction is completed) [IV.1 ¶9].

Identified with: dissolve, calcine, tinge, whiten, renew, bathe, wash, coagulate, imbibe, fix, grind, dry, distill [III.3 ¶60]

References: I.2 ¶46, I.3 n7, III.1 ¶37, III.1 ¶53, III.3 ¶60, IV.1 ¶9

Coelum Terrae

treatise

Cited for reference only.

References: III.4 n35

Colcothar

term

In a passage from Hermes, named as one of several substances that are also sulphur.

In the passage quoted from Hermes, colcothar is named as a kind of sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20].

Identified with: Sulphur [I.3 ¶20]

References: I.3 ¶20

Collective

term

In Iamblicus, the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations and pertaining to Illumination.

Iamblicus, as quoted, calls the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations, Collective. It pertains to Illumination and “was called Collective, having for its object to gather the mental powers into accord with their leader” [III.4 ¶24]. Compare Communion of Operation, the second class.

References: III.4 ¶24

Colour

term · colours, colors, coloring

The stages of colour the work passes through; in Hermes’ division of the Water, colour is a third part, a coagulating moisture.

The colours are the stages the work must pass through. In Hermes’ division of the Water, colour is one third part: “the one third part of which is colour, that is to say — a coagulating moisture” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast says Hermes divides the colours “into three red spirits and three white, which have their growth all from the same identical water” [I.3 n5].

Identified with: a coagulating moisture [I.3 ¶6]

References: I.3 n5, I.3 ¶6

Commixtion

term

In Norton’s Ordinal, a mixing-in of something, to be avoided.

Norton’s Ordinal warns: “Beware of Commixtion that nothing miscape.” [IV.1 ¶28]. Commixtion is a mixing-in of something that must be avoided.

References: IV.1 ¶28

Common soul

term

For Atwood, the agent at work in present-day mesmerism and also the Alchemists’ subject-matter: indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will.

Atwood identifies the Common Soul with “the identical agent which is spread abroad in the present day mesmerizing, the photogenic medium, our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul”. She says it is “also the subject-matter of the Alchemists aforesaid” [II.2 ¶18]. It is indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will: “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” [II.2 ¶18]. This is a central identity for her method: the mesmeric agent and the alchemical matter are one.

Identified with: the agent of present-day mesmerizing / photogenic medium / New Imponderable [II.2 ¶18]; subject-matter of the Alchemists [II.2 ¶18]

See also: Soul

References: II.2 ¶18

Common trance

term · common entranced life, entranced

In the Appendix, the entranced life of sleep-walkers, produced by fermenting present life by its similar; the third life is not known in it.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says that fermenting present life by its similar “leads into the common trance, or is entranced” [APP ¶3]. She equates the common trance with “the common entranced life, i.e., the life of the sleep-walkers” [APP ¶2]. The third life is not known in it. Compare clairvoyant life.

Identified with: life of the sleep-walkers [APP ¶2]

See also: Trance

References: APP ¶2, APP ¶3

Communion

term

The connection the work requires; it is disturbed by air currents, and communion with superiors needs a heavenly way of life.

Atwood says that “Strong currents of air are well known to disturb communion” [III.4 ¶42]. She also warns that a heavenly way of life is needed, “otherwise thou canst have no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

References: III.4 ¶42, III.4 ¶44

Communion of operation

term

In Iamblicus, what the second class of prayer pertains to; it effects the bonds of concordant spirits.

Iamblicus, as quoted, says that the second class of prayer pertains to a Communion of Operation: “the second, to a Communion of Operation” [III.4 ¶24]. This class effects the bonds of concordant spirits before intellectual alliance. Compare Collective.

References: III.4 ¶24

Complexions

term

In Vaughan, what is to be sought where extremes meet; not further defined.

Vaughan, as quoted, advises: “where extremes meet, there look for complexions” [III.4 ¶44]. The text does not define the term further.

References: III.4 ¶44

Compound of art

term

In Eudoxus, the compound the Wise man makes by secret union of the fixed with the volatile; Geber’s mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur.

Eudoxus says of the compound of Art: “it is the Wise man who makes it by the secret union of the fixed with the volatile” [IV.3 ¶9]. It is always made by the Artist and is not altogether the same in the Second and Third Work. He adds: “Geber defines it, a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9]. Compare compound of Nature.

Identified with: mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur (per Geber) [IV.3 ¶9]

References: IV.3 ¶9

Compound of nature

term

In Eudoxus, the compound treated in the First Key, made by Nature in ways the Artist cannot understand; he only aids her by external things.

Eudoxus says: “The first is the compound of Nature, whereof I have spoken in the First Key” [IV.3 ¶9]. Nature makes it in a way the Artist cannot understand, and he only aids her by external things. Compare compound of Art.

References: IV.3 ¶9

Compound simple

term

Atwood’s term for the art’s matter: one essence containing everything yet separated in each particular, the ground of the magians’ elements.

Atwood calls the art’s matter “the compound simple of this art”. The hen’s egg corresponds to it, except in catholicity [I.3 n26]. In Part II she describes it as “an essence all comprehending, yet separated in each particular, by so great an interval from itself” [II.2 ¶19]. She identifies it with the Monster and the Eternal Riddle: “This is the Monster and the Eternal Riddle explained to common sense as suits it, but misunderstood to this day; that Compound Simple”. She also calls it the ground of the elements: “that Compound Simple and ground of the magians’ elements” [II.2 ¶19].

Identified with: the Monster / the Eternal Riddle [II.2 ¶19]; ground of the magians’ elements [II.2 ¶19]

References: I.3 n26, II.2 ¶19

Compounded

term · compound creature

Whatever is mixed or impure; it cannot approach the divine Fire, which destroys and separates it.

In a passage drawing on Sendivogius, compounded means whatever is mixed or impure: “nothing that is filthy or compounded, or blemished may come near Him” [II.4 ¶39]. The divine Fire destroys and separates what is compounded. It is unclear whether this view is Atwood’s own or reported from Sendivogius; the records tag both voices. Compare coacervation.

References: II.4 ¶39

Concauses

term

In Iamblichus, contributing causes: the soul’s best dispositions and purity, which accompany the work without being its principal cause.

Iamblichus, as quoted, names “all the best dispositions of the soul, and also the purity pertaining, as certain concauses” [II.4 ¶31]. They are contributing causes that accompany the work without being its principal cause.

References: II.4 ¶31

Concentration

term

Degrees of concentration through which, Atwood says, the agent is promoted and fortified; she does not explain them further.

Atwood speaks of the agent being fortified “when promoted through a second to a third of concentration” [III.4 ¶9]. The text names these degrees but does not explain what each involves.

References: III.4 ¶9

Conceptive medium

term

The receiving medium through which universal principles are conceived; Atwood says nature lacks a true one, and that truth depends on its purity.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “There is no such thing as truth absolute in nature, because she has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]. The receiving medium must be pure and simple if truth is to be conceived: “Thus everything depends on the purity of the receiving power.” [APP ¶43]. See also conceptive vehicle.

See also: Medium

References: APP ¶43

Conceptive vehicle

term

The vehicle of conception; Atwood blames the ancients’ obscure teaching about it for great error, and says the soul may dissolve its own, the parental bond.

Atwood says that “the obscure instructions of the ancients concerning the nature of their conceptive vehicle, has caused incalculable error and confusion” [II.1 ¶8]; she does not define it further there. Elsewhere she treats it as the soul’s vehicle from conception, which the soul may dissolve, and identifies it with the parental bond: “she may dissolve her own conceptive vehicle, even the parental bond” [II.3 ¶37]. In the Appendix (a later layer) she says nature “has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]; see conceptive medium.

Identified with: parental bond [II.3 ¶37]

See also: Vehicle

References: II.1 ¶8, II.3 ¶37

Concord

term · Concordaunce

In Norton’s verses, an agreement or fit between the art and its requisites, numbered as successive Concords (ministers, places, instrument).

The term comes chiefly from Norton, quoted by Atwood. He numbers the Concords: “The Second Concord with this Arte is,” [III.4 ¶36] (concerning apt ministers), and “The Fourth Concord is full notable Between this arte and places convenable” [III.4 ¶41]. He also speaks of the fit of the art with its instrument: “Without full concord of arte with hys instrument” [III.4 ¶39]. Atwood herself uses ‘concord’ for the joining of prayer, self-sacrifice and the faculties of the mind [III.4 ¶28].

References: III.4 ¶36, III.4 ¶39, III.4 ¶41

Condillac

person

Cited once, critically: Atwood rejects his sensual system, together with Locke’s.

Atwood names Condillac only to criticize his sensual system, along with Locke’s [II.1 ¶34].

References: II.1 ¶34

Conditionate

term

What man can do in the work: prepare the conditions by patient, disciplined labour, without being able to compel the Divine blessing.

Atwood: “Man may conditionate: — ought, by patient labour disciplining, to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20]. The context sets this human preparation against the Divine blessing, which man cannot compel. See conditionating.

References: III.4 ¶20

Conditionating

term

Placing oneself under conditions in obedience to the Divine Will, as opposed to searching in one’s own will alone.

Atwood contrasts searching in one’s own will alone with proceeding “by conditionating, in obedience to the Divine Will” [IV.4 ¶23]. See conditionate.

References: IV.4 ¶23

Confection

term

The mixture or compound of the work; Hermes says the ferment whitens it, and Atwood warns that a premature permanent confection yields an offspring that does not abide.

Hermes, quoted by Atwood, says “the ferment whitens the confection” [I.3 ¶58], and protects it from combustion. Atwood uses the word for a permanent fixing that must not come too early: “if any permanent confection is made or suffered to take place beforehand, the immature offspring does not abide” [IV.1 ¶48].

References: I.3 ¶58, IV.1 ¶48

Congenial sight

term

A fitting faculty of sight without which, Atwood says, the research cannot be carried on; she does not define it.

Atwood says of the research: “nor can it be prosecuted without a congenial Sight” [IV.4 ¶32]. The text gives no further definition.

References: IV.4 ¶32

Conjunction

term · conjunctions, Conjonction

The union of the principles in the work, in stages, consummated in a final indissoluble Conjunction that generates a more perfect offspring; Atwood equates it with the circulated Form of Gold.

In Atwood’s account, conjunction is the union of the principles (in III.3, of Mars and Venus [III.3 ¶11]), during which a spirituous vapour rises; “in the various hours of conjunction” come Darkness, Saturn and the Head of the Crow [III.3 ¶13].

She distinguishes stages: “In the first conjunction the Spirit predominates; in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light” [III.3 ¶30]. The final Conjunction cannot be dissolved and produces an offspring unlike and more perfect than its parents: “that Conjunction will generate a branch of unlike shape to its parents” [III.3 ¶29].

She gives it several names: “This then is the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation — the true circulated Form of Gold” [III.3 ¶33]; and “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In III.4 the agent goes on “further multiplying in the Conjunction” [III.4 ¶9], and Norton, quoted there, speaks of unions man may not undo without grace: “For God’s conjunctions man my not undoe” [III.4 ¶10]. Atwood also describes a stage at which the work passes beyond human control: “There is a period too, when in conjunction, the Spirit transcends all earthly control” [III.4 ¶20], recreating under the Divine Hand alone.

Identified with: true circulated Form of Gold [III.3 ¶33]; tetraptive (Ripley); fountain of Pythagoras; Divine Tetractys [III.3 ¶33]

References: III.3 ¶13, III.3 ¶29, III.3 ¶30, III.3 ¶33, III.4 ¶10, III.4 ¶20, III.4 ¶9

Connate spirit

term

The inborn spirit of the soul, whose attractive grace subdues the self-willed agent; Julian says the deified soul strengthens it, making it the safety of the whole body.

Atwood says the self-willed agent is subdued and brought to self-mortification because “it is by the attractive grace of the connate spirit” [III.1 ¶63]; the following ‘This Spirit’, which has self-motion and intelligence, very probably refers to the connate spirit (an inference from context).

Julian, quoted by Atwood, says of the deified soul that “she transfuses a certain vigorous strength into her connate spirit” [IV.3 ¶30], which then becomes the cause of safety to the whole body.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes what happens “when the connate spirit is deprived of its understanding spirit” [APP ¶109]: its life flows away until it rallies from a new center by self-realization.

See also: Spirit

References: III.1 ¶63, IV.3 ¶30, APP ¶109

Conscience

term

The inner faculty that, through persevering inward search, reveals higher objects of pursuit.

Atwood urges inward search “until Conscience reveal to us those higher objects of pursuit, and truer attractions” [IV.3 ¶50]. See also contrition, where she places the manifestation of Light in the distress of the sensible nature in the conscience [III.3 ¶24].

References: IV.3 ¶50

Conscious Intuition

term

The mode of knowing by which, Atwood says, Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation, as opposed to teaching or inference.

Atwood says Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation “not by outward teaching or rational inference from effects, but by the Conscious Intuition” [III.3 ¶49].

See also: Intuition

References: III.3 ¶49

Constellation

term

In Norton’s verses, the celestial influence to which the Stone’s elements are most obedient during its generation.

Norton, quoted by Atwood, says the elements of the Stone during generation “Have most obedience to constellation” [IV.2 ¶34].

References: IV.2 ¶34

Consubstantial

term

Sharing one substance: Atwood says all things, however various, are consubstantial in their Cause.

Atwood: “all things, however various in manifestation, are consubstantial in their Cause” [III.2 ¶35].

References: III.2 ¶35

Consuming fire

term

The burning, wrathful state of the Prester below, which it ceases to be when placed in the supreme Ether.

Atwood describes the Prester placed in the supreme Ether as “not burning as below, or wrathful; but vital, calm, transmuting, recreating, and no longer a Consuming Fire” [II.3 ¶56]. ‘Consuming Fire’ thus names its lower, destructive state.

See also: Fire

References: II.3 ¶56

Continental life

term

The containing life which must be preserved when the spirit’s external forms are dissolved.

In a footnote Atwood describes the task as being “to dissolve without destroying the continental life” [I.3 n62]: the spirit’s external forms are to be dissolved while the containing life is kept.

See also: Life

References: I.3 n62

Contrition

term · contritions

The distress of the sensible nature in the conscience, the great darkness in which Light appears; in the Appendix, repeated contritions absorb the sensuous medium.

Atwood says “the Light is made manifest in great darkness, viz., in the contrition or distress of the sensible nature in the conscience” [III.3 ¶24], so identifying contrition with that great darkness. The flinty conscience “feels no contrition, but by the fiery well-tempered steel” [III.3 ¶11]. The word is also applied to the fretting of particles in fermentation.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), contrition is stirred in the surrounding spirit by the growing Light of the Salt, and “reiterative contritions absorbing the sensuous medium” [APP ¶78] change the circulation of the blood.

Identified with: great darkness [III.3 ¶24]

References: III.3 ¶11, III.3 ¶24, APP ¶78

Conversion

term

In Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, the purified soul’s turning to associate with its generator: the only way to scientific knowledge of true Being.

Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, describes the purified soul’s turning toward its generator as the only route to scientific knowledge of true Being, “which cannot be obtained either otherwise or without such a conversion” [II.3 ¶43].

References: II.3 ¶43

Conversion of the elements

term · Converte elementa, Convert the elements

The reversal of natures, making light things heavy and active passive and the reverse; Atwood calls by this name all diversity proceeding from and returning to the One.

Arnold, quoted by Atwood, tells the seeker to “understand the conversion of the elements, to make light things heavy, and to make spirits no spirits” [I.2 ¶22], and says that “our operation is nothing else than a mutation of natures” [I.2 ¶25], reducing them to their first root.

Atwood gives her own account: “a conversion of the elements in this respect is just to make active passive and passive active” [III.3 ¶29], the occult manifest and the manifest occult. She widens the term to the whole cycle: “all diversities of things are seen to proceed from and return to this only One; which is called a conversion of the elements” [III.3 ¶29].

Identified with: mutation of natures [I.2 ¶25]; procession from and return to the One [III.3 ¶29]

See also: Elements

References: I.2 ¶22, I.2 ¶25, III.3 ¶29

Cooperation

term

In Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, the mental labour that accompanies prayer, so that prayer is not a tempting of God.

Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, defines it: “when you incline your mind to this or that, variously discussing and meditating many things, this is cooperation” [III.4 ¶22]. This labour must go with prayer, so that prayer is not ‘a tempting of God’.

Identified with: variously discussing and meditating many things [III.4 ¶22]

References: III.4 ¶22

Corner Stone

term · Chief Corner Stone, perfected Corner Stone, ethereal corner stone, rejected Corner Stone

The imperishable quintessential virtue of the New Life and first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art, rejected by ignorance and known only to those who have it in themselves.

Atwood identifies the Corner Stone with the foundation and fruit of the work: it “is the Corner Stone or first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶66]; “the New Life thence arises whose quintessential virtue, imperishable and perpetually victorious, is the Corner Stone” [III.1 ¶66]. It is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise, because they alone can know it who have it in themselves” [III.1 ¶66].

It is brought to light by the work in a proper vessel; without this “the ethereal corner stone would never have been brought to light” [II.1 ¶8], and it is raised within the ‘living temple’: “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8]. Atwood calls for “faith to resuscitate the Corner Stone, which ignorance has rejected from immemorial time” [IV.3 ¶37].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), she says “Everything is in the perfected Corner Stone” [APP ¶134], the state in which the whole regenerate life-force is brought up into head-consciousness, and treats the Hermetic Stone as the analogue of the Chief Corner Stone.

Identified with: first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art [III.1 ¶66]; quintessential virtue of the New Life [III.1 ¶66]

See also: Stone

References: II.1 ¶8, III.1 ¶66, IV.3 ¶37, APP ¶134

Corporeal

term

The sensual principle, predominant in the mundane conception, which hides the divine original from consciousness.

Atwood glosses the word herself: “by the corporeal, i.e., the sensual principle which is predominant in the mundane conception” [III.3 ¶52]. In the passage this principle obscures the divine original from consciousness.

Identified with: sensual principle [III.3 ¶52]

References: III.3 ¶52

Corpus solutum

term

The dissolved body, which a Latin sentence in the text calls a perennial water congealing Mercury.

The text gives the Latin “Corpus solutum est aqua perennis congelans Mercurium perpetua congelatione.” [III.3 ¶21], with no translation in the book and no clear speaker. Our rendering: ‘The dissolved body is a perennial water, congealing Mercury with a perpetual congelation.’ The identity of the dissolved body with perennial water rests on this translation, which is ours.

Identified with: aqua perennis (perennial water) [III.3 ¶21]

References: III.3 ¶21

Correspondence

term

A term Atwood borrows from the Swedenborgians for the relation of the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood relates the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit, and adds: “There is, as the Swedenborgians would say, a correspondence between them.” [APP ¶15].

References: APP ¶15

Corrosives

term

In Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, the agents wrongly credited with the single combat of dissolution; the real agent is a specific loosening virtue.

Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, rejects reliance on Corrosives acting through ‘Second qualities’: “They err, therefore, who ascribe this single combat only to Corrosives” [IV.1 ¶39]. The true agent, he says, is a specific virtue of loosening.

References: IV.1 ¶39

Corruption

term · corruptible

Dissolution, which belongs only to composites; in a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses, artificial corruption especially manifests the underlying subject.

In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses: “This therefore Corruption manifests (especially the artificial), for corruption is of that which is composite” [III.2 ¶48]. Corruption, then, is dissolution of what is composite, and the artificial kind reveals the subject beneath.

References: III.2 ¶48

Coruscation

term · coruscant

The sudden flashing of the released light; Atwood calls the life at the center of the lower life, Apollo, coruscant.

Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood calls the flashing center of the lower life Apollo: “Apollo is that life, and it is coruscant” [APP ¶49]; setting it free produces harmony. Of the released light she says “it shines forth with a sudden coruscation feeding on the surrounding ether” [APP ¶126].

References: APP ¶126, APP ¶49

Cosmopolite

person

An authority Atwood cites with approval on reconciling fire and water and, through his allegory of the old man, on purifying the Mercury.

Atwood cites Cosmopolite in support on reconciling fire and water: “All things must therefore being purged make Fire and Water to be Friends, which they will easily do in their earth, which had ascended with them.” [IV.3 ¶7]. She also uses his ‘ingenious allegory’ of the old man (Mercury) on purifying the Mercury and the whole magistery: “if you shall give our old man gold and silver to swallow, that he may consume them, and at length he also dying may be burnt” [IV.3 ¶10]. She draws on his naming of the Mercury as water, steel and lodestone, on gold coupling eleven times, and on the Chalybes. She offers all of this as confirmation of the secret of the two mercuries [IV.3 ¶10].

References: IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶7

Creative essence

term

That in and with which, Atwood says, the third life moves.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3].

See also: Essence

References: APP ¶3

The Critic

treatise

A publication (new series, No. 13, 1845) that Atwood cites as the source of the English translations of an epitaph.

Atwood cites The Critic, new series, No. 13 (1845), as the source of the English translations of an epitaph she gives [I.1 ¶22] [I.1 n30]. It is a reference only.

References: I.1 n30, I.1 ¶22

Crito

person

A cited source (Idem, p. 248) used to support the view that Intellect is a God-given sight which mortals lack through generation.

Atwood cites Crito (as “Idem, page 248”) in support of the view that Intellect is a sight given by God, which mortals lack through generation: “gave him a sight called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God” [II.1 ¶38] [II.1 n35]. She uses the passage approvingly.

References: II.1 n35, II.1 ¶38

Crollius

person · J. Crollius, Oswald Crollius

A disciple of Paracelsus whose Philosophy Reformed Atwood cites repeatedly and approvingly on the vital spirit in man, the true physician, and what the operator must be.

Atwood names Crollius among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, with Van Helmont, Fludd, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. She notes that The Philosophy of J. Crollius carries the Addresses to the Athenians in English [I.1 ¶64]. She lists him as an adept, citing Philosophy Reformed in Pinnel’s translation [I.1 ¶70] [I.1 n81].

She quotes him with approval on several points:

  • The vital spirit in man. In Philosophy Reformed he holds that the gold-producing vapour is in man: “the same is the generating spirit of all creatures”. He also describes the true physician [II.1 ¶12] [II.1 n9] [II.1 ¶14] [II.1 n13].
  • Fire and the physician. From The True Physic, chap. 1: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated”. Atwood uses this for trial by fire, for the separation made by the natural inbred chemist, and for the physician born of the light of grace [III.1 ¶10] [III.1 n8].
  • Means of the work. In the Admonitory Preface of Oswald Crollius, great things come from preparation, contemplation, handiwork and grace: “by a holy assiduity of preparations, joining thereto diligent contemplation of natural causes” [III.1 ¶13] [III.1 n12].
  • Who can do the work. The slothful and profane are unfit: “these Chemical Secrets will never be fingered by those slothful or sottish despisers of them” [IV.1 ¶6] [IV.1 n4].

References: I.1 n81, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶70, II.1 n13, II.1 n9, II.1 ¶12, II.1 ¶14, III.1 n12, III.1 n8, III.1 ¶10, III.1 ¶13, IV.1 n4, IV.1 ¶6

Cross

term

The passage or condition under which the old life is crucified and a new one germinates: all is sown under it, and the soul must pass under it before regeneration.

Quoting Jacob Boehme, Atwood gives the Cross as what one must enter “in the Fourth Form”, where Sol and Luna are together, in order to seek gold: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48]. Her own gloss speaks of crucifixion: “out of that crucifixion, by reunion of the principles under another law, the new life is elicited” [III.1 ¶49].

In her own voice, “All is sown under the cross and completed in its number” [III.3 ¶13]. Under the cross fire and water fall together and germinate. A reader’s translation (ours, not the book’s) has true Wisdom coming under it [III.3 ¶14]. She links this to “out of the crucifixion of the cerebral life” [III.3 ¶15].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the soul passes under its Cross before the residuum supplies its regenerate body, and the earth becomes its punctum saliens: “after that the soul has passed under its Cross” [APP ¶110].

The context suggests that the Cross stands for a death of the ordinary, cerebral life. A new life, joined under another law, then comes out of it.

References: III.1 ¶48, III.1 ¶49, III.3 ¶13, III.3 ¶15, APP ¶110

Crow

term

In Hermes as glossed by Atwood, the chief principle of the art: the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state early in the work; one with the vulture.

In a passage of Hermes that Atwood glosses, the Crow is the chief principle of the art. It is the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state, at the early stage where the revived spirit is joined with its solar ferment: “the crow is also in the infancy of that work wherein the revivified spirit is united with its solar ferment” [I.3 n12].

It is identified with the vulture: “The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate” [I.3 n12].

Identified with: Vulture [I.3 n12]

References: I.3 n12

Crowned king

term

Atwood’s gloss on Hermes: the first visible resplendence of the vital tincture, the king triumphing over death when the colours appear.

Atwood explains the image directly: “By the crowned king, Hermes signifies the first manifested resplendence of the vital tincture” [I.3 n22]. The figure is the king triumphing over death when the colours appear. The meaning is stated by the text.

Identified with: first manifested resplendence of the vital tincture [I.3 n22]

See also: King

References: I.3 n22

Crystalline diaphaneity

term

The transparent state to which all things must be reduced before the Work truly begins.

Atwood writes that, before the Work truly begins, “all things are reduced to a crystalline diaphaneity” [IV.1 ¶48]. It apparently names a necessary preliminary state of complete clarity in the matter.

References: IV.1 ¶48

Curse

term · original curse

The condition matter has lain under since the fall; the work aims to redeem matter from it.

For Atwood, the curse is the condition matter has lain under since the fall, and the aim of the work is to free matter from it: to “deliver matter from the original curse” and “to redeem matter from the curse, and to raise it from the dead” [IV.3 ¶38].

References: IV.3 ¶38

Cyril

person · Cyrillus, St Cyrillus

A Church Father whom Atwood cites as taking up the rites of the Mysteries and veiling the church’s mysteries in enigmas.

Atwood cites St Cyrillus as a Church Father who adopted the rites of the Mysteries. She uses him to support her claim that the church hid its mysteries in enigmas: “except in obscure terms, in such a manner, however, as that the faithful who are initiated may comprehend, and the rest be discouraged” [II.2 ¶3] [II.2 ¶5] [II.2 n9].

References: II.1 ¶52, II.2 n9, II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶5

D

D. Fabianus de Monte

person — S. Severin · D. Fabianus de Monte, S. Severin

Author of Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione (Quest. 5), cited in a footnote for a definition of Alchemy.

Atwood cites Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione, Quest. 5, in a footnote. The words quoted are “Alchimia est ars perspicaci” [I.1 n52] (our rendering: Alchemy is an art for the perceptive). It is a reference only.

References: I.1 n52

Dactyli Idaei

collective voice — fable · Fingers of Mount Ida

A fable Atwood uses to illustrate the hand and fiery art bringing the metallic veins to light, as the hand expresses a thought formed beforehand.

Atwood uses the fable as an illustration: “Such were those Dactyli Idaei, literally the Fingers of Mount Ida” [IV.1 ¶34]. They stand for the hand and fiery art that bring the metallic veins to light, in the way the hand expresses a thought already formed.

References: IV.1 ¶34

Dagon

term

In a passage of Ricardus, something overthrown by the enigmas; the text does not define it.

In a sentence by Ricardus about study wiping away ignorance: “by these enigmas the Dagon is overthrown” [III.4 ¶20]. The text does not define it. The context suggests it stands for the ignorance that study removes.

References: III.4 ¶20

Dark Aleph and light Aleph

term · dark Aleph, light Aleph

In Reuchlin as quoted: dark Aleph is the hidden essence, which becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension.

Atwood quotes Reuchlin. Dark Aleph is the hidden essence. It becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension: “is dark Aleph converted into light Aleph” [III.2 ¶10].

References: III.2 ¶10

Dark world

term

In Boehme’s scheme of the Three Worlds, a procreation or outer birth: a substance expressed from the internal and spiritual worlds.

In Boehme’s Three Worlds, as Atwood gives them, the dark world is “a procreation or extern birth or, as it were, a substance expressed or spoken forth from the internal and spiritual worlds” [III.2 ¶16]. It is identified with the outer (“extern”) birth.

Identified with: extern birth [III.2 ¶16]

References: III.2 ¶16

Darkness

term

In a passage of the Master, what the stone brings forth after Light: the clouds, called the mother of all things.

In a passage of the Master that Atwood quotes, the stone after the Light “brings forth the clouds, or darkness, which is the mother of all things” [III.1 ¶49]. Darkness is here equated with the clouds.

Identified with: clouds [III.1 ¶49]

References: III.1 ¶49

Darkness upon the Abyss

collective voice — unattributed in the text

An unattributed image Atwood uses as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light in the hyperphysical work.

Atwood uses the image, without naming a source, as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light during the hyperphysical work: “as there was darkness upon the Abyss when the Divine Spirit moved upon the Water’s face” [III.1 ¶60].

References: III.1 ¶60

David

person

Cited, via the 68th Psalm, on the Divine presence driving out what is alien, within Ripley’s verse, and among the Hebrew prophets on the Wheel of Fire.

Atwood names David with Ezekiel, Moses, Zachariah and the Hebrew prophets in illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. He is cited inside Ripley’s verse about the waters passing away: “Abierunt in sicco flumina” [III.1 ¶57] (our rendering: the rivers went away into dry land). In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the 68th Psalm illustrates the alien being driven out when the Divine presence arises: “as wax before the fire” [APP ¶157].

References: II.3 ¶54, III.1 ¶57, APP ¶157

De Lapide Physici Condit.

treatise

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n2

De St Martin

person · St Martin, Se St Martin

A writer cited throughout the Appendix with approval, on numbers, the divine names, regeneration, and the earth as crucible of souls.

All citations fall in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood praises him as having entered the centre of substantial life [APP ¶112–115]. She cites him approvingly on the following points:

  • The Crown. With Behmen, he is the source of the phrase “the Crown” [APP ¶104].
  • Numbers. From Corresp., p. 298: “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]. Atwood extends this to outer nature and to scriptural tradition.
  • Correspondence, letter 30, and Theos. Correspondence, p. 117. With Eckhartshausen, he is cited on the change in the circulation of the blood. He is also a reference on The Name speaking in us and on the mineral earth [APP ¶78] [APP ¶88] [APP ¶89].
  • The two Testaments. From Theos. Corresp., p. 244: their foundation lies “in the true pronunciation of the two great names” [APP ¶98]. Atwood glosses this as the revealed utterance of the life of God in man.
  • The regenerate body. From Tableau Naturel, vol. 2, p. 230 (spelled “Se St Martin” there): “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]. He is cited on the residue of the sensual medium giving body to the regenerate soul.
  • Law and inquiry. From Reply, p. 364, he is cited on a perfect law that works by degrees. His answers to a friend’s particular question illustrate universal truth exploding questions, like the Hermetic inquiry [APP ¶112] [APP ¶113] [APP ¶115].

References: APP ¶104, APP ¶107, APP ¶110, APP ¶112, APP ¶113, APP ¶115, APP ¶78, APP ¶88, APP ¶89, APP ¶98

Dead and revived god

collective voice — Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris · Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris, Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris

Figures Atwood names as the god dead and revived among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians.

Atwood names Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis and Osiris as instances of the god dead and revived, among the Cabiri, in Phrygia, in Lydia and among the Egyptians [III.3 ¶69].

See also: Fable of Isis and Osiris, Gods, Osiris

References: III.3 ¶69

Dead clay

term

In Norton, clay that has been heavily roasted; ground and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.

Norton, quoted by Atwood: “Dead clay is called such a thing, As hath suffered great roasting” [III.4 ¶31]. Ground to powder and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.

References: III.4 ¶31

Decad

term

In a quoted adept’s verse, where the nucleus of Salt lies, to be guarded in holy silence; not explained.

A quoted adept, called “the mysterious adeptest”, speaks of Salt “whose nucleus in the Decad guard in holy silence” [III.3 ¶50]. The text does not explain the Decad.

References: III.3 ¶50

Defunct philosophers

collective voice

The dead philosophers whose testimony, Atwood says, is the only evidence on which Alchemy can be imagined to be real.

Atwood says the testimony of defunct philosophers is the only evidence on which Alchemy may be imagined real [IV.4 ¶12].

See also: Philosophers

References: IV.4 ¶12

Deification

term

In Aristotle as reported by Atwood, the condition reached when the understanding touches its cause; only the duly initiated are capable of it.

In Atwood’s report of Aristotle, deification is attained by contact of the understanding with its cause. Only the initiated can reach it: “duly initiated and capable of this deification” [II.1 ¶37].

References: II.1 ¶37

Demiurgic fire

term

The creative fire the gods manifest through Intellect in Light, borne by Minerva as Phosphor; hidden from man by sensual conception.

In Atwood’s account, the gods manifest the Demiurgic Fire through Intellect in Light. “Minerva is sometimes called Phosphor, as being the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [II.4 ¶26]. To Theurgists the gods show a self-visible Fire: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

It is the creative fire borne by Wisdom. Ordinary sense-bound thinking hides it, “that Fire which the sensual conception occultates, and so forcibly restricts, that man does not suspect it even” [III.3 ¶71]. The context suggests it is the hidden fire the method seeks to release.

See also: Fire

References: II.4 ¶26, II.4 ¶29, III.3 ¶71

Demiurgic Intellect

term

That with which Theurgic sacrifice seeks to be joined; not further defined.

Atwood says Theurgic sacrifice seeks “a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She does not define it further.

See also: Intellect

References: III.4 ¶25

Democritus

person · Democrit, Democritus of Abdera, Abderite

A philosopher Atwood treats as an adept of the sacred art: his reduction of matter, the Fable of Proteus, and his pyrographic portrayal of the work.

Source and standing. Atwood presents Democritus of Abdera, author of a book of Sacred Physics (de Arte Sacra), as treating the Hermetic art and the occult discovery under ancient philosophy.
