She names him as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶12] [I.1 ¶20] [I.1 n14] [I.1 n20]. Synesius wrote a commentary on him [I.1 ¶27]. Norton’s verse lists “Democrit” among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Norton also reports him as naming the Water: “Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient;” [III.3 ¶74].

The method. Atwood endorses his proposal, as Bacon reports it, to reduce matter almost to annihilation and so free the spirit [I.2 ¶24]. Through the Fable of Proteus the matter, near annihilation, restores itself by an inbred force [I.3 n7]. The fable also supports binding the matter: “that method of working with nature is the most effectual that makes use of manacles and fetters” [I.3 n37]. He is cited for “Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36]. With Hermes, he repeats the process of the Vital Spirit [II.1 ¶25]. He hints that the changes stop only when Art brings the Matter into the fixity of its Final Cause [III.2 ¶22]. Following Bacon, Atwood calls the Experiment “the Art of Democritus” [III.3 ¶61].

The Vulcanic action. The Flammelli Summula gathers sayings from him. It shows, in operative language, the burning of the Brazen Body and Venus becoming golden: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily” [I.3 n49] [I.3 n53]. Atwood says he portrays the Vulcanic action “before all, and as it were pyrographically”: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily, instructs this Abderite” [IV.1 ¶43] [IV.1 n40]. She calls him “our Abderite”.

Having seen it, he laughed at other things [IV.4 ¶27].

References: I.1 n14, I.1 n20, I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶20, I.1 ¶27, I.2 ¶24, I.2 ¶36, I.3 n37, I.3 n49, I.3 n53, I.3 n7, II.1 ¶25, III.1 n2, III.2 ¶22, III.3 ¶61, III.3 ¶74, IV.1 n40, IV.1 ¶43, IV.4 ¶27

Demogogon

term · Demogorgon

Atwood’s term for ‘the whole’ that is first not yet animated by its own returning light, later animated and shining from the dark abyss; apparently the whole subject of the work.

Atwood uses the name in two linked passages (spelled two ways). First: “For it is the whole Demogogon, as yet not actually animated by contact of his own returning light” [II.3 ¶30]. Later: “For it is the whole Demogorgon, now actually animated, which before was made visible without its subject light” [II.3 ¶52]. There it is ignited and shines from the dark abyss of being as a luciferous wheel. The text does not otherwise define it. The context suggests it names the whole subject of the work before and after its own light returns to it.

References: II.3 ¶30, II.3 ¶52

Demons

term · Demon, revenging Demon

Apparitional beings arising from the enclosed vapour of imagination, children of matter at war with the truth-seeking soul; also Hermes’ revenging Demon that torments the wicked.

Atwood’s account. The demons of antiquity are apparitional beings born of a confined vapour of imagination: “all the race of demons, so much celebrated by antiquity, appear to have their origin in a life of this kind, viz., from an included vapor of the imagination” [II.3 ¶22]. They are called the children of matter: “as the progeny of matter, and as having an energetic virtue, but at natural war with the truth-seeking soul” [II.3 ¶24]. They are said to have sense, arts and an operative life, which they use to deceive, and they are given life by desire. The Chaldaic oracle also speaks of “pure demons”.

Hermes (Poemander). Among the wicked, the Mind gives way to the Demon: “giving place to the revenging Demon, which, applying unto him the sharpness of fire, tormenteth such a man sensibly” [III.3 ¶57]. When the body dissolves, this Demon receives the “idle manners”.

References: II.3 ¶22, II.3 ¶24, III.3 ¶57

Des Septchenes

person · De Septchenes

Cited for reference only.

References: II.2 n8, II.2 n9, IV.2 n12

The desirable

term

That toward which even Matter extends, identified with the Good.

The text says even Matter is “extended to the desirable, i.e., to the Good” [III.4 ¶28]. It identifies the desirable with the Good. The speaker is unclear from the record.

Identified with: the Good [III.4 ¶28]

References: III.4 ¶28

Desire

term

For Atwood, the longing of the mind for its object, through which the research is ultimately made manifest and which prayer enlarges.

Atwood speaks of the inquiry as “a research which is so much wrapped in and about the Desire as to be ultimately made manifest through its means” [III.4 ¶20]. She treats every desire as a kind of prayer, and prayer in turn works “(by enlarging the desire)” [III.4 ¶24]. The record suggests Desire is the motive force of the method: the research depends on it and comes to light through it.

References: III.4 ¶20, III.4 ¶24

Deuteronomy

treatise

Scriptural book Atwood cites in support of the unfigured form of the Divine Essence.

Atwood cites Deuteronomy 4:15, “Take good heed unto yourselves, for ye saw no manner of similitude on the say that the Lord spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n52], to support her point that the Divine Essence is without figure.

References: II.3 n52, II.3 ¶48

Dew of heaven

term

In Eudoxus, what the wise make fall upon the earth so that it yields precious fruit; not further explained.

Spoken by Eudoxus (quoted): the wise make it fall upon the earth, “knowing how to make the dew of Heaven fall upon it” [IV.3 ¶12], so that it bears precious fruit. The text does not explain the expression further; its plain meaning in the method is unclear.

See also: Heaven

References: IV.3 ¶12

Dew of light

term · dew

In Rabbi Ben Jocahi, the dew shaken from the head of the hidden principle, which awakens the dead and nourishes the saints; identified with manna.

Quoted from Rabbi Ben Jocahi: “Thy dew is the dew of light” [III.2 ¶3]. This dew falls from the head of the hidden principle, awakens the dead, nourishes the saints and is white as the diamond. It is identified with manna: “It is this which nourishes the most exalted saints, the manna which descends into the field of sacred fruits” [III.2 ¶3].

Identified with: manna [III.2 ¶3]

See also: Light

References: III.2 ¶3

Diana

term

For Atwood, a figure of the First Matter and refulgent Light: the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature personified, containing all elements of being.

Atwood presents Diana as the First Matter and the refulgent Light, personifying the whole Fundamental Nature, inferior and superior together: “she is the wholeness of the Fundamental Nature at once personified, the knot and link of all the elements o being” [III.1 ¶70].

Identified with: Fundamental Nature (its wholeness personified) [III.1 ¶70]

References: III.1 ¶70

Dianoia

term

A term in a Proclus passage, named alongside ‘our individual reason’; not further defined.

Appears in a passage of Proclus (quoted), where the spirit “becomes perfectly everything from which dianoia and our individual reason consist” [II.2 ¶15]. The text gives no further definition; it is apparently a reasoning faculty listed beside individual reason.

References: II.2 ¶15

Dickenson

person

Author of de Quintessentia, cited by Atwood for an account of powder of transmutation found in Lully’s Westminster cell.

Atwood cites E. Dickenson’s de Quintessentia for the story of powder of transmutation discovered in Lully’s cell at Westminster [I.1 ¶47; I.1 n57]. She uses it as reported testimony; the records show no comment from her on it.

References: I.1 n57, I.1 ¶47

Digby

person · John Digby, Digby’s Ed.

John Digby, given as translator of the French edition of Sendivogius’ New Light of Alchemy (London 1722), which adds the Treatise on Salt and a Dialogue.

Named in a note on Sendivogius’ New Light of Alchemy, London 1722: Digby translated from the French edition, which adds the Treatise on Salt and an instructive Dialogue [I.1 ¶71; I.1 n91]. Atwood refers to this as Digby’s edition.

References: I.1 n91, I.1 ¶71, I.3 n30, III.4 n21, IV.1 n10, IV.1 ¶7

Digestion

term

An operation by which the powder is multiplied, and a measured process required before perfect dissolution and before extraction of the Fixed Salt.

Two quoted voices use the term. An adept (quoted) says the white or red powder is multiplied tenfold with each digestion, and “each digestion is made in tenfold shorter time than the preceding” [II.1 ¶25]. Eudoxus (quoted) requires digestion before perfect dissolution in the Second Key, “after a proportioned digestion and putrefaction” [IV.3 ¶5], and before extracting the Fixed Salt in the Third Key, by “a convenient digestion and a slow distillation” [IV.3 ¶7]. In both cases it is a measured, staged operation within the work.

References: II.1 ¶25, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶7

Dionysius

person

Authority cited by Atwood for the divine darkness, visible yet incomprehensible, and for the True Thing of negative theology.

Atwood cites Dionysius in support of the divine darkness, the “caligo divina” [III.2 ¶13], which is visible yet beyond comprehension. She also draws on him for the True Thing of negative theology, whose possession is the happiest life [III.2 ¶15]. She uses him with approval.

References: III.2 ¶13, III.2 ¶15

Dionysius of Syracuse

person

Plato’s correspondent; Atwood thinks a practical science drew him to Plato.

Named as Plato’s correspondent. Atwood suggests he was drawn to Plato by a science she believes was practical [I.1 ¶17].

References: I.1 ¶17

Diotima

person

Speaker in the Banquet, cited by Atwood in support of the idea that the wise mind possesses its object within itself.

Atwood cites Diotima in the Banquet in support of the idea that a wise mind holds its object within itself: “that mind which is become wise needs not to investigate any further” [II.1 ¶37]. She uses the passage with approval.

References: II.1 ¶37

Disappointed chemists

collective voice

Critics of Alchemy whose ‘learned cavils and clamours’ Atwood dismisses.

Atwood criticizes the disappointed chemists for their learned cavils and clamours against Alchemy [IV.4 ¶12]. She rejects their view.

References: IV.4 ¶12

Disciple

collective voice

Anonymous voice, endorsed by Atwood, who treats material gifts as tokens of the Spirit’s love.

A quoted disciple says of the Spirit: “then he sends us these things as tokens and pledges of his love” [IV.3 ¶46]. Atwood endorses this reading of material gifts as signs of the Spirit’s love.

References: IV.3 ¶46

Disciple of Cornelius Agrippa

collective voice — not named

An unnamed disciple of Cornelius Agrippa, cited for ‘more suggestive language’ on the work’s sequence and for Agrippa’s poverty after his failure.

Atwood cites Agrippa’s unnamed “ingenious disciple” as expressing, in more suggestive language, the joining, siege and creature sequence of the work: “Take our two serpents, which are to be found everywhere on the face of the earth” [III.1 ¶50]. She cites him again on Agrippa’s poverty resulting from his failure: “This was it, adds his disciple, that made his necessities so vigorous and his purse so weak” [IV.1 ¶36].

See also: Agrippa

References: III.1 ¶50, IV.1 ¶36

Discovery of the Father

term · discovery

In Proclus, meeting, union with and direct sight of the Father; not opinion or science but Intellectual Vision; the Paternal Port.

Defined by Proclus (quoted): “For discovery is this, — to meet with him, to be united to Him, and to see Him Himself” [II.4 ¶41]. It is not opinion and not science but Intellectual Vision of the Father or Maker. Proclus equates it with the Paternal Port: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father” [II.4 ¶41].

Identified with: Paternal port [II.4 ¶41]

References: II.4 ¶41

Discursive energy of reason

term

In Plotinus, the ordinary reasoning into which the soul falls back from Intellect after the divine state.

Plotinus (quoted) describes the soul after the divine state as “falling off from Intellect into the discursive energy of reason” [III.2 ¶50]. It names ordinary step-by-step reasoning, a lower condition than Intellect.

See also: Reason

References: III.2 ¶50

Discursive faculty

term

The reasoning faculty which, Atwood says, plays no part in discovering and assenting to universal propositions.

Atwood says that in discovering universal propositions and assenting to them “there is no use of the discursive faculty or of external facts to witness” [II.1 ¶34]. Knowledge of this kind does not come by reasoning or from outside evidence.

References: II.1 ¶34

Dissolution

term · dissolve, dissolved, solution

For Atwood, the core operation of the first work: an artificial loosening of the vital bond that dissolves the fixed sensual compact so the spirit can be renovated and perfected.

Atwood treats dissolution as the central operation of the first work. “The beginning of the whole work is a perfect solution” [IV.1 ¶4]: the subject is dissolved in its own blood, or own mercury, to remove superfluities. The dissolution must be total, for “nothing short of dissolution can give it rest” [IV.1 ¶7].

She takes the term from the old doctrine: “We adopt the term dissolve here in accordance with the old doctrine” [II.3 n2]. She applies it to the change in the vital relation during trance, and notes that the Alchemists say the sensible medium ought to be dissolved. She calls it “an artificial dissolution of the vital bond, by means of Alchemy” [I.3 n64]. The philosophic work begins after it, and by it vapour, blackness and death are driven out: “and this by dissolution” [I.3 ¶56].

In the process, “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved, and that which is dissolved is renovated”, and “by Dissolution thou shalt possess a triumphant reward” [II.3 ¶37]. The process is repeated: “the process by which the spirit is carried on from each succeeding dissolution into a more perfect form of being” [I.3 n19]. In the same note Atwood says a radical dissolution of the spirit reveals the evil of original sin, and that dissolution by the water is the key of restoration [I.3 n19].

She also describes it as the breaking-up of the light’s body and of the natural-born life, in which the three principles separate: “an eclipsation of the light takes place, and a dissolution of its body” [III.1 ¶53]. The context suggests its cause is vital heat artificially stirred in the blood [III.1 ¶53].

See also: Generation and dissolution, Solution

References: I.3 n19, I.3 n64, I.3 ¶56, II.3 n2, II.3 ¶37, III.1 ¶53, IV.1 ¶4, IV.1 ¶7

Dividual

term

For Atwood, the divided condition reached by ‘falling off’, in which one ceases to be the Universe.

Atwood writes that by falling off, “in becoming dividual, he ceases to be the Universe” [IV.4 ¶27]. It names the separated state opposed to unity with the whole.

References: IV.4 ¶27

Divine art

term

Atwood’s name for the Art in its higher purposes: working in and with the Universal Spirit, joined with universal theosophy, beyond its mineral uses.

Atwood uses Divine Art as a name for the Art. Boehme gives the “principles of the Divine Art” and a ground of experience for it [I.1 ¶68]. She separates its mineral uses (quickening and perfecting) from “the higher purposes and application of the Divine Art, and universal theosophy” [I.1 ¶42]. It requires a representative of the rebellious Principle: “that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64]. Nearby text speaks of “the Hermetic Art”, but the records do not say the two names are identical [III.1 ¶66].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “the Divine Art works in and with the Universal Spirit” [APP ¶140]. There it brings forth various states of life that offer allurements to the will, and it uses instruments as well as vessels [APP ¶140].

References: I.1 ¶42, I.1 ¶68, III.1 ¶64, APP ¶140

Divine art of separation

term

For Atwood, the loosening of the bond between spirit and its bodily media, which Paracelsus speaks of and mesmerism imitates externally.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls mesmeric practice “an imitation of the Divine Art of the separation of which Paracelsus speaks” [APP ¶73]. The Art apparently loosens the bond between spirit and its bodily media; mesmerism imitates it only outwardly.

See also: Separation

References: APP ¶73

Divine conjunction

term

For Atwood, a state in which, while it lasts, subject and object are not two in consciousness.

Atwood writes that “as in the Divine conjunction, whilst it lasts, there are not two things as of subject and object in the consciousness” [III.2 ¶66]. In it, the life that understands and the light understood are one.

See also: Conjunction

References: III.2 ¶66

Divine ecstasy

term

For Atwood, an ecstasy kindled in connection with its Source, which draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art.

Atwood speaks of “that kindling of Divine Ecstasy, in connection with its Source” [III.1 ¶70]. It draws nature to its desire and works the whole miracle of the Hermetic Art. It is apparently the active power that accomplishes the work.

References: III.1 ¶70

Divine essentiality

term · Essentiality

For Atwood, that with which the resigned Spirit is clothed; it qualifies the true Adept and is identified with the material of the Corner-Stone.

Atwood says the resigned Spirit is clothed with the Divine Essentiality: “And this Essentiality it is which qualifies the true Adept” [III.3 ¶24]. It also sanctifies the Adept. She identifies it with the material of the Corner-Stone: “It is this material of the Corner-Stone which links reason to Divinity” [III.3 ¶24].

Identified with: material of the Corner-Stone [III.3 ¶24]

References: III.3 ¶24

Divine Exemplars

term

The first and most beautiful objects of Wisdom: undecaying and invariable, with other things beautiful by participating in them.

The phrase is Atwood’s gloss on Iamblicus (quoted): Wisdom is “conversant with the first and most beautiful objects (i.e., the Divine Exemplars)” [II.1 ¶39]. They do not decay or vary, and other things are beautiful by participating in them.

Identified with: the first and most beautiful objects [II.1 ¶39]

References: II.1 ¶39

Divine experience

term

Addressed by Atwood as the august Mother of all things; at the Substant Unity, Experience is present with Power.

Atwood addresses it directly: “And thou august Mother of all things, Divine Experience.” [III.3 ¶79]. She describes the Substant Unity as the place “where Experience is present with Power, and Effect in substance to bear them witness” [III.3 ¶79].

Identified with: Mother of all things [III.3 ¶79]

See also: Experience

References: III.3 ¶79

Divine eye

term

For Atwood, the inner faculty of perception which, purified and strengthened, perceives the truth of all beings.

Atwood, citing Plato, speaks of “that divine eye which, as Plato says, is better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶8]. Purified and strengthened, this inner faculty perceives the truth of all beings.

References: II.2 ¶8

Divine fiat

term

For Atwood, the divine command that blesses the union of Soul and Passive Spirit, in which the sensual dominant is occultated and subdued.

Atwood writes that “the Divine Fiat comes mercifully to bless the union” of Soul and Passive Spirit [III.3 ¶10]. In it the sensual dominant is subdued: “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15].

References: III.3 ¶10, III.3 ¶15

Divine fire

term

In Iamblicus, what is received in perfect plenitude through the third class of prayer, the final seal of union.

Iamblicus (quoted) writes that “through the energy of the third, we receive a perfect plenitude of Divine Fire” [III.4 ¶24]. The third class of prayer is the final seal of union.

See also: Fire

References: III.4 ¶24

Divine germ of humanity

term

For Atwood, the divine seed in man, beheld in a deformed condition under the evils of its birth.

Atwood refers to “the divine germ of humanity said to be beheld under the thousand evils of its birth” [II.3 ¶30]. In that state it appears deformed.

References: II.3 ¶30

Divine ground

term

Atwood’s term for the ground where the Scriptural phrase is seen and proved; there man may work but cannot compel the Divine Blessing.

Atwood speaks of what is “as seen and proved on the Divine Ground” [IV.1 ¶40]. On this ground, she says, man may experiment, plough, plant and irrigate, but he cannot compel the Divine Blessing [IV.1 ¶40].

References: IV.1 ¶40

Divine I am

term

The affirmation in which Life feels itself to Be; Atwood says the Kabalah uses it to signify the Substant Unity of all that is.

In Atwood’s account, “Life springs forth with motion, feeling itself to Be.” [III.3 ¶79]. She identifies the Divine I Am with the Substant Unity: “in the Divine I Am, is by the Kabalah signified the Substant Unity of all that is” [III.3 ¶79].

Identified with: Substant unity [III.3 ¶79]

References: III.3 ¶79

Divine idea

term

What, according to Atwood, those who live profanely and without self-knowledge cannot attain, entertain or think self-actively.

Atwood says that those living profanely and without self-knowledge cannot “attain to the Divine Idea; either to entertain or think It self-actively is impossible” [III.3 ¶78].

See also: Ideas

References: III.3 ¶78

Divine imagination

term

In Boehme as quoted, that through which all things arose from the Tincture.

Quoted from Boehme: “All things are thence arisen through the Divine Imagination” [III.2 ¶16]. The context ties this arising to the Tincture [III.2 ¶16].

See also: Imagination

References: III.2 ¶16

Divine Intuition

term

Atwood’s name for the passive reception of the divine, raised by love, hope and faith, as opposed to self-active comprehension of Deity.

Atwood contrasts “the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] with a self-active comprehension of Deity. In this mode the divine is received passively, and the soul is raised by love, hope and faith [II.4 ¶40].

See also: Intuition

References: II.4 ¶40

Divine inversion

term

A term Atwood names as the subject of a Rabbi’s advice and links to creation out of nothing, but does not define.

Atwood refers to advice “concerning the true nature of Divine Inversion” [III.2 ¶31] and connects it with creation out of nothing. The passage does not define the term.

See also: Inversion

References: III.2 ¶31

Divine light

term

The formless divine light that the initiate sees; Atwood says it is held captive in this life and that it turns the Quintessence into living gold. In the Appendix she calls it the Essence of Gold.

Quoted (Psellus; the Oracle). In the Introspection, “the initiated person sees the Divine Light itself without any form or figure” [II.3 ¶46]. The oracle calls this Sacro Sancto [II.3 ¶46], and speaks of it: “When thou seest a Fire without Form” [II.3 ¶47]; this light, the quoted voices say, will not deceive.

Atwood. Without this revelation the operator’s purpose is blind. She warns against “he who presumes without the revelation of the Divine Light to introduce his own blind purpose” [III.1 ¶38]. The new life “needs only the corroborative virtue of the Divine light which it draws” [III.1 ¶49], and this turns the Quintessence into living gold. ¶40 also mentions a guardian of the Light [III.1 ¶40]. In this life the light is kept behind “the barriers by which the Divine Light is here held in thralldom” [IV.4 ¶17], and the means of the ancients remove those barriers. “When once the Divine Light is loosened in life” [IV.3 ¶39], everything prospers so long as her Rule is kept; the text leaves unclear whether “her” means the Light or Wisdom.

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood says the Divine Light is hidden in the self-begotten life, which takes the Divine Life for itself instead of serving it. She identifies it with gold: “The Divine Light, the Essence of Gold” [APP ¶70].

Identified with: Essence of Gold [APP ¶70]; Sacro Sancto [II.3 ¶46]

See also: Light

References: II.3 ¶46, II.3 ¶47, III.1 ¶38, III.1 ¶49, IV.3 ¶39, IV.4 ¶17, APP ¶70

Divine light region

term

In the Appendix, the highest sphere, above the pure Ether, where high Reason dwells, informed by Love and purified by humiliation.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes a scale of spheres: “Above that is the Divine Light region” [APP ¶170]. It lies above the pure Ether and is the dwelling of high Reason, informed by Love and purified by humiliation [APP ¶170].

References: APP ¶170

Divine media

term

The real means by which, Atwood says, Theurgists are joined to the Divine nature, as opposed to a mental conception.

Atwood insists that the Theurgists’ union with the Divine nature is real: “it is indeed by divine Media, and not a mere conception of the mind or metaphysical abstraction” [II.4 ¶31].

References: II.4 ¶31

Divine monarchy

term

Something Atwood says is established from the triune-essence principles she has just set out.

After her passage on the triune essence, Atwood writes: “Hence the Divine Monarchy consists, and is established” [IV.2 ¶12]. Its primary principles are those she has just announced there.

References: IV.2 ¶12

Divine Oracle

collective voice · divine oracles

An oracular voice Atwood cites as ratifying the Platonic instruction on how to apprehend the Intelligible.

Atwood cites the Divine Oracle in support of the Platonic teaching on how to apprehend the Intelligible: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶42]. The citation continues across [II.4 ¶43–48]. She uses it approvingly.

Divine oracles. In a footnote, Atwood cites the divine oracles in support: they teach that fire obliterates the strains from generation [II.3 n40].

See also: Oracles

References: II.3 n40, II.4 ¶42, II.4 ¶43, II.4 ¶44, II.4 ¶45, II.4 ¶46, II.4 ¶47, II.4 ¶48

Divine original

term

The divine source in which contraries always coexist; Atwood says the common elements of Nature hide it and chemistry cannot identify it.

Atwood says that “contraries are always consubsistent in the Divine Original” [III.2 ¶60], such as small and great, deficient and exceeding. Elsewhere she writes: “The common elements of Nature obscure their Divine Original” [IV.1 ¶47]. In that context, chemistry cannot identify this source [IV.1 ¶47].

References: III.2 ¶60, IV.1 ¶47

Divine reason

term

A principle said to have been originally resident in man’s life, which ranked him high, reported from cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience.

Reporting cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood describes man as ranked high for “a Divine Reason, on occult principle of Causal Efficience, said to be originally resident in his life” [II.1 ¶32]. This passage identifies the Divine Reason with that occult principle of Causal Efficience.

Identified with: occult principle of Causal Efficience [II.1 ¶32]

See also: Reason

References: II.1 ¶32

Divine science

term

The knowledge whose temple, Atwood says, admits whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing.

Atwood says that whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing “is already admitted to the temple of Divine Science, and joins in with the whole conclave” [IV.4 ¶32].

References: IV.4 ¶32

Divine seed

term

What the matter brought into the right condition attracts, and (in the Appendix) what the spirit that has died to all receives.

In the main text, the matter is brought into the right condition by action and reaction, so as “to supply the right condition for attracting the Divine Seed” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the spirit dies to everything, even its own identity, and becomes “a simple receptacle and magnet for the Divine Seed” [APP ¶87]. Both passages describe a prepared receiver that draws in the Seed.

See also: Seed

References: IV.1 ¶41, APP ¶87

Divine silence

term

In Trismegistus as quoted, the knowledge of the First Cause: a rest of all the senses in which the soul is changed into the Essence of God.

Atwood quotes Trismegistus on the First Cause: “the knowledge of it, says Trismegistus, is a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33]. In this state the soul is drawn from the body and changed into the Essence of God [IV.2 ¶33].

References: IV.2 ¶33

Divine substantiality

term

In the theosophist as quoted, the pure spirit that nourished the flame-like life of Adam before the fall.

The theosophist, as quoted, says that unfallen Adam’s flame-like life was “nourished by that pure spirit of the divine substantiality” [IV.3 ¶38].

References: IV.3 ¶38

Divine Superstructure

term

Atwood’s name for the completed work; the returned Instrument gives it its force and integral perfection.

Atwood says the returned Instrument makes up “the force and integral perfection of the Divine Superstructure” [III.1 ¶61]. The term apparently names the finished work.

References: III.1 ¶61

Divine Teacher

collective voice

Cited from the Scriptures to support keeping the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy.

Atwood cites the Divine Teacher of the Scriptures to justify withholding the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine” [I.3 n10]. She uses it with approval.

References: I.3 n10

Divine union

term

Union with the reality that images stand for. Julian, as quoted, says it is achieved only with the help of Divine Works.

Quoted (Julian). “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52]. The assistance meant here is Divine Works.

Atwood. Divine Union joins the soul not to an image but to the reality that images represent. Afterwards, what was in the mind before returns heightened: “subsequent to the Divine Union, there recurs That also which was in the mind prior to the union, exalted and multiplied” [III.2 ¶66].

See also: Union

References: II.1 ¶52, III.2 ¶66

Divine water

term

In Hermolaus Barbarus as quoted, the chemists’ celestial water, an ethereal spirit from which potable gold and the philosophers’ stone begin.

Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus: “There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20]. It is distinct from every other water or liquor, and Democritus and Trismegistus knew it. It is called by other names, “calling it divine water, Scythian latex, &c.” [I.1 ¶20]. He calls it a spirit “which is a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. Potable gold and the philosophers’ stone begin from it. If the outside air is kept out, its ether burns forever: “concerning this water; and he devoutly affirms, that the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

Identified with: Scythian latex [I.1 ¶20]; a spirit of the nature of the ether [I.1 ¶20]; praeter-perfect aqueous body [I.1 ¶20]

See also: Water

References: I.1 ¶20

Divine works

term

In Synesius as quoted, the help without which the Divine union can neither be achieved nor understood.

Synesius, as cited, “bears witness to the efficacy of Divine Works” [II.1 ¶52]. Without this help the Divine union is neither effected nor understood [II.1 ¶52].

See also: Works

References: II.1 ¶52

Doctors

collective voice · our doctors

Cited for the view that the Art is perfected by multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether.

‘Our doctors’ are cited in support of the view that the Art’s perfection lies in multiplying the Prester and placing him in the supreme Ether [II.3 ¶56].

References: II.3 ¶56

Doctrine of Wisdom

term

The Greeks’ teaching, which Atwood praises as unequalled in its scientific explanation of the divine source.

Atwood praises the Greeks as unequalled in “their doctrine of Wisdom in perspicuity, grace of utterance, and scientific explication of the divine source” [I.1 ¶70].

See also: Wisdom

References: I.1 ¶70

Double nativity

term

In Vaughan as quoted, a twofold birth, visible and invisible, without which the Matter cannot be brought to its final purpose.

Vaughan, as quoted, speaks “of a double nativity, visible and invisible” [IV.2 ¶35]. Without it the Matter cannot be altered to its final purpose. The passage does not explain the expression further.

References: IV.2 ¶35

Doves of Diana

term

In Eirenaeus as quoted, a sign to watch for; the passage does not explain it.

Eirenaeus, as quoted, names “your signal the Doves of Diana” [III.1 ¶14]. The passage does not say what they are.

See also: Diana

References: III.1 ¶14

Doves of Venus

term

In the Appendix, Atwood’s gloss for the maternal instinct, through which the light finds the Paternal Life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: the light finds the Paternal Life “through the maternal instinct (the doves of Venus)” [APP ¶167]. Her stated meaning is the maternal instinct.

Identified with: maternal instinct [APP ¶167]

See also: Venus

References: APP ¶167

Doxastic

term

In Proclus as quoted, what belongs to opinion: uncertain, close to irrational life, and not true discovery.

Quoting Proclus, Atwood separates true discovery from what is “not that which is doxastic, or pertaining to opinion” [II.4 ¶41]. Such opinion is uncertain and close to irrational life [II.4 ¶41].

References: II.4 ¶41

Dr Dee

person · Dee

Diarist whose diary Atwood cites as evidence of Kelly’s projection and of Kelly possibly revealing the secret to him.

Atwood cites Dee’s Diary (n74: Sept. 1586) as a source for Kelly’s projection and for the possible discovery of the secret: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me, God be thanked.” [I.1 ¶66] [I.1 ¶67] [I.1 n74].

See also: Spirit to Dr Dee

References: I.1 n74, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶67

Dr Everard

person

Translator of the Hermetic books into English; Atwood praises the translation.

Atwood praises Dr Everard’s English translation of the Hermetic books [I.1 ¶7].

References: I.1 ¶7

Dragon

term · dragons

For Atwood, the self-willed spirit that came into nature with the fall into generation and appears as the matter’s blackness; Hermes, Bloomfield and a French adept, as quoted, describe it differently.

Atwood. In her own words: “The dragon is the self-willed spirit” [I.3 n31]. It entered nature through the fall into generation. It lives in water, oily tincture and faeces, and it rises through blackness. It is the matter’s blackness at the first ascension. It is poisonous: “like a poisonous dragon it destroys all that it touches” [I.3 n31]. It watches the crevices and shuns the sunbeams. As the internal light rises, the dragon is hidden: it “becomes so occultated in the rising of the internal light to manifestation” [I.3 n43]. The Dragon therefore apparently marks the dark first stage, which gives way as the light appears.

Quoted (Hermes). “The Dragon dwells in all the threefold nature, and his houses are the darkness and blackness that is in them” [III.1 ¶61]. In the same passage, the French adept describes two dragons biting each other until they become a Fifth Essence [III.1 ¶61].

Quoted (Bloomfield). The Dragon is the first of the three, and it slays and quells the other two: “The first one is the Dragon fell” [IV.2 ¶36].

The sources don’t agree on the details. Atwood treats the Dragon as the self-willed spirit and the blackness, Hermes as a principle dwelling in the threefold nature, and Bloomfield as the first of three, which overcomes the others.

Identified with: self-willed spirit [I.3 n31]

References: I.3 n31, I.3 n43, III.1 ¶61, IV.2 ¶36

Dry liquor

term

In Sendivogius, what the living metals are to be made into in Our Fire; the text does not explain it further.

Quoted from Sendivogius: of the living metals “let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21], in connection with Our Fire. The text gives no further explanation.

References: IV.3 ¶21

Dry soul

term

Atwood’s term for the soul that has left nature and its moisture, turns to itself and radiates its own light; Heraclitus calls it the wisest.

Atwood describes the soul that has withdrawn from nature and its moisture: turning to itself, it radiates its own light — “then she becomes a dry splendor from exhalation” [II.3 ¶27]. She cites Heraclitus: “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27].

See also: Soul

References: II.3 ¶27

Dry water

term · aqua sicca

A philosophers’ name for the ‘living water’ that the Stone is; also one of the forms the subject takes in its changes.

Quoted from Geber, dry water is the philosophers’ name for the living water that the Stone is: “living water, which we have named dry water” [I.2 ¶11] (= living water). Atwood herself lists aqua sicca among the forms the subject takes in its mutations — “a stone, a vapor, or an aqua sicca” [I.2 ¶37] — without further explanation.

Identified with: living water [I.2 ¶11]

See also: Water

References: I.2 ¶11, I.2 ¶37

Dry water of the sea of the wise

term

In Eudoxus, that with which the extracted water is joined by a ‘magical union’, dissolving it into the viscous mercurial liquor.

Quoted from Eudoxus: the extracted water is dissolved into the viscous mercurial liquor “by a magical union of the dry water of the sea of the wise” [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not explain the expression further.

See also: The Wise

References: IV.3 ¶16

Dryden

person

Cited for his English verse rendering (Aeneid, lib. 6) of a Latin passage Atwood quotes.

Atwood gives Dryden’s English verse from his Aeneid, lib. 6, as a rendering of the Latin quoted in the same paragraph: “Deep forests and impenetrable night Possess the middle space” [II.3 ¶6; II.3 n3].

References: II.3 n3, II.3 ¶6

Duad

term

The generating pair: if the divine Idea brought forth directly in it, the offspring would be imperfect and discordant; in the oracle it sits beside the Monad.

Atwood treats the Duad as the generating pair: “For if in the Duad the divine Idea were suffered immediately to bring forth, an imperfect offspring would result” [IV.2 ¶20] — imperfect and discordant through the predominance of either extreme. In the oracle she cites, the Duad stands beside the Monad: “For the Duad sits beside him and glitters with intellectual sections,” [IV.2 ¶22].

References: IV.2 ¶20, IV.2 ¶22

Dual contemplation

term

Reflective contemplation, which is excluded, together with multitude, when Matter is called ‘one so far as one’.

Atwood glosses dual contemplation as reflective contemplation (= reflective contemplation): Matter is called one so far as one by “depriving the idea of multitude and dual, i.e., reflective, contemplation” [III.2 ¶52].

Identified with: reflective contemplation [III.2 ¶52]

References: III.2 ¶52

Dufresnoy

person · l’Englet Dufresnoy

Author of the Histoire Hermetique, cited for a skeptic’s praise of English Hermetic writers and for Lully material, yet criticized as ignorant of the subject.

Atwood cites his Histoire Hermetique several times. As a skeptic’s testimony to English Hermetic writing she quotes: “les Anglois n’ecrivent sur la science hermetique avec beaucoup de lumiere et de profondeur” [I.1 ¶72; I.1 n92] (our rendering: the English write on the hermetic science with much light and depth). He is cited in support of the Lully story; his catalogue lists about 200 of Lully’s alchemical treatises; and he is a reference for the laws forbidding transmutation [I.1 ¶47; I.1 ¶48; I.1 n58; I.1 n61]. He is also cited (vol. 2) for transmutation stories [I.1 n104]. But Atwood criticizes his Catalogue (tom. iii, Paris, 1762): he reduced the count of authors, was ignorant of the subject, and excluded writers by title rather than matter [I.1 ¶75; I.1 n97].

References: I.1 n104, I.1 n1742, I.1 n34, I.1 n58, I.1 n61, I.1 n92, I.1 n97, I.1 ¶47, I.1 ¶48, I.1 ¶72, I.1 ¶75

E

Eagle

term

In the quoted fraternity of the Rosy Cross, one of two mutually devouring yet loving creatures; tortured, it yields tears, and its ‘embers’ are obtained at the second gate.

Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the Eagle is one of two creatures that devour yet love each other; tortured, it weeps — “Torture the Eagle till she weeps” [III.3 ¶63] — and its embers are obtained at the second gate. The text gives no plain meaning.

References: III.3 ¶63

Early Christians and the wisest Ethnics

collective voice · early Christians, the wisest Ethnics

Group voices cited together as agreeing that the Mysteries were instituted pure and for the noblest ends.

Atwood cites them in support of the original purity of the Mysteries: “early Christians concurring with the wisest Ethnics in declaring that they proposed the noblest ends” [II.4 ¶56].

See also: Ethnics

References: II.4 ¶56

Earth

term · our earth, Philosophic Earth

For Atwood, the crucible for souls as well as bodies; in Hermes, ‘our earth’, the body of spirit and soul, the feminine earth of the masculine.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]; it is that into which power is turned to be made integral, and “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110].

In the quoted Hermes, ‘our earth’ has sulphur as its fatness; the earth begot between water (spirit) and redness (soul) is the body of both — “the earth begot betwixt them is the substance or body of both” [I.3 n21] (= substance or body of both); “the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶22]; and Magnesia is sown in the Philosophic Earth. Earth is also identified with the residue: “the faeces or earth which remains below” [I.3 ¶23] (= faeces).

Identified with: substance or body of both [I.3 n21]; Faeces [I.3 ¶23]

See also: Our earth

References: I.3 n21, I.3 ¶22, I.3 ¶23, APP ¶110

Earth of the wise

term

The Hermetists’ earth, located within their heaven and named so to distinguish it from the ‘feculent dead soil’.

Atwood says the Hermetists place their earth within their heaven and “call it magical, the Earth of the Wise, Olympus, Our Earth” [III.2 ¶36] (= magical earth, Olympus, Our Earth), “in order to distinguish from the feculent dead soil” [III.2 ¶36].

Identified with: magical earth / Olympus / Our Earth [III.2 ¶36]

See also: The Wise

References: III.2 ¶36

Earthly vessel

term

In the Benedictine Monk, the vessel containing fire, air and water in the work, glossed as the gross body or composition.

Quoted from the Benedictine Monk: fire, air and water are contained “in their earthly vessel, i.e., in their gross body or composition” [III.3 ¶24] (= gross body or composition).

Identified with: gross body or composition [III.3 ¶24]

See also: Vessel

References: III.3 ¶24

Eastern temples and the priests at Eleusis

collective voice · Eastern temples, the priests at Eleusis

Named as the places and celebrants of the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries.

Atwood names the Eastern temples and the priests at Eleusis as where the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries were celebrated [II.2 ¶24].

References: II.2 ¶24

Eccles.

treatise

A source cited in footnotes for honoring the physician and for Wisdom’s secret being with the Faithful.

Cited (Eccles. 8; Idem., 1) in support of honoring the physician and of the saying that Wisdom’s secret belongs to the Faithful: “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36; IV.3 n14; IV.3 n15].

References: II.3 n40, IV.3 n14, IV.3 n15, IV.3 ¶36

Ecclesiasticus

person

Cited (1:6-8) in support of Wisdom as created by God, poured on all his works and given to those who love him.

Atwood cites Ecclesiasticus 1:6-8 on Wisdom: “He created her and numbered her, and poured her out upon all his works.” [III.3 ¶48; III.3 n33] — and given to those who love him.

References: III.3 n33, III.3 ¶48

Eckhartshausen

person

Cited in the Appendix in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterated contritions.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Eckhartshausen is cited in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterative contritions [APP ¶78].

References: APP ¶78

Efficient

term · true efficient, Rational Efficient

Atwood’s term for the active, working cause within the total essence, to be drawn forth, known in co-identity, and related to mind rather than generative life.

Atwood uses the Efficient for the active cause the method seeks to recover. It is to be drawn forth from within: the aim is to “draw forth the true Efficient and to know it in co-identity” [II.3 ¶5]. It lies in the intelligible substance of reason’s Law: “For there the true Efficient is to be found, which is not externally developed” [II.3 ¶46]. Knowledge and the efficient rise together: “It is from within that the knowledge springs together with the true efficient” [III.1 ¶40], the two “which are indeed one in principle” [III.1 ¶40] (= knowledge), though distinguished in practice for the sake of offspring. The “Rational Efficient, armed with a bright intelligence” [III.1 ¶47] discovers the evil of its first conception and dissolves the Vital Bond; the text does not explicitly say this is the same as the ‘true efficient’.

In the dissolution, “the newly roused Efficient is exceeding wrathful” [III.1 ¶56], reducing the body of Light (Osiris) to vapor. It is universal: there is “not the smallest grain of sand without the Efficient which is in all” [III.2 ¶43], and without it numbers and figures produce nothing substantive. One who mingles with it keeps a remnant of it: “whoever thus becomes One by mingling with the Efficient, will have a remnant of it with himself” [III.2 ¶66]. The Platonic Successor, quoted, calls it the soul’s cause: “the soul, being in such a condition, associates with her Efficient” [III.3 ¶26], gaining a similitude of it. Once Mind attains Self Knowledge, “the Efficient proceeds out wards to image its motive in operation” [IV.1 ¶48].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says this life-power is now dislocated downward: “The Efficient must be regained. That is, it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life.” [APP ¶134].

Identified with: knowledge [III.1 ¶40]

See also: Voluntary efficient

References: II.3 ¶46, II.3 ¶5, III.1 ¶40, III.1 ¶47, III.1 ¶56, III.2 ¶43, III.2 ¶66, III.3 ¶26, IV.1 ¶48, APP ¶134

Efficient power

term

Atwood’s name, in the Appendix, for Causality, of which we ordinarily have no experience; contact with universal power initiates regenerate life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates it with Causality: “We know noting of Causality — i.e., we have no experience of the Efficient Power.” [APP ¶175] (= Causality). The individual mind’s contact with power universal initiates regenerate life [APP ¶175].

Identified with: Causality [APP ¶175]

See also: The Power

References: APP ¶175

Efflorescent spirit

term

In Khunrath, something in vegetables that the Stone increases; not further defined.

Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone acts on “vegetables, by an increase of their efflorescent spirit” [IV.3 ¶28]. Not further defined.

See also: Spirit

References: IV.3 ¶28

Egg

term · our egg

In Hermes, ‘our egg’ holds the one disposition sought; the hen’s egg is the nearest natural analogue to the art’s compound simple.

Quoted from Hermes: ‘our egg’ holds the one disposition sought. The hen’s egg, made of four elements, is the closest natural analogue, “which answers in all respects, excepting the catholicity, to the compound simple of this art” [I.3 n26].

References: I.3 n26

Egg of philosophers

term

Atwood’s name for the subject when it is ‘nothing’: a formless, potential state amid its mutations.

Atwood says the subject, among its mutations, is at one stage nothing “but a potential chaos and egg of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37] (= potential chaos).

Identified with: potential chaos [I.2 ¶37]

See also: Philosophers

References: I.2 ¶37

Egyptian relics

collective voice

Cited to illustrate the rebellious Principle depicted in human form with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes.

Atwood cites Egyptian relics as depicting the rebellious Principle in human semblance, with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes [III.1 ¶64].

See also: Egyptians

References: III.1 ¶64

Egyptians

collective voice

Cited approvingly for teaching self-knowledge and placing the Sphinx before Isis, but in the Appendix criticized as an example of self-willed magic.

Atwood cites the Egyptians in support of the precept “that Man should know himself” [II.1 ¶39], meant experimentally and ontologically. They placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, which she reads as Ether guarding Wisdom [III.1 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) they are criticized as an example of the magic of the self-will: their magicians’ “enchantments” drew only on their own strength, and so Egypt fell [APP ¶2; APP ¶4; APP ¶5].

See also: Egyptian relics

References: II.1 ¶39, III.1 ¶5, APP ¶2, APP ¶4, APP ¶5

Eighth sphere

term

In Poemander’s account given by Hermes, Intellect, reached when the ascending part is stripped of all operations; above it powers sing praises to God.

Quoted from Poemander in Hermes’ account: the ascending part, naked of all operations, “cometh to the eighth sphere, which is Intellect” [III.3 ¶57] (= Intellect); above it are powers singing praises to God.

Identified with: Intellect [III.3 ¶57]

References: III.3 ¶57

Eirenaeus

person · Eirenaeus Philalethes, Philalethes, Eiranaeus, E. Philalethes, Eiraneaeus, Eiraneaus, Eireanaeus, Author of the Open Entrance, the Cosmopolite Eirenaeus

The adept Atwood calls the most celebrated later adept and a ‘perfect artist’; she draws heavily on his verse and prose for fire, matter, operations, multiplication and projection.

Atwood presents Eirenaeus Philalethes as the most celebrated later adept, a perfect artist whose identity is unknown, listing works including An Open Entrance to the Shut Palace of the King, Ripley Revived and The Marrow of Alchemy [I.1 ¶73]; he is the ‘foregoing’ adept with whom Vaughan is confounded [I.1 ¶74]. She qualifies his Ripley Revived as practically explanatory for the initiated but sophistical to beginners [I.1 ¶64; I.1 n67], and quotes him that “our books are made for those who have been or intend to become conversant about the search of nature” [I.2 ¶50; I.2 n50]. He is among adepts warning against practice before full understanding [I.1 ¶86]; “Few, very few, Philalethes said, there were in his day” [II.2 ¶25] who understood the principle.

On the agent: “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45; I.2 n44]; nature’s one secret agent — “For she her secret agent doth possess, Which in the universe is only one” [II.2 ¶28; II.2 n19]; “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold” [III.1 ¶13]; “For in our water is our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69; III.1 n73]. He supplies the account of fire, waters, menstruals, regimen and signs [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood finds ‘a profound mystery’ in “To Saturn, Mars with bond of love is tied,” [III.1 ¶58; III.1 n64]. Other uses: “Separate, says Eiraneaus, the light from the darkness seven times” [I.3 n39]; “Never grudge, then, that thou hast destroyed thye gold” [III.3 ¶22; III.3 n12], glossed as the first fruits of reason; the one key — “That ‘t is a fountain sealed, Which one thing only can unlocke;” [III.3 ¶67; III.3 n46]; the gross understanding’s false light — “that darkness I now perceived had a false fore of its own” [III.4 ¶16; III.4 n11].

On practice: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5], distinct from the Second, where Nature works alone [IV.1 ¶11]; two contrary works done apart then reconciled — “For what one doth concoct t’other will drive away;” [IV.1 ¶42; IV.1 n37]; a favored case — “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17; IV.1 n18]. For multiplication and projection: “But one at last ting’d ninety thousand more” [IV.3 ¶25; IV.3 n6]; “you will no longer be able to calculate the strength of the medicine” [IV.3 ¶18; IV.3 ¶20; IV.3 n1] — the text attributes ¶18 to the Author of the Open Entrance and ¶20 to E. Philalethes’ Introitus Apertus without stating they are one. He is cited for a universal medicine — “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7] — after which Atwood tells gold-seekers to disregard such testimony. Within the Adept’s words he is cited for the menstruum in the sphere of Saturn that can calcine gold, identified with the Salt [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “Take that matter which is gold” [APP ¶89] is glossed as finding the magical earth at one’s own center. Whether ‘the Cosmopolite Eirenaeus’ [III.1 ¶64] is a further source or a co-source of the Lion Hunt poem is unclear.

Election

term

In Norton, the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator’s nativity may contradict.

Quoted from Norton: the Election is the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator’s own nativity may oppose — “In contrariety of this Election” [IV.2 ¶34].

References: IV.2 ¶34

Elective attraction

term

The name given to chemical affinity, which a reader records as ruled by the three principles.

The text identifies it with chemical affinity: “chemical affinity, called Elective Attraction” [II.1 ¶19]. The reader’s record adds that this affinity is ruled by the three principles; the voice of the passage is unclear.

Identified with: chemical affinity [II.1 ¶19]

References: II.1 ¶19

Elementary ignition

term

Ordinary, sensible fire, which Atwood distinguishes from true fire as a mere effect of an antecedent potency.

Atwood sets true fire apart from the fire of common experience, “distinct from that elementary ignition with which we are sensibly familiar” [I.2 ¶15]. Per the reader’s record, such ignition is not true fire but only an excitation or effect of the antecedent potency [I.2 ¶15].

References: I.2 ¶15

Elementary world

term

The world over which the regenerate soul gains rule and through which it can pass.

Atwood speaks of the soul attaining a state “wherein it can rule over the elementary world and pass through it” [IV.4 ¶20]. The context suggests the regenerate soul is meant.

References: IV.4 ¶20

Elements

term · element, four elements

In Hermetic usage not common elements or chemical simples, but properties of the universal spirit in the Mercury; the true element is a spirit of life.

Atwood’s definition. The elements of the adepts are not bodily substances: “We must not limit, says Paracelsus, an element to a bodily substance or quality” [I.2 ¶26]. Rather, “the elements they speak of, as being introverted and transformed are the elements of the Mercury, properties of the universal spirit”, and “the true element is a spirit of life, and grows in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; the visible is only its receptacle. Water, air, earth and gold are not true elements; of Nature she writes “but Her, the true element, they have never found” [III.3 ¶65], i.e. the chemists. In verse she cites, the four are divided from a first mass: “And from that lump divided I foure sundry elements,” [III.3 ¶76]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Alchemists refer to the four elements of the Universal Ether” [APP ¶69].

Quoted authorities. Hermes says the elements are to be taken “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]; Atwood glosses: “The philosophic water then, being divided into four parts or hypostatic relations, they are called elements” [I.3 n5]. The author of The Triumph and the Master speak of their conversion and dissolution: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6]; “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14]. Eudoxus describes the Second Key, which separates the Stone’s constituents and converts them in sequence: it “makes Water of Earth, Air of Water, and Fire of Air” [IV.3 ¶5].

Identities asserted: elements of the Mercury / properties of the universal spirit; spirit of life [I.2 ¶26]; four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water [I.3 n5]; Nature (“Her”) as the true element [III.3 ¶65]; four elements of the Universal Ether [APP ¶69].

Identified with: elements of the Mercury, properties of the universal spirit [I.2 ¶26]; spirit of life [I.2 ¶26]; four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water [I.3 n5]; Nature (‘Her’) [III.3 ¶65]; four elements of the Universal Ether [APP ¶69]

References: I.2 ¶26, I.3 n4, I.3 n5, III.3 ¶65, III.3 ¶76, IV.2 ¶14, IV.2 ¶6, IV.3 ¶5, APP ¶69

Eleusian Mysteries

collective voice — accounts of

Accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries, cited by Atwood in support of Wisdom as the offspring of a vital experiment into nature.

Atwood invokes accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries to support her view that Wisdom is the offspring of a vital experiment into nature [II.1 ¶52].

See also: Mysteries

References: II.1 ¶52

Elias Artista

term · Elias, the artist

A figure the Adepts declare already born: a forerunner baptizing with water, foreshowing all things to the wise, born miraculously and before the Divine Light.

Atwood reports the saying of the Adepts: “Natus est jam Elias Artista (5); Elias, the artist, is born already” [IV.2 ¶12] (the book’s own translation). In the same passage, per the reader’s record, he is described as a forerunner who baptizes with water, foreshows all things to the wise, and is born miraculously and prior to the Divine Light [IV.2 ¶12]. The voice is that of the Adepts as quoted.

References: IV.2 ¶12

Elias spirit

term

A spirit said in the Table Talk to be born when the metal bond is broken, whose work is to prepare for something higher.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that when the metal bond is broken “the Elias spirit is born and his work is to prepare for something higher.” [APP ¶139]

See also: Spirit

References: APP ¶139

Elixir

term

The healing, life-prolonging and transmuting product of the Art, named in many reports of adepts and in quoted verse; also used of the soul’s immortal fortification.

Reports of adepts (Atwood). Artephius, “by the use of the elixir, is reported to have lived throughout the period of a thousand years” [I.1 ¶36]; the phrase “elixir of life” also appears in a quotation in that paragraph. “Alain de l’Isle is said to have obtained the Elixir” [I.1 ¶45]. Paracelsus is mentioned with “the elixir he boasts” [I.1 ¶64], in a sentence about “one who was in the habit of taking a potent spiritual medicine” whose effects worsened with depravity [I.1 ¶64]. Of Seton, “a report was spread about of the Elixir” [I.1 ¶66], in a passage that also speaks of the medicine he gave the sick; Starkey speaks of “the White and Red elixir” [I.1 ¶73]. Vaughan reportedly died “from an overdose of the elixir” [I.1 ¶74]. These records suggest a product that can be taken and that both heals and transmutes, though the passages do not define it.

Quoted authorities. Ripley: the separated elements of Mercury, “again commixed by equal weight or proportion, make the elixir complete” [I.2 ¶25]; the purged stone becomes “in whytenes Elixir of great might” [III.1 ¶62]. Bloomfield lists it among names of the privy quintessence: “Our great Elixir most high of price, Our Azot, our Basiliske, and our Adrop, our Cockatrice.” [I.2 ¶41]. Norton: “In this wise Elixir, of whom ye make mencion, Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34], i.e. engendered when celestial and elemental virtues accord.

Atwood’s spiritual use. The soul, re-entering the body through death, fortifies it “with the elixir of an immortal life” [II.3 ¶39].

Identities asserted: Azot, Basiliske, Adrop, Cockatrice and other names (Bloomfield) [I.2 ¶41]; a thing of Second Intention (Norton) [IV.2 ¶34].

Identified with: a thing of Second Intention [IV.2 ¶34]

References: I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶45, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73, I.1 ¶74, I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶41, II.3 ¶39, III.1 ¶62, IV.2 ¶34

Elixir and gold

term

Intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment, called vital products, whose exhibition without disclosure of source astonished common chemistry.

Atwood treats elixir and gold together as intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment: “Both of which are vital products” [II.4 ¶58]. Exhibited without discovery of their source, they caused much astonishment to common chemistry [II.4 ¶58].

See also: Gold

References: II.4 ¶58

Elixir of light

term

Light set free from the central essence, said to prolong life and cure disease and moral and physical defects.

Atwood: “This is the elixir of Light from the central essence” [I.3 n18]. In the same note it is identified with the tincture of many dyes and with the union of the purified spirit with its course, and is said to prolong life and to cure disease and moral and physical defects [I.3 n18].

Identified with: tincture of many dyes / union of the purified spirit with its course [I.3 n18]

See also: Light

References: I.3 n18

Elysian Fields

term · Elysium

A condition of being beyond corporeal life and generation, the place of the third, intellectual vision and the goal of the hidden labours.

For Atwood, Elysium is a state transcending corporeal life and generation, the goal of the hidden labours, and the place of the third, intellectual vision: “this third vision of the light is in Elysium” [II.4 ¶15].

Identities asserted: the Islands of the Blessed — “is denominated the Islands of the Blessed; and these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3]; the enclosed garden of Solomon and the Terrestrial Paradise — “This is Elysium, the enclosed garden of Solomon, where God condescends to walk and drink of the sealed fountain; the true Terrestrial Paradise” [II.4 ¶9].

Identified with: Islands of the blessed [II.4 ¶3]; enclosed garden of Solomon [II.4 ¶9]; Terrestrial Paradise [II.4 ¶9]

References: II.4 ¶15, II.4 ¶3, II.4 ¶9

Elysian light

term

The light reached after passing through the dark region; the object of inquiry and the state into which the liberated soul passes.

Atwood says the dark region must be traversed “before inquiry can hope to meet its object in the Elysian light” [II.3 ¶5]. It is the state into which the liberated soul passes; she illustrates with Aeneas “going forth to meet his father in the Elysian fields” [II.4 ¶21], where he receives the Epopteia. See also Elysian Fields.

See also: Light

References: II.3 ¶5, II.4 ¶21

Emanation

term

The doctrine by which the physical universe proceeds from the superstantial Light or will and is extended and corporified by multiplication of the unit.

Atwood presents an essential emanation as Kabalistic doctrine: “according to the doctrine of an essential emanation, the whole physical universe is extended and corporified” [III.2 ¶3], through multiplication of the indeficient unit into its parts under the Law of its own proceeding Light [III.2 ¶3]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) she speaks of “emanation from the superstantial Light or will” and says “The darkness is the emanation” [APP ¶66], the flat and qualitated becoming cubic by multiplication into itself [APP ¶66].

Identity asserted: darkness [APP ¶66].

Identified with: Darkness [APP ¶66]

References: III.2 ¶3, APP ¶66

person

Author of Wuthering Heights, criticized in the Table Talk as a Saturnine mass of power lacking the clearing Jupiter element.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Wuthering Heights is criticized as a Saturnine mass of power in potentiality, wanting the clearing Jupiter element; Emily is called Saturn [APP ¶175].

References: APP ¶175

Emotion

term

A mid-point between mind and matter, by which mind is moved into matter.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says: “Emotion is a mid-point between the two” [APP ¶80], i.e. between mind and matter, mind being moved into matter by it.

References: APP ¶80

Empedocles

person

Cited by Atwood, mainly from his Physics, in support of the soul’s exile from the light, concealed harmony manifested by ether, and the twofold order of union and strife.

Atwood cites Empedocles approvingly on several points. On our desertion of the best life by turning to externals: “Heaven’s exiles straying from the orb of light.” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 ¶10]. From the Physics, called “a poet”, he illustrates a concealed harmony made manifest by the motion of ether: “Then all the members of the god appeared” [II.4 ¶26–28, II.4 n16]. He also serves as an instance of “the physiologist” who substitutes elements as principles, differing from others in expression only [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶34]. From Physics, cap. 1, she draws support for a twofold intelligible and sensible order, perpetual interchange, and the One formed from the many: “All things in union now thro’ love conspire, And now thro’ strife divulsed are borne along” [III.2 ¶38, III.2 ¶39, III.2 n35].

Empirical

term

Used pejoratively of knowledge lacking the experience, gained only by observing remote effects.

Atwood: “All our knowledge without the experience is empirical, the result only of observation of remote effects” [IV.4 ¶12].

References: IV.4 ¶12

term

Something Hermes says is made from the golden matter; not explained in the text.

Hermes, quoted: “of them we make the encaustic of which we have written” [I.3 ¶59]; the reference is apparently to the golden matter. The text does not explain the term.

term

The handling of the work, which has particular turnings in which Eirenaeus says he often erred.

Eirenaeus, quoted: “in some particular turnings of the Encheiresis I erred often” [IV.1 ¶17]. The context suggests it means the manual handling or conduct of the work.

person

A visionary criticized in the Table Talk for lacking education of the intellect and so having little gauge for truth.

References: APP ¶105

term · enigmas

The veiled teaching and its hidden meaning, whose solution comes through desire and labour and opens the mystery of all things.

The first class of prayer is described as “seeking a clue whereby it may enter the intelligible profundity of the Enigma” [III.4 ¶24]. Its solution arises from labour and desire, even from attempts “which were not the solution of the Enigma, the solution itself arose” [III.4 ¶22]; unfolding it opens the mystery of all things. The voice of these passages is unclear in the records.

The riddle whose solution is to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of one’s natural understanding; Mind is its Key.

Atwood glosses the riddle plainly: “to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx; in other words, to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of his natural understanding” [IV.1 ¶48]. And: “For Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48].

References: III.3 n24, III.3 ¶36

Ens

term · last ens

An entity; in the Table Talk, such an ens is said to underlie the philosophic stone and to be the final term to which the sensual medium is brought.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says “such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone” [APP ¶108], and speaks of the sensual medium “brought to its pivot, to its last ens” [APP ¶110].

References: APP ¶108, APP ¶110

Ens of light

term

An entity of light, the purer conscious ens carried back to God; named with the rejected Corner Stone as what the wise raise.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the purer conscious ens of light” [APP ¶78] carried back to God, and per the reader’s record relates it to the excruciated Philosophic Matter and the real Stone [APP ¶78]. In the main text the wise “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8] in the living temple; it is not separately defined there.

See also: Light

References: II.1 ¶8, APP ¶78

Enthusiasm

term · enthusiastic energy

The state of being agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, contrary to phantasy; distinguished by the ancients from fanaticism.

Olympiodorus, quoted: “when we are agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, and the phantasy intervenes, the enthusiastic energy ceases” [II.2 ¶12]. Atwood notes the ancients drew a line “between enthusiasm and fanaticism” [II.4 ¶29], parallel to that between imaginative vision and the light of the true gods; she does not otherwise define it.

References: II.2 ¶12, II.4 ¶29

term

The person in trance, susceptible to imaginative impressions that linger in a place.

Atwood: “the entranced Subject is more or less susceptible of all imaginative impressures” [III.4 ¶42], including, per the reader’s record, those lingering in the place.

See also: Subject

References: III.4 ¶42

Envious

term

Said of philosophers in a special sense: they withhold the truth only from the ignorant and vicious, not from the just or wise.

Hermes, quoted, explains why philosophers withhold truth only from fools and the vicious, not from the just or wise: “For this reason are philosophers said to be envious” [I.3 ¶11]; again, “For this reason are the philosophers said to be envious” [III.4 ¶9].

References: I.3 ¶11, III.4 ¶9

Epictetus

person

Cited by Atwood in support of the view that the Mysteries become venerable when believed to be provided for the perfection of human life.

Atwood cites Epictetus in support: the Mysteries become venerable when one believes they were provided for the perfection of human life [II.4 ¶57].

References: II.4 ¶57

Epidaurian

collective voice

An initiate whose account, cited from Apuleius’s Metamorphoses Book 11, Atwood uses to illustrate what was done in the Mysteries.

Atwood cites, from Apuleius, Metam. Book 11, the Epidaurian’s first-person account as an initiate’s report of what was done in the Mysteries (quoted voice): “I approached the confines of death, and, having trod the threshold of Proserpine, I returned from it” [II.3 ¶45; II.3 n49].

References: II.3 n49, II.3 ¶45

treatise

A work quoted from its end in support of the claim that the all-begetting Spirit dwells within us.

Cited from the end of the Epistle to Trithemius (quoted voice) in support of the view, which Atwood adopts, that the all-begetting Spirit dwells in us: “But the Spirit begetting all doth in us dwell” [II.1 ¶27; II.1 n27].

References: II.1 n27, II.1 ¶27

Epopteia

term

The final grade of initiation, following telete and muesis, in which initiates are fixed as spectators of the intelligible and shown the Universal Nature and the soul.

In Atwood’s account (ATWOOD voice), epopteia is the last of three grades of initiation: “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. The record describes it as being fixed as spectators of the intelligible, its content being the revelation of the Universal Nature and of the soul [II.4 ¶23].

References: II.4 ¶23

Equilibriate virtue

term

In Khunrath’s words, the Stone’s balancing power by which it drives out suffering and disease of mind and body.

Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone “by its own equilibriate virtue expels suffering and every disease whether of mind or body” [IV.3 ¶28]. The context suggests a link with the health described nearby, from Julian, as a symmetry or equilibrium of nature [IV.3 ¶30]; the connection is the reader’s comparison, not stated outright.

See also: Virtue

References: IV.3 ¶28

Erasmus

person

Cited for his burlesques, which Atwood uses to illustrate the alchemical mania of the age.

Atwood mentions Erasmus’s burlesques as illustrating the alchemical mania of the age [I.1 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶64

Eros

term

In the passage given by the metropolitan of Memphis, Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle and called chief of the Immortals.

In the passage quoted from the metropolitan of Memphis (quoted voice), Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle: “the amiable Eros, chief of the Immortals” [III.3 ¶46].

References: III.3 ¶46

Esdras

person

Book of Esdras, cited to show that few attain the work and for the ‘outgoings of paradise’, identified with the seven mystic mountains.

Atwood quotes Esdras (Book 1, cap. 3) to illustrate that few attain the work: “The earth giveth much mould, whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of” [II.2 ¶29; II.2 n20]. She also cites Esdras for the ‘outgoings of paradise’, which are identified with the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9].

References: II.2 n20, II.2 ¶29, II.4 ¶9

Essence

term

In Eirenaeus, what gold and Mercury are recongealed into, healing all griefs; in Aristotle and Porphyry, separate particular subsistence and one’s own Essence to be established in.

The word appears in quoted voices with different senses.

  • Eirenaeus: gold and Mercury are recongealed “Both to an Essence which all griefs canheal.” [III.1 ¶69].
  • Aristotle (as quoted): “a separate subsistence as this or that particular thing especially belongs to what we call essence, (that is to say, composition of subject and object is necessarily implied in the idea of true intelligence)” [III.2 ¶53]; in this passage Matter is not essence [III.2 ¶53].
  • Porphyry: the reader is to be “being established in yourself and in your own Essence” [III.2 ¶59].

These uses are not reconciled in the records.

References: III.1 ¶69, III.2 ¶53, III.2 ¶59

Essence of light

term

What the Stone is made manifest as; identified with the true Form or Idea of Gold (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says the Stone is made manifest as an Essence of Light, “which Essence is the true Form or Idea of Gold” [APP ¶6].

Identified with: true Form or Idea of Gold [APP ¶6]

See also: Light

References: APP ¶6

Essential Intellect

term

In the Aristotle passage, the intellect to which human reason is subordinate.

Quoted from Aristotle: human reason is described as subordinate “on account of its subordination to essential intellect” [II.1 ¶34].

See also: Intellect

References: II.1 ¶34

Eternal essence

term

In Porphyry, an essence infinite in power, self-established and self-sufficient, to which nothing can be added and which place or relation would diminish.

Atwood quotes Porphyry (spelled here “Prophyry”): “When you have assumed to yourself an Eternal Essence, says Prophyry, infinite in itself according to power” [III.2 ¶59]. Such an essence is self-established and self-sufficient, seeking nothing but itself; nothing can be added to it, and adding place or relation diminishes it; “it is much more sufficient than any perpetually flowing fountain can be conceived to be” [III.2 ¶59].

See also: Essence

References: III.2 ¶59

Eternal Word

term

In the theosophist’s account, Adam’s leader, which had dominion in him in his Paradisiacal innocency.

Quoted from the theosophist: in Adam’s Paradisiacal innocency “The Eternal Word was his leader, and had dominion in him” [IV.3 ¶38].

See also: Word

References: IV.3 ¶38

Ether

term · Free Ether, Universal Ether, pure Ether, Aether, Aethera, Ethe, most supreme Ether, passive Ether

Atwood’s universal subtle medium: an all-pervading perfective essence, vehicle of the world-soul, which, separated and purified, is the matter of the Stone and rises into Light.

Nature and authorities. With Homberg, Boerhaave, Boyle and Berkeley, Atwood describes Ether as a distinct, universally diffused substance, sensible only in its mixtures and effects, source and bond of the elements, giving air its vitalizing power: “the occult virtues of the Ether; its all-pervading essence and perfective power” [I.2 ¶12]; one authority calls it “ether, and a pure invisible fire” [I.2 ¶14]. The Free Ether (voice of the Greeks) is “freed from the prison of gross matter, and able to work of itself intimately by the virtue of its own included light” [I.2 ¶16]; Euripides calls it Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17]. Ovid’s verse gives “liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera, non quicquam terrenae faecis habentum” (ours: liquid and weightless ether, having nothing of earthly dregs) [III.2 ¶37].

In the Art (ATWOOD). Separated and purified it is the matter of the Stone: “the Formal Light, by multiplication in its Ethe, is said to produce gold” [I.2 ¶46]; the Stone has “its foundation in the free Ether” [IV.4 ¶2]. Alchemists are “our Oedipus distillers of this Ether” [III.1 ¶13], ending in “the final resurrection of the pure Ether into Light” [III.1 ¶21], “depriving the ether of its wild affections and impressures” [IV.1 ¶4]. Pseudo-alchemists tried “to compress and entice the ether by mangetical disposition” and failed [II.1 ¶6]. Asserted identities: the alchemists’ mineral tree [II.3 ¶18]; “that Augean palace” of the multiplied Prester [II.3 ¶56]; “the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; non-being, the “simple Understanding of its ether” [III.3 ¶15].

In man and cosmos. “what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5], vehicle of the world-soul. Wholeness comes “from equilibriate circulation in their Ether” [II.4 ¶29]; rites work “by the medium of the passive Ether” [II.4 ¶36]; Intellect rides “secure in its Ether” [IV.1 ¶33]; see also “the liquid crystal of the understanding ether” [III.3 ¶10]. Imaginations can “pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode” [III.4 ¶42]; ether also names the anaesthetic [IV.1 ¶4]. In Boehme the Tincture “stays in its ether” [III.2 ¶16]; in Khunrath’s source (voice unclear) ether in the divine water “will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, later layer). “The Ether is two-fold: the mundane, which is full of the false forms; the pure, which is not of this world” [APP ¶64]; it is “a quintessence of those very four principles” and “the Quintessence of both worlds” [APP ¶69]; each has “a scrap of that ether shut in at our birth-conception”, “the omnia in omnibus of the Hermetic Riddle” [APP ¶119]; the spirit-man’s work “is to move the Ether” [APP ¶139]; of Lucifer, ether is identified with Heaven: “burn up the ether which was Heaven.” [APP ¶133]; “The Ether is the universal extended Matter; the Divine posit everywhere; life.” [APP ¶179].

Identified with: quintessence of the four principles called elements [APP ¶69]; Quintessence of both worlds [APP ¶69]; omnia in omnibus of the Hermetic Riddle [APP ¶119]; Heaven [APP ¶133]; universal extended Matter; life [APP ¶179]; pure invisible fire [I.2 ¶14]; mineral tree [II.3 ¶18]; Augean palace [II.3 ¶56]; Sphinx of the Universe [III.1 ¶5]; Non-being [III.3 ¶15]; Jove [I.2 ¶17]

References: I.1 ¶20, I.2 ¶12, I.2 ¶14, I.2 ¶16, I.2 ¶17, I.2 ¶46, II.1 ¶6, II.3 ¶18, II.3 ¶56, II.4 ¶29, II.4 ¶36, II.4 ¶40, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶5, III.2 ¶16, III.2 ¶37, III.3 ¶10, III.3 ¶15, III.3 ¶9, III.4 ¶42, IV.1 ¶33, IV.1 ¶4, IV.4 ¶10, IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶4, APP ¶119, APP ¶133, APP ¶139, APP ¶170, APP ¶179, APP ¶64, APP ¶69

Ether natural

term

In the Appendix, the first Ether arising from nature, through which thoughts, images, passions and desires rise to their own sphere, beneath the pure Ether and the Divine Light.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says thoughts, images, passions and desires “all rise up through this first Ether Natural and abide on a sphere of their own above it” [APP ¶170]. Above it lies the pure Ether, related to the moral nature, and then the region of Divine Light [APP ¶170].

References: APP ¶170

Etheral quintessence

term · Ethereal Quintessences

The ethereal which art separates from mortal existence, read as Plato’s One Whole and Aristotle’s perfect world; its estates rise successively, figured in Hesiod’s generations.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice) reads Plato and Aristotle as pointing to it: “Plato yet more plainly alluding to the Etheral Quintessence, in Timaeus, says, that of four elements the Demiurgus assumed One Whole from wholes” — perfect and free from age and disease; of such descriptions she asks “what other, therefore, should they either mean but the ethereal” [III.2 ¶38].
