In the plural, the Ethereal Quintessences are successive estates called forth by the light and heat of the superincumbent mind: “the several estates of the Ethereal Quintessences arising one above another”, figured in Hesiod’s generations [III.3 ¶42].

Identified with: One Whole from wholes (Plato) [III.2 ¶38]

See also: Quintessence

References: III.2 ¶38, III.3 ¶42

Ethereal being

term

The one being whose relation, action and passion the authors mean by sulfur, mercury, earth, and twofold or third matter.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice) says the authors’ various names (sulfur, mercury, earth, twofold or third matter) refer to “the magnetic relation, action, and passion of the Ethereal being in itself” [I.2 ¶42].

See also: Being

References: I.2 ¶42

Ethereal element

term

The subject described by negations (no form, quality, body, reason or bound, but a certain Infinity) in Atwood’s discussion of Matter.

Continuing her discussion of Matter, Atwood writes: “But since the ethereal element is described by so many ablative characteristics” [III.2 ¶53], namely that it is neither form, quality, body, reason nor bound, but a certain Infinity. The text does not state that the ethereal element is the same as Matter, though the context suggests a close link.

See also: Elements

References: III.2 ¶53

Ethereal glass

term

Something passive to intellect as a mirror is to images, subsisting without imagination, felt rather than known; the Passive Nature is said to be of this kind.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice) compares it to a mirror: “so is this ethereal glass to intellect, subsisting according to processure and in defect of all imagination” [III.2 ¶60]. It is felt, not known, and the Passive Nature is said to be a thing of this kind [III.2 ¶60].

See also: Glass

References: III.2 ¶60

Ethereal humidity

term

The moisture that nourishes and educates the Solar Light, set beside Luna as ‘Domina Humiditatis’.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “The ethereal humidity nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]; it is set beside Luna, called Domina Humiditatis (ours: mistress of moisture) [IV.1 ¶29].

References: IV.1 ¶29

Ethereal hypostasis

term

The Greek counterpart of the alchemists’ first matter: the one life-substance divided into three principles in dissolution, which revolves in its First Cause when the Stone is confirmed.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice) treats it as the Greek counterpart of the alchemists’ first matter: “that ethereal hypostasis we were before discussing” [III.1 ¶3]. In the dissolution, “the ethereal hypostasis is divided against itself and brought to a separation even as these three” principles [III.1 ¶53]. When the Stone is confirmed, rising in rational supremacy over sense and finite reflection, “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62]; that passage does not define it further. See also “filling the Ethereal Hypostasis with acme and power” [II.4 ¶29].

See also: Hypostasis

References: III.1 ¶3, III.1 ¶53, IV.3 ¶62

Ethereal Quadrangle

term

That which, in the Fifth Essence, becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice): in the Fifth Essence “the Ethereal Quadrangle becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity” [III.3 ¶32].

References: III.3 ¶32

Ethereal spirit

term · Etherial Spirit

The sought spirit, never existing separately on earth but hidden in the beings it sustains; in Synesius, the intermediate nature joining divine and lowest, phantastic until purified by art.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “the ethereal spirit does not subsist of itself, separate or tangibly on earth” [I.2 ¶20], but is hidden and defiled within the beings it sustains. She equates its subjugation with that of the Sphinx: the trial “ends in her subjugation; in other words, the Ethereal Spirit abandons her phantasy” [III.1 ¶20], yielding the clear light of understanding to the trained investigator. Quoting Synesius, it is the intermediate nature between rational and brutal life, corporeal and incorporeal: “it is the medium which conjoins divine natures with the lowest of all” [II.2 ¶10]. It is identified with “the phantastical condition also of the natural understanding essence, before it is purified by art and exalted. This Etherial Spirit” [II.2 ¶10].

Identified with: Sphinx [III.1 ¶20]; natural understanding essence [II.2 ¶10]

See also: Spirit

References: I.2 ¶20, II.2 ¶10, III.1 ¶20

Ethereal vehicle

term

The prepared medium in which the seed of gold is planted so as to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the seed of gold must be “planted in its proper ethereal vehicle, well prepared and fallow” to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase [I.3 n40]. Elsewhere the divine unions “tried the ethereal vehicle to its utmost susceptibility” [II.4 ¶40].

See also: Vehicle

References: I.3 n40

Ethereal waters

term

The waters on which the displaced sulfur floats while they tear, decoct and soften the sensual dominant.

Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the displaced sulfur is made “to float upon the ethereal waters, whilst these continue to tear, decoct, and soften the sensual dominant” [III.1 ¶53].

See also: Water

References: III.1 ¶53

Ethics

treatise

A work cited for Tartarus as the region next beyond Hades.

Cited for Tartarus as the next region beyond Hades [II.3 ¶36].

References: II.3 ¶36

Ethnics

collective voice · Ethnic

A group whose Anima Mundi doctrine Atwood says agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine.

Atwood says the Ethnics’ doctrine of the Anima Mundi agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine [I.2 ¶14].

Ethnic. Used by Atwood in contrast to Christian, “both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]; the text does not define it further.

See also: Early Christians and the wisest Ethnics

References: I.2 ¶14, II.2 ¶5

Eudoxus

person

Speaker of The Six Keys of Eudoxus, which Atwood quotes as practical instruction on the Art until its defective final Keys make her turn elsewhere.

Atwood cites Eudoxus’s introduction to the Six Keys in support of the view that the difficulty lies in learning the Art from books and that the seeker needs deep knowledge of Nature: “the practice of our Art is the most difficult thing in the world, not in regard to its operation” [IV.2 ¶4]. The Six Keys of Eudoxus, Opening Into the Most Secret Philosophy is named in a chapter heading [IV.3 ¶1], which makes him the first-person speaker of the quoted text that follows; Atwood presents it as instruction on the practice [IV.3 ¶10; IV.3 ¶12; IV.3 ¶14; IV.3 ¶16]. She qualifies its usefulness: its last Keys, on Multiplication and Projection, are avowedly defective, “The Keys of Eudoxus open no more” [IV.3 ¶17], so she turns to another source.

References: IV.2 ¶4, IV.3 ¶1, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶12, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶17

Eudoxus in Plutarch

person

Eudoxus as reported in Plutarch’s De Iside et Osiride, cited for the myth of Jupiter’s grown-together feet freed by Isis, which Atwood reads as an allegory of the Art.

Atwood cites Eudoxus in Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride, for the myth in which Isis frees Jupiter’s grown-together feet; she reads it as an allegory of the Art. The interpretation quoted: “the mind and reason of the Supreme God, which in nature is invisible and dwelling in obscurity, by being put in motion becomes known” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n28].

See also: Plutarch

References: III.1 n28, III.1 ¶23

Euripides

person

Quoted for Ether called Jove, for the felicity of seeing the Mysteries, and from the Bacchis on death, purification and initiation.

Atwood quotes Euripides (quoted voice) in support of her account of Ether as all-nourishing and called Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17; I.2 n16]. To show that the people placed their chief felicity in the Mysteries, she quotes a line spoken by Hercules and one from the Bacchis: “I was blessed when I got a sight of the mysteries” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8]. From Bacchis she also takes “a dream of death” for the threshold where the Lesser Mysteries end [II.3 ¶36; II.3 n48], and Bacchae verses supporting purification and initiation [II.3 ¶43; II.3 ¶44].

References: I.2 n16, I.2 ¶17, II.2 n8, II.2 ¶5, II.3 n48, II.3 ¶36, II.3 ¶43, II.3 ¶44

Evestrum

term · Divine evestrum

Paracelsus’s term, used by Atwood in the Appendix for the dream of its whole afterlife the soul brings into the body, its destiny; God’s grace is the Divine evestrum relative to man.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood takes up Paracelsus’s term: “the soul comes into this body with the dream of its whole afterlife presented to it” [APP ¶57]. This is its destiny, which moves a will that does not see beyond it. Against it stands “God’s grace (the Divine evestrum, relatively to man)” [APP ¶57], by which, Atwood says, we overcome it.

References: APP ¶57

Exalted energy

term

What the abusers of the art succeeded in inducing before denying the Light its fulfilment; not further defined.

Atwood (her own voice) says the abusers of the work denied the Light its fulfilment after “having succeeded in inducing an exalted energy” [III.4 ¶6]. The text does not define the expression further.

References: III.4 ¶6

Excrements

term

In the verse Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the residue taken away once the matter has grown very dry, before the young Child is lodged in a bright bed.

The word occurs in the quoted verse of The Hunting of the Greene Lyon: when the matter has grown very dry, “The excrements be tane away;” [III.1 ¶65], before the young Child is laid in a bright bed. The voice is the quoted poem, not Atwood’s own.

References: III.1 ¶65

Exemplary Law

term

The law of Universal nature, whose fountain Atwood names as the Substant Unity.

Atwood speaks of the Substant Unity as “the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law” [III.3 ¶79]. The text gives no further definition.

See also: Law

References: III.3 ¶79

Exemplary light

term

That without which, Atwood says, every plan of improvement is defective; not further defined.

Atwood judges “every plan defective without the Exemplary Light” [IV.4 ¶18]. The expression is not further defined in the records.

See also: Light

References: IV.4 ¶18

Exemplary Logos

term

In Atwood’s words, the Logos hidden and slain from the foundation in the fiat of our Identity, occulted in two diametrically reverse poles or principles.

Atwood writes that “the exemplary Logos is hidden, — slain from the foundation in the exterminating fiat of our Identity” [III.3 ¶79]; its occultation lies in two diametrically reverse poles or principles. The text does not define it further.

See also: Logos

References: III.3 ¶79

Exoteric

term

Atwood’s qualifier for Part I’s outer view of the progress and theory of alchemy, used in the heading.

The word appears in the heading of Part I: “An Exoteric View of the Progress and Theory of Alchemy” [I.1 ¶1]. Its sense is not further explained in the records; the heading apparently marks Part I as the outward, historical treatment.

References: I.1 ¶1

Experience

term

In the verse Tablet, a personified creative power that framed all things from nothing; in Atwood’s prose, the resulting experience of life, third of the alchemical Three.

The voice is unclear. In the verse rendering of the Tablet the speaker addresses Experience as a creative power: “That thou art the very same, That didst from nothing all things frame;” [III.3 ¶76], having made the One Thing. In the following prose Atwood speaks of the Matter proved simple in experience and of “the resulting experience of life” [III.3 ¶77] as the third of the alchemical Three. How the personified power and the third principle relate is not stated; the records leave both readings side by side.

References: III.3 ¶76, III.3 ¶77

The experienced

collective voice

An unnamed authority Atwood relies on for man’s connection to the fountain of Universal Nature.

Atwood appeals to “the experienced” without naming them, on the point of our connection to the fountain of the Universal Nature [II.4 ¶19].

References: II.4 ¶19

Experiment

term · experimental, Divine Experiment, vital experiment, this Experiment

Atwood’s word for the practical hermetic work itself, seldom attempted and more rarely completed, through which the ancients found their whole philosophy and the Fathers came into Experience.

In Atwood’s own voice the Experiment is the practical work: “That was the Experiment that led our Fathers into Experience” [III.3 ¶61], and experience is the proper test of philosophy. She insists on perseverance for it (“than perseverance for this experiment” [III.4 ¶45]). She explains “why the Divine Experiment has been so seldom attempted and more rarely brought to a legitimate conclusion on this earth” [IV.4 ¶7], and says “In the course of this vital experiment the ancients discovered the whole of the philosophy they teach” [IV.4 ¶9]. She identifies it with a “pyrotechnical induction” of “the quintessence of Universal nature and her fruitful springs” [IV.4 ¶9].

The adjective “experimental” carries the same weight in Part I: Democritus is styled “the father of experimental philosophy” and “Pliny bears witness to the experimental fame of Democritus, and his skill in the occult sciences and practice of them” [I.1 ¶12]; Aristotle “led mankind astray from the path of true experiment” [I.1 ¶16]; the theosophic schools are “based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17], where practical science is set against abstracts. Contrast Atwood’s critical use of “experimental philosophy” for modern science [IV.4 ¶30].

Identified with: Pyrotechnical induction [IV.4 ¶9]

See also: Vital experiment

References: I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, III.3 ¶61, III.4 ¶45, IV.4 ¶7, IV.4 ¶9

Experimental adeptist

collective voice

The voice cited from the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C., cited for the reversal of death in the work.

Atwood cites the title page of the Philosophical Epitaph of W.C. to illustrate the overcoming of death in the work: “O death how art thou vanquished” [I.3 n43].

See also: Adept

References: I.3 n43

Experimental knowledge

term

What the soul has not yet attained while she regards her image objectively and is ‘in Hades’.

Atwood describes the soul, while she regards her image objectively and is in Hades, as being “before attaining to the experimental knowledge” [II.3 ¶36]. The term is not further defined here; the context suggests a knowing by inward experience as opposed to outward regard.

References: II.3 ¶36

Experimental philosophy

term

Atwood’s name for modern science following Lord Bacon’s ‘exterminating chase’, which she says labours for selfish aggrandizement.

Atwood, in her own voice, criticizes modern science led by Lord Bacon’s “exterminating chase”: “experimental philosophy labours for selfish aggrandizement” [IV.4 ¶30].

See also: Philosophy

References: IV.4 ¶30

Experimental proof

term

The practical stage of the art, which follows study of the doctrine.

Atwood distinguishes study of the doctrine from what “is afterwards needed for the experimental proof” [III.4 ¶15], that is, the practical stage of the art.

References: III.4 ¶15

Expiation

term

A required means of approaching the secrets of the highest causes, which Atwood compares to Charon’s fee.

Atwood states: “neither are the secrets of the highest causes approached without a mean of expiation” [III.2 ¶44], comparing it to the fee paid to Charon. What the expiation consists of is not spelled out in the record.

References: III.2 ¶44

Expounders

collective voice

Unnamed interpreters of the Mysteries whose narcotic explanation of initiatory transfiguration Atwood rejects.

Atwood reports the expounders’ view that “all this splendid delirium and transfiguration in the Mysteries was the effect of narcotic liquors” [II.4 ¶56], and rejects it as common sense acting Procrustes-like.

References: II.4 ¶56

Exstasis

term

In the Appendix, the means by which the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes the desire of the lower life “opening up into the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life, by exstasis” [APP ¶97]. The four names given there are apparently treated as equivalent.

References: APP ¶97

External and internal worlds

term

Outer and inner reality, which at the completion of the work are seen to blend and confirm each other.

Atwood writes that at the completion “the External and Internal Worlds were seen to blend together in confluent harmony” [III.3 ¶82], each confirming the other.

References: III.3 ¶82

External fire

term

In Eirenaeus, the well-regulated outward heat that alone assists Nature in the Second operation.

Quoting Eirenaeus, Atwood gives the Second operation as performed by Nature “by the sole assistance of a well-regulated external fire” [IV.1 ¶11].

See also: Fire

References: IV.1 ¶11

External man

term

Boehme’s term for the outward self, which could hardly grasp or express what he had seen inwardly.

In a passage Atwood quotes from Boehme, he says of his inward vision: “I could very hardly apprehend the same in my external man” [III.2 ¶16].

References: III.2 ¶16

F

Faber

person

A Hermetic writer Atwood lists among Paracelsus’s worthy disciples and in the ‘golden chain’ of Hermetic philosophers who traced the poets’ allusions.

Faber is listed in a note with the work Opera Medico-Chimica [I.1 ¶70; I.1 n88]. Atwood names him with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Helvetius as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Tollius and Michael Maier in the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers” who traced the poets’ allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own; she cites them in support [III.1 ¶25]. In an aside on Ripley’s method the text remarks: “Faber is so wise that he will not understand him” [IV.1 ¶36].

References: I.1 n88, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶25, IV.1 ¶36

Fable of Isis and Osiris

collective voice · Egyptian Fable of Isis and Osiris, Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris, Isis, Osiris

Cited to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring, represented by the birth of Horus.

Atwood uses the fable to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring; the birth of Horus represents the metaphysical offspring [IV.2 ¶6; IV.2 ¶7; IV.2 ¶11].

Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris. Named as the mythology that Synesius is said to explain by the enigma of the two pairs of eyes [III.1 ¶45].

Isis and Osiris. Atwood uses the pair as an image: reason constantly seeks her true Hypostasis “as Isis for Osiris” [II.3 ¶46].

Fable (Typhon, Osiris, Isis; the Egyptian monarch). Atwood reads the fable that “Typhon killed Osiris, his uterine brother, and scattered his members to the four winds” [III.1 ¶53] as illustrating the threefold division of the ethereal hypostasis; the hair grown in Ethiopia figures the fire allowed to grow [III.1 ¶56]; and Isis figures the reconciling of the opposites [III.1 ¶63].

See also: Dead and revived god (Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris), Isis, Osiris

References: II.3 ¶46, III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶63, IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 ¶6, IV.2 ¶7

Fable of Mars and Venus taken together by Vulcan

collective voice

The fable cited to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, with fuller explanation deferred.

Atwood cites the fable of Mars and Venus caught together by Vulcan to illustrate the need of the masculine tincture with Venus, promising to explain it later [I.3 n49].

See also: Vulcan

References: I.3 n49

Fabricate Intellect

term

The intellect which, Atwood says, is not born without Motion, figured by Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan’s aid.

Atwood writes: “without the instrumentality of Motion, which the lame god personates, the Fabricate Intellect is not born” [IV.1 ¶34]. The figure is Pallas brought forth from Jove with Vulcan’s help; Vulcan, the lame god, stands for Motion (stated).

See also: Intellect

References: IV.1 ¶34

Faculty of Wisdom

term · Wisdom

In the cabalistic scriptures and antique schools Atwood reports, a higher faculty latent in man which, revealed, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her source.

Reporting the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood speaks of “the germ of a higher faculty or Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32] in man, which, revealed and set alone, knows nature intuitively and works magically as her substratal source. It is identified with “This Being” (“This Being, moreover, or Faculty of Wisdom” [II.1 ¶32]).

Identified with: This Being [II.1 ¶32]

See also: Wisdom

References: II.1 ¶32

Faeces

term

The earthy residue of the matter: in Hermes the third from two, from which death is removed; in Sendivogius cast away; in Eudoxus kept and washed, as hiding the Balm of Life.

The records come from three quoted authorities, who differ on its handling. In a Hermetic passage it is the third of the three that come from two, the earth that remains below, and death is to be taken away: “death from the faeces” [I.3 ¶23]. Sendivogius has the residue discarded after putrefaction, before the spirit is returned to the water: “the faeces being cast away” [III.3 ¶29]. Eudoxus, by contrast, says the black earthy residue at the bottom of the vessel must not be discarded: “The Balm of Life is hid in these unclean faeces” [IV.3 ¶8]; it is washed with the celestial water until it is no longer black. Whether these describe different stages or different practices is not settled by the records.

References: I.3 ¶23, III.3 ¶29, IV.3 ¶8

Faith

term

For Atwood, faith is a real ideal conception that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge, not blind credulity; it is a common witness inferring a reality beyond experience, to be directed by reason.

Atwood insists that “The faith we invite is no blind credulity” [III.3 ¶64]. Faith is a real ideal conception, however small, that leads experimental inquiry and grows into knowledge and practical experience. It is a liberty of thought that bears its own evidence. She equates it with the ideal conception: “without faith, without the ideal conception, nothing is or can be proven” [III.3 ¶64].

Later she presents faith as a witness common to all: “we have a witness which believes and infers, a reality beyond present experience” [IV.4 ¶15]. It draws the other faculties after it: “faith is the very attracting loadstone which hope pursues” [IV.4 ¶19], drawing hope, desire and reason. Faith must nevertheless be directed by reason [IV.4 ¶15–19].

Faith. The doctrine of Faith is invoked as an analogy: as the soul is permanently united with the glorified body, so spirits and purified bodies are joined, and “there shall be no more separation or death” [IV.3 ¶10].

Identified with: ideal conception [III.3 ¶64]

References: III.3 ¶64, IV.3 ¶10, IV.4 ¶15, IV.4 ¶19

Fall

term

In the Table Talk, Atwood treats the Fall as Nature’s being taken from the primal source into a will, a fall that was spiritual before it was sensible.

Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes: “Nature has taken from the primal source into a will is the history of the Fall.” [APP ¶48]. The sentence is garbled as printed; apparently the Fall is Nature’s being taken from the primal source into a will. She also holds that “the Fall was not at first sensible, but spiritual; the principle of the Fall is a long way back behind its effects” [APP ¶121]. Birth into this life is a continuous image of it [APP ¶121]. See also feminine principle, which she calls the cause of the Fall [APP ¶98].

References: APP ¶121, APP ¶48

False imagination

term

What remains of sense impressions even in trance, which must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity.

Atwood (II.2) describes the remnant of sense impressions that persists even in trance as “a false imagination, which it is requisite to destroy” [II.2 ¶10]. It must be destroyed before the understanding spirit can receive Divinity [II.2 ¶10].

See also: Imagination

References: II.2 ¶10

Famous Christian philosophers

collective voice · these famous Christian philosophers

Unnamed philosophers who supply the mountain allegory. Atwood qualifies them: their promises of gold drew futile public searches.

Atwood gives their allegory of the mountain: wind, earthquake, fire, calm, then the tincture. It begins “When you have discovered the mountain, the first miracle that will appear is this” [II.3 ¶33]. She qualifies their use: their promises of gold drew the public into futile searches [II.3 ¶34].

See also: Philosophers

References: II.3 ¶33, II.3 ¶34

Faraday Society

collective voice — opening meeting address, 1846

An address at the Faraday Society’s opening meeting, cited by Atwood as an example of the modern view of alchemists as deluded crucible-brooders, which she criticizes.

Atwood cites this address as a sample of the modern view that the alchemists were deluded crucible-brooders, and she criticizes it [I.1 ¶33]. The passage she quotes derives a word from an alchemist’s obscure style: “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33].

References: I.1 ¶33

Fawkes

person

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n35

Feminine principle

term · feminine spirit, passive feminine principle

In the Table Talk, the feminine principle is that which is above, drawing the self-willed source upward by love; it is the cause of the Fall and, advanced, of restoration.

Both points come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood identifies the feminine principle with Wisdom and the heart life: “that which is above (the feminine principle, — Wisdom, — the heart life)” [APP ¶98]. It draws the self-willed source upward by love, and the self-willed source thereby becomes a passive feminine principle [APP ¶98]. It works both ways: “As the feminine spirit is the cause of the Fall”, so, advanced, it is the cause of restoration [APP ¶98].

Identified with: Wisdom; the heart life [APP ¶98]

See also: Principles

References: APP ¶98

Ferment

term · fermented, ferments, fermenting, fermented spirit, fermenting principle, fermental, Firment, brazen ferment

The active agent by which one life works on another (or a thing on itself), opening and dissolving it so that a higher life is freed and exalted; Hermes calls it the Key of the philosophers.

Atwood’s usage. A ferment is a superior power that frees the subject-matter: “being set free by the force of a superior ferment or attraction” [I.2 ¶4]. The Ether is called fermenting, and “the fermented Spirit assimilates the Light throughout” [I.2 ¶8]. It is a thing’s own agent of change and converts it into another nature with nothing foreign added. In the Art the Spirit is raised “by its won prepared must or leaven” and gains virtue “in proportion to the virtue which it has acquired in the fermentation” [I.2 ¶48]. The Stone is exalted by fermentation within its own kind, and “every ferment begets its own exaltation” [I.3 n55]. Reason acts as a ferment and “would gather all up, as a ferment” into its Light [III.1 ¶21]. She contrasts “that body which is gold (not a brazen ferment)” [III.1 ¶19]. Sulfur is called the golden ferment, and the rising light keeps “a fermental odor of the body” so that the soul does not depart altogether [III.1 ¶53]. The result depends on the agent: “according to the virtue of the fermenting principle is the result obtained”. The philosophic matter “is purified by successive interchanging of ferments”, as sap becomes wine [IV.1 ¶44, ¶46].

Hermes compares the ferment to leaven in dough: “see how the ferment in this case doth change the former natures to another thing” [I.3 ¶58]. It must be kindred, since “there is no ferment otherwise than from a kindred nature” [I.3 ¶58]. It whitens, prevents combustion, holds the tincture and joins bodies, and it is the Key of the philosophers [I.3 ¶58].

Other voices. In a note whose voice is unclear, “the inquisitive light once entering as a ferment” meets its proper pole and converts the medium into itself [II.3 n40]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon requires that “Which Ferment must be of such a thing, As was the workes begyning;” [III.1 ¶65]. In the poem this means Luna for the white and Sol for the red, each worked alone with the Lion’s blood. It is added warm to the Magnet as a fourth part, and continual fermentation multiplies the Medicine [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood’s “Rational Ferment” [III.1 ¶66] is a separate term.

Table Talk (APP, later layer). Here a ferment is the action of one life on another: “When one life being fermented throws its life to another equally fermented” [APP ¶42]. Seven is “a Rest from the ferment or action of the Vitalizing or Divine principles” [APP ¶69]. The reader is told to “so ferment the whole including spirit of your life that it, the former, opens, corrupts, dissolves” [APP ¶126], and “each fermented spirit advances upon its origin” [APP ¶111]. Fermented = elaborated: “perfectly elaborated — i.e., fermented”, said of the individual Logos that transmutes the whole being [APP ¶101].

Identified with: elaborated [APP ¶101]

References: I.2 ¶4, I.2 ¶48, I.2 ¶8, I.3 n55, I.3 ¶58, II.3 n40, III.1 ¶19, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶65, IV.1 ¶44, IV.1 ¶46, APP ¶101, APP ¶111, APP ¶126, APP ¶42, APP ¶69

Ferment of philosophers

term

In a passage quoted from Aristhenes, that into which the ‘least’ thing is to be drawn by artifice; the text does not define it.

Atwood quotes Aristhenes, who says to “draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26]. The thing to be drawn in is the ‘least’ thing. The passage does not define the term further. See ferment.

See also: Philosophers

References: II.2 ¶26

Fermentation

term · fermentative process, fermentative law, fermental principle, Fermentacion, Firmentation

The core operation in which a life worked by a kindred life dissolves and passes into a higher state; Atwood’s best image of the Divine Art and the final cementing of the Stone’s union.

Main text (Atwood). Fermentation is the subject’s artificial progress to perfection: “In its artificial fermentation and progress towards perfection” [I.2 ¶37]. Liquid analogies denote “the fermental principle of the spirit and her distilled quintessence” [I.2 ¶33]. The chapter title names “the spontaneous fermentation which the Vital Spirit undergoes, and the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” [III.1 ¶9]. Modern practice does not push this process to the uttermost [III.1 ¶9]. Atwood distinguishes two kinds: “there is a twofold fermentation — a spiritual and a bodily” [IV.3 ¶21]. The spiritual kind multiplies the tinctures, and the bodily kind incorporates the medicine into gold or silver. Fermentation is the last operation, in which the Stone’s union is finally cemented and its parts agree and relate to the external world: “which union or consummation of its transmutative virtue is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. She asserts an identity with the Kabalah: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God, that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27]. The Stone is fermented with its own metal (silver for the White, gold for the Red), which Atwood reads as Light [IV.3 ¶27].

Eudoxus. His Fifth Key operation is “the Fermentation of the Stone with the perfect body” [IV.3 ¶14]. The Stone is joined, as leaven and through the Spirit, with the Perfect Body, so that the whole becomes a leaven able to multiply.

Table Talk (APP, later layer). Here fermentation is the core operation: a life fermented by its similar passes into a further state, and this is repeated over and over. “The word fermentation conveys an idea of the perfecting principle and of the possibility of transmutation beyond any other word”, and “it is the best image of the Divine Art which earthly processes give” [APP ¶27]. One life is worked by another so that both dissolve and are reproduced in a third. Unlike ordinary generation, the result is exalted: “spiritual generation is according to the fermentative law”, an ascending process [APP ¶132].

Identified with: the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God (Kabalah) [IV.3 ¶27]

References: I.2 ¶33, I.2 ¶37, III.1 ¶9, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶21, IV.3 ¶27, APP ¶132, APP ¶27

Fermentative virtue

term

The power of vital melioration that man possesses whole within himself, for the rectification of Nature’s Law.

Atwood holds that man has within himself “the whole fermentative virtue, motive, and principle of vital melioration” for the rectification of Nature’s Law [IV.4 ¶3].

See also: Virtue

References: IV.4 ¶3

Festina lente and Ne quid nimis

collective voice — sayings · Festina lente, Ne quid nimis

Proverbial sayings cited in the Table Talk in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, higher or lower.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood cites “Festina lente, Ne quid nimis” in support of avoiding haste and excess in the work, whether higher or lower [APP ¶110].

References: APP ¶110

Fichte

person

A philosopher named with Kant and Schelling, whose metaphysics Atwood criticizes as falling short of objective realization; in the Table Talk he saw the Absolute ground without experiencing it.

In the main text Atwood groups Kant, Fichte and Schelling and criticizes their metaphysics. It ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Fichte broke through into the Absolute ground, seeing it but without experiencing it [APP ¶96]. He appears again in the same list as one who ‘knew it’ [APP ¶117].

References: III.2 ¶31, APP ¶117, APP ¶96

Ficinus

person · Ficinus the Platonist, Marsilii Ficini

Translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes, whose Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander Atwood cites; he explained the art theoretically.

Atwood cites Ficinus’s Latin version of the Asclepian Dialogues and the Poimander [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n11]. She calls him the translator of Plato and of the works imputed to Hermes. He explained the art theoretically, and she cites his Liber de Arte Chemica (Marsilii Ficini Florent.) [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n68]. He also appears as “Ficinus the Platonist” in a list [I.1 ¶39].

References: I.1 n11, I.1 n68, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶7

Fiery bath of love

term

In a quoted monk’s continuation of Basil Valentine, something instituted by one who has befriended Vulcan; the text does not explain it.

The monk who continues Basil Valentine says that only one who has “firmly contracted friendship with Vulcan, and instituted the Fiery bath of Love” can demonstrate the separation of venom from the Medicine [IV.1 ¶40]. The expression is not explained.

References: IV.1 ¶40

Fiery Dragon

term

In a recipe quoted from Eirenaeus, an ingredient (four parts) bearing the Magic Steel in its belly, joined to nine parts Lodestone; the text does not explain it.

Atwood quotes Eirenaeus: “Take four parts of our Fiery Dragon, which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The Fiery Dragon is to be conjoined to nine parts Lodestone [IV.1 ¶43]. The passage does not explain it.

See also: Dragon

References: IV.1 ¶43

Fiery essence

term

In Eudoxus, what animates the Water once the faeces are washed free of blackness; it works all the wonders of the Art.

Eudoxus says that once the faeces are washed free of blackness, “your Water shall be animated with this Fiery Essence, which works all the wonders of our Art” [IV.3 ¶8].

See also: Essence

References: IV.3 ¶8

Fiery ordeal

term

The trial that reason is artificially constrained not to escape.

Atwood speaks of reason “being artificially constrained, lest it should escape the fiery ordeal” [I.3 n50].

References: I.3 n50

Fifth essence

term

What the two warring dragons become when decocted in their own venom; for Atwood, a state beyond the four degrees, neuter from all yet partaking of all.

A French adept quoted by Atwood says the two warring dragons, “being decocted totally in their own venom, are turned into a Fifth Essence” [III.1 ¶58]. Atwood describes it as made beyond the four precedent degrees of perfection: “neuter from all, yet partaking of all in perpetuity of union” [III.3 ¶32]. It is embodied but not subject to gross corporeity [III.3 ¶32].

See also: Essence

References: III.1 ¶58, III.3 ¶32

Final cause

term · Final Causes

The end or purpose into whose supernatural fixity Art brings the Matter; hidden in ordinary life but manifest in Alchemy.

For Atwood, the Matter’s alterations end when it “is brought by Art into the supernatural fixity of its Final Cause” [III.2 ¶22]. Final causes are ends or purposes. They are hidden in ordinary life, but in Alchemy, in act as in effect, “Final Causes are of all things most manifestly revealed” [III.4 ¶9]. The superior power filling the soul is “proximate to the Final Cause” [III.4 ¶6].

In IV.2 a passage of the Master carries a gloss whose voice is unclear: “the boundary of hearts (i.e., the Final Cause)” [IV.2 ¶14]. It enters above the Foliated Sulphur when fire is poured on it. Compare the generated Being, “perceiving itself indeed to be the Final Object of its own First Cause, is good” [IV.2 ¶8]. See also First Cause.

Identified with: boundary of hearts [IV.2 ¶14]

See also: Causes

References: III.2 ¶22, III.4 ¶6, III.4 ¶9, IV.2 ¶14, IV.2 ¶8

Fire

term · our fire, Fires, internal Fire, philosophic fire

The secret, vital fire of the philosophers, distinct from common fire; variously identified with Intellect, the life of man, the essence of life, the sulfur and seed of gold.

Atwood. “Our fire” is the philosophers’ own fire, “magical, creative, vital” [I.3 n41]. It is most subtle and extremely volatile, and it vivifies, depurates and segregates; it is distinct from common fire. “Some call it the miracle of the world” [I.3 n41]. The True matter is discovered by “no other Fire but that of Intellect” [III.2 ¶62], sublimed and fortified in its efficient source. She takes “the life of man therein circulating to be a pure fire” [IV.4 ¶4], incorporated in an ethereal vapour and containing the Universal Efficient. The method of ascent is “that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) fire is the medium through which the Divine Will conducts Light: “the fire here is our chaotic will in potentiality”, and “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

Quoted authorities. For the scholiast, “the essence of life, says the scholiast, is nothing else than a pure, naked, unmingled Fire” [I.3 n22]. It is celestial and generating, not elementary, and it is “the temperate unguent, which is fire” [I.3 ¶24]. Sendivogius says: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]. “It is also in all things indiscernibly.” [II.4 ¶39], moved only by God’s will. It bears God’s seal and is the death and separation of everything compounded. Eirenaeus urges: “be not so careful of the fire of the Athanor as of your internal Fire” [III.1 ¶14]. He identifies it: “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold, says Eirenaeus”, and “this is the seed of gold, involved in many links, and held prisoner, as it were, in a deep dungeon” [III.1 ¶14]. This fire is imprisoned in the hard, dry body and freed by our water, and it appears in the Third Menstrual [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood names Eirenaeus’ ‘internal fire of the sulfur of thy water’ as the vital perscrutinator [III.1 ¶13]. Pontanus says: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul, that so thou mayest attain to thy desire; for it is the key of all the philosophers” [III.1 ¶37]. Vaughan writes that “the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing”, yet it holds all the secrets of corruption and generation [III.4 ¶38]. An Adept names “the natural, unnatural, and the supernatural Fires”, which must be lit quickly so that none puts out another; a Fourth supervenes over them [IV.2 ¶11]. Sendivogius also says to “put them into Our Fire and let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21]. See also Fire of the Wise.

Identified with: our chaotic will in potentiality [APP ¶97]; essence of life [I.3 n22]; temperate unguent [I.3 ¶24]; true sulfur of Gold [III.1 ¶14]; seed of gold [III.1 ¶14]; key of all the philosophers [III.1 ¶37]; Intellect [III.2 ¶62]; the life of man [IV.4 ¶4]; the miracle of the world [I.3 n41]

See also: Internal fire

References: I.3 n22, I.3 n41, I.3 ¶24, II.4 ¶39, III.1 ¶14, III.1 ¶37, III.2 ¶62, III.4 ¶38, IV.2 ¶11, IV.3 ¶21, IV.4 ¶4, IV.4 ¶8, APP ¶97

Fire of life

term

In the Paracelsian passage Atwood quotes, the life-fire in man, called Antimony by adepts, which does nothing excellent while immured but flows forth as panacea after purgation.

In a Paracelsian passage the fire of life is the life-fire in man: “our fire of life (called Antimony by adepts, can effect nothing comparatively excellent whilst it is immured” [III.1 ¶10]. Like unlit fuel, it does nothing while immured. After purgation the pure life flows forth as panacea [III.1 ¶10]. The same passage asserts the identity with Antimony.

Identified with: Antimony [III.1 ¶10]

See also: Life

References: III.1 ¶10

Fire of nature

term

A fire named in several contexts: what drew the Magians toward nature’s central source, what besieges the bound serpents, and that by which the Matter brings forth Orus; it is not defined.

Atwood says the Magians were “drawn about the fire of nature, as it were, into communication with her central source” [I.1 ¶39]. Cornelius Agrippa’s disciple advises: “Thou must incamp against them with the fire of nature”, meaning against the bound serpents [III.1 ¶50]. The text does not say whether this is the ‘fire of the natural life’ of III.1 ¶43. The Matter brings forth Orus “by the Fire of nature lawfully conceived” [III.3 ¶62]. None of these passages explains the term.

References: I.1 ¶39, III.1 ¶50, III.3 ¶62

Fire of putrefaction and generation

term

In Sendivogius, the fire of the second operation, different from that of the first.

Sendivogius directs the work to be set on “the fire of putrefaction and generation, not on such a one as thou didst in the first operation” [IV.3 ¶21].

See also: Generation

References: IV.3 ¶21

Fire of the wise

term · Secret Fire

In Eudoxus, the secret fire that is the only instrument of sublimation, dissolving the Stone gently into Water; no philosopher has openly revealed it.

Eudoxus calls it “the Fire of the Wise, which is the only instrument which can work this sublimation” [IV.3 ¶5]. It dissolves the Stone naturally and without violence into Water. It is the Secret Fire: “No philosopher has ever openly revealed this Secret Fire” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is also called “this Secret Fire, and this powerful agent, which works all the wonders of the Art” [IV.3 ¶5]. It is known by its described characters and by divine gift. Eudoxus also says “the whole compound, is made perfect by the action of our Fire” [IV.3 ¶7], but he does not assert that this is the Fire of the Wise.

Identified with: Secret fire [IV.3 ¶5]; powerful agent [IV.3 ¶5]

See also: The Wise

References: IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶7

Fire spirit

term

In a quoted adept, a spirit rooted in the spiritual fire earth, from which it is fed by a secret influx.

The adept Atwood quotes says the Fire Spirit is rooted in the spiritual fire earth and “receives from it a secret influx upon which it feeds” [II.3 ¶41].

See also: Spirit

References: II.3 ¶41

Fire world

term

The region consciousness enters after the middle region (Atwood) or after the Aquaster (a quoted adept), where invisible things are seen; the text does not define it further.

Atwood says that after the middle region, at the dark descent, consciousness “enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]. The adept she quotes places it after the Aquaster: one who has “entered the Fire World, sees what is both invisible and incredible to common men” [II.3 ¶41]. Neither passage defines it further.

References: II.3 ¶16, II.3 ¶41

First and Second Commandments

treatise · 1st and 2nd Commandments

Cited in the Table Talk, where Atwood reads graven images as the practical result of self-centering and stopping in finite gifts as idolatry.

Both citations come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood interprets graven images (the Second Commandment) as the practical result of self-centering, which violates the First [APP ¶100]. She also cites the commandments for the view that stopping in finite gifts is idolatry [APP ¶135].

References: APP ¶100, APP ¶135

First cause

term · First Cuase

The cause of a being’s existence, which each has in himself; the top of the ascending series of causes, into which Reason re-enters and the only proper object of seeking.

Atwood places the First Cause at the top of the ascending series of causes, the ‘Final Cause of all’. The lowest effect reverses it: “the last and lowest effect, in which all the attributes of the First Cause are not only deficient but reversed” [III.2 ¶54]. Selfhood is raised into it. In a passage whose voice is unclear, expulsive life draws consciousness away from it: “drawn without to a debilitated consciousness away from its First Cause” [II.1 ¶21]. In IV.2 it is essence, the subsisting as a particular thing. “cause and principle form the First Why” [IV.2 ¶7]. “the speculative Motive of the first Cause is finally produced in reversionary order from the Third” and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶8]. It is the only proper object of seeking. The aim is to “attain to that supremacy of Reason which re-enters to its First Cause” [IV.2 ¶18], and “the consummating knowledge of the First Cause” comes in quietude and cessation of mental energy [IV.2 ¶33]. At the end of the work “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62], and the upright Mind of Man “co-operates with the First Cause” [IV.4 ¶32].

Aristotle, quoted on deliberation, uses the phrase differently: men work back from the proposed end through its media “until they arrive at the first Cause which is discovered in the last place” [IV.1 ¶30].

In the Table Talk (APP, later layer) each being has the cause of its existence in himself. Since Existence is one, knowing it is knowing the cause of all: “the consciousness can be brought into contact with its First Cause” [APP ¶6]. See also Final Cause.

Identified with: First Why [IV.2 ¶7]

See also: Causes

References: II.1 ¶21, III.2 ¶54, IV.1 ¶30, IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 ¶33, IV.2 ¶7, IV.2 ¶8, IV.3 ¶62, IV.4 ¶32, APP ¶6

First ens

term

What the dissolving water reduces all metals into, glossed as water.

Atwood says the dissolving water “reduces them into their first ens, or water”, speaking of all metals [I.3 n12]. The first ens is thus identified with water.

Identified with: Water [I.3 n12]

See also: Ens

References: I.3 n12

First entrance

term

An initial step whose knowledge, together with volatilizing the fixed tincture, admits one to the temple of Divine Science; the text does not explain it.

Atwood writes: “He who knows the first entrance” and how to volatilize the fixed tincture is admitted to the temple of Divine Science [IV.4 ¶32]. The text does not explain what the first entrance is.

References: IV.4 ¶32

First filosophie

term

In Norton’s verse, the foundational knowledge required of anyone who hopes ‘to come by Lakimie’.

Norton, quoted by Atwood, requires of anyone hoping ‘to come by Lakimie’: “He must know hys first filosophie,” [IV.2 ¶5].

References: IV.2 ¶5

First foundation

term

Basil Valentine’s term for what nature holds concealed, to be sought with one’s own eyes and hand as the basis for judging rightly.

Spoken by Basil Valentine (“the monk”), as quoted by Atwood: “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” [III.1 ¶13]. The record presents it as something to be sought personally, with one’s own eyes and hand, and as the basis for philosophizing with judgment.

References: III.1 ¶13

First God

term

In the Platonic Successor’s account, the highest principle, beyond all and more ineffable than all, celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe.

A view quoted from the Platonic Successor [II.4 ¶41]. The First God is celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe and only last as producing earth, heavens and souls. He is praised “as the God of all gods, the Unity of all unities, and beyond the First Adyta” and “as more ineffable than all silence, and more Unknown than all recondite essence” [II.4 ¶41].

See also: Gods

References: II.4 ¶41

First life

term

Atwood’s term for the original life about whose penetralia consciousness is drawn in Hades, and from whose perpetual motion the nether darkness flows.

In Atwood’s own voice: consciousness in Hades is drawn about the penetralia of the first life, and the nether darkness is described as “flowing out from the perpetual motion of the first life” [II.3 ¶18].

See also: Life

References: II.3 ¶18

First light

term

In Plotinus as quoted, the light shining primarily in itself, at once illuminating and illuminated, and the foundation of every intellect.

Quoted from Plotinus [III.2 ¶66]. The First Light shines primarily in itself and “at one and the same time illuminates and is illuminated” [III.2 ¶66]. It is identified with the ground of intellect: “this First Light, which is the foundation of every intellect and primarily knows itself” [III.2 ¶66].

Identified with: the foundation of every intellect [III.2 ¶66]

See also: Light

References: III.2 ¶66

First material of the metals

term

Albertus Magnus’s definition: an unctuous subtle humidity forcibly incorporated with a subtle earthy part.

Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “the first material of the metals is an unctuous subtle humidity, forcibly incorporated with a subtle terrestreity” [I.2 ¶29].

References: I.2 ¶29

First matter

term · First Mater, prima material, primam materiam

The one subject of the Art: the common root substance of all natures, not found on earth or among sensible things, reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life.

Atwood’s account. The First Matter is the common basis to which bodies can be reduced and from which they take new form — “their common basis or mercurial first matter” [I.2 ¶3] — and so the true subject of transmutation; she equates it with the “Universal Subject” [I.2 ¶7] and the “Universal Matter of the adepts”, which ordinary analysis does not discover [I.2 ¶3]. It is not any sensible thing but a middle substance generated from the Universal Spirit’s active and passive relations, “the simple generated substance of life and light, immanifestly flowing throughout nature” [I.2 ¶34]; “the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits” [I.2 ¶33]; “Thus obscure, after all, is the true Matter of the Alchemists” [I.2 ¶34]. Albert describes it “with the characteristic minuteness of personal observation” [I.1 ¶39]; Vaughan’s Lumen de Lumine gives “an allegorical display of the first matter” [I.1 ¶74]. The alchemists claim for it extreme attributes and miraculous origin, as the Greeks do for the ethereal hypostasis [III.1 ¶3].

Identities. It is generated by an emancipation of the Fontal Source, “and this is Diana, and that refulgent Light which eclipses every other light but that of its proper Reason” [III.1 ¶70]. It is “the abyssal Darkness”, brought forth by God as First Matter [III.2 ¶56]; it is not known in energy “but flies from him, indeed, who wishes intently to behold” [III.2 ¶57]. Beyond all things it is “That which is prior to all things” [III.2 ¶66]. Footnoted identities: “very natural true sperm of the greater world”, and Sendivogius’s “water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]. Chapter III.3 treats its manifestation and “Information by Light” [III.3 ¶1].

Quoted voices. Mylius: God “creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus” (ours: created one substance; this we name the first matter) [III.2 ¶2; also III.2 ¶56]. Basil Valentine: the all-containing water formed into earth by the dryness of its fire and air is “the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19]. Vaughan: “The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape” [II.3 ¶30], calling it the mineral nature; knowing it is discovering “the Sanctuary of Nature” [III.4 ¶44]. The Rosy Cross: “O, most excellent subject! Out of which all things in the world are generated” — poison named “the flying eagle”, and “the Seed of Divine benediction”, hidden from the wicked by its vestures, parent of the philosophical Sun and Moon [III.3 ¶63]. Arnold: the Stone is dissolved “that it may be reduced into its first Matter” [IV.1 ¶7]; Khunrath: the Azoth “reduces bodies to their First Matter” [IV.3 ¶28] and it appears as wet, impure “mud earth” partaking of Adam [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: Mercury, “Our Old Man”, “is the first matter of all metals” [IV.3 ¶10]. Flamel: “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶57].

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). It is not found on earth but reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life. “It is immediately antecedent to the first consciousness” and presents itself “as the extreme of bound and definiteness reverting to non- being” [APP ¶137]; its attributes are transmutable forms, hence seeming contradictions. Elsewhere, “the First Mater which is humanly producible” may be unlawfully formed for a finite end [APP ¶37].

Identified with: Universal subject [I.2 ¶7]; Universal matter [I.2 ¶3]; union of masculine and feminine spirits [I.2 ¶33]; mineral nature [II.3 ¶30]; Diana [III.1 ¶70]; refulgent Light [III.1 ¶70]; one substance [III.2 ¶2]; this water containing all [III.2 ¶19]; abyssal Darkness [III.2 ¶56]; unam substantiam (one substance created by God) [III.2 ¶56]; very natural true sperm of the greater world [III.2 n43]; water of our sea; water of life [III.2 n43]; That which is prior to all things [III.2 ¶66]; Seed of Divine benediction [III.3 ¶63]; flying eagle (the name it bears at first sight) [III.3 ¶63]; mud earth [IV.1 ¶36]; Mercury / Our Old Man [IV.3 ¶10]; First principles [I.1 ¶57]

See also: Matter

References: I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶74, I.2 ¶3, I.2 ¶33, I.2 ¶34, I.2 ¶7, II.3 ¶30, III.1 ¶3, III.1 ¶70, III.2 n43, III.2 ¶19, III.2 ¶2, III.2 ¶56, III.2 ¶57, III.2 ¶66, III.3 ¶1, III.3 ¶63, III.4 ¶44, IV.1 ¶36, IV.1 ¶7, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶28, APP ¶137, APP ¶37

First matter of the elements

term

In Paracelsus as quoted, the invisible, intangible life present in all things — the life the creatures have.

Quoted from Paracelsus: “This is the First Matter of the elements, which can neither be seen nor felt, and yet is in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; it is “nothing else but that life which the creatures have” [I.2 ¶26].

Identified with: that life which the creatures have [I.2 ¶26]

See also: Elements

References: I.2 ¶26

First Mover

term

In Atwood’s words, the One with whom one would move and whose Will one would be, at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all.

Atwood asks who can “move One with the First Mover, and Be His Will, who is at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all” [III.3 ¶78].

Identified with: Antecedent and Final Cause of all [III.3 ¶78]

References: III.3 ¶78

First operation

term

In Eirenaeus as quoted, the laborious manual first stage of the work, disposing the matter as first found, contrasted with the Second where Nature works alone.

Eirenaeus’s term, as quoted: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6], and “nothing can be achieved in the First Operation without sweating and much labor” [IV.1 ¶11]. It concerns disposing the matter as first found and is contrasted with the Second Operation, in which Nature works alone.

References: IV.1 ¶11, IV.1 ¶6

First preparation

term

In Vaughan as quoted, the first part of the Gross Work, which Agrippa knew and made clear; not described further.

Vaughan says Agrippa “knew the First Preparation, and has clearly discovered it” [IV.1 ¶36]. The packet gives no description of the preparation itself.

See also: Preparation

References: IV.1 ¶36

First prepared subject

term

Atwood’s term for the subject in its first prepared state, which she says is meant by the Lunar Vulcan and is also called Diana.

In Atwood’s voice: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject”, “which is also called Diana, and the secret natural interior Fire of Adepts” [IV.1 ¶29].

Identified with: Lunar Vulcan [IV.1 ¶29]; Diana [IV.1 ¶29]; secret natural interior Fire of Adepts [IV.1 ¶29]

See also: Subject

References: IV.1 ¶29

First principle

term

What the theurgically prepared seeker rises to: the most united in nature, its Flower, through which it is Deity.

Atwood, following “the doctrine of the ancients”: “if any one wish to discover the First Principle, according to the doctrine of the ancients, he must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. It is described as the most united in nature, its Flower, that through which it is Deity, suspended from its fountain and holding the Universe in sympathetic consent with itself [III.3 ¶59].

See also: First principles, Principles

References: III.3 ¶59

First principles

term

Lully’s name for the chaotic, monster-shaped spirits, which Atwood explains by the Seed of Spirit found in their purified material extreme.

Atwood reports: “But Lully, indeed, calls these chaotic forms first principles” [II.3 ¶30], and calls the first principles of the Art “Spiritus fugitives in aero condensators” (fugitive spirits condensed in the air) [II.3 ¶30]. Atwood explains the name: they are so called because the Seed of Spirit is found in their purified material extreme, not because they are permanent or rational [II.3 ¶30].

Identified with: fugitive spirits condensed in the air [II.3 ¶30]

See also: First principle, Principles

References: II.3 ¶30

First rotary wheel of life

term

Atwood’s phrase for the stage of life in which the true Light, as distinct from common light, becomes efficient.

Atwood speaks of the true Light, distinct from common light, as “that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30]. Not further explained.

See also: Life

References: IV.3 ¶30

First source

term

Atwood’s term for the origin from which every advance in externals leads man further away.

Atwood: “every advance we make in externals leads us further off from the First Source” [IV.4 ¶18].

References: IV.4 ¶18

First truth

term

In Atwood’s words, what man may know really and experimentally — the highest privilege he can propose.

Atwood presents as man’s highest privilege “to know the First Truth of things really and experimentally” [IV.4 ¶22].

See also: Truth

References: IV.4 ¶22

First unity

term

What the sought insoluble, transmuting, uniting union requires; voice unclear.

Voice unclear in the record: “such a tie cannot be without the first unity” [III.1 ¶50]. The context links creating and transmuting without violence to the first power, wisdom and love.

References: III.1 ¶50

First vegetative life

term

In the Appendix, the green first stage of life, identified with hope as the first aspiration to progress, whose ripened Life is purple.

From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), in Atwood’s voice: “The first vegetative life is green, it arises with hope; it is hope” [APP ¶119]; “The purple color is its ripened Life” [APP ¶119].

Identified with: hope [APP ¶119]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶119

First work

term

In Eirenaeus as quoted, the work accomplished by assiduity and industry, with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.

Eirenaeus: “it is by assiduity and industry that we accomplish the First Work” [IV.1 ¶6], with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.

See also: Works

References: IV.1 ¶6

First-fruits

term

In the Appendix, the early results of the work: real but not permanent, to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.

From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The first-fruits, tough perfectly real, should not be accepted as permanent” [APP ¶74]; they are to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.

References: APP ¶74

Fixation

term

In Atwood’s account, the third operation: after calcinations, a reunion into a more permanent form of Being.

Atwood describes fixation as the operation in which “after calcinations there is a reunion into a more permanent form of Being” [III.2 ¶64].

References: III.2 ¶64

Fixed and volatile

term · fixed, volatile, volatile and fixed, Fixity, unfixed, fixum, volucrem

The two contrary states the work inverts and unites: the fixed made volatile and the volatile fixed, until both reach perfect Fixity.

Atwood describes the work as “that which is fixed becoming volatile and the volatile nature fixed” [I.2 ¶20]. In Part IV (voice unclear) “the fixed is made volatile” in the dissolution, wholly so in the Second Operation [IV.1 ¶36], and the fixed must be separated “from the unfixed” [IV.1 ¶40]; fixed Antimony reaches fixed disease [IV.1]. Eudoxus, quoted, makes the compound of Art from the union of the two, which act on each other until they “are volatilized and fixed reciprocally into a perfect Fixity” [IV.3 ¶9].

References: I.2 ¶20, IV.1 ¶36, IV.1 ¶40, IV.3 ¶9

Fixed brass

term

In the Democritus passage, material drawn out and worked on the coals until it appears Golden.

Quoted from Democritus: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily” [IV.1 ¶43], it is worked on the coals until it appears Golden.

See also: Brass

References: IV.1 ¶43

Fixed metals

term

In the Author of the Open Entrance, silver (for the white) or gold (for the red), melted with the Stone in projection.

The Author of the Open Entrance directs “four parts of one of the fixed metals, i.e., silver of it be for the white, or gold if it be for the red” [IV.3 ¶20] to be used with the Stone in projection.

Identified with: silver or gold [IV.3 ¶20]

References: IV.3 ¶20

Fixed Salt

term · fiery salt

In Eudoxus as quoted, the salt extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, in which Mercury’s whole energy consists; the Blood of our Stone.

Eudoxus calls it “the Fixed Salt, which is the Blood of our Stone” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, and the whole energy of Mercury consists in it; distilled water “carries up with it a part of this fiery salt” [IV.3 ¶9].

Identified with: Blood of our Stone [IV.3 ¶7]

See also: Salt

References: IV.3 ¶7, IV.3 ¶9

Fixed sulphur

term

The balsam of nature that preserves bodies (per the Scholiast), and the Philosophers’ Stone into which fixed Mercury turns (per The Triumph).

Atwood reports the Scholiast’s view: “The fixed sulfur of adepts, according to our Scholiast, is the true balsam of nature” [I.3 n61]; “The more anything abounds with this balsam, the longer it lives and is preserved from perishing” [I.3 n61], and the universal medicine is concreted from things rich in it. The author of The Triumph makes the fixed and nourished Mercury become “the fixed Sulphur, which is the Stone of Philosophers” [IV.2 ¶6].

Identified with: balsam of nature [I.3 n61]; Stone [IV.2 ¶6]

See also: Sulphur

References: I.3 n61, IV.2 ¶6

Fixed tincture of life

term

Something fixed which must be rendered volatile and returned free; knowing how admits one to the temple of Divine Science.

Atwood speaks of knowing “how to render the fixed tincture of life volatile, and to return it, being free” [IV.4 ¶32] as admission to the temple of Divine Science. Not further explained.

See also: Life

References: IV.4 ¶32

Fixt, Variable, fugitive

term · Fixt, Variable, Fugitive

In Bloomfield as quoted, the three ‘persons’ to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.

Quoted from Bloomfield: “The Fixt, the Variable, and the Fugitive” [IV.2 ¶36] are three persons to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.

References: IV.2 ¶36

Flamel

person · Flammel, Nicholas Flamel, Nic. Flamel

An adept whose own account of finding, preparing and projecting the Stone Atwood quotes at length, and whom she cites repeatedly as an authority on the matter and fire.

Atwood quotes Nicholas Flamel’s own account at length as a remarkable, well-known case: the book, its explanation, the preparation, projection and the moral effect of the Stone — “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶56, I.1 ¶57]. Sources named are his Hieroglyphics and Testament; listed writings include La Sommaire Philosophique (in French verse, translated in the Theatrum Chemicum), Le Desir desiree and Le Grand Eclaircissement [I.1 ¶58]. His Summario Philosophico gave extracts from Democritus [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n16]. He is named with Rupicessa, De Meun, Pontanus, Basil Valentine and Ripley among genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

Atwood uses him as an example: though he had matter, fire and furnace from Abraham the Jew, he still wandered three years [III.1 ¶37]. His Summula supports the alchemists’ garden, “where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 n4], and the nature of the fire — not coal or wood but “a bright shining fire like the Sun itself, whose heat must neither be excessive, but always of one and the same degree” [IV.1 ¶41, IV.1 n35]. His Second Book is cited for learned discretion [IV.1 ¶29]. He is cited alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7] and speaks “more particularly” on the two Mercuries: “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red”, warning he was himself deceived until the Jew informed him [IV.3 ¶10]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is compared for the macrocosm’s image evolved before the mental eye in regeneration [APP ¶55].

References: I.1 n16, I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶49, I.1 ¶56, I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶58, II.4 n4, II.4 ¶9, III.1 ¶37, IV.1 n35, IV.1 ¶29, IV.1 ¶41, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶7, APP ¶55

Flos Salis Albi

term · Flower of White Salt

An Arabian name for the Matter which Atwood says truly designates the substant hypothesis, identified with Magnesia and the water that wets not the hands.

In Atwood’s voice, by this Arabian name “thus the substant hypothesis is said very truly to be designated” [III.2 ¶8]. She equates it with several names: “the white sand, Quellum, which Van Helmont speaks of”; “this salt is the Water that wets not the hands”; “that identical Magnesia that was exhibited in the Mysteries”; and “the White Island of Vishnu; the Lord of Radha; the White Paradise” [III.2 ¶8].

Identified with: white sand, Quellum [III.2 ¶8]; Water that wets not the hands [III.2 ¶8]; Magnesia [III.2 ¶8]; White Island of Vishnu; Lord of Radha; White Paradise [III.2 ¶8]

References: III.2 ¶8

Flower of Intellect

term

What the rectified circulation makes manifest, turned back toward its Archetypal Source.

Atwood speaks of the operation aiming “to make manifest the Flower of Intellect retrospectively to its Archetypal Source” [IV.2 ¶20]; apparently the fruit of the rectified circulation, directed back to its origin.

See also: Intellect

References: IV.2 ¶20

Flower of thy mind

term

In the Divine Oracle Atwood quotes, the faculty with which the Intelligible must be understood.

Quoted from the Divine Oracle: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶43]. The passage associates it with an empty mind and a pure turning eye; the text does not define it further.

See also: Mind

References: II.4 ¶43

Fludd

person

Named by Atwood, with Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber, as an intelligent and worthy disciple of Paracelsus.

Atwood lists Fludd among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, alongside Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. The book says nothing more about him here.

References: I.1 ¶64, II.3 n58

Flying volatile

term

In a Hermes passage, the volatile to be drowned while flying and separated from its rust; Atwood reads the images as about the freed spirit and its soul.

Hermes, quoted: “Take the flying volatile and drown it flying” [I.3 ¶16], separating it from its rust. Atwood takes these images to concern the freed spirit and its soul [I.3 ¶16].

References: I.3 ¶16

Foliated sulphur

term

In the Master’s words, the substance on which the Fire is poured, so that the Final Cause enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted.

Quoted from the Master: “when thou shalt pour forth thy Fire upon the Foliated Sulphur” [IV.2 ¶14]. The Final Cause then enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted [IV.2 ¶14].

See also: Sulphur

References: IV.2 ¶14

Fontal light

term

The source-light in whose evolution the Universal Nature appears white, as all colours united.

Atwood: “just so is the Universal Nature, described as appearing in the evolution of her Fontal Light” [III.2 ¶5]. In that evolution the Universal Nature appears white, all colours united.

See also: Light

References: III.2 ¶5

Fontal nature

term

The source-nature which the reflective faculty craves but cannot reach; those who know it by experience truly understand why God is to be feared.

Atwood says that “they only who have become conversant by experience in the Fontal Nature” truly understand why God is to be feared [I.3 n19]. Elsewhere, the reflective faculty is disabled “in the inquiry after that Fontal Nature which, by a necessary criterion, it craves” [II.1 ¶33]. Apparently, then, it is reached by experience rather than by reflection.

References: I.3 n19, II.1 ¶33

Fontal reason

term

The source from which the individual springs as an outbirth; obscured by the sensual principle and rediscovered in regeneration.

Atwood describes the individual as an outbirth “from that Fontal Reason whence it springs” [III.3 ¶52]. The sensual principle obscures it; in regeneration it is discovered, rising through self-perceivance with creative attributes and powers [III.3 ¶52].

See also: Reason

References: III.3 ¶52

Fontal source

term

That whose emancipation produces the First Matter.

Atwood calls the First Matter “an emancipation of the Fontal Source” [III.1 ¶70]; it is not further defined here.

References: III.1 ¶70

Fontal spirit of nature

term

Nature’s source-spirit, distinct from its manifestation and from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.

Atwood distinguishes “the fontal Spirit of nature, apart from its manifestation” [I.2 ¶15] from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.

References: I.2 ¶15

Form

term · Forms

The specifying, inward agent that matter lacks; joined to matter it begets a seed. Atwood identifies it with Light and with the sulfurs.

Atwood treats Form as what specifies a body: subject-matter is withdrawn from inferior Forms, and “one form being expelled, another may be introduced” [I.2 ¶5]. She calls it an error that “the alchemists extracted from the Form out of these metals to transmute and increase with” [I.2 ¶9].

Form is the inward agent: “This agent is the form that matter wanted” [I.2 ¶45]. Joined to matter, it begets a seed. Its identity is stated outright: “This Form is Light” [I.2 ¶45]. One material takes many specific shapes: “though the material is one throughout, forms are diverse” [I.2 ¶46]. Forms are also called sulfurs: “her forms or sulfurs are perplexed” [I.2 ¶48].

In the practice, putrefaction makes the body “to corrupt and to lose its Form” [IV.1 ¶41]. Conversely, the Universal Element’s invisible vapor is compressed “into a tangible Form” [IV.1 ¶47].

Identified with: Light [I.2 ¶45]; sulfurs [I.2 ¶48]

References: I.2 ¶45, I.2 ¶46, I.2 ¶48, I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶9, IV.1 ¶41, IV.1 ¶47

Form of gold

term

The ray of motive Light, which Atwood calls the alone universal principle of increase and perfection: the transmutative ferment and Stone.

Atwood says the chemists tried “to extract the Form of gold” with salt, sulfur, mercury and antimony [I.1 ¶86]. Her own account: “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9], “the alone universal principle of increase and perfection” [IV.4 ¶9]. When it dominates the circulatory system it is made concrete in life, and it is the transmutative ferment and Stone [IV.4 ¶9].

Identified with: ray of motive Light [IV.4 ¶9]; universal principle of increase and perfection [IV.4 ¶9]

See also: Gold

References: I.1 ¶86, IV.4 ¶9

Form of light

term

The new, concentric, finally immortal form in which the subject is established when it is rectified at the end of the operations.

Atwood says sublimation ends the operations by “establishing her in a new and concentric Form of Light” [II.2 ¶27]. The philosophic matter is finally “rectified into a consummate and immortal Form of Light” [IV.1 ¶46].

See also: Light

References: II.2 ¶27, IV.1 ¶46

Form of man

term

In Rabbi Ben Jochai’s words, quoted by Atwood, the Form of man contains all that is in heaven and earth.

Quoted: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42].

References: II.1 ¶42

Formal agent

term

What true generation would simply represent; Atwood says nothing in nature is generated so as to represent it alone.

Atwood: nothing in nature is generated “simply so as to represent the Formal Agent alone” [III.2 ¶61].

See also: Agent

References: III.2 ¶61

Formless subject

term

Matter as perceived in the Night of Matter: obscure, vast and infinite.

The passage reads: “her perception of the Formless Subject is obscure, and vast, and infinite” [III.2 ¶55]. In the same passage the intellect is “sinking into the Abyssal Subject” [III.2 ¶55]; the two may be the same, but no identity is asserted. Who is speaking is unclear.

See also: Subject

References: III.2 ¶55

Fountain

term · crystal fountain

In Eirenaeus’s verse, a fourfold distilling spring that washes the king and carries him up, also named May-dew and Eve; Atwood’s notes speak of a well, not explicitly identified with it.

Atwood describes the crowned king resting over the fountain and drawing auripigment from it. Her notes speak of a well: “the well is, as the catholic spirit of life, inexhaustible” [I.3 n22], with the occult Causality at its center; another note speaks of the deep well from which the philosophic water is drawn: “because the well is deep out of which it is drawn” [I.3 n36]. The text does not explicitly identify the fountain with the well.

Eirenaeus, quoted: “O crystal fountain! Which with fourfold spring Rubs down the valleys with its pearly drops Distilling” [III.1 ¶69]. The fountain washes the king and carries him up. The same verse names it “This our May-dew which our earth doth move To bring forth fruit, which fruit is perfect gold” and “This is our Eve, whom Adam doth so love” [III.1 ¶69].

Identified with: May-dew [III.1 ¶69]; Eve [III.1 ¶69]

References: I.3 n22, I.3 n36, III.1 ¶69

Four philosophic elements

term

In Maria’s words, what the matter in which the science is most easily found contains most evidently.

Maria, quoted: the science is most easily found in “that matter which most evidently contains the four philosophic elements” [I.3 n48].

See also: Elements

References: I.3 n48

Four winds

term

The philosophers’ name for the vapor into which the body of Light is reduced, which condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually.

Atwood: the body of Light is reduced to “a mere vapor, called by the philosophers, on account of its origin, the Four Winds” [III.1 ¶56]. The vapor condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually. In the fable, Typhon scatters Osiris’s members to the four winds [III.1 ¶56].

References: III.1 ¶56

The Fourth

term

A fourth agent, partaking of the aerial fiery element, that comes over the three fires to complete the work.

In the Adept’s account, “the Fourth, partaking of the aerial fiery element, supervenes for the accomplishment o the work” over the three fires [IV.2 ¶11]. Atwood then speaks of “the form of the Fourth in that Burning Fiery Furnace” [IV.2 ¶12], which she says can be conceived only from what is written. The text does not say these are the same, and a Fourth cause also appears at [IV.2 ¶7–8]; how these readings relate is left open.

References: IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 ¶12

Fourth form

term

Emanated by the Identity after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding: truthful, godlike, the express image of its motive.

Jacob Boehme, quoted: “enter I even to the cross in the Fourth Form, there you have Sol and Luna together” [III.1 ¶48]; he does not explain it further.

Atwood: after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding, the Identity emanates the Fourth Form: “It emanates a Fourth Form, truthful, godlike” [IV.2 ¶18], the express image of its motive. Later she writes: “And the Fourth, as the artist, applies it to the work in the furtherance” [IV.2 ¶32]. The text does not say that this Fourth is the same as the Fourth Form, or as Boehme’s.

See also: Form

References: III.1 ¶48, IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 ¶32

Fourth monarchy

term

A prophesied coming age, the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace, when the Mother of sciences comes forth and greater things are discovered.

Atwood names the “Fourth Monarchy, which is the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace” [IV.3 ¶49]. It is the time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth, and greater things be discovered than have been hitherto in the past monarchies of the world” [IV.3 ¶49].

Identified with: Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace [IV.3 ¶49]

References: IV.3 ¶49

Franck

person · Ad. Franck, Frank

Author of La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux, a history of the Kabalah Atwood recommends; her source for the Zohar translations she cites.

Atwood recommends Franck’s La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux as a history of the Kabalah, to be read with no less instruction than delight. It is the source of the Zohar translations she cites [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n2; III.2 n3; III.2 n4]. She uses it approvingly, as a supporting source.

References: III.2 n2, III.2 n3, III.2 n4, III.2 ¶3, III.3 n39, III.3 n50

Free masonry

term

What, Atwood says, the alchemists establish on the same substantial foundation as Greek philosophy.

Atwood: “In just such a foundation do the Alchemists establish their Free masonry” [III.1 ¶3], meaning the same foundation as Greek philosophy. The term is not explained further.

See also: Masons

References: III.1 ¶3

Free spirit

term

The spirit released in trance, which can range through its sphere, reveal hidden things and philosophize, though its freedom does not guarantee truth.

Atwood speaks of “the intrinsic intelligence and power of the Free Spirit which can expatiate into the whole circumference of its sphere and reveal hidden things” [II.3 ¶4]. This is the spirit released in trance; it can philosophize, but she warns that its freedom does not guarantee truth [II.3 ¶4].

See also: Spirit

References: II.3 ¶4

Free will

term

Not motiveless choice but the operative power freed from bondage, whose effects follow the will in full accord: the Almighty Magnet.
