Atwood: “That was free Will, not the motiveless chimera which human fancy has been prone to coin, but the operative Almighty Magnet” [III.3 ¶71]. Free will is thus the operative power freed from bondage, with effects that follow the will in full accord.

Identified with: Almighty Magnet [III.3 ¶71]

See also: Will

References: III.3 ¶71

Freed will

term

The liberty, in life, into which souls emerge from Lethe and Egyptian darkness.

Atwood speaks of souls emerging from Lethe and Egyptian darkness into “the glorious liberty of the Freed Will in life” [III.1 ¶70].

See also: Will

References: III.1 ¶70

Freher

person · D.A. Freher

Named by Atwood among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed.

Atwood lists Freher among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27], citing him in support of her own view.

References: I.3 n49, I.3 n53, I.3 n67, I.3 n69, IV.3 n16, IV.3 ¶27

French adept

collective voice

An anonymous adept Atwood cites for the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.

Atwood quotes the French adept: “the two dragons do bite one another very cruelly” [III.1 ¶58]. She uses the image to show the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: III.1 ¶58

Freton

term

In Norton’s verse, the harder kind of glass, made from clippings of other glasses.

Norton, quoted: “The harder stuffe is called Freton, Of clipping of other glasses it come” [III.4 ¶31].

References: III.4 ¶31

Fugitive ens

term

In a passage given in Hermes’ voice, the volatile element that flies away, which sulphurs and albuminous bodies hold and detain.

Quoted from Hermes: sulphurs and albuminous bodies are said to be those “which hold also and detain the fugitive Ens” [I.3 ¶21]. The context suggests the term means the volatile principle that tends to escape and must be fixed.

See also: Ens

References: I.3 ¶21

Fumosities

term

In Geber’s account, what fills a fanciful soul so that it cannot receive the true intention of natural things.

Geber, as quoted by Atwood among the impediments to the Art, says that a fanciful soul, “because there is replete with fumosities, it cannot receive the true intention of natural things” [III.4 ¶3]. Apparently a mental cloudiness that unfits the mind for the work.

References: III.4 ¶3

Furnace

term · furnaces

An instrument of the work; Atwood says the old writers devised furnaces for every part, many misleadingly, while the true furnace is a little simple shell.

Atwood says the old writers devised a furnace for every part of the work, many of them misleadingly, but “The true furnace has been described as a little simple shell” [III.4 ¶38], small enough to be carried in one hand. She notes that “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38], so Athanor is another name for it. She criticizes those who followed Geber’s example and described the furnace with a misleading subtlety [III.4 ¶38].

Identified with: Athanor [III.4 ¶38]

References: III.4 ¶38

Fusil Salt

term · fusil kind of salt

In a quoted adept’s account, a transparent salt seen in the waters of the vessel, said to be no different from pumice stone.

An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (identified in n26 as Grasseus) describes the waters of the vessel as “full of a certain transparent salt” [III.2 ¶25], and judges “that fusil kind of salt to be not different from pumice stone” [III.2 ¶25]. So the text equates fusil salt with pumice stone. The plain meaning beyond this is not stated.

Identified with: pumice stone [III.2 ¶25]

See also: Salt

References: III.2 ¶25

G

Galen

person

Named in a passage from Helmont that criticizes measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold, the method of Galen’s art.

In the Helmont material Atwood cites, physicians are criticized for “being allured with the facility of the art of Galen” [IV.3 ¶34], that is, for measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold. The view is Helmont’s; Galen’s method is the thing rejected.

References: IV.3 ¶34

Galileo

person

Named by Atwood in a contrast: she would as soon have lived in Galileo’s days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism.

Atwood says she would as soon have lived in Galileo’s days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism [III.4 ¶12]. Galileo is used only as this point of comparison.

References: III.4 ¶12

Garden

term

The alchemists’ name for the meadow of Divine Ideas, a place of sweet dew where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated.

Atwood says of the meadow of Divine Ideas (the Pratum) that “the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. She describes it in the alchemists’ words: “the philosophers have indeed a garden where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9]. In her account it is where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated [II.4 ¶9].

Identified with: meadow of Divine Ideas / Pratum [II.4 ¶9]

References: II.4 ¶9

Garment of light

term

Something that, in Atwood’s account, must be dissected and shorn, in parallel with stripping the Orient Animal’s skin.

Atwood writes that “the whole garment of Light must be dissected, shorn, and the signal of victory be heroically transferred” [III.1 ¶64], in parallel with the stripping of the Orient Animal’s skin. Apparently an image for laying open the vital or luminous covering of the subject. The text does not state this meaning directly.

See also: Light

References: III.1 ¶64

Gate of blackness

term · happy gate of Blackness

The passage at the beginning of the work through which the great change happens, which Atwood ties to the soul’s willed dissolution of her bond to the body.

Atwood quotes the adept’s cry: “O happy gate of Blackness! Cries the adept, which art the passage to so glorious a change!” [II.3 ¶37]. She equates it with the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics: “That was the way to “precious death”, spoken of by the Hebrews and Academics, this the “happy gate of blackness” celebrates by the old adepts” [II.3 ¶37]. She also equates it with the head of Hermes’ crow: “the “happy gate of blackness” celebrates by the old adepts, the “head of Hermes’ crow”, which is in the beginning of the work” [II.3 ¶37]. In her context it is the soul’s willed dissolution of her bond to the body, at the opening of the work. That reading comes from the surrounding passage, not from a stated definition.

Identified with: precious death [II.3 ¶37]; Head of Hermes’ crow [II.3 ¶37]

References: II.3 ¶37

Gate of putrefaction

term

The common name, per Atwood, for a stage of dissolution in the work: a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit.

Atwood describes a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit, and adds: “This is commonly called the Gate of Putrefaction” [III.1 ¶58]. In context it names the stage of dissolution.

See also: Putrefaction

References: III.1 ¶58

Gates

term · gate

In the Rosy Cross fraternity’s account, the five contested stages of the work, from knowledge of the true matter to projection.

Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the work is accomplished by “entering in by five litigious gates” [III.3 ¶63]. These are knowledge of the true matter, preparation, fire to maturity, multiplication and projection [III.3 ¶63].

References: III.3 ¶63

Gebelin

person

Author of Monde Primitif, whose agricultural interpretation Atwood criticizes.

Atwood cites Gebelin’s Monde Primitif to criticize its agricultural interpretation [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n3].

References: II.2 n3, II.2 ¶4

Geber

person

An authority the adepts rank next after Hermes. Atwood defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils and draws on him throughout for doctrine, the work’s impediments and its terms.

Standing and veiling. Atwood reports that the adepts rank Geber greatest after Hermes, and she defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils [I.1 ¶31–33; works cited at I.1 n37]. In Norton’s verse he is among the masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Ripley’s verse calls failed practitioners “as one of Geber’s cooks” [I.1 ¶65]. Read literally, his receipts led seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86]. From the Summa Perfect. she quotes his exclusion of the unworthy: “Ye sons of Avarice and Ignorance, cries Geber, and ye of evil manners, avaunt and fly from this science” [III.4 ¶18, III.4 n14]. On the word gibberish, see E0670.

Doctrine. Atwood uses him to support these points:

  • The work is verified by experiment: “we have searched out and found, and have seen with our eyes and handled with our hands” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n101–102].
  • “All is made of Mercury” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n12].
  • Metals can be perfected: “In metals,says Geber, is lesser perfection than in animals” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n47].
  • Theory must come first: “he who knows the principles and the way of generation, which consists according to the intention of nature, is but a very short way from the completement” [I.3 n2].
  • The root lies in the operator: “he has not the true root in him whereon to base his labor and intention” [II.1 ¶11, II.1 n7].
  • The work fails through ignorance: “men have thought the confection of fold impossible, because they have not know the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47, II.1 n43].
  • The compound of Art is “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9].

She reinterprets his “the thing which perfects in minerals, is the substance of argent vive and sulfur, proportionally commixt in the bowels of clean inspissate earth” [I.2 ¶42, I.2 n39] as relations of the Ethereal being, not literal substances. Elsewhere he is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25] and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

Impediments. She follows his list of bodily and mental impediments: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3–6, III.4 n1]. She also follows his ranking of the unfit [III.4 ¶12–16]. His “necessary charges” she reinterprets as giving up selfhood [III.4 ¶6]. Geber gives the furnace the name Athanor: “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38]. She faults later writers who copied him in describing it with misleading subtlety.

References: I.1 n101, I.1 n102, I.1 n37, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶31, I.1 ¶32, I.1 ¶33, I.1 ¶65, I.1 ¶76, I.1 ¶86, I.2 n12, I.2 n39, I.2 n47, I.2 ¶11, I.2 ¶42, I.2 ¶49, I.3 n2, II.1 n43, II.1 n7, II.1 ¶11, II.1 ¶47, III.1 n25, III.1 ¶21, III.2 ¶60, III.4 n1, III.4 n14, III.4 ¶12, III.4 ¶15, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶18, III.4 ¶3, III.4 ¶38, III.4 ¶4, III.4 ¶6, IV.3 ¶9

Genealogical method of ascent

term

Atwood’s name for the method of the work, indicated by the order of her exposition and identified with the artistic fabrication of the Promethean Fire.

Atwood says the order of her exposition indirectly indicates “the genealogical method of ascent; even that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. The method is thus identified with the fabrication of the Promethean Fire.

Identified with: artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan [IV.4 ¶8]

References: IV.4 ¶8

Generation

term

Embodied, born mortal life, into which souls descend and from whose bond and strains they must be freed. It is also the process through which every creature is brought into life.

Atwood. Generation is the realm of birth into mortal life. Souls descend into it: “souls descending into the realms of generation” [II.4 ¶7]. They must be freed “from the bond of its earthly geniture” [II.4 ¶3] and redeemed “from the oblivious realms of generation” [II.3 ¶36]. In the work, “those strains are all finally obliterated that accede to the soul from generation” [II.3 n40]. She also uses the word for a process in which each being’s central spirit is separated off: “the separation of this is constantly enacted in generation” [III.3 ¶52]. Through that process every creature is brought into life and operation. For her paired saying on generation and dissolution, see E0662.

Quoted voices. Crito says Intellect is withheld from every mortal nature in this life, “this however is not deprived by God but by the essence of generation” [II.1 ¶38]. Iamblicus says prayer “expels whatever is prone to generation, and retains nothing of the dregs of mortality” [III.4 ¶24].

See also: Generation and dissolution

References: II.1 ¶38, II.3 n40, II.3 ¶36, II.4 ¶3, II.4 ¶7, III.3 ¶52, III.4 ¶24

Generation and dissolution

term · generation, dissolution

Atwood’s principle that what generation binds, the inbred evil, only dissolution can unloose.

Atwood: “That which generation binds dissolution only can unloose” [IV.4 ¶17]. In context, what generation binds is the inbred evil. See also generation (E0661).

See also: Dissolution, Generation

References: IV.4 ¶17

Generative life

term

In the later Appendix, the life into which the life-force is now wasted when it should be related to mind.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer of the book. There Atwood says the life-force should be directed to mind: “it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life” [APP ¶134]. In the Aristaeus story, the bees are lost along with “all the faculties of his soul, with the generative life” [APP ¶144].

See also: Life

References: APP ¶134, APP ¶144

Generative virtue

term

A power which, drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light, marks the origin of matter for the Platonists. It is alienated and later reunited to mind.

Reporting the philosophers’ view, the text speaks of the origin of matter “when the generative virtue is drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. In a later passage, whose speaker is unclear, the primary motion of the ebbing life brings it about that “the Generative Virtue, which was alienated, becomes re- united to mind” [III.2 ¶66]. Compare generative life (E0663).

See also: Virtue

References: III.2 ¶66, III.2 ¶9

Genesis

treatise

The biblical book, which Atwood cites to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom and to liken the work to the creation of the world.

Atwood cites Genesis 2:10, “that land of Havilah where good gold is” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n4], to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom. She cites chapter 1, “And the Spirit of God moved upon the Face of the Waters.” [IV.2 ¶30, IV.2 n19], to liken the work to the creation of the world.

References: III.1 n4, III.1 ¶8, IV.2 n19, IV.2 ¶30

Genesis of light

term

Atwood’s term for the real, not imaginary, production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis.

Atwood presents the production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis as real rather than imaginary: “but as the true Genesis of Light” [III.2 ¶26].

See also: Light

References: III.2 ¶26

Gentile Mythology

collective voice

Cited by Atwood as carrying, in symbol, the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing.

Atwood says Gentile Mythology carries in symbol the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing [III.3 ¶69].

References: III.3 ¶69

George Von Welling

person

Listed by Atwood as a persecuted adept and friend of Fichtuld, author of the Opus mago-Cabbalist.

Atwood lists George Von Welling among persecuted adepts and as a friend of Fichtuld [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70]. The footnote gives his work as Opus mago-Cabbalist [I.1 n80].

References: I.1 n80, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70

Georgic

treatise · Georgics

A Latin poem, its author not named here, whose fourth book Atwood quotes for the binding of a shape-changing captive (Proteus) with force and bonds.

Atwood quotes the fourth book of the Georgics (no author named) on the binding of the shape-changer. The captive held in bonds changes into varied shapes: “Verum,ubi correptum minibus, vinclisque tenebis” [III.2 ¶21, III.2 n21]. Only force and bonds compel it: “vim duram et vincula capto Tende” [III.2 ¶23, III.2 n24], and “Orando flectes: vim duram et vincula capto” [I.3 n37]. The more it turns into all forms, the tighter the bonds must be: “Et, quanto illa magis formas se vertet in omnes,” [I.2 ¶38, I.2 n37].

References: I.2 n37, I.2 ¶38, I.3 n37, III.2 n21, III.2 n24, III.2 ¶21, III.2 ¶23

Gibberish

term

A word that a quoted Faraday Society address derives from Geber’s mysterious style. For Atwood, that style is deliberate veiling.

Atwood quotes an address to the Faraday Society that names Geber as the one “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33]. The derivation is the address’s own. Atwood’s point is that Geber’s obscurity was a deliberate veil (see Geber, E0659).

References: I.1 ¶33

Glass

term · glasse, glasses

In Norton’s verse, the vessel material that keeps spiritual matters from escaping, named as the vessel God gave. Vaughan adds that the glass is one.

Norton is quoted: “But other vessels be made of glasse, That spiritual matters should not outpasse” [III.4 ¶31]. Norton’s Master identifies glass with the vessel God gave: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶31]. In our translation (by: ours), the Latin reads: if God had not given us the vessel, he would have given us nothing. The better kind of glass is called morning stuffe, and the harder kind Freton [III.4 ¶31]. Vaughan is quoted saying “the glass is one, and no more” [III.4 ¶38].

Identified with: vas (the vessel God gave) [III.4 ¶31]

References: III.4 ¶31, III.4 ¶38

Glauber

person

Named by Atwood as one whose receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice.

Atwood says Glauber’s receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86].

References: I.1 ¶86

Gnostic energy

term

In a Proclus passage, an energy of the soul that faith surpasses, set beside intelligence and judgment.

Proclus is quoted saying faith is “which is then better than every Gnostic energy” [II.4 ¶40]. It is set beside intelligence and judgment. The term is not defined further.

References: II.4 ¶40

Gods

term

For Atwood, manifestations of the Demiurgic Fire made distinct in Light through Intellect, and the unities of all being. They appear as simple light, not phantasms.

Atwood asks: “what are all the gods but manifestations of this same Fire germinating through the projecting energy of Intellect distinct in Light?” [II.4 ¶26]. She also calls them “the genus of the gods, which are the unities of all being” [II.4 ¶29]. In her account each god is an aspect of that Fire. Intellect makes the gods visible and nourishes them. They are an intelligible union and Truth, and they appear as simple light, not as phantasms [II.4 ¶26–29].

Identified with: manifestations of the Demiurgic Fire [II.4 ¶26]; unities of all being [II.4 ¶29]

References: II.4 ¶26, II.4 ¶29

Gold

term

In Atwood’s usage, the adepts’ name for the Soul, meaning its Light, in the second conjunction. It is also the seed that must be destroyed to be multiplied.

Atwood gives a stated identity: “in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light; which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. So Gold is the Soul’s Light, predominant in the second conjunction. Its formal virtue stays sealed until Mercury penetrates it [III.3 ¶30]. Elsewhere gold must be destroyed as seed in order to be multiplied: “he that saves his gold, that is to say, remains satisfied in the first fruits of his reason” [III.3 ¶22]. Saving one’s gold thus means resting content in the first fruits of reason. See also Gold Alchemical (E0676).

Identified with: first fruits of his reason [III.3 ¶22]; Soul, i.e., its Light [III.3 ¶30]

See also: Gold

References: III.3 ¶22, III.3 ¶30

Gold

term · this gold

The finished product of the work, endued with a magnetical virtue that draws divine increase; also called the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun and the Stone of Fire.

The finished product: “this gold is endued with a magnetical virtue” [II.1 ¶25] that draws divine increase. The passage gives it other names: “Whence it has been called likewise the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun, the triumphal Chariot of Antimony” [II.1 ¶25], and “this is the Stone of Fire seen in bright lines” [II.1 ¶25]. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or the source she follows is speaking.

Identified with: terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun; triumphal Chariot of Antimony [II.1 ¶25]; Stone of Fire [II.1 ¶25]

See also: Gold

References: II.1 ¶25

Gold Alchemical

term

In the later Appendix, the first conceived Paternal Light and the metaphysical seed of mineral gold.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “The Gold Alchemical is the first conceived Paternal Light” [APP ¶20], and “it is the seed metaphysical of mineral gold” [APP ¶20]. Compare gold (E0675).

Identified with: first conceived Paternal Light [APP ¶20]; seed metaphysical of mineral gold [APP ¶20]

References: APP ¶20

Gold of the wise

term · our gold, Aurum Sapientum

In the author of Lucerna Salis, the gold of the Wise is not vulgar gold but a clear, pure water that becomes spiritual.

Atwood reports the author of Lucerna Salis as declaring “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold; but it is a certain water clear and pure” [III.3 ¶32]. On the packet’s reading, this water bears the Lord’s lightning, from which all things receive life, and passes through the Alembic; hence, the quoted author says, “this is the reason, continues he, why our gold is become spiritual” [III.3 ¶32]. The gold of the Wise is thus identified with that water (QUOTED: the author of Lucerna Salis).

Identified with: a certain water clear and pure [III.3 ¶32]

See also: Philosophers’ gold, The Wise

References: III.3 ¶32

Gold philosophical

term

In a Rosicrucian passage, Gold philosophical is named as the husband of Mercury; the text does not explain it further here.

In a passage attributed to the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, Mercury speaks: “my husband is Gold philosophical” [III.3 ¶64]. The text gives no further explanation at this point (QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross).

References: III.3 ¶64

Golden Bough

term · Ramus

The Golden Bough, the offering and talisman by which Aeneas descends; Atwood reads it as a ray of living light, the intellect, and a passport into hidden realms.

Atwood treats the Golden Bough as what the Sybil sends Aeneas to find, “he may discover and bring to her the Golden Bough” [III.1 ¶15], and offers it as a parallel to the hidden object of the work. It is the required propitiation for the descent; literally part of the sacred equipage, “connected with the Mercurial caduceus” [II.3 ¶11], but read by Atwood ontologically as the intellect: “a ray of living light, golden and flexible, the true Brancha Spiritualis of Raymond Lully” [II.3 ¶11].

It is one of the “golden passports” into the hidden realms, and it is the bough, not the tree, that is to be taken, the small portion to start from: “Ramus, non arbor — The bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken” [III.1 ¶32]. Atwood sets it beside other emblems: “Such was the Caduceus of Hermes — the Golden Bough, the ferrying Cup of Hercules” [III.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Aeneas passes Tartarus to Elysium “By propitiation, through the offering of the Golden Bough” [APP ¶168], which he is to “take as his talisman to pass through the Infernal Regions to Elysium” [APP ¶171]; there its tree appears identical with Proteus’ last transformation [APP ¶171]. All voices are ATWOOD.

Asserted identities: = Brancha Spiritualis [II.3 ¶11]; = Caduceus of Hermes and ferrying Cup of Hercules (set in apposition) [III.1 ¶36].

Identified with: Brancha Spiritualis [II.3 ¶11]; Caduceus of Hermes; ferrying Cup of Hercules [III.1 ¶36]

References: II.3 ¶11, III.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶32, III.1 ¶36, APP ¶168, APP ¶171

Golden branch

term

Something drawn to its native soil that passes through death and darkness, takes root, and blossoms into illuminating light; not explicitly identified.

Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the Golden Branch as drawn to its native soil, which “through death and darkness enters; and taking root at last, gathers strength to germinate and blossom, as a radiant flower” [II.4 ¶7]. The passage does not explicitly say what the branch is.

References: II.4 ¶7

Golden fleece

term

In the Table Talk, the purplish outward appearance of the light of Life diffused over the seeker’s body in the third life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood states: “The Golden Fleece is the outward appearance presented by the light of Life diffused over the body of the seeker in the third life” [APP ¶22]; the appearance is described as of a purplish luster (ATWOOD).

References: APP ¶22

Golden seed

term

In Basil, the one thing holding mercury, salt and sulphur, knowledge of which gives the root of life; called also a magnet.

Quoting Basil (QUOTED: Basil), the text presents the golden seed as the one thing that holds mercury, salt and sulphur; whoever knows it has the root of life. It is equated with a magnet: “this golden seed or magnet” [II.1 ¶11].

Identified with: Magnet [II.1 ¶11]

See also: Seed

References: II.1 ¶11

Golden water

term

The adept’s water, found not in wells or depths but in higher places, as ripe Mercury rises.

Atwood quotes an adept: “Our golden water, says the adept, is not found in wells, nor in profundities, but in higher places” [III.3 ¶17]; the context connects this with ripe Mercury rising (QUOTED: the adept).

See also: Water

References: III.3 ¶17

Gordian knot

term

Atwood’s name for the central difficulty of the Hermetic Mystery: knowing the Salt and its solution.

Having treated the Salt and its solution, Atwood (ATWOOD) declares: “Here then liest the Gordian Knot of the Hermetic Mystery” [IV.1 ¶37]. The knot is thus the crux of the method: knowing the Salt and how it is dissolved.

References: IV.1 ¶37

Gospel

treatise

Cited as carrying the Christian doctrine of fulfillment, which Atwood adds to the other traditions as agreeing with them.

Atwood adds “the Christian doctrine of fulfillment” of the Gospel to the other traditions she has surveyed, as agreeing with them in the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

References: IV.4 ¶28

Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ

collective voice

The Gospel account of Christ’s life, to which, Atwood says, the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work and human redemption.

Atwood notes that the Adepts compare the phenomena of their work to the Gospel tradition of the Life of Christ and to human redemption [IV.3 ¶27]; she cites it as illustration.

References: IV.3 ¶27

Grace

term

The divine gift by which alone, according to Norton and Kelly, the Art is found and obtained, rather than by study or will.

Two quoted authorities make grace the condition of the science. Norton’s Ordinal calls it “A singular grace and gift of the Almightye;” and says of the science, “But only by grace, she is holy in her kind.” [III.4 ¶10]; on the packet’s reading, the student must be proved able to receive it, and it is needed to undo God’s conjunctions (QUOTED: Norton’s Ordinal). Kelly likewise says the Art comes not by reading, sitting still, fancy or will: “But, as I said, by grace it is obtained:” [IV.1 ¶19]; it is to be sought (QUOTED: Kelly). The records do not show Atwood qualifying either view.

References: III.4 ¶10, IV.1 ¶19

Grafting and transplanting

term

The ancients’ exact art of growing and subliming the Spirit to higher degrees of concentrated essentiality in successive vessels or forms.

Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “that exact art of grafting and transplanting which the ancients practiced” [III.1 ¶9]: the Spirit is grown and sublimed to a third, fourth and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality, in as many representative vessels or forms. The horticultural image apparently stands for the stepwise concentration of the Spirit in the method.

References: III.1 ¶9

Grand Mysteries

term

In a passage from Stoboeus via Dr Warburton, the next initiation, which affects the mind as death does.

In a passage cited from Stoboeus through Dr Warburton (QUOTED: Stoboeus / Dr Warburton), the next initiation, “initiation into the Grand Mysteries” [II.3 ¶37], is said to affect the mind as death does.

See also: Mysteries

References: II.3 ¶37

Grasseus

person · J. Grasseus, Grsaeus

Adept reputed author of the Water Stone, said to be Boehme’s friend; Atwood cites his eyewitness vessel account and endorses his Stone/Christ analogy.

Atwood lists Grasseus as reputed author of the Water Stone and a personal friend of Boehme [I.1 ¶70]; the note gives titles Das Wasser-Stein des Weissens, Arca Arcano and Lillium inter Spina [I.1 n83]. As J. Grasseus, his Water Stone of the Wise Men is said to have been published with the Aurora [I.1 ¶64].

Called “an ancient and much esteemed Adeptus”, he supplies (Theatr. Chem. 6:294) an eyewitness account of a world in miniature in the vessel: “Within this fabric (i.e., the consecrated vessel), was a certain mass moving circularly” [III.2 ¶25, III.2 n26]. Atwood reads this as the whole Hermetic laboratory.

He is named among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), under the spelling Grsaeus, his Aquarium supplies the analogy of the Stone with Christ the Head Corner Stone, which Atwood endorses as a “versimilitude” [APP ¶46].

References: I.1 n83, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶70, III.2 n26, III.2 ¶25, IV.3 ¶27, APP ¶46

Graven image

term

In the Table Talk, inwardly a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit; outwardly its weakened material form, common idolatry.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) gives an inward meaning: “A graven image means a vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit” [APP ¶100], one worshipped by the heart. Outwardly, its weakened material form is common idolatry.

Identified with: vocal utterance carved into the understanding spirit [APP ¶100]

See also: Image

References: APP ¶100

Great art

term

The ancients’ art, which, Atwood says, Bacon knew nothing of, together with its subject.

Atwood (ATWOOD) says of Bacon that “he knew nothing of their Great Art, or of its subject even, and naturally mistook their hidden ground” [I.2 ¶24].

References: I.2 ¶24

Great Salt sea

term

In the Table Talk, Wisdom, the Universal Will, which dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) glosses the expression herself: “The great Salt Sea (Wisdom, the Universal Will)” [APP ¶94]. It dissipates the impure sulphurs in the individual will. Asserted identities: = Wisdom; = Universal Will [APP ¶94].

Identified with: Wisdom [APP ¶94]; Universal will [APP ¶94]

References: APP ¶94

Great secret

term · the secret

The secret of the art, mentioned in the accounts of Kelly, Dee and Philalethes; the text does not say what it is.

Atwood (ATWOOD) relates that “the secret of making of the Powder was confided to Kelly some years afterwards by a dying monk” [I.1 ¶67], and quotes Dee: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me” [I.1 ¶67]. Philalethes is said to have possessed “the secret” when young [I.1 ¶73]. These passages do not say what the secret is.

References: I.1 ¶67

Great theologist

collective voice

An authority cited within Proclus’s passage on the soul’s entry into the Adytum of Life.

The great theologist is cited within the Proclus passage on the soul’s entry into the Adytum of Life [II.4 ¶29]; the text gives no further identification.

References: II.4 ¶29

Great unknown

term

The highest reality, unknown because concealed in this life; it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.

Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of those who “seek to prove Reality in the Great Unknown — unknown, because concealed in this life” [II.4 ¶42]. According to the passage, it becomes known in Identity when the soul concentrates herself.

See also: Unknown

References: II.4 ¶42

Great whole

term · Whole

The totality contained proportionally in every portion of existence; simple, and known by contact and intuition in self-knowledge.

Atwood (ATWOOD) holds “every portion of existence to be continent and comprehended proportionally of the Great Whole” [III.2 ¶45]. Being simple, “it is simple, and not so much therefore an object of reason as of contact and intuition” [III.2 ¶46]; it is reached in self-knowledge.

References: III.2 ¶45, III.2 ¶46

Greater and lesser good

term

Paired terms: man prepares the way of the Greater Good in the Lesser, and the Lesser is blessed by the Greater.

Atwood (ATWOOD) gives man’s task as “to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20], adding that “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater” [III.4 ¶20].

References: III.4 ¶20

Greater Mysteries

term

The higher grade of ancient initiation, alone promising assimilation and final contact with the first principle; its doctrine concerned the whole universe.

Atwood (ATWOOD) says assimilation and final contact with the first principle were promised “to those who were initiated in the Greater Mysteries only” [II.2 ¶5]. Citing Clemens Alexandrinus with approval: “The doctrine of the Greater Mysteries, says Clemens Alexandrinus, related to the whole universe” [II.2 ¶5]. Later she says the revelations she has gathered partly describe “the visions, and awful accompaniments which took place in the celebration of the Greater Mysteries” [II.3 ¶49].

See also: Mysteries

References: II.2 ¶5, II.3 ¶49

Greater Orb and Lesser World

term · Greater Orb, Lesser World

In the monk continuing Basil Valentine, two domains each with its Vulcan; the Lesser World’s Vulcan amends what the Greater Orb’s leaves crude.

The monk, continuing Basil Valentine (QUOTED: the monk), says: “Whatsoever the Vulcan in the Greater Orb leaves crude and perfects not, that in the Lesser World must be amended by a certain other Vulcan” [IV.1 ¶40]. Apparently the Lesser World’s fire completes what the Greater Orb’s leaves imperfect; the text does not gloss either domain further here.

See also: Lesser world

References: IV.1 ¶40

Greater world

term

In a quoted adept, the world whose virgin womb, Earth without form and water, is where Ruach Elohim is made body.

A quoted adept (QUOTED: the mysterious adeptest) speaks of “the virgin womb of the greater world, viz., that Earth which is without form and water” [III.3 ¶50], where Ruach Elohim is made body; then “The Son, born into the light of the macrocosm” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage uses “macrocosm”, but the text does not explicitly identify it with the greater world. Asserted identity: its virgin womb = Earth without form and water [III.3 ¶50].

Identified with: Earth which is without form and water (its virgin womb) [III.3 ¶50]

References: III.3 ¶50

Grecian fables

collective voice — Midas · Midas

Greek fable of Midas, which Atwood reads in the Table Talk as the will starved in possession of the aurific life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the Grecian fable of Midas to illustrate the will starved in possession of the aurific life [APP ¶159].

See also: Greek fable (Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas), Midas

References: APP ¶159

Greek and Alexandrian Platonists

collective voice — with the mystics of the middle ages and the Fathers of the Church · mystics of the middle ages, the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church

Groups of writers whose works, Atwood says, give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report.

Atwood says the writings of the Greek and Alexandrian Platonists, the mystics of the middle ages and the enlightened Fathers of the Christian Church give much evidence that the Eleusinian rites differed widely from common report [II.4 ¶56]. She cites them in support.

See also: Platonists

References: II.4 ¶56

Greek Aristhenes

person · Aristhenes

Cited to support that the subject is least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, and that preparation removes superfluities.

Atwood cites the Greek Aristhenes in support of her account of the subject: least valued and outwardly dead but alive within, with preparation removing its superfluities: “Take that which is least, and draw it by artifice into the true ferment of philosophers” [II.2 ¶26, II.2 n18].

References: II.2 n18, II.2 ¶26

Greek Catholics’ hymn for St John’s day

collective voice

A hymn cited to illustrate the tradition that St John made gold and gems.

Atwood cites the Greek Catholics’ hymn for St John’s day to illustrate the tradition of St John making gold and gems: “Qui de virgis fecit aurum Gemmas de lapidibus” [I.1 ¶24, I.1 ¶25]. Translation (ours): Who made gold from rods, gems from stones.

References: I.1 ¶24, I.1 ¶25

Greek Divine

collective voice

An unnamed Greek authority cited as agreeing with others concerning the Matter of the work; the text does not otherwise identify him.

Cited in support: the Greek Divine is said to have agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. The text does not otherwise identify him.

References: III.2 ¶60

Greek fable

collective voice — Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas · Greek fables

The Greek heroic fables of Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas, which Atwood decodes as figures of the mind’s faculties in the work.

Atwood decodes these fables: the heroes are those “who represent the Rational Ferment”, while their associates stand for the other faculties of the mind [III.1 ¶66].

See also: Grecian fables (Midas), Heroes of the ordeal (Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus), Heroic fables (Theseus, Ariadne, Jason, Medea, Hercules, Eurystheus, Achilles, Ulysses, Minerva, Aeneas, the Sybil), Labouring heroes (Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason)

References: III.1 ¶66

Greek Ontologists

collective voice

Greek philosophers whose course Atwood says guided her in following Nature back to her Initial Source.

Cited in support: Atwood says the course of the Greek Ontologists guided her in following Nature to her Initial Source [IV.4 ¶6].

References: IV.4 ¶6

Greek philosophers

collective voice

Greek philosophers whose authority Atwood invokes, in part, to ground the inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious.

Their authority partly grounds Atwood’s inference that the Mysteries were real and efficacious [II.2 ¶24].

See also: Philosophers

References: II.2 ¶24

Greek temples

collective voice — to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus · Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo, Bacchus

The Greek temples to Ceres, Minerva, Apollo and Bacchus, cited by Atwood as institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom.

Atwood cites these temples as illustration: institutions that ministered to defects of mind and disciplined the understanding for Wisdom [IV.3 ¶36].

References: IV.3 ¶36

Greeks

collective voice · Greek philosophy

The Greeks as a collective voice whose doctrine of Wisdom Atwood holds unequalled and whose names and doctrines she repeatedly cites in support of the Hermetic view.

Atwood holds up the Greek doctrine of Wisdom as unequalled, promising to discuss it later [I.1 ¶70]. She cites Greek usage repeatedly in support: they name the essence freed from gross matter “the Free Ether” [I.2 ¶16]; they call Intelligible Causes gods [II.4 ¶39]; Isis was “by the Greeks called Myrionymous”, the goddess with a thousand names [III.3 ¶62]. Greek philosophy substantializes mind as the substratal matter of existence, and its ethereal hypostasis parallels the alchemists’ first matter [III.1 ¶2, III.1 ¶3]. By contrast, the Greeks kept silent about, or poetized, the physical revealments of the Tartarean realms, out of fear of vulgar curiosity [II.3 ¶34].

See also: Greeks (these Greeks, these philosophers), Greeks and eastern sages (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics)

References: I.1 ¶70, I.2 ¶16, II.3 ¶34, II.4 ¶39, III.1 ¶2, III.1 ¶3, III.3 ¶62

Greeks

collective voice — these Greeks, these philosophers · These Greeks, these philosophers

Greek philosophers whose contradictory statements about Matter Atwood explains and defends, comparing them with the Hermetic adepts.

These Greeks say contradictory things about Matter: that it is one and all, everywhere and nowhere. Atwood explains and defends these statements and compares them with the Hermetic adepts [III.2 ¶51, III.2 ¶52].

See also: Greeks

References: III.2 ¶51, III.2 ¶52

Greeks and eastern sages

collective voice — Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics · Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Peripatetics, Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics

The Greek and eastern sages and the philosophical schools (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics) cited together for the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source.

Cited in support of the ancient doctrine of the Ether as universal source, described as “a certain pure and hidden fire” [I.2 ¶12].

See also: Greeks, Platonists, Pythagoreans, Sage

References: I.2 ¶12

Green Duenech

term · Duenech

In Khunrath’s words, a matter that appears with the Vitriol of Venus when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed; together they are the true matters of the Blessed Stone.

A term from Khunrath, quoted by Atwood: when the bonds of coagulation are relaxed there appear “the Green Duenech and the Vitriol of Venus, which are the true matters of the Blessed Stone” [IV.1 ¶36]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

Identified with: true matters of the Blessed Stone (with the Vitriol of Venus) [IV.1 ¶36]

References: IV.1 ¶36

Green Lion

term · Grene Lyon, Greene Lyon, Lyon Greene, our Lyon

A name for the matter when first sublimed, so called for its strength and crude vitality; central agent of the Hunting of the Greene Lyon and figured also by Khunrath and Ripley.

Atwood: the matter when first sublimed “is called a serpent, dragon, or green lion, on account of its strength and crude vitality” [I.2 ¶40].

In the quoted poem The Hunting of the Greene Lyon it is the central agent: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” — green for being unripe, not for its colour; and it is not common quicksilver: “For they weene that our Lyon ys Common Quicksilver, but truly they miss:” [III.1 ¶65]. The poem also has it swift, devouring and eclipsing the Sun (turning red to white) yet perfecting him; as Priest it weds Sun and Moon, who were born in its Bed; it supplies the Lion’s Blood; and it beguiles most who hunt it [III.1 ¶65].

Khunrath (quoted): “The Green Lion, lurking and concealed, is drawn forth from the Cavern of his Saturnine Hill” by allurements suited to his nature, pierced with a lance, and his blood collected [IV.1 ¶36]; not otherwise explained.

Ripley (quoted) says that fools give the name to vitriol: “vitriall, Which folys doe call the Grene Lyon” [I.1 ¶65]; the passage apparently rejects this vulgar identification without saying what the true Green Lion is.

Identified with: vitriall (as named by fools) [I.1 ¶65]

See also: Lion

References: I.1 ¶65, I.2 ¶40, III.1 ¶65, IV.1 ¶36

Gross work

term · Gross Worke, Grosse worke

The preliminary preparation of the matter, before the dissolution, after which the philosophic work proper begins; long, foul, costly and perilous per Norton.

Atwood: “the preliminary preparation of the matter being very generally termed the gross work”, and “The philosophic work is not considered to begin until after the dissolution” [I.3 n56]. Of the many called at first, “few, it will be understood, are chosen to proceed beyond the exigencies of the preliminary Gross Work” [III.4 ¶32]; Norton describes “the needful qualification and numbers of individuals employed about the Gross Work” [III.4 ¶36].

Norton’s Ordinal (quoted): “For the Gross Worke is foule in her kinde,” [IV.1 ¶25] — a long phase (three years would be a blessed chance), perilous and costly, a handicraft full of possible faults: “But handie crafte, called Art mechanical,” [IV.1 ¶28]; once completed it need not be begun again.

Atwood also calls it “this said hyper-physical Gross Work” [IV.1 ¶36], with a First Preparation and a Second part, the Second being one of the Art’s greatest subtleties.

Identified with: preliminary preparation of the matter [I.3 n56]

See also: Works

References: I.3 n56, III.4 ¶32, III.4 ¶36, IV.1 ¶25, IV.1 ¶28, IV.1 ¶36

Ground of Wisdom

term

The understanding which Atwood says must be properly conceived before any experiments are undertaken.

Atwood advises to “leave off experiments until the ground of wisdom is properly conceived” [I.1 ¶86]: understanding must precede practice.

See also: Wisdom

References: I.1 ¶86

Growth spirit

term

The spirit of growth in children, identified with the vegetable spirit, more phantastic than the animal, allowing free imagination until the circle of life closes.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Children have the growth spirit in them (the vegetable spirit which is more phantastic than the animal)” [APP ¶122]. It allows free imagination until the circle of life closes. Identified with the vegetable spirit.

Identified with: Vegetable spirit [APP ¶122]

See also: Spirit

References: APP ¶122

Gustavus Adolphus

person

A figure before whom, the book reports, a transmutation took place in 1620, the gold being coined into medals; cited as evidence for transmutation.

Cited in support of the reality of transmutation: one was performed before him in 1620 and the gold coined into medals [I.1 ¶77, I.1 n104].

References: I.1 n104, I.1 ¶77

H

H. O’Brien

person — author of the Round Towers · H. O’Brien, author of the Round Towers, O’Brien

Author of the Round Towers of Ireland, mildly criticized by Atwood for mistaking the White Paradise for his Emerald Home, yet praised as an estimable work.

Atwood cites the Round Towers of Ireland (chap. 22, p. 327) and mildly criticizes its author for mistaking the White Paradise for his ‘Emerald Home’ — an exclusiveness she pardons for its enthusiasm — while calling the book ‘an estimable work’ [III.2 ¶8, III.2 n10].

References: III.2 n10, III.2 ¶8

Habbakuk

person

A figure quoted by Atwood to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise.

Quoted to illustrate power acting through the hand of the wise: “he had horns coming out of his hand, and there was the hiding of his power” [IV.3 ¶39].

References: IV.3 ¶39

Hades

term

Not fleshly existence but a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries: the dark, image-loving lower world and unpurified aerial moisture of life, the soul’s state while her hypostasis remains dark.

In the quoted Sacred Discourse, through downward will or evil agencies “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶14].

Atwood’s own reading: Hades is not the corporeal nature or fleshly existence but “a state of vital submersion in the Mysteries, when the consciousness is artificially drawn about the penetralia of its first life”; she equates it with Lethe — “by Hades, or that profound Lethe” [II.3 ¶7]. She describes “Hades dark all over, squalid, delighting in images, unintelligible, precipitous” [II.3 ¶26], where consciousness wrapped by the Mysteries is anxious and perplexed. It is the aerial moisture of life unpurified: “which moisture in its native state, before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason, is that Hades we are treating of, the Purgatory of the wise” [II.3 ¶29]. And “the soul is said to be in Hades all the while that her hypostasis continues in darkness” [II.3 ¶36] — that is, while she regards her image objectively, before experimental knowledge.

Identities: Lethe [II.3 ¶7]; the Purgatory of the wise; the aerial moisture in its native state [II.3 ¶29].

Identified with: Lethe [II.3 ¶7]; Purgatory of the wise [II.3 ¶29]; aerial moisture in its native (unpurified) state [II.3 ¶29]

References: II.2 ¶14, II.3 ¶26, II.3 ¶29, II.3 ¶36, II.3 ¶7

Haly

person · Hali

An authority cited on the necessity of the vessel or place, and, in the Appendix, for the noise accompanying the Alchemical solution.

With Morien and Albert, Hali supports the necessity of the vessel or place: “the place is the principle also of the supernatural generation” [II.1 ¶8]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Haly is cited as saying the Alchemical solution is accompanied with noise [APP ¶50].

References: II.1 ¶8, APP ¶50

Handicraft

term

The ancients’ more scientific practical art by which, Atwood says, they experimentally entered the temple of Divine Wisdom.

Atwood: “a more scientific Handicraft enabled the ancients experimentally to enter” the temple of Divine Wisdom [IV.3 ¶37].

References: IV.3 ¶37

Hands of the ether

term

The transverse poles of the Ether, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; in man a natural fire, the fire of the Ether in our life organism.

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The hands of the Ether are its transverse poles”, formed by the divine differentiation everywhere; “in man a natural fire —i.e., the fire of the Ether in us, or of our life organism” [APP ¶177].

Identified with: transverse poles [APP ¶177]

See also: Ether

References: APP ¶177

Harprecht

person

An adept named among the persecuted, sometimes confused with Philalethes.

Named as a persecuted adept, sometimes confused with Philalethes [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73].

References: I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73

Head life

term

The one life we presently live, the animal and rational life, out of three possible lives; the Hermetically regenerated give it up.

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “We live in but one life, the head life, but there are three possible lives” [APP ¶45]. We have no right to be efficient in it, and the Hermetically regenerated give it up. Identified as “the Head life or the animal, the rational life” [APP ¶60]. Contrast heart life.

Identified with: animal, rational life [APP ¶60]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶45, APP ¶60

Head of Hermes’ crow

term · Hermes’ crow

Per a quoted modern exponent, the black, motionless state at the beginning of the work, after three months’ circulation.

Quoted from “our modern exponent”: “the head of Hermes’ crow is said to be in the beginning of this work” [II.1 ¶23] — the black, motionless state reached after three months’ circulation. See also Head of the Crow.

See also: Crow

References: II.1 ¶23

Head of the crow

term

Named by Atwood with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and Obscurity as present in the hours of conjunction; not defined there.

Atwood lists it with Darkness, Night, Saturn, the Antimony of the Wise and “Obscurity and the Head of the Crow in the various hours of conjunction” [III.3 ¶13]. Not defined in the record; compare head of Hermes’ crow.

See also: Crow

References: III.3 ¶13

Head Stone

term

The stone whose virtues Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber celebrate, mentioned by Atwood in connection with Reason acting as a ferment.

Atwood says Lully, Arnold, Bacon and Geber were “abundantly celebrating the virtues of their Head Stone” [III.1 ¶21], in a passage on Reason acting as a ferment; the context apparently links the two, though the record does not state the identity.

See also: Stone

References: III.1 ¶21

Head-consciousness

term

The consciousness into which the whole force of regenerate life is brought up in the perfected Corner Stone.

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the whole force of regenerate life is “brought up into the head-consciousness, what they call in the north” [APP ¶134], in the perfected Corner Stone.

References: APP ¶134

Healing art

term

Medicine as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing.

Atwood presents the Healing Art as once perfectly attained and divinely gifted, then lost through ambition, gain and Galenic theorizing: “So the origin, decline, and fall of the Healing Art has been pictured by one of its brightest ornaments” [IV.3 ¶35].

References: IV.3 ¶35

Heart life

term

The higher life into which the lower opens: that which is above and attracts, identified with the feminine principle and Wisdom.

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: the higher life into which the lower opens, “that which is above (the feminine principle, — Wisdom, — the heart life)” [APP ¶98], which attracts. She also writes “the heart life, or the medial life, or the celestial life, or the vegetable life” [APP ¶97]; whether these are strict synonyms or a series is uncertain from the text. Contrast head life.

Identified with: feminine principle, Wisdom [APP ¶98]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶97, APP ¶98

Heat

term

In Vaughan’s words, the heat the operator applies, which must not exceed the natural proportion; its literal nature is not stated.

Vaughan (quoted) warns of the operator’s heat: “if thy heat exceeds the natural proportion” [III.4 ¶44]. The record does not say what this heat literally is.

References: III.4 ¶44

Heaven

term

Per Proclus, intellectual contact with the intelligible; Aristotle distinguishes three senses of the word, and the Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven.

Proclus (quoted): “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36]. Aristotle distinguishes three senses, including “we are accustomed likewise to call that heaven, which is composed from every natural and sensible body” [III.2 ¶36]. The Hermetists, like Plato, place their earth within heaven [III.2 ¶36].

Identified with: intellectual contact with the intelligible [III.2 ¶36]

References: III.2 ¶36

Heaven and earth

term

Two principles which Hermes says are to be joined through the Water; Atwood reads them as the two invisible poles of the Spirit.

Hermes (quoted): “the Heaven is to be joined mediately with the Earth” [I.3 ¶55], that is, through the Water. Atwood reads the passage as signalizing the two invisible poles of the Spirit [I.3 ¶55].

See also: Earth

References: I.3 ¶55

Heaven and earth philosophical

term

An expression, in a quoted adept’s voice, for the agent and patient of the work, which must be united in friendship and love.

Voiced by the Adept Atwood quotes: the Heaven and Earth philosophical are treated as agent and patient, “the Heaven and Earth philosophical, even as agent and patient” [IV.2 ¶30], which must be united in friendship and love. Asserted identity: = agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30].

Identified with: Agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30]

References: IV.2 ¶30

Heavenly fire

term

The Benedictine Monk’s own fire, which stirs up the elemental fire; set against coals and common fire.

In the words of the Benedictine Monk (quoted): “For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one” [III.3 ¶24]. This fire excites the elemental fire as the matter desires a fitting Form, and is contrasted with coals and common fire [III.3 ¶24].

See also: Fire

References: III.3 ¶24

Heavenly Flyer

term · heavenly bird

With ‘the fire’, one of the two agents of the work, glossed by the scholiast as the external and internal agents of the Hermetic work.

A quoted scholiast reads the pair: “By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified, says the scholiast, the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work” [I.3 n16]. The heavenly Flyer (or bird) is thus paired with the fire as one of these agents; the text does not say which of the two is external and which internal.

References: I.3 n16

Hebrew doctrine

collective voice

The Hebrew teaching, which Atwood says differs from the Ethnic Anima Mundi only in words.

Atwood compares the Hebrew doctrine with the Ethnic Anima Mundi and finds that it differs from it only in words [I.2 ¶14].

References: I.2 ¶14

Hebrew Kabalists

collective voice — Rabbis · Rabbis

Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis, cited by Atwood in support of absolute Idealism, the fall and reunion of creation, reason over authority, and self-inquiry.

Atwood cites the Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis in support of absolute Idealism, of creation’s fall and reunion, of reason over authority, and of self-inquiry [II.1 ¶40; II.1 ¶41].

See also: Ben Jochai (the learned Rassbi; his disciples), Kabalistic commentators (mystics of the middle ages; the Rabbis), Kabalists

References: II.1 ¶40, II.1 ¶41

Hebrews and Academics

collective voice

A group voice whose ‘precious death’ Atwood equates with the gate of blackness.

Atwood equates the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics with the gate of blackness [II.3 ¶37].

References: II.3 ¶37

Hegel

person · the German philosopher

A modern metaphysician whose doctrine of pure Being Atwood contrasts with the Hermetic way, and whom the Appendix lists among moderns who drew on the Mystics.

Atwood quotes “the German philosopher (Hegel)”: “All things, says the German philosopher (Hegel), have their commencement in pure Being” [III.2 ¶30]. She uses this as a contrast: abstraction reaches pure Being, which is equal to non-Being, but only as a void [III.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named among modern metaphysicians who took their starting point from the Mystics [APP ¶96], and appears again in the same list as one who ‘saw it’ [APP ¶117].

References: III.2 ¶30, APP ¶117, APP ¶96

Heliodorus

person

Author to whom the mystical romance Theagenes and Chariclea is attributed; named among writers of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone.

The mystical romance Theagenes and Chariclea is attributed to Heliodorus, who, the book says, resigned his bishopric of Tricca rather than disavow it [I.1 ¶28; I.1 n34]. He is also named with Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras, Zosimus and Archelaus as an author of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

References: I.1 n34, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶28

Helvetius

person

‘The acute Helvetius’, cited by Atwood as a witness of transmutation and of the transcendent Light found at the centre; a worthy disciple of Paracelsus.

Atwood names Helvetius with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Faber as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and cites his explicit transmutation story in support [I.1 ¶77]. His ‘Armed Magnet’ is identified with the Wheel of Fire or inner Sun [II.3 ¶54]. From his Vitulus Aureus, ‘the acute Helvetius’ is cited as testifying to the transcendent Light and to finding the mystery, by experience, at the centre: “that most recreant Beauty can never be blotted out from my mind” [III.1 ¶70; III.1 n74]; how far the cited words are his own is not clear from the passage.

References: I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶77, II.3 ¶54, III.1 n74, III.1 ¶70

Heraclitus

person

Philosopher Atwood cites repeatedly in support: the dry soul, living the death of others, the principle named fire, and the Well where Truth lies hidden.

Atwood says Heraclitus’ metaphysics agrees in essentials with Aristotle’s [I.1 ¶16], and cites him as supporting that the theurgic media are medicines of imperfect souls [II.2 ¶5]. For the dry, self-turned soul she quotes “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27]; for nox corporis, souls dead to this life and alive in the other, “we live their death and die their life” [II.4 ¶9]. He is cited as naming the principle, according to essence, fire: “have denominated it to be fire” [III.2 ¶35]. The Wisdom is ‘that Well of Heraclitus’ where Truth lies hidden, ‘whence also those philosophic tears’ [IV.4 ¶27]. Atwood uses him in support or illustration throughout.

References: I.1 ¶16, II.2 ¶5, II.3 ¶27, II.4 ¶9, III.2 ¶35, IV.4 ¶27

Hercules

person

Figure whose cleansing of the Augean Stable figures, in the Appendix, the cleansing of the mineral soul.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Hercules’ labour of cleansing the Augean Stable figures the cleansing of the mineral soul [APP ¶71], and his grief for Hylas illustrates the same point as the Iliad [APP ¶109]. In the main text, Hippocrates is said to have been honored by the Athenians with the same gifts as Hercules and Aesculapius [IV.3 ¶34].

See also: Heroes of the ordeal (Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus), Labouring heroes (Perseus, Theseus, Bacchus, Ulysses, Hercules, Jason)

References: IV.3 ¶34, APP ¶109, APP ¶71

Herman Conringius

person

Author of De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina, criticized by Atwood for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention.

Atwood criticizes Herman Conringius, author of De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina., for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n1].

References: I.1 n1, I.1 ¶3

Herman Fichtuld

person · Fichtuld

Author of Probier Stein, listed by Atwood among persecuted adepts.

Herman Fichtuld, cited for his Probier Stein, is listed among persecuted adepts [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n79].

References: I.1 n79, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70

Hermes

person · Hermes Trismegistus, Trismegistus, Thrice Great Hermes, the ancient Hermes, Hermes the King

The adept king credited with the Hermetic writings, whose Golden Treatise Atwood prints and glosses, and a constantly cited authority on the work, its agents and its moral conditions.

Hermes (Trismegistus) is the starting point of the Hermetic story, an adept king credited with the Hermetic writings [I.1 ¶6; I.1 ¶7]; the works imputed to him were translated from Greek into Latin by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. Geber ranks after him, and Artephius learned the art from his books [I.1 ¶31; I.1 ¶36]; Norton’s verse lists him among masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

Golden Treatise (Tract. Aur.). Introduced as an ancient epitome of the whole Art of doubtful authorship [I.2 ¶50], it is printed in full as the main text of I.3 and glossed in Atwood’s notes [I.3 ¶1–¶58]; she calls it a fair, less sophistical example of alchemical writing, yet veiled [I.3 ¶46]. Its key lines: “the work is both with you and about you” [I.3 ¶1]; “the masculine truly is the heaven of the feminine, and the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶15]; “the whole matter I know to be one only thing” [I.3 ¶36]; “that which is born of the crow is the beginning of this Art” [I.3 ¶46]. ‘Hermes the King’ first declared that Mercury cannot be mortified alone [I.3 n17]. Atwood reinterprets its Water as the ethereal body, not common water [I.2 ¶43; I.2 n41], and cites it throughout: the vessel is the water, “vas philosophorum est aqua eorum” [II.1 ¶8]; “Extract from the ray its shadow and its obscurity” [II.3 ¶27]; two natures mortified together [III.1 ¶43]; “Take, my son, the flying bird and drown it flying” [III.1 ¶53; IV.1 ¶15], where she notes he ‘does not speak of it openly’ [III.1 n67]; the chain binding the matter [III.2 ¶22]; secrecy toward the vicious [III.4 ¶9]; the science as “the sole gift of the living God” [III.4 ¶20].

Other works. The separation precept (cited with the Tract. Aur., the Smaragdine Tablet and the Asclepius), “Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross”, is read as Mind the Separator [III.1 ¶21; III.1 n22]; the Tablet is quoted in full as summary instruction, “That which is above is as that which is below” [IV.2 ¶43]. The Poemander (Pymander) testifies to inward regeneration: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; “Conceive well the Light in thy Mind, and Know It.” [III.3 ¶52]; each principle carries “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. Knowledge of the First Cause is “a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33].

Practice (IV.3). He supports the First Key and beheading the Raven [IV.3 ¶3], the Stone as “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶5], keeping the earthy residue [IV.3 ¶7], “The first of all is the water which issueth out of this Stone.” [IV.3 ¶8], and the permanent union of purified bodies and spirits [IV.3 ¶10]. He names the Spirit of Universal nature “a Quintessence” [III.2 ¶36]. Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): the Poemander on the downward-born nature [APP ¶18]; the Golden Treatise cap. 4 [APP ¶51].

Also cited. Trismegistus as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶20]; the Stone generated with light and bringing forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30]; furnace and glass making a new world, via Fludd’s Mosaica [II.3 ¶52; II.3 n58]; “our Son, as Hermes calls him”, a personification of the intellectual purpose [III.1 ¶36]; equal Spirits, “both need the help of the other” [III.1 ¶41]; the necessity of labor, via Eirenaeus [IV.1 ¶6], and his toil for ‘the blessed Lunary of Diana’ [III.2 ¶64]; in Norton’s verse, the water of crude Mercury [III.3 ¶74] and “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [IV.2 ¶13].
