Introspection

term

Psellus’s term, as cited, for the initiate’s inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure, distinguished from the Superinspection.

Atwood cites Psellus for the initiate’s inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure: “This is the Introspection which Psellus speaks of, as distinguished from the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” [II.3 ¶46].

References: II.3 ¶46

Introspective proof

term

Inward testing, without which inbred evil cannot truly be discovered.

Atwood holds that inbred evil cannot be truly discovered without inward testing: “or even discover it truly without introspective proof” [IV.4 ¶17].

References: IV.4 ¶17

Introversion

term

A complete process that must be passed through before the work is perfected; not further defined.

Atwood states that “it is not perfected unless the whole introversion is passed through” [III.1 ¶21]. The text here does not define the process further.

References: III.1 ¶21

Intuition

term · Intuitive faith

Direct, self-evident knowing, which Atwood treats as the evidence and end of all rational proof and the highest human certainty.

Atwood’s own term for direct, self-evident knowing. She holds that “intuition is the evidence and end of every rational proof” [II.1 ¶33], and that “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. On her account it is the highest certainty open to a human being.

References: II.1 ¶33, II.1 ¶34

Intuitional life

term · intuitional

The level of life reached by cutting off the sensuous life; dissolving the sensuous reaches the intuitional, called divine.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “You cut off the sensuous life and get into the intuitional” [APP ¶176]. Dissolving the sensuous life is said to reach the intuitional, which she calls divine. A reader linked it with the “medial life” of [APP ¶182], but that identity is inferred from the parallel, not stated in the text.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶176

Inversion

term

The reversal of nature’s ordinary order: Atwood calls it our present state, a requirement for perfect manifestation, and reason turning back on itself.

Atwood uses the word in three related ways.

  • Our condition. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “Our present state is one of inversion.” [APP ¶45]
  • A requirement of the work. The ordinary order of nature’s procedure has to be reversed, and this lies beyond ordinary art and nature: the work proceeds “by a real experimental inversion” [I.2 ¶22], since “the order of natural procedure ought to be introverted for a true and perfect manifestation” [I.2 ¶27].
  • Reason turning back on itself. Logic “becomes bounded about its own inversion” [III.2 ¶67], while the experiment actually carries the inversion out. Followed strictly, both lead to the First Source [III.2 ¶67].

The text does not say whether these are one process seen from different sides.

References: I.2 ¶22, I.2 ¶27, III.2 ¶67, APP ¶45

Invisible artist

term

The true worker of the work, according to a quoted Adept: the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature.

A quoted Adept speaks here: “The work is performed by an invisible Artist; for there is a secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature” [IV.2 ¶18]. The invisible Artist is thus identified with the secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature, which is the real agent behind the work.

Identified with: secret incubation of the Spirit of God upon nature [IV.2 ¶18]

See also: Artist

References: IV.2 ¶18

Invisible hand

term

The inner hand of which the outward hand is the image and clothing; it works effects according to what it has attained.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The hand outward is an image of the invisible hand, its clothing” [APP ¶177]. The invisible hand works its effects according to what it has attained.

References: APP ¶177

Invisible Mercury

term · invisible Universal Mercury

In Bohme’s account, the agent that prepares the Antimonial Spirit, also called the spiritual air of Antimony.

Bohme is quoted here. The Invisible Mercury prepares the Antimonial Spirit. It works when condensed in its vehicle, and its operation brings the three principles into harmony [II.1 ¶21]. Identity: “the invisible Universal Mercury, or spiritual air of Antimony” [II.1 ¶21].

Identified with: spiritual air of Antimony [II.1 ¶21]

See also: Mercury

References: II.1 ¶21

Isaacs

collective voice — J. I. Hollandus, I. Hollandus · J. I. Hollandus, I. Hollandus, Hollandus

Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked successfully; Atwood gives their works as references.

Atwood names the Isaacs (J. I. Hollandus and I. Hollandus) as Dutch adepts, father and son, who are said to have worked the art successfully [I.1 ¶58]. She gives their works, de Lapide Philosophico and Opera Universalia, as references [I.1 n63].

References: I.1 n63, I.1 ¶58

Isaiah

person

Cited twice: for the overflowing of the dark power, and for gradual purifying and perfecting.

Atwood cites Isaiah twice.

  • Isaiah, Chap. 8, verse 8 illustrates how the dark power overflows at this stage of the work: “He shall overflow the channels, and go over all the banks” [III.1 ¶60, III.1 n65].
  • Isaiah 38:13 supports gradual purifying and perfecting: “Line upon line, Precept upon precept” [IV.3 ¶39, IV.3 n19].

References: III.1 n65, III.1 ¶60, IV.3 n19, IV.3 ¶39

Isis

term · Queen Isis, fable of Isis

The goddess Atwood identifies with nature, Minerva, Athena and the Wisdom under inquiry, and the name of the Matter once it becomes intelligent and convertible to every form.

In Apuleius (quoted). Isis appears to Lucius and names herself: “call me by my true name, Queen Isis” [II.4 ¶17]. She calls herself nature: “I, who am nature, the parent of all things” [II.4 ¶17]. She is also queen of the elements, the one goddess “whose one divinity the whole orb of the earth venerates under a manifold form, by different rites and a various of appellations” [II.4 ¶17]. Among those appellations are Pessinuntica, Cecropian Minerva, Paphian Venus, Diana Dyctynna, Stygian Proserpine, Ceres, Juno, Bellona, Hecate and Rhamnusia.

Atwood’s identifications. The Sphinx stood in “the vestibule of Isis, who is the same with Minerva and that Wisdom we are investigating” [III.1 ¶5]. So Isis is equated with Minerva and with the Wisdom that is the subject of the inquiry.

In the fable and the work. In the fable, Isis gathers Osiris’s scattered members: “but Isis, recollecting, hides them in a chest” [III.1 ¶53]. In the work, the Lunar Vulcan plays her part. It tempers Typhon and reconciles the opposed principles, which then circulate with her in equilibrium [III.1 ¶63]. She is “as Isis in the Mysteries, where she is also called Athena” [III.1 ¶63]. That second name is given “to express that self-motion and intelligence with which this Spirit is endowed” [III.1 ¶63].

Name of the Matter. After the process described in [III.3 ¶61], the Matter is endowed with understanding, can be converted into any Form, and is the pre-existent mother of all. “Then she is Isis, the Divine I Am” [III.3 ¶62]. She is also “by the Greeks called Myrionymous, or the goddess with a thousand names” [III.3 ¶62]. Yet “As respects herself, she is Nothing” [III.3 ¶62].

All of these are Atwood’s statements except the Apuleius passage, which she quotes.

Isis (the old mythology). Atwood brings in Isis of the old mythology to illustrate the divine beauty that is pursued. Isis is the Goddess whose temple is Reason [II.1 ¶50].

Fable of Isis. Atwood cites the fable in which “she brought forth Horus, even feeding him with fire” [I.3 n41], to illustrate the nourishing of the son with fire.

Identified with: nature [II.4 ¶17]; Pessinuntica, Cecropian Minerva, Paphian Venus, Diana Dyctynna, Stygian Proserpine, Ceres, Juno, Bellona, Hecate, Rhamnusia [II.4 ¶17]; Minerva [III.1 ¶5]; Wisdom [III.1 ¶5]; Athena [III.1 ¶63]; Divine I am [III.3 ¶62]; Myrionymous (goddess with a thousand names) [III.3 ¶62]

See also: Fable of Isis and Osiris

References: I.3 n41, II.1 ¶50, II.4 ¶17, III.1 ¶5, III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶63, III.3 ¶62

Islands of the blessed

term

In Olympiodorus, a figure for a condition above corporeal life and generation, the same as the Elysian Fields.

Olympiodorus is quoted here. The Islands of the Blessed stand for a condition above corporeal life and generation, just as “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He adds that “these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3].

Identified with: Elysian Fields [II.4 ¶3]

References: II.4 ¶3

Ixir

term

In Hermes, the ferment made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water; it tinges and fixes, and bodies cannot be made pure without it.

Hermes is quoted here. Ixir is the ferment, made from the gold of the wise with a fiery water. It tinges and fixes, and it is that “without which bodies cannot be made pure” [I.3 n63].

Identities stated:

  • gold and ferment: “gold, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶58]
  • Sericum: “we make of them Sericum, i.e., Ixir” [I.3 ¶59]
  • seriacum: “we make seriacum, which is the ferment Ixir” [I.3 ¶62]
  • Elixir, true Ferment: “This is the Elixir, Ixir, or true Ferment tinging and fixing” [I.3 n63]

Identified with: ferment / gold [I.3 ¶58]; Sericum [I.3 ¶59]; seriacum [I.3 ¶62]; Elixir, true Ferment [I.3 n63]

References: I.3 n63, I.3 ¶58, I.3 ¶59, I.3 ¶62

J

J. Tollius

person · Tollius

A Dutchman and elegant classical expositor of Hermetic matters; Atwood counts him in the golden chain of Hermetic philosophers.

Atwood calls Tollius a Dutchman and an elegant classical expositor on the same ground [I.1 ¶70]. His works listed are Tollii Fortuita, Manudcutio ad Coelum Chemicum and Sapientia Insanies, sive Promissa Chemica [I.1 n87]. Alongside Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Michael Maier, he belongs to the “golden chain of Hermetic philosophers”. These writers traced the poets’ allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own, and Atwood cites them in support [III.1 ¶25].

References: I.1 n87, I.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶25

J.J. Beccher

person · Beccher, Becher

An author Atwood lists, with his works.

Beccher appears in a list of writers [I.1 ¶70]. His works given are Physica Subterranea, Oedipus Chemicus Aperius Mysteria and Laboratorium Chemicum [I.1 n86].

References: I.1 n86, I.1 ¶70, III.2 n38

Jacob

person

Cited in support of self-renunciation as the way to union.

Atwood cites words she attributes to Jacob in support of self-renunciation as the way to union: “Wherefore I abhor myself, cries Jacob” [IV.3 ¶58].

References: IV.3 ¶58

Jesus Christ and his apostles

collective voice · Jesus Christ

Atwood holds that the Theurgic Art comes nearest to their doctrine of regeneration.

Atwood makes a comparison: the Theurgic Art comes nearest to “the perfect doctrine of regeneration preached by Jesus Christ and his apostles” [III.1 ¶11].

See also: Apostle

References: III.1 ¶11

Jew

collective voice

The person who told Flammel the truth on this point.

The Jew is mentioned as the one who told Flammel the truth on this point [IV.3 ¶10].

References: IV.3 ¶10

Job

person

Job and his book, cited often: his story is a type of the regenerate’s sacrifice in faith, and his texts on Wisdom, Leviathan, gold and humbling support Atwood’s argument.

Atwood cites Job and the Book of Job often.

  • Job 28, on Wisdom. Quoted at length to illustrate a contrast. Precious things hidden in the earth are brought to light, but the place of Wisdom is hidden from all living and known to God. For man, “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is Wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n5].
  • Job 41, Leviathan. Quoted at length right after the account of how Typhon is subdued, with no commentary: “Canst thou draw out Leviathan with an hook?” [III.1 ¶63, III.1 n71].
  • Job 31 and 33. Cited for the accountability of moral evil and the condemnation of trusting in gold: “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [III.4 ¶7, III.4 ¶8, III.4 n5]. Note n6 goes with Adam hiding his iniquity in his bosom [III.4 n6].
  • Job 40:14. Supports the humbling of the proud, followed by the promise of saving power: “THEN WILL I ALSO CONFESS UNTO THEE THAT THINE OWN RIGHT HAND CAN SAVE” [IV.3 ¶58, IV.3 n27]. The note marker follows the end of the quotation, and the text does not say how far back the citation reaches.
  • An objection answered. The saying “no one by searching can find out the Almighty to perfection” holds, Atwood says, for a man searching by his own will. It does not hold for one conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will [IV.4 ¶23].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Job’s story is “all a type” of the sacrifice in faith made by the Hermetically regenerated [APP ¶60]. His words illustrate the contrast between the perfection of the Law of Light and human defection: “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth Thee; therefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes” [APP ¶90].

References: III.1 n5, III.1 n71, III.1 ¶63, III.1 ¶8, III.4 n5, III.4 n6, III.4 ¶7, III.4 ¶8, IV.3 n27, IV.3 ¶58, IV.4 ¶23, APP ¶60, APP ¶90

John Andre

person — J. Andraeas · J. Andraeas, Andraeas

Cited as a witness to Arnold’s conversion of iron bars into gold at Rome.

Atwood cites John Andre as testifying that Arnold turned iron bars into gold at Rome [I.1 ¶43]. The source is in addit. ad Speculum Rub de crim. Falsi: “Nostris diebus habuimus magnum” [I.1 n52]. Our rendering, not the book’s: In our days we had a great [one].

References: I.1 n52, I.1 ¶43

John Cremer

person — Abbot of Westminster · John Cremer, Abbot of Westminster, Cremer, Cremeri

Abbot of Westminster: a long-labouring seeker, misled by the adepts’ enigmas, who found enlightenment by seeking Lully; his Testament supports the Lully story.

Atwood presents John Cremer, Abbot of Westminster, as an example. He laboured for a long time, was misled by the adepts’ enigmas, and found enlightenment by seeking out Lully [I.1 ¶46]. His Testament (Cremeri Testamentum) supports the Lully story, and in it Cremer openly condemns the king’s breach of faith [I.1 ¶47, I.1 n56].

References: I.1 n56, I.1 ¶46, I.1 ¶47

John French

person · French

A practitioner who translated Sendivogius as The New Light of Alchemy, with a preface Atwood calls bold and striking.

Atwood names John French as a practitioner who translated Sendivogius (The New Light of Alchemy) and wrote a “bold and striking” preface [I.1 ¶71]. French’s Art of Distillation is also cited [I.1 n90].

References: I.1 n90, I.1 ¶71

John Trithemius

person · Abbot Trithemius, Trithemius

Listed among the great spirits; Atwood names him as Agrippa’s source for the means and principles of Occult Science.

Trithemius is listed among the great spirits [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood says that Abbot Trithemius was Agrippa’s source for the means and principles of Occult Science [I.1 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶64, II.3 n20, II.3 ¶24

Julian

person · the Emperor Julian

The Emperor Julian, cited on vital rectification and on Divine union needing assistance; Atwood counts him among the Alexandrian revival figures.

Julian is one of the Alexandrian revival figures (with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Apuleius) who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge and are quoted later [I.1 ¶27].

  • From the Oration to the Extra-Mundane Mother (Julian’s Orations II), illustrating vital rectification: the purified soul receives Divine Light and strengthens its connate spirit, and disease comes from erroneous motion of the spirit. “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature” [IV.3 ¶30, IV.3 n10].
  • The Emperor Julian’s arguments, preserved by Cyril, support the view that Divine union needs such assistance: “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 n46].

References: I.1 ¶27, II.1 n46, II.1 ¶52, IV.3 n10, IV.3 ¶30

K

Kabalah

collective voice · Kabbalah, the Hebrew Kabbalah

The Hebrew tradition Atwood cites in support at several points: Boehme’s agreement with it, the Divine I Am, union with God as Fermentation, and going forth and returning.

Atwood cites the Kabalah consistently in support:

  • Boehme’s testimony is said to agree “in all particulars with the most ancient Kabalah and profound experimental divinity” [III.2 ¶17].
  • The Kabalah supports the view that in the Divine I Am is signified the Substant Unity of all that is [III.3 ¶79].
  • Its union of man with God is identified with Fermentation: “that which in the Kabalah is denominated the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27].
  • From Sephir Jezirah, cap. 1, going forth and returning, with closed-eye meditation, forms part of the final passage into accord: “Egredere et regredere, et propterea pactum praecisum est” [IV.3 ¶60, IV.3 ¶61, IV.3 n28]. Our rendering, not the book’s: Go forth and return, and for this reason the covenant is cut.
  • The Hebrew Kabbalah is described as “profound yet simple metaphysics”, “partially transmitted”, and agreeing within the same tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

See also: Cabalistic, Cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience

References: III.2 ¶17, III.3 ¶79, IV.3 n28, IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶60, IV.3 ¶61, IV.4 ¶28

Kabalistic commentators

collective voice — mystics of the middle ages; the Rabbis · Kabalistic commentators and mystics of the middle ages, the Rabbis

The Kabalistic commentators, medieval mystics and Rabbis, who Atwood says reached the same ideas as German metaphysics by ontological experiment.

Atwood cites these figures in support: they hold the same ideas as German metaphysics, but reached them by ontological experiment [III.2 ¶29].

See also: Ben Jochai (the learned Rassbi; his disciples), Hebrew Kabalists (Rabbis), Kabalists

References: III.2 ¶29

Kabalistic Interpreter

collective voice

Cited, by way of Blackwell’s Mythology, on creation as the Divine Will producing itself into material form.

Atwood cites the Kabalistic Interpreter (by way of Blackwell’s Mythology, letter 7) for creation as the Divine Will producing itself into form out of inane Identity: “the Divine Will, then alone operating, says the Kabalistic Interpreter, produces itself into a material form and recreation” [III.3 ¶43, III.3 n29].

See also: Kabalists

References: III.3 n29, III.3 ¶43

Kabalists

collective voice · the Kabalist

Kabalistic writers Atwood cites in support on the Quintessence, man as prototype, the Abyss as the Matter, uniting end and beginning, and the Law’s hidden soul.

Atwood cites the Kabalists in support at several points:

  • They name the pure Quintessence “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light” [I.2 ¶16].
  • They raise man up as containing the prototype of creation [II.1 ¶42].
  • Their Abyss is identified with the Matter, “styled also by them Unknown, Void, Nothing, Infinite” [III.2 ¶60].
  • From Liber Jezirah, cap. 1, the completed work unites end and beginning: “Unite the end to the beginning as the flame is united to the coal” [III.1 ¶50, III.1 n55].
  • From the Zohar, part 3, fol. 152, verso, a view Atwood endorses: the Law’s narrative clothes a sublime mystery, its Soul. “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n39].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Kabalists celebrate the White Light as belonging to the Ancient of Days, the primeval Light [APP ¶157].

See also: Hebrew Kabalists (Rabbis), Kabalistic commentators (mystics of the middle ages; the Rabbis), Kabalistic Interpreter, Modern Kabalists

References: I.2 ¶16, II.1 ¶42, III.1 n55, III.1 ¶50, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n39, III.3 ¶59, APP ¶157

Kant

person

Criticized by Atwood: his metaphysics stops short of objective realization and never got past the negative margin of intellectual intuition.

Atwood criticizes Kant together with Fichte and Schelling. Their metaphysics ends in void non-entity and skepticism and falls short of objective realization, though she ranks Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Kant is criticized for never getting past the negative margin of intellectual intuition [APP ¶96]. He is also said to have “saw that”, but the text does not state what he saw. Apparently it is the preceding point about intellect and the Universal Reason [APP ¶117].

References: III.2 ¶31, APP ¶117, APP ¶96

Key

term · Keys

The decisive secret that opens the Mystery and the Art; also, among the authorities, the name for successive numbered operations of the practice and for explanatory texts.

Atwood’s usage. For Atwood the Key is what opens the Mystery and alone passes its wards: without it the Mystery can neither be entered nor explained, and with it the Adepts’ writings become instructive — “If, however, the Key is wanting, how may we presume to enter” [IV.4 ¶32]. She identifies it with Light: “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]. Even holding it does not guarantee more than entry to the vestibule when the texts are scrambled, “even to those who had already become possessed of the true key” [I.1 ¶82]. The Alchemists “delivered many Keys, whereby, as they say, we may enter into the sanctuary of philosophy”, but these do not unfold the first approach [IV.1 ¶3]. She also calls the six texts she then presents Keys: “The six following Keys, delivered into the safe hand of the intelligent inquirer” [IV.2 ¶45].

Quoted authorities. Basil Valentine, with Kirchringius and Madathan, makes the key the decisive secret, opening the first and the last gate, so that missing it ruins the whole course: “this key is the principal part of the whole Art; this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last” [III.1 ¶37]. Eudoxus uses Keys for six successive, numbered operations, each ending at a stated point — the First at the whitening of the Stone, the Second at digestion and putrefaction — and placed within works: “the operation of the Second Key of the First Work is ended” [IV.3 ¶5]. He also speaks of the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Keys, and says that whoever knows the Stone and Our Fire has “the Keys of the Art”; the mercurial liquor is “the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16].

The records thus show two senses: a single decisive secret (Atwood, Basil Valentine), and a sequence of operational stages or texts (Eudoxus; Atwood’s six Keys).

Identified with: Light [IV.4 ¶32]

References: I.1 ¶82, III.1 ¶37, IV.1 ¶3, IV.2 ¶45, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶5, IV.4 ¶32

Key of David

term

Held by the one competent to minister, who opens and no man shuts; Atwood does not explain it further.

Atwood says the one competent to minister is “he that hath the Key of David”, who opens and no man shuts [IV.3 ¶39]. The text gives no further explanation. Compare the Appendix’s “Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97] (see Key to the Work).

See also: David

References: IV.3 ¶39

Key of the philosophers

term

In a passage quoted from Hermes, the ferment’s action of whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies.

Quoting Hermes, Atwood gives the ferment’s action — whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies — and Hermes says “this is the Key of the philosophers and the end of their works” [I.3 ¶58].

See also: Philosophers

References: I.3 ¶58

Key of the restoration

term

In the Master’s words, the dissolution of the composition by the power of the Water.

In a passage given as the Master’s, the dissolution of the composition by the Water is named: “when by the power of the Water the composition is dissolved, it is the Key of the Restoration” [IV.2 ¶14].

References: IV.2 ¶14

Key to the work

term

In the Appendix, entry into the work or into another life, gained when the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life by exstasis.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the entry into the work, or into another life, is gained from the desire of the lower life opening into the heart life by exstasis. She equates it with the Key of the House of David: “The Key to the Work, or into another life, the Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97].

Identified with: Key of the House of David [APP ¶97]

See also: Works

References: APP ¶97

Keystone

term

Something “rejected” that regains “her Head place” only after the labours of the Heroic Intellect; the text does not decode it.

Atwood writes of the labours of the Heroic Intellect, which must come “before the rejected Keystone regains her Head place” [II.2 ¶29]. The text does not say plainly what the Keystone is.

References: II.2 ¶29

Khunrath

person · H. Khunrath, Henry Khunrath

A pious German adept, author of the Ampitheatrum Sapientae Eternae, whom Atwood treats as a main authority on the Azoth, the Stone’s virtues, and the practice.

Atwood lists Henry Khunrath among the German adepts, a pious adept embittered by mistreatment; works named include the Ampitheat. Sapientiae Eternae and Magnesia Catholica [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n84].

What she takes from him (endorsed).

  • The Azoth as tangible; he received the universal tincture and healed with it, and argued against self-deception: “I write not fables” [I.1 ¶81; I.1 n106]. He cites an ancient author on the perpetually burning ether: “the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20; I.1 n28].
  • The threefold secret, separation, no manual labour, the Azoth, and the colour sequence ending in the glorified Stone: “Seek Three in One, and again seek One in Three, dissolve, congeal” [III.3 ¶9; III.3 n3; III.3 ¶19; III.3 n11].
  • The adept’s discipline: indefatigable labour at his own expense, learning from error, book interpreting book, note-keeping, constant meditation — “What was wrong taught me what was right” [IV.1 ¶29; IV.1 n24].
  • A detailed account of the first act and the Second Operation: “In the first act of the physico-chemical works, explains Khunrath” [IV.1 ¶36; IV.1 n29].
  • An epigraph (“Enigma”) on a first-second-third transmission that introduces the threefold order: “Omnia in omnibus primum, omni Tertio traditit” [IV.2 ¶2].
  • He is named among Adepts linking the work to the Creed, and is her main authority for the Stone’s universal virtues, the Azoth and the fermentation with its metal; rightly conceiving the azoth is half the work. “It is the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27; IV.3 ¶28; IV.3 ¶29; IV.3 n8; IV.3 n9].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): he names the preserved principle of body (Caput Mortuum) “‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’”, and Atwood thinks he also calls it Duanach [APP ¶26]. He teaches that the Art perfects the mineral life and typifies the Divine; with Grsaeus he insists on the Stone/Christ analogy, which Atwood defends as “more than pardonable” [APP ¶44; APP ¶46]. She compares him for Behmen’s law: “the Enigma Omia in omnibus” [APP ¶73].

References: I.1 n106, I.1 n28, I.1 n84, I.1 ¶20, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70, I.1 ¶81, I.3 n13, I.3 n70, I.3 n9, III.3 n11, III.3 n20, III.3 n3, III.3 ¶19, III.3 ¶9, IV.1 n24, IV.1 n29, IV.1 ¶29, IV.1 ¶36, IV.2 ¶2, IV.3 n8, IV.3 n9, IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶28, IV.3 ¶29, APP ¶26, APP ¶44, APP ¶46, APP ¶73

Kibric and Zibeth

term

In Maria’s words, the soul and spirit: two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body.

In a passage quoted from Maria, “Kibric and Zibeth (the soul and spirit)” are “the two fumes which comprise and embrace each other in the two luminaries”; they are two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body [I.3 n67].

Identified with: the soul and spirit [I.3 n67]; the two fumes [I.3 n67]

References: I.3 n67

King

term

A figure for the ruling principle: the Rational Efficient, the soul as man’s centre, and the source of the soul’s faculties, held captive until it is restored.

Atwood. In a note, the crowned speaker chained to his mother, who makes occult matter appear, is explained: “By the king, the Rational Efficient is signified” [I.3 n50]. She observes that the adepts keep his secret and “make little or no mention of the king at all” [II.1 ¶7]. In Part IV the soul’s faculties are “engaged voluntarily in the restitution of their King”, “for the sake of him who is their source”, who is otherwise held in “an illegitimate thralldom under all”; he is renewed together with his ‘brethren’ [IV.4 ¶20].

Sendivogius. The King is the soul in man, his centre, seated in the vital spirit in the purest blood: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10].

The Hunting of the Greene Lyon (quoted). The King is the child of Sun and Moon wedded by the Lion: “And yet thys King was begott by none other, But by Sun and Moone hys owne Sister and Brother.” He is fed on the Lion’s Blood, dies (paired with blackness) and rises, and is fed with Luna if white, the Sun if red [III.1 ¶65]. The same sequence calls the matter ‘this young Chylde’ or ‘Child’; the text does not say outright that King and Child are the same.

The readings fit together (rational principle, soul as centre, source of the faculties), but the text does not join them explicitly.

Identified with: Rational Efficient [I.3 n50]; the soul in man [II.1 ¶10]

References: I.3 n50, II.1 ¶10, II.1 ¶7, III.1 ¶65, IV.4 ¶20

King of Prussia

person

Cited in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710.

Atwood cites the king of Prussia in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710 [I.1 ¶77; I.1 n104].

References: I.1 n104, I.1 ¶77

term

Glossed by Atwood: Hermes means the great Law of Light or universal reason, impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature.

Atwood explains it in a note: “By the King’s seal, Hermes signifies the great Law of Light or universal reason”, which is impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature [I.3 n69].

Identified with: great Law of Light / universal reason [I.3 n69]

References: I.3 n69

Kirchberger

person

Correspondent in the Theos. Correspondence, cited in the Appendix with approval on the physical problem and the Divine Will, but criticized as a seeker who did not wholly convert into the Light.

All citations are in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). From the Theos. Correspondence, p. 168, Atwood takes the naming of ‘the physical problem’, making the invisible spirit visible [APP ¶93]. From p. 236 she endorses: “the Divine Will makes use of the human voice as an organ for conducting the Light, through the fire”, glossing the fire as our chaotic will [APP ¶97]. From p. 359, said “for de St Martin”: “there is no true government but a Theocracy”, which she calls a great truth but qualifies. She criticizes Kirchberger himself as an intellectual seeker who did not convert wholly into the Light [APP ¶112; APP ¶114].

Kirchringius

person

An adept and commentator on Basil Valentine, whose Latin version underlies the only good English Valentine; cited on the key and on prayer in the work.

Atwood calls Kirchringius ‘the adept’ and his commentaries ‘useful’ [I.1 ¶27]. His Latin version of Valentine, with its ‘admirable commentary’, is the basis of the only good English translation [I.1 ¶61]. She cites him with approval: the key is the principal part of the Art, and “this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last”; its method is called Manual Operation [III.1 ¶37]. From his Annotations on Basil Valentine she takes the efficacy of prayer, both in the work and in solving enigmas: prayer as desire plus cooperation, yielding revelation — “even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed, says Kirchringius” [III.4 ¶22; III.4 n24].

References: I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶61, II.1 n22, II.1 n8, III.1 ¶37, III.4 n24, III.4 ¶22, IV.1 n1, IV.1 n34

See also: The Wise

Latex

term

A name for the Matter as liquid, equated by the quoted authorities with the sharp vinegar and blessed water, which the alchemical reduction uncovers.

In a passage given from Synesius and the New Light: “this Latex is the sharp vinegar which makes gold a pure spirit, seeing she is even that blessed water which engenders al things” [I.2 ¶33]. The Alchemists seek “such a reducation of nature as shall discover this Latex without destroying her vehicle, but the modal life only” [II.1 ¶47]; this passage does not define it further.

Identified with: sharp vinegar; blessed water [I.2 ¶33]

References: I.2 ¶33, II.1 ¶47

Latitude

term

The union of Altitude and Profundity at their extreme poles, by which the wheel of Life is turned.

Atwood: “Altitude and Profundity, being united at their extreme poles, make Latitude”, and by it the wheel of Life is turned [III.3 ¶72].

References: III.3 ¶72

Laus Hermonaeus

person

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n1

Law

term · Law of Wisdom

The intelligible law of reason or soul, whose revelation is the soul’s own self; in the Kabalist’s sense, the scriptural Law, whose real substance is its Soul.

Atwood. The perfected soul, “percipiently included in the circular necessity of her Law, believes its revelation which is her very self” [II.3 ¶46]. The wisely simple are those “who have subdued their will to the Law of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶55].

The Kabalist (endorsed by Atwood). The scriptural Law has an outer story that clothes it: “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law”, and each word cloaks a sublime mystery “under the Bark of the Law”. Its real substance is its Soul: “the Soul, which is the basis of all rest; which is the Law itself” [III.3 ¶59].

Identified with: Soul [III.3 ¶59]

References: II.3 ¶46, II.3 ¶55, III.3 ¶59

Law of conscience

term

What the priests forsook when they tried to wield magic power without it, which led to confusion.

Atwood says the priests, “having forsaken the law of conscience, attempted to wield without it the rod of magic power”, which led to confusion [I.1 ¶30].

See also: Conscience

References: I.1 ¶30

Law of Divine manifestation

term

Behmen’s law: an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself; the Hermetic Work follows the same order.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Law of Divine Manifestation is expressed in those striking words of Behmen” — an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself. Atwood says the Hermetic Work follows the same order [APP ¶73].

References: APP ¶73

Law of dual generation

term

Where, Atwood says, ‘the strength of sin’ lies; the text does not explain it further.

Atwood: “the strength of sin is in the Law of dual generation” [III.2 ¶62]. The text does not explain it further.

See also: Generation

References: III.2 ¶62

Law of justice

term

The law that exacts exact retribution (‘eye for an eye’) in the spheres of the work.

Atwood: “so does the Law of Justice exact retribution in those spheres”, that is, an eye for an eye [III.4 ¶9].

References: III.4 ¶9

Law of light

term

A law that must move through Love in the will; for the Kabalists, the superstantial law from which the world emanates as an efflux of Mind.

Atwood (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer): “there is a law of Light, which must move through Love in the will” and act on the will-moved mind; the mind must be subservient to it or become demoniacal [APP ¶9].

Hebrew Kabalists (reported): in their Idealism “the whole world was before their eyes as an efflux of Mind, an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. Compare King’s seal, glossed as “the great Law of Light or universal reason” [I.3 n69].

See also: Light

References: II.1 ¶40, APP ¶9

Law of nature

term · Laws of Nature

Nature’s simple and harmonious law, which baffles the operator who brings his own blind purpose; the moral, physical and organic laws are one at the root.

Atwood: “The Law of Nature, being simple and harmoniously framed, will baffle him” — the operator who brings his own blind purpose is baffled and condemned [III.1 ¶38]. The Laws of Nature — “the moral, the physical, and the organic are well reasoned, as in their constitutional consequences, apart from each other” — seem independent at nature’s circumference but are one at the root [III.4 ¶8].

References: III.1 ¶38, III.4 ¶8

Lawgiver

collective voice

The voice of Deuteronomy, cited by Atwood to warn those favoured in the work against presumption and forgetting God in prosperity.

Atwood cites the Lawgiver (footnote: Deuteronomy 8:10) on the Israelites’ suffering for rebellion and the warning against forgetting God in prosperity: “Beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God” [IV.3 ¶57; IV.3 n26]. She applies it by analogy to those favoured in the work, as a warning against presumption; she endorses it.

References: IV.3 n26, IV.3 ¶57

Laws of art

term

The scientific laws of the Art, whose study together with the Hermetic records Atwood makes the needed foundation before any trial.

Atwood names the “study of the Hermetic records and scientific Laws of Art” [IV.3 ¶54] as the foundation required before anyone attempts a trial of the work.

References: IV.3 ¶54

Leaven

term · old leaven

The assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; Atwood also invokes purging out the old leaven.

Atwood treats leaven as the assimilating ferment by which bodies are transformed, spiritualized and preserved; bodies are “preserved by the assimilating must or leaven” [III.3 ¶23], which makes must another name for it. The old leaven is to be purged: “Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump” [III.3 ¶23].

Identified with: must [III.3 ¶23]

References: III.3 ¶23

Lepidem Aetherium

term

In Palingenius’ Latin verse, the ethereal stone that the worthiest art fashions, forbidden to the profane and granted to few.

In Latin verse quoted from Palingenius, the Lepidem Aetherium is the object of the worthiest art, to be fashioned: “Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium, quem scire profanes Haud quaquam licet” [IV.3 ¶55]. It is forbidden to the profane, sought in vain by the wicked and granted to few. Translation (ours): “Ethereal Stone”; the book gives none.

References: IV.3 ¶55

Lesser Mysteries

term · lesser

The first, popular grade of initiation, open to all, revealing only the internal life and ending with the soul on the borders of Tartarus.

For Atwood the Lesser Mysteries are the first grade of initiation. In them, it appears, the revelations of the natural spirit’s first sphere were passed: “passing these, as it appears, in the Lesser Mysteries” [II.2 ¶8]. It was “the only popular initiation open to all” [II.3 ¶3], revealing only the internal life, a field of natural contemplation without rule. It ended with the soul on the borders of the Stygian lake in view of Tartarus: “And here the Lesser Mysteries ended” [II.3 ¶36].

See also: Mysteries

References: II.2 ¶8, II.3 ¶3, II.3 ¶36

Lesser world

term

In the mysterious adeptest’s words, the lesser world is the father of the Son, or what the Son is likened to; possibly linked with the microcosm.

The mysterious adeptest, quoted by Atwood, says the Son is “consubstantial nevertheless, and like his father the lesser world” [III.3 ¶50]. The phrase may name the lesser world as the Son’s father or only liken the Son to it. The same passage calls the Stone “wonderfully salutary to the microcosm in universal triunity” [III.3 ¶50], but the text does not explicitly identify the microcosm with the lesser world. Not defined further.

See also: Greater Orb and Lesser World

References: III.3 ¶50

Lethe

term · drink of Lethe

In Agrippa’s words, the drink of forgetfulness that is to be cast out.

Agrippa, quoted by Atwood: “Cast out the drink of Lethe” [II.4 ¶19]. Lethe is the drink of forgetfulness.

References: II.4 ¶19

Life

term

Atwood calls Life the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery.

Atwood: “And Life is the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery” [IV.4 ¶32].

References: IV.4 ¶32

Ligature of natures

term

A secret binding of natures, paired with their magical dissolution, which Atwood says Bacon discovered; not explained.

Atwood credits Bacon with discovering “the secret ligature of natures, and their magical dissolution” [I.1 ¶38]. The text does not explain it further.

References: I.1 ¶38

Light

term · Central Light, Divine Light, Light within

The hidden, self-multiplying formal Light that perfects matter, is the Form of Gold and the Key of the Hermetic Mystery, and is to be freed.

Physical role. An adept quoted by Atwood says “It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied, for this ascends and descends from the first fountain of multiplication and generation” [I.2 ¶8]; once perfected by art it exalts any body in its kind. Atwood makes it the forming, fermenting agent: “Light is the true fermental principle which perfects the Ether in its proper kind” [I.2 ¶44]; “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45]; “the universal magnet of its own infinite self-multiplicative Light” [I.2 ¶48]. Albertus Magnus (via Becher) calls it “Light, which is the formal essence of all things, and most abundant in gold” [III.2 n38].

Hidden and to be freed. “To find this Light, and to free it from captivity” [III.1 ¶11] was the adepts’ aim: “the Central Light and Wisdom was all their aim” [III.1 ¶13]. It is “not common Light, but that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30], latent in every kingdom of nature; Atwood asks, “is not Light the true Aurific Seed” [IV.3 ¶30], and calls it the Stone’s own metal, its ferment. “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9]; Nature is to “establish a stable monarchy upon her redeemed Light” [IV.4 ¶6].

Inner and divine. All Nature is its Efflux [III.3 ¶78]; Thought emanates it [III.3 ¶79]; recreation is “a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], with “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light” [III.3 ¶80]. The practice develops “by rational inquisition of the Light within” [IV.1 ¶18]; “Some have met the Light sooner, some later” [IV.1 ¶17]; one passes “by a living experience into the Light” [III.4 ¶15]. Quoting Plotinus, the soul receives a sudden Light: “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41]; Atwood also calls the magistery “a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37].

Key. “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]; Atwood says “we pretend only to have signalized the Light” [IV.4 ¶2], and that she has shown “the golden ore” of it [IV.4 ¶32]; “for those to whom it is addressed the Light will attract” [IV.4 ¶31]. The selfish “have willfully denied the Light its true fulfillment” [III.4 ¶6]; in its vision the philosophers despised gold and silver [IV.3 ¶26]. In the later Appendix (Table Talk), “It requires Light to throw Light upon Light” [APP ¶118]; it is “the light which comes into every soul born into the world” [APP ¶126].

Identified with: Form [I.2 ¶45]; fermental principle [I.2 ¶44]; formal essence of all things [III.2 n38]; God [IV.2 ¶41]; Aurific seed [IV.3 ¶30]; the Stone’s ‘own metal’ (its ferment) [IV.3 ¶30]; Form of gold [IV.4 ¶9]; Key [IV.4 ¶32]

See also: Divine light

References: I.2 ¶44, I.2 ¶45, I.2 ¶48, I.2 ¶8, III.1 ¶11, III.1 ¶13, III.2 n38, III.3 ¶78, III.3 ¶79, III.3 ¶80, III.4 ¶15, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶6, IV.1 ¶17, IV.1 ¶18, IV.1 ¶25, IV.2 ¶37, IV.2 ¶41, IV.3 ¶26, IV.3 ¶30, IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶31, IV.4 ¶32, IV.4 ¶6, IV.4 ¶9, APP ¶118, APP ¶126

Light and love fire

term

In the theosophist’s words, the other principle in everything, the woman’s seed, to be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.

The theosophist, quoted by Atwood, names “the woman’s seed the light and love fire” [IV.3 ¶38]: the other principle in every thing, which must be raised up to shine through and subdue the wrath.

Identified with: the woman’s seed [IV.3 ¶38]

See also: Fire

References: IV.3 ¶38

Light essential

term

What the quintessences lack, so that they resolve and die (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says quintessences “uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23]. Not further defined.

References: APP ¶23

Light of Alchemy

term · true Light of Alchemy

What Atwood says is discovered by inquiring into the substance and practical evolution of the psychical experience.

Atwood: “It is into the substantiality of this and for its practical evolution that we must inquire, if we would discover the true Light of Alchemy” [II.1 ¶47]; the “this” is the psychical experience.

See also: Alchemy

References: II.1 ¶47

Light of God

term

In Boehme’s words, the Light needed to understand the Tincture, which nature cannot grasp by its own ability.

Boehme, quoted by Atwood: “the understanding and capacity is not in nature’s own ability without the Light of God” [III.2 ¶16]. To those in it the matter is plain: “it is very easy to be understood by those who are in the Light” [III.2 ¶16].

See also: Gods

References: III.2 ¶16

Light of life

term

The light exhibited in the true Eleusinian initiations, which they could kindle and fortify.

Atwood: “The light exhibited in the Eleusinian msteries, i.e., in the true initiations as is plainly to be gathered from the sense of the ancients, was the Light of Life” [II.4 ¶56], the light “which these could kindle and fortify” [II.4 ¶56].

Identified with: The light exhibited in the Eleusinian msteries [II.4 ¶56]

See also: Life

References: II.4 ¶56

Light of nature

term

In Sendivogius’ words, nature’s own light, hidden by the body of sense, which when it enlightens someone clears the cloud and penetrates inward things.

Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood: “nature, having her proper light, is by the shadowy body of sense, hidden from our eyes” [II.1 ¶10]. When “the light of nature doth enlighten any one, presently the cloud is taken away from before his eyes” [II.1 ¶10]; “so far doth the light of nature penetrate and discover inward things” [II.1 ¶10]. The philosophers see all things in it as in a mirror.

References: II.1 ¶10

Light of reason

term

The light that flows into and purifies the aerial moisture and re-enters in the Mysteries; Atwood identifies it with the Sulfur of adepts.

Atwood speaks of the aerial moisture “before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason” [II.3 ¶29], and of “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts” [II.3 ¶30]. The ignorant scoffer lacks it, and so “without the Light of Reason, would be least of all able to precipitate its downfall” [IV.3 ¶56].

Identified with: Sulfur of adepts [II.3 ¶30]

See also: Reason

References: II.3 ¶29, II.3 ¶30, IV.3 ¶56

Light of universal nature

term

The light kindled by the catholic torch; not further defined.

Atwood says the catholic torch “kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]. Not further defined.

References: IV.4 ¶32

Linear life

term

Our present life going forth in a line, which must be taken up into a circle back to its first source (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “Our life goes forth into a line at present, it has to be taken up into a circle” [APP ¶48], that is, back into its first source.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶48

Linear way

term · linear decoction, dissolution by line, decocted linearly

The single uniform course of dissolution throughout the work, in one matter and one vessel, which the Adepts also call Manual.

Atwood describes “one linear decoction throughout and dissolution by line” [IV.1 ¶3] and “one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9], in one matter and one vessel. It is “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5]. Not further explained.

Identified with: Manual operation [IV.1 ¶5]

References: IV.1 ¶3, IV.1 ¶5, IV.1 ¶9

Lion

term · green and red lion

In the words of the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, the creature whose blood, joined with the Eagle’s tears, is the treasure of the whole earth.

In the fraternity of the Rosy Cross, quoted by Atwood, the Lion is the other creature; weakened, it bleeds: “The blood of this Lion incorporated with the tears of the Eagle is the treasure of the whole earth.” [III.3 ¶63]. A green and red lion is drawn from the Dragon’s body. Not further explained.

References: III.3 ¶63

Lion’s sweat

term · Lyons sweate

In The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the liquid given to the pure matter at each imbibition.

The verse The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, quoted by Atwood: “A portion of your Lyons sweate Must be given it for to eate:” [III.1 ¶65], i.e. at each imbibition of the pure matter. Not further defined; how it relates to the Lion’s Blood is unclear.

References: III.1 ¶65

Liquor of the sages

term · precious liquor, liquor

In Eudoxus’ words, the liquor hidden under the Stone that contains all the work needs, which has over a thousand names and is the great Alcahest.

Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood: “search the source of the Liquor of the Sages, which contains all that is necessary for the work; it is hidden under the Stone” [IV.3 ¶10]. He calls it “this precious liquor, to which the philosophers have given more than a thousand different names, which is in sum the great Alcahest” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether it is the liquor from which the two Mercuries are made is not stated.

Identified with: Alkahest [IV.3 ¶10]

See also: Sage

Lives of the Alchemists

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: Alchemists

Living gold of the philosophers

term · living gold

What the Quintessence becomes with the Divine light’s virtue: transmuting, multiplicative gold, the concrete form of what is valued in dead metal.

Atwood: with the virtue of the Divine light the Quintessence becomes “the living gold of the philosophers, transmuting and multiplicative — the concrete form of that which in the dead metal we esteem” [III.1 ¶49].

See also: Philosophers, Philosophers’ gold

References: III.1 ¶49

Living light

term

The Light which, Atwood says, became known to Solomon together with the mysteries of universal creation.

Atwood says Solomon “celebrates the revelation of that Living Light which became known to him” [III.3 ¶49], together with the mysteries of universal creation.

See also: Light

References: III.3 ¶49

Living temple

term

The inner place, guarded by the adepts’ equivocations, where the wise raise the Corner Stone and where desire is addressed from the Divine Light within.

Atwood: the adepts’ equivocations protect “that living temple wherein alone the wise of all ages have been securely able to raise their rejected Corner Stone” [II.1 ¶8]. Effectual desire is “addressed within the Living Temple from the Divine Light within” [III.4 ¶27]. The context suggests an inner place; it is not further defined.

References: II.1 ¶8, III.4 ¶27

Locke

person

Author of the Essay, cited by Atwood in support of intuition as the highest certainty, though she criticizes his ‘sensual system’.

Atwood cites Locke’s Essay in support of intuition as the highest certainty: “Intuitive faith is certain beyond all doubt, and needs no proof beyond itself” [II.1 ¶34]. She also criticizes Locke’s ‘sensual system’, so her endorsement is partial.

References: II.1 ¶34

Lodestone

term · loadstone

An image of attraction and a cover-name: the enlightened see the point of the philosophers’ lodestone; Cosmopolite gives the name to the Mercury.

Agrippa and Sendivogius, quoted by Atwood, use it as an image of attraction. Man is to “draw and bring them to himself as a loadstone, iron” [II.1 ¶9]. The enlightened man “can behold the point of our lodestone, answering to each center of the beams” [II.1 ¶10] of the philosophical sun and moon. Eirenaeus (“the same author”) prescribes “conjoin to nine parts of our Lodestone” [IV.1 ¶43] with the Fiery Dragon; not explained. Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite gives the Mercury (Our Old Man) “also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. In a passage of unclear voice, “as steel draws the loadstone and the loadstone in like manner turns toward steel” [IV.2 ¶30] is compared to freed Will and Understanding; our loadstone has Salt at its center, turning to the Pole, and our Magnet shows “that Polar Star which our Magnet exhibits” [IV.2 ¶30].

Identified with: Mercury (Our Old Man) [IV.3 ¶10]

References: II.1 ¶10, II.1 ¶9, IV.1 ¶43, IV.2 ¶30, IV.3 ¶10

Lodge

term

Used by Atwood of those whom Ripley’s Twelve Gates edified; apparently an inner circle of the initiated.

Atwood says Ripley’s Twelve Gates “little edified any without the Lodge” [I.1 ¶64]. The context suggests the Lodge is an inner circle of the initiated, but the text does not say so; other readings are possible.

References: I.1 ¶64

Logos

term

The Logos: for Philo, the seal by which the world was framed and of which the soul is an impression; for Atwood (Appendix), each man’s fundamental faith and the Crown.

Quoting Philo, Atwood gives the Logos as that “by whom the world was framed”, “the seal after the impression of which everything is made” [II.1 ¶43]; accordingly “the soul of man is an impression of this seal of which the prototype and original characteristic is the everlasting Logos” [II.1 ¶43].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood speaks in her own voice of “his fundamental faith, which is his individual Logos” [APP ¶101]: each man’s individual Logos is his fundamental faith, to be fermented until it transmutes his whole being. She also identifies it with the Crown: “The Crown, to use Behmen’s and de St Martin’s phrase, is the Logos.” [APP ¶104].

Identified with: fundamental faith [APP ¶101]; the Crown [APP ¶104]; the seal [II.1 ¶43]

References: II.1 ¶43, APP ¶101, APP ¶104

Lord

person · our Lord

Christ, cited in the Appendix (Table Talk) for sayings Atwood applies to the Hermetic Art and the Stone.

Cited only in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). His words “The wind bloweth where it listeth” are cited as an analogy, Christ the Head Corner Stone is named as the analogue of the Stone, and the regenerated are said to enter his life [APP ¶41, APP ¶46, APP ¶60]. His saying “Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things shall be added unto you” supports Atwood’s point that seeking the Universal first is the shortest and truest road in the Hermetic Art [APP ¶134]. His use of the language of David — “I have said ye are gods, if (says our Lord) ye called them gods unto whom the Word of God came” — illustrates powers subordinate to God evolved where the Word comes, with the danger of self-centers [APP ¶100].

References: APP ¶100, APP ¶134, APP ¶41, APP ¶46, APP ¶60

Lord Bacon

person

Lord Bacon, cited repeatedly by Atwood: partly as a witness favourable to the philosophers’ stone and the ancients’ wisdom, partly criticized for mechanical methods and ignorance of the Great Art.

Atwood uses Lord Bacon both as support and as a foil.

Support. He reportedly experimented toward the philosophers’ stone and recognized its possibility in the Advancement of Learning, without condemning the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. From the same work she takes his advice to regard the early sages with more reverence [III.2 ¶33; III.2 n30]. His Fable of Proteus (De Sapientia Veterum / Wisdom of the Ancient) supports, via Democritus, the principle of torture and restoration — to “torture and vex it in order to its annihilation” [I.2 ¶23] — and is quoted again with endorsement: matter, forced to extremity, runs through all forms and restores itself; he “lays hold of and works upon matter in the extremest degrees” [III.3 ¶61; III.3 n44], which Atwood glosses as the last exigence of life.

Criticism. She faults him for proposing mechanical dissolution and for not knowing the Great Art or its subject [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n19]; his “particular digesters applied to the fire” (Sylva Sylvarum; History of Rarity and Density) would expel the very nature prized [I.2 ¶24; I.2 n20]. His supposition (Instauration of the Sciences) that the understanding is too polluted by the fall to reflect total reason raises a difficulty, since introspection would then be useless [II.2 ¶21; II.2 n17]. Finally she calls him leader of the ‘exterminating chase’ of experimental philosophy, yet notes he recommended the pursuit of Causes and inquiry after the ancients’ hidden Wisdom, ‘though he knew it not’ [IV.4 ¶30].

See also: Bacon

References: I.1 ¶82, I.2 n19, I.2 n20, I.2 ¶23, I.2 ¶24, II.2 n17, II.2 ¶21, III.2 n30, III.2 ¶33, III.3 n44, III.3 ¶61, IV.4 ¶30

Lorenz Oken

person · Oken

Lorenz Oken, praised in the Appendix for treating nature ‘in that higher way’ and for an apparent inspiration into the science of created nature.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) Atwood praises Lorenz Oken (cited in a Ray Society edition, London, 1847) as dealing with nature ‘in that higher way’ and as best evolving Causal Truth into the outward forms of life [APP ¶31]. Elsewhere she says he appears to have had an inspiration into the science of created nature [APP ¶96].

References: APP ¶31, APP ¶96

Lower life

term

The generative, fallen life, whose desire, opened upward, yields the Key.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of “the desire of the lower life, the generative, the fallen life” [APP ¶97]; this lower life is thus identified with the generative and the fallen life, and its desire, opened upward, is said to yield the Key.

Identified with: the generative, the fallen life [APP ¶97]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶97

Lucerna Salis Phil.

treatise · Lucerna Salis, Lucerna Solis

Lucerna Salis Phil., a verse treatise Atwood quotes on the one universal matter (the Sages’ salt), the stone, and its dissolution without corrosive.

Atwood quotes this treatise (also given as Lucerna Solis, with a note referring to ‘Lucerna Salis, from the Latin verse’) in support of several points:

  • The one universal matter, called the Sages’ salt: “A certain thing is found in the world” [I.2 ¶9; I.2 n10].
  • The stone, its growth, the Red Lyon and red Sulfur: “It is a stone and no stone, In which the whole art consists;” [I.2 ¶30; I.2 n32].
  • The Stone is to be dissolved after the mind of the wise, “Nullo corrosivo adhibito” [III.2 ¶63; III.2 n46] (ours: ‘with no corrosive applied’).

Elsewhere Arnold, Lully and Artephius are said to agree with its description of whitening [III.2 ¶5].

See also: Author of the Lucerna Salis

References: I.2 n10, I.2 n32, I.2 ¶10, I.2 ¶30, I.2 ¶9, I.3 n61, I.3 n63, I.3 n70, III.1 n42, III.2 n46, III.2 ¶63

Lucidity

term

One of the ordinary mesmeric phenomena, named alongside prevision and community of sense, will and thought.

Atwood lists lucidity among “The ordinary phenomena of lucidity, prevision, community of sense, will, and thought” [II.2 ¶6].

References: II.2 ¶6

Lucius Agatho Priscus

person

Named in a companion inscription declaring that corpse and sepulcher, contained and container, are the same.

A companion inscription under the name Lucius Agatho Priscus is quoted to the effect that contained and container are one: “Both corpse and sepulcher the same!” [III.3 ¶66].

References: III.3 ¶66

Lully

person · Raymond Lully, Raymond, Reymond, R. Lulli, R. Lully

Raymond Lully, a confessed adept Atwood cites very often and with approval on the subject, the agent, secrecy, the inner work and the need for divine revelation.

Atwood treats Lully as a major authority and endorses his testimony throughout.

Witness to the art. His own declarations are evidence for the England story; his alchemical writings are obscure but numerous and favourable to the art [I.1 ¶47–48; I.1 ¶76]. In the Ultimum Testamentum he is a confessed adept of known Christian zeal, with the story of gold for Edward II: “Converti una vice in aurum 50 millia pondo argenti vivi, plumbi, et stannic.” [I.1 ¶39, ¶46; I.1 n55] (ours: ‘I once converted into gold 50,000 pounds of quicksilver, lead and tin’). She calls his Theoria et Practica one that “appears to us one of the very best pieces of Alchemical philosophy extant” [I.1 n58]. Norton’s verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely [I.1 ¶15]; Ripley’s verse names him as an authority, as having determined the science true, and as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [I.2 ¶6; II.1 ¶13; III.1 ¶62], and as one who revered Geber [I.1 ¶32].

The subject. An apparent contradiction (De Arte Magna) is explained: he denies only to a false position of the art [I.2 ¶7; I.2 n8]. The subject is of another nature and needs human art — “Imo argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18; I.2 n17] (ours: ‘indeed our quicksilver is a water of another nature’) — Hyle, a clear compounded water, a third thing (tertium) [I.2 ¶29, ¶31, ¶42]. He agrees concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; a quoted adept identifies his Lunaria with the authors’ mercury [III.2 ¶25]. In the Appendix (a later layer) he supports the claim that nature has no pure conceptive vehicle: “The pure matter of the philosophers is not to be found on earth” [APP ¶43].

Method. He teaches patient rational inquiry and intimates Reason as a ferment; the golden bough is read as the subtle intellect: “Intellectus naturam habens subtilem ad intelligendum res intelligibles” [III.1 ¶13, ¶21; III.1 n26; cf. II.3 ¶11] (ours: ‘the intellect, having a subtle nature for understanding intelligible things’). He warns against too strong a fire: “Let the heavenly power or agent be such in the place of generation, or mutation” [III.1 ¶55]. The Mercury “comes not but by help of ingenuity, and the Manual operations of man” [IV.1 ¶5]. First principles appear as cloud-like monstrous spirits, which Atwood reads as known from inner self-inspection [II.3 ¶30]. He adds “a sufficiency of the Divine Favour, and books to open the understanding and give it zest for truth” to Arnold’s requisites [III.4 ¶20]; after a tedious common process he performed the Solution in nine days by the secret from God, which only God can reveal [IV.1 ¶36, ¶39]. He also charged strict secrecy [I.3 n15].

References: I.1 n55, I.1 n58, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶32, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶46, I.1 ¶47, I.1 ¶48, I.1 ¶76, I.2 n17, I.2 n25, I.2 n29, I.2 n33, I.2 n8, I.2 ¶18, I.2 ¶29, I.2 ¶31, I.2 ¶42, I.2 ¶6, I.2 ¶7, I.3 n15, I.3 n4, II.1 ¶13, II.3 n7, II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶30, III.1 n11, III.1 n25, III.1 n26, III.1 n60, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶55, III.1 ¶62, III.2 ¶25, III.2 ¶5, III.2 ¶60, III.4 n20, III.4 ¶20, IV.1 n28, IV.1 n3, IV.1 ¶36, IV.1 ¶39, IV.1 ¶5, APP ¶43

Lumen de Lumine

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: Author of the Lumen de Lumine

References: I.3 n14, III.2 n27, III.3 n41

Luminaries

term · Luminary

In Synesius, two lights made manifest, one fixed and one volatile; when the lower rises upon the upper an incomparable Luminary issues.

Quoting Synesius, Atwood records that “there are made manifest two luminaries, the one fixed, the other not” [III.3 ¶60]: one fixed (male, below), the other volatile (above, ever moving). When the lower rises upon the upper, “there then issues forth an incomparable Luminary” [III.3 ¶60].

References: III.3 ¶60

Lunar Vulcan

term

The agent that takes the principal part when Sol is eclipsed, like Isis in the Mysteries; Atwood says it means the first prepared Subject, the Adepts’ secret interior Fire.

Atwood writes that, “Sol being eclipsed, the Lunar Vulcan acts a principal part, as Isis in the Mysteries” [III.1 ¶63].

Later she says the Stone is “prepared by those who trace nature with the assistance of the Lunar Vulcan” and explains: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject” [IV.1 ¶29] — also called Diana and the Adepts’ secret interior Fire. As ‘Lunar Caustic’ it needs outward stimulus: “this same Lunar Caustic is brought into act by an exterior excitation” [IV.1 ¶29]. The identity with the first prepared Subject is stated by Atwood herself.

Identified with: Isis (acts her part) [III.1 ¶63]; First prepared subject [IV.1 ¶29]; Lunar Caustic [IV.1 ¶29]

See also: Vulcan

References: III.1 ¶63, IV.1 ¶29

Lunaria

term

Lully’s term, identified by a quoted adept with the quicksilver that authors call mercury.

An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (Grasseus, per n26), quoted by Atwood, holds “that quicksilver, which authors call mercury, to be the same with Lully’s Lunaria” [III.2 ¶25].

Identified with: quicksilver / mercury [III.2 ¶25]

References: III.2 ¶25

Lunary of Diana

term

What Hermes suffered and toiled to obtain; not otherwise explained in the text.

Atwood reports that “to obtain the blessed Lunary of Diana, he had suffered much, and toiled incessantly” [III.2 ¶64], of Hermes. The text does not explain the expression further.

See also: Diana

References: III.2 ¶64

Lustrations

term

Purificatory rites of the Mysteries by which the soul is liberated into a divine condition.

Atwood writes that “by the lustrations in the Mysteries, as they describe, the soul becomes liberated and passes into a divine condition of being” [II.2 ¶9].

References: II.2 ¶9

M

M. Dunstani

person

Cited for reference only.

References: II.1 n22

Macrocosmic image of the microcosm

term

An image thrown forth, passive and ephemeral, identified with the downward-born nature and with Eve brought forth by Adam.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood describes an image thrown forth, macrocosmic, passive and ephemeral for want of consubstantiality; its perfect beauty attracts the soul and, united to it, brings the ideal forth as actual offspring. She identifies it: “The macrocosmic image of the microcosm is the downward-born nature” and “It is the Eve which Adam brought forth” [APP ¶18].

Identified with: downward-born nature [APP ¶18]; Eve [APP ¶18]

See also: Microcosm

References: APP ¶18

Madathan

person

An adept who failed for five years and received the key by revelation; also rebuked by Nature for seeking the Stone without dissolution.

Atwood cites Madathan (Mus. Hermeticum, Lumen de Lumine) as an example: after failing for five years, he says, “I was entrusted with the Key of Power, by a secret revelation from Almighty God” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n41]. She also quotes Nature rebuking him for trying to make the Stone without dissolution: “Dost thou think, says she, to eat the oysters, crabs, shells and all?” [III.2 ¶61].

References: III.1 n41, III.1 ¶37, III.2 ¶61

Magian

collective voice

A voice quoted from Agrippa supporting the view that reason needs divine illumination.

Atwood quotes from Agrippa’s Third Book of Occult Philosophy: “All is one soul, says the Magian, but reason, unless it be illuminated, is not free from error” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n29], in support of reason’s need for illumination.

References: III.1 n29, III.1 ¶23

Magic

term · magia, magical, magician

Magic: an imputation against Bacon, in Paracelsus a natural secret of separation, the ‘service of the gods’, and in one passage the inward union of the elements.

The records show several uses:

  • As imputation (Atwood). Against Bacon “the imputation of magic has seemed ridiculous” [I.1 ¶38]; Atwood suggests that reducing it to natural skill may be as wrong as the old superstition. The medieval adepts are called “Magians, who were drawn about the fire of nature” [I.1 ¶39]. Ashmole “exposes certain principles of magic” [I.1 ¶62], and of Agrippa: “there stood the magician at last” [I.1 ¶64].
  • Paracelsus (quoted). A natural, not specially divine, secret giving entrance into nature: “if that magic then were natural, certainly it was most wonderful, very excellent for quickness of separation” [I.2 ¶25].
  • Plato; Psellus (quoted). The magic of Zoroaster, whose use is to perfect the soul by the power of materials; the cited view “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51].
  • Its end (voice unclear). The elements, unless united through the first love, “will never inward and essentially unite; which is the end and perfection of magic” [III.1 ¶50]. Boehme’s phrase “bruise that composed magical body” [III.1 ¶48] describes a body that, bruised, becomes ‘magical and hungry after nature’.

Identified with: the service of the gods [II.1 ¶51]

References: I.1 ¶38, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶62, I.1 ¶64, I.2 ¶25, II.1 ¶51, III.1 ¶48, III.1 ¶50

Magic Key

term

The key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus to open the Hermetic garden, said to have been lost by the Masons.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood speaks of a magic Key prepared by the anonymous author of the Tractatus Aureus “to open the door into the Hermetic garden” [APP ¶100], and says the Masons lost it.

See also: Key

References: APP ¶100

Magic region

term

A region in which every desire becomes prolific and embodies itself by the ethereal conception.

Atwood writes that “every desire is, in the magic region, made prolific” [IV.4 ¶10], embodying itself by the ethereal conception.

References: IV.4 ¶10

Magic steel

term

Something the Fiery Dragon carries in its belly, in a passage quoted from Eirenaeus; not explained.

Quoting the same author (Eirenaeus, per n37), Atwood mentions the Fiery Dragon “which bears in his belly the Magic Steel” [IV.1 ¶43]. The text gives no explanation.

See also: Steel

References: IV.1 ¶43

Magical earth

term · magic earth, terra magica

The pure earth found at one’s own center that commences Regeneration; also the Matter as an earth containing the recreative fire, the Land of Havilah.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood places the magical earth at one’s own center, quoting “nascitur in aere terra magica; in aethere clarificatur” [APP ¶89] (ours: ‘the magic earth is born in the air; in the ether it is clarified’). She explains that there “you find that which is in the air or the vegetable life, that pure earth which commences the Regeneration” [APP ¶89], in contrast with the mineral earth of the lower life.

Earlier she calls the Matter “the true magic earth wherein is the recreative fire” [III.2 ¶8] and identifies it with the ‘Land of Havilah, where good gold is’ [III.2 ¶8].

Identified with: pure earth [APP ¶89]; Land of Havilah [III.2 ¶8]

See also: Earth

References: III.2 ¶8, APP ¶89

Magical solution

term

The dissolution which, with human aid, enables the Spirit to leave its extraneous forms.

Atwood writes of the Spirit that “Without the magical solution and human aid to fortify” [III.2 ¶61] it cannot leave its extraneous forms.

See also: Solution

References: III.2 ¶61

Magistery

term · Magistry, Maistery

The accomplished work or mastery of the Hermetic art, its goal and product; Atwood calls it a fiery form of Light inspisate and a type of the Christian Creed.

Magistery is the adepts’ name for the whole work, its mastery and its product.

Atwood. Wisdom guards “her universal magistery from an incapable and dreaming world” [I.1 ¶33], and men were “unable to perfect the same magistery” through the philosophers’ obscurity [I.1 ¶36]; the word also appears in Geber’s title ‘The Sum of the Perfect Magistery’ [I.1 ¶33, ¶36]. It is reached by communion with the ruling Spirit of nature [I.3 n19]. Man’s virtue within himself to prove the Universal Source “was the foundation of the whole Hermetic magistery”, and “without this knowledge no one can attain to the magistery” [II.1 ¶8] — the knowledge of the vessel. In it the luminaries pass “through many phases from imperfection to perfection in the true magistery” [II.2 ¶26]; only those with “this passport can attain to the Magistery of life” [III.1 ¶13]. She defines it: “Which magistery is a fiery form of Light inspisate” [IV.2 ¶37], made manifest by triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit. The Adepts claim “their magistery not only corresponds, but is in every deed a type, and promise, and foundation of our Christian Creed” [IV.3 ¶27].

Quoted authorities. Flamel: “Having this, I easily accomplished the magistery.” [I.1 ¶57]. Geber: “the completement of matters sought after in our magistery” [I.1 ¶76]. Synesius: the soul is “drawn by our magistery out of its mine” [III.1 ¶70; cf. I.2 ¶33]. Bloomfield: “Our magistery is Three, Two, and One — The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “the knowledge of our Magistery comes rather by the Inspiration of Heaven” [IV.3 ¶16]. An unattributed verse: “Material of our Magistry a substance insensible.” [III.1 ¶7].

Identified with: the Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone [IV.2 ¶36]; a fiery form of Light inspisate [IV.2 ¶37]

References: I.1 ¶33, I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶76, I.2 ¶33, I.3 n19, II.1 ¶8, II.2 ¶26, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶7, III.1 ¶70, IV.2 ¶36, IV.2 ¶37, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶27

Magnesia

term

A name for the matter calcined by its proper fire, also called lead of the wise; sown in the Philosophic Earth it dies and corrupts.

Atwood says the matter calcined by its proper fire “is called magnesia and lead of the wise” [I.2 ¶40]. A quoted scholiast writes: “our Magnesia, continues he, being sown in the Philosophic Earth, dies and corrupts” [I.3 n21], to conceive itself anew. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon says the old philosophers described its making at large while concealing how to order it afterwards: “To create Magnesia they made no care, In their Bookes largely to declare;” [III.1 ¶65].

Identified with: lead of the wise [I.2 ¶40]

References: I.2 ¶40, I.3 n21, III.1 ¶65

Magnet

term · magnets

In Atwood’s Appendix, a will as center of attraction (two magnets in man are two wills); in the Greene Lyon verse, the fair white part left in the midst.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes that “self becomes the magnet” [APP ¶122] and that “There are two magnets in man, i.e., two wills contending for man” [APP ¶124].

In The Hunting of the Greene Lyon (quoted), the Magnet is the white part left when the matter separates from its black, light ‘vile Erth’: “Your magnet in the midst wilbe, Of Collour faire and white trust me;” [III.1 ¶65]; it must show full white, and the ferment is put into it as one fourth part.

Identified with: wills [APP ¶124]

References: III.1 ¶65, APP ¶122, APP ¶124

Magnetic

term

Used in Atwood’s phrase ‘the chain of the magnetic series’, which moves when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit.

Atwood writes that when the Soul is drawn back into the Passive Spirit, “the first link in the chain of the magnetic series moves” [III.3 ¶10]. See also magnetic chain.

References: III.3 ¶10

Magnetic chain

term

The continuum from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to the darkness of Matter; the ladder of Celsus and Zoroaster.

Atwood describes Matter as lying at “the opposite extreme of the magnetic chain, which is extended a non gradu ad non gradum” [III.2 ¶54] (ours: ‘from no degree to no degree’), from infinite pure light above all intelligence down to darkness. She identifies it: “this is that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

Identified with: ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster [III.2 ¶54]

References: III.2 ¶54

Magnetical virtue

term

Apparently the drawing power by which the gold attracts divine increase; the Stone is likened to an armed magnet.

The voice is unclear in the record. The Stone is likened to “an armed magnet included and circulating in a perpetual heaven” [II.1 ¶25]; the context suggests magnetical virtue is the gold’s drawing power by which it attracts divine increase.

See also: Virtue

References: II.1 ¶25

Malachi

person

The prophet whose Elijah prophecy frames Atwood’s discussion of Elias the artist.

Atwood quotes Malachi 4:5–6, “Behold I will send you Elijah, the prophet” [IV.2 ¶12; IV.2 n4], to frame Elias the artist. The Refiner’s-Fire messenger passage (Malachi 3:1–4) closes the section without comment [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n9].

References: IV.2 n4, IV.2 n9, IV.2 ¶12, IV.2 ¶14

Malden

person — Philalethean Lion Hunt · Philalethean Lion Hunt

Attribution attached to The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, an allegorical verse account of the whole practice that Atwood gives ‘by way of recreation’.

Atwood gives The Hunting of the Greene Lyon ‘by way of recreation’ [III.1 ¶64] — ‘in part’, though the text is headed as unabridged — as an allegorical account of the whole practice: Green Lion, Sun and Moon, black/white/red, imbibition, ferment and multiplication [III.1 ¶65]. Its opening explains the name: “But our Lyon wanting maturity, Is called greene for unripenes trust me,” [III.1 ¶65]. She does not comment on it there. The attribution to Malden and the label ‘Philalethean Lion Hunt’ are uncertain from the records.

References: III.1 ¶64, III.1 ¶65

Mammon

term

In Atwood’s account, Mammon is the downward-looking spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work astray.

Atwood names Mammon as the spirit that led the depraved abusers of the work: “Mammon led them on; mammon that least erected sprit that fell” [III.4 ¶4]. The phrase pictures it as the least upward-looking spirit.

References: III.4 ¶4

Manacles and fetters

term

A figure that Bacon, writing on Democritus, glosses as laying hold of matter and working on it to the utmost degree.

In Bacon’s account of Democritus, quoted in the book, the figure carries its own gloss: “manacles and fetters; i.e., lays hold and works upon matter in the extremist degree” [I.2 ¶23]. The text therefore states the plain meaning: working on matter to the extreme.

Identified with: working upon matter in the extremist degree [I.2 ¶23]

References: I.2 ¶23

Manget

person

Cited for reference only.

References: III.1 n25

Manget’s collection

treatise

A collection cited as containing works by Philalethes and Grasseus.

Atwood cites Manget’s collection as the place where works by Philalethes and Grasseus are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

References: I.1 n83, I.1 ¶73

Manilius

person

An author cited from the Astronomicon to support the view that men hold the world within them and are each a small image of God.

Atwood cites Manilius (Astronomicon, lib. 10) in support. He holds that men contain the world within them and are each a small image of God: “Quid mirum noscere mundum” [II.1 ¶29; II.1 n28]. That reading rests on our own translation of the Latin, not one the book gives.

References: II.1 n28, II.1 ¶29

Manual artifice

term

A practical technique of the work that Ashmole’s notes allude to; the book does not describe it here.

Atwood says Ashmole’s notes allude to the manual artifice “without much disguise” [I.1 ¶62]. The passage does not describe the technique itself.

References: I.1 ¶62

Manual operation

term · Manual, Manual operations

The name for the method of using the key (Kirchringius); for Atwood, the literal handwork needed chiefly in the first work, also called the Linear way.

The book quotes Kirchringius on the key and “the method, which is called Manual Operation, by which to use it” [III.1 ¶37]. Speaking in her own voice, Atwood says that in the first work “Manual operation is chiefly required” [IV.1 ¶2]. She treats it as the one way of Purification, “called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5], and so equates it with the Linear way. Readers took her to mean literal handwork by the operator, but that sense is an inference from context.

Identified with: Linear way [IV.1 ¶5]

References: III.1 ¶37, IV.1 ¶2, IV.1 ¶5

Manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme’s works

collective voice

A verse eulogy, found in manuscript in a volume of Boehme’s works, praising Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom; Atwood accepts it with a qualification.
