Atwood quotes a manuscript eulogy found in a volume of Boehme’s works. It praises Boehme for renewing all ancient wisdom: “In Boehme’s wondrous page we view, Discoverd and revealed anew” [I.1 ¶68]. It names the Eastern Magi, Orpheus, Hermes, Confucius, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Plato, Socrates and Epictetus [I.1 ¶68–¶70]. Atwood accepts its praise only “theosophically, but not intellectually” [I.1 ¶70].

See also: Works

References: I.1 ¶68, I.1 ¶69, I.1 ¶70

Marcus

person

Author of the Defensio Idearum Operaticium, cited on the impress and on a plant born, dying and reborn in a glass vessel.

A footnote quotes Marcus’s Defensio Idearum Operaticium on the impress and on a plant that is born, dies and is reborn in a glass vessel: “Quid quaesco dicerunt hi tanti philosophi, si plantam quasi momento nasci in vitreo case viderent” [III.3 n27].

References: III.3 n27

Maria

person

A Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, linked with Democritus at Memphis; Atwood often cites her Practica on the matter, the vessel and the order of the work.

Atwood describes Maria as a Hebrew woman advanced in the Hermetic Art, associated with Democritus at Memphis, whose treatises are extant [I.1 ¶13; I.1 n20]. She cites Maria repeatedly, mostly in support:

  • Matter: “this science may be found in all bodies”, most easily in matter that plainly holds the four elements [I.3 n48].
  • Order of the work: Maria illustrates white before red and the rectification of Kibric and Zibeth, which are soul and spirit and the two fumes at the root of the science. Atwood quotes “Take the white, clear, and dignified herb, says Maria, which grows upon the little mountains” [I.3 n67].
  • The vessel: a divine secret that cannot be done without and is never openly revealed. “Philosophers have spoken sufficiently of all that is necessary concerning the work, with exception of the vessel” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1].
  • Shortness of the work: Maria is cited for the work’s shortness as the reason philosophers say little about it [II.1 ¶14].
  • The poison: once resolved, the deadly poison becomes productive. “when this poison is resolved into a subtle water, it coagulates our Mercury into most pure silver” [III.1 ¶61; III.1 n68].
  • Latin verse: on fixing the fugitive and binding it in three hours, “Gummis cum binis fugitivum figit in imis,” given without comment [IV.2 ¶31; IV.2 n20].

References: I.1 n20, I.1 ¶13, I.3 n31, I.3 n48, I.3 n67, I.3 n9, II.1 n1, II.1 ¶14, II.1 ¶8, II.4 n4, III.1 n68, III.1 ¶61, IV.2 n20, IV.2 ¶31

Maria Practica

treatise

Maria’s treatise, cited for the vessel of Hermes as the ‘measure of thy fire’, placed after the Passive Understanding.

Atwood cites the end of the Maria Practica, to support or illustrate the vessel of Hermes as the measure of thy fire, which she places after the Passive Understanding: “Istud est vas Hermetis, quod Stoici occultaverunt” [III.1 ¶40; III.1 n44]. The treatise is cited elsewhere under Maria.

References: III.1 n44, III.1 ¶40

Marriage

term · nuptials

The union of Mind and Universe, in which solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether; ancient mythic marriages prefigure it.

For Atwood, the marriage is the union of Mind and Universe: “This is the union supersentient, the nuptials sublime, Mentis et Universi” [III.3 ¶15]. In the readers’ summary, solitary Thought unites with the simple Understanding of its ether, and ancient mythic marriages prefigure this. Her figure for it is “the bridegroom crowneth the bride in the North” [III.3 ¶15].

Identified with: union of Mind and Universe (Mentis et Universi) [III.3 ¶15]

References: III.3 ¶15

Marrow of Alchemy

treatise

A verse treatise cited to illustrate that a small quantity of the composition is sealed in one glass.

Atwood quotes a line from Book 3 to illustrate that a small amount of the composition is sealed in one glass: “And it sufficeth in one glasse to put” [IV.3 ¶23; IV.3 n4].

See also: Alchemy

References: IV.3 n4, IV.3 ¶23

Mars and Venus property

term

Planetary properties of temperament whose dominance, Atwood says, draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood speaks of “People in whom the Mars and Venus property is dominant” [APP ¶113]. She says that in such people the dominance draws consciousness near the Sol principle and gives knowledge by experience.

References: APP ¶113

Masculine tincture

term

The tincture that fixes the light of Venus in manifestation; it rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.

Atwood says the light of Venus cannot hold “without the masculine tincture to fix it in manifestation” [I.3 n49]. In the same note she says the tincture rises from death out of the black darkness, united with the white virginal spirit.

See also: Tincture

References: I.3 n49

Masons

collective voice

Criticized in the Appendix: they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key, keeping an absurd outward form.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood criticizes the Masons. She says they ape the words of power but have lost the magic Key. Their outward form is absurd, she says, and survives only through a secret response of common sense to the original mystery [APP ¶100].

See also: Free masonry, Master mason

References: APP ¶100

Master

collective voice — author of the Tractatus Aureus

The author of the Tractatus Aureus, quoted on the stone generated with Light and on dissolution by the watery Form.

Atwood quotes the Master’s Tractatus Aureus twice:

  • Cap. 3, after her own gloss on Boehme, on Nature’s middle principle: “Our stone comes with Light, and with Light it is generated” [III.1 ¶49; III.1 n54]. The stone is generated with Light and brings forth darkness.
  • Cap. 2, in support of dissolution by Water, fire on the Foliated Sulphur, the King’s Tincture and revival: “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14; IV.2 n7].

See also: Masters, Tractatus Aureus

References: III.1 n54, III.1 ¶49, IV.2 n7, IV.2 ¶14

Master Key

term

That whose application moves the first link in the chain of vital causes; also the concealment under which the Adepts kept the three operations.

Atwood writes: “The first link in the chain of vital causes moves, as we apply the Master Key.” [III.4 ¶47]. She does not explain the key there. Elsewhere she says the Adepts kept the three operations “reserved strictly under the Master Key of their Dilemma” [IV.2 ¶3], so the term also names their concealment.

See also: Key

References: III.4 ¶47, IV.2 ¶3

Master mason

term · Grand Architects

Only a Master mason can ‘erect structures in the air’; in context this apparently means Mind working by its own reflective energy, too hard for inferior craftsmen.

Atwood writes: “it is the work only of a Master mason, of Grand Architects, as the Brethren have it, to erect structures in the air” [IV.2 ¶14]. She equates the Master mason with the Grand Architects of the Brethren and says the task is too onerous for inferior craftsmen. The context suggests the image stands for Mind working by its own reflective energy, but that reading is inferred, not stated.

Identified with: Grand Architects [IV.2 ¶14]

See also: Masons

References: IV.2 ¶14

Masters

collective voice

A group voice whose term “benedicta viriditas” Atwood applies to the green or purple vegetative life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood applies the masters’ term “benedicta viriditas” to the green or purple vegetative life [APP ¶119].

See also: Master (author of the Tractatus Aureus)

References: APP ¶119

Material

term · the matter

What the work is done on: all men have it and live by it, but few can handle it.

The material is what the work is done on: all men have it, but few can handle it. Atwood: “because all men have the material and live by it” [III.4 ¶2]. She does not identify the material further in this passage. See also Matter.

See also: Matter

References: III.4 ¶2

Material of mind

term

Atwood’s name for the subject whose development her Kabalistic and Greek concordances are meant to support.

Atwood speaks of “the development of this Material of Mind” [III.1 ¶71]. She says the Kabalistic and Greek concordances that follow will support it.

See also: Mind

References: III.1 ¶71

Material rites

term

For Psellus, the only means of strengthening the soul’s vehicle: perfecting the soul by the power of materials on earth.

Atwood quotes Psellus, who calls material Rites the only means of strengthening the soul’s vehicle. Their aim is “To initiate or perfect the human soul by the power of materials here on earth” [II.1 ¶51].

References: II.1 ¶51

Maternal intelligence

term · Maternal

The celestial instinct that first conceived the tree of life; it alone reveals the tree and leads into the Paternal light of life.

Atwood equates Maternal intelligence with the celestial instinct. She speaks of “the celestial instinct only to reveal; that subtle Maternal; intelligence which originally conceived it” [III.1 ¶34]. This intelligence first conceived the tree of life, alone reveals it, and leads into the Paternal light of life [III.1 ¶34].

Identified with: celestial instinct [III.1 ¶34]

See also: Intelligence

References: III.1 ¶34

Mathematician

collective voice

An unnamed voice quoted in Latin, praising the Creator’s laws and foundations.

Atwood quotes the mathematician in Latin, illustrating praise of the Creator’s laws and foundations: “En tibi Norma Poli — ! en divae Libramina Molis!” [II.4 ¶30]. The rendering is our translation, not one the book gives.

References: II.4 ¶30

Mathesis

term

Atwood’s word for the emanation’s passage from flat to cubic, in the phrase ‘Mathesis becoming geometric’.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood describes the emanation passing from flat to cubic: “It is Mathesis becoming geometric.” [APP ¶66]. She gives the term no further gloss.

References: APP ¶66

Matrix

term

That on which the sulphur must return for any effect to be produced.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood says an effect requires “a return of the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life) on its matrix” [APP ¶183].

References: APP ¶183

Matter

term · One Matter, Material Principle, subject-matter, True matter

The Hermetic subject: one simple substance under all forms, identified with our Identity, known only in the experience and by the Fire of Intellect, not in nature.

Atwood’s main account. The Matter is diffused everywhere and partly obtainable anywhere, but the aim is to perfect it. In her words, “there is but One Matter truly qualifiable or capable of qualifying matter to be harmonized in this way” [II.1 ¶20]. It is no common water but “an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting” [III.2 ¶7]. She identifies it with “the Thing itself, which is our Identity. This is the true Hermetic material” [III.2 ¶7]. In the same passage it is the power borne by Cheiron, it is Pan, and by rhetorical question it is the Water of our Sea of the old Alchemists [III.2 ¶7]. The Arabians call it Flos Salis Albi [III.2 ¶8]. Readers note that it first appears in vision in demoniacal forms [III.2 ¶7].

The philosophers’ Matter. Atwood sets out, apparently with approval, the view of these philosophers. Matter is “the Material Principle which, according to these philosophers, the Divine experience imparts” [III.2 ¶51]. It is one and all, everywhere and nowhere, uncompounded, an Infinity, describable only by negations and apprehended by ablative reasoning and negation: “that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity, nor any one of those things, by which Being is defined” [III.2 ¶53]. It is the last and lowest effect, the inverse of the First Cause, yet “somewhat; and real” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it with the Quintessence of Plato, the Water of Thales, the Non-Being of Parmenides and the Abyss of the Kabalists [III.2 ¶60]. “For in the natural world there is no such Matter to be found” [III.2 ¶61]. Life and the Fire of Intellect discover “the True matter of the adepts” [III.2 ¶62].

Matter (the One). “The Matter of all things is One and proved simple in the experience” [III.3 ¶65]. It is Nature, “one and the same Unknown Identity through all” [III.3 ¶65], the true element chemists have never found. As non-being, it arises by severance from real being [III.3 ¶77]. When it is sacrificed in the reunion, it supplies body to the Divine.

Other voices. The metropolitan of Memphis says “Matter appeared: and inseparable from it attraction instantly began to operate” [III.3 ¶48]. Vaughan speaks of that without which “the Matter is not alterable as to our final purpose” [IV.2 ¶35], namely the sublimations and double nativity. A passage whose voice is unclear says the Matter must be fed leisurely, cleansed and given wings that are held back: “Cause, therefore, wings to be prepared for the Matter” [IV.1 ¶15].

Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860). “The Matter is seen with the inner eye” [APP ¶162], with agent and patient alternating. In handling it, it flows from the new-born consciousness through the hands to ferment another life [APP ¶164].

Identified with: Water of our Sea (by rhetorical question) [III.2 ¶7]; unctuous mineral vapour [III.2 ¶7]; Thing itself / our Identity / true Hermetic material [III.2 ¶7]; power borne by Cheiron [III.2 ¶7]; Pan [III.2 ¶7]; Flos Salis Albi [III.2 ¶8]; Quintessence of Plato [III.2 ¶60]; Water of Thales [III.2 ¶60]; Non-Being of Parmenides [III.2 ¶60]; Abyss of the Kabalists [III.2 ¶60]; Nature, the Unknown Identity [III.3 ¶65]; Non-being [III.3 ¶77]

See also: Material, Subject matter, True matter

References: II.1 ¶20, III.2 ¶51, III.2 ¶53, III.2 ¶54, III.2 ¶60, III.2 ¶61, III.2 ¶62, III.2 ¶7, III.2 ¶8, III.3 ¶48, III.3 ¶65, III.3 ¶77, IV.1 ¶12, IV.1 ¶15, IV.2 ¶35, APP ¶162, APP ¶164

Matter and form

term

For the prince, what is perfected and corrupted; full knowledge of this is the goal of study.

Atwood quotes the prince, who makes the goal of study “a plenary knowledge of the verity of perfecting and corrupting Matter and Form” [III.4 ¶20].

See also: Form

References: III.4 ¶20

Maximus Olybius

person

Maker of the perpetual lamp found near Alestes, whose urn inscription Atwood cites as speaking of elements digested by laborious art.

Named as the maker of a perpetual lamp found near Alestes [I.1 ¶18]. His urn inscription is cited for its line about elements enclosed and digested by heavy labour: “Namque elementa gravi clausit digesta labore” [I.1 ¶19]. Our rendering (by: ours): for he enclosed the elements, digested with heavy labour. Atwood cites it for its mention of elements digested by laborious art.

References: I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶19

Maya

term

In an Indian record Atwood quotes, whatever appears or does not appear in the mind apart from the First Cause: the mind’s image or delusion.

A term from a quoted Indian record, not Atwood’s own: whatever appears or does not appear in the mind, other than the First Cause, is to be known as “the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48]. The gloss “image or delusion” is the text’s own.

References: II.3 ¶48

Meadow

term · meadows, Pratum

The meadow of Divine Ideas: the prolific power of life and the grasp of the first efficient causes of life and Forms; the Alchemists call it their garden.

Atwood, drawing on Plato, says “the Meadow is the prolific power of life, according to Plato” [II.4 ¶16]; she describes it as the comprehension of the first efficient causes of life and of Forms. She identifies it with the Alchemists’ garden: “this meadow of Divine Ideas, or Pratum, as the Oracle denotes it, is a place well known to philosophers; the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. So in her reading the Platonic/Oracular Meadow (Pratum) and the alchemical garden name the same place.

Identified with: garden (of the Alchemists) [II.4 ¶9]

References: II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶9

Medial gold

term · almost or medial gold

In Hermes as quoted, the third product from the Stone after water and gold, nobler than the water with the faeces.

Hermes, as quoted, lists it as the third product from the Stone: “the third is our almost or medial gold which is more noble than the water with the faeces” [I.3 ¶55]. The text does not explain it further.

See also: Gold

References: I.3 ¶55

Medial life

term · vegetable or medial life

The middle or second life, between the mineral and the higher life, reached by dissolving the sensuous medium, through which the third life is raised and born.

Atwood’s term for an intermediate level of life. Most records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).

In the Appendix. It is the second life: “Dissolve the sensuous medium and you have the second or medial life.” [APP ¶182]. The third life is born “through the medial or celestial life” [APP ¶35], so it is equated with the celestial life. The exalted spirit is “the spirit in the medial life” [APP ¶15]. When life is drawn inward, “the medial spirit is changed; life is attracted in, instead of out” [APP ¶24]. It sits between the mineral and the higher life; the Salt “must be translated or drawn up into the medial life” [APP ¶77], and the heart centre is “the heart of the celestial medial vegetable life” [APP ¶95]. It is also the life in which we ought to be efficient, so as to be efficient for the divine life above us; Atwood equates this with faith: “efficient in the medial life — in faith” [APP ¶45].

In the main text. In the order of the Mysteries, “Close upon the revealment of the Medial Life then, as we take it, in order of the Mysteries followed the Purificative Rites” [II.2 ¶20]; the passage does not define it. Following the Platonists, the generative virtue forms an “intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. Atwood glosses Enoch’s wooden receptacles as this life: “the wooden receptacles (the vegetable or medial life)” [III.2 ¶12].

Whether the II.2 usage means the same as the Appendix’s second life is not stated.

Identified with: Celestial life [APP ¶35]; exalted spirit (the spirit in this life) [APP ¶15]; Faith [APP ¶45]; wooden receptacles [III.2 ¶12]

See also: Life

References: II.2 ¶20, III.2 ¶12, III.2 ¶9, APP ¶15, APP ¶182, APP ¶24, APP ¶35, APP ¶45, APP ¶77, APP ¶95

Medial light

term

The senses’ own light, in which they are entranced at the start of the practice.

Atwood speaks of “entrancing the senses in their own medial light” [IV.1 ¶3] at the start of the practice. The text gives no further gloss.

See also: Light

References: IV.1 ¶3

Medial region

term

The middle region of life into which the hidden Sulphur must be transplanted before it can grow and become manifest.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the Sulphur “has to be drawn forth and transplanted into the medial region before it can grow and become manifest” [APP ¶125], and that something follows “When the medial life draws the hidden central light” [APP ¶125]. The context suggests the medial region is the place of the medial life (see medial life).

References: APP ¶125

Medial spirit

term

A spirit whose forms and properties are extinguished in the fermentation; not further explained.

Atwood describes the fermentation as taking place “by an extinguishing of the forms and properties of the Medial Spirit” [III.2 ¶28]. It is not explained further here; compare the Appendix’s “medial spirit” that is changed when life is drawn inward (see medial life).

See also: Spirit

References: III.2 ¶28

Mediate dispositions

term

In the Lucerna Salis as quoted, the means by which God grants the art: instruction and the labour of the hands.

The author of the Lucerna Salis, as quoted, says God grants the art not immediately “but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20].

References: III.4 ¶20

Medicine

term · medicines, White medicine, universal medicine

The transmuting and healing product of the work, the Stone in its tinging form, whose virtue grows with each dissolution and multiplication.

The medicine is the agent that transmutes metals and also heals. Its strength is spoken of as its height or virtue: “the true height of the medicine” [I.1 ¶66]; “the White medicine of sufficient virtue to convert 120,000 times its weight into the purest silver” [I.1 ¶73], also called a tincture in the same account [I.1 ¶73].

Quoted authorities. The Lucerna Solis and the monk of the Rosary make it from the salt of the world and call it one thing: “the medicine is one, in which the whole mystery consists” [I.2 ¶11]; “Of it is made that medicine which will preserve you from all maladies” [I.2 ¶10]. The Scholiast says the bodies are reduced into it, it tinges 10, 100, 1000 parts, and “the oftener the medicine is dissolved, by so much more it increases in virtue” [I.3 n38]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon keeps ferment in the fire “That thy Medicine augment mayst aye;” [III.1 ¶65]. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The third gate is the fire which conduceth to the maturity of the medicine.” [III.3 ¶63]; at the fourth gate it is a universal medicine for all diseases. In IV.3 it is the Stone in working form; diluted in mercury “you will have the medicine, though of an inferior order” [IV.3 ¶20]; Vaughan speaks of “the Stone and magic medicine” and calls it “such a subtle moist fire” that only its proper glass can hold it [IV.3 ¶22].

Atwood. Philosophers, “when they have obtained this medicine”, did not care to lengthen their days or parade riches [IV.3 ¶48]. She also reports Heraclitus calling the theurgic media medicines: “Heraclitus calls these medicines, as being the help and remedy of imperfect souls” [II.2 ¶5]; these also healed the body.

Identified with: Tincture [I.1 ¶73]; subtle moist fire [IV.3 ¶22]

See also: True medicine, Universal medicine, White medicine

References: I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73, I.2 ¶10, I.2 ¶11, I.3 n38, II.2 ¶5, III.1 ¶65, III.3 ¶63, IV.3 ¶20, IV.3 ¶22, IV.3 ¶48

Medium

term · Mediums, media, sensible medium, photogenic medium

A mean or intermediary: the precepts demand one between the two; in the practice, the sensible medium released by entrancing and purified; also any means toward an end.

The word carries several senses.

A mean between two. Hermes, as quoted: “for the precepts demand a medium” [I.3 ¶23]; “the temperate unguent, which is fire, is the medium between the faeces and the water” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood repeats “for the precepts demand a medium” [III.1 ¶41] as why the two Spirits need each other. Compare “medium and bond”.

The sensible medium. Atwood uses it of the mesmeric agent, the photogenic medium. Quoting an adept, one who has the Art “and hath the medium, will be richer than any other” [II.2 ¶18]; the purified principle becomes “the medium of that holy and sublime experience” [II.2 ¶25]. In regeneration “the sensible medium, which in this present birth is dominant, being made occult” [III.1 ¶50]. It is released by entrancing: “the medium in its natural state is volatile, immanifest, phantastic, irrational, and important” [IV.1 ¶4], so it must be purified; there are “many ways of including the sensible medium” [IV.1 ¶5]. In IV.1 ¶7 the word is also used for the means by which the Royal Diadem is extracted.

A means toward an end. Aristotle, as quoted: in deliberation “they consider how and by what Medium it may be obtained” [IV.1 ¶30], tracing media back to the first Cause. Atwood applies this: “That Medium, therefore, which is last in the analysis is first in generation” [IV.1 ¶31]; inquiry ends at the medium immediately in the operator’s power, and there the work begins. Zachary, quoted: “Mediums nevertheless are to be employed” [III.4 ¶20] besides prayer.

How far these senses are one in Atwood’s mind is not stated.

Identified with: temperate unguent [I.3 ¶24]

See also: Sensible medium

References: I.3 ¶23, I.3 ¶24, II.2 ¶18, II.2 ¶25, III.1 ¶41, III.1 ¶50, III.4 ¶20, IV.1 ¶30, IV.1 ¶31, IV.1 ¶4, IV.1 ¶5

Medium and bond

term

What Atwood says any increase of the Spirit requires.

Atwood: “neither is there any increase of the Spirit, as we have already shown, without a medium and a bond” [III.4 ¶30]. See medium.

References: III.4 ¶30

Melioration

term

Improvement: the natural life needs it, and the operator must have its principles in himself.

Atwood speaks of “how much such a life is in need of melioration” [II.2 ¶18], and of those “wanting the very principles of melioration in themselves” [II.2 ¶29], meaning the operator must have these principles within.

References: II.2 ¶18, II.2 ¶29

Melissus

person

Reported via Aristotle as holding the One according to Matter; the view is dismissed as rustic.

Known in the text only through Aristotle’s report: Melissus takes the One according to Matter, a view dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

References: III.2 ¶40

Memphian prophet

collective voice

A figure teaching the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than words.

Atwood uses the Memphian prophet as the teacher of the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than by words [III.3 ¶44].

See also: Prophet

References: III.3 ¶44

Menstrual

term · menstruals, Third Menstrual

In Eirenaeus as quoted, one of three menstruals; the freed fire appears visibly in the third, which only one who knows the first two can see.

Eirenaeus, as quoted, speaks of three menstruals. The freed fire “appears visibly in our Third Menstrual” [III.1 ¶14], but “he that knows not our two first menstruals is altogether shut out” [III.1 ¶14]. The text does not say what the menstruals are.

References: III.1 ¶14

Menstruum of the world

term

What ‘that water’ must be: drawn out of the sphere of the Moon and rectified until it can calcine gold.

In a passage of uncertain voice: “Now that water must be the menstruum of the world” [IV.3 ¶21], “out of the sphere of the Moon so often rectified until it can calcine gold” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is not explained further.

Identified with: that water [IV.3 ¶21]

References: IV.3 ¶21

Mercurial liquor

term

In Eudoxus as quoted, the viscous water into which the secret fire’s water dissolves; the beginning, foundation and Key of the Art.

Eudoxus, as quoted: the water drawn out by the secret fire, through magical union with the dry water of the sea of the wise, “is dissolved into a viscous water – into a mercurial liquor” [IV.3 ¶16], “a mercurial liquor, which is the beginning, the foundation, and the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16]. It is thus equated with the viscous water. See Mercury.

Identified with: viscous water [IV.3 ¶16]

References: IV.3 ¶16

Mercurizate

term

In Ripley as quoted, said of mineral and metallic bodies reduced to their beginning; apparently ‘turned into mercury’.

Ripley, as quoted: “Mineral and metalline may be mercurizate” [I.2 ¶6], said of fusible bodies once reduced to their beginning. The text does not gloss the word; the context suggests made into mercury in the philosophers’ sense (see Mercury).

References: I.2 ¶6

Mercury

term · Mercury of the Wise, Mercury of the Philosophers, philosopher’s Mercury, philosophic mercury, Mercurius, Mercurius Philosophorum, Mercurial Spirit, our Mercury

One of the three principles with Sulphur and Salt; in the philosophers’ sense the first matter, a living spirit-water, not common mercury, in which the art begins and ends.

Not common mercury. The philosophers never teach that “mercury as mercury specificate, can be changed into gold” [I.2 ¶4]. Their Mercury is the first matter to which bodies are reduced: “reduce the body into water, that is, into mercury” [I.2 ¶5], also called argent vive [I.2 ¶5]; it is the root of gold and silver [I.2 ¶11]; “All is in Mercury which the wise men seek” [I.2 ¶12] (Bacon, Rosarium, Geber, Aquinas, endorsed by Atwood). Atwood: “the Mercury of the philosophers is not found of itself on earth” [I.2 ¶49]; it is “the Universal Spirit or Mercury” [I.2 ¶49], also called Proteus and quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; the preparation includes “multiplying the Mercury by its proper Light” [I.2 ¶39]. Albertus calls it permanent water, unctuous vapour and spirit of body [I.2 ¶29]; Lully calls it Hyle [I.2 ¶29].

Living agent. The Scholiast: “philosophic, fiery, vital, running” [I.3 n9]; the art begins and “finishes in the same” [I.3 n55]. The adepts call it “the recreated body of the spirit, passive and pure” and “the earth of the wise” [I.3 n29]. After preparation the vulgar Matter becomes “pure, agile, intelligent, living” [II.2 ¶16]. Atwood: it is “the impure vapor of life” that the sulphuric Spirit putrefies [III.1 ¶24]. The Alchemists say it comes only “by help of ingenuity and industry” [III.1 ¶13]; Lully, by ingenuity and manual operation [IV.1 ¶5]. Boehme, Agrippa and Paracelsus’ disciples: “the Mercurial Spirit is everywhere” [II.1 ¶9], though not equally extractable from all. Eiraneaus: separating light from darkness seven times, “the creation of the philosophic mercury will be complete” [I.3 n39]. Eudoxus: its whole energy lies in “the fixed salt of our compound” [IV.3 ¶9].

Identities. Atwood: in the first conjunction the Spirit predominates, in the second its Light, “which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. Eirenaeus: “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69], the first matter of metals, a water dry. Grasseus: quicksilver, the same as Lully’s Lunaria [III.2 ¶25]. The Rosy Cross Dragon: “I am called of the philosophers Mercury: my husband is Gold philosophical.” [III.3 ¶64], also Egg and Light of nature. Eudoxus: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10], first matter and water of metals, white and red, carrying “in its centre its own Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶12]; “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. Sendivogius: the water into which earth is resolved [IV.3 ¶21]. Atwood names it with the Sal Sepientum [II.4 ¶39], and Behmen’s Mercurius as “spirit of the Sound” [APP ¶49, Appendix layer].

In the work. The adept: it rises “to her superior habitation” [III.3 ¶17]. The author of The Triumph: it is whitened, citrined and fed “with its own blood” [IV.2 ¶6]; the theosophist says it “doth all this itself” as “the workman which is in it already” [IV.3 ¶38]. The bottomless Mercury of Eirenaeus [III.1 ¶19; APP ¶89] is not decoded. Whether the fixed philosopher’s Mercury of III.3 ¶32 is the same as Mercury-as-Spirit is open.

Identified with: Water [I.2 ¶5]; Argent vive [I.2 ¶5]; first original (of Sol) [I.2 ¶11]; root of gold and silver [I.2 ¶11]; Proteus; quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; Philosophic water [I.3 n5]; Earth of the wise [I.3 n29]; first matter of metals [III.1 ¶69]; water dry [III.1 ¶69]; our water / our secret fire [III.1 ¶69]; quicksilver [III.2 ¶25]; Lunaria [III.2 ¶25]; Spirit [III.3 ¶30]; Old Dragon [III.3 ¶64]; poisonous dragon [III.3 ¶64]; Egg of nature [III.3 ¶64]; Light of nature (within) [III.3 ¶64]; carbuncle of the Sun; clarified Earth [III.3 ¶64]; Our old man [IV.3 ¶10]; first matter of all metals [IV.3 ¶10]; water of the metals [IV.3 ¶10]; Spirit [IV.3 ¶12]; the workman which is in it already [IV.3 ¶38]; Permanent water [I.2 ¶29]; Hyle [I.2 ¶29]; Universal spirit [I.2 ¶49]; Water [IV.3 ¶21]; spirit of the Sound [APP ¶49]; Sal Sepientum [II.4 ¶39]; impure vapor of life [III.1 ¶24]

References: I.2 ¶11, I.2 ¶12, I.2 ¶29, I.2 ¶37, I.2 ¶39, I.2 ¶4, I.2 ¶49, I.2 ¶5, I.3 n29, I.3 n39, I.3 n5, I.3 n55, I.3 n9, II.1 ¶12, II.1 ¶9, II.2 ¶16, II.4 ¶39, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶14, III.1 ¶19, III.1 ¶24, III.1 ¶61, III.1 ¶69, III.2 ¶25, III.3 ¶17, III.3 ¶30, III.3 ¶32, III.3 ¶64, III.3 ¶81, IV.1 ¶5, IV.1 ¶7, IV.2 ¶6, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶12, IV.3 ¶21, IV.3 ¶38, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶9, APP ¶49, APP ¶89

Mercury and Jupiter

term

Planetary properties to which perception and intuition belong: clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres, weaker in feeling and realization.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood assigns “perception or intuition, which are the property of Mercury and Jupiter” [APP ¶113]; these are clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres but weaker in feeling and realization.

References: APP ¶113

Mercury of the first work

term

In the Open Entrance as quoted, what is added, three or four parts to one of Perfect Matter, in Multiplication.

The Author of the Open Entrance, as quoted, directs adding “three or four parts at most of the Mercury of the First Work” [IV.3 ¶18] to one part of the Perfect Matter in Multiplication. Not further defined.

See also: Works

References: IV.3 ¶18

Merlin

person — St Ambrose

Listed among the great spirits; his Prophecies are reported to refer solely to Hermetic arcana, and Norton names him among masters who wrote obscurely.

Atwood lists Merlin (given as St Ambrose) among the great spirits, and reports that his Prophecies refer solely to Hermetic arcana [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n54]. Norton’s verse names him with Hermes, Rasis, Geber, Avicen, Hortolan, Democrit, Morien, Bacon and Raymond as masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

References: I.1 n54, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45

Mesmerism

term · mesmeric, mesmerizing

The modern art that uses the same agent as the Mysteries but for inferior ends; Atwood’s first key and Door-keeper to the vestibule of antique science.

Atwood treats Mesmerism as a real but external, preliminary form of the same art. It works with the same agent, but “the object was different and immeasurably superior to those proposed by modern Mesmerism” [II.2 ¶24]. In its preliminary practice “the modern art, called Mesmerism, strikingly accords” with the Mysteries and Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

She ranks it as a beginning only: “This Mesmerism, in respect of our Mystery then, may be regarded as a first key” [III.1 ¶8], one that opens only into the vestibule and shows the labyrinth of life, since its practitioners mesmerize one another without knowing how to amend the Thing. “Mesmerism, as it is mechanically practiced in the present day, is a first step indeed” [IV.3 ¶37] before the temple of Divine Wisdom.

She credits it personally: “We allude to Mesmerism: not ashamed, but grateful to acknowledge the neglected Door-keeper” [III.4 ¶13], “the neglected Door-keeper that gave us first introduction to the vestibule of antique science” [III.4 ¶13]; it relieves suffering and offers the multitude a new guide to knowledge and felicity.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The action of mesmerism is a very external way” [APP ¶73]: by vertical passes it loosens spirit from its corporeal media for the moment, an external imitation of the Divine Art of separation.

Mesmerism. Atwood notes that the phenomena of Mesmerism have revived belief in an Odic Force, which she does not assume here [I.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she says Aesculapius is its only just pride [IV.3 ¶36]; whether this is praise or a limitation is unclear. See the main Mesmerism entry.

Identified with: Door-keeper [III.4 ¶13]

See also: Pioneers of Mesmerism (De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet)

References: I.2 ¶16, II.2 ¶24, III.1 ¶8, III.4 ¶13, IV.3 ¶36, IV.3 ¶37, IV.4 ¶5, APP ¶73

Mesothesis

term

What the soul is said to be: a mesothesis between two spheres, its ultimate perfection.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the soul: “it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres” [APP ¶178]. The term is not glossed; the context suggests a middle position between two spheres.

References: APP ¶178

Metal bond

term

Something whose breaking precedes the birth of the Elias spirit; not explained.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “When the metal bond is broken” [APP ¶139], the Elias spirit is born. Not explained further.

References: APP ¶139

Metallic humidity

term

What Atwood says the soul’s angelic essence is.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The soul’s angelic essence is a metallic humidity.” [APP ¶181]. Not explained further.

Identified with: the soul’s angelic essence [APP ¶181]

References: APP ¶181

Metalline perfection

term

The perfection reached in metals, belonging only to the primary evolution of life and distinct from the ultimate Divine association.

Atwood speaks of “the metalline perfection, which belongs to the primary evolution of life only” [IV.3 ¶27], and warns against confusing it with the ultimate Divine association.

References: IV.3 ¶27

Metalline radix

term

The metallic root, which appears first in the experimental process and is most easily apportioned.

Atwood: “the metalline radix first presents itself in the experimental process” [I.2 ¶49], and it is the most easily apportioned.

See also: Radix

References: I.2 ¶49

Metals of the philosophers

term

In the Appendix, Atwood identifies the philosophers’ Metals with the ethereal metals, the Ether’s progressive stages from lower to higher forms.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood states: “The Metals of the philosophers are the ethereal metals; the Ether’s progressive stages” [APP ¶180]. So the Metals = ethereal metals = the Ether’s progressive stages, apparently its processes from lower to higher forms.

Identified with: ethereal metals; the Ether’s progressive stages [APP ¶180]

See also: Philosophers

References: APP ¶180

Metaphysical alienation

term

Atwood’s term for the condition, proved by ancient experience, of passing beyond ordinary consciousness toward deification.

Atwood speaks of “Such is the condition and metaphysical alienation which ancient experience sublimely proved, as passing to deification” [II.4 ¶49]. The context suggests a passing beyond this life’s consciousness; the text links it directly to deification.

References: II.4 ¶49

Metaphysical body of gold

term

Something to be found and made profitable by joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other.

Atwood describes the procedure of joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other: “this is the true way and means by which the metaphysical body of gold will be made profitable” [III.1 ¶50].

See also: Gold

References: III.1 ¶50

Metaphysical embryo

term

That which undergoes abyssal regeneration and contest in the intermediate stages before birth into sense perception, and on which the geometric procedure operates.

Atwood speaks of “the abyssal regeneration and contest of the metaphysical Embryo before it is born into the perception by the eye of sense” [III.1 ¶56], placing it in the intermediate stages of the work, before anything becomes visible. Elsewhere she refers to “the geometric method of procedure with the Metaphysical Embryo, through its complex parts” [III.3 ¶37], i.e. the circle–square–triangle–circle procedure; the term is not further defined there.

References: III.1 ¶56, III.3 ¶37

Metaphysical ferment

term

A small, purified, fire-tested portion that re-enters its native life and transmutes the whole into its own Aurific Light.

Atwood: “a small grain of the metaphysical ferment leavens the whole lump” [III.1 ¶24]. In the same paragraph she calls it a graft: “the metaphysical graft, already purified and passed the fire, re-enters to redeem its congenital life” [III.1 ¶24], transmuting it all into its own Aurific Light. Leaven and graft are images used for it here, not separate terms.

See also: Ferment

References: III.1 ¶24

Metaphysical offspring

term

The one born in the third vessel, triply covered, represented by the birth of Horus.

Atwood, discussing the birth of Horus, writes: “even so is the metaphysical offspring said to be involved” [IV.2 ¶11], i.e. triply covered and born in the third vessel. Compare the ‘supernatural offspring’ that Intellect begets [IV.2 ¶7].

References: IV.2 ¶11

Metaphysicians

collective voice — inductively arguing · metaphysicians, inductively arguing

Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood criticizes for reducing the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence.

Atwood rejects their attempt to reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence, saying human instinct opposes it [IV.4 ¶15].

See also: Metaphysicians

References: IV.4 ¶15

Metaphysicians

person · our metaphysicians

Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood sets in contrast: they lamented natural reason’s inadequacy but could not free it from dependence on sense.

Atwood cites them by way of contrast: they lamented the inadequacy of natural reason but could not free it from its dependence on sense [II.1 ¶32].

See also: Metaphysicians (inductively arguing), Modern metaphysicians

References: II.1 ¶32

Metaphysico-chemical analysis

term

The analysis of the Universal Subject: separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord, displayed in Valentine’s allegory.

Atwood says that in Valentine’s allegory “the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis of the Universal Subject is displayed — the separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord” [III.2 ¶20]; she also inserts “[viz., in the metaphysico-chemical analysis]” into a quoted passage [III.2 ¶19]. These three phases apparently outline the method as she reads it here.

References: III.2 ¶19, III.2 ¶20

Metaphysico-chemistry

term

Atwood’s name for the Hermetic science, whose ‘Fermentation’ she matches with the Kabalah’s union with God.

Atwood equates the Kabalah’s union with God with “that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27].

References: IV.3 ¶27

Metempsychosis

term

In the Ancient Schools of Divinity, the human Identity’s passage out of animal terrene existence through ethereal elements toward the Reason re-entering its First Cause.

Atwood distinguishes the common acceptance of metempsychosis, which she says has bred many errors, from its sense in the Ancient Schools of Divinity: “a transmigrating of the human Identity out of this animal terrene existence through the ethereal elements of its original fundamentals of nature” [IV.2 ¶18], toward the Reason that re-enters its First Cause.

References: IV.2 ¶18

Metropolitan of Memphis

collective voice

A quoted speaker whose cosmogony (Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit stirring the mass) Atwood uses as illustration, footnoted to Blackwell’s Mythology.

Atwood quotes him: “And know, consecrated Youth, adds the metropolitan of Memphis” [III.3 ¶46]. His account — Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit’s breath stirring the mass, and the separation of congenial from heterogeneous parts — illustrates her reading of the work [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶48]; the source is footnoted to Blackwell’s Mythology.

References: III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶48

Michael Maier

person · Maier

Hermetic writer whom Atwood ranks first among those explaining ancient fable by the Hermetic key, and cites repeatedly for emblems and supporting passages.

Atwood ranks Maier first among those who explained ancient fable by the Hermetic key, though he was profoundly guarded [I.1 ¶70, I.1 n89; works named: Symbola Aurea Mensae, Ulysees, Septimana Philosophica]. He detailed the whole allusion of the epitaph [I.1 ¶24; n31 gives Symbola Auriae Mensa]. She lists him among writers giving specimens of the preliminary lessons, citing Atalanta Fugiens, Emblem 18, for the gold/Mercury passage [III.1 ¶13, III.1 n18]. His Emblema 21 supplies the geometric symbol of the procedure (circle, square, triangle, circle) yielding the Stone: “Fac ex mare et foemina circulum; inde quadrangulum” [III.3 ¶31, III.3 n21]; Atwood calls it ‘epigrammatically symbolized by Michael Maier’ [III.3 ¶37, III.3 ¶38, III.3 n25]. She places him, with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Tollius, in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who traced the poets’ allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25]. His Emblems support the affinity of body and spirit and the agriculture analogy: “Naturam natura docet, debellat ut ignem” [I.3 n37, I.3 n40]. His Hierog. Egypt. Graec. supports the stripping of the Orient Animal: “Animal de Oriente pelle sua leonine spoliari debet” [III.1 ¶64, III.1 n72], given in Latin untranslated (ours: ‘the Animal of the East must be stripped of its lion’s skin’). Atwood uses him throughout with endorsement.

References: I.1 n31, I.1 n89, I.1 ¶24, I.1 ¶70, I.3 n37, I.3 n40, III.1 n18, III.1 n70, III.1 n72, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶25, III.1 ¶63, III.1 ¶64, III.3 n21, III.3 n25, III.3 ¶31, III.3 ¶37, III.3 ¶38

Microcosm

term · microcosmos, Microcosmic

Man as the lesser world, comprehending and representing the whole of the macrocosm; the small world in which the work’s mysteries are consummated.

Several voices agree that man is the microcosm. Sendivogius calls it “the lesser world or microcosm” and says “Thou hast in thy body the anatomy of the whole world” [II.1 ¶10]; he also says “man, after the creation of all things, was created into a particular world or microcosm” [II.4 ¶39], on account of the fiery rational soul infused into him. Atwood reports the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience: “man is a perfect microcosm, wherein, as it was said, the great world and all its creatures might be summarily discerned” [II.1 ¶31]; “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32] — while noting this cannot now be proved. In the same context Atwood uses “celeberrimus ille microcosmos et Adam” [II.4 ¶39] (ours: ‘that most celebrated microcosm and Adam’) alongside the hidden Reason; the referent is unclear.

In her own voice the Microcosm is set against the Great World: it is the scene of “the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation” [III.3 ¶33], and the Archetypal Law is “Perfect in the Microcosmic Unit as in the total Deity of the Great World” [III.3 ¶39]. In the Appendix (later layer): “man, being a microcosm, comprehends and represents the whole and each” of the three Lives, its limbs a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶35]; and “The whole image of the macrocosm is formed, and has consequently its typical representation, in the Microcosm” [APP ¶55].

Identified with: Lesser world [II.1 ¶10]

See also: Microcosm and macrocosm

References: II.1 ¶10, II.1 ¶31, II.1 ¶32, II.4 ¶39, III.3 ¶33, III.3 ¶39, APP ¶35, APP ¶55

Microcosm and macrocosm

term · microcosm, macrocosm, microcosmic, macrocosmic

The pairing of individual and universal: the microcosmic experiment yields knowledge of the macrocosmic Cause, and the microcosm’s fire continues where the macrocosm’s ends.

Atwood: “by the microcosmic experiment into It, the knowledge if the macrocosmic Cause also was derived” [III.1 ¶23] — knowledge of the universal is gained through experiment on the individual. She also speaks of “the corporeal fire of the microcosm” [III.1 ¶37], which takes over where the macrocosm’s operative fire ends.

See also: Microcosm

References: III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶37

Microcosmic centers

term

Three centers in man: head (animal rational life), heart (celestial medial vegetable life), and lumbar region (inferior mineral life).

In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “There are three microcosmic centers in man” [APP ¶95] — the head, the eye of the Divine and seat of the animal rational life; the heart, of the celestial medial vegetable life; and the lumbar region, of the inferior mineral life. Compare mineral life.

See also: Center

References: APP ¶95

Microcosmic heaven

term

The inner heaven according to whose magnetic virtue the Spirit displays its properties, and where the rainbow-token of reconciliation appears.

Atwood says the Spirit displays its universal properties internally “according to the magnetic virtue, action, and passion of the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.2 ¶16]; this is not further explained. By analogy with the sky after storm, “the same beautiful token of reconciliation is made apparent in the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.3 ¶13], i.e. the rainbow appears there.

See also: Heaven

References: III.2 ¶16, III.3 ¶13

Microcosmic life

term

The life in the individual, which in its natural state resembles the world’s vitality taken into the blood by respiration, and needs melioration.

Atwood: “the microcosmic life is not dissimilar from the vitality of the greater world” [II.2 ¶18], which respiration takes into the blood; in its natural state it needs melioration.

See also: Life

References: II.2 ¶18

Microcosmic recreation

term

The inner re-creation of man, whose basis is the will as fire.

In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood says of the will as fire: “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

See also: Recreation

References: APP ¶97

Microcosmical tradition

term

The tradition Atwood suggests arose from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.

Atwood proposes to show “how the microcosmical tradition arose” [III.3 ¶77]: from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.

See also: Tradition (mythological antique devices)

References: III.3 ¶77

Midas

person

Cited as a contrast: one who preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god.

Atwood uses Midas as a negative example: he preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god [IV.3 ¶48].

See also: Grecian fables (Midas)

References: IV.3 ¶48

Middle Age Adeptists

collective voice

Cited in support: their ‘refined enthusiasm’ agrees with the same divine tradition.

Atwood says the ‘refined enthusiasm’ of the Middle Age Adeptists agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

References: IV.4 ¶28

Middle principle

term

The specificative form by which a thing is generated as its own kind; the principle in which Nature contains and separates natures.

In the grain analogy Atwood identifies it: “in its middle principle, that is to say, in the specificative form” [I.3 n40] — the form by which a thing is generated as its own kind. Nature is addressed as that “which containest and separatest natures in a middle principle” [I.3 ¶33]; the Master, quoted, has “which containest and separatest all things in a middle principle” [III.1 ¶49]. So = specificative form.

Identified with: specificative form [I.3 n40]

See also: Principles

References: I.3 n40, I.3 ¶33, III.1 ¶49

Milton

person

Poet quoted from Paradise Lost to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.

Atwood quotes Milton (paradise Lost, 1:676): “That riches grow in hell” [II.3 ¶35, II.3 n41], to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.

References: II.3 n41, II.3 ¶35

Mind

term

The divine in man, identified with God and Poemander; for Atwood the true Separator, the efficient and regimen of the work, and the Key of the Hermetic Enigma.

Quoted Hermetic voice: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; Atwood seeks entrance to “the shut palaces of Mind” [II.1 ¶53]. In Hermes’ account Poemander says “I am, quoth he, Poemander, the Mind of the Great Lord” [III.3 ¶52] and “I am that Light, the Mind, they God” [III.3 ¶54]; and “That which, in thee, seeth and heareth the Word of the Lord, and the Mind, the Father, God, differ not one from another” [III.3 ¶54]. Mind is always present, comes into the holy and pure, and is “the Porter and Door-keeper” against evil works [III.3 ¶57]. So, per Poemander, Mind = Poemander = Light = God the Father = Porter and Door-keeper. The Rabbi in the Zohar says the articulate voice proceeding from Spirit “comes from the Mind” [III.3 ¶78].

In her own voice, Atwood: “we observe Mind to be the true Separator, the efficient as well as the regimen of the work” [III.1 ¶21]; nothing foreign enters it. And: “Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48]; “no sooner does it attain to Self Knowledge, by proper inquiry within” than the Efficient acts outward [IV.1 ¶48].

Identified with: God [II.1 ¶43]; Poemander [III.3 ¶52]; Light; God [III.3 ¶54]; Porter and Door-keeper [III.3 ¶57]; Key of this Hermetic Enigma [IV.1 ¶48]

References: II.1 ¶43, II.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶21, III.3 ¶52, III.3 ¶54, III.3 ¶57, III.3 ¶78, IV.1 ¶48

Minera

term

That from which the quintessence is drawn by the magistery; not glossed.

Quoted from Synesius / the New Light: the quintessence is “drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]. The term is not glossed; the context shows only that it is that from which the quintessence is drawn.

References: I.2 ¶33

Mineral life

term

The third and lowest life in man, which the Hermetic Art perfects; it contacts the macrocosmic mineral life and first appears in introspection as a dark vapour.

In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “The third life, the mineral or lowest life in man” [APP ¶59]; “The Vegetable and Animal lives are higher than the mineral life in us.” [APP ¶59]. The Art is “a perfectioning of the third or lowest or the mineral life in man” [APP ¶44]. It brings one into contact with the Macrocosmic mineral life and is first seen by introspection as a dark vapour. Identity: “The mineral soul or the lowest form of life in us” [APP ¶71] — so = mineral soul. Compare microcosmic centers (lumbar region).

Identified with: third life; lowest life in man [APP ¶59]; mineral soul; lowest form of life in us [APP ¶71]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶44, APP ¶59, APP ¶71

Mineral radix

term

What is carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury: the root and true matter of the Hermetic Art.

Atwood: “the mineral radix and true mater of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶19], carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury. So = the true matter of the Art.

Identified with: true mater of the Hermetic Art [III.1 ¶19]

See also: Radix

References: III.1 ¶19

Mineral soul

term

The inner ‘secret chamber’ guarded by horrors and phantoms.

Atwood speaks of horrors and phantoms “guarding the secret chamber of their mineral soul” [II.3 ¶29]. In the Appendix the mineral soul is identified with the lowest form of life in us (see mineral life).

See also: Soul

References: II.3 ¶29

Ministering spirit

term

The Spirit that acts without intervention or concealment throughout the work.

Atwood: “without intervention or concealment in the ministering Spirit throughout” [III.4 ¶9]. The ‘highly effective agent’ springing from ourselves, mentioned directly after, apparently refers to it (inferred). Whether ‘the Spirit’ that some were “compelling the Spirit to their private ends” [III.4 ¶6] is the same is not stated.

See also: Spirit

References: III.4 ¶6, III.4 ¶9

Ministers

term · Minister

In Norton, the assistants who carry on the work, with stated moral and practical qualifications, numbers and conduct.

Quoted from Norton: “When ye can finde apt Ministers” [III.4 ¶37]; “Noe Minister is apt to this intent But he is sober, wise, and diligent” [III.4 ¶37]. Norton sets out their qualifications, numbers and conduct.

References: III.4 ¶37

Mirific Word

term

In Atwood’s words, the Word that contains the two catholic natures, the changeable and the immutable.

Atwood speaks of “the two catholic natures contained in the mirific Word” [III.2 ¶24]. From the context of her record, these two natures are the changeable and the immutable. The text gives no further definition here.

See also: Word

References: III.2 ¶24

Modal life

term

In the Alchemists’ teaching as reported, the part of nature that the reduction destroys, as distinct from her vehicle.

This is a view reported from the Alchemists. The modal life is what the reduction destroys, as opposed to nature’s vehicle. The context suggests it is her superfluous forms, since nature is said to be addressed “where nature may be addressed in order to the rejection of her superfluous forms” [II.1 ¶47]. That equation is an inference, not the text’s own statement.

See also: Life

References: II.1 ¶47

Modern adept

collective voice

An unnamed modern adept whom Atwood cites to support her claim that hiding the truth let ignorance spread.

Atwood cites an unnamed modern adept in support of her point that concealment spread ignorance: “this bushel being placed over the light, the darkness of it invited ignorance abroad” [I.1 ¶64]. She endorses the view.

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: I.1 ¶64

Modern Alchemists

collective voice · the Alchemist

The Alchemist as agreeing with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, contrasted with modern Alchemists who are mostly silent on their Art’s metaphysics.

Atwood says the Alchemist agrees with the Greeks on a universal pure matter, while modern Alchemists are mostly silent on the metaphysics of their Art [III.2 ¶46].

See also: Alchemists

References: III.2 ¶46

Modern exponent

collective voice · our modern exponent

An unnamed modern writer whom Atwood cites to confirm and illustrate Hermes’ process in terms of the three principles.

Atwood cites this unnamed modern exponent as confirming and illustrating Hermes’ process in terms of the three principles: “in three months circulation, says he, by digestion, the powder becomes black” [II.1 ¶23].

References: II.1 ¶23

Modern interpreters

collective voice — unnamed

Unnamed modern interpreters whom Atwood criticizes for explaining the lights of the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy.

Atwood rejects the reading of unnamed modern interpreters (“as some say”) who explain the lights shown in the Mysteries as orreries and astronomy [II.3 ¶49].

References: II.3 ¶49

Modern Kabalists

collective voice · some modern Kabalists

Unnamed modern Kabalists whom Atwood cites to explain the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether.

Atwood cites some modern Kabalists for their explanation of the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether as “an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity” [III.2 ¶13].

See also: Kabalists

References: III.2 ¶13

Modern metaphysicians

collective voice

Modern metaphysicians, whom the Appendix contrasts with its own view because they make Time a condition of thought.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), modern metaphysicians are set in contrast because they make Time a condition of thought [APP ¶172].

See also: Metaphysicians

References: APP ¶172

Modern metaphysics

collective voice

Modern metaphysics, which Atwood contrasts with her own view because it treats mind as only abstract or inferential.

Atwood sets modern metaphysics against her own position because it treats mind only as abstract or inferential [III.1 ¶2].

References: III.1 ¶2

Moderns

collective voice — empirical chemists · empirical chemists

The moderns and empirical chemists, whom Atwood criticizes: their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean.

Atwood criticizes the moderns and empirical chemists. Their elements and distilled waters are not what the adepts mean, “as the empirical chemists formerly imagined” [I.2 ¶39; I.2 ¶43].

References: I.2 ¶39, I.2 ¶43

Moist fire

term

The fire the matter is to be boiled in, named in Hermes’ precept and not explained at that point.

Hermes’ precept, which Atwood repeats, says: “Put the matter into a moist fire” [I.3 ¶10]. The moist fire is the fire the matter is boiled in. The passage does not explain it: the nature, origin and “artificial excitation” of the philosophic fire are put off until later.

See also: Fire

References: I.3 ¶10

Moist nature

term · moist natures

In the Poemander, what the descending darkness turns into: an unspeakably troubled moist nature that gives off smoke, with Light before it.

Hermes speaks in the Poemander. The descending darkness changes into “a certain moist nature unspeakably troubled, which yielded a smoke, as from fire” [III.3 ¶53]. It is “that moist nature, that appeareth out of the darkness”, and the Light is before it. When the Word joins Nature, pure fire flies upward out of it [III.3 ¶54].

Moist natures. Vaughan warns that too much heat provokes the moist natures: “thou hast stirred up the wrath of the moist natures, and they will stand up against the central fire” [III.4 ¶44]. This is a caution about managing the fire.

References: III.3 ¶53, III.3 ¶54, III.4 ¶44

Moist spirit

term

Venus’s spirit, to which metalline bodies cling so that it may give them life.

In a footnote, Atwood says metalline bodies cling to Venus’s moist spirit so that it can give them life: “they gladly adhere to this moist spirit, that it may vivify them” [I.3 n49].

See also: Spirit

References: I.3 n49

Monad

term · Monadic

The simple unity to which the Ternary is reduced, Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, and man is reduced in union with God.

Atwood treats the Monad as the simple unity at the end of the reduction. The Ternary is reduced, and Nature is brought back by rejecting the Binary, “to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18]. She also speaks of “the Monadic simplicity of her Element” [IV.2 ¶20]. In the Chaldaic oracle she cites, the (Paternal) Monad generates Two and rules the Triad: “The Monad is enlarged which generates Two,” [IV.2 ¶22]. Discussing the Kabalah, she cites the union it describes, “the union of man, reduced to the simplicity of the Monad, with God” [IV.3 ¶27]. On this reading, reducing man to the Monad and reducing Nature to it seem to be the same aim. The text sets the two passages side by side but does not state that link.

References: IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 ¶20, IV.2 ¶22, IV.3 ¶27

Monarchy of light

term

The ordered state in which the renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord under Light.

Atwood uses the phrase for the outcome of renewal. The renewed faculties and every dignified sentiment are brought into accord “to testify and maintain the triumphant Monarchy of Light” [IV.4 ¶20].

See also: Light

References: IV.4 ¶20

Monk in his Rosary

collective voice · Rosary, Rosar.

The monk who wrote the Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv), cited for the teaching that Stone and medicine are one.

Atwood cites the monk in his Rosary (Rosar., Abbrev. Tract. iii and iv) in support of the teaching that the Stone and the medicine are one, with nothing added or taken away: “The Stone is one” [I.2 ¶11; I.2 n11]. She endorses it.

See also: Author of the Rosarium

References: I.2 n11, I.2 ¶11

Monks

collective voice

The monks, whom Atwood criticizes for promoting Agrippa’s Vanity as if it were a recantation.

Atwood criticizes the monks for promoting Agrippa’s Vanity as a recantation [I.1 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶64

Moon

term · Luna, Lune, Moone

The passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven: in Atwood’s account the Passive Intelligence, paired with the Sun, and named by many authorities in veiled forms.

Atwood’s statements. In Alchemy “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40]. With the Sun, it is one of the pair that “sound the depths together”. Citing Plutarch, she writes that “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason, and to proceed from Wisdom” [III.1 ¶45]. She also reports that Boehme finds Sol and Luna together at the cross.

Hermes, glossed by Atwood. “Luna after fifteen days is diminished; and in the third, she is augmented” [I.3 ¶7]. Atwood explains this Luna as “that ethereal light, which is the passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven” [I.3 n7]. Its waning and waxing match the moon’s, and the philosopher names it after the moon by analogy. Elsewhere Hermes says: “My own Luna, also, is my light, exceeding every other light” [I.3 ¶37]. This is the Stone’s own light, and it is not explained further.

Other quoted authorities.

  • The Hunting of the Greene Lyon: the Moon is sister and bride of the Sun, born with him in the Lion’s Bed, and with him a parent of the King. Luna holds parallel positions in the poem. She is fed to the Lion with Sol and worked alone with the Lion’s blood, “Worke Luna by her selfe alone, With the blood of the Greene Lyon:” [III.1 ¶65], for the white ferment, and she feeds a white King. The passage does not assert that Luna and the Moon are identical.
  • Eirenaeus: when the soul imprisoned in Saturn is set free, a shining vapour arises, “A Vapour shining, like pearl orient, Which is our Moon and sparkling Firmament” [III.1 ¶69]. Elsewhere he pairs Sol and Lune as what projection produces: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” [IV.3 ¶25]. The next line says they will prove both gold and silver pure.
  • The author of the New Light: “our lune or silver, not common silver” [I.3 n40], which receives the seed of gold.
  • Pierce, the Black Monk, names Lune among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].

Asserted identities: Moon = Passive Intelligence [III.1 ¶40]. Luna = the ethereal light or passive luminary of the Philosophic Heaven [I.3 n7]. Moon = the shining Vapour and sparkling Firmament (Eirenaeus) [III.1 ¶69]. Lune = silver, not common silver (New Light) [I.3 n40].

Identified with: Passive intelligence [III.1 ¶40]; Vapour shining / sparkling Firmament [III.1 ¶69]; ethereal light / passive luminary in the Philosophic Heaven [I.3 n7]; silver (not common silver) [I.3 n40]

See also: Saturn, Jupiter, Venus and Lune

References: I.3 n40, I.3 n7, I.3 ¶37, I.3 ¶7, III.1 ¶40, III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶65, III.1 ¶69, III.4 ¶21, IV.3 ¶25

Moon of the Firmament

term

In Vaughan, a middle Nature that is placed equally within two elements in the vital heat-operation.

Vaughan, as quoted, gives the instruction: “take the Moon of the Firmament, which is a middle Nature” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the vital heat-operation it is placed equally within two elements. He asserts its identity with a middle Nature in the same place.

Identified with: middle Nature [IV.1 ¶41]

References: IV.1 ¶41

Moorish philosopher

collective voice · Centrum Naturae Concentratum

The author of Centrum Naturae Concentratum, cited for the claim that man is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature.

Atwood cites the Moorish philosopher (Centrum Naturae Concentratum) in support of the claim that man himself is the best subject and can draw the Central Salt of nature. The cited passage speaks of what “contains not so great mysteries and excellences as Man reformed by God into his image” [II.1 ¶9; II.1 n3]. She endorses this.

See also: Philosophers

References: II.1 n3, II.1 ¶9

More experienced observers

collective voice

Unnamed observers whose testimony Atwood cites: very few people are naturally suited to the research.

Atwood relies on the testimony of more experienced observers that very few people are naturally suited to the research [III.4 ¶2].

References: III.4 ¶2

More modern class of adepts

collective voice

Later adepts whom Atwood cites for the view that man’s life is a fire capable of improvement.

Atwood cites the more modern class of adepts in support of the view that man’s life is a fire capable of improvement: “a pure, naked, and unmingled fire of infinite capability” [II.1 ¶17].

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: II.1 ¶17

More modern experimentalist

collective voice

An unnamed experimentalist cited for the sign of the Arcanum: the masculine tincture rising from the black and uniting with the white spirit.

In a footnote, Atwood cites a more modern experimentalist. When the masculine tincture rises from the black and unites with the white spirit, the operator “will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53].

References: I.3 n53

Morien

person · Morienus, Morieni

An adept who taught King Calid. Atwood cites him often for the teaching that the matter is taken from man himself, and on the operation.

Story. Morienus was the disciple of an adept, Adfar, and later initiated King Calid. Their dialogue is cited as Morienus Eremita Hierosol. De Transfiguratione Metallorum [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n38]. Atwood says his biographer’s story is too long to extract.

The matter. Atwood takes his advice to Calid as pointing to the matter being taken from man: “This matter, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶8; II.1 n1] and “The thing, O king, is extracted from thee” [II.1 ¶16; II.1 n15]. She says Sendivogius diverted this hint. Morien also supports her vessel and place doctrine [II.1 ¶8], and he is counted among the authorities who agree about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

The operation. “Our operation, concludes Morien, is nothing else but extracting water from the earth and returning it again” [IV.1 ¶41; IV.1 n36]. This is an alternating extraction and return of moisture that leads to putrefaction. Atwood then glosses it as action and reaction.

Other uses. As cited by Eirenaeus, he warned Calid that many philosophers were overcome by the fatigue of this work [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5]. He supports the teaching that the magistery is God’s secret of secrets, entrusted to the prophets: “Scire etiam tibi convenit, O bone rex” (ours: It is fitting also for you to know, O good king) [II.4 ¶39; II.4 n27]. Norton’s verse names him among masters who wrote obscurely, “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Atwood uses him mainly as a supporting authority.

References: I.1 n38, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶35, II.1 n1, II.1 n15, II.1 ¶16, II.1 ¶8, II.4 n27, II.4 ¶39, III.2 ¶60, IV.1 n36, IV.1 n5, IV.1 ¶41, IV.1 ¶6

Morienus’s biographer

collective voice

The unnamed writer of Morienus’s story, which Atwood mentions but finds too long to extract.

Atwood mentions that Morienus’s biographer tells his story, but she judges it too long to extract [I.1 ¶35].

References: I.1 ¶35

Mortify

term · mortification, self-mortification, mortifying

Putting the matter to death as a necessary step of the work. For Atwood, it is the death of the fiery self-willed agent once it is ripe.

Hermes makes mortification necessary, together with generation: “except one understandeth how to mortify and induce generation” [I.3 ¶26]. That is, the matter must be put to death through its proper nature. Atwood applies the term to the fiery, self-willed agent. It grows to its full extent “until the time for his mortification is ripe and ready at hand” [III.1 ¶56]. The connate spirit then finally brings the agent to this death, so it becomes a self-mortification.

References: I.3 ¶26, III.1 ¶56

Mosaic

treatise — Scripture

The Mosaic Scripture. Some learned writers held it to be the only revealed truth; Atwood would still revere it if all cosmogonies share one divine source.

Atwood reports that some learned writers judged that “the Mosaic was the only revealed truth of all” [III.3 ¶42]. She qualifies this view. If all cosmogonies share one divine source, she would still revere Scripture.

References: III.3 ¶42

Moses

person

A figure whom Atwood cites as one who taught under a veil and whose legitimate power she sets against the Egyptians’ enchantments.

Like Hermes, Moses gives his instruction under a veil [I.3 n40]. In the Apostle’s text she quotes, the Law is read under a veil: “when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart” [III.3 ¶59]. Atwood compares him on the waters: those on which the Spirit of God moved are not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He appears with Ezekiel, David and Zachariah as illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. Boehme names him with the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles as teaching what Boehme finds in his inner book [III.2 ¶16]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Moses’ legitimate power under God’s law, “might in word and deed”, is set against the Egyptians’ enchantments [APP ¶2; APP ¶4].

References: I.2 ¶43, I.3 n40, II.3 ¶54, III.2 ¶16, III.3 ¶59, APP ¶2, APP ¶4

Most enlightened philosophers

collective voice

Philosophers whom Atwood cites in support of the difference between common and natural calcination.

Atwood appeals to the most enlightened philosophers in support of the difference between common and natural calcination [IV.3 ¶16].

See also: Philosophers

References: IV.3 ¶16

Mother of all beings

term

The great mystery in which, Atwood says, we stand even now.

Atwood writes: “And so far we stand even now in the great mystery, in the Mother of all beings” [III.3 ¶52]. The passage does not define the term further.

See also: Being

References: III.3 ¶52

Mother of sciences

term

Something Atwood expects to come forth in the Fourth Monarchy; the text does not define it further.

Atwood looks ahead to a time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth” [IV.3 ¶49], in the Fourth Monarchy. The term is not defined further.

References: IV.3 ¶49

Motive

term

The operator’s motive, which Atwood calls the true spiritual ferment: everything depends on it, and the Work truly begins only when the right Motive is found.

For Atwood, the Motive is decisive: “Everything depends upon the Motive, which is the true spiritual ferment” [IV.1 ¶44]. The result corresponds to the virtue of the Motive, and the Work truly begins only then, since “it is not until the right Motive is discovered” [IV.1 ¶48]. She identifies the Motive with the spiritual ferment [IV.1 ¶44].

Identified with: spiritual ferment [IV.1 ¶44]

References: IV.1 ¶44, IV.1 ¶48

Motive light

term

An expression Atwood uses once, for the purpose towards which conviction is steeled. The text does not define it further.

Atwood speaks of “conviction steeled to the purpose of her Motive Light” [IV.4 ¶19]. The record gives no further definition.

See also: Light

References: IV.4 ¶19

Motive reason

term

Atwood’s term for man’s life, set against man seen as the individualized multiplication of a blind will.

Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “tat Motive Reason which is his life” [II.1 ¶42], so she identifies Motive Reason with man’s life. She sets it against man as the individualized multiplication of a blind will [II.1 ¶42].

Identified with: his life [II.1 ¶42]

See also: Reason

References: II.1 ¶42

Motto

collective voice

A Latin motto cited in support of the First Matter as the one substance God created in the beginning.

The motto is cited (QUOTED) in support of the First Matter as the single substance God created: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, Creavit unam substantiam, Hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶56]. Our translation, which the book does not give: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. The same sentence also stands as the epigraph credited to Mylius [III.2 ¶2].

References: III.2 ¶56

Mountain of the seven

term · seven mystic mountains, Mountain of the Seven metals

Flammel’s seven-fold mountain, with a royal herb at its top. Atwood equates it with several other symbols: Esdras’s outgoings of paradise, Sendivogius’s Planetary Sphere and the Sapphiric Mine’s tincture.

Atwood (ATWOOD) describes Flammel’s seven-fold mountain, at whose top a royal herb is found [II.4 ¶9]. She then equates it with other names: “Those seven mystic mountains, whereupon grow the roses and lilies, are the outgoings of paradise mentioned in Esdras” [II.4 ¶9]. She adds “and the Planetary Sphere of Sendivogius” and “and that most famous tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [II.4 ¶9]. So the text treats these as several names for one thing. It does not state the plain meaning.

Identified with: outgoings of paradise (Esdras) [II.4 ¶9]; Planetary Sphere of Sendivogius [II.4 ¶9]; Tincture of the Sapphiric mine [II.4 ¶9]

See also: Seven

References: II.4 ¶9

Muesis

term · muoumetha

In Proclus and the Phaedrus passage, the second grade of vision. It is seeing stable appearances with closed eye, through the pure soul, and comes through silence imparted by faith.

This term comes from quoted voices, not from Atwood. In the passage from Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus), muesis is the second grade: “But we view with closed eye, i.e., with the pure soul itself (muoumetha) entire and stable appearances” [II.4 ¶23]. These appearances come through the connective gods [II.4 ¶23]. Proclus (QUOTED) says that “muesis, in short, is neither through intelligence nor judgment, but through the uncial silence imparted by faith” [II.4 ¶40], so faith is named as its cause. The text gives no further definition.

References: II.4 ¶23, II.4 ¶40

Multiplication

term · multiplied, multiply, multiplying, Multeplied, Multeplie

Increasing the finished Stone or Medicine without limit by repeating the same operation: dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Atwood also uses it of frauds’ promises and of Light’s assimilative virtue.

Most records come from quoted authorities. Several describe it as the stage after the Stone is made, when its virtue is increased.

  • Norton speaks of the Red Stone: “Him to increase in multiplication” [I.1 ¶60].
  • Paracelsus says the tincture stays “immutable in the multiplication” [I.1 ¶76].
  • The Hunting of the Greene Lyon says the Medicine is increased without restarting the work, best by continual fermentation: “It’s so well Multeplied as with continuall Firmentation:” [III.1 ¶65].
  • The fraternity of the Rosy Cross makes it the fourth gate, together with augmentation: “The fourth gate is that of multiplication and augmentation in which proportions and weights are necessary.” Reaching this gate gives a universal medicine [III.3 ¶63].
  • Eudoxus makes it the Sixth Key, “the Multiplication of the Stone, by the reiteration of the same operation”, which raises its virtues without limit [IV.3 ¶16].
  • The Author of the Open Entrance writes: “It remains only for the work of Multiplication” [IV.3 ¶18]. He describes joining the Stone with Mercury of the First Work, then dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Each round multiplies its virtue and goes faster [IV.3 ¶18].

A footnote of unclear voice describes the same repeated dissolution and coagulation by the water of the medicine’s mercury, which raises its tinging virtue. It also says that “the multiplication of its internal form has rubified it” [I.3 n67].

Atwood herself (ATWOOD) uses the word in two other ways. First, frauds cheated merchants out of gold, silver and gems, “which they lost, in vain hope of getting them multiplied” [I.1 ¶55]. Second, she makes multiplying a property of Light alone: “Or what else should possibly transmute or multiply by its own assimilative virtue?” [IV.3 ¶30].

References: I.1 ¶55, I.1 ¶60, I.1 ¶76, I.3 n67, III.1 ¶65, III.3 ¶63, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶18, IV.3 ¶30

Multiplication of gold

term

The purely mineral goal to which many gave up their lives. Atwood contrasts it with the art’s higher purposes.

Atwood (ATWOOD) describes those “sacrificing their whole life’s hope to the multiplication of gold” [I.1 ¶42]. She treats it as a merely mineral aim, set against the higher purposes of the art.

See also: Gold

References: I.1 ¶42

Mundane spirit

term · universal Mundane Spirit

The universal Spirit as it is first consciously revealed in humanity’s receptive life. It can receive anything and be converted to anything, and it is equated with Aristotle’s passive intellect.

Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the universal Mundane Spirit, as it is at first consciously revealed in the recipient life of humanity” [II.2 ¶17]. She says it can receive anything and be converted to anything. She equates it with what Aristotle names: “which Aristotle, in his Metaphysics, calls passive intellect” [II.2 ¶17].

Identified with: Passive Intellect [II.2 ¶17]

See also: Spirit

References: II.2 ¶17

Mundified

term · mundification

Purified or cleansed. The Spirit’s mundification must be completed “in both kinds” before the Philosophic Work truly begins.
