Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. In context the word apparently means purified. She also says the Philosophic Work does not truly begin “until the mundification of the Spirit is completed in both kinds” [IV.1 ¶48]. The text does not say what the two kinds are.

References: II.2 ¶15, IV.1 ¶48

Musaeus

person

The person addressed in an Orphic fragment as “offspring of the bright Silene”.

Musaeus appears only as the addressee of the Orphic fragment cited at [II.4 ¶40], where he is called the offspring of the bright Silene.

References: II.4 ¶40

Musai

term

A term used once for what appeared during the evaporative process of purification. What exactly it refers to is unclear.

Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “And that such actually appeared to be the Musai, during the evaporative process of purification” [II.3 ¶22]. This comes in connection with the material images seen during that purification. The text does not make clear whether the Musai are those images or something else.

References: II.3 ¶22

Museum Hermeticum

treatise · Musaeum Hermeticum

A collection Atwood cites as containing works by Philalethes and the Water Stone.

Atwood cites this collection as the place where works by Philalethes and the Water Stone are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

References: I.1 n83, I.1 ¶73

Mustai

term

The Greeks’ name for the aspirants, whom the Hierophant passed on to the immortal abode.

Atwood (ATWOOD) gives Mustai as the Greek name for the aspirants: “the aspirants, by the Greeks called Mustai” [II.3 ¶36]. The Hierophant passed them on to the immortal abode [II.3 ¶36].

Identified with: aspirants [II.3 ¶36]

References: II.3 ¶36

Mylius

person

Author cited for the epigraph saying that God created one substance, the first matter.

Mylius (QUOTED), Phil. Reform., Pars. VI, Lib. 1, gives the epigraph: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶2]. Our translation: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. Atwood uses it in support of the one First Matter. The same words are cited again as a motto at [III.2 ¶56].

References: III.2 ¶2

Mystae

term

The initiates who, according to the expounders, were given narcotic liquors before the shows.

This is the expounders’ view (QUOTED: the expounders), which Atwood reports. They say narcotic liquors were given “which were administered to the Mystae before the shows commence” [II.4 ¶56].

References: II.4 ¶56

Mystae and Teleioi

term

The initiates whose inner experience, Atwood says, the Neo-Platonists did not make public.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says: “It was not their practice to declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi” [APP ¶122]. “Their” refers to the Neo-Platonists.

References: APP ¶122

Mystere de la Croix

treatise · Mystere de la Crois

A French treatise Atwood cites in support of the conjunction of Mars and Venus yielding solar sulphur, repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear, and the magnetic work.

Atwood cites Mystere de la Croix, chap. 13 (spelled ‘Mystere de la Crois’ in n10), in support of three points. The first is the conjunction of Mars and Venus, which yields a solar sulphur. The second is repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear. The third is that the work is magnetic: “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶11; III.3 n4; III.3 ¶18; III.3 n10]. Our translation: This work is called Magnetic. She uses it as support for her own view.

References: III.3 n10, III.3 n4, III.3 ¶11, III.3 ¶18

Mysteries

term · higher Mysteries, temple mysteries, the wise hierophants

The ancient initiatory rites, Ethnic and Christian, held at Eleusis and in Eastern temples. Atwood treats them as real, scientific inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.

Atwood (ATWOOD) treats the Mysteries as real and effective, not as ceremony. They were initiatory rites, “both Ethnic and Christian”, that kept a secret apart from ordinary worship: “There was undoubtedly a secret, hanging about these celebrations, both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]. Their object was Ontological Wisdom, and they really obtained it [II.2 ¶5].

She holds that “the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries, celebrated in the Eastern temples and by the priests at Eleusis, were real and efficacious” [II.2 ¶24]. Their stages ran in order: revealment of the Medial Life, Purificative Rites, then final initiations [II.2 ¶24]. They worked a vital change in those who sought wisdom and immortality, and “the conduct of the Mysteries was uniform and entirely scientific” [III.1 ¶9].

In them, apparitions come before divine illumination, “wherein the consciousness, becoming artificially wrapped by the Mysteries” is held in Hades [II.3 ¶29]. She reads the Rosicrucian letter as describing a passage of initiatory progress within them [II.3 ¶29]. A passage of unclear voice speaks of Intellect “descending into the bosom of the Mysteries” when it perceives the Formless Subject [III.2 ¶55].

Historically, “Necessity, at length, compelled an abandonment of the Mysteries” after the fall of Alexandria, along with the banning of Theurgic rites [I.1 ¶30]. Synesius “was careful, however, to protect the mysteries of his religion from vulgar abuse” [I.1 ¶27]. Yet “the Mysteries of Antiquity changed their form only to appear more resplendent when Christianity came to be the prevailing religion” [IV.2 ¶17]. In Christianity they took the form of effectual baptismal regeneration and the Eucharist [IV.2 ¶17].

Atwood asks that the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest be understood “not as mere external ceremonials, pictured scenes of suffering and beatitudes, but as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source” [IV.4 ¶5]. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

Mysteries. Atwood cites the Mysteries twice. In them Isis is called Athena, which expresses the Spirit’s self-motion and intelligence [III.1 ¶63]. Their mandate forbade passing the revelation on to the profane [III.2 ¶46].

Mysteries and the wise hierophants. Atwood cites the mysteries and the wise hierophants as an illustration. The Aspirant leaves the statues behind to behold the Adytum, and this shows the mind leaving all images; it is “the order in which Divinity is perceived” [III.2 ¶66].

References: I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶30, II.2 ¶24, II.2 ¶5, II.3 ¶29, III.1 ¶63, III.1 ¶9, III.2 ¶46, III.2 ¶55, III.2 ¶66, IV.2 ¶17, IV.4 ¶5

Mysteries celebrated at Eleusis and the rest

collective voice

The Eleusinian and other Mysteries, which Atwood reinterprets as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.

Atwood reinterprets the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, not as external ceremonies. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5]. See also Mysteries.

References: IV.4 ¶5

Mysterious adeptest

collective voice

An adept, cited from Khunrath’s Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern., who defines the philosopher’s stone as embodied Ruach Elohim. Atwood admits such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown.

Atwood quotes him: “The philosopher’s stone, says the mysterious adeptest, is Ruach Elohim” [III.3 ¶50]. The note cites Khunrath, Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern., Isag. in fig. [III.3 n35]. He calls the Stone embodied Ruach Elohim, names Salt as its principle and calls it Wisdom [III.3 ¶50]. Atwood uses him in support but admits that such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown [III.3 ¶50].

See also: Adept

References: III.3 n35, III.3 ¶50

Mystery

term

The object of Agrippa’s search. The Rosy Cross fraternity calls it the most ancient knowledge, breathed into nature by God’s Word, and equates it with the Fire of Life and the Wise men’s red gold.

Atwood (ATWOOD) says Agrippa reached his final conviction by “searching and proving the magnitude of the Mystery” [I.1 ¶64].

The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (QUOTED) describes the mystery as the most ancient knowledge, “a knowledge which God Almighty, by his Word, breathed into nature” [III.3 ¶63]. It is given to few, though it lives and moves daily in sight of all [III.3 ¶63]. They equate it with “a miraculous power, the blessed Fire of Life” and with “the transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men” [III.3 ¶63].

Identified with: Fire of life [III.3 ¶63]; transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men [III.3 ¶63]

References: I.1 ¶64, III.3 ¶63

Mystery of regeneration

term

The regenerative mystery, of which, Atwood says, the Reformers kept little more than a traditional faith.

Atwood (ATWOOD) says the Reformers kept little of it, “retaining, indeed, little more of the mystery of regeneration than a traditional faith” [I.1 ¶26].

See also: Regeneration

References: I.1 ¶26

Mystical analysis

term · ultimate alchemical analysis

The one analysis that resolves a pot into gold and gold into an indissoluble water. It agrees with hermetic doctrine in both inner and outer senses, and its final stage yields Light.

Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “For by no other analysis either is a pot resolved into gold, or gold into a water which is indissoluble.” [III.2 n38]. She holds that this analysis agrees with hermetic doctrine in both its internal and external senses, and that its ultimate stage yields Light [III.2 n38].

References: III.2 n38

Mystical death and regeneration

term

A topic Atwood deliberately leaves aside at this point. She says it will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject is made manifest.

Atwood (ATWOOD): “We omit many things here relating to the mystical death and regeneration” [II.3 ¶56]. She says these will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject has been made manifest.

See also: Regeneration

References: II.3 ¶56

Mystical problem of the Trinity

term

The Trinity’s “three in one and one in three”, cited as an analogy for agent, patient and offspring in all created things.

A footnote uses the mystical problem of the Trinity, “three in one and one in three”, as an analogy for the agent, patient and offspring found in all created things [I.3 n30]. The voice is not specified.

References: I.3 n30

Myth of Oedipus

collective voice

Cited in the Appendix as foreshadowing the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother”.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the myth of Oedipus is said to foreshadow the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother” [APP ¶73].

See also: Oedipus

References: APP ¶73

Myths

collective voice

The Myths, cited in the Appendix for showing Vulcan as lame. This is explained as halting motion.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Myths are cited for showing Vulcan as lame, which is explained as halting motion [APP ¶129].

References: APP ¶129

N

N. Barnaud

person · Barnaud

A commentator cited by Atwood for his commentary on an enigmatic epitaph, printed in the Theatrum Chemicum.

Cited as having commented on the epitaph discussed in the text [I.1 ¶24]; the footnote names his commentary in the Theatrum Chemicum, Commentariolum in Enigmaticum quoddam Epitaphium Bononiae studiorum [I.1 n32].

References: I.1 n32, I.1 ¶24

The Name

term

The Name that, Atwood says, we have no business to speak; if it speaks in us, it works its own change.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), insists: “We have no business whatsoever to speak The Name.” [APP ¶88] Her point, as the record gives it, is that it is not for us to utter; if it speaks in us, it works its own change [APP ¶88].

References: APP ¶88

Natal bond

term

The soul’s bond in life, which she must give up, with dread, during the transition.

Atwood speaks of the soul about to “relinquish her natal bond in life” [II.3 ¶37]. The record glosses it as the soul’s bond in life, which she gives up with dread during the transition.

References: II.3 ¶37

Natalius

person

A figure who, the text says, would not teach Agrippa despite his entreaties.

Cited as having refused to teach Agrippa despite his entreaties [IV.1 ¶36].

References: IV.1 ¶36

Natural Alembic

term

That through which the impure Instrument is brought and returned; the wording also suggests the Instrument then itself constitutes it.

Atwood writes of the Instrument that “when finally brought through the natural Alembic, and returned, it constitutes the natural Alembic” [III.1 ¶61]. Two readings are possible. On one, the natural Alembic is the passage through which the impure Instrument goes and returns. On the other, the Instrument itself becomes the natural Alembic. The repeated phrase may be a printing slip, so the text leaves this open.

See also: Alembic

References: III.1 ¶61

Natural fire

term · fire of the natural life

The vital fire of the natural life, which when fermented and opened frees the celestial Life and Light; in Eudoxus, the fire the Stone sympathizes with.

Atwood (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer): the natural fire is the vital fire of the natural life. Fermented by the same life from another, it is opened and “sets free the celestial Life and Light” [APP ¶38].

Eudoxus (quoted): the Stone, an Astral Fire, sympathizes with Natural Fire, and “the igneous spirit of the natural fire is corporified in the substances which are analogous to it” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Stone grows in an ‘Elementary Fire’ geometrically proportioned to it [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not say that Natural Fire and Elementary Fire are the same.

See also: Fire

References: IV.3 ¶16, APP ¶38

Natural Impotency

term

Geber’s term for a natural unfitness for the work, caused by defects of body or of soul.

Atwood reports Geber’s term for a natural incapacity for the work, caused by bodily defects or defects of soul: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3].

References: III.4 ¶3

Natural inbred chemist

term · inbred chemist

In Crollius, the agent that separates each mystery into its own receptacle and frees the medicine from impure outside elements.

Crollius (quoted): “the natural inbred chemist teaches to segregate every mystery into its own reservacle” [III.1 ¶10]. It frees the medicine from impure external elements. The text gives no further definition. The phrase apparently names an inner, natural agent of separation, though what exactly it is stays open.

References: III.1 ¶10

Natural intelligent spirit

term · natural Spirit

Man’s ‘phantasic’ Spirit, the vestibule of Reason, which in man matches the Ether in the universe; it is imperfect and its Light is hidden.

Atwood: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5]. She calls it ‘phantasic’ and the vestibule of Reason [III.1 ¶5]. Earlier chapters have shown “the imperfection of the natural Spirit in his world, the occultation of its Light” [III.1 ¶4].

See also: Spirit

References: III.1 ¶4, III.1 ¶5

Natural life

term

The soul’s ordinary, unregenerate state, where no lasting leader rules and passing motives take control.

Atwood: “the government of the natural life is oligarchical, almost an anarchy” [II.4 ¶38]. In this state no permanent leader rules and passing motives take control.

See also: Life

References: II.4 ¶38

Natural reason

term · natural Intellect

Ordinary reason: needed at the threshold but dull and idle in the work, unable to purify the phantastic Spirit; it is the image of the supernatural reason.

Atwood treats natural reason as necessary but only an aid at the threshold. In the work itself it is dull and inoperative [III.1 ¶20–21]. It cannot purify the phantastic Spirit: “But the natural Intellect cannot do this” [III.1 ¶20]. It is the image of the higher faculty: “these things which the natural reason as an image enacts theoretically, this supernatural reason is said to do as an archetype essentially” [III.1 ¶21].

= iron key: “as it were an iron key, intended to unlock the golden treasury of light within” [III.1 ¶13].

Identified with: iron key [III.1 ¶13]

See also: Reason

References: III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶20, III.1 ¶21

Necessary charges

term

What the avaricious are afraid to ‘interposit’; Atwood glosses this as giving up the life of selfhood and turning the product to a benevolent and truthful end.

In the passage from Geber, on the avaricious: “but are afraid to interposit the necessary charges” [III.4 ¶3]. In Geber’s wording the failure is covetousness of money. Atwood reinterprets the charges in her own voice: “i.e., to abandon the life of selfhood, and return the product to a benevolent and truthful end” [III.4 ¶6]. Her gloss apparently makes the cost moral and inward rather than financial.

References: III.4 ¶3, III.4 ¶6

Nemean Lion

term

A Lion said to be born of ‘her foam’ and identified with what the sentence before describes; the exact referent is unclear.

Atwood: “and this is that Nemean Lion said to be born of her foam” [IV.1 ¶29]. The Lion is identified with what the sentence before describes. It is unclear from the record what that is, and whose foam is meant.

See also: Lion

References: IV.1 ¶29

Neoplatonists

collective voice · Neo-Platonists

Philosophers Atwood cites for a hidden Principle of Universal Science and for teaching principles while keeping silent on the Practice.

Atwood cites them as support for a latent Principle of Universal Science that can be known under certain conditions [II.1 ¶39]. They spoke of Principles and of how the mind proceeds while avoiding the Practice; their images stir inward faith [III.2 ¶46].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she qualifies this. They set out principles scientifically and went through long-perfected Initiation, but did not declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi. They kept to psychological investigation, and Behmen surpassed them here [APP ¶122].

References: II.1 ¶39, III.2 ¶46, APP ¶122

Nether confines

term

A region reached after the first barriers, where one must choose Light; the text does not explain it further.

Atwood mentions “approaching to the Nether confines, to make choice of Light” [IV.1 ¶25]. The region comes after the first barriers. The text does not explain it further.

References: IV.1 ¶25

New birth

term

The moment when extremes are present and Light springs forth out of the abyssal Darkness.

Atwood: “extremes are said to be present at the new birth, when Light springs forth to manifestation out of the abyssal Darkness” [III.2 ¶56].

References: III.2 ¶56

New generation

term

The new beginning that the former life, all but destroyed, draws to itself through a new seed.

Atwood describes the former life, nearly annihilated, “which at length, in its extreme exigence, draws a new seed to begin a New Generation” [III.2 ¶28]. The new start comes out of the extreme destruction of the old.

See also: Generation

References: III.2 ¶28

New Imponderable

term

Atwood’s name for the agent of mesmerism, which she identifies with the Common Soul.

Atwood uses this name for the agent at work in mesmerism and identifies it with the Common Soul: “our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul” [II.2 ¶18].

Identified with: Common soul [II.2 ¶18]

See also: Imponderable

References: II.2 ¶18

New life

term

What arises once the evil of Original Sin is overcome by subtle stratagems; its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone.

Atwood: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems, the New Life thence arises” [III.1 ¶66]. Its quintessential virtue is the Corner Stone [III.1 ¶66].

See also: Life

References: III.1 ¶66

New Light

treatise · New Light of Alchemy

The New Light of Alchemy, cited as one of the sources of a summary passage.

Cited as one of the sources of the summary passage [I.2 ¶33]; the footnote names it as the New Light of Alchemy [I.2 n36].

References: I.2 n36, I.2 ¶33

New man

term

In Boehme, the regenerate inner seer who looks into the astral birth, as opposed to the external man.

Boehme (quoted): “for the new man speculates into the midst of the astral birth or geniture” [III.2 ¶16]. The new man is contrasted with the external man, so the context suggests the regenerate inner seer.

References: III.2 ¶16

Newton

person · Sir Isaac Newton

Cited as recognizing the possibility and not condemning the tradition; also used once for comparison.

Atwood cites Sir Isaac Newton as support: he recognized the possibility and did not condemn the tradition [I.1 ¶82]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named for comparison only [APP ¶122].

References: I.1 ¶82, APP ¶122

Night of Hippocrates and Day of Orpheus

term · Night of Hippocrates, Day of Orpheus

Paired images: the radical destruction leads back to the Night of Hippocrates and on into the Day of Orpheus.

Atwood calls the radical destruction “the way of the recedure to the Night of Hippocrates, leading thenceforth into the Day of Orpheus” [III.2 ¶28]. The text does not explain the two terms further. The context suggests a return to darkness that is followed by light.

See also: Orpheus

References: III.2 ¶28

Night of matter

term

The state of the mind beholding Matter: it receives the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely, feeling without understanding.

The passage opens: “When therefore the mind is in the Night of Matter” [III.2 ¶55]. In this state the mind suffers the reception of the formless and perceives obscurely, vastly, infinitely; it feels without understanding [III.2 ¶55]. The voice is unclear: the record does not show whether this is Atwood or a cited authority.

See also: Matter

References: III.2 ¶55

No less experienced adept

collective voice

An unnamed adept cited for the view that Venus’s light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture.

Atwood cites this unnamed adept in support. Venus’s light alone is imperfect without the masculine tincture, though at that stage “the artist is rejoiced, and thinks perhaps his work is finished” [I.3 n49].

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: I.3 n49

No less subtle than experienced adept

collective voice

An unnamed adept cited for water turning into air and back, and for the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver.

Atwood cites this unnamed adept to illustrate water turning into air and back again: “the central heat may change the water into air” [I.3 n31]. The adept also gives the image of the old man swallowing gold or silver [I.3 n31].

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: I.3 n31

Noah

person

Used as an illustration of the principle kept safe in the water through destruction, which then renews all things.

Atwood uses Noah to illustrate the principle preserved in the water through destruction, which renews all things: “as Noah in the Ark” [III.3 ¶71].

References: III.3 ¶71

Noble Master

collective voice — of the poem’s narrator

In a quoted poem, the narrator’s master, whose deathbed oath is the narrator’s reason for veiling the secrets.

Inside the quoted poem, the narrator gives his master’s deathbed charge as his reason for veiling: “At his death he made me sweare hym to, That all the secrets I schould never undoe” [III.1 ¶65].

See also: Masters

References: III.1 ¶65

Nobles of the rose

term

Coins struck from Lully’s gold, about 10 ducats each, of the finest metal, with a marginal inscription said to mark their miraculous origin.

Atwood reports that from Lully’s gold “a coinage of the gold was struck in pieces weighing about 10 ducats each, called Nobles of the Rose” [I.1 ¶47]. They were of the finest metal, and their marginal inscription was said to denote their miraculous origin [I.1 ¶47].

References: I.1 ¶47

Non-being

term · primitive non-Being

In Parmenides, what neither mind nor speech can reach; in Hegel, the empty abstraction of pure Being; for the Kabalists, the primitive non-Being, the Cause of causes.

The text quotes three distinct views.

Parmenides: Non-being is what neither mind can see nor speech reveal, “since, as of Being void, ‘Tis not the object of the mental eye” [III.2 ¶14].

Hegel: “this pure Being is no other than a pure abstraction, it is a term absolutely negative, which may also in its immediate conception be called non-Being” [III.2 ¶30]. So for Hegel pure Being = non-Being.

The Kabalists (the Rabbi): non-Being is not nothing in the ordinary sense. It is not produced “from nothing in the common-sense acceptation of that word; for Being could never be produced from non-Being (deficiently understood), but by non-Being they mean” [III.2 ¶32] something else. It cannot be conceived as cause or essence, “but yet is in fact the Cause of causes: it is that which we call the primitive non-Being; because it is anterior to the universe” [III.2 ¶32]. It is not corporeity: “by it we do not signify corporeity either, but that Principle or Wisdom on which it is founded” [III.2 ¶32]. It holds no distinction. Identities asserted: = Cause of causes; = Principle or Wisdom [III.2 ¶32].

The readings differ: Parmenides calls it unknowable, Hegel calls it an empty abstraction, and the Kabalists call it the Cause of causes and the Principle or Wisdom.

Identified with: nothing (in the Kabalists’ sense) [III.2 ¶32]; pure Being (Hegel) [III.2 ¶30]; Cause of causes [III.2 ¶32]; Principle or Wisdom [III.2 ¶32]

References: III.2 ¶14, III.2 ¶30, III.2 ¶32

Nonentity

term

The initial nothingness of all things, which Atwood says Parmenides and others were cited to prove, and at which the soul does not stop but passes into true Being.

Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “Parmenides and the rest cited to prove the same initial nonentity of all” [III.2 ¶54]. The soul, she continues, “not enduring any longer to stop at nonentity, becomes into true Being” [III.2 ¶55]. Nonentity is thus apparently a stage the soul passes through, not its goal.

References: III.2 ¶54, III.2 ¶55

Norton

person

Author of the verse Ordinal of Alchemy, an authority Atwood cites throughout and endorses on secrecy, the few chosen, patience, purity, learning and the requisites of the work.

Norton’s Ordinal is cited throughout the book, almost always in support of Atwood’s own positions.

Secrecy and the few chosen. From the Proheme Atwood takes the point that masters wrote under coverts, while “Yet Anaxagoras wrote plainest of them all In his boke of Conversions Naturall;” [I.1 ¶14, I.1 n21]. He supports the view that few are chosen and covetousness disqualifies: “Quod inter mille millia, vix subt tres electi” [I.1 ¶40, I.1 n47]; “Scarcely seven men maie this science finde.” — the science being granted to few faithful, lowly men and withheld from proud clerks who then call it fable [III.4 ¶14, III.4 n9]. Secrecy is a duty because “If one evil man had hereof his will, All Christian peace he might easily spill;” [I.3 n15]; the art is a holy gift taught orally under oath to the proven [III.4 ¶9–10, III.4 n8]: “Wherefore old Fathers, conveniently, Called this science Holy Alkimy”.

Name and profundity. “For it is most profounde philosophye This subtill science of holy Alkimy” [I.1 ¶49, I.1 n59; cf. I.2 ¶51]. In chap. 1 he also illustrates the universal craze for alchemy, the ruin of hasty seekers and the damage done by a monk’s book of false receipts [I.1 ¶49–54].

Order of the work. He supports white-before-red: “Till the white medicine be fully wrought;” [I.1 ¶59–64, I.1 n64]; Atwood praises the Ordinal as candid and orderly except for the concealed Subject Matter. He notes that the parts are divided among authors: “Every and each of them disclosed but a parte” [I.1 ¶83, I.1 n107]. Verse on the never-wasting Water cites Democrit and Hermes [III.3 ¶73–74, III.3 n48].

Conditions and practice. Only those of stable wit finish [III.4 ¶16–17]; the Work begins only after purity: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49, IV.1 n42]; “Greate neede hath he to be a clerke” [IV.2 ¶5, IV.2 n6]. He is the main authority on vessels, ministers, furnaces and places: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶30–41]; Atwood calls his account of the Preparatory Practice naive and “without much envy”. He also supports astrological election and the Elixir as a thing of Second Intention [IV.2 ¶34, IV.2 n23], and advice on servants [IV.1 ¶9].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for the name Holy Alchemy [APP ¶29] and against over-haste: “Haste is the Devil’s part” [APP ¶103].

See also: Authorities in Norton (Philosophers, Astrologers, Auctors), Norton’s Master (my good Master)

References: I.1 n107, I.1 n21, I.1 n47, I.1 n59, I.1 n60, I.1 n64, I.1 ¶14, I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶40, I.1 ¶49, I.1 ¶52, I.1 ¶54, I.1 ¶59, I.1 ¶60, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶83, I.2 n51, I.2 ¶51, I.3 n15, I.3 n2, I.3 n4, I.3 n6, III.1 n10, III.3 n41, III.3 n42, III.3 n48, III.3 ¶73, III.3 ¶74, III.4 n12, III.4 n28, III.4 n31, III.4 n33, III.4 n34, III.4 n8, III.4 n9, III.4 ¶1, III.4 ¶10, III.4 ¶14, III.4 ¶15, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶17, III.4 ¶30, III.4 ¶31, III.4 ¶36, III.4 ¶37, III.4 ¶39, III.4 ¶40, III.4 ¶41, III.4 ¶9, IV.1 n3, IV.1 n42, IV.1 ¶49, IV.1 ¶9, IV.2 n23, IV.2 n6, IV.2 ¶13, IV.2 ¶34, IV.2 ¶4, IV.2 ¶5, IV.3 n3, APP ¶103, APP ¶29

Norton’s Master

collective voice — my good Master

Norton’s master, quoted inside Norton’s verse as revealing the secret that the vessel is glass.

Inside Norton’s verse, his “good Master” is quoted (QUOTED) as revealing that the vessel is glass: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset” [III.4 ¶31]. Our translation, which the book does not give: If God had not given us the vessel, he would have given nothing.

Norton’s Ordinal

treatise · Ordinal

Norton’s verse treatise, cited in IV.1 as the main verse authority on the conduct and hazards of the Gross Work.

Cited from chap. 4 (as Ordinal or Norton’s Ordinal) as Atwood’s main verse authority on balanced, unhasty feeding of the work, its cost, patience and simmering, the three-year Gross Work, and the Gross Work as a foul, perilous handicraft needing experience, uniformity and able ministers [IV.1 ¶12–28, IV.1 n14, n17, n22, n23]: “Excess of one half quarter of an hour May destroy all”. See also Norton.

Nothing

term

In Atwood’s usage, that which is before all things, in which the Eternal Will arises and into which Wisdom returns; knowing Nothing means having the All.

Atwood (ATWOOD) writes of “bringing back into the Nothing which is before all things” as Wisdom’s end; the Eternal Will arises in it [APP ¶90, Appendix, later layer]. Earlier she says: “For he who in such wise knows Nothing — no one apostate particular — has the All” [IV.4 ¶27], so knowing Nothing apparently means holding to no separated particular.

term

“Night of body or corporeal sleep”: a name Atwood reports for the Terrestrial Paradise, where souls are dead to this life and more alive in that.

Atwood (ATWOOD) identifies it with the Terrestrial Paradise or Elysium: “the true Terrestrial Paradise, which some have called nox corporis, the night of body or corporeal sleep” [II.4 ¶9]. The text glosses the Latin itself. Souls there are dead to this life and more alive in that [II.4 ¶9].

term · number, weight, and measure

term · Numerical numbers

Outwardly mere ‘bark’ of things; theosophically, the order in which the Divine Law develops in creative operation, known through theurgic art.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]; understood theosophically, numbers are the order of development of the Divine Law in creative operation, known through theurgic art [APP ¶107].

Nuysement

person

Author cited from Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi and Tractatus de Vero Sale on the mineral spirit, gold’s magnetical virtue, and innate heat.

Introduced as “another” authority on the power of the pure mineral spirit, which “it will work such an alteration in things of like nature with themselves, that they shall equalize the Philosophical Elixir” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n49] (Sal, Lumen et Spiritus Mundi, ed. Combachius). The Tractatus de Vero Sale is footnoted as the source for gold’s magnetical virtue and the names Microcosmic Sun and Stone of Fire [II.1 n21]. From the Latin of Combachius Atwood takes that the effective heat is innate, a terrestrial sun, not external: “sed potius solis terrestris innatus calor” [IV.1 ¶43, IV.1 n39]. She cites him in support throughout.

The state of the mental eye when all thought is submerged: a crass, obscure vacuity, called the Original of Life, related to true Being as night to day.

Atwood (ATWOOD) describes the objectless mental eye, all thought submerged, becoming one with darkness as the eye does: “a crass, obscure vacuity” [III.2 ¶54]. She identifies it: “that obscure oblivion which is the Original of Life” [III.2 ¶54]. It stands to true Being as night to day [III.2 ¶54].

Identified with: Original of Life [III.2 ¶54]

person

person · Borrichius, Borricius

treatise

person · Oldranus

Authority cited (lib. Concilio, Quest 74) as having praised the Hermetic Art and Arnold’s wisdom.

Olympic fire

term

In Khunrath’s words, a fire with which the internal and external fire must be in sympathy; the text does not define it.

Voice: QUOTED: Khunrath. The internal and external fire must be “in harmonious sympathy with the Olympic Fire” [III.3 ¶9]. The passage does not say what the Olympic Fire is.

Olympiodorus

person

‘The Egyptian Olympiodorus’, cited in support on phantasy as an impediment, allegorical readings of Elysium and Tartarus, and reason’s rule over the soul.

Atwood cites him approvingly. Phantasy opposes divine enthusiasm, and perceiving Universals proves the soul can act without it: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12, II.2 n13]. From his Commentary on the Gorgias she takes an allegorical reading of Hercules’ last labour and of the Islands of the Blessed / Elysian Fields as a state above corporeal life: “islands stand out of, as being higher than the sea” [II.4 ¶3]. He also supports an ethical/physical reading of Tartarus: “souls, in which reason does not preside as a charioteer, are changed according to the subject temperament of the body” [III.2 ¶9, III.2 n11]. He is listed among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].

References: I.1 n34, I.1 ¶27, II.2 n13, II.2 ¶12, II.4 ¶3, III.2 n11, III.2 ¶9

One

term · Unit

The philosophers’ absolute unit, Fountain of all being, implied in every multitude and each part; reported from Xenophanes as God.

Atwood (ATWOOD) says “the One of these philosophers is the Fountain of all being” [III.2 ¶45], implied in every multitude and each part; “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45]. She also reports Xenophanes, via Aristotle (QUOTED), identifying it with God: “looking to the whole heaven, he says, the One is God” [III.2 ¶40].

Identified with: Fountain of all being [III.2 ¶45]; God (according to Xenophanes, as reported by Aristotle) [III.2 ¶40]

See also: Unit

References: III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶45

One blessed Stone

term

In Agrippa’s words, the single thing besides which there is no other, the subject of the most holy stone, of which to speak rashly is sacrilege.

Voice: QUOTED: Cornelius Agrippa. He speaks “of the one blessed stone alone, besides which there is no other thing, the subject of the most holy stone of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶64], treating rash speech of it as sacrilege [I.1 ¶64].

Identified with: subject of the most holy stone of the philosophers [I.1 ¶64]

See also: Stone

References: I.1 ¶64

One element

term

The ancient theory of a single vitalizing principle in air and all things, which Atwood says moderns deride because it escapes their analyses.

Atwood (ATWOOD) notes that “the ancient theory of the One Element has been very much derided” [I.2 ¶14], because the single vitalizing principle in air and all things escapes modern analyses [I.2 ¶14]; her tone implies she does not share the derision.

See also: Elements

References: I.2 ¶14

One only matter

term

The single matter of all things in the Beginning, which the process imitates as all diversities come from and return to the One.

Atwood (ATWOOD): “as in the Beginning there was said to be one only matter of all things” [III.3 ¶29], so in the process all diversities proceed from and return to the One [III.3 ¶29].

See also: Matter

References: III.3 ¶29

One principle

term

In Proclus’ words, the principle found only by becoming assimilated to it, the most united in nature, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent.

Voice: QUOTED: Proclus. “if any one wish to discover the One Principle he must become first assimilated to it” [III.2 ¶50]. It is the most united in nature, through which it is Deity, uniting the universe in sympathetic consent [III.2 ¶50].

See also: Principles

References: III.2 ¶50

One thing

term · One only Thing, one things

The single subject from which, after the Smaragdine (Emerald) Table, all things proceed by adaptation; Atwood identifies it with the Identity made in regeneration and, later, with our psychical essence.

The term comes from the Hermetic Table, cited as the Smaragdine, Emerald or Smagardine Table (also as the Smaragdine Tablet of Thrice Great Hermes): it speaks of “for performing the miracles of the One Thing whence all the rest proceed by adaptation” [III.1 ¶41; cf. I.1 ¶9, I.2 ¶48]. The Table as quoted makes the Sun its father, the Moon its mother, the Wind its carrier and the Earth its nurse, and says “This is the father of all perfection and consummation of the whole world.” [IV.2 ¶44]. A quoted master, whom Atwood follows, says “the whole matter I know to be One only Thing” [III.1 ¶21]; in that passage folly, phantasy, passion and Reason are its modes of being.

Boehme, as quoted, says the first something was “a certain cloud or darkness, which was condensed into water”, and that “this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained” [III.2 ¶15]. Atwood takes this up herself: “God of nothing created something which was made that one thing in which are all”, and she adds that “this One Thing appears to be nothing less or more than that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16]. For the creature it is the first divine manifestation out of the abyss.

Atwood says that “The same tradition of the manifold powers and preservation of the One Thing runs in symbol” through the Gentile Mythology [III.3 ¶69]. The verses she quotes make it the only key to the sealed Art (“Which one thing only can unlocke; This one things learn to know,” [III.3 ¶68]) and “A mass confused and darkly clad, That in itself, all Nature had”, called “The first Material Mother of all.” [III.3 ¶76]. The verses call it indestructible, easy to find and hard to get.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says plainly: “The One Thing; it is our psychical essence; our nervous system.” [APP ¶176].

Identified with: psychical essence; nervous system [APP ¶176]; Water [III.2 ¶15]; Identity [III.2 ¶16]; first Material Mother of all [III.3 ¶76]

See also: The Thing

References: I.1 ¶9, I.2 ¶48, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶41, III.2 ¶15, III.2 ¶16, III.3 ¶68, III.3 ¶69, III.3 ¶76, IV.2 ¶44, APP ¶176

Ontological Wisdom

term

Atwood’s name for philosophy in the true sense: the knowledge of true Being that was the object of initiation.

Atwood equates the two terms directly: “philosophy, that is to say, Ontological Wisdom” [II.2 ¶4]. She calls it “the Wisdom of true Being” [II.2 ¶5]. In that passage it is the knowledge that initiation aimed at.

Identified with: Philosophy [II.2 ¶4]

See also: Wisdom

References: II.2 ¶4, II.2 ¶5

Operator

term

In Agrippa’s phrase, the worker of all wonderful effects, which is located within us.

Atwood quotes Agrippa: “in us is the Operator of all wonderful effects” [II.1 ¶26]. The Operator is inward, not an outside agent.

References: II.1 ¶26

Opposive principle

term

A principle that, once freed, draws the mind’s other faculties into its vortex, revels with them until satiated, and is then more easily ensnared.

Atwood says the faculties are “drawn away afterwards into the vortex of the Opposive Principle, rapidly attracting them when it is freed” [III.1 ¶66]. It revels with them, becomes satiated and is then more easily ensnared. She illustrates this with Orpheus’s tale of Saturn bound in fetters while drunk [III.1 ¶66]. The text does not say outright that this is the same as the ‘rebellious Principle’ of III.1 ¶64.

See also: Principles

References: III.1 ¶66

Oracle of Apollo

collective voice — from Eusebius · Oracle of Apollo, from Eusebius

An oracle of Apollo, taken from Eusebius, used as the epigraph of II.2: the path to Deity is hard, and the Egyptians and other ancient peoples disclosed it.

Atwood uses it as an epigraph: “The Path by which to Deity we climb Is arduous, rough, ineffable, sublime;” [II.2 ¶1]. The verses go on to say the path was disclosed by the Egyptians and other ancient peoples.

See also: Apollo

References: II.2 ¶1

Oracle to Amelius

collective voice

The oracle given to Amelius, which Atwood quotes to show the place where the soul of Plotinus dwells.

Atwood quotes the oracle given to Amelius about where the soul of Great Plotinus is. It describes the place in Latin: “Ubi Amicitia est, ubi cupido visu mollis” [II.4 ¶11, II.4 ¶12] (ours: where Friendship is, where desire is gentle to behold).

References: II.4 ¶11, II.4 ¶12

Oracles

collective voice · the oracle, Oracula Chaldaica, Zoroastri Oracula

Oracular sayings that Atwood cites often, including the Oracula Chaldaica and Zoroastri Oracula, to support her teaching on the soul’s ascent, the formless Fire, purification and piety.

Atwood treats the oracles as supporting authorities. One urges the soul to turn upward, away from the image-loving Hades: “Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards” [II.3 ¶26, II.3 n27; footnote cites Zoroastri Oracula, Anima, Corpus, Homo]. Another, from the Oracula Chaldaica, names the true vision as the formless Fire: “When thou seest a Fire without Form, Shining flashingly through the depths of the World, Hear the voice of Fire” [II.3 ¶46–47, II.3 n50]. It is cited again for the Fire as the derivation and dispenser of Fire [II.3 ¶52–53].

The Oracle also gives the name ‘Pratum’ (meadow) to the meadow of Divine Ideas [II.4 ¶9]. It warns about the infinite End of the principle: “Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth” [III.2 ¶15]. The oracles are said to teach that the impure perceptive medium needs ‘alternation and solution’ before it can tell good from evil [II.2 ¶15]. On piety, Atwood writes: “Thus piety is available for all things, as the oracles declare” [III.4 ¶22]. In that passage prayer is piety’s chief exercise and is profitable for great undertakings. With Julian, the oracles support the claim that “through purifying ceremonies bodies become worthy of receiving divine assistance and health” [IV.3 ¶30–31, IV.3 n10]. An oracle is also reported to have called Socrates the wisest of mankind because of that Nothing [IV.4 ¶27].

See also: Divine Oracle, Truth-telling Oracle, Zoroastri Oracula

References: II.2 ¶15, II.3 n27, II.3 n50, II.3 ¶26, II.3 ¶46, II.3 ¶47, II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶53, II.4 ¶9, III.2 ¶15, III.4 ¶22, IV.3 n10, IV.3 ¶30, IV.3 ¶31, IV.4 ¶27

Orgies

term

In Clemens Alexandrinus’s words as Atwood quotes them, the rites or celebrations of the Mysteries.

Atwood quotes Clemens Alexandrinus: “These are the orgies of the Mysteries” [II.2 ¶5]. The word means the Mysteries’ rites.

References: II.2 ¶5

Orient animal

term · Animal de Oriente

The adepts’ figure of an animal that must be skinned by the Hand; in the Table Talk, Atwood explains it as the opposite will clothed in Light.

In III.1, Atwood reports the adepts’ saying: “For the Orient Animal must be stripped of his skin, not with arrows or clubs, but with the Hand, as Adepts say” [III.1 ¶64]. The skin is a lion’s skin. The Latin in that passage adds that the animal then enters the great salt sea and comes out again with beauty. The figure is not explained there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood herself gives the meaning: “The ‘orient animal’ means the animal (that is, the opposite) will which is clothed in Light”. She also calls it “the third which rises in opposition to the first” [APP ¶21].

References: III.1 ¶64, APP ¶21

Oriental quicksilvers

term · two oriental quicksilvers

A Hermetic expression quoted from Hermes: two oriental quicksilvers that hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies.

Hermes, as quoted, speaks of “the fat of the two oriental quicksilvers, which hunt the sulphurs and contain the bodies” [I.3 ¶20]. The text does not explain the expression further.

References: I.3 ¶20

Origen

person

Named in the story about Ammonius.

Origen is named only in the story of Ammonius [III.2 ¶64].

References: III.2 ¶64, III.3 n39

Original light

term

Nature’s Original Light: the infallible touchstone by which the capable can tell what is rationally possible.

Atwood speaks of Nature’s “infallible touchstone of her Original Light” [IV.3 ¶54]. The able use it to discern what is rationally possible.

See also: Light

References: IV.3 ¶54

Original matter

term

The state to which bodies must be reduced, by introversion of the generated life, before they can be truly manifested and made permanent.

Atwood names as a condition of true manifestation and permanence “the reduction of bodies to their original matter, by introversion of the generated life” [I.2 ¶49].

See also: Matter

References: I.2 ¶49

Original sin

term

An evil that is overcome by subtle stratagems, after which the New Life arises.

Atwood writes: “The evil of the Original Sin being overcome by so many subtle stratagems” [III.1 ¶66], after which the New Life arises. The context suggests that the stratagems are those just described for ensnaring the Opposive Principle.

References: III.1 ¶66

Original virtue

term

The real power that the types signify; without understanding it and cooperating with it, the types only mimic efficacy.

Atwood says the types need “a true understanding and cooperation of that original virtue, apart from which they do but mimic an efficacy” [I.1 ¶26].

See also: Virtue

References: I.1 ¶26

Orpheus

person

An authority whom Atwood cites often for mythic illustrations that she reads hermetically: Pan, the Cave of Mercury, Saturn’s fettering, and the Day that follows the Night.

Atwood quotes Orpheus to illustrate Pan as the whole of nature: “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis” [I.2 ¶28, I.2 n26, Orpheus Hymni] (ours: strong, subtle Pan, whole and universal). From the Argonautics she cites prudent entry into the Cave of Mercury (“Mercurii ingedier spuluncam” [III.1 ¶17–18]), which she interprets hermetically. In the same vein, Orpheus is said to have recommended taking the Hermetic material in the cave of Mercury [III.2 ¶7].

She draws on Orpheus for the tale of Saturn, bound in fetters while drunk by his son through a stratagem: “and by the advice of the goddess, too, according to Orpheus, the subtle stratagem was contrived” [III.1 ¶66]. It illustrates how the satiated Opposive Principle is ensnared. She also cites ‘the Day of Orpheus’, which follows the Night [III.2 ¶28].

See also: Heroes of the ordeal (Cadmus, Deucalion, Osiris, Bacchus, Hercules, Orpheus)

References: I.2 n26, I.2 ¶28, III.1 ¶17, III.1 ¶18, III.1 ¶66, III.2 ¶28, III.2 ¶7

Orpheus Eucharisticus

treatise

An emblem work (Emblema LVI) that Atwood cites to support the point that the corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.

Atwood cites the Apodosis of Emblema LVI: “Cui scelerum viru mens moribunda tumet” [III.3 ¶11–12, III.3 n5] (ours: whose dying mind swells with the poison of crimes). It supports her point that a corrupt mind cannot draw the healthful waters.

References: III.3 n5, III.3 ¶11, III.3 ¶12

Orphic Fragment

treatise

An Orphic fragment that Atwood cites on purity and contemplation of the One, while qualifying its claim that He is never seen by mortal eyes.

The fragment opens: “I open a secret to the Initiated, but let the doors be shut.” [II.4 ¶40, II.4 n28]. Atwood uses it in support of purity and contemplation of the One. She qualifies its statement that He is ‘never seen by mortal eyes’: the Initiated, she says, did behold Him.

See also: Orphic oracles

References: II.4 n28, II.4 ¶40

Orphic oracles

collective voice

Cited for the teaching that Pan, of necessity, evolves every property and form out of his central will.

Atwood cites the Orphic oracles in support of the teaching that Pan evolves every property and form out of his central will, of necessity [I.2 ¶36].

See also: Oracles, Orphic Fragment, Orphic poet

References: I.2 ¶36

Orphic poet

collective voice

An unnamed Orphic poet, quoted in Latin, on what blessed Eurotas heard while Phoebus (Apollo) meditated.

Atwood quotes the Orphic poet’s verse on Apollo contemplating such rivers: “Omnia quae Phoebo quondam meditante beatus Audiit Eurotas” [II.4 ¶13–14] (ours: all that blessed Eurotas once heard while Phoebus meditated).

See also: Orphic oracles, Poets

References: II.4 ¶13, II.4 ¶14

Orphic verse

collective voice

An Orphic verse cited for the radiant return of Bacchus.

The verse shows Bacchus returning “triumphant, and appearing in splendour to mortals” [II.4 ¶54].

References: II.4 ¶54

Orus

term

The offspring that the Matter brings forth by the Fire of nature, lawfully conceived; Atwood calls it the Philosophic Sun.

Atwood says what the Matter brings forth by the lawfully conceived Fire of nature “is Orus, the Philosophic Sun” [III.3 ¶62].

Identified with: Philosophic Sun [III.3 ¶62]

References: III.3 ¶62

Osiris

term

In the fable, the brother whom Typhon kills and scatters; applied to the work, Atwood identifies him with the Divine Light, the foreign body of Light.

In the fable, Typhon kills Osiris and scatters his body. Applying it to the work, Atwood identifies Osiris with “the foreign body of Light, which is Osiris” [III.1 ¶56] and “Osiris, i.e., the Divine Light” [III.1 ¶63]. The Efficient reduces this Light to vapor, and it suffers restraint as it passes through the voluntary axle [III.1 ¶56–63].

Identified with: foreign body of Light [III.1 ¶56]; Divine light [III.1 ¶63]

See also: Dead and revived god (Cadmillus, Atys, Adonis, Osiris), Fable of Isis and Osiris

References: III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶63

Ostanes

person

A Persian sage who, as Atwood reports from Pliny, first brought the Persian spirit into Greece.

Citing Pliny, Atwood names Ostanes as the Persian sage who first brought the Persian spirit into Greece [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n13].

References: I.1 n13, I.1 ¶12

Our earth

term

In Sendivogius’s words, the source of the water and the salt-nitre, holding a river of living water.

Sendivogius, as quoted, speaks of “Our Earth in which there is a river of living water” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is the source of the water and the salt-nitre. The text does not define it further.

See also: Earth

References: IV.3 ¶21

Our old man

term

Cosmopolite’s allegorical name for the Mercury, as reported by Eudoxus; apt because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals.

Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). He explains that Cosmopolite’s allegory — “give our old man gold and silver to swallow” — names the Mercury: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]. The name fits, he says, because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals [IV.3 ¶10].

Identified with: Mercury [IV.3 ¶10]

References: IV.3 ¶10

Our paste

term · philosophical paste, paste

Eudoxus’ name for the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, with the Spirit uniting them, compounded in proportions learned from bread-making.

Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). The paste is the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, the Spirit uniting them; it is composed of several matters whose proportions are learned from the analogy of bread-making — “the matters which compose our philosophical paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. Once fermented, all the philosophic confection becomes itself a leaven [IV.3 ¶14].

References: IV.3 ¶14

Ours

term — living gold and silver

Sendivogius’ term for the philosophers’ own gold and silver, called living, as opposed to common gold and silver, called dead.

Voice: Sendivogius (quoted). The philosophers’ own gold and silver are called living, against common gold and silver, called dead: “take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21]. The text does not positively define them here.

References: IV.3 ¶21

Ovid

person · Ovidii

Poet whom Atwood calls an initiated poet and quotes from the Fasti and Metamorphoses on Chaos, the Aether, man’s origin and the steep first way.

Atwood presents him as an initiated poet, inspired, “as he declares, by that same universal deity of the two-faced Janus” [III.3 ¶44]. From the Fasti she quotes “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” — Chaos as the primeval thing, opening the cosmogony [III.3 ¶45, III.3 n30]. From the Metamorphoses: “Ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo”, illustrating man made from divine seed or from earth holding seeds of heaven [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶47, III.3 n31]; “Haec super imposuit liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera”, placing the dreg-free Aether above the rest and introducing the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶37, III.2 n33]; and “Ardua prima via est”, the steepness of the first way [IV.1 ¶8, IV.1 n11]. (Renderings of the Latin are readers’ own, not the book’s.) Elsewhere he is named with Virgil, Horace and Vitruvius among Augustan men accused of sorcery, illustrating Rome’s limited achievement [I.1 ¶18].

References: I.1 ¶18, III.2 n33, III.2 ¶37, III.3 n30, III.3 n31, III.3 ¶44, III.3 ¶45, III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶47, IV.1 n11, IV.1 ¶8

P

Palingenius

person — Manzoli · Manzoli

A poet whose verse, Atwood says, divulges the artificial method; she says his name means ‘one regenerated’. His Zodiacus Vitae is cited on the Ethereal Stone.

Atwood cites Manzoli, called Palingenius, in support. She says his verse divulges the artificial method, quoting “Take this Arcadian slippery lad that’s apt to fly.” [III.1 ¶26]. She also says the name Palingenius means one regenerated [III.1 ¶27]. From the Zodiacus Vitae she cites the art of fashioning the Ethereal Stone: “Invenere artem, qua non ars dignior ulla est, Fingendi Lepidem Aetherium” [IV.3 ¶54; IV.3 n25]. In the readers’ account, this art is found only after long trial and cost, is closed to the profane and is granted to few [IV.3 ¶54–¶55].

References: III.1 ¶26, III.1 ¶27, IV.3 n25, IV.3 ¶54, IV.3 ¶55

Pan

term · Alchemical Pan, Pana

The one universal Nature: in the Orphic hymn the whole that is all elements; for Atwood the Alchemical Pan, one in himself and multitudinous in offspring.

In the Orphic hymn Atwood quotes, Pan is “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis; Et totus ignis, aura, terra, sive aqua,” — the beginning and end of all [I.2 ¶28]. Atwood then turns to “the most Ancient Nature”, speaking of it as he: “Yet not in his elementary immanifest diffusion let us invoke the most Ancient Nature”, but as the Hermetic masters found it [I.2 ¶29]. In her own voice the subject is a single being with manifold offspring: “so is it said to be with the Alchemical Pan, who, being but one himself, is in his offspring multitudinous” [I.2 ¶34]; he contains Proteus and evolves all forms from his central will [I.2 ¶34].

References: I.2 ¶28, I.2 ¶29, I.2 ¶34

Panacea

term

What the purged, pure life flows forth as, in a declaration Atwood reports.

In an unattributed declaration (“as is declared”), the purged pure life flows forth as “a pure panacea from the god of Light” [III.1 ¶10].

References: III.1 ¶10

Pancirollus

person

Writer Atwood cites as describing several perpetual lamps.

Cited as describing several perpetual lamps [I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶20].

References: I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶20

Paphia

term

A figure in Democritus’ image who appears golden under the fire and is then called such a Venus.

Voice: Democritus (quoted). In his image Paphia, under the fire, appears golden, and is then identified with Venus: “Perchance, it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus” [I.3 n53].

Identified with: Venus [I.3 n53]

References: I.3 n53

Paracelsians

collective voice · Paracelsian Alchemists

A group named in a chapter title, cited for the view that the true medicine and fire of life are bound in man.

Named in the chapter title. Atwood cites them in support of the view that the medicine and fire of life (called Antimony) are in man and are freed by purgation: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶1, III.1 ¶10].

References: III.1 ¶1, III.1 ¶10

Paracelsus

person · Theophrastus Paracelsus, Paracelsi

Authority Atwood cites often, chiefly on Separation as the Art’s primary object and on the tincture, while criticizing his deliberately misleading writings.

Atwood calls him “our doctor” and draws on him chiefly for Separation. From the addresses To the Athenians: “The greatest miracle of all in philosophy is separation”, with the true element as the spirit of life and First Matter of the elements [I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶26, I.2 n21, I.2 n24]; and “Separation is the greatest miracle in philosophy”, the Art’s primary object, with free will as friend or foe and the sequestatrix [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n20]. In the Signatura Rerum he describes the tincture’s astral fire, signs, and transmuting and medicinal power: “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n99]. He supports whiteness as the simple ground of diversity whereon to recreate: “Omnia in Dei manu alba sunt; is eas tingit ut vult” [III.2 ¶5]; and he is said to agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. With Van Helmont he corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea — “by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit” — though Atwood qualifies this as only a secondary witness [III.3 n27].

She also criticizes him for deliberately misleading writings, names his best works (the three Addresses to the Athenians, Aurora) and discusses his death [I.1 ¶64]. Cited with his Libro de Vita longa, he is compared to Avicenna’s ill-directed genius and appears to credit Artephius’s tale [I.1 ¶35, I.1 ¶36, I.1 n41]. His De Natura Rerum was published with French’s New Light, 1650 [I.1 ¶71]. He is mentioned as calling Crollius a natural divine, with “salem Paracelsi” in the Latin [II.1 ¶14, II.1 ¶21].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “the Archaeus of Paracelsus” is set in apposition to the solar plexus, workshop of the Celestial life [APP ¶32]; he is the source of “evestrum” for the soul’s destiny-dream [APP ¶57] and of the name Evester for the analogical sphere [APP ¶105]; and mesmerism is said to imitate the Divine Art of separation he speaks of [APP ¶73].

References: I.1 n41, I.1 n99, I.1 ¶35, I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶71, I.1 ¶76, I.2 n21, I.2 n24, I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶26, I.3 n4, II.1 ¶14, II.1 ¶21, III.1 n20, III.1 ¶21, III.2 n27, III.2 ¶5, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n27, APP ¶105, APP ¶32, APP ¶57, APP ¶73

Paracelsus’ disciples

collective voice

Followers of Paracelsus who, Atwood says, applied alchemy to human life and suggested the method and medium of attraction.

Cited as having applied alchemy to human life and suggested “the method and medium of attraction” [II.1 ¶9].

See also: Disciple

References: II.1 ¶9

Paradise Lost

treatise — author not named

Work (author not named in the text) quoted to illustrate Mammon as the downward-looking spirit leading the depraved operators.

Atwood quotes it on Mammon, the downward-looking spirit who leads the depraved operators: “for e’en in heaven his looks and thoughts Were always downward bent” [III.4 ¶4, III.4 ¶5, III.4 n2]. The author is not named.

References: III.4 n2, III.4 ¶4, III.4 ¶5

Paris

person — Venus, Juno, Minerva

Paris, who preferred Venus to Juno and Minerva, invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) in the Democritus passage.

Invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) of the Democritus passage: “Perchance it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus, he did prefer her both to Juno and Minerva” [IV.1 ¶43]. Whether Atwood or the quoted source speaks here is unclear.

References: IV.1 ¶43

Parmenides

person

Authority whose Non-Being Atwood identifies with the Matter, cited on non-being and the initial nonentity of all.

Atwood quotes his Fragments on “Non-being, which nor mind can see”, as a check on intellectual notions along this path [III.2 ¶13, III.2 ¶14, III.2 n14]. Via Aristotle she reports that he touched the One according to Reason and saw more than Xenophanes and Melissus [III.2 ¶40]. He is cited with the rest to prove the initial nonentity of all [III.2 ¶54], and “the Non-Being of Parmenides” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

References: III.2 n14, III.2 ¶13, III.2 ¶14, III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶54, III.2 ¶60

Particular Spirit and Universal

term · Particular Spirit, Universal

Vaughan’s term for an individual spirit that a certain Art unites to the Universal; distinguished from the divine spirit.

Voice: Vaughan (quoted): “a certain Art by which a Particular Spirit may be united to the Universal” [II.1 ¶26]. The Particular Spirit is distinguished from the divine spirit [II.1 ¶26].

See also: Universal, Universals

References: II.1 ¶26

Passified spirit

term

The Spirit made passive, into which the supernatural reason infuses itself throughout.

Atwood: the supernatural reason works “by pure infusion of Itself to the passified Spirit throughout” [III.1 ¶21].

See also: Spirit

References: III.1 ¶21

Passive Intellect

term

Aristotle’s term, as Atwood reports and adopts it, for an intellect capable of receiving and being converted to all things.

Aristotle’s term as Atwood reports it (and adopts): the intellect he “calls passive intellect, because capable of receiving and being converted to all” [II.2 ¶17].

See also: Intellect

References: II.2 ¶17

Passive intelligence

term

The receptive intelligence, identified with the Moon, which, freed by art and in conjunction, answers the Will of her seeking Reason.

Atwood: the Passive Intelligence, spoken of as her, once freed by art and set in conjunction, “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason”, finds the way, removes obstacles and passes with him through the abyss [III.1 ¶40]. Identity asserted: “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40].

Identified with: Moon [III.1 ¶40]

See also: Intelligence

References: III.1 ¶40

Passive nature

term

The pure, indeterminate receptive nature that should reflect the Divine Light unrefracted; identified as the Alchemists’ Matter.

Atwood: “And the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind, pure and indeterminate” [III.2 ¶60], reflecting the Divine Light without refraction or mixed images. Identity asserted: “Such was the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].

Identified with: the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists [III.2 ¶60]

References: III.2 ¶60

Passive spirit

term

The receptive spirit, spoken of as herself, whose returning faith and desire draw the Soul back into itself at the extreme of tribulation.

Atwood: at the extreme of tribulation, “the returning faith and desire of the Passive Spirit attracts the Soul again into herself” [III.3 ¶10].

See also: Spirit

References: III.3 ¶10

Passive spirit of nature

term

Nature’s receptive spirit, enclosed and impure in its ordinary state, made a right recipient by dissolution.

Atwood: in its ordinary state “the passive spirit of nature is included and impure” [I.2 ¶48]; dissolution makes it a right recipient [I.2 ¶48].

References: I.2 ¶48

Passive subject

term

That which the Vital Spirit’s fermentation changes; not further defined.

Atwood speaks of “the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” by the Vital Spirit’s fermentation [III.1 ¶9]. The text does not define it further.

See also: Subject

References: III.1 ¶9

Passive understanding

term

Understanding gained in transcendental contemplation of herself, which directs the mode of analysis and supplies most of its means.

Atwood: “the Passive Understanding gotten in transcendental contemplation of herself” directs the mode of analysis and provides most of its means [III.1 ¶40]. The passage does not explicitly identify it with the Passive Intelligence discussed alongside it.

References: III.1 ¶40

Paternal

term

The first source of life and the last initiation, goal of every step of ascent, whose rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites.

Atwood: “the paternal is the first source of life, and the last into which the conscience is initiated” [II.4 ¶25]. It is the goal of all steps of ascent, and its rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites [II.4 ¶25].

References: II.4 ¶25

Paternal fountain

term

In the Chaldaic Oracle, the source from which intellectual notions crop the Flower of Life.

Voice: the Chaldaic Oracle (quoted): “Intellectual notions from the Paternal Fountain cropping the Flower of Life” [II.4 ¶32]. Not further explained.

See also: Fountain

References: II.4 ¶32

Paternal life

term

In the Appendix, the fundamental life sought by the light; related expressions Paternal ens and Paternal Spirit dwell in liberty in Elysium.

Appendix only (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood speaks of “seeking the Paternal Life, the fundamental life” [APP ¶167]. Related expressions name what dwells there: “where the Paternal ens resides in liberty” [APP ¶168] and “to Elysium, where the Paternal Spirit lives” [APP ¶171]; the text does not state in so many words that these are the same as the Paternal Life.

Identified with: the fundamental life [APP ¶167]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶167, APP ¶168, APP ¶171

Paternal light of life

term

The soul’s original, more central light, antecedent to the Maternal intelligence; identified with the generative light.

Atwood calls it “the yet more central, antecedent Paternal, light of life”, into which the Maternal intelligence leads [III.1 ¶34]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) it is the soul’s original light, obscured by the vaporous vehicle to bring it into sense, and identified: “the pure paternal light of life — the generative light” [APP ¶121].

Identified with: the generative light [APP ¶121]

See also: Life

References: III.1 ¶34, APP ¶121

Paternal port

term

In Proclus as reported by Atwood, the soul’s undefiled union with the Father, in which it rests established in him as in a harbour.

A term Atwood reports from Proclus: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41]. The image is of “locating the soul in the Father, as in a port” [II.4 ¶41]. So the text itself identifies the Paternal Port with undefiled union with the Father.

Identified with: undefiled union with him [II.4 ¶41]

References: II.4 ¶41

Paternal principle

term

In the Appendix, Atwood’s name for the seed of this life, which is said to be drawn up.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates the paternal principle with the seed of life: “The seed of this life, the paternal principle, is drawn up.” [APP ¶98]. The text gives no further explanation here.

Identified with: the seed of this life [APP ¶98]

See also: Principles

References: APP ¶98

Paternal source

term

That which Intellect seeks in the allegory of the descent, according to Atwood.

Atwood reads the allegory of the descent as “an inquiry of Intellect after its Paternal Source” [II.3 ¶13]. The context suggests the term names the origin to which Intellect seeks to return. The text does not define it further.

References: II.3 ¶13

Patient

term

Paired with ‘agent’: that in which the agent’s sin is multiplied and lives on in the ‘unhappy offspring’.

Atwood uses ‘patient’ as the counterpart of ‘agent’. The records show it as that in which the agent’s sin is multiplied, so that “it should survive in the unhappy offspring unto the third or fourth generation” [IV.3 ¶56]. The text does not define the term further here.

See also: Agent and patient, Spiritual agent and spiritual patient

References: IV.3 ¶56

Perfect body

term

In Eudoxus, the leaven needed to ferment the Stone in the Fifth Key.

Eudoxus speaks here, quoted by Atwood: “the Perfect Body is a necessary leaven of Our Paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. So the text identifies the Perfect Body with the leaven of Our Paste, the leaven by which the Stone is fermented in the Fifth Key.

Identified with: leaven of Our Paste [IV.3 ¶14]

See also: Body

References: IV.3 ¶14

Perfect matter

term

In the Author of the Open Entrance, the matter joined with the Mercury of the First Work in the Multiplication.

This comes from the Author of the Open Entrance, quoted by Atwood. In the Multiplication one is told to “take one part of the Perfect Matter” [IV.3 ¶18] and join it with the Mercury of the First Work. The term is not defined further here.

See also: Matter

References: IV.3 ¶18

Permanent water

term

Whitened water made red by conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit; its Art is called ‘our brass’.

In a footnote, Atwood gives the reddening of the whitened water: “By a conjunction with its own permanent prepared spirit, the albified water is made red” [I.3 n54]. The same note links the Art of the permanent water with ‘our brass’.

See also: Water

References: I.3 n54

Perpendicular line

term

In the Appendix, the Divine line in all things, which withdraws from sense in mesmerizing, as opposed to the transverse line.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says: “The perpendicular line is the Divine line in all things” [APP ¶13]. In mesmerizing it withdraws from sense. Were it stronger in us than the transverse line, we would no longer be in sense [APP ¶13].

Identified with: Divine line [APP ¶13]

References: APP ¶13

Perpendicular Magnetism

term

In the Appendix, the magnetism (‘altitude’) that dissolves the sensuous vehicle, freeing the soul and moving consciousness into another medium.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that Perpendicular Magnetism dissolves the sensuous vehicle and moves consciousness into another medium: “By the former the soul is set free” [APP ¶173]. It is linked with ‘altitude’. The context suggests it is set against another, contrasting kind of magnetism.

References: APP ¶173

Perpetual lamps

term

Ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, which Atwood takes as proof that the Romans knew chemistry and the occult laws of light.

Atwood describes ancient lamps found still burning in tombs and urns, kept alight by a pure liquor. She treats them as evidence: “the perpetual lamps best prove, and without offence, that the Romans understood something of chemistry and the occult laws of light” [I.1 ¶18].

References: I.1 ¶18

Perscrutination

term

Thorough, searching investigation: the means by which reason proves all things, and something the stiff-necked lack.

Two voices use the word. Geber, quoted by Atwood, describes the stiff-necked as “void of ingenuity and every sort of perscrutination” [III.4 ¶3]. Atwood herself makes it reason’s task: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15]. In her method, then, searching inquiry is required, and its absence disqualifies.

References: III.4 ¶15, III.4 ¶3

Perscrutinator

term · perscrutinating Intellect

Hermes’ name for the searching inner fire or secret sulfur that stirs up and purifies the matter; Atwood identifies it with the investigating Intellect that works the change.

In a footnote, Atwood, citing Hermes, describes a secret sulfur: “It is the stirrer-up of the whole power and efficacy and purifier of the matter; hence Hermes calls it the Perscrutinator” [I.3 n32]. Hermes calls this temperate unguent or fire ‘the Perscrutinator of the water’. Atwood adds that it is what is “eminently distinguishing the Rational Ferment” [I.3 n32].

In III.1 she takes the term inward. It is “that same perscrutinating Intellect which Hermes speaks of” [III.1 ¶21], the searching intellect that brings about the whole change. The sequestration that gives form and essence belongs to it [III.1 ¶21]. She also equates it with Eirenaeus’ phrase: “It is this vital perscrutinator, the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water, as Eirenaeus calls it” [III.1 ¶13].

Asserted identities: the secret sulfur [I.3 n32]; the internal fire of the sulfur of thy water [III.1 ¶13]; the perscrutinating Intellect [III.1 ¶21].

Identified with: secret sulfur [I.3 n32]; internal fire of the sulfur of thy water [III.1 ¶13]

References: I.3 n32, III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶21

Petri Apiani

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n27

Petri Norelli

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n95, I.1 ¶75

Petris

person — the Persian · Petris, the Persian

Author of an epistle addressed to Artaxerxes, cited for its account of Hippocrates’ divine nature and healing.

Atwood cites an epistle by Petris, the Persian, addressed to Artaxerxes. It tells of Hippocrates’ divine nature and healing: “this man is the prince of divine knowledge” [IV.3 ¶32]. See also [IV.3 ¶34]. The footnote points to Helmont, Tumulus Pestis [IV.3 n12]. Atwood uses the epistle as illustration.

References: IV.3 n12, IV.3 ¶32, IV.3 ¶34

Petronius Arbiter

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n19

Phantasmagoric region

term

In the Appendix, a region passed before entering the world’s solution, after which the inner vision is the same for all.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that the inner vision is the same for all “after they have passed the phantasmagoric region” [APP ¶144] and entered the world’s solution. The text does not explain the term further.

References: APP ¶144

Phantasms

term · figured phantasms

Figured images produced by the mind’s own fancy, or by nature and the demiurgic intellect, as distinct from the gods’ true self-manifestation.

Atwood separates phantasms from the gods’ true self-manifestation. Phantasms are figured images that come from the mind’s own fancy, or from nature and the demiurgic intellect. She speaks of the case “if various phantasms are hurled forth before the presence of them” [II.4 ¶29].

References: II.4 ¶29

Phantastic spirit

term · phantasic

The imaginative spirit, the natural vehicle of our life and the vestibule of Reason; confusing and possessive while impure, it can be purified and refined by Intellect.

In II.2 Atwood describes the imaginative spirit in man and animals. While impure it produces a ‘phantastic life’ and confusion and possession of the mind, and it is likened to the Sphinx: “such is said to be the nature of the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. It can be cleansed: “But the phantastic Spirit may be purified, even in brutes” [II.2 ¶13]. She links it with what Iamblicus calls the mundane spirit: “Thus Iamblicus, speaking of this mundane spirit, says” [II.2 ¶15].

In III.1 she places it in the soul’s anatomy: “the Phantastic Spirit, which is the natural vehicle of our life” [III.1 ¶5]. She also links it to the natural intelligent Spirit: “for what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe; and this intelligence, phantasic as it is and drawn without, may be called the vestibule of Reason” [III.1 ¶5].

Synesius, as Atwood quotes him, gives Intellect the work of purifying it: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20]. Intellect thins it and extends it toward Divinity. The text does not say it is the same as the Ethereal Spirit.

Asserted identities: mundane spirit [II.2 ¶15]; natural vehicle of our life [III.1 ¶5]; natural intelligent Spirit [III.1 ¶5].

Identified with: Mundane spirit [II.2 ¶15]; natural vehicle of our life [III.1 ¶5]; Natural intelligent spirit [III.1 ¶5]

See also: Spirit

References: II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶15, III.1 ¶20, III.1 ¶5

Phantasy

term

The imagination: a region of notions and instincts that hinders intellectual conception and, if it prevails, turns the inner life to folly.

Olympiodorus, quoted by Atwood, calls it a hindrance: “The phantasy, says he, is an impediment to our intellectual conception” [II.2 ¶12]. He also sets it against enthusiasm.

The ancients, as she reports them, describe “the region of the phantasy, with its notions and instincts” [II.2 ¶22]. Its contents are often more false, fleeting and evil than sense images, and it is dangerous to dwell in passively.

In her own voice, Atwood counts phantasy as a mode of the One Thing, alongside folly and passion: “the phantasy, if suffered to prevail, will convert all to her own folly in the internal life” [III.1 ¶21]. Once phantasy is subdued, the Ethereal Spirit abandons it.

References: II.2 ¶12, II.2 ¶22, III.1 ¶21

Pharisees, Katharoi, Devotes and Puritans

collective voice · Pharisees, Katharoi, Devotes, Puritans, Pharisees, Katharoi, Devotes, Puritans

Religious groups Atwood names together in the Appendix as examples of religious self-will in history.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names these groups as historical examples of religious self-will [APP ¶110].

References: APP ¶110

Phillips

person

Cited for reference only.

References: II.1 n17

Philo

person — the Jew Philo · the Jew Philo, Philo-Judaeus

‘The Jew Philo’, whom Atwood cites for the rational part of man as God’s temple and the soul as the impression of the Logos-seal.

Atwood cites Philo in support of two points: that the rational part of man is God’s temple, and that the soul bears the impression of the Logos-seal. “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]. The works named in her footnotes are De Praemiis et Poenis, De Nobilitate, De Profugis and De Plantatione Noe [II.1 n39, II.1 n40].

Elsewhere she lists Philo-Judaeus with Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus, Julian and Apuleius. These are Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, and she says she will quote them later [I.1 ¶27].

References: I.1 ¶27, II.1 n39, II.1 n40, II.1 ¶43

Philosopher

collective voice — unnamed voice

An unnamed ‘philosopher’ cited throughout the book for a range of maxims on the work, the soul and illumination, usually in support of Atwood’s points.

The phrase ‘the philosopher’ stands for an unnamed authority at many points. The text does not show that it is always the same person.

  • Within Hermes’ text, the philosopher is cited for the permanent works [I.3 ¶30] and for the Botri saying: “Botri is made from the Citrine” [I.3 ¶41].
  • On the soul, citing Plotinus’s Select Works (Taylor, page 387) in a footnote: “When the soul is situated in the body, says the philosopher, she departs from self-contemplation” [II.1 ¶50, II.1 n44]. The point supported is that the purified soul recollects what it forgot.
  • “Dimidium facti qui bene coepit habet” [III.1 ¶24], i.e. (ours) a good beginning is half the work.
  • On the Night of Matter: “By no means, says the philosopher” [III.2 ¶55]. Here the point is that the mind receives the formless rather than understanding nothing.
  • The worker should work faithfully until it be the Divine pleasure to make the work appear [III.3 ¶80].
  • On the Gordian Knot: “who is he that is bale to untie it, enquires the philosopher?” [IV.1 ¶37].
  • “Labor to know causes” [IV.1 ¶44]. Atwood endorses this as the condition of success.
  • On self-preparation, invitation and sudden illumination: “Fit thy roof to thy God in all thou canst” [IV.2 ¶39, IV.2 ¶41].
