See also: Authorities in Norton (Philosophers, Astrologers, Auctors), Philosophers

References: I.3 ¶30, I.3 ¶41, II.1 n44, II.1 ¶50, III.1 ¶24, III.2 ¶55, III.3 ¶80, IV.1 ¶37, IV.1 ¶44, IV.2 ¶39, IV.2 ¶41

Philosophers

term · philosopher

Genuine seekers of the Stone, as against knaves and sordid chemists; the disciplined, proven person to whom alone Nature gives up her casket.

Atwood separates true philosophers from impostors. Experiments went on in secret “both by knaves and philosophers” [I.1 ¶55], and the philosopher stands apart from idlers and ‘sordid chemists’. In her account Nature gives her secret only to the qualified: “she will surrender to none but a philosopher, one too that has been disciplined in her schools” [III.4 ¶13]. That is someone tried and proven able to bear the sacred trust.

Philosophers. Atwood cites ‘the philosophers’ as a group for several doctrines:

  • The First Matter is sought inwardly: “The First Matter is not to be found on earth, as the philosophers say” [APP ¶137] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer).
  • As Hermes reports, they praise gold: “this gold, in relation of other bodies, is as the sun amongst the stars” [I.3 ¶58].
  • Spirit and body must be joined for generation: “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7].
  • In ancient times they dug out the saving Salt and exalted it by circulating media [IV.4 ¶20].

She also points out their limits. None of them shows how to obtain the two mercuries. They pass over that point ‘very slightly’ and treat the preparation of Mercury ‘in silence’. The Adepts say more about the last operations than about the First, so reading them alone will hardly suffice [IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶16].

See also: Authorities in Norton (Philosophers, Astrologers, Auctors), Famous Christian philosophers, Philosopher (unnamed voice), Philosophers of tyme old (olde Fathers), Renowned philosophers of various ages and nations

References: I.1 ¶55, I.3 ¶58, III.4 ¶13, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶14, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶7, IV.4 ¶20, APP ¶137

Philosophers’ gold

term · gold of the philosophers, philosopher’s gold, gold of the wise, our gold, living gold

Not common gold but a living, luminous, purified substance that ripens and perfects other bodies; also the transmuting powder in Van Helmont’s projection.

In Van Helmont’s account, quoted by Atwood, it is a transmuting powder: he projected “one grain of the philosophers’ gold upon some thousands of grains of boiling quicksilver” [I.1 ¶76]. In Khunrath’s words it is identified with “the blood of the Lion, which is the gold of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶81]. It may also be read as the universal tincture; the text leaves this open.

Atwood’s own account, drawing on the adepts, makes it a living substance, not metal: “Our gold is not common gold, says the adept, but a depurated substance” [I.3 n63]. It has a heavenly complexion, and it ripens and perfects other bodies. Paradoxically “the gold of the wise is more heavy than lead” [I.3 ¶61], and it is made into Ixir with a fiery water.

Asserted identities: living gold, “The gold of the philosophers, or living gold, as they sometimes call their luminous concrete” [I.3 n65]; our earth, “our earth is gold” [I.3 ¶62]; the blood of the Lion [I.1 ¶81].

Identified with: Blood of the Lion [I.1 ¶81]; living gold [I.3 n65]; Our earth [I.3 ¶62]

See also: Gold, Gold of the wise, Living gold of the philosophers

References: I.1 ¶76, I.1 ¶81, I.3 n63, I.3 n65, I.3 ¶61, I.3 ¶62

Philosophers of tyme old

collective voice — olde Fathers · olde Fathers

Earlier authorities criticized inside a quoted poem for describing the making of Magnesia while hiding imbibition.

Inside a poem Atwood quotes, the ‘Philosophers of tyme old’ or ‘olde Fathers’ are faulted for describing the creation of Magnesia while concealing imbibition: “The secret of Imbibition never out tould;” [III.1 ¶65].

See also: Philosophers

References: III.1 ¶65

Philosophic body

term

The body of the work, which carries a shadowy darkness with it until it is purified of sensual defilements.

Atwood writes in a footnote: “A shadowy darkness passes always along with the philosophic body” [I.3 n21]. The darkness stays with it until the body is purified of sensual defilements.

See also: Body

References: I.3 n21

Philosophic calcination

term · philosophical calcination

In Eudoxus, a purely natural calcination of the Stone that sublimes and distills it and increases its radical humidity, unlike destructive common calcination by fire.

Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, calls it “a philosophic calcination which is purely natural” [IV.3 ¶16]. He contrasts it with common calcination by violence of fire, which destroys the body: “this philosophical calcination, which sublimes and distills the Stone in calcining it, much augments its humidity” [IV.3 ¶16]. It preserves and increases the Stone’s radical humidity.

Identified with: natural calcination [IV.3 ¶16]

See also: Calcinations

References: IV.3 ¶16

Philosophic Eagles

term

In Eirenaeus, things whose exact preparation is the first degree of perfection in the Art; not explained further.

Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, says: “the exact preparation of the philosophic Eagles may be considered the first degree of perfection in this Art” [IV.1 ¶11]. The text does not explain what the Eagles are.

See also: Eagle

References: IV.1 ¶11

Philosophic fermentation

term

The process in which Life’s substance is wholly transmuted, its threefold property developed and the forms of the Medial Spirit put out, followed by radical destruction and New Generation.

Atwood writes: “as Life passes through the philosophic fermentation, its substance is entirely transmuted” [III.2 ¶28]. In this process the threefold property of Life is developed and its heterogeneous parts are divided. The forms of the Medial Spirit are extinguished, and a radical destruction and a New Generation follow [III.2 ¶28].

See also: Fermentation

References: III.2 ¶28

Philosophic field

term

The field where, in Atwood’s figure, the Prototypes of the sacrificial beasts remain feeding and fattening; the text does not explain it further.

Atwood speaks of the sacrificial beasts “whilst their Prototypes remain feeding and fattening in the Philosophic Field” [III.2 ¶44]. The passage gives no further explanation of the expression.

References: III.2 ¶44

Philosophic heaven

term

The realm whose powers, Atwood says, are shaken and defiled during the putrefaction.

In Atwood’s account of the putrefaction, “the powers of the Philosophic Heaven are so wonderfully shaken and defiled” [III.1 ¶58]. The text does not define the Philosophic Heaven further here.

See also: Heaven

References: III.1 ¶58

Philosophic matter

term · Philosophical matter

The subject of the Hermetic work: hidden in the central motion of mineral life, called by many names, properly the Stone in concrete form, and described as an excruciated ens of Light.

Atwood treats the philosophic matter as the subject of the work. It lies hidden “in the central motion of the mineral life, where the spirit is first coagulated and conceives itself into a concrete form” [I.3 n13]. It has many names: she notes one author who “eloquently identifies the philosophic matter, calling it mens sublimes et mare patens” (a mind sublime, and an open sea) [I.3 n13], and says that “in the concrete form, and for reasons before given in part, it has been properly called the Stone” [I.3 n16].

In Part IV she describes it as “the philosophic matter, drawn in part from the heterogeneous air and defiled breath of vitality” [IV.1 ¶46], which is purified into an immortal Form of Light. She mentions that Basil Valentine goes on to describe it after the passage she quotes (“before proceeding to a description of the Philosophic Matter” [III.2 ¶19]), but that description is not given there.

Quoted voices: in Hermes, the Son bears the Matter, which has a fixed watery form; the Master says “For this Son is the treasury, bearing even (in his hand) the Philosophic Matter” [IV.2 ¶14].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood gives two definitions: “The Philosophic Matter is an excruciated ens of Light”, “alight extracted through anguish from Life” [APP ¶84]; and “The Philosophical matter is the entelechy of body bearing the spirit” [APP ¶178].

Asserted identities: = the Stone [I.3 n16]; = mens sublimes et mare patens [I.3 n13]; = excruciated ens of Light [APP ¶84]; = entelechy of body bearing the spirit [APP ¶178].

Identified with: excruciated ens of Light [APP ¶84]; mens sublimes et mare patens (a mind sublime, and an open sea) [I.3 n13]; Stone [I.3 n16]; entelechy of body bearing the spirit [APP ¶178]

See also: Matter

References: I.3 n13, I.3 n16, III.2 ¶19, IV.1 ¶46, IV.2 ¶14, APP ¶178, APP ¶84

Philosophic process

term

In the Appendix, being conversant with the soul in her philosophy: the recreative, or rather separative, process.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood glosses the philosophic process as being “conversant with the soul in her philosophy — i.e., the recreative, or rather separative, process” [APP ¶181].

Identified with: recreative, or rather separative, process [APP ¶181]

References: APP ¶181

Philosophic Proteus

term

A figure in the Art whose will, unlike natural species, is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light; the text does not define it directly.

Atwood writes that “the will of the philosophic Proteus is free to be drawn without hindrance” [I.2 ¶48]. Unlike natural species, it is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light. The context apparently ties it to the fermented Vital Spirit, but the passage does not define it.

See also: Proteus

References: I.2 ¶48

Philosophic Salt

term · Salt

A Salt discovered in the work, glossed as the voluntary bond; its solution is the Second Work, and knowing it is the secret of the Ancient Sages.

Atwood says that the stated periods of the work are often metaphorical: “the periods are often to be understood metaphorically with respect to the discovery of the philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶17]. She glosses it as the voluntary bond, writing of “the Solution of the Philosophic Salt (i.e., the voluntary bond)” [IV.1 ¶36]. This solution is the Second Work, and “He who knows the Salt and its solution, knows the secret of the Ancient Sages.” [IV.1 ¶37].

Asserted identity: = the voluntary bond [IV.1 ¶36].

Identified with: the voluntary bond [IV.1 ¶36]

See also: Salt

References: IV.1 ¶17, IV.1 ¶36, IV.1 ¶37

Philosophic subject

term · our subject

The Matter considered as the subject of the work: universal, with perfective virtues, burdened with superfluities, and prepared by slow, gentle, continuous trituration.

Atwood uses the term for the Matter as the subject on which the work is done. She speaks of “the alleged virtue and perfective properties of the Philosophic Subject” [I.2 ¶34], which go beyond ordinary light phenomena, and calls it universal, so that every epithet fits it: “inasmuch as nothing can be said amiss of a Universal Subjet” [I.2 ¶37].

She defers its full treatment, saying the mystical death and regeneration will become clearer “when we come to treat of the manifestation of the Philosophic Subject” [II.3 ¶56]. The ass’s qualities are “very applicable and necessary to be found in the Philosophic Subject” [III.2 ¶64] if it is to carry out the Divine behests.

In Part IV the subject is prepared by hand (“Preparation of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶2]). It is burdened with “such a mass of heterogeneous superfluities adhering to our subject” [IV.1 ¶7], and is worked by “the trituration of the Philosophic Subject, which ought to be slow, gentle, and continuous” [IV.1 ¶13].

See also: Subject

References: I.2 ¶34, I.2 ¶37, II.3 ¶56, III.2 ¶64, IV.1 ¶13, IV.1 ¶2, IV.1 ¶7

Philosophic vessel

term

The vessel of the work, concealed by Hermes, described as having an apparatus of nerves, veins and alembics, and best when it accords with the vessel of nature.

Atwood notes that “Hermes has chosen to conceal the philosophic vessel” [I.3 n48]. The context places the science in all bodies and its preparation in the innermost chamber of life.

Later she describes “the Philosophic Vessel and its multiform distillatory apparatus, of nerves, veins, and alembics” [III.4 ¶30]. The best vessel is “She that concordeth with vessel of nature” [III.4 ¶31]. It is finally constructed and vitrified by the Spirit and is called ‘oracular’. The described apparatus apparently suggests a vessel within the living body, but the records do not state this directly.

See also: Vessel

References: I.3 n48, III.4 ¶30, III.4 ¶31

Philosophic water

term · Aqua Philosophica

The one water from which all things grow and into which they dissolve, containing its own sulfur; Hermes’ Aqua Philosophica that dissolves the elements.

Atwood speaks of things “which have their growth all from the same identical water, and are resolved into the same again” [I.3 n5]. This water is divided into four relations and contains its own sulfur: “this water or mercury of the adepts has, within itself, its own good sulfur” [I.3 n5].

In the voice of Hermes it is addressed: “O, blessed watery pontic form, that dissolvest the elements” [I.3 ¶27]. Its dissolution of the composition is the key of restoration. Atwood’s note on this passage adds: “Great is the reputed virtue of this Aqua Philosophica, which distills itself finally to manifestation by the Art of Life” [I.3 n36]. It cleanses inwardly and itself, and, joined in consciousness with the central Efficient, becomes the key of every magic art. It is learned only by practice.

Asserted identity: = mercury of the adepts [I.3 n5].

Identified with: mercury of the adepts [I.3 n5]

See also: Water

References: I.3 n36, I.3 n5, I.3 ¶27

Philosophic work

term · Subtle Work, Subtill Werke

The work proper, begun only after right motive and complete purification, with a threefold order of operation concealed by the Adepts and distinct from the preliminary practice.

Zachary, as quoted, advises reading the philosophers and praying “before thou extendest thy Hand to the Philosophic Work” [III.4 ¶20]. An unclear voice equates the work with the practice: “the practice (that is of the ultimate Philosophic Work)” [III.4 ¶44].

Atwood says “few are chosen to proceed with the Philosophic Work” [IV.1 ¶31] out of those who consult on the means. It begins only after the right Motive, complete mundification and crystalline diaphaneity, so that only then can it be said “that the Philosophic Work has been said truly to being” [IV.1 ¶48]. Everything before is preparatory. She supports this with verse: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49].

Part IV.2 is headed “Of the Philosophic or Subtle Work” [IV.2 ¶1]. There Atwood says that “in the Philosophic Work, preceding her, there is a threefold order of legitimate operation” [IV.2 ¶3], which the Adepts concealed. Norton’s verse calls it ‘this Subtill Werke’.

Asserted identities: = Subtle Work [IV.2 ¶1]; = the practice [III.4 ¶44].

Identified with: Practice [III.4 ¶44]; Subtle Work [IV.2 ¶1]

See also: Works

References: III.4 ¶20, III.4 ¶44, IV.1 ¶31, IV.1 ¶48, IV.1 ¶49, IV.2 ¶1, IV.2 ¶3

Philosophical contrition

term

A process out of which the Matter first appears pure and white; the text does not explain it further.

Atwood reports that the Matter comes forth “pure, as they say, and white, out of the philosophical contrition” [I.2 ¶36]. The term is not further explained there.

See also: Contrition

References: I.2 ¶36

Philosophical dissolution

term

In the Appendix, the dissolution in which soul and spirit separate from the breathless body, held to it as by a thread until refixation.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “In the Philosophical dissolution of the body, soul and spirit are separate” [APP ¶96]. They remain joined to the breathless body as by a thread until refixation.

See also: Dissolution

References: APP ¶96

Philosophical Elixir

term

A product of the work whose divine virtues wise men admire; things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it.

Atwood mentions “the Philosophical Elixir, whose divine virtues wise men so much admire” [I.2 ¶49]. Things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it. Nearby she separately names ‘the elixir of the wise’ as the result of superior skill and coction in vegetal life [I.2 ¶46]; the text does not say the two are the same.

See also: Elixir

References: I.2 ¶49

Philosophy

term

Reason’s desire for its antecedent light.

Atwood defines philosophy as reason’s longing for its source: “philosophy was a desire of this kind, an appetition of reason for its antecedent light” [II.1 ¶44].

Asserted identity: = an appetition of reason for its antecedent light [II.1 ¶44].

Identified with: an appetition of reason for its antecedent light [II.1 ¶44]

References: II.1 ¶44

Philosophy and Experience

treatise

A piece in Ashmole’s collection that Atwood counts among the most instructive.

Atwood lists Philosophy and Experience among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole’s collection [I.1 ¶64].

See also: Experience

References: I.1 ¶64

Phoebus

term · Orient Phoebus

In quoted verse, the bright appearance that follows the blackness and its strange colours, and the coming God whom only the pure can endure.

The term appears in quoted verse. Bloomfield, as quoted, says that after the blackness and its strange colours, “Then shall Phoebus appear first out” [IV.2 ¶36], signalling the joy to come. In the hymn (Callimachus) Phoebus is the coming God whom only the pure endure: “Bright Phoebus comes and thunders at the gate.” [IV.2 ¶38]. In context this apparently marks the light that follows the dark stage of the work.

References: IV.2 ¶36, IV.2 ¶38

Phoenix

term

Atwood’s figure for something with a reviviscent spirit that passed from East to West, apparently alchemy; in a quoted source, the deep red bird that appears after the fire.

Atwood writes that “our Phoenix too bestirred herself, and passed into the West” [I.1 ¶37], around the twelfth century, and gives it a ‘reviviscent spirit’. The context suggests the Phoenix here stands for alchemy itself, but this is an inference.

Cornelius Agrippa’s ingenious disciple, as quoted, describes the Phoenix that appears after the fire is fortified: “It is a red bird of a most deep color with a shining fiery hue.” [III.1 ¶50]. It is fed with the fire of its father as meat and the ether of its mother as drink.

References: I.1 ¶37, III.1 ¶50

Physic

term

Medicine as Crollius describes it: a knowledge to be tried by fire, inseparable from pyrotechny, and practised by the physician.

Crollius, as quoted, says “the trial of the knowledge of physic is to be made by fire” [III.1 ¶10]. In his account physic cannot be separated from pyrotechny, and it is practised by the ‘physician’.

References: III.1 ¶10

Physical and moral sciences

term

Atwood’s two divergent kinds of science, physical (external, sensory, utilitarian) and moral (inward); neither can prove or disprove the other, and the Hermetic Science would include both.

Atwood contrasts the two. The Physical sciences rest on an external basis, take the senses as evidence and practical utility as their end. The Moral sciences have their evidence and object within the mind and slight worldly benefits. The two diverge, with “the Spiritual unable to prove itself absolutely, or the Material to disprove the other practically” [IV.4 ¶11]. The Hermetic Science would include both.

References: IV.4 ¶11

Physical problem

term

Kirchberger’s term, endorsed by Atwood: making the invisible spirit visible, by taking the infinite Light-nature into bound through hypostatic multiplication of its image.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood adopts Kirchberger’s term. The physical problem is “the making visible the invisible spirit” [APP ¶93]: taking the infinite Light-nature into bound by hypostatic multiplication of its image.

References: APP ¶93

Physician, heal thyself

collective voice — maxim · maxim ‘Physician, heal thyself’

A maxim quoted within Basil’s passage, where the praise of the science lies in experience.

The maxim “Physician, heal thyself” appears inside a passage Atwood quotes from Basil. There, the praise of the science consists in experience [IV.1 ¶2].

References: IV.1 ¶2

Physico-Chemical art

term

The Art whose ‘obstetric hand’ assists the Stone’s own regenerative self-manifestation.

In the words of the mysterious adeptest, the Stone is “made manifest by itself regeneratively by the obstetric hand of the Physico-Chemical Art” [III.3 ¶50]. The Art apparently assists, as a midwife does, a manifestation the Stone accomplishes itself.

References: III.3 ¶50

Picus di Mirandola

person · Picus, prince di Mirandola, Pico di Mirandola

A writer whose De Auro Atwood cites to link Alchemy with profound metaphysics and to report a friend making gold and silver in his presence.

Picus di Mirandola is named in a list of authorities [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his de Auro (Opus Aureum de Auro) to support the link of Alchemy with profound metaphysical science [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n69]. She also cites De Auro for his testimony that a friend made gold and silver in his presence: “I have seen it and done it myself” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n103]. Atwood uses him as a supporting witness.

References: I.1 n103, I.1 n69, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶76

Pierce the Black Monk

person · Pierce, the Black Monk, Pierce, the Black Monke

A writer on the Elixir in Ashmole’s collection whom Atwood cites on the Matter and the Stone, and on the piety needed by the seeker.

Atwood names Pierce the Black Monk among the ‘ecclesiastics of different orders’ who agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She counts his Fragment among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole’s collection [I.1 ¶64].

From his verses on the Elixir she quotes a recipe for the Stone with the Water of Might: “In Arsenic sublimed there is a way straight” [III.3 ¶16, III.3 n6]. From the same work in Ashmole’s Theatr. she takes support for the view that the subject is a seed from a body, not common gold and silver. The seeker must be pious, charitable and prayerful, and covetous men never find it: “Therefore there ys no other waye But to take thee to thy beades and pray:” [III.4 ¶21, III.4 n23]. Atwood cites him in support.

See also: Monks

References: I.1 ¶64, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n6, III.3 ¶16, III.4 n23, III.4 ¶21

Pioneers of Mesmerism

collective voice — De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet · De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet

A group Atwood praises as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism; she says the science has gone backward since them.

Atwood praises De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend and Dupotet as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism. She says the science has gone backward since their time [II.2 ¶6].

See also: Mesmerism

References: II.2 ¶6

Plato

person

A philosopher Atwood cites widely, for veiled hyperphysical philosophy, self-knowledge, philosophic death, intellectual intuition and the Matter; she declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.

Atwood cites Plato many times, almost always in support.

Veiled philosophy. From many dialogues and Epistle II she takes his hyperphysical, veiled philosophy and his dread of writing the truth: “it is a parturition respecting this ingenerated in the soul, from which he who is not liberated will never in reality acquire truth” [I.1 ¶17, I.1 n23]. She suggests the science behind it was practical but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher. She mentions him as translated by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. She also places him in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who traced the poets’ allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25].

Self-knowledge and the Mysteries. From the First Alcibiades: “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n33]; he “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51]. From the Phaedo: assimilation through the Greater Mysteries and the divine eye, “better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶5, II.2 ¶8], and philosophic death, “it is the business of philosophers to study how to be dead” [II.3 ¶37]. Wisdom belongs to old age, meaning intuitive Intellect free of imaginative error; he condemns ‘two-fold ignorance’ [II.2 ¶13].

Descent and ascent. “It is necessary that a man should have his right opinion as firm as adamant in him when he descends into Hades” [II.3 ¶12]. He likens the soul’s descent into generation to an earthquake [II.3 ¶20], and compares Glaucus deformed by weeds to the viscous soul [II.3 ¶30]. On intuition: “on a sudden a light, as it were a leaping fire, will be enkindled in the soul, and will there itself nourish itself” [II.3 ¶50]. Pure souls see visions “resident in a Pure Light” [II.4 ¶29]. “Plato beautifully unfolds the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] through love, hope and faith. Atwood reads his “there are many more thrysus bearers than Bacchic souls” [II.4 ¶54] as meaning that many have the fire but cannot draw it forth.

The Matter. He places earth within heaven: he “calls it the most ancient element within the heaven” [III.2 ¶36]. Matter is grasped “by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53]. The Timaeus is read as alluding to the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶38], and “the Quintessence of Plato” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. Via Olympiodorus his Tartarus is read ethically, physically and psychically [III.2 ¶9], and via Proclus the Meadow is the prolific power of life [II.4 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for alchemy being understood only by those “conversant with the soul in her philosophy” [APP ¶181].

References: I.1 n23, I.1 ¶17, I.1 ¶64, II.1 n33, II.1 ¶37, II.1 ¶51, II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶5, II.2 ¶8, II.3 n36, II.3 n55, II.3 n56, II.3 n8, II.3 n9, II.3 ¶12, II.3 ¶20, II.3 ¶30, II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶50, II.4 n18, II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶29, II.4 ¶40, II.4 ¶41, II.4 ¶54, III.1 ¶25, III.2 n38, III.2 ¶35, III.2 ¶36, III.2 ¶38, III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶53, III.2 ¶60, III.2 ¶9, APP ¶181

Platonic discourses

collective voice

Cited for reference only.

References: II.3 ¶36

Platonic Successor

person

A late Platonic writer Atwood cites for Sacred Arts replacing lost revelation, an exhortation to inner stillness, and the soul’s ascent from image to Archetype.

Atwood cites the Platonic Successor, via Iamblichus on the Mysteries and Taylor’s notes, for the view that Sacred Arts replace lost spontaneous revelation: “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53, II.1 n46]. She praises the ‘magnificence of thought and diction’ of his exhortation to inner stilling and adoration of the First: “Now, if ever, to remove from ourselves multiform knowledge” [II.4 ¶41]. She also cites him on the soul’s ascent from image to Archetype and its recovery after falling from the vision of God: “he will again, says the Platonic Successor, be elevated” [III.3 ¶26]. In every case she endorses him.

See also: Platonic successors, Platonists

References: II.1 n46, II.1 ¶53, II.4 ¶41, III.3 ¶26

Platonic successors

collective voice

The later Platonists, whose ‘highly elevated philosophy’ Atwood says agrees in the same divine tradition.

Atwood cites the Platonic successors to show that their ‘highly elevated philosophy’ agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

See also: Platonic Successor

References: IV.4 ¶28

Platonic theology

collective voice

Cited by Atwood as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being.

Atwood cites Platonic theology as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being [III.2 ¶33].

References: III.2 ¶33

Platonist and the Kabalist

collective voice

Paired voices Atwood cites for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or known only as nothing.

Atwood cites the Platonist and the Kabalist together for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or is known as nothing [III.2 ¶57].

See also: Kabalists

References: III.2 ¶57

Platonists

collective voice · the Platonist

The Platonic school, cited by Atwood for the whiteness of true Being, the origin of matter, the Epic Cycle as a secret of creation, and the Mysteries as Initia.

Atwood cites the Platonists in support: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9], and she draws on their view of the origin of matter [III.2 ¶9]. She reports them as saying that the Epic Cycle includes the true philosophic secret of creation [III.3 ¶42]. ‘The Platonist’ is cited again for the Mysteries having been called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she contrasts them with Behmen: the Platonists are more scientific and less descriptive [APP ¶62].

See also: Greek and Alexandrian Platonists (with the mystics of the middle ages and the Fathers of the Church), Greeks and eastern sages (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics), Platonic Successor

References: II.2 ¶4, III.2 ¶9, III.3 ¶42, APP ¶62

Pliny

person

Author of the Hist. Nat., whom Atwood cites on Ostanes bringing the Persian spirit to Greece, Democritus’ fame and occult practice, and Caligula’s failed attempts.

Atwood cites Pliny’s Hist. Nat. (lib. xxx, cap. I; lib. 33, cap. 4) in support of three points: Ostanes brought the Persian spirit to Greece; Democritus was famous for experiment and practised in secret; and Caligula’s attempts failed [I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶18, I.1 n13, I.1 n17, I.1 n26]. She quotes: “Plenum miraculi et hoc pariter utrasque artes effloruisse, medicinam dico, magiciemque eadem aetate” (our rendering: this too is full of wonder, that both arts flourished together, medicine, I mean, and magic, in the same age) [I.1 ¶12].

References: I.1 n13, I.1 n17, I.1 n26, I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶18

Plotinus

person

Neoplatonist philosopher Atwood cites heavily in support of inward withdrawal, sudden divine Light, union with the source and pure Matter; the later Appendix qualifies his account of First Matter.

Named among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27], and among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9]; Atwood calls him ‘the graceful Plotinus’ [II.1 ¶39]. She cites him in support throughout: on the same doctrine while condemning suicide [II.3 ¶37]; on the soul’s participation of Deity, perceiving “that the supplier of life is present” [II.3 ¶46]; on the beauty of the gods seen through Intellect — “All the gods, says Plotinus, are beautiful, and their splendour is intense.” [II.4 ¶29; II.4 n17]; on the sudden arrival of the One: “He comes, says Plotinus, suddenly alone” [II.4 ¶50]. From the Select Works and Ennead 5 she takes the sudden Light of Intellect — “a sudden Light, and this Light is from Intellect, and is also It” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n31] — and approach to the universal subject through an image, a portion of gold [III.1 ¶32; III.1 n37]; and again “For the Light is with Power, and is God.” [IV.2 ¶41; IV.2 n28]. With Porphyry he is the source of her summary on the Subject of bodies, analysis and pure divine Matter, that “there should be a Nature primarily vital which is also formless, indestructible and immortal” [III.2 ¶46–49; III.2 n38–39]; n38 says he alludes to the mystical analysis. He supports knowledge of real beings by self-investigation, where “the reality is testified by reminiscence” [III.2 ¶50], and asks how the infinite is conceived — the Indefinite by the Indefinite [III.2 ¶53]; and inward conversion, union with Divine nature, the soul’s middle order and the value of its fall from the treatise on the Descent of the Soul: “Often when by an intellectual energy, I am roused from body and converted to myself” [III.2 ¶50; III.2 n41]; union as experimental ingress requires that one “separate body from the man and its defilements” [III.2 ¶66]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is referred to on how pure matter is generated [APP ¶43] but qualified: he gives only the metaphysic of the First Matter’s generation, never realized so — “a recessure of reason behind itself into the indefinite intermediate between reason and the Absolute” [APP ¶137].

References: I.1 ¶27, II.1 ¶39, II.2 ¶9, II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶46, II.4 n17, II.4 ¶29, II.4 ¶50, III.1 n26, III.1 n31, III.1 n37, III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶32, III.2 n38, III.2 n39, III.2 n41, III.2 ¶46, III.2 ¶47, III.2 ¶48, III.2 ¶49, III.2 ¶50, III.2 ¶53, III.2 ¶66, IV.2 n28, IV.2 ¶41, APP ¶137, APP ¶43

Plutarch

person

Author Atwood cites, as ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, on Chemia, the passions as impediments, the Moon and Sun, Typhon’s names and the fable’s meaning.

Atwood cites Plutarch for the etymology of Chemia: Egypt was called Cham/Chemia for its black soil, and “by the word Chemia, says Plutarch, the seeing pupil of the human eye was also designated” [I.1 ¶5]. From De Iside et Osiride, calling him ‘well initiated in these mysteries’, she takes support for senses and passions as impediments, the rites preparing the aspirant for knowledge of the Supreme Mind: “the souls of men are not able to participate of the Divine nature whilst they are thus encompassed about with senses and passions” [II.1 ¶50; II.1 n45]. He supports the Moon as reason and Wisdom, the Sun as force: “the influence of the Moon, says Plutarch, seems to reflect the works of reason” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n49]; he explains that Typhon’s names Seth and Bebo import violent restraint, contrariety and subversion [III.1 ¶63]; and he is cited, with the Adepts, as witness to the fable’s meaning [IV.2 ¶7].

See also: Eudoxus in Plutarch

References: I.1 ¶5, II.1 n45, II.1 ¶50, III.1 n49, III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶63, IV.2 ¶7

Pneumatic vehicle

term

The soul’s subtle vehicle which, when humid and condensed, presents apparitions to the inner sense.

Atwood speaks of “our pneumatic vehicle, becoming humid and condensed beneath her heaven” [II.3 ¶22]; in this state it presents apparitions to the inner sense, and the soul looking outward “beholds the shadow and images of her vaporous vehicle” [II.3 ¶27]. Whether the ‘vaporous vehicle’ is the same as the pneumatic vehicle is apparently implied by the context, not stated.

See also: Vehicle

References: II.3 ¶22, II.3 ¶27

Poemander

treatise · Divine Poemander, Divine Poimander, Peomander

The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus, praised for sublime doctrine and cited as testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect.

Atwood praises the Divine Poimander for sublimity of doctrine, though it concerns divine capabilities and regeneration rather than their physical ground [I.1 ¶7]. From book 2 she takes a testimony of the operative revelation of Intellect to which, she says, nothing can be added: “For the sleep of the body was the sober watchfulness of the mind” [III.3 ¶58; III.3 n36]. It supplies language for the real suffering passions cause in the revealed light — they “do force the inwardly placed man to suffer sensibly” [III.3 ¶71]. From book 10, introduced with ‘Yet’ against an impossibility she has stated, it teaches that one must enlarge the self beyond body and time to understand God, self-limitation being the obstacle and knowing, willing and hoping the way: “for the like is intelligible by the like” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n51]. A passage cited with the Book of Wisdom (chap. 11, ver. 22) illustrates the world held before divine vision: “The whole world is before thee, O God! As a little grain of the balance” [III.3 ¶39; III.3 n26].

References: I.1 ¶7, III.3 n26, III.3 n36, III.3 n51, III.3 ¶39, III.3 ¶58, III.3 ¶71, III.3 ¶78

Poet

collective voice — unnamed voice

An unnamed poet quoted for a line on the black soot bringing light and a phrase on the remoteness of the discovery.

An unnamed poet supplies a couplet illustrating that the black soot brings light: “Adferet haec Phoebi nigra favilla jubar.” [I.3 n22] (ours: ‘This black ash will bring the radiance of Phoebus’). Another phrase illustrates how remote the discovery is: “reclusa resedet longius” [III.1 ¶13] (ours, roughly: ‘withdrawn, it lies further off’).

See also: Poets

References: I.3 n22, III.1 ¶13

Poets

collective voice

Poets in general, whose fables Atwood reads as veils of the vaporous estate, the Intelligible Sun, and receptive versus presumptuous approach.

Atwood reads the poets’ Pan as a veil for the vaporous estate and its frightening disguises [II.3 ¶20]. Within the Platonic Successor’s passage the Sun from which the Intelligible gods proceed is described as “emerging, as the Poets say, from the bosom of the ocean” [II.4 ¶41]. The stories of Actaeon and Endymion illustrate that presumptuous striving repels while sleeping receptivity receives the presence: “to the sleeping Endymion she vouchsafed her willing presence” [III.2 ¶57].

See also: Initiated poet, Poet (unnamed voice), Poets and traditionalists, Wise poet (in his Georgics)

References: II.3 ¶20, II.4 ¶41, III.2 ¶57

Poets and traditionalists

collective voice

Poets and traditionalists who, by the Walls of Troy built by Apollo’s music, meant the insphering of the lower life (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Walls of Troy, said to be built by Apollo’s music, are what the poets and traditionalists meant as a figure of the insphering of the lower life [APP ¶49].

See also: Poets

References: APP ¶49

Point of passivity

term

A point in the process with no attraction, only indifference to life and death, when the Artist must stir up the Motion.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Alchemists, with Atwood’s endorsement, say “there is a point of passivity” [APP ¶82]: a point in the process with no attraction but indifference to both life and death, at which the Artist must stir up the Motion.

References: APP ¶82

Poison

term · greatest poison, deadly poison

The adepts’ name for what is entered for the dissolution, ‘the greatest poison’; the root of the Science is also called ‘a deadly poison’.

Atwood reports that the adepts call what is entered for the dissolution the greatest poison — “adepts describe it indeed as the greatest poison” [III.1 ¶56] — and that the root of the Science is called deadly: “because the root of this Science is a deadly poison” [III.1 ¶61]. The text does not say outright whether these are the same thing. Resolved into a subtle water, the poison coagulates our Mercury into silver [III.1 ¶56].

Identified with: root of this Science [III.1 ¶61]

References: III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶61

Pole

term · Central Pole

In the Adept’s loadstone figure, the point toward which the center turns, where the steel’s virtue strengthens and the heart of the mercury, a true Fire, lies.

Speaking through a quoted Adept: “This center turns naturally towards the Pole where the virtue of the steel is gradually strengthened.” [IV.2 ¶30]; “In this Pole is the heart of the mercury, which is a true Fire” [IV.2 ¶30], in which its Lord rests. The figure is the loadstone and steel; its plain meaning is not stated in the record.

References: IV.2 ¶30

Pondus

term

The just weight or proportion in which, per Eirenaeus, the first water is joined to the body.

Quoting Eirenaeus: one is “to join it to the body in a just pondus” [III.1 ¶14] — the first water joined to the body in just weight or proportion.

References: III.1 ¶14

Pontanus

person · John Pontanus

Author Atwood cites as a genuine seeker: he erred two hundred times, held the Fire the unrevealed key, and taught nothing in the subject is discarded.

Pontanus’s Epistola appears to credit Artephius’s tale [I.1 ¶36; I.1 n41]. He is listed with Rupicessa, De Meun, Flamel, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]. From his Epistle (Theat. Chem.) Atwood takes in support that he erred two hundred times, that the Fire is the unrevealed key found only by profound meditation: “seek to know this Fire with all thy soul” [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n40]. He also supports that nothing in the subject is to be discarded, superfluities being converted into essence by the Fire: “he who pretends to separate anything from our subject knows nothing of philosophy” [IV.3 ¶7].

References: I.1 n41, I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶49, III.1 n40, III.1 ¶37, IV.3 ¶7

Pontic medium

term

Something without which, along with Theurgic assistance, one cannot transcend the consciousness of this life; not explained further here.

Atwood writes: “Without the Pontic Medium, without Theurgic assistance we are unable to transcend the consciousness of this life” [II.4 ¶49]. The passage does not explain the term.

See also: Medium

References: II.4 ¶49

Pontically

term

The manner in which the Argent vive is generated: by a reciprocal alternation, passing its virtue hand to hand.

Atwood says the Argent vive “is generated pontically, as it were by a reciprocal alternation” [IV.1 ¶11], distributing its advanced virtue by hand to hand. Not otherwise explained.

References: IV.1 ¶11

Pontick water

term · ponticity

Eudoxus’s name for the viscous liquor thickening under repeated affusion, also called Water of Life and the great Lunaria.

Quoting Eudoxus: “the philosophers give this viscous Liquor the name of Pontick Water” [IV.3 ¶9]; the liquor thickens under repeated affusion, and its exuberant ponticity is the character of its virtue. Asserted identities: = Water of Life — “It has been called the Water of Life, because it gives life to the metals” [IV.3 ¶9]; = great Lunaria — “it is properly called the great Lunaria, because of its brightness wherewith it shines” [IV.3 ¶9].

Identified with: Water of Life [IV.3 ¶9]; great Lunaria [IV.3 ¶9]

See also: Water

References: IV.3 ¶9

Pope

person

Pope, whose Homer’s Iliad Atwood quotes while criticizing his rendering of the heroic tears as ‘unavailing’.

Atwood quotes Pope’s Iliad, book 18 — “Patroclus dead, Achilles hates to live.” [III.1 ¶29; III.1 n35] — and criticizes him for rendering the heroic tears ‘unavailing’ [III.1 ¶30].

References: III.1 n35, III.1 ¶29, III.1 ¶30

Pope John XXII

person

Pope said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it.

Atwood reports that Pope John XXII is said to have practised the art he interdicted and enriched the treasury by it, illustrating its continued secret pursuit [I.1 ¶55].

References: I.1 ¶55

Pope’s Homer’s Odyssey

treatise · Odyssey

Pope’s Homer’s Odyssey, book 8, read as figuring the dominion of Intellect and the sea barring the goal.

Atwood quotes Pope’s Odyssey, book 8 — “In wondrous ships self-moved, instinct with mind;” [IV.1 ¶20; IV.1 n20] — reading the Phoeacian ships and Alcinous’ court as the dominion of Intellect and the vast sea as the barrier before the goal [IV.1 ¶21–24; IV.1 n21].

References: IV.1 n20, IV.1 n21, IV.1 ¶20, IV.1 ¶21, IV.1 ¶22, IV.1 ¶24

Pordage

person

Author of Mundorum Explicatoio, quoted for verse on the sphere where God displays himself to himself.

Atwood quotes Pordage’s Mundorum Explicatoio (p. 320): “Here ‘tis that God himself t’ himself displays” [III.2 ¶18; III.2 n19], illustrating the sphere of divine self-display.

References: III.2 n19, III.2 ¶18

Pordage and Lead school

collective voice

A school Atwood says is not to be undervalued, on the same original track as Boehme.

Atwood says the Pordage and Lead school is not to be undervalued, being on the same original track as Boehme [I.1 ¶68].

References: I.1 ¶68

Porphyry

person · Prophyry

Neoplatonist whose Auxiliaries to Intelligibles and Cave of the Nymphs Atwood cites on purification, the twofold death, the soul’s reunion with its source and pure Matter.

Named among the Alexandrian revival figures [I.1 ¶27], the Neoplatonists who dilate on the same ground [II.1 ¶39] and whose writings show the Mysteries [II.2 ¶9], and in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25]. His Auxiliaries supply a chapter motto: “It s necessary that the soul, when purified, should associate with its Generator.” [II.3 ¶2; cf. II.3 ¶43]. A moist spirit binds the soul to images and earth: “If the soul on its departure, says Porphyry, still possesses a spirit turbid from humid exhalations, it then attracts to itself a shadow and becomes heavy” [II.3 ¶27; II.3 n29]; leaving nature makes it a dry splendor. He explains the twofold death, which Atwood glosses — “the other peculiar to philosophers, in which the soul is liberated from the body” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n45]. His Hymn to Plotinus illustrates waking vision: “Nor was the vision like the dreams of sleep, But seen whilst vigilant you brave the deep” [II.3 ¶51; II.3 n57]. The Cave of the Nymphs supports the northern and southern gates as descent into generation and ascent to divinity [II.4 ¶7; II.4 n2]; the self-reflexive vision is “a fountain, not flowing outwardly, but circularly scattering its streams into itself” [II.4 ¶15; II.4 n6]. When discipline is complete “the motions themselves will be dissolved through their proximity to the reasoning power” [II.4 ¶36–37; II.4 n25]. Additions of place or selfhood veil the Eternal Essence; “being established in yourself and in your own Essence, you will be assimilated to the Intelligible Universe” [III.2 ¶59; III.2 n44]. With Plotinus he is co-source of the summary on pure Matter [III.2 ¶46], and ‘the Greek Porphyry’ appears in the Ammonius story [III.2 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶27, II.1 ¶39, II.2 n13, II.2 ¶9, II.3 n24, II.3 n29, II.3 n45, II.3 n57, II.3 ¶2, II.3 ¶24, II.3 ¶27, II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶43, II.3 ¶51, II.4 n2, II.4 n25, II.4 n6, II.4 ¶15, II.4 ¶36, II.4 ¶37, II.4 ¶7, III.1 ¶25, III.2 n44, III.2 ¶46, III.2 ¶59, III.2 ¶64

Potable gold

term

A product which, like the philosophers’ stone, takes its beginning from the divine water (per Hermolaus Barbarus).

Quoting Hermolaus Barbarus, the divine water is that “whence potable gold, and the stone of philosophers, takes its beginning” [I.1 ¶20].

See also: Gold

References: I.1 ¶20

Powder of projection

term

The transmuting agent in the Dee/Kelly story, found at Glastonbury and so strong its true height had to be found by trial.

In the Dee/Kelly story Atwood relates the finding of “a large quantity of the Powder of Projection in a niche amongst the ruins of Glastonbury Abbey” [I.1 ¶66]; it was so strong (1 upon 272,330) that its ‘true height’ had to be found by trial.

See also: Projection

References: I.1 ¶66

Powder of transmutation

term

Transmuting powder said by Dickenson to have been found in Lully’s cell, enriching the workmen.

Per Dickenson, “a certain quantity of the powder of transmutation” [I.1 ¶47] was found in Lully’s cell and enriched the workmen.

See also: Transmutation

References: I.1 ¶47

The Power

term

What secrecy ensured could be discovered only by the long labour of an experienced, upright mind.

Atwood says secrecy was kept “that the Power might only be discovered through the long labour of an experienced and upright mind” [III.4 ¶9].

References: III.4 ¶9

Power and motive in alliance

term

The double capacity figured by Cheiron, who educates the Heroic Fire and rectifies the Armed Magnet.

Atwood describes Cheiron “in his double capacity of Power and Motive in alliance” [IV.1 ¶33], educating the Heroic Fire and rectifying the Armed Magnet.

References: IV.1 ¶33

Power hidden in man

term

The Light shining in darkness within man, identified with the true Light; an enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple.

Atwood: “This therefore is that Power which is hidden in man, the true Light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [II.3 ¶55] — thus = the true Light. It is “An enchanted treasury known only to the wisely simple” [II.3 ¶55].

Identified with: True light [II.3 ¶55]

References: II.3 ¶55

Power life

term

One of three modes of consciousness, with the sensible and perceptive, which conjoined to them makes them efficient (Appendix).

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood names three modes: “either in the sensible, the perceptive, or the power life; this last conjoined to the other two makes them efficient” [APP ¶45].

See also: Life

References: APP ¶45

Practice

term

The operative procedure of the Hermetic work, which Atwood seeks to understand rather than exhibit, touching only certain particulars.

Atwood distinguishes understanding from exhibiting the operative procedure: “But we are not yet proposing to exhibit the Practice, but only to understand it” [III.1 ¶56]. She sets out impediments and endowments “before we enter on the routine of Practice” [III.4 ¶2], and at the close says she has “suggested certain particulars concerning the Practice at this latter end” [IV.3 ¶54], which may be unfamiliar to the reader.

References: III.1 ¶56, III.4 ¶2, IV.3 ¶54

Praetextus

person

Cited for reference only.

References: II.2 n8

Praxithea

person

Mother of Hippocrates, of the race of the Heraclides.

Named as Hippocrates’ mother, of the race of the Heraclides [IV.3 ¶32].

References: IV.3 ¶32

Prayer

term · prayers, pray, prayed

Desire directed to its object, above all to God for wisdom; it collects the mind and, joined with labour, brings revelation, and esoterically works within the operations themselves.

Atwood treats prayer first in a broad sense: “every desire of the mind is in its kind a prayer and preparative for the acquirement of its object” [III.4 ¶22]. Directed especially to God for wisdom, it collects the mind and, joined with labour (cooperation), brings revelation; “prayer especially, which is its principle exercise, is profitable for great undertakings” [III.4 ¶22]. She then goes further: “But the esoteric ground brings us acquainted with prayer in a far deeper sense” [III.4 ¶22], where prayer works within the operations of the Art; she reports that Iamblicus distinguishes three classes of prayer leading to union and the Divine Fire.

Asserted identities: prayer = the great desire of knowing — “for if you burn with a great desire of knowing them, that is prayer” [III.4 ¶22]; and prayer as the Divine Key — “It likewise is the Divine Key which opens to men the penetralia of Wisdom” [III.4 ¶24]. In the method, prayer thus appears both as the disposing desire of the operator and, in the deeper sense, as an active part of the work (the exact mode of that working is not spelled out in these records).

Identified with: great desire of knowing [III.4 ¶22]; Divine Key [III.4 ¶24]

References: III.4 ¶22, III.4 ¶24

Preacher

collective voice

The Preacher, cited by Atwood for the veiled, pointed nature of wise writings and for the need of a companion in the work.

Atwood cites the preacher twice. First, to illustrate the pointed, veiled character of the writings of the wise: “The words of the wise are as goads” [III.4 ¶19]. Second (with the reference Eccels. 4:8,9), in support of her point that the work needs a companion, a medium and a bond, since one alone labours endlessly: “Behold, two are better than one, says the Preacher” [III.4 ¶30; III.4 n27]. In both she uses him approvingly as support for her own position.

References: III.4 n27, III.4 ¶19, III.4 ¶30

Preliminary practice

term · preliminary work

The earlier, preliminary part of the practice, handed down inconsistently; Atwood holds that knowing it is insufficient without the ultimate theory.

Atwood speaks of the preliminary practice as handed down inconsistently, and insists that mastery of it does not suffice without the ultimate theory: there are “many even with a perfect knowledge of the preliminary work, and having the true Matter in Hand also and means of purification” [IV.2 ¶4] who nevertheless fail.

See also: Practice

References: IV.2 ¶4

Preparation

term · preparations

The preparatory stage of the work: for Flamel, preparing the prime agents, the hardest part; for Atwood, a stage exercising every faculty of the mind, sometimes lasting years.

Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood, makes the preparation of the first principles or prime agents the most difficult part of the work, after which the magistery is easy: “For knowing the preparations of the prime agents, and then literally following the directions in my book, I could not then miss the work if I would.” [I.1 ¶57].

In Atwood’s own voice the Preparation is a stage in which no part of the concord may be left out: one must not “deny any faculty of the mind its due exercise in the Preparation” [III.4 ¶28]. She also notes its length: “Years have been employed by some in the Preparation” [IV.1 ¶17]. Whether her Preparation is the same as Flamel’s preparation of the prime agents is not stated in these records See also Preparatory Practice and prime agents.

References: I.1 ¶57, III.4 ¶28, IV.1 ¶17

Preparatory practice

term

A practice Atwood defers to a later discussion, there to show the value of assistance; Norton describes it.

Atwood (ATWOOD) postpones discussion of the Preparatory Practice to a later point, where the value of assistance will be clearer: “when we come to speak of the Preparatory Practice which Norton, naively, and without much envy, describes” [III.4 ¶36].

See also: Practice

References: III.4 ¶36

Preparing spirit

term · the Spirit preparing its body

In an adept’s account, the spirit that dissolves and cleanses the body of Light and draws from it a second, tinging Spirit.

Voice: an adept quoted by Atwood. The Preparing Spirit dissolves and purifies the body of Light and extracts from it a Second, tinging Spirit: “The Preparing Spirit dissolves the body of Light, and cleanses it from the corrupting causes” [IV.1 ¶10].

See also: Spirit

References: IV.1 ¶10

Prester

term

Zoroaster’s term, which Atwood reads as the Fire Spirit of Life, the supernatural centre of every living thing, which the Art sought to multiply and exalt.

An adept quoted by Atwood pairs the Prester with the Sun: “the miraculous conspiracy that is between the Prester and the Sun, the external and internal fire of life, the thing desiring and the thing desired” [II.3 ¶41].

Atwood herself identifies it: “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54] — the identity sustaining all things, the supernatural centre of every living thing. The perfection of the Art was “to multiply the Prester and place him in the most supreme Ether” [II.3 ¶56].

In a Chaldaic oracle she quotes, the Prester is the Flower of glowing Fire drawn from the matter springing from “The Matrix containing all things” [IV.2 ¶28]: “Whence is extracted a Prester the Flower of glowing Fire,” [IV.2 ¶28], flashing into the cavities of the world. The oracle passage is not further explained there.

Identified with: Fire Spirit of Life [II.3 ¶54]; Flower of glowing Fire [IV.2 ¶28]

References: II.3 ¶41, II.3 ¶54, II.3 ¶56, IV.2 ¶28

Presters of intellectual fire

term · Intellectual Presters of Intellectual Fire

In Chaldaic oracle language used by Atwood, the powers of intellectual fire to which all things are subject and which follow their First Cause in order.

The phrase comes from the Chaldaic Oracle, taken up in Atwood’s own discussion (the records do not separate the two voices sharply): “to these Intellectual Presters of Intellectual Fire all things are subservient by the persuasive will of the Father” [II.4 ¶33]; and “the Presters of Intellectual Fire follow in radiant order the will of their First Cause” [II.4 ¶38]. See Prester.

See also: Fire

References: II.4 ¶33, II.4 ¶38

Prime agents

term

In Flamel’s account, the initial agents of the work, whose preparation must be known before the work can succeed.

Voice: Nicholas Flamel, quoted by Atwood. The preparation of the prime agents is the key requirement: “knowing the preparations of the prime agents” [I.1 ¶57]. In the same account Flamel apparently uses the phrase in place of first principles, though the identity is not explicitly asserted. See Preparation.

See also: Agent

References: I.1 ¶57

Primitive ether

term

For some modern Kabalists cited by Atwood, the pure attracting vacuum or understanding, born of the concentrated Divinity, that draws the central efficient into will and operation.

Voice: some modern Kabalists, reported by Atwood. The primitive Ether is born of the concentrated Divinity like a shower from a cloud, and is identified as “the primitive Ether, which is the pure attracting vacuum, or understanding” [III.2 ¶13], which draws the central efficient to will and operation.

Identified with: pure attracting vacuum / understanding [III.2 ¶13]

See also: Ether

References: III.2 ¶13

Prince

collective voice

An author cited from the Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection, whom Atwood uses to show that the student must gather the dispersed teaching and test it.

Atwood quotes the prince (work given as Epilogue to the Invest. Of Perfection) in support of her view that the student must collect the dispersed teaching and test it by experiment: “let the sapient artificer, concludes the prince, studiously peruse our books, collecting our dispersed intention” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n15].

References: III.4 n15, III.4 ¶20

Principiating substance

term

In Reuchlin, the second of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word: incorruptible, immutable and always subsistent.

Voice: Reuchlin, quoted by Atwood. Of the two catholic natures in the mirific Word, the second is set against the visible, changing nature: “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24].

References: III.2 ¶24

Principium

term

The beginning or principle of the work, which Atwood identifies with the intention; hard to find because the rational ferment lies hidden in our life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood identifies the principium with the intention: “The difficulty is to find this principium, the intention” [APP ¶35]. The difficulty arises because the rational ferment is hidden in our life.

Identified with: the intention [APP ¶35]

References: APP ¶35

Principle

term · Principe

The one source to which all things, thoughts and actions are resolved and from which every particular can be recomposed; the final term of the soul’s ascent.

Atwood presents the Principle as the end of the soul’s ascent — the ascent rises “afterwards to the Principle of things” [III.3 ¶26] — and as the one source into which all things, thoughts, passions and actions are resolved. Whoever reaches it gains more than possession: “he will not alone have that Principle, and be able to compose and renumerate every former particular out of the same” [III.3 ¶39]. The method apparently involves resolving everything into its source and recomposing from it. See also Principle of things.

See also: Principles

References: III.3 ¶26, III.3 ¶39

Principle of reunion

term

For the Hebrew Kabalists, a principle remaining in the life of fallen individuals that will in time restore them to their source in higher perfection.

Voice: the Hebrew Kabalists / Rabbis, as Atwood reports them. Even after the fall, “the principle of reunion nevertheless abides in the generated life of individuals” [II.1 ¶41], and in time it will restore them to their source in a higher perfection.

References: II.1 ¶41

Principle of things

term

That with which the intellectual energy of the intelligible world keeps perpetual, tranquil contact, and from that contact generates Light.

Atwood writes that the intellectual energy of the intelligible world “generates Light through a perpetual tranquil and quiet contact with the Principle of things” [II.4 ¶16]. See Principle, where the same phrase names the final term of the soul’s ascent [III.3 ¶26].

See also: The Thing

References: II.4 ¶16

Principle of universal science

term

A real and efficacious principle that Atwood holds lies latent in human life and can be known only under specified conditions.

Atwood asserts “a Principle of Universal Science latent in human life, real and efficacious” [II.1 ¶39], which can be known only under specified conditions.

References: II.1 ¶39

Principles

term

What the Hermetic names Sulphur, Salt, Mercury and the elements refer to, as opposed to qualities; in Eudoxus, the principles of ‘our Mercury’ separated in the Third Key.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood states that the Hermetic names — Sulphur, Salt, Mercury, water, air, fire — refer to principles, not qualities, though “in the spirit they become qualities” [APP ¶81].

Eudoxus, quoted by Atwood, speaks of the principles of ‘our Mercury’ (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury), extracted after sublimation and then separated and purified in the Third Key: “the separation and the purification of the Principles of our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶7].

See also: Principle

References: IV.3 ¶7, APP ¶81

Principles of Eternity

term

In Boehme, the three leaves of the inner book (the image of God) in which he finds all that scripture teaches.

Voice: Boehme, quoted by Atwood. The inner book he opened, the image of God, holds everything scripture teaches: “my book hath only three leaves, the same are the Principles of Eternity” [III.2 ¶16].

Identified with: three leaves of the inner book [III.2 ¶16]

References: III.2 ¶16

A priori

term · a priore

Inquiry from the inner, causal ground: for Atwood the true method for first truths, which then proves itself a posteriori by its effects.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the a priori method, inquiry from the inner causal ground, against the inductive method: “The a priori method is the true one for the discovery of the first truths” [APP ¶120]. Only the soul’s lapse into selfhood hinders it. Once established, “it proceeds to prove itself a posteriori by efficient procedure, as it were by what is commonly called miracle” [APP ¶120]. See a priori ground.

References: APP ¶120

A priori ground

term

The ancients’ philosophical method, contrasted with modern inductive science; long neglected, it is the ground Atwood wants philosophy to return to.

Atwood contrasts the ancients’ method with modern inductive science and wants philosophy to “return with her instruments to work as formerly on the a priori ground” [III.1 ¶8], a ground long left uncultivated. See a priori.

References: III.1 ¶8

Proclus

person

Author of works on Plato whom Atwood cites often on the Mysteries, initiation, the soul’s purification and its union with the One, almost always in support.

Atwood names Proclus among the Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge, to be quoted later [I.1 ¶27]. She also lists him among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9], and in the ‘golden chain of Hermetic philosophers’ who traced the poets’ allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25].

She uses him throughout in support of her own account:

  • The mundane or phantastic spirit: “it folds itself about the indivisibility of true intellect (which is in its center)” [II.2 ¶15].
  • Why Theseus and Pirithous were detained in Hades, a reading she endorses [II.3 ¶13].
  • Deceptive images come before illumination: “In the most holy Mysteries, says he, before the presence of the god, the impulsive forms of certain terrestrial demons appear” [II.3 ¶22; II.3 n17]. She applies the same to the speculation of Wholes. In the Hymn to the Sun, demons keep souls in the body, forgetful of their origin: “Demons who machinate a thousand ills,” [II.3 ¶24; II.3 ¶25].
  • Astonishment at the mystic spectacles: “Beauty shining forth astonishes those that behold it, converts the soul to itself” [II.3 ¶50; II.3 n53].
  • Hercules’ purification, the Elysian fountains and the Meadow as the prolific power of life: “the plain of Truth, he says, is intellectually expanded to intelligible Light” [II.4 ¶3; II.4 ¶16; II.4 n8].
  • Grades of initiation and the soul’s inward conversion: “there are indeed many steps of ascent, but all of them extend to the Paternal port and the Paternal Initiation” [II.4 ¶23; II.4 ¶29; II.4 n15, n21, n22]. Initiation comes through faith-given silence: “what else than faith is the cause of this ineffable muesis?” [II.4 ¶40; II.4 n29]. The goal: “This, then, is the Paternal Port and the discovery of the Father, according to Proclus, viz., an undefiled union with him” [II.4 ¶41].
  • The twofold Apollonical Intellect, paralleling Wisdom and Power: “the prophetic power unfolds the simplicity of truth and takes away the variety of that which is false” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n50].
  • “Heaven, he says, is the intellectual contact with the intelligible” [III.2 ¶36; III.2 n31].
  • To discover the One Principle one must be assimilated to it: “he must raise himself to that which is most united in nature, and to its flower” [III.2 ¶50].
  • The god torn, preserved and renewed (Hymn to Minerva): “The heart of Bacchus, swiftly slaughtered king, Was saved in Aether” [III.3 ¶70; III.3 n47].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says he develops the ontological basis of the Iliad [APP ¶157]. She also praises his Commentary on the Timaeus, which treats Time as the image’s participation of the Paradigm, against the relational view held by her addressee and by modern metaphysicians [APP ¶172].

References: I.1 ¶27, II.1 n33, II.1 ¶39, II.2 ¶15, II.2 ¶9, II.3 n17, II.3 n22, II.3 n30, II.3 n53, II.3 ¶13, II.3 ¶22, II.3 ¶24, II.3 ¶25, II.3 ¶27, II.3 ¶50, II.4 n15, II.4 n21, II.4 n22, II.4 n29, II.4 n8, II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶23, II.4 ¶29, II.4 ¶3, II.4 ¶40, II.4 ¶41, III.1 n50, III.1 ¶25, III.1 ¶45, III.2 n31, III.2 n34, III.2 ¶36, III.2 ¶50, III.3 n47, III.3 ¶70, APP ¶157, APP ¶172

Profundity

term

One of the alchemists’ three periods, which Atwood identifies with the subjective life, the water below.

Atwood names the Profundity as one of the alchemists’ three periods and explains it: “the Profundity is the subjective life, the water that is below” [III.3 ¶72].

Identified with: the subjective life, the water that is below [III.3 ¶72]

References: III.3 ¶72

Projection

term · projections, Projeccion, projected, project, projecting

The final operation: casting the Stone, powder or medicine onto a metal or mercury to tinge or transmute it, which Atwood also extends to ‘the imperfect metal of any life’.

Projection is the application of the finished Stone, powder or medicine to a substance to transmute it. In Atwood’s historical accounts: Arnold’s “wonderful projections he made with the transmuting powder” [I.1 ¶43]; “In Dee’s diary we have the account of Kelly making projection with one small grain” [I.1 ¶66]; “However, I made projection of a part” [I.1 ¶73]. Flamel, after the magistery: “Having attained this, I came now to the Projection; and the first time I made projection, was upon mercury” [I.1 ¶57], turning it to silver, and with the Red Stone to gold. Van Helmont: “I have made projections divers times” [I.1 ¶76], casting a little powder on boiling quicksilver.

Technical conditions: an adept says the medicine must first be fermented with pure gold, or “there would ensue loss and damage in the projection” [I.3 n70]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon says continually fermented medicine grows stronger: “And sure far it will be exalted at the last, And in Projeccion ren full fast:” [III.1 ¶65]. Atwood advises that “it is always best to make projection by degrees until the Stone yields no more tincture” [IV.3 ¶20], onto purified metal. She gives an alternative name: “the final Projection, as the metalline perfectibility of the matter is sometimes called” [IV.3 ¶19].

Some sources limit its importance. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The fifth and last gate is projection.” [III.3 ¶63], which serves only for metals. Eudoxus deliberately leaves “the Projection of the Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16] undescribed, since success does not depend on it.

Atwood also applies the term beyond metals: the Mercury “projected on the imperfect metal of any life, dissolves, drawing away the foundation into itself” [III.3 ¶32].

Identified with: metalline perfectibility of the matter [IV.3 ¶19]

References: I.1 ¶43, I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶73, I.1 ¶76, I.3 n70, III.1 ¶65, III.3 ¶32, III.3 ¶63, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶19, IV.3 ¶20

Prometheus, Vulcan and Minerva

collective voice · Prometheus, Vulcan, Minerva

Mythic figures Atwood uses to picture the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire.

Atwood illustrates the method of ascent as the artistic fabrication of the Fire, which Prometheus received from Vulcan and Minerva disseminated [IV.4 ¶8].

References: IV.4 ¶8

Promised land

term

Atwood’s image for the goal beyond the sea of sense, which a haven and signal marks direct one to.

Atwood (ATWOOD) writes that beyond the sea of sense “there is a haven and signal marks to direct where the Promised Land is to be found” [IV.4 ¶32].

References: IV.4 ¶32

Prophecies

collective voice

Prophecies of the Fourth Monarchy that Atwood notes but does not dwell on.

Atwood reports prophecies foretelling the Fourth Monarchy — “Many prophecies there are of times to come” [IV.3 ¶49] — but does not tarry on them.

References: IV.3 ¶49

Prophet

collective voice

A prophetic voice cited from the Book of Enoch on those who misuse secrets, and in the Ordinal on the feeding of the matter.

Atwood cites the prophet (Book of Enoch, cap. 64, sect. 2) in support: those who discover secrets and turn them to ill account are judged — “They have discovered secrets, and these are they who are to be judged” [III.4 ¶6; III.4 n3]. She identifies them with Geber’s avaricious. In the Ordinal, as quoted, the prophet’s words are cited as a wondrous mention of the feeding of the matter, ‘If ye apply it to this intention’: “Visitasti terram et inebriasti eam,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: ‘Thou hast visited the earth and watered it’).

References: III.4 n3, III.4 ¶6, IV.1 ¶12

Proserpine

term

In Atwood’s reading, the intellect’s congenial life: our lapsed soul, hidden in her dark hypostasis.

Atwood glosses Proserpine as the intellect’s “own congenial life, which is Proserpine, and that lapsed soul of ours, seated in her dark hypostasis unknown” [II.3 ¶11].

Identified with: lapsed soul [II.3 ¶11]

References: II.3 ¶11

Prosopopoeia of the Stone

treatise

A verse piece, apparently spoken by the Stone, cited by Atwood for the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation.

Atwood cites the Prosopopoeia of the Stone (references given as Theatr. Chem., Tome 3, p. 764; Processus Chiica, Carmen Elegans; Vaughan’s magia Adamica) to illustrate the balanced state in which the principles neither die nor live during the severation: “I am not dead although my spirit’s gone,” [III.1 ¶53; III.1 ¶54; III.1 n59].

See also: Stone

References: III.1 n59, III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶54

Protean life

term

In the later Appendix, Atwood’s name for the shape-shifting life sought in the work, which she says is very hard to discover.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says “The Protean life is very difficult of discovery” [APP ¶171]. Its last shape, she indicates, is a tree [APP ¶171].

See also: Life

References: APP ¶171

Proteus

term

Atwood’s figure for the one ever-changing universal entity of life, the subject of the work, identified with Mercury, the quintessence and the mercury of the Philosophers.

Atwood uses Proteus as an image of the one subject in all its changing forms. In Part I she says “For Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36], citing the verse “Etherial, watery, earthy general soul, Immortal Fire! Even all the world is thine And pars of thee, O Proteus, power divine;” [I.2 ¶35]. She equates it with the Mercury and the quintessence: “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37]. In a footnote Proteus is the image of the one agent that is a serpent on earth, a fish in water and a bird in air, “yet is, not withstanding, One throughout the multiformity of nature” [I.3 n55].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) makes the same identification. Proteus is “the one universal entity of life, the omnia in omnibus before manifestation and individuality, the thing of which you may assert everything; Proteus.” [APP ¶138]. All descriptions of the Matter refer to it, and the work is said to be mechanical as well as alchemical, using instruments and vessels. It is also the world’s “dissolved essence which is the mercury of the Philosophers, Proteus.” [APP ¶144].

Identities asserted: = Mercury, = quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; = one universal entity of life, = omnia in omnibus [APP ¶138]; = mercury of the Philosophers [APP ¶144].

Identified with: one universal entity of life [APP ¶138]; omnia in omnibus [APP ¶138]; Mercury [APP ¶144]; Mercury; quintessence [I.2 ¶37]

References: I.2 ¶35, I.2 ¶36, I.2 ¶37, I.3 n55, APP ¶138, APP ¶144

Proto-chemistry of Hermes

term

The field in which an adept cited by Atwood claims to have manual experience.

Atwood cites an adept’s claim to “his own manual experience in the proto-chemistry of Hermes” [II.1 ¶11]. The packet gives no further explanation. Compare protochemistry and Protochemic Artifice.

See also: Hermes

References: II.1 ¶11

Protochemic artifice

term · Proto-chemic artifice

The practical art through which, according to Vaughan, the true foundation is found; Atwood sums up its whole performance as solution, sublimation and fixation.

In a passage attributed to Vaughan, a knowledge of this art comes before the philosophy of Wisdom: “a knowledge of the Protochemic Artifice; for that by means of this, and this only, the true foundation is discoverable” [II.1 ¶26]. Atwood, in her own voice, reduces it to three operations: “All that is performed in the Proto-chemic artifice may be comprehended in three terms” [III.2 ¶64]. These three terms are solution, sublimation and fixation.

References: II.1 ¶26, III.2 ¶64

Protochemistry

term

The protochemistry of Hermes, which Atwood says is the ground of Vaughan’s discourse on the nature of man.

Atwood says that Vaughan’s discourse on the nature of man is “grounded on the protochemistry of Hermes” [I.1 ¶74]. The term is not explained there. Compare proto-chemistry of Hermes and Protochemic Artifice.

References: I.1 ¶74

Proverbs

treatise · Proverbs of Solomon

A biblical book Atwood quotes in support of seeking Wisdom and Self-Knowledge, and which she applies to the Mercury or water of the work.

Atwood cites Proverbs ii, 4, 5 in support of the call to Self-Knowledge: “If thou seekest for her as silver, and searchest for wisdom as for hidden treasures” [I.3 n46]. She uses Proverbs 8, introduced “as Solomon says”, for the worth and promises of Wisdom: “I love them that love me, and those that seek me early shall find me” [IV.3 ¶47; IV.3 n21; IV.3 n24]. She applies Proverbs iv, 8, 9 to the Mercury or water, which crowns the one who exalts her: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n8]. In each case Atwood quotes the text approvingly.

References: I.3 n46, III.3 n8, III.3 ¶17, IV.3 n21, IV.3 n24, IV.3 ¶47

Psalmist

person

Quoted by Atwood in support of the view that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.

Atwood quotes the Psalmist with approval: “I called upon the Lord, exclaims the Psalmist, and He heard me out of His holy temple” [III.4 ¶28]. She uses the line to show that prayer from the inner temple is heard and brings understanding and the Spirit of Wisdom.

References: III.4 ¶28

Psalms

treatise

Praised in the Appendix for their depth of Divine experience, which Atwood says the Mystics have neglected.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Psalms are praised for their “surpassing depth of Divine experience”, and Atwood says the Mystics have neglected them [APP ¶97].

References: APP ¶97

Psellus

person

Commentator on the Chaldaic Oracles whom Atwood cites on material rites, on the Mysteries as Initia, and on apparitions and introspection in the Chaldaic rites.

Atwood cites Psellus’ commentary on the Chaldaic Oracles in support of the view that the soul is perfected by material rites together with divine illumination: “there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites” [II.1 ¶51]. She cites him again as having said that the Mysteries were called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In Part II, ch. 3 she uses his commentary (footnoted as “Pesllus de Oraculis”) on the apparitions of the Chaldaic rites, superinspection among them, as empty products of the soul’s passions: “mere appearances, having no substance, and therefore not signifying anything true” [II.3 ¶20; II.3 n15]. She also contrasts “the Introspection which Psellus speaks of”, the formless Divine Light, with Superinspection in Hades [II.3 ¶46]. In all these places she uses him as support.

References: II.1 ¶51, II.2 ¶4, II.3 n15, II.3 n21, II.3 ¶20, II.3 ¶24, II.3 ¶46

Pseudo-alchemists

term

Atwood’s name for false seekers who followed receipts literally, without theory, in search of gold, as opposed to the true adepts.

Atwood sets the pseudo-alchemists against the true adepts. Their motives were “as those of the pseudo-alchemists, on the other hand, were reckless and despicable” [I.1 ¶41]. They took the receipts literally and, with no theory, worked with mineral sulfur, mercury and salt to make gold: “The pseudo-Alchemists dreamed of gold, and impossible transformations” [II.1 ¶6].

References: I.1 ¶41, II.1 ¶6

Psychical quintessence

term

The threefold separated essence that equals the whole dissolved compound it comes from; it is known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.

Atwood describes the Psychical Quintessence as “being in its own threefold segregated essentiality equal to the whole dissolute compound whence it arises” [III.2 ¶44]. It casts off what is superfluous, and she reads Pythagoras’ hecatomb for his theorem as a symbol of its discovery [III.2 ¶44]. Identity asserted: = Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine (“that miraculous Psychical Quintessence, known to the wise as the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.2 ¶44]).

Identified with: Tincture of the Sapphiric mine [III.2 ¶44]

See also: Quintessence

References: III.2 ¶44

Ptolemy

person

Mentioned only once in the Appendix, where his astronomy is compared with Newton’s.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Ptolemy appears only in a comparison between his astronomy and Newton’s [APP ¶122].

References: APP ¶122

Punctum saliens

term

In the Appendix, the higher Cause of life, which Reason reaches through secondary causes; Atwood also says the earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross.

Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood writes that “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110], and does not explain this further. Elsewhere she identifies the term with “the higher Cause, the punctum saliens of life” [APP ¶152]. Reason reaches it by way of secondary causes and there consciously finds its own roots. Identity asserted: = higher Cause [APP ¶152].

Identified with: higher Cause [APP ¶152]

References: APP ¶110, APP ¶152

Pure crystalline matter

term

In Crollius’ account, the separated and purified medicine that is to be given to our bodies.

Speaking in Crollius’ voice, the passage describes separating and purifying the medicine “that the pure crystalline matter may be administered to our bodies” [III.1 ¶10].

See also: Matter

References: III.1 ¶10

Pure matter

term · pure and divine Matter
