The universal matter that subsists about Intelligibles and mediates between causes and their gross effects; the Theurgic Art makes it manifest, and in the Appendix it is the first, passive product of the work.

In Part III Atwood describes “a certain pure matter subsisting about Intelligibles which is universal” [III.2 ¶46]. It is the origin of all vital and corporeal existence. It is hidden but can be made manifest to sense, and the Theurgic Art makes it manifest. It is connascent with the gods and receives Divinity. She also calls it “a certain pure and divine Matter mediately subsisting between primary and secondary causes and their gross effect” [III.2 ¶49].

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds that, according to Lully, pure matter is not found on earth, and that “You may find out in Plotinus how that pure matter is generated.” [APP ¶43]. There it is the first product of the work: “a pure matter which is passive, having no power of perfecting itself; it is the attractive power” [APP ¶182]. Identity asserted: = the attractive power [APP ¶182].

Identified with: the attractive power [APP ¶182]

See also: Matter

References: III.2 ¶46, III.2 ¶49, APP ¶182, APP ¶43

Purgation

term

The purification of the soul, of which Atwood says Will is the greatest part; for the Paracelsians, the separation of the pure life from impurity, as metal from ore.

Atwood says that “Will is the greatest part of purgation” [II.2 ¶13], where purgation means the purification of the soul. In a passage given in the voice of the Paracelsians, purgation separates the pure life from the impure: “by a due purgation, the pure life is separated, as metal from the dark and sordid ore” [III.1 ¶10].

References: II.2 ¶13, III.1 ¶10

Purification

term · purifications

The cleansing of souls, which Servius says the Bacchic rites served and which was a chief benefit of the Mysteries.

Atwood quotes Servius on the function of the Bacchic rites: “the sacred rites of Bacchus pertained to the purification of souls” [II.2 ¶5]. In the same paragraph the benefits of the Mysteries are given as “moral enlightenment and purification of life” [II.2 ¶5].

See also: Vital purification

References: II.2 ¶5

Purificative rites

term

The stage of the Mysteries that follows the revealing of the Medial Life; it restores the rule of reason and frees the inclination from sense before the deeper initiations.

Atwood places the Purificative Rites after the revealing of the Medial Life. They were rites “which were designed also to restore the monarchy of reason in the soul” [II.2 ¶20], and they prepare for the final initiations. The deeper mysteries require them, because after them comes “the inclination being already freed from the dominion and all the superficial progeny of sense” [II.3 ¶9].

References: II.2 ¶20, II.3 ¶9

Purified spirit or intelligence

term

The agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward; Atwood identifies it with Isis.

Atwood describes the purified spirit or intelligence as the agent that dissolves the vital medium and draws the Voluntary Efficient upward. Identity asserted: = Isis (“the purified spirit or intelligence, that is Isis” [III.1 ¶23]).

Identified with: Isis [III.1 ¶23]

See also: Intelligence

References: III.1 ¶23

Putrefaction

term · putrefied, putrefy

The decay and death that, according to Atwood, comes before every new form: linked with blackness (the ‘gate of blackness’, the ‘blackness of the night’), in which the matter dies and corrupts before it rises again.

Atwood states that “putrefaction precedes the generation of every new form into existence” [I.3 n42], and links it with the ‘gate of blackness’. In the crow image she explains: “The blackness of the night is the putrefaction of the same” [I.3 n12]. The matching ‘clearness of the day’ is resurrection to a relative purity. In a passage quoted from Hermes, the darkened matter “lives in the putrefaction” [I.3 ¶48], and its dark clouds are changed.

In Part III Atwood applies the term to the decay of the vital vapour under the ferment. More generally, she applies it to the death and corruption that every life passes through before rising better, as a seed does: “Does not the grain putrefy in the moist earth before it springs?” [III.1 ¶30]. Morien, quoted in Part IV, describes the earth as having its water drawn off and returned again and again “until the earth is completely putrefied” [IV.1 ¶41]. The earth is then corrupt, without its Form, and dead for a season.

Identity asserted: = blackness of the night [I.3 n12].

Identified with: blackness of the night [I.3 n12]

References: I.3 n12, I.3 n42, I.3 ¶48, III.1 ¶30, IV.1 ¶41

Pyrotechnical induction

term

Atwood’s name for the vital experiment, through which powers, the regenerative original and temptations were revealed to conscience.

Atwood uses the phrase for the vital experiment: “by this pyrotechnical induction, powers were revealed to conscience” [IV.4 ¶9]. What was revealed included the regenerative original and the temptations.

References: IV.4 ¶9

Pyrotechny

term

A term Crollius pairs with physic, saying the two cannot be separated, in the context of trial by fire.

In a passage given in Crollius’ voice, and in the context of trial by fire: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated” [III.1 ¶10].

References: III.1 ¶10

Pythagoras

person · Pythagorus

Greek philosopher whom Atwood cites on Wisdom, on initiatory ordeals and on the Tetractys; she reads his hecatomb symbolically as the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence.

Atwood names Thales and Pythagoras among the early Greek philosophers who sought eastern wisdom, and notes that their writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She cites Pythagoras’ definition of Wisdom as “the science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39; II.1 n36]. She also uses him as an example of the long preparations and ordeals required before admission to the deeper mysteries, and of the purifying of disciples’ souls [II.2 ¶11].

She reports that Aristotle criticized him for explaining essence by number [III.2 ¶40]. She then reads his hecatomb, offered for the right-angle theorem, as a symbol of the discovery of the Psychical Quintessence [III.2 ¶43; III.2 ¶44]. She identifies the Conjunction with “that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer, spelled “Pythagorus”), his Tetractys is obtained by theurgic multiplication and is the kind of ens that underlies the stone. Atwood calls it “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108]. Throughout, Atwood uses him as support.

See also: Biographer of Pythagoras

References: I.1 ¶12, II.1 n36, II.1 ¶39, II.2 ¶11, III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶43, III.2 ¶44, III.3 ¶33, APP ¶108

Pythagoreans

collective voice

Cited in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries bring about assimilation and final contact with the first principle.

Atwood cites the Pythagoreans in support of the view that the Greater Mysteries lead to assimilation and final contact with the first principle [II.2 ¶5].

See also: Greeks and eastern sages (Stoics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics), Pythagoric precept

References: II.2 ¶5

Pythagoric precept

collective voice

A precept Atwood quotes as a warning to would-be practitioners, alongside ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.

Atwood quotes the Pythagoric precept “Neither break a superficies” [IV.3 ¶56] as a warning to would-be practitioners and sets it beside the counsel ‘Enlarge not thy destiny’.

See also: Pythagoreans

References: IV.3 ¶56

Q

Quadrature of the circle

term

Impossible by natural means, Atwood says, but demonstrated supernaturally by transmuting the hypostatic relations; whoever finds it perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature.

Atwood writes that “the Quadrature of the Circle was supernaturally demonstrated; which naturally it cannot be” [III.3 ¶30]. It is demonstrated only by transmuting the hypostatic relations. The one who finds it has resolved all things into one Principle and perceives the Universal Mystery of Nature [III.3 ¶30].

References: III.3 ¶30

Qualitate

term · qualitated, qualitates

In the Appendix, to give something specific quality and form: essence is qualitated by Ideas, and the speech of Mind qualitates in the pure Ether.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: “essence is qualitated, i.e., specificated, and receives form from Ideas” [APP ¶37]. Elsewhere she writes: “The speech of Mind uttered into the pure Ether qualitates and specificates.” [APP ¶64]. Identity asserted: = specificate [APP ¶37].

Identified with: specificate [APP ¶37]

References: APP ¶37, APP ¶64

Qualitative virtues

term

The elements as they exist at their source; they multiply into distributive powers whose remote subjects are the sensible elements.

Atwood describes the source as “making elements there to subsist as qualitative virtues, which, multiplying into being, become distributive powers” [III.2 ¶38]. The remote subjects of these powers are the sensible elements.

See also: Virtue

References: III.2 ¶38

Quaternary

term · Quaternarius

In the Adept’s words, the fourfold through which the Ternary is reduced; it is identified with the four elements.

In a passage given in the voice of an Adept, the instruction is to “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18]. Identity asserted: = four elements (“the Quaternarius, or four elements, as some call them” [IV.2 ¶18]).

Identified with: Elements [IV.2 ¶18]

References: IV.2 ¶18

Quellum

term

Van Helmont’s white sand, which Atwood describes as showing itself in a vital soil that no spade or mattock has ever pierced.

Atwood describes Van Helmont’s Quellum, his white sand, as “manifesting itself forth in a vivid vital soil, which spade or mattock never pierced” [III.2 ¶8].

References: III.2 ¶8

Quintessence

term · quintessences, quintessence of philosophers

The essence drawn out by the work: the celestial soul or arising Spirit of universal nature, identified with Mercury, the Elixir of Life, the Free Ether and Lumen Vestimenti.

Atwood treats the Quintessence as no mere speculation: “that elder Quintessence of the magi which they introduce, not as a being of speculation merely, but of experimental science” [I.2 ¶16], obtainable as a compact, tangible essence. In the same passage she reports other names for it: the Kabalists’ “Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light”, and “the Greeks, the Free Ether, that is to say, freed from the prison of gross matter” [I.2 ¶16].

It is identified with the soul: “the quintessence is no other than our viscous celestial and glorious soul drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]; Synesius is quoted to the same effect, “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70]. It is also “This Proteus, then, or Mercury, or quintessence of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37], and a name of the whitened stage: “which, whitening, is called milk, dew, quintessence” [I.2 ¶40].

In the method it is the new life elicited from the crucifixion of the old: “which life is a very real and pure Quintessence, the Mercury so much sought after, even the Elixir of Life” [III.1 ¶49]. After seven repetitions comes “the final resurrection of the Quintessence into a permanent form of life” [I.3 n40]. Atwood says Hermes calls by this name “the arising Spirit of the Universal nature which, persisting separately, bounds as it were, by an invisible summit, every corporeal subsistence” [III.2 ¶36]. An adept reads “the dust of the earth” as “the arising quintessence of the universal nature” [I.3 n51].

It must be handled gently: Vaughan calls it “the sweet spirit of Peace, the true eternal Quintessence”, which “will depart from the elements, leaving both of them and thee to confusion” [III.4 ¶44]. A passage of uncertain voice (possibly the author of The Triumph) directs one to “convert and congeal the new-born Quintessence or mercurial water into an incombustible fixed unguent” [IV.2 ¶6]. Artephius credits his long life to “the use of this admirable quintessence” [I.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “As man was the Quintessence of the whole creation, so woman was the Quintessence of man — the love-spirit was in her” [APP ¶72]; and of the lower spherical quintessences, “these world forms are unstable and, uninformed with the Light Essential, resolve and die” [APP ¶23].

Identified with: Lumen Vestimenti, the Vehicle of Light [I.2 ¶16]; Ether [I.2 ¶16]; Soul [I.2 ¶33]; Proteus; Mercury [I.2 ¶37]; dust of the earth [I.3 n51]; Mercury [III.1 ¶49]; Elixir of Life [III.1 ¶49]; our viscous celestial and glorious soul [III.1 ¶70]; arising Spirit of the Universal nature [III.2 ¶36]; spirit of Peace [III.4 ¶44]; mercurial water [IV.2 ¶6]

References: I.1 ¶36, I.2 ¶16, I.2 ¶33, I.2 ¶37, I.2 ¶40, I.3 n40, I.3 n51, III.1 ¶49, III.1 ¶70, III.2 ¶36, III.4 ¶44, IV.2 ¶6, APP ¶23, APP ¶72

Quintessence of things

term

Phrase from Hermolaus Barbarus’s gloss on the divine water, describing it as of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things.

Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus, who glosses the divine water as “a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. The grammar leaves it unclear whether the water is the quintessence of things or only of its nature.

See also: The Thing

References: I.1 ¶20

Quintessential nature

term

What is found when the elements of the compound creature are divided; further opened, it yields the angelical spirit.

In a quoted adept’s counsel: “divide the elements, and you shall find the quintessential nature” [II.3 ¶52]; opened further, this nature yields the angelical spirit. Atwood also speaks of the son as the quintessential nature concentrated [I.3 n40].

References: II.3 ¶52

R

R. Constantius

person

Author cited as containing allusions that support the story of Lully.

Cited by Atwood as containing allusions supporting the Lully story [I.1 ¶47].

References: I.1 ¶47

R.C.

collective voice

Voice of the Famma et Confessio, cited to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place.

Cited from the Famma et Confessio to illustrate philosophers visiting the Elysian place: “Vidi aliquando Olympicos domos” [II.4 ¶11; II.4 n5] (ours: I once saw the Olympic houses).

References: II.4 n5, II.4 ¶11

Rabbi Ben Jochai

person · Rabbi Ben Jocahi

Rabbi cited from the Zohar on man as the Celestial Prototype and on the dew of light shaken from the hidden head.

Atwood cites the Rabbi (from the Zohar) approvingly for the doctrine of man as Celestial Prototype and image of God: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42; II.1 n38]; he reads ‘The Eternal has founded the earth upon his wisdom’ as referring to the human prototype. Under the spelling “Rabbi Ben Jocahi” he is cited for the white form of the hidden principle and the dew of light: “From his head he shakes a dew which awakens the dead” [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n4].

See also: Ben Jochai (the learned Rassbi; his disciples)

References: II.1 n38, II.1 ¶42, III.2 n4, III.2 ¶3

Rabbi in Zohar

collective voice

Voice of the Zohar cited for Thought as the hidden Principle unfolding into Spirit and articulate voice, which Atwood takes up as her theme.

Atwood quotes: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78; III.3 n50]. She takes up this account of Thought unfolding into Spirit or Intelligence and articulate voice as her theme, calling it a ‘Magnificent, yet impervious assertion’.

See also: Zohar

References: III.3 n50, III.3 ¶78

Radical dissolution of life

term

The dissolution the operator enters once self-will and the other vices have been removed from his mind.

Atwood requires that self-will and the other vices “be removed from the mind of him who is to enter into the radical dissolution of Life” [IV.1 ¶40].

See also: Life

References: IV.1 ¶40

Radical element

term

Something discovered and set free through the adepts’ theory once the superfluities are discharged.

Atwood speaks of “the medium by which the radical element is discovered and set free to the accomplishment of its inclusive law” [I.3 n4], once the superfluities are discharged. Elsewhere the ‘radix’ is to appear under the moist fire [I.3 ¶10]; the text does not explicitly link the two.

See also: Elements

References: I.3 n4

Radical essence

term

What the prophet Enoch beheld in the Place to which he was snatched up, paired with the mystical Adamic Soil.

Atwood mentions “what he beheld of the Radical Essence, and the manifold glories of that mystical Adamic Soil” [III.2 ¶12], of the prophet (Enoch) snatched up to that Place.

See also: Essence

References: III.2 ¶12

Radical humidity

term

In Eudoxus, the body’s essential moisture, consumed by common calcination but preserved and increased by philosophic calcination.

Quoted from Eudoxus: common calcination “consumes the greatest part of its radical humidity” [IV.3 ¶16], whereas philosophic calcination preserves and increases it. In the Fourth Key the earth is moistened with its own humidity [IV.3 ¶16].

References: IV.3 ¶16

Radical moisture

term

The substance of which metals are uniformly composed, which can be withdrawn from inferior forms and pass into a more perfect form.

Atwood equates it with the metals’ subject-matter: “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4]; it can be withdrawn from inferior Forms. Under a fermentive test it passes into a more perfect Form: “The radical moisture of the metal likewise, obeying the fermentive virtue of such a test when applied” [III.2 n38]. Khunrath is quoted that the Stone benefits metals “by transference of their radical moisture” [IV.3 ¶28], removing their terrestreity; this is not further defined.

Identified with: Subject matter [I.2 ¶4]

References: I.2 ¶4, III.2 n38, IV.3 ¶28

Radical moisture of the metals

term

In Sendivogius, what remains after the philosophers’ water consumes the gold and silver.

Quoted from Sendivogius: what remains (‘the tenth part with one part’) after the philosophers’ water consumes the gold and silver — “this shall be the radical moisture of the metals” [IV.3 ¶21].

References: IV.3 ¶21

Radical substance

term

The homogeneous root substance of all things, whose homogeneity is the ground of transmutation.

Atwood grounds transmutation in “the homogeneity of the radical substance of things” [I.2 ¶3].

References: I.2 ¶3

Radix

term

In Geber, the true root of the science, found only by a subtly searching mind.

Quoted from Geber: those without a subtly searching mind “cannot find the true Radix of this most precious science” [III.4 ¶3].

References: III.4 ¶3

Rapport

term

A connection by which one in this state meets the whole image-world of his sphere; the change to a spiritual body comes by divine rapport.

Atwood writes that “each by rapport in this state becomes conversant with the whole phantasmagoric universe of his sphere” [II.3 ¶22], and that one “is changed from an earthly to a spiritual body, by rapport divine” [II.3 ¶29].

References: II.3 ¶22, II.3 ¶29

Rational analysis

term

The operation which, repeatedly passed through, alters the Vital Spirit and dissolves the whole natural born hypostasis.

Atwood: “a true Rational Analysis, which, repeatedly passed through, leads on to a dissolution of the whole natural born hypostasis” [III.1 ¶50]. Elsewhere ‘the mode of analysis’ is said to be directed by the Passive Understanding [III.1 ¶40]; the text does not explicitly link the two phrases.

References: III.1 ¶50

Rational boundary

term

That by which the Matter returns in the Freed Will to consciousness and manifests the Supreme Cause.

Atwood speaks of the Matter “returning by its Rational Boundary in the Freed Will to consciousness” [III.2 ¶60], so manifesting the Supreme Cause. Not further explained.

References: III.2 ¶60

Rational ferment

term

The pure aurific seed of Light hidden in ordinary life, represented by Cadmus, Jason, Orpheus and Aeneas; also named Perscrutinator.

Atwood names the Rational Ferment (also called Perscrutinator) as something “concerning which it will be our purpose to inquire hereafter” [I.3 n32]. In myth it is represented by heroes; of Cadmus: “identified him with Jason, Orpheus, Aeneas, and the rest, who represent the Rational Ferment;” [III.1 ¶66]; the other faculties of the mind are originally attendant on it. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she explains why the principium is hard to find: “the rational ferment, the pure aurific seed of Light, is hidden in this life of ours” [APP ¶35].

Identified with: pure aurific seed of Light [APP ¶35]

See also: Ferment

References: I.3 n32, III.1 ¶66, APP ¶35

Rational form

term

The inbred form according to which the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself.

Atwood: the Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature to itself “according to the Rational Form inbred” [IV.3 ¶29].

See also: Form

References: IV.3 ¶29

Rational light

term

The strongest of lights, the One Leader which, discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit to overcome the corporeal; also the aurific seed.

Atwood: “The Rational Light, once discovered and set in motion, actuates the Spirit” [III.3 ¶23], which then overcomes the corporeal. It is the sole deliverer of the veiled spirit: “there is but One Leader, who should undertake the deliverance; one only, we repeat; he that is allied — the same Rational Light” [III.4 ¶19]; strengthened in practice, it is raised to the ‘allegoric siege of life’ and kindled to overcome the stronghold of evil there.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): Saturn must be satiated from without with plenty “of the honey of the bees“, the aurific seed, the Rational Light” [APP ¶72]; “The Rational Light is the strongest of all lights, and overcomes every other.” [APP ¶168], and once realized all life orders itself round it, constituting re-integration of being. In the inner combat it acts last: deprived of its understanding essence, “the rational intellect goes forth to avenge it and die” [APP ¶153].

Identified with: honey of the bees; aurific seed [APP ¶72]; One Leader [III.4 ¶19]

See also: Light

References: III.3 ¶23, III.4 ¶19, APP ¶153, APP ¶168, APP ¶72

Rational magnet

term

Something moved about by the Almighty force, set beside the image of an established monarch whom inferior powers follow.

Atwood mentions “the Almighty force that moves about the Rational Magnet” [II.4 ¶38], alongside the image of an established monarch followed by the inferior powers. Not further defined.

See also: Magnet

References: II.4 ¶38

Rational part

term

In Porphyry, that which is present with a man himself; being present with it, and absent from externals, is presence with true Being.

Quoted from Porphyry (spelled ‘Prophyry’): one should be “present with that which is present with himself, that is to say, with his rational part” [III.2 ¶59]; such presence, with absence from the external, is presence with true Being.

Identified with: that which is present with himself [III.2 ¶59]

References: III.2 ¶59

Rational permeation

term

The way, by reflexive analysis of the analyzer, of penetrating through Nature’s Understanding into her Causal Light.

Atwood, of reflexive analysis of the analyzer: “this is the way of rational permeation, by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20].

References: IV.1 ¶20

Rational skepticism

term

Reason’s inquiry that proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true; better called discrimination, and required of the Hermetic Student.

Atwood distinguishes it from its mock ally: “Rational skepticism has quite another object and never exhibits itself in the refractory form of its mock ally.” [III.4 ¶15]. It proves all things, rejecting the false and holding the true, and is required of the Hermetic Student: “Such skepticism, more properly perhaps called discrimination” [III.4 ¶15].

Identified with: discrimination [III.4 ¶15]

References: III.4 ¶15

Rational soul

term · animam rationalem

In Sendivogius, the reasons of life and understanding in fire, infused by God into man, by which alone he differs from other creatures and resembles God.

Quoted from Sendivogius: “This soul was of that most pure fire, infused by God into the vital spirit” [II.4 ¶39]; “In it are the reasons of life and understanding, which are distributed in the first infusion of man’s life, and these are called the rational soul” [II.4 ¶39]. By it alone man differs from other creatures and is like God. A Latin line of unclear voice reads “Deus nunquam creavit rem nobiliorem sub coelo praeter animam rationalem” [III.3 ¶81] (ours: God never created a nobler thing under heaven except the rational soul); per this rendering it is ranked against ‘our Mercury’, but the reading is uncertain.

Identified with: the reasons of life and understanding (in Fire) [II.4 ¶39]

See also: Soul

References: II.4 ¶39, III.3 ¶81

Re-integration of being

term

The state in which all life moves orderly round the realized Rational Light.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), once the Rational Light is realized and all life orders itself round it: “This constitutes the re- integration of being” [APP ¶168], called there ‘the manifestation of the **** in man’.

See also: Being

References: APP ¶168

Reason

term · Root of Reason

The superior, supernatural ruling principle in man, temple of the Deity, which as ferment gathers all into its Light; called Wisdom, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture.

Atwood makes Reason the rightful ruler of the soul, around which the inferior powers settle; in this life it is hidden and latent. One “will so venerate this Reason” [II.4 ¶36], and she names it: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39]. It is the dwelling of Deity: “God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace” [II.1 ¶43]; “For this Reason is her temple wherein the Eternal Self-existent dwells” [II.1 ¶50]; and “Reason, which is, as it were, the temple of that Intellectual Ilumination” [III.1 ¶5], entered through the phantasic vestibule.

The superior, supernatural Reason (of which natural reason is the image) works as ferment: “this Reason gaining the ascendancy, would gather all up, as a ferment, into the superior essence and traction of her own Light” [III.1 ¶21], separating false forms and assimilating the inferior life. “It is of this the ancients speak, calling it Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture”; “For it is Light indeed, and an occult splendor of existence transcendentally pure”; it is conceived as “the Intellectual sun” [III.1 ¶21].

It is the one universal faculty consciously distinguishable by itself: “this root of reason which is truly catholic”; “in our mere individual consciousness it is the foundation of all law” [III.1 ¶23]; cut off from its source it is weak and unaware of it. Completed by the work, “reason BECOMING A BRIGHT Light in the periphery of her fiery essence remains immortal, and is the Mistress of Life” [III.3 ¶80], “leaving reason nothing more to doubt of” [III.3 ¶82].

In practice it is man’s “especial prerogative of Reason and rectitude of purpose” [IV.4 ¶12], with “the Reason also, purified and singled out by Art for the encounter” [IV.4 ¶9]. The upright mind submits to the universal Rule, “including all in the catholic perceivance of this Reason”: “let him search for the Root of Reason rationally, and hold by it, and conspire with It” [IV.4 ¶32].

Identified with: her temple [II.1 ¶50]; Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum [II.4 ¶39]; Wisdom, Intellect, Gold, Sol, Sulfur, Tincture [III.1 ¶21]; Light [III.1 ¶21]; Intellectual sun [III.1 ¶21]

See also: Root of reason

References: II.1 ¶43, II.1 ¶50, II.4 ¶36, II.4 ¶39, III.1 ¶21, III.1 ¶23, III.1 ¶5, III.3 ¶80, III.3 ¶82, IV.4 ¶12, IV.4 ¶32, IV.4 ¶9

Rebellious principle

term

A principle with stolen forces provoking conflict in life, whose identical representative the Divine Art requires so those forces can be drawn forth and spent.

Atwood describes a rebellious Principle whose ‘stolen forces’ provoke a bloody conflict in life; the Divine Art requires an identical representative of him so those forces may be drawn forth and spent. Egyptian relics show “innumerable similitudes belonging both to this rebellious Principle and to that identical representative of him which the Divine Art requires” [III.1 ¶64], depicted in human semblance between foes.

See also: Principles

References: III.1 ¶64

term

The recipes of mercenary pretenders, which led people into error and crime.

Atwood blames mercenary pretenders for error and even “the commitment even of egregious crimes by their receipts” [I.1 ¶64].

References: I.1 ¶64

term

In the Appendix, the place where the originals of the true tools are; outward tools only represent these.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of outward tools “they are representatives of these that are in the Recess of Light” [APP ¶100]. The originals of the true tools are thus placed in the Recess of Light; the text gives no further explanation.

See also: Light

References: APP ¶100

collective voice

Plato cites the records of the Mysteries as witness to the saying about the thrysus-bearers [II.4 ¶54].

term

A metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light, in which the visible springs from the invisible.

Atwood: “the recreation was seen to be a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], in which the visible springs from the invisible.

References: III.3 ¶79

term

The fire within the magic earth that spontaneously binds its parts, coagulates them and stops their flux.

Atwood describes the fire within the magic earth: “this fire binds the parts thereof spontaneously to himself, coagulates them, and stops their flux” [III.2 ¶8]. Arresting the flux of the matter is thus this fire’s work.

See also: Fire

References: III.2 ¶8

Recreative force

term

The force the alchemists claim man has brought into action through rational conditioning.

A claim Atwood reports for the Alchemists: “man, by rationally conditionating, has succeeded in developing into action the Recreative Force” [II.1 ¶47]. The text does not define the force further.

References: II.1 ¶47

Red

term · red root

The Red, named as the source of the Citrine; its root, the red root, is identified with the Terra Adamica.

Atwood names the Red as the source of the Citrine and asserts an identity: “The red root is the Terra Adamica” [I.3 n52].

Identified with: Terra Adamica [I.3 n52]

term

Atwood reports that Basil Valentine found “a new method of working the Red Elixir” [I.1 ¶59]; the process had previously been laborious and rarely achieved. She also cites Norton’s lines on the Red Stone as evidence on this point [I.1 ¶60] (see Red Stone).

term

In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., something possessed, together with pure Mercury, by whoever has the vapour of the subject.

References: I.2 ¶30

In Eudoxus, one of the two Mercuries, identified with the most sharp Vinegar and called by others the bath of the Sun.

Eudoxus (quoted) speaks of two Mercuries and identifies one: “the most sharp Vinegar is the Red Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]; he adds that “the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun” [IV.3 ¶10], a name others give it. Asserted identities: = most sharp Vinegar; = bath of the Sun.

Identified with: most sharp Vinegar [IV.3 ¶10]; bath of the Sun [IV.3 ¶10]

term

In Eudoxus, what is struck upon the Stone so that a clear fountain issues from it.

term

What Kelly is believed to have had, whether by secret information or by making it himself.

Atwood reports the belief that Kelly “became possessed of the Red Powder by some secret kind of information” [I.1 ¶66], or else made it himself. The text does not state outright that it is the same as the Powder of Projection.

References: I.1 ¶66

Red Salt

term

What Ripley tried to putrefy by alternate heat and cold, and which he called his Gold.

The text (voice unclear) says Ripley tried to putrefy “this Red Salt which he enviously calls his Gold” [IV.1 ¶36] by alternate heat and cold. Asserted identity: = Gold (Ripley’s name for it).

Identified with: Gold (Ripley’s name) [IV.1 ¶36]

See also: Salt

References: IV.1 ¶36

Red Stone

term · Res Stone

The final perfection of the matter, the form of the Stone that turns mercury into gold; also called phoenix, salamander and royal essence.

Nicholas Flamel (quoted) reports: “I made projection of the Red Stone, on a like quantity of mercury” [I.1 ¶57], yielding gold, where the earlier projection had yielded silver. Norton (quoted) says scarcely one in fifteen kingdoms possesses it — “In fifteen kingdoms hath our Red Stone.” — that it is not to be sought until the white medicine is fully wrought, and that it can be increased in multiplication; the passage also has the form “Had not of our Res Stone consideration” [I.1 ¶60]. Atwood cites these lines as evidence about the Red Elixir. In her own voice the Red Stone is the final perfection of the matter: “it is henceforth a phoenix, salamander, their royal essence and Red Stone” [I.2 ¶40]. Asserted identities: = phoenix; = salamander; = royal essence.

Identified with: phoenix; salamander; royal essence [I.2 ¶40]

See also: Stone

References: I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶60, I.2 ¶40

Red sulphur

term

In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., the red Sulfur contained in the subject, knowledge of which gives the whole foundation.

From the verses quoted from Lucerna Salis Phil.: “And he who knows the red Sulfur which it contains, Has within his power the whole foundation” [I.2 ¶30]. The text does not explain it further.

See also: Sulphur

References: I.2 ¶30

Redness

term

In Hermes, a redness corrupted with water, held like fire in a live coal, to be purified by repeated withdrawal; called the soul.

Hermes (quoted) instructs: “Take, my Son, this redness, corrupted with the water” [I.3 ¶17]; it holds its fire like a live coal and is to be purified by repeated withdrawal. A note identifies it: “the redness is its soul” [I.3 n21], the soul of the passive spirit. Asserted identity: = soul.

Identified with: Soul [I.3 n21]

References: I.3 n21, I.3 ¶17

Refixation

term

In the Appendix, what brings the philosophical dissolution to an end.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the philosophical dissolution that “this continues until the refixation takes place” [APP ¶96].

References: APP ¶96

Reflection

term

Exclaimed over as a most mighty and surpassing magic, right after the account of life’s return to its source; not defined.

Atwood exclaims “Most mighty and surpassing magic of Reflection.” [III.3 ¶79], directly after describing life’s return to its source. The term is not defined there.

References: III.3 ¶79

Regardant subject

term

The inferior nature, i.e. the person engaged in the rite, from whom divine things do not take their principle of energy.

The text (voice unclear) glosses the term itself: divine things do not take their principle of energy “from an inferior nature (i.e., to say, from the regardant subject)” [II.4 ¶31]. The regardant subject is the one engaged in the rite. Asserted identity: = inferior nature.

Identified with: inferior nature [II.4 ¶31]

See also: Subject

References: II.4 ¶31

Regenerate life

term

In the Appendix, the life that begins when the individual mind contacts universal power, ferments the sensorium of this life and lives on its decease.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the contact of the individual mind with power universal is its start: “that experience is the initial of the regenerate life” [APP ¶175]. This life ferments the sensorium of the present life and lives upon its decease. See regeneration.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶175

Regenerate soul

term

The soul that puts on the Stone as a new body.

Atwood says the Stone is what “the regenerate soul puts on as a new body” [IV.4 ¶20]. See regeneration.

See also: Soul

References: IV.4 ¶20

Regenerate Wisdom

term

In the Moorish philosopher, the wisdom of a man reformed into God’s image, by which he possesses all things and unlocks nature’s mysteries.

The Moorish philosopher (quoted) says the man reformed into God’s image “in his regenerate Wisdom possesseth all things, and with this light can unlock the most hidden and recluse mysteries of nature” [II.1 ¶9].

See also: Wisdom

References: II.1 ¶9

Regeneration

term · regenerate, regenerated, regenerating, regeneratively, Hermetic regeneration

The recreative process, physical and spiritual, by which the vital principle is reconstructed, the natural life dissolved and the Identity made; the process the Hermetic Art serves.

Atwood’s term for the process the Art serves. Already in Part I she says the Poimander and Asclepian books “denote rather our divine capabilities and promise of regeneration than the physical ground of either” [I.1 ¶7], that physical ground being treated with the practical method in the Tractatus Aureus; and in early Christianity “the mystery of human regeneration, so zealously proclaimed, was also rationally understood” [I.1 ¶11]. Only by it can an immortal essence “pass into immortality” [II.4 ¶7].

As process: it is the miraculous principle “by which the relationships of the vital elements are exchanged” [III.1 ¶50] — the sensible medium becomes occult and the occult, catholic reason of life becomes manifest. In it is made “that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16], by reprocedure into experience out of an artificially induced dissolute void of life. Upon dissolution of the natural life, “in the regeneration this Reason is said to be discovered” [III.3 ¶52], arising through self-perceivance; the Stone is made manifest regeneratively. It is the physical secret the Mysteries refer to; its first principle: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will” [III.3 ¶77]. It is renewal by Water and the Spirit; “baptismal regeneration was an effectual rite” [IV.2 ¶17], and Christ is brought forth anew as “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. With the fall it is “the ancient doctrine” [IV.3 ¶38], understood only through self-knowledge.

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds: the vital principle is reconstructed “through a regeneration” [APP ¶68] in “the recreative process of the regeneration” [APP ¶55], the macrocosm’s image being evolved before the mental eye; the Hermetically regenerated give up the head life. It brings the whole of life into the Sonship: “It is the death to sin with a new birth awakened in us” [APP ¶79]; begun by the pure earth, it is highest when the spirit, dead to its identity, re-arises as the Divine image — “the condition of the highest regeneration” [APP ¶87]. The philosophic birth “is known in Regeneration, individually proven and proving all” [APP ¶108]; regenerate bodies are penetrated with Light, and the regenerate soul receives body from the residuum of the sensual medium. “The mystery is an art revealed to regenerating men, to advance them on to perfection” [APP ¶146]; it gives freedom to realize every volition, later surrendered to the Father’s Will, and involves “a drawing of power and life up through the feet” [APP ¶158].

References: I.1 ¶11, I.1 ¶7, II.4 ¶7, III.1 ¶50, III.2 ¶16, III.3 ¶52, III.3 ¶77, IV.2 ¶17, IV.2 ¶18, IV.3 ¶38, APP ¶108, APP ¶146, APP ¶158, APP ¶55, APP ¶68, APP ¶79, APP ¶87

Regiment of the colors

term

In the Author of the Open Entrance, the succession of colours the matter passes through, run through again in each multiplication.

The Author of the Open Entrance (quoted) says that in multiplication “every regiment of the colors will in that brief space be passed through” [IV.3 ¶18]: the whole succession of colours recurs, but quickly.

References: IV.3 ¶18

Regio Phantastica

term

In the Appendix, the wise men’s name for the analogical sphere, of only relative truth, valued by Hermetists only for its derived light stripped of phantasmagoric form.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “There is a certain truth in the analogical sphere, but it is only relative. The wise called it the Regio phantastica” [APP ¶105]. For the Hermetists “it was as a pabalum for them, but only when deprived of all phantasmagoric form” [APP ¶105] — valued for the derived light of its essence. Some visionaries “misconceive this Evester, as Paracelsus calls it” [APP ¶105]. Asserted identities: = the analogical sphere; = Evester (Paracelsus’s name).

Identified with: the analogical sphere [APP ¶105]; Evester [APP ¶105]

References: APP ¶105

Religion of Intellect

term

The religion whose pursuit was punished by death once the Mysteries were abandoned, as the Asclepian prophecy foretold.

The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes (quoted) prophesies that in a degenerate age “a capital punishment shall be appointed for him who applies himself to the Religion of Intellect” [I.1 ¶10]. Atwood takes up the phrase, in quotation marks, for the time when the Mysteries were abandoned and Theurgic rites proscribed: “a punishment, no less than death, was menaced against him who dared to pursue the “Religion of Intellect”” [I.1 ¶30]; then “tradition and secular delirium had taken place of intellectual enthusiasm, and idle dreams were set up as oracles in the place of Divine inspiration” [I.1 ¶30]. The term is not further defined.

See also: Intellect

References: I.1 ¶10, I.1 ¶30

Reminiscence

term

The soul’s recovery of what it forgot in embodied life — the awakened recollection of the intellect that the rites produce, sought by Reason in her root of Light.

Atwood: the soul “will recollect all those things, the remembrance of which she loses in the present life” [II.1 ¶50]; souls allied to antecedent realities feel it, “thrilling into reminiscence, as of some long past life forgotten” [II.1 ¶53]; it is also the recovery of the ancient experiment. The rites work by “awakening intellect into reminiscence” [II.4 ¶36], but the hidden Reason cannot “be awakened to reminiscence without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. Reason, roused from lethargy, goes “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15].

References: II.1 ¶50, II.1 ¶53, II.4 ¶36, II.4 ¶39, IV.4 ¶15

Renowned philosophers of various ages and nations

collective voice · individuals of various ages and nations, whose names are renowned in philosophy

Atwood’s description of the witnesses gathered in the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience.

Atwood uses this phrase for the witnesses she has gathered for the Inquiry, many of whom attest the Stone from personal experience [IV.4 ¶2]. She relies on them as support.

See also: Philosophers

References: IV.4 ¶2

Reuchlin

person · John Reuchlin

Author of The Mirific Word and De Arte Cabalistica, whom Atwood cites approvingly for the purified principle, Wisdom as darkness turned to light, and the mirific Word’s two natures.

Atwood lists John Reuchlin among those who blended alchemy and therapeutics with neoplatonism and cabala [I.1 ¶39]. From The Mirific Word she takes support for the purified principle as medium of divine experience: “Ex natura et divino factum est” [II.2 ¶25] (ours: ‘it is made from nature and the divine’; the book’s own rendering is not in the packet). From De Arte Cabalistica, third book: “Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.” [III.2 ¶10] (ours: ‘there is nothing in the beginning but Wisdom’), with Wisdom as Ain in darkness and the dark Aleph turned to light Aleph. From de Verbo Mirificao: two natures in the mirific Word, the changeable and the immutable — “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24; III.2 n25] — which is said to allude to arresting the flux. She uses him throughout as supporting authority.

References: I.1 ¶39, II.2 ¶25, III.2 n25, III.2 ¶10, III.2 ¶24

Revelation

term

In Kirchringius, the sudden arrival of a solution after persistent desire and labour, given only to one who prays with great desire and labour.

Kirchringius (quoted): after persistent prayer, desire and labour, “at length, in a moment, the solution will fall in; this is a revelation” [III.4 ¶22]. Asserted identity: = the solution falling in.

Identified with: the solution falling in [III.4 ¶22]

See also: Bible, Book of Revelation

Reviviscent spirit

term

The reviving spirit of the Phoenix from which, Atwood says, Bacon filled his lamp; the text does not explain it further.

Atwood speaks of Bacon being able to “fill his lamp from her reviviscent spirit” [I.1 ¶38], the spirit belonging to the Phoenix, which he worked by ascending and descending. The passage leaves the expression unexplained; it apparently names a vivifying principle drawn from the Phoenix, but the text gives no plain meaning.

Rhasis

person · Rasis

An Arabian alchemist the book cites for public transmutations, as a master who wrote obscurely, and in the Ordinal for the dietary of the matter.

Atwood names Rhasis as an Arabian alchemist famous for public displays of transmutation [I.1 ¶34]. As “Rasis” he appears in Norton’s verse among masters (with Hermes, Geber, Avicen, Morien, Bacon, Raymond and others) who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the Ordinal, Rasis is cited as having “set the dietary”: the matter must not eat hastily — “Non tamen comedat res festinanter,” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: yet let the thing not eat hastily). He is also named in Eirenaeus’ allegory as read by those sitting in darkness [III.4 ¶16].

Ricardi Anglici Libellus

treatise

Cited for reference only.

References: III.4 n20

Ricardus

person

An adept (Richardi Ang. Libel.) cited to support the view that study of the philosophers’ writings must precede practice.

Atwood quotes “the adept Ricardus” from Richardi Ang. Libel. cap. 3: “I beg of thee, my son, says the adept Ricardus, to examine the writings of the philosophers” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n16]. She uses him with approval to support her point that study of theory precedes practice and that study overthrows ignorance.

References: III.4 n16, III.4 ¶20

Ripley

person · the Canon Ripley

An adept, author of the Twelve Gates, Medulla and verses to King Edward, whom Atwood cites often on the First Matter, solution, putrefaction and concealment, while criticizing the Gates’ disorder.

Ripley is one of Atwood’s most-cited authorities.

On concealment and honesty. His Fifth Gate supports her view that a plain art is veiled to protect it from the unworthy: “In horrid metaphors veiled are an art most plain” [I.1 ¶85; I.1 n111]. In his Epistle to King Edward IV he offers, conditionally, to show his king the Stone’s working and argues against wilful deceit: “Never trewly for merke nor for pounde Make yt I common” [I.1 ¶79–80; I.1 n105].

Against ignorant practice. His Admonition of Erroneous Experiments illustrates the failures of working on vulgar substances: “But profytt found I right none therein.” [I.1 ¶64–65; I.1 n72]. Via Ashmole he is cited for verses against those who prate “Of Robin Hood, and of his Bow” without practice [I.1 ¶64]. Yet Atwood criticizes the Twelve Gates as disorderly and misleading [I.1 ¶62–63].

On the Matter. Stanza 10 of the Epistle supports reduction to the first matter: “Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable” [I.2 ¶5–6; I.2 n7]. The Medulla, cap. i, supports that separation and recombination of Mercury’s elements make the elixir: “The elements of Mercury being separated” [I.2 ¶25; I.2 n23]. He calls the First Matter a middle or third thing: “Aquosa substantia sicca reperta” [I.2 ¶31, ¶42] (ours: a watery substance found dry). The Admonition supports that man is the mine of the natural mercury: “Out of hy myner by arte yt most be brought” [II.1 ¶13; II.1 n11]. “The Canon Ripley” is among those agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

On the operation. The Second and Fifth Gates and Ripley Revived illustrate the vapor running down in the vessel, the sun obscured with waters like Noah’s flood, and purgation to a white Elixir: “Ryght so to water minerall reduced ys our gold” [III.1 ¶56–62; III.1 n61, n63, n69]; Atwood glosses his phrase “by Crafte occasionate” [III.1 n69]. The consummating Conjunction is “by Ripley called tetraptive” [III.3 ¶33]. In contrast, his attempt to putrefy his Red Salt by alternate heat and cold is called a “singular” method [IV.1 ¶36].

He is listed among genuine seekers, against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): he warns against haste under the similitude of red poppies [APP ¶103].

References: I.1 n105, I.1 n111, I.1 n72, I.1 ¶49, I.1 ¶62, I.1 ¶63, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶65, I.1 ¶79, I.1 ¶80, I.1 ¶85, I.2 n23, I.2 n7, I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶31, I.2 ¶42, I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶6, I.3 n4, I.3 n6, II.1 n11, II.1 ¶13, III.1 n61, III.1 n63, III.1 n69, III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶57, III.1 ¶62, III.2 ¶60, III.3 ¶33, IV.1 ¶36, APP ¶103

Robert Vallensis

person · R. Vallensis

Author of De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae in the Theatrum Chemicum, cited for the antiquity of alchemy.

Atwood cites Robert Vallensis’s De Veritate et Antiquitate Artis Chemiae, in the first volume of the Theatrum Chemicum, in support of alchemy’s antiquity [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n4]. A further footnote refers to the same work as a source, closing “Haec ille Andaeas” [I.1 n52] (ours: thus that Andaeas).

References: I.1 n4, I.1 n52, I.1 ¶3

Rock in the wilderness

term

Atwood’s expression for that which is so called because it lies in great obscurity and is hard to reach, surrounded by darkness and clouds.

Atwood explains the name herself: “This is the rock in the wilderness,, because in great obscurity and difficult to find the way of” [II.3 ¶30]. It is surrounded by darkness, clouds and exhalations, as though in the bowels of the earth. The text states the reason for the name (obscurity and inaccessibility); what “this” is must be taken from the surrounding passage.

References: II.3 ¶30

Roger Bacon

person · Friar Bacon, Freer Bacon, R. Bacon

The ‘experimental Friar’, an adept Atwood cites on concealment, the Matter, solution, the operator’s purification and the primacy of understanding over experiment.

Atwood treats Roger Bacon as a genuine adept who produced gold; Friar Bacon said he saw and touched the perfect thing transmuting [I.1 ¶76]. His maxim justifies concealing the practice: “truth ought not to be shown to every ribald, for then that would become most vile, which, in the hands of a philosopher, is the most precious of all things” [I.1 ¶38–39; I.1 n43, n44]; conscience led him to withhold his gift. His Libro de Mirab. Natur. Operib. contains extracts from Rhasis and appears to credit Artephius’s tale [I.1 ¶34, ¶36; I.1 n41].

On method, he supports leaving off experiments until understanding is attained: “operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding” [I.1 ¶86; I.1 n112]. Called “the experimental Friar”, he supports that the beginning is dissolving and investigating the philosophic man: “Volo ovum philosophorum dissolvere et partes philosophici hominis investare, nam hoc est initium ad alia” [II.3 ¶5; II.3 n1] (ours: I will dissolve the philosophers’ egg and investigate the parts of the philosophic man, for this is the beginning of the rest). The Radix Mundi and Speculum support that subject-matter, not species, is transmuted, and that the first work is Solution: “Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime” [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n1] (ours: species are not transmuted, but the subjects of species best and most properly). The Radix Mundi also supports the operator’s moral requirements: “it is impossible for you to attain this immortal essentiality, unless you become sanctified in mind and purified in soul” [III.3 ¶28; III.3 n19].

As “the experimentalist” he is agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]; something warned him “from the error of his ways” [IV.4 ¶27]. Norton’s verse names “Freer Bacon” with Albertus, and Agrippa followed Friar Bacon’s example in proving principles [I.1 ¶60, ¶64].

See also: Bacon

References: I.1 n112, I.1 n41, I.1 n43, I.1 n44, I.1 ¶34, I.1 ¶36, I.1 ¶38, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶60, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶76, I.1 ¶86, I.2 n1, I.2 ¶5, I.3 n15, II.3 n1, II.3 ¶5, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n19, III.3 ¶28, IV.4 ¶27

Root

term

In quoted authorities, the one root from which all metals and minerals descend, identified with the metallic seed.

Quoted from Basil and Geber: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11]. The same passage equates it with the seed: “this metallic seed, or root” [II.1 ¶11]. The record suggests that this root is also the inner basis the operator must find in himself, though that is the context’s implication rather than a stated definition.

Identified with: metallic seed [II.1 ¶11]

References: II.1 ¶11

Root of light

term

Atwood’s term for the source in which Reason is to seek genuine reminiscence.

Atwood says Reason is “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15]. Apparently the same source she elsewhere calls the Root of Reason [IV.4 ¶20], though the text does not equate the two expressly.

See also: Light

References: IV.4 ¶15

Root of reason

term

The Source and proper object of the rational faculty, buried in the life of sense and resuscitated by Hermetic Artifice; identified with Wisdom and the saving Salt.

Atwood: “the proper object of the rational faculty is in its Source, which lies profoundly buried in this life of sense” [IV.4 ¶20]; Hermetic Artifice resuscitates it. She identifies it directly: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20] — so = Wisdom and = saving Salt.

Identified with: Wisdom [IV.4 ¶20]; saving Salt [IV.4 ¶20]

See also: Reason

References: IV.4 ¶20

Rosicrucian Fraternity

collective voice · Rosicrucians

A secret association, known through the Fame and Confession, into which some adepts carried their work for protection.

Atwood says some adepts carried their work into a secret association, the Rosicrucian Fraternity of the Fame and Confession, for protection [I.1 ¶66]. She also notes that certain Rosicrucians were alarmed by the books of Agrippa’s and Paracelsus’ disciples [II.1 ¶9].

See also: Brethren of the Rosy Cross

Royal artist

collective voice

A voice cited (Calid in Salmon) for the view that the art belongs to those who understand and cannot be bought or sold.

Atwood cites the royal artist, per the footnote from Calid in Salmon, p. 30: “this treasure is not to be bought with money; and as it cannot be bought, so neither can it be sold” [III.4 ¶18; III.4 n13]. She uses it in support: the art is for those who understand.

See also: Artist

References: III.4 n13, III.4 ¶18

Royal diadem

term

In Urbigeranus and other adepts, that which is extracted from ‘our Sordid Subject’ by the medium the Arcanum shows.

Quoted from Urbigeranus and other Adepts: the Arcanum shows “the medium by which the Royal Diadem may be extracted from our Sordid Subject” [IV.1 ¶7]. The text does not explain the expression further; it apparently names the precious product hidden in the base subject.

References: IV.1 ¶7

Royal herb

term

In Flammel, the herb found triumphing at the summit of the mountain of the Seven, called mineral, vegetable or saturnine and being ‘either and all’.

Quoted from Flammel: at the summit of the mountain of the Seven is “a royal herb triumphing, which some call mineral, some vegetable, some saturnine” [II.4 ¶9]; it is said to be either and all. The text gives no plainer gloss.

References: II.4 ¶9

Royal road

term

Atwood’s name for the single path toward which all Hermetic treatises direct once it is found.

Atwood says the Hermetic treatises are “all directing on the same Royal Road when this is found” [III.4 ¶15]. The expression is not otherwise defined here.

References: III.4 ¶15

Ruach Elohim

term

In a quoted adept, that which moved upon the waters, made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identified with the Stone.

Quoted from “the mysterious adeptest”: “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters, the firmament being in the midst” [III.3 ¶50]. The same passage has it conceived and made body in the virgin womb of the greater world, and identifies it with the Stone.

References: III.3 ¶50

Rule

term

The God-given standard for discerning right from wrong; the superior Reason is called ‘the Reason of our Rule’.

The Alchemists’ counsel: “Take hold of that Rule which God hath given thee for direction” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood links it to the superior Reason: “the superior virtue of that which is the Reason of our Rule” [III.1 ¶21]. Compare Rule of Reason.

References: III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶21

Rule of reason

term

Atwood’s term for Reason as guide of the pursuit: under it every step progresses, it alone enters the true Form of Gold, and it proves all things.

Atwood: “every step is progressive where the Rule of Reason is pursued” [III.4 ¶11]; of the true Form of Gold, “Reason alone can enter into it” [III.4 ¶11]. Reason’s office is inquiry: “It is the province of reason to inquire and endeavor, by perscrutination, to prove all things” [III.4 ¶15].

See also: Reason

References: III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶15

Ruling spirit of nature

term

Atwood’s term for that Spirit, communion with which is the way to the magistery, and whose Law is to be feared and obeyed.

Atwood presents “communion with the ruling Spirit of nature” [I.3 n19] as the way to the magistery; its Law is to be feared and obeyed.

References: I.3 n19

Rupecissa

person · Rupicessa

An adept named among genuine seekers and cited in support of Basil Valentine’s view.

Rupecissa is cited as supporting Basil Valentine’s view [I.2 ¶31]. As “Rupicessa” he is listed with De Meun, Flamel, John Pontanus, Basil Valentine, Ripley, Lully and Cremer as genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

References: I.1 ¶49, I.2 ¶31

S

Sacred art

term · Sacred Arts

The ancients’ art practised in the Mysteries, which Atwood connects with Alchemy and Mesmerism and seeks to revive.

Atwood speaks of the ancients’ Sacred Art practised in the Mysteries, comparing it with Mesmerism: “if we connect it with the ancients’ Sacred Art” [II.2 ¶7]. She says her chapter aimed “to indicate the connection of the Sacred Art and Alchemy” [II.4 ¶58]. At the close she describes her work as reviving “these lights and relics of the Sacred Art long buried in oblivion” [IV.4 ¶30], and holds that whoever “can understand the language of the philosophers, will understand their Art” [IV.4 ¶32].

The Platonic Successor (quoted) says Jupiter, after spontaneous revelation ceased, “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53] for communication with the gods.

References: II.1 ¶53, II.2 ¶7, II.4 ¶58, IV.4 ¶30, IV.4 ¶32

Sacred Discourse

treatise

A treatise cited for the labours of Hercules as the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and for the Spirit’s sinking when the will inclines downward.

Atwood cites the Sacred Discourse in support: the labours of Hercules are the trials of whoever contends for liberty, and when the will inclines downward “the Spirit grows heavy and sinks into profound Hades” [II.2 ¶13–14].

References: II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14

Sacred Mysteries

term

Sacred knowledge and rites which, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified.

Atwood: “sacred mysteries, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified by their abuse” [I.1 ¶11] — a ground for the secrecy she defends.

See also: Mysteries

References: I.1 ¶11

Sacred science

term

In a quoted adept, the name for the genuine art which fraudulent books blasphemed.

Quoted from the adept, on fraudulent writers: “they have blasphemed the Sacred Science, and by their errors have brought contempt on men philosophizing” [I.1 ¶53].

References: I.1 ¶53

Sage

collective voice · the adept

An anonymous voice whose sayings Atwood cites on sense-life, the purified internal fire, and putrefaction.

Atwood reads the sage’s saying “Visitabis interiora terrae rectificando” [II.3 ¶28–29] (ours: you will visit the interior of the earth by rectifying) as referring to sense-life. Another saying supports the superiority of the purified internal fire: “Si pariat ventum valet auri pondera centum” [III.1 ¶43] (ours: if it brings forth wind, it is worth a hundred weights of gold). Via Ripley Revived, 5th Gate, the sage/adept supports putrefaction as the key, and tincture as coagulated blood: “O happy gate of blackness” [I.3 n42, n43].

See also: Adept, Adepts (cited voice)

References: I.3 n42, I.3 n43, II.3 ¶28, II.3 ¶29, III.1 ¶43

Sage in Enoch

collective voice

The voice of the Book of Enoch, cited to illustrate the guarded mineral soul.

Atwood cites the Book of Enoch, chap. 64: 7, 8: “there is an angel standing upon it, and that angel struggles to prevail” [II.3 ¶29; II.3 n32], illustrating the guarded mineral soul.

See also: Book of Enoch

References: II.3 n32, II.3 ¶29

person · St Croix

Author of a two-volume work on the Mysteries whom Atwood criticizes as thorough in research but astronomical and superficial in reading.

Atwood cites Sainte Croix’s des Mysteres (2 vols, 8vo) and criticizes it: the research is thorough, but the reading of the Mysteries is astronomical and superficial [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n2].

Invoked for their gift of healing, which Atwood notes is absent today.

Atwood contrasts the saints and apostles’ gift of healing with its absence today, promising the reason in the sequel [III.1 ¶9].

Sal Sepientum

term

Salt of the Wise (our rendering): Atwood’s name for what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened, identified with Mercurius Philosophorum.

Atwood: “This is the Sal Sepientum et Mercurius Philosophorum” [II.4 ¶39] — so = Mercurius Philosophorum. The rendering Salt of the Wise is ours. In context it names what arises when the hidden Reason is awakened.

Identified with: Mercury [II.4 ¶39]

References: II.4 ¶39

Salamander

term

In quoted adepts, an image of the Stone as born and nourished in fire, enduring it unharmed and curing diseases of men and metals.

The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (quoted) says the Eagle and Lion together take on the Salamander’s nature, “which, if it remains in the fire without any detriment, cures all the diseases of men and metals” [III.3 ¶63]. Eudoxus (quoted) uses it as an image of the Stone, which “as a true Salamander receives it nativity, is nourished and grows in the Elementary Fire” [IV.3 ¶16].

References: III.3 ¶63, IV.3 ¶16

Salt

term · Salts, Sal, Slat

One of the three principles (with Sulphur and Mercury); identified by Atwood with Will, Wisdom and the Root of Reason, and by quoted adepts as the most ancient principle of the Stone.

Salt is one of the three principles with Sulphur and Mercury; Atwood lists it third in the series of [III.1 ¶53], in the same position as the body principle and the proceeding substance (how these relate is left open), and the Adept she cites says “yet without Salt no man can attain to this Sacred Science” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius’s fable “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56].

Atwood’s identifications. In the main text she speaks of the Saturnian Salt which, developed to intellect and made erect, subdues all nature, equating it with “the internal spiritual Sun which is the Perpetual Motion of the Wise, and that Saturnian Salt” [II.3 ¶52], and with “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She calls it “that saving Salt which philosophers were wont anciently to excavate and by so many circulating media to exalt”, identifying it with the Root of Reason and Wisdom: “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20].

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Salt = Will: “There is no true body but Will; it is the principle of the body — the Salt.” [APP ¶65]. “The Slat is the voluntary substance”, bound in the generative mineral life; drawn up into the medial life, “the Salt thus transplanted becomes Light and grows” [APP ¶77]. “The Salt, the will, opens it secondfold.” [APP ¶182] (the sense of ‘secondfold’ is unclear).

Quoted voices. The mysterious adeptest calls it “Salt, that most ancient principle of the Stone” and “The Salt of Saturn, the Universal son of Nature”, “always and everywhere universal through its own fusibility, self-existent in nature”; “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom”; its nucleus in the Decad is to be kept secret; with the Sun, it is that “than which, together with the Sun, nothing is found more useful” [III.3 ¶50]. The Adept speaks of an immortal Salt in the mind’s machinery, “that marvelous Salt, which is that menstruum in the sphere of Saturn mentioned by Eirenaeus, which can calcine gold” [IV.2 ¶30]. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

Identified with: Will [APP ¶65]; voluntary substance [APP ¶77]; Will [APP ¶182]; Astrum solis [II.3 ¶52]; Universal son of Nature [III.3 ¶50]; most ancient principle of the Stone [III.3 ¶50]; Wisdom [III.3 ¶50]; menstruum in the sphere of Saturn [IV.2 ¶30]; Root of reason [IV.4 ¶20]; Wisdom [IV.4 ¶20]

See also: Philosophic Salt

References: II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54, III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶61, III.3 ¶50, IV.2 ¶30, IV.2 ¶35, IV.4 ¶20, APP ¶182, APP ¶65, APP ¶77

Salt of Saturn

term

The most abstruse principle of the Stone: deprived of light, the central earth whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe; identified with Demogorgon and the mineral soul.

In a passage whose voice is unclear, “The Salt of Saturn, that most abstruse principle of the Stone — the most ancient Demogorgon” [II.3 ¶41] is said to be deprived of light, the one “whose perpetual motion emanates the first material universe, and is the mineral soul” [II.3 ¶41]. It is also the central earth whose Being is Tartarus: “This is the earth, distinguished by Anaxagoras, which abiding durably in the center” [II.3 ¶41]. Compare Salt, where a quoted adept calls the Salt of Saturn the “Universal son of Nature” [III.3 ¶50].

Identified with: Demogogon [II.3 ¶41]; Mineral soul [II.3 ¶41]; the earth, distinguished by Anaxagoras [II.3 ¶41]

See also: Saturn

References: II.3 ¶41

Salt of the Sages

term · their salt, salt of the world

In the Lucerna Solis verse, the Sages’ name for the one universal thing containing all nature and Life, extracted from their earth, and not vulgar salt.

Quoted from the Lucerna Solis: the one universal thing, present everywhere, containing all nature and all Life and extracted from ‘their earth’, is known only to the Sages: “The band of Sages only have known it, And they call it their salt.” It is explicitly not common salt: “Nor the vulgar salt in any manner, But rather the salt of the world” [I.2 ¶10].

See also: Sage

References: I.2 ¶10

Salt, Sulphur and Mercury

term · Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, Salt, Mercury, Sulphur, Mercury, salt and sulphur, Sulphur, Mercury and Salt, Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt, three principles

The three principles of the Adepts: modes of being of one Matter, related as agent, patient and offspring; not the literal substances chemists misapplied.

Atwood. Literal chemists failed to extract the Form of gold “by salt, sulfur and mercury, or the three combined with antimony” [I.1 ¶86]. Properly, “The three principles, the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, are merely different as modes of being of the same thing” [I.2 ¶39], exhibited by nature from the Matter’s unity after the annihilate condition, as agent, patient and offspring. They are contained in the first matter of metals, a doctrine “of which so much has been spoken and ignorantly misapplied” [I.3 n22]; they are “the paternal, maternal, and proceeding ens of life. And there are the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury of the Adepts” [I.3 n30]; “thou hast in these three principles, says Sendivogius, a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]. Per Vaughan they are hidden intrinsical natures, not literal ‘pot-principles’ [I.3 n30]. At [III.3 ¶77] she names them “the Sulphur and Mercury and Slat, the active and the passive, and the resulting experience of life”: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will”; “the second is of the Humanity, i.e., of the selfhood, prepared and sanctified”; “the result of these two in unison is the Bodily Substance of things thenceforth created” — three powers in one seat. In the mind’s machinery she lists “wheel within wheel revolving vitally, Mercury, Sulphur, and an immortal Salt” [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) they are the three principles of the vital force in the blood: “Attraction, Circulation, Repulsion — the Alchemical Salt, Mercury, Sulphur” [APP ¶24].

Quoted. Basil and Crollius: “the mercury, slat and sulfur — spirit, body and soul — lie hid together in one thing” [II.1 ¶11]; “there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found in the salt, mercury, and sulfur thereof” [II.1 ¶14]. Eudoxus: they are present, seemingly but not truly united, in the apparently homogeneous Water — “Salt, Sulphur and Mercury — which are the spirit, the soul, and the body” [IV.3 ¶7]. Note the sources differ on which principle is spirit, soul or body.

Identified with: paternal, maternal, and proceeding ens of life [I.3 n30]; body, spirit, occult soul [I.3 n30]; Attraction, Circulation, Repulsion [APP ¶24]; spirit, body and soul [II.1 ¶11]; Three Powers in one seat [III.3 ¶77]; the active, the passive, and the resulting experience of life [III.3 ¶77]; Word of God (the first) [III.3 ¶77]; the selfhood (the second) [III.3 ¶77]; Bodily Substance (the result) [III.3 ¶77]; the spirit, the soul, and the body [IV.3 ¶7]

See also: Mercury, Three principles, Three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)

References: I.1 ¶86, I.2 ¶39, I.3 n22, I.3 n30, II.1 ¶11, II.1 ¶14, III.3 ¶77, IV.2 ¶30, IV.3 ¶7, APP ¶24

Quoted from Sendivogius: “water and salt-nitre, which comes from Our Earth” [IV.3 ¶21]; the radical moisture is put upon it. Not further explained.

Sanctuary of nature

term

In Vaughan, the place of Nature’s treasures, behind a Door that must be opened through knowledge of the First Matter.

Saturn

term · Saturnine

In the Appendix, the self-willed life or Will, which entraps the Light and holds the key to Sulphur’s prison.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Saturn or the self-willed life” [APP ¶72], “the selfish Saturnine life in man”, entraps the Light and craves more; it is overcome by satiation and then transmuted [APP ¶72]. “a Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]. As a planetary property, nothing can be felt or realized “without the voluntary dominance of Saturn and Luna” [APP ¶113]. Compare Saturnian Will and Salt of Saturn.

Saturn, Jupiter, Venus and Lune

term · Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, Lune, Saturnine

Planetary names used in the Appendix as qualities of character and work: Saturnine dark potentiality cleared by the Jupiter element.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood, judging a work or character: “It is a Saturnine mass of power in mere potentiality; a dark cloud; chaos before Light strikes through it.” and “It wants the Jupiter element to clear it.” [APP ¶175].

term

Something founded on the Matter (as Pan), once circumscribed in Intellect for the manifestation of its Light; not further explained.

Atwood says the Matter, as Pan, is “the foundation of the great Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will, which was once circumscribed in Intellect, for the manifestation of its Light” [III.2 ¶7]. Not further explained.

term

The Will, figured by the drunken Saturn of the verse, which revels without rational restraint through the subordinate faculties until sated and asleep.

Atwood reads the drunken Saturn of the verse as the Will: “For the Saturnian Will, being allowed to revel without limitation or rational restraint” through the subordinate faculties, until “his desires are more than satisfied, and, as the image runs, from the effect he sleeps” [III.1 ¶68]. term

The knowledge the few wise took with them into obscurity.

Atwood says the wise preserved their knowledge “by burying themselves with their saving science in profound obscurity” [I.1 ¶30].

Savior

person · the Saviour

Cited for the command to have Salt in ourselves and for the honour of the ass at his triumph.

Atwood cites the Savior’s order to have Salt in ourselves, “that Salt which the Savior orders that we should have it in ourselves” [II.3 ¶54]. She also cites the Saviour’s choice of the ass ‘on the occasion of his greatest earthly triumph’ to illustrate that animal’s honour [III.2 ¶64].
