Schelling

person

Named by Atwood with Kant and Fichte as falling short of objective realization, though ranked above them; quoted on awakening from Intellectual Intuition.

Atwood criticizes Kant, Fichte and Schelling for a metaphysics ending in void non-entity and skepticism, short of objective realization, while ranking Schelling above the other two [III.2 ¶31]. She cites him in support of the view that after the intuition only the remembered vision remains, owing to the limits of human reason: “We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death” [IV.2 ¶33]. The Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) mentions him with Fichte by way of contrast [APP ¶96] and in the same list as ones who ‘saw it’ [APP ¶117].

References: III.2 ¶31, IV.2 ¶33, APP ¶117, APP ¶96

Scholiast

collective voice · our Scholiast

The glossator of the Scholium, Atwood’s main and approved commentator in I.3, cited for practical and spiritual readings of the Hermetic text.

Atwood cites the Scholiast throughout I.3 with approval (‘our Scholiast’, ‘the wise Scholiast’), taking the Scholium as giving full instructions. He interprets the elements, colours, recipe, Mercury, vulture, mountain, fire and bird, “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]–[I.3 n16]. He locates the work in life — “It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life” [I.3 n48] — and glosses ‘as vinegar makes vinegar’ [I.3 n48–n55]. He supports practical readings of the Athanor and Hermetic seal — “The matter, he says, is to be decocted in the philosophic furnace called Athanor, with a continual fire.” — the treasury of nature in the breast, fixed sulfur as balsam of nature, and the soul of gold as aurific principle [I.3 n57–n67]. He is cited on entering the Spirit (“Thou must enter with thy whole spirit into the center of nature”), the repeated opening of the body, Magnesia, the essence of life as Fire, the Dragon as first blackness, secret sulfur and the rarity of the philosophic water [I.3 n19–n36]; and on the affinity of body and spirit — “The bodies of the metals, explains our Scholiast, are the domiciles of their spirits” — dissolution, multiplication and the parents nursed [I.3 n37–n42].

References: I.3 n11, I.3 n12, I.3 n16, I.3 n19, I.3 n20, I.3 n21, I.3 n22, I.3 n26, I.3 n27, I.3 n29, I.3 n30, I.3 n31, I.3 n32, I.3 n36, I.3 n37, I.3 n38, I.3 n39, I.3 n4, I.3 n40, I.3 n41, I.3 n42, I.3 n48, I.3 n49, I.3 n5, I.3 n50, I.3 n51, I.3 n53, I.3 n54, I.3 n55, I.3 n57, I.3 n6, I.3 n60, I.3 n61, I.3 n63, I.3 n65, I.3 n66, I.3 n67, I.3 n9

Schoolmen

collective voice

Named only in a phrase borrowed within Vaughan’s quotation.

Mentioned only within a quotation from Vaughan: “bad news (as the schoolmen phrase it)” [IV.2 ¶35].

References: IV.2 ¶35

Scotus Erigina

person

Listed by Atwood among the confessed adepts.

Named in Atwood’s list of confessed adepts [I.1 ¶39].

References: I.1 ¶39

Scripture

person · the Scriptures, Holy Scripture

Cited by Atwood throughout as supporting authority: on Wisdom, blessing from God, purity, the conversion of darkness to light, and as analogue of the Hermetic Work.

Atwood cites Scripture as endorsed authority. It promises Wisdom, following Solomon’s panegyric, with other such places [II.1 ¶45]; the Scriptures teach a faith bestowing Wisdom, God’s sentence on the Serpent (“I will put enmity between thee and the woman”), and promises of Wisdom and material fruits, and are to be read as obscure and mystical [IV.3 ¶37–¶46]. Blessing and increase come from God: “the Lesser is blessed by the Greater”, with ‘Every good gift…’ and ‘God alone giveth the increase’; the talent is taken from him who does not use it [III.4 ¶20]. It supports the conversion of darkness into light: “The night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are all alike to Him” [III.2 ¶10]; number, weight and measure as Nature’s three dimensions: “Thou hast disposed all things, in number, weight, and measure.” [III.3 ¶67]; and that the healer must first be healed: “Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in thy field; and afterwards build thy house” [III.1 ¶9, III.1 n7] (the note refers to the Wisdom of Solomon and Proverbs 24), with the beam and mote and ‘Physician, heal thyself’. For purity she cites “He that hath clean hands and a pure heart”, saying she quotes it as apt, ‘proved on the Divine Ground’, not because it is popular [IV.1 ¶39–¶40]. The ancestors found the Word of Life, “which their neglected Scriptures everywhere testify of” [IV.2 ¶43]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the Work revealed in Holy Scripture is the analogue of the Hermetic Work, and the Stone of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139].

References: II.1 ¶45, III.1 n7, III.1 ¶9, III.2 n27, III.2 ¶10, III.3 ¶67, III.4 ¶20, IV.1 ¶39, IV.1 ¶40, IV.2 ¶43, IV.3 ¶37, IV.3 ¶38, IV.3 ¶40, IV.3 ¶46, APP ¶139

Sea of the wise

term

The Matter in its flowing, moist state, passive to every impression of the light.

Atwood: “In its flowing, humid state it is called the sea of the wise, passive to all impression and influences of the light” [I.3 n16].

See also: The Wise

References: I.3 n16

Sea water

term · our sea water

In Synesius and the New Light, the precious thing congealed in gold and silver and abiding in the sea of the world.

Quoted (Synesius; the New Light): the precious thing is “a ting more precious than the whole world; which I plainly tell thee is nothing else than our sea water” [I.2 ¶33]; it is congealed in gold and silver and abides ‘in the sea of the world’.

Identified with: a ting more precious than the whole world [I.2 ¶33]

See also: Water

References: I.2 ¶33

Seal of God

term

In Boehme, the concealment set before the true ground of the art to prevent its misuse.

Quoted from Boehme: “the Seal of God lieth before it, to conceal the true ground” [II.1 ¶25], so that the art may not be misused.

See also: Gods

References: II.1 ¶25

Second Adam

term

Greater than the first Adam: the restoration exceeds what was lost.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “for the second Adam is greater than the first” [APP ¶98] — the restoration exceeds what was lost.

References: APP ¶98

Second intention

term

In Norton, the character of the Elixir as engendered by the concord of virtues; not further explained.

Quoted from Norton: from the concord of virtues “Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34]. Not further explained.

References: IV.2 ¶34

Second operation

term

The stage in which Nature alone works, without hands, by regulated external fire; for Atwood, the main reference of the Ordinal’s period of years.

Eirenaeus: “In the Second, however, Nature alone operates, and without any imposition of hands” [IV.1 ¶11], by well-regulated external fire. Khunrath likewise: after the first act, in one vessel, furnace and fire, body, spirit and soul dissolve and reunite, they “rot of themselves and without manual cooperation, by the sole labors of nature” [IV.1 ¶36]. Atwood says the Ordinal’s period of years: “This is meant chiefly in reference to the Second Operation” [IV.1 ¶17], linking it to the discovery of the philosophic Salt. Its relation to the Gross Work is not stated. Compare Second Work.

References: IV.1 ¶11, IV.1 ¶17, IV.1 ¶36

Second principle

term

The Paradisiacal Life, lived under the Cross.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “Living in the Second Principle means living the Paradisiacal Life” [APP ¶94]; it is lived under the Cross, the heart life below the extended arms representing it.

Identified with: Paradisiacal Life [APP ¶94]

See also: Principles

References: APP ¶94

Second qualities

term — specifical qualities · specifical qualities

In Van helmont, second qualities misleadingly trusted, contrasted with specifical (appropriated) qualities acting only on their proper object.

Quoted from Van helmont: those go astray who, “they too much trusting to Second qualities, as being ill secure, do sleep thereupon”, neglect the “specifical qualities, also appropriated ones (which are only extended on their proper object)” [IV.1 ¶39].

Identified with: appropriated ones (for specifical qualities) [IV.1 ¶39]

References: IV.1 ¶39

Second spirit

term · tinging spirit

In the Adept, a spirit subsisting and tinging in the body, extracted by the Preparing Spirit.

Quoted from the Adept: the Preparing Spirit “extracts a Second Spirit subsisting and tinging in the body”, “extracting from it the tinging spirit” [IV.1 ¶10].

See also: Spirit

References: IV.1 ¶10

Second work

term

The continuation of the First Work, perfecting the new embryo and multiplying its light; for Atwood, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt.

Atwood: “the Second Work, which is only, in continuation of the First, to perfect the newly informed embryo and multiply its vivific light” [I.3 n7]. It is one of the Art’s greatest subtleties: “By the Second Work we are to understand, therefore, the Solution of the Philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: “The Fourth Key of the Art is the entrance to the Second Work” [IV.3 ¶12], in which the Water is reduced to Earth. Compare Second Operation.

Identified with: Solution of the Philosophic Salt [IV.1 ¶36]

See also: Works

References: I.3 n7, IV.1 ¶36, IV.3 ¶12

Secret fire

term

In Eirenaeus, the fire contained in, and identified with, ‘our water’.

Quoted from Eirenaeus: “For in our water is our secret fire.” and “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69]; the water is apparently Mercury. Compare secret Fire of the Wise.

Identified with: Water [III.1 ¶69]

See also: Fire, Fire of the wise

References: III.1 ¶69

Secret fire of the wise

term

The only agent the Art grants for purifying Nature; without knowing it, one fails even with the true matter.

In a passage whose voice is unclear (Atwood, or continuing ‘our author of The Triumph’, cited in the next sentence): “the secret Fire of the Wise, which is the only agent granted by Art to purify and dispose Nature to a sacrifice of her last life” [IV.2 ¶6]. Eudoxus: it makes a water that does not wet the hands run out of the dry-looking ‘plant’, and many fail “for want of knowing the secret fire of the wise” even after knowing the true matter [IV.3 ¶16]. The same paragraph names “the Understanding of Our Fire, which is both secret and natural” as one of two things that give the Keys; whether this is the same fire is not stated outright.

See also: The Wise

References: IV.2 ¶6, IV.3 ¶16

Secret menstrual

term

In Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, what Argent Vive prepared by art gives: the mother of the Stone, known by several names.

Eirenaeus, quoted, says that Argent Vive prepared by art “gives the secret menstrual: The mother of our Stone which is so rare.” [III.1 ¶69] He gives it further names: “Our oil, our unguent, and our marchasite; Which we do name also our fountain bright.” [III.1 ¶69] So, in his verse, secret menstrual = mother of the Stone = oil, unguent, marchasite, fountain bright.

Identified with: mother of our Stone [III.1 ¶69]; oil, unguent, marchasite, fountain bright [III.1 ¶69]

See also: Menstrual

References: III.1 ¶69

Secret of secrets

term · Secretu, Secretorum, secretum secretorum

The philosophers’ name for what the Art teaches but never teaches openly; in Morieni, the magistery itself, God’s secret.

Artephius, quoted, rebukes the literal reader: “you, fool, believe we teach the secret of secrets openly” [I.1 ¶84]. Atwood records Secretu Secretorum as a philosophers’ name for the same thing, and cites Morieni identifying it with the magistery: “hoc magisterium nihil aliud est, nisi Arcanum et secretum secretorum Dei altissimi et magni” [II.4 ¶39] (our rendering: this magistery is nothing else but the Arcanum and secret of secrets of God most high and great). In Morieni, then, the secret of secrets = the magisterium, God’s secret entrusted to the prophets [II.4 ¶39].

Identified with: magisterium [II.4 ¶39]

References: I.1 ¶84, II.4 ¶39

Seed

term · seed of gold, metalline seeds

What Form (Light) clothed with matter begets, impressing its character on matter; the seed of gold is called the Stone of Fire.

Atwood presents seed as what Form, or Light, begets when clothed with matter: “Which clothed with mater doth a seed beget.” [I.2 ¶45] The seed impresses its character on matter; metals arise from metalline seeds out of the Universal Spirit, while vulgar gold lacks seed until art helps it [I.2 ¶45]. An adept, cited by her, identifies the seed of gold with the Stone of Fire: “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44].

Identified with: Stone of Fire [I.2 ¶44]

References: I.2 ¶44, I.2 ¶45

Seed of nature

term

In Sendivogius, quoted, that of which man’s body is a shadow.

Sendivogius, quoted, says “the body of man is a shadow of the seed of nature” [II.1 ¶10].

References: II.1 ¶10

Seed of spirit

term

What is at last found within the purified material extreme of this life, described as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star.

Atwood: “within the material extreme of this life, when it is purified, the Seed of Spirit is at last found” [II.3 ¶30]. It is described there as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star [II.3 ¶30].

See also: Spirit

References: II.3 ¶30

Seeking reason

term

The active principle whose Will the Passive Intelligence answers and accompanies through the abyss.

Atwood speaks of the Passive Intelligence which “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason” [III.1 ¶40]; the seeking Reason is the active partner (spoken of as him), which she accompanies through the abyss.

See also: Reason

References: III.1 ¶40

Select Works

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: Works

References: III.2 n40

Self-begotten life

term

This life of ours, in which the Divine Light is hidden and which appropriates that Light instead of serving it.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls our life self-begotten, the life in which the Divine Light is hidden: “This life of ours, instead of administering to the Divine Life, appropriates it.” [APP ¶70]

See also: Life

References: APP ¶70

Self-centers

term

Centers that gifted beings in whom the Word gives power tend to set up; key to the Second Commandment as the result of violating the First.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood warns that “the danger is the tendency in such gifted beings to set up self-centers” [APP ¶100], beings in whom the Word gives power. She treats this as the key to the Second Commandment, as the outcome of violating the First [APP ¶100].

References: APP ¶100

Self-desire

term

What adulterates vision in the phantastic sphere.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says of vision in the phantastic sphere: “it is self-desire that adulterates” [APP ¶105].

References: APP ¶105

Self-Knowledge

term

Atwood’s name for the Hermetic method itself: inner revelation in a purified soul, the root of alchemical tradition and the narrow way of regeneration.

For Atwood, Self-Knowledge is the Hermetic method: “the Hermetic method of Self-Knowledge” [I.3 n46], which alone enables man to know, understand and possess divine things. She holds “Self-Knowledge to be at the root of all Alchemical tradition” [II.1 ¶30], formerly taken as a way to knowledge of Universal Nature.

It is the object of the inward search whose method she seeks from the ancients: “the true method and conditions of Self- Knowledge” [II.1 ¶46]. She sets it apart from trance or vision and equates it with the true psychical experience: “For it is this, no common trance or day-dream, or any fanatical vision of celestials, that we propose to scrutinize, but the true psychical experience” [II.1 ¶46].

It is among the goods of the higher Mysteries: “the Self-Knowledge and perfection of life and immortality promised” [II.2 ¶7]. Atwood names by it the method of inner revelation in a purified soul, “the narrow way of regeneration into life” [II.4 ¶19]. The Greeks reached “an experimental conception of its reality in the self-knowledge” [III.2 ¶46], i.e. of the reality of the Whole. Its condition is total privation: “Self-knowledge is impossible unless every other knowledge is deprived” [III.2 ¶56].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Self-knowledge is the first contact of consciousness in the ground of life.” [APP ¶137]

Identified with: the true psychical experience [II.1 ¶46]

References: I.3 n46, II.1 ¶30, II.1 ¶46, II.2 ¶7, II.4 ¶19, III.2 ¶46, III.2 ¶56, APP ¶137

Self-perceivance

term

That through which the Reason arises, with creative attributes and powers, in regeneration.

Atwood says the Reason “arises through the self-perceivance, with creative attributes and powers” [III.3 ¶52]. Whose self is perceived the text does not specify here.

References: III.3 ¶52

Self-spiration

term

The individual’s distinct subsistence as separated, or outborn, from the Fontal Reason.

Atwood describes the individual as “a distinct self-spiration, severation, or outbirth, as it were, from that Fontal Reason” [III.3 ¶52]: self-spiration is thus equated with severation and outbirth.

Identified with: severation; outbirth [III.3 ¶52]

References: III.3 ¶52

Self-sufficiency

term

The forbidden regions into which depraved minds climbed by the clue of life.

Atwood says depraved minds, given the clue of life, “climbed by it into forbidden regions of self-sufficiency” [III.4 ¶4].

References: III.4 ¶4

Self-will

term · self-willed

The individual, self-centred will acting for itself rather than under God’s law, at war with the Divine Will; to be brought into subjection.

All records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood describes self-will as will acting for itself rather than under God’s law: “The magic of the self-will is that which the Egyptians practiced in the days of Moses” [APP ¶2], and power “taken into the self-will and used accordingly it becomes diabolical” [APP ¶4].

When the Wisdom-life is stirred, “what takes it is the self-will” [APP ¶82]; it wars with the Universal Will and, as patient, has its false forms dissolved. Drawn upward by love it becomes passive; acting before its time it destroys: “There is a swiftness in the self-willed magnet working powerfully and to destruction” [APP ¶103]. The Divine purpose is to “bring the self-willed opposition into subjection” [APP ¶104], through man’s consent. In religion it distorts: “The action of the self-will on the soul which exaggerates its religious life” [APP ¶110].

It is the principle we are born into: “This war is the war between two principles of the self-will and the Divine Will.” [APP ¶154]

References: APP ¶103, APP ¶104, APP ¶110, APP ¶154, APP ¶2, APP ¶4, APP ¶82

Self-willed Identity

term

The inner self-will that arrests the entering light; it must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice and is finally subdued by the connate spirit.

Atwood describes the light “penetrating to meet the self-willed Identity within, is arrested” [III.1 ¶53]. This Identity must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice, “humiliation of the Selfhood under the exemplary cross of Christ” [III.1 ¶60], and the connate spirit at last subdues it to self-mortification [III.1 ¶60].

See also: Identity

References: III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶60

Selfhood

term

The separate, self-centred individual self into which the soul has fallen; it must be dissolved, subverted and abandoned to the Divine Will for regeneration.

Atwood treats selfhood as the separate self that must be undone. Its “dark dominion” [II.3 n2] is dissolved by the magnetic friction of its proper light. Reiterated reflexive analysis serves so that “it may resolve the separable Selfhood” [IV.1 ¶20]; rectification and sublimation are completed “by an actual subversion of the selfhood” [IV.1 ¶47]. The work requires one “to abandon the life of selfhood” [III.4 ¶6], the necessary charges, and return to the Universal by “abandoning the selfhood” [IV.4 ¶27]. Immortality is consummated by “the abandonment of the dual selfhood and its volition to the Divine Will” [IV.3 ¶58]; then “from the separable selfhood, the Identity passes into universal accord” [IV.3 ¶60].

In III.2 (voice unclear) the selfhood is obliterated in the attraction into the First Cause: “as this selfhood likewise is obliterated in the overwhelming attraction, which raises it into the First Cuase” [III.2 ¶56]; and non-being is glossed as the subjective selfhood, whose additions bring poverty [III.2 ¶59].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the soul’s fall is “the fall away of it into selfhood, which has defaced the image” [APP ¶120], and the converting light shines on “the darkness of the selfhood on which it shines” [APP ¶114]. The Midas-will holds the life it possesses “holding it as he did the selfhood” [APP ¶159].

Identified with: Non-being [III.2 ¶59]

References: II.3 n2, III.2 ¶56, III.2 ¶59, III.4 ¶6, IV.1 ¶20, IV.1 ¶47, IV.3 ¶58, IV.3 ¶60, IV.4 ¶27, APP ¶114, APP ¶120, APP ¶159

Sendivogius

person · Michael Sendivogius, the author of the New Light

An adept and author of the New Light of Alchemy, among Atwood’s most cited and generally endorsed authorities on the matter, water and practice of the Art.

Atwood names him Michael Sendivogius, author of Novum Lumen Chemicum / The New Light of Alchemy; his imprisonment illustrates persecution, and his book is praised as attractive but deliberately disordered, needing repeated study; some identify him with Philalethes and with Alexander Seton [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶71, I.1 ¶73].

On method of reading: from his Preface, one must read from the possibility of nature, not the words, for “this Art is for the wise, not for the ignorant” [I.1 ¶84]; from his Epilogue, philosophers teach indirectly and contradict on purpose, “it being the custom of philosophers to use them; thou hast need of them” [I.1 ¶84].

On the matter: “Our water is heavenly, not wetting the hands, not of the vulgar, but almost rain water” [I.2 ¶33]; his saying that the matter of metals is twofold Atwood reinterprets as relation within the Ethereal being [I.2 ¶42]. One must seek the hidden thing yielding a moisture “which doth dissolve gold without violence or noise” [I.2 ¶48]. “Vulgar gold Sendivogius compares to a herb without seed” [I.2 ¶49]. The three principles are one substance in triple relation, “a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]; and “our lune or silver, not common silver, is that which receives the seed of the gold” [I.3 n39]. He describes the Water of our Sea, “that water was as white as snow” [III.2 ¶7], “the water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]; and the enigmatic conversion of elements: “who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join a spirit thereto” [III.3 ¶29].

Atwood criticizes him once as diverting readers from Morien’s hint [II.1 ¶8], but endorses him on man as microcosm: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10]; on Fire: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]; and on prayer with work: “Pray, says Sendivogius, pray; but work.” [III.4 ¶20]. He also supplies “Urinus Saturni” for the Black Saturn [II.3 ¶18], his Planetary Sphere = the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9], and the fight in which “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56], yielding white milk [III.1 n62]; per n66 he is also the source of the Adept’s saying that without Salt no man attains the Science [III.1 n66]. His friends disbelieved that “there was any water in our sea” [III.4 ¶16]. In IV.3, the wary Artist, he teaches spiritual fermentation: “thou takest not common gold or silver, for these are dead; take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21], admitting that his experience stopped there. In the Appendix (later layer) he is cited for the Philosopher who “looks not out on nature with the eyes of common men” [APP ¶67].

References: I.1 n109, I.1 n110, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶71, I.1 ¶73, I.1 ¶84, I.2 n35, I.2 n36, I.2 n40, I.2 n46, I.2 n48, I.2 ¶33, I.2 ¶42, I.2 ¶48, I.2 ¶49, I.3 n30, I.3 n31, I.3 n39, I.3 n40, I.3 n5, II.1 n2, II.1 n5, II.1 ¶10, II.1 ¶8, II.3 ¶18, II.4 n26, II.4 ¶39, II.4 ¶9, III.1 n62, III.1 n66, III.1 ¶56, III.1 ¶61, III.2 n27, III.2 n43, III.2 n8, III.2 ¶7, III.3 n20, III.3 ¶29, III.4 n18, III.4 n32, III.4 ¶16, III.4 ¶20, IV.3 n2, IV.3 ¶21, APP ¶67

Seneca

person

Cited, from his Epistola xci, as witness to Democritus’ making of artificial precious stones.

Atwood cites Seneca (Epistola xci) for Democritus’ “his artificial confection of precious stones” [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n18].

References: I.1 n18, I.1 ¶12

Senior

person

Cited for the precept that the volatile must be united with the fixed, which Atwood says deserves attention.

Atwood cites Senior’s precept on uniting volatile with fixed, “the highest fume should be reduced to the lowest” [IV.3 ¶8], as one which deserves attention.

References: IV.3 ¶8

Sense

term

Sense perception and its beguilements, made the beacon of modern thought; the turbulent sea beyond which the haven lies.

Atwood laments that modern thought follows “the beguilements of sense” [IV.4 ¶28] and places the haven “beyond the turbulent sea of sense” [IV.4 ¶32].

References: IV.4 ¶28, IV.4 ¶32

Sensible medium

term

The medium of sense-consciousness that trance dissolves, beneath which consciousness is later translated.

Atwood says trance can “dissolve the sensible medium and convert it to the experience of another life” [II.3 ¶5]; consciousness is afterwards translated beneath it.

See also: Medium

References: II.3 ¶5

Sensual compact

term

What is fixed and must be dissolved in the work.

Atwood glosses the alchemical fixed thing as the sensual compact: “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved” [II.3 ¶37].

Identified with: that which was fixed [II.3 ¶37]

References: II.3 ¶37

Sensual dominant

term

The dominance of sense-life, identified with the corporeal; softened by the ethereal waters and subdued by Spirit in regeneration.

Atwood says the ethereal waters soften the sensual dominant to “make it more fit for the returning reason and understanding to work upon” [III.1 ¶53]. It is subdued “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15], and she identifies it with the corporeal: Spirit “overcomes the corporeal, which is the sensual dominant, in the regeneration” [III.3 ¶23].

Identified with: Corporeal [III.3 ¶23]

References: III.1 ¶53, III.3 ¶15, III.3 ¶23

Sensual spirit of life

term

What is without a person; it must be made flexible and hidden.

Atwood glosses that which is without: “that which is without, viz., the sensual spirit of life must be made flexible and occultated” [I.3 n8].

Identified with: that which is without [I.3 n8]

See also: Life

References: I.3 n8

Sensuous medium

term · sensual medium

The principle of sense in the blood, dissolved by magnetizing and reiterated contritions; its residuum supplies body to the regenerate soul.

Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood identifies it as “the principle of sense or the sensuous medium in the blood” [APP ¶109], against which the senses are turned. Absorbed by reiterative contritions and dissolved by magnetizing, “it dissolved the sensuous medium and opens the consciousness to the Divine life” [APP ¶91]. Brought to its last ens, “The residuum from this medium supplies body to the regenerate soul” [APP ¶110].

Identified with: principle of sense [APP ¶109]

See also: Medium

References: APP ¶109, APP ¶110, APP ¶91

Sensuous spirit

term · sensuous and sensible spirit

The spirit in the blood through which life acts; taken up into the will, it dies so that new life, the Phoenix, may arise.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood describes the spirit in the blood through which life acts, to be taken up into the will so that new life grows from its death: “Out of the ashes of this present sensuous spirit arises the Phoenix.” [APP ¶91]

See also: Spirit

References: APP ¶91

Sentient medium

term

In Atwood’s modern exponent, what was at first fixed and is dissolved in the blackening.

Quoting our modern exponent, Atwood reports that in the blackening “that which at first was fixed, viz., the sentient medium, is dissolved” [II.1 ¶23].

See also: Medium

References: II.1 ¶23

Separation

term · Separabis

The primary object of the Art: separating pure from impure and subtle from gross, which Atwood takes to be apparently identical with the Mysteries’ ordeal of the death of the natural life.

Paracelsus, quoted, held that “separation was the principle and beginning of all generation” [I.2 ¶25], the greatest miracle in philosophy; it is the first half of Ripley’s procedure before recombination [I.2 ¶25].

Atwood: “This Separation is indeed the primary object of the Art” [III.1 ¶21], the separating of pure from impure and subtle from gross, done by mind, not mechanical dissolution. She identifies it with the Mysteries: it “appears to be identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries, when the great ordeals are passed through during the decomposition and death of the natural life” [III.1 ¶21].

Identified with: the ordeals of the Mysteries (decomposition and death of the natural life) [III.1 ¶21]

References: I.2 ¶25, III.1 ¶21

Separator

term · divine Separator

The true separating agent, whose finding is the greatest difficulty; in Boehme, a divine artist of great subtlety within lovers of the Art.

Atwood: “To find the true Separator is described, in fact, as the greatest difficulty” [III.1 ¶32], which she likens to Virgil’s hidden tree. Jacob Boehme, quoted, speaks of lovers of the Art “whose Separator is an artist of great subtlety in them” [III.1 ¶39], a divine agent that must not be given into the bestial hand.

References: III.1 ¶32, III.1 ¶39

Sepentary

term

In the Adept’s words, the seven made when Three and Four unite; the true Sabaoth, the rest of God the creature shall enter.

The Adept, quoted: “Three and Four make seven.” [IV.2 ¶18] (the four elements with Unity and Ternarius). He identifies it: “This Sepentary is the true Sabaoth, the rest of God” [IV.2 ¶18], which the creature shall enter.

Identified with: Sabaoth, the rest of God [IV.2 ¶18]

References: IV.2 ¶18

Sephiroth

term

In a passage quoted from Agrippa, the Sephiroth, glossed as Hochma, are that on which the ass’s influence occultly depends.

Voice: Agrippa, as quoted. The ass’s influence is said to depend occultly on the Sephiroth, glossed in the same breath: “Sephiroth, i.e., Hochma” [III.2 ¶64]. So the text equates Sephiroth with Hochma here; it does not explain either further.

Identified with: Hochma [III.2 ¶64]

References: III.2 ¶64

Sequestatrix

term

In a passage quoted from Paracelsus, the sequestatrix is that which gives each thing its form and essence; Atwood links it to the special part of Intellect.

Paracelsus is quoted: “that is the sequestatrix, which gives to every thing its form and essence” [III.1 ¶21]. In the same passage Atwood seems to call either this sequestatrix or the Separation the special part of Intellect. The text leaves unclear which of the two she means.

References: III.1 ¶21

Serpents

term · Angues

Two serpents found everywhere on earth, a living male and a living female, to be understood spiritually and not bodily.

Voice: Cornelius Agrippa’s ingenious disciple, as quoted. The two serpents are found everywhere on earth: “they are a living male and a living female (understand in relation to the spirit always without all corporeal allusion)” [III.1 ¶50]. The text itself instructs a spiritual reading, without any bodily reference.

References: III.1 ¶50

Servius

person — commenting on Virgil · Servius, commenting on Virgil

Servius, commenting on Virgil, is cited to support the point that the Bacchic rites served to purify souls.

Atwood cites Servius’s comment on Virgil in support of her point that the Bacchic rites were meant to purify souls: “Libris patris sacra ad purgationem animarum pertinebant” [II.2 ¶5]. A rough rendering (ours, not the book’s): the sacred rites of Father Liber pertained to the purification of souls. The claim rests on Atwood’s own use of the line, not on our rendering.

References: II.2 ¶5

Seven

term

Atwood says the great principle of the number seven is a Rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The great principle of the number seven is a Rest” [APP ¶69]. This is a rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.

References: APP ¶69

Seven bodies

term

In Hermes, seven bodies of which gold is first; Atwood reads them as the inferior spheres of vitality in which the soul of gold moves.

Atwood cites Hermes: “there are seven bodies — of which gold is the first, the most perfect, the king of them, and their head” [I.3 ¶58]. In a note she explains what the bodies stand for. The aim is to “perfect all the other seven bodies; i.e., to signify here, according to Hermes, the inferior spheres of vitality in which it moves” [I.3 n65]. So she identifies the seven bodies with the inferior spheres of vitality in which gold’s soul moves.

Identified with: inferior spheres of vitality [I.3 n65]

References: I.3 n65, I.3 ¶58

Seven letters

term

Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, marked by color and quality.

Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, distinguished by color and quality. She notes that writers name them differently: “some call them planets, others metals (for the radical life of the spirit is indeed mineral)” [I.3 n47].

References: I.3 n47

Severation

term

The period in which the principles are separated, during which a coction goes on amid flood, eclipse and confusion.

Atwood uses severation for the period in which the principles are separated: “during this period of the severation, a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. In her account this period is marked by flood, eclipse and confusion.

References: III.1 ¶53

Sharp vinegar

term

A solvent known only to philosophers; Atwood says Cleopatra dissolved her earring in it.

Atwood tells how Cleopatra dissolved her earring in “such a sharp vinegar as is only known to philosophers on the ground of nature” [I.1 ¶18]. The text gives it no further identification.

References: I.1 ¶18

Siege of life

term

The ‘allegoric’ siege of life, to which the Rational Light is raised and where it overcomes the stronghold of evil.

Atwood says the Rational Light “afterwards is raised to the allegoric siege of life” [III.4 ¶19], where it overcomes ‘the stronghold of evil’. The term is not explained further here.

See also: Life

References: III.4 ¶19

Signature

term

Atwood says an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding to know things in their roots.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding for “the knowledge of things in their roots” [APP ¶63]. The term is not defined further here.

References: APP ¶63

Simperings

term · simper

In Norton’s Ordinal, the simperings of the Stone must be known until it can no more simper.

Voice: Norton’s Ordinal, as quoted: “To know the simperings of our Stone, Till it may no more simper do, nor cease,” [IV.1 ¶12]. The verse apparently sets simmering against boiling. This is the reader’s inference; the text does not state it.

References: IV.1 ¶12

Simple element of nature

term

What Van Helmont was led to perceive in his dream-like vision.

Atwood says Van Helmont, in a dream-like vision, was “led along into a perception of the simple element of nature” [III.2 ¶17].

References: III.2 ¶17

Simplicius

person

Named as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage that Atwood cites.

Atwood names Simplicius as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage she uses [III.1 ¶21]. Nothing more is said of him.

References: III.1 ¶21, III.2 n36

Sir Edward Kelly

person · Kelly

An adept whom Atwood cites as having reportedly possessed the Powder; she judges his book weak and his lavishness blameworthy, but uses his verses on the Art coming by grace.

Atwood names Kelly, author of De Lapide Philosophorum, as an adept who reportedly possessed the Powder, but she judges his book of little value and criticizes his lavishness [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶67]. Elsewhere she cites Kelly’s verses in Ashmole’s Theatrum in support of her view that the Art is not obtained by reading or by will: “by grace it is obtained” [IV.1 ¶19; IV.1 n19].

References: I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶67, IV.1 n19, IV.1 ¶19

Sir William Jones

person — translator of an Indian record · William Jones

Translator of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1) that Atwood cites: all mental appearances except the First Cause are image or delusion.

Atwood cites Sir William Jones’s translation of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1, p.241) as giving the same instruction: every mental appearance except the First Cause is image or delusion. The record says: “know that to be the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n51]. She uses it as agreeing with her own position.

References: II.3 n51, II.3 ¶48

Siretz

term

In Hermes, a kind of sulphur, identified with lions’ and cats’ claws.

Voice: Hermes, as quoted. Siretz is a sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It is also identified with “the lions’ and cats’ claws, which is siretz” [I.3 ¶20]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

Identified with: Sulphur [I.3 ¶20]; lions’ and cats’ claws [I.3 ¶20]

References: I.3 ¶20

Skeptics

term · skepticism, modern skeptics

Those Geber condemns next above the Covetous: they stay ignorant by choice and hinder others; Atwood calls their skepticism the mock ally of rational skepticism.

Atwood reports Geber’s judgment: “next above the Covetous, Skeptics are condemned by Geber” [III.4 ¶12]. In her account they remain ignorant by choice and hinder others. She adds her own view that modern skeptics only ‘ape’ sound reason, and that their skepticism is the ‘mock ally’ of rational skepticism. She apparently shares Geber’s condemnation.

References: III.4 ¶12

Smaragdine Tablet

treatise · Smaragdine Table, Emerald Table, Smagardine Table, Smagardine Tablet, Tabula Smaragdina Hermetis

Hermes’ Tabula Smaragdina, quoted in full as comprising the working principle and total subject of the art; Atwood calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art.

Atwood quotes the Tablet in full (as the Smaragdine Table, also spelled ‘Smagardine table’, or the Emerald Table). She treats it as containing the working principle and total subject of the art, and calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art. Its key line: “that which is above is as that which is below” [I.1 ¶3; I.1 ¶7–10]. She endorses it and uses it repeatedly:

  • As the Emerald Table, to show that agent and patient are one after dissolution, the One Thing: “That which is below is as that which is above” [I.2 ¶48].
  • As the Smagardine Table, to show that both the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient must be prepared: “That which is above is as that which is below, and that which is below is as that which is above” [III.1 ¶41].
  • In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), for the point about earth or the residuum: “The power is integral if it be turned into earth” [APP ¶110].

References: I.1 ¶10, I.1 ¶3, I.1 ¶7, I.1 ¶8, I.1 ¶9, I.2 ¶48, I.3 n23, II.3 n59, III.1 ¶41, APP ¶110

Socrates

person

Cited from the Republic, Theaetus and Phaedrus for Wisdom generating truth, for the grades of initiation, and as the one who knew the Nothing that is Wisdom.

Atwood draws on Socrates:

  • From the Republic and Theaetus: Wisdom generates truth, perfects imperfect things and calls forth latent Intellections. “Wisdom is generative of truth and intellect” [II.1 ¶37].
  • From the Phaedrus, as explained in a passage from Proclus: the ordered grades of initiation. “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. He is also the narrator of Plato’s ascent to Intelligible Beauty [II.4 ¶29].
  • Atwood identifies the Wisdom with the Nothing that Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27].

She uses all three in support of her own position.

References: II.1 ¶37, II.4 ¶23, II.4 ¶29, IV.4 ¶27

Sol

term · Sun, Sol’s

Sol or the Sun: hidden inwardly in the Stone, imprisoned until penetrated by the mercurial Spirit, partner of the Moon, and given to the reduced body as its soul.

Several voices speak of Sol:

  • Hermes, as quoted: the Stone’s sun and beams lie hidden within it. “My Sol and my beams are most inward and secretly in me” [I.3 ¶37]. Sol is also said to ‘follow’ in the seven letters, but this is not explained.
  • Atwood, explaining how Mercury acts on gold: “the formal virtue of Sol is sealed; his sulphur is imprisoned” [III.3 ¶30]. Sol is unaware of himself until the mercurial Spirit penetrates him; then he sends forth his Light.
  • Atwood on the Sun as the Moon’s partner in the work. Citing Plutarch, she says “the operations of the Sun are seen to resemble those strokes which by mere dint of strength and force bear down all before them” [III.1 ¶45]. In a passage from Boehme, Sol is given to the reduced body as its soul: “give it Sol, viz., the soul” [III.1 ¶48].
  • The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, as quoted: the Lion devours and eclipses the bright Sun and brings him to greater perfection. The Sun is the Moon’s brother and bridegroom; with her he is parent of the King, and he feeds a red King. “This Lyon maketh the Sun sith [fith] soone To be joined to hys Sister the Moone:” [III.1 ¶65]. ‘Sol’ appears in parallel positions in the same verse, but the text does not state that it is the same as the Sun.
  • Pierce, the Black Monk, as quoted, lists Sol among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].
  • Eirenaeus, as quoted, pairs Sol and Lune as the products of projection: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” and “Innumerable parts to Sol’s estate.” [IV.3 ¶25]. Their effect will prove ‘both gold and silver pure’.

Identified with: Soul [III.1 ¶48]

References: I.3 ¶37, III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶48, III.1 ¶65, III.3 ¶30, III.4 ¶21, IV.3 ¶25

Sol principle

term

Atwood equates the Sol principle with the vortex of life, to which Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely in consciousness.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), equates the two: “the vortex of life —the Sol principle” [APP ¶113]. Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely to it in consciousness.

Identified with: vortex of life [APP ¶113]

See also: Principles

References: APP ¶113

Solar and Lunar Mercury

term

In Flamel, two Mercuries, one planted in the other, cherished in the Alembic over a constant sun-like fire.

Voice: Flamel, as quoted. He speaks of “the Solar and Lunar Mercury, and the plantation of the one in the other” [IV.1 ¶41]. Both are cherished in the Alembic over a constant fire like the sun’s. The text does not explain this further.

See also: Mercury

References: IV.1 ¶41

Solar light

term

Light that the ethereal humidity nourishes and educates; set beside Sol as the source of all heat.

Atwood says the ethereal humidity “nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]. In the same passage she sets the Solar Light beside Sol as the source of all heat.

See also: Light

References: IV.1 ¶29

Solar sulphur

term · souphre solaire

In the Mystere de la Croix, a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold, drawn by subtle operations from the vitriol left after Mars and Venus are conjoined.

Voice: the Mystere de la Croix, as quoted. After Mars and Venus are conjoined, subtle operations draw from the leftover vitriol “un souphre solaire ou or philosophique vivant” [III.3 ¶11]. Our rendering, not the book’s: a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold. The phrasing equates solar sulphur with living philosophic gold.

Identified with: living philosophic gold [III.3 ¶11]

See also: Sulphur

References: III.3 ¶11

Solar tincture

term · Tinctura Solaris

Atwood equates the Solar Tincture with the Aurific Light.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The Solar Tincture (Tinctura Solaris) is the Aurific Light.” [APP ¶92]. The term is not explained further.

Identified with: Aurific light [APP ¶92]

See also: Tincture

References: APP ¶92

Solomon

person · the wise king

The wise king, cited throughout as a voice on Wisdom: its nature, its gift from above, its increase, and seeing all things in its Spirit.

Atwood often cites Solomon, also called the wise king, in support of her own view of Wisdom:

  • Wisdom of Solomon, chap. 7: a panegyric of Wisdom as pure, all-pervading and renewing, entering holy souls. “Wisdom, says the wise king, is more moving than any motion” [II.1 ¶44; II.1 n42].
  • Wisdom of Solomon 8: 9: knowledge of creation comes by Conscious Intuition, taught by Wisdom. “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49; III.3 n34].
  • Wisdom of Solomon, 21: Wisdom must be given from above, and it preserves the righteous. “Or what man is he, asks Solomon, that can know the counsel of God?” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n18].
  • Atwood reads “the fear of God is the beginning of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶37] as the awe of the soul perceiving itself in its source.
  • Proverbs iv, 8, 9 illustrates the increase of the fermenting light: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [I.3 n45].
  • Proverbs 24, 27 and Eccles. 4: Wisdom joined with strength, and two are better than one. “A wise man is strong, says the wise king, and knowledge increaseth strength” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n51].
  • The ‘enclosed garden of Solomon’ and the sealed fountain are identified with Elysium [II.4 ¶9].

Others cite him within passages she quotes:

  • Charnocke’s verse on the faithful servant: “A good servant, saith Solomon, let him be unto thee, As thine own hearte,in each degree” [III.4 ¶35].
  • Eirenaeus, against idleness: “The desire of the idle shall cause him to perish” [IV.1 ¶6].
  • Helmont, on the physician as created by the Lord: “Honor the physician with the honor due unto him” [IV.3 ¶34].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Solomon illustrates seeing the nature and virtues of all things in the Spirit of Wisdom [APP ¶67]. He also supports not exceeding the capacity one is given: “Be not righteous overmuch” [APP ¶110].

References: I.3 n45, II.1 n42, II.1 ¶44, II.3 ¶37, II.4 ¶9, III.1 n51, III.1 ¶45, III.3 n34, III.3 ¶49, III.4 ¶35, IV.1 ¶6, IV.3 n18, IV.3 ¶34, IV.3 ¶39, APP ¶110, APP ¶67

Solution

term · solve, solved

The dissolving that is the first work and foundation of the art: the body reduced to water or mercury; for Atwood, also the separation of the sensuous medium and a converting comprehension.

Friar Bacon and the Rosarium, as quoted, call Solution the first work: the body is reduced into water, that is, mercury, and “this is called Solution, which is the foundation of the whole art” [I.2 ¶5].

Atwood’s own uses:

  • She glosses the verb directly: “solve, that is comprehend, it on its own ground” [II.2 ¶15]. The impure perceptive medium needs this: “it needs alternation and solution, as the oracles teach” [II.2 ¶15]. And “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution” [II.2 ¶16].
  • On the operation itself: “Solution dissolves and liquifies the included Spirit” [III.2 ¶64].
  • Lully dissolved the Philosophic Salt: “he performed the Solution in nine days” [IV.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer):

  • Solution is both the answer to a question and a dissolving that enters and converts the enquirer, as light dissolves darkness: “every solution is a convertive process and progress in entity and hypostatic relation” [APP ¶115].
  • Past the phantasmagoric region one is to “enter into its solution, i.e., in its dissolved essence” [APP ¶144], the world’s dissolved essence.
  • “Solution refers to the separation of the sensuous medium itself.” [APP ¶176]. This separation is repeated on the intuitional or medial life to reach the divine.

Identified with: dissolved essence [APP ¶144]; separation of the sensuous medium [APP ¶176]; comprehend [II.2 ¶15]

See also: Dissolution

References: I.2 ¶5, II.2 ¶15, II.2 ¶16, III.2 ¶64, IV.1 ¶36, APP ¶115, APP ¶144, APP ¶176

Solve, Coagula, Fige

term

A formula closing a verse on the fixed and the volatile, linked there to the inversion of fixed and volatile.

A verse on the fixed and the volatile closes with this formula: “Solve, Coagula, Fige.” [I.2 ¶21]. Our rendering, not the book’s: dissolve, coagulate, fix. The passage ties it to the inversion of fixed and volatile. The voice is unclear from the text.

References: I.2 ¶21

Son

term

In Hermes, the son of king and red daughter, who takes his tincture from the fire and bears the Philosophic Matter: the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified.

Voice: Hermes, as quoted. The son is conceived of the king and the red daughter and takes his tincture from the fire. He is the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified: “this son is himself the treasury, even himself bearing the Philosophic Matter” [I.3 ¶35].

Voice: the Master, as quoted. The Son is dead and then lives: “The Dragon shuns the sunbeams which dart through the crevices, our dead Son lives.” [IV.2 ¶14]. He takes his Tincture from fire and death, comes forth from the Fire, rejoices with his spouse, becomes a warrior in the Fire, and bears the Philosophic Matter. The same passage gives two identities: “Our Son the King” and “For this Son is the treasury” [IV.2 ¶14].

Identified with: King [IV.2 ¶14]; treasury [IV.2 ¶14]

References: I.3 ¶35, IV.2 ¶14

Son of Dirach

person

Cited authority (Eccles.) whom Atwood uses to show that Wisdom first tries her follower with fear before revealing her Secret.

Cited by Atwood (Eccles. 1:20; 4:17, 18, 28) in support of the point that Wisdom first tries a man with fear and only then reveals her Secret: “at first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him” [II.3 ¶37; II.3 n43]. Atwood attributes this to the same intimate experience she is describing, and uses it approvingly.

References: II.3 n43, II.3 ¶37

Song of Sol.

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: Sol

References: APP ¶119

Sons of art

term

Basil’s name for practitioners of the Art, who all aim at the ‘harbor’ reached when the Matter’s bonds are loosed after its due time.

In a passage quoted from Basil, the sons of Art are the practitioners of the Art, whose common goal is the loosing of the Matter’s bonds after its due time: “loose its bonds towards which all sons of Art aim to arrive as to their long-desired and sought for harbor” [IV.1 ¶15].

References: IV.1 ¶15

Sophia

term

In Atwood’s Table Talk, that which alchemy seeks in the mind.

Atwood speaks of alchemy as “the seeking of The Sophia in the mind” [APP ¶183] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer). The text gives no further definition here.

References: APP ¶183

Sophocles

person

Cited by Atwood to illustrate the same point: that life is to be had only there, all other places being full of misery and evil.

Cited by Atwood as illustrating the same point as the surrounding passage: “Life only is to be had there, all other places are full of misery and evil” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8].

References: II.2 n8, II.2 ¶5

Soul

term · human soul

In Atwood’s Table Talk, the soul is the body’s ultimate perfection, a mesothesis between two spheres, and in its metalline perfection the philosopher’s stone.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The human soul is more than a mere resultant of body; it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres.” [APP ¶178]. Its angelic essence is described as a metallic humidity, and she identifies the perfected soul with the philosopher’s stone: “The soul in its metalline perfection is the philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

Identified with: Stone [APP ¶181]

References: APP ¶178, APP ¶181

Soul of Deity

term

In Sendivogius as quoted, what man possesses and other creatures, which have only spirit, lack.

Sendivogius, as quoted, distinguishes man from other creatures, which “have only spirit and not the soul of Deity” [II.1 ¶10]; man alone has the soul of Deity.

References: II.1 ¶10

Soul of gold

term

An ingredient in Hermes’ recipe, identified with the Meridian Redness and, by the Scholiast, with the true aurific principle that perfects the seven bodies.

In Hermes’ recipe as quoted, the soul of gold is one ingredient, identified with the Meridian Redness: “the Meridian Redness, that is the soul of gold” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast, who reads the whole recipe as a matter of distillation, explains it as “our soul of gold, writes the Scholiast, which is the true aurific principle” [I.3 n65]: a medium that perfects the seven bodies as the sun perfects sublunary nature.

Identified with: Meridian Redness [I.3 ¶6]; true aurific principle [I.3 n65]

See also: Gold

References: I.3 n65, I.3 ¶6

Spagyric works

term

Works in which, Atwood says, the adepts esoterically credit prayer with efficacy when the mind is lifted up; not further defined.

Atwood notes that “adepts are eloquent in their imputations of its efficacy in Spagyric Works, when the mind is lifted up” [III.4 ¶22], referring to prayer. The text does not define Spagyric Works further.

See also: Works

References: III.4 ¶22

Species

term

The specific kind of a thing (lead as lead); indestructible and not transmutable, contrasted with the Universal Subject to which transmutation actually relates.

Atwood uses species in a special sense: the specific kind of a thing, as lead considered as lead. Species are indestructible, not liable to corruption and not transmutable: “It is not species that they profess to transmute” [I.2 ¶4]. Transmutation instead concerns what underlies them, “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

References: I.2 ¶4, IV.4 ¶2

Speculation of wholes

term

Contemplation in which, according to Proclus, the same order holds as in the Mysteries: phantasms first, illumination afterwards.

Proclus, as quoted, says that “the same method takes place in the speculation of Wholes” [II.3 ¶22] as in the Mysteries: phantasms appear first and illumination comes later.

References: II.3 ¶22

Sperme

term

In Pierce the Black Monk’s verse, a seed taken out of a body that contains all things, set against common gold and silver.

In verse quoted from Pierce, the Black Monk, the sperme is a seed drawn from a body, set against common gold and silver: “But a sperme owte of a body I take,” [III.4 ¶21]. It contains all: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light, Water and Erth, Fyre and Fryght:” [III.4 ¶21].

References: III.4 ¶21

Sphinx

term

Atwood’s figure for the Ether, Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries, whose enigma must be fully solved lest she regain dominion over the work.

Atwood says the Egyptians placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, and identifies her with the Ether: “so is that Ether then the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; “Such was the Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries” [III.1 ¶6]. She is the passive counterpart of the inner light: “And she is all things passively which the internal light is impassively.” [III.1 ¶6]. Her animal form with a human face shows a twofold life, and her ‘winds’ image the elevating power of imagination; the ancients mastered her [III.1 ¶6].

In the practice, the Sphinx is a power that must be fully overcome: if the dissolution is left incomplete before the total solution of her enigma, “the Sphinx should retrieve her dominion unawares and frustrate the work begun” [IV.1 ¶7].

Sphinx. Atwood cites the Sphinx as the barrier at the vestibule that perplexes intruders and admits only philosophers [IV.4 ¶5]. She uses Oedipus’ solving of the riddle to illustrate the rational penetration of one’s own natural understanding: one who, “like Oedipus, is able to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx” [IV.1 ¶48]. See also the term Sphinx.

Identified with: Ether [III.1 ¶5]; Door-keeper of the Egyptian Mysteries [III.1 ¶6]

See also: Sphinx’s fables

References: III.1 ¶5, III.1 ¶6, IV.1 ¶48, IV.1 ¶7, IV.4 ¶5

Sphinx’s fables

collective voice

Fables cited by Atwood to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being.

Atwood cites these fables to illustrate the reduction to a simple estate of Being, with the image of something “carried within the temple upon the back of an ass” [III.2 ¶64].

See also: Sphinx

References: III.2 ¶64

Sphinx’s lair

term

Atwood’s figure for that to which her preceding exposition has served as introduction; not explained.

Atwood closes a section: “we conclude our introduction, as it may be called, to the Sphinx’s lair” [III.4 ¶47]. The figure is not explained.

References: III.4 ¶47

Spinoza

person

Named by Atwood as a metaphysician who speculated on the same experimental ground.

Atwood names Spinoza among metaphysicians and speculators on the same experimental ground [I.1 ¶39]; the text says nothing further about him.

References: I.1 ¶39

Spirit

term · spirits

The life-principle of the matter, whose association sums up the Art; in the work it wakes, unifies, builds its own vessel, and (per Eudoxus) is the tie of soul and body, called Eve and Mercury.

In the work. The Spirit’s removal is the matter’s death and its return is its life; it must be kept from escaping the vessel: “In the life and death thereof we work with the spirits” [I.3 ¶49]. The Art is summed up in it: “In a scientific association of the Spirit the Hermetic Art has been said summarily to consist” [I.3 n59]. Atwood also speaks of its superior life, its two invisible poles and its external forms (voice partly unclear in these records).

Atwood’s account. The Spirit wakes in the congress of allied mind: “the Spirit wakes to consciousness” [III.4 ¶27]; “these diversified parts of the Spirit are in the renascent harmony made one” [III.4 ¶28]. It cannot increase without a medium and a bond. “The Spirit finally constructs its own vessel and vitrifies it” [III.4 ¶32], and it tests the instruments, “as by the Spirit they are proved fit” [III.4 ¶40].

The Zohar. The Rabbi in the Zohar, as quoted: “When the Thought begins to develop itself forth, it arrives at that degree when it becomes Spirit.” At this point it is no longer shut up in itself: “Arrived at this estate, it takes the name of Intelligence” [III.3 ¶78].

Eudoxus. Joined with body to form the Stone, the Spirit is the soul and body’s only tie, “of whom the Spirit is the only tie which works this conjunction”, and is used to wash the earth; “the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. It is corporified (turned to earth) in the Fourth Key, and in the Fifth it unites paste and leaven. In the plural, the spirits of the bodies are the Bath and unite permanently with purified bodies: “the spirits desire to be in the cleansed bodies, and having them, they enliven and dwell in them” [IV.3 ¶10].

Identified with: Intelligence [III.3 ¶78]; Eve [IV.3 ¶7]; Mercury [IV.3 ¶12]

References: I.3 n59, I.3 ¶49, III.3 ¶78, III.4 ¶27, III.4 ¶28, III.4 ¶32, III.4 ¶40, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶12, IV.3 ¶7

Spirit of nature

term

In Atwood’s Table Talk, nature’s spirit is all imagination, realizing its imaginings in aromal essences; literal chemists vainly hoped to sublime it with lifeless instruments.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The spirit of nature is all imagination, ideality, fancy.” [APP ¶122]. It wraps itself in aromal essences to realize its imaginings. It is a personality in particulars, and “when regarded universally it is the same in the being of the orb soul” [APP ¶122]; it grows more phantastic the more power it is given from the Central Source.

In the main text she criticizes literal chemists who worked with stills and furnaces “in hope by such lifeless instruments to sublime the Spirit of Nature” [I.1 ¶86], implying that such instruments cannot do it.

References: I.1 ¶86, APP ¶122

Spirit of the Lord

term

In the Apostle’s words as quoted, the Spirit that brings liberty and changes its beholders into the same image; identified with the Lord.

The Apostle, as quoted: where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty, and its beholders are changed into the same image, “even as by the Spirit of the Lord” [III.3 ¶59]. It is identified with the Lord: “For the Lord is that Spirit” [III.3 ¶59].

Identified with: the Lord [III.3 ¶59]

See also: Lord

References: III.3 ¶59

Spirit of the natural life

term

Spirit in its natural state, which Atwood calls degraded and incapable of true intelligence: diseased, falsifying and dulled until clarified.

Atwood reports the condemnation of “the Spirit of the natural life as degraded and incapable of true intelligence” [II.2 ¶8], and asks “in what the disease of the Spirit consists” [II.2 ¶9]. In this state the spirit is diseased, falsifying and dulled until it is clarified.

See also: Life

References: II.2 ¶8, II.2 ¶9

Spirit of Wisdom

term

A vindicative power upholding Wisdom’s Rule, fulfilling it lovingly but confounding whoever abandons the Divine purpose for private ends.

Atwood writes of “the vindicative Spirit of Wisdom for the justification of her Rule” [IV.3 ¶56]. “The Spirit of Wisdom runs lovingly by her own Rule to fulfill it” [IV.3 ¶56], but leaves in confusion whoever turns from the Divine purpose to private ends.

See also: Wisdom

References: IV.3 ¶56

Spirit to Dr Dee

collective voice

The Spirit’s words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.), cited by Atwood in support of steadfastly continuing the labor to its end.

Atwood cites the Spirit’s words to Dr Dee (Dee’s Conversat.) in support of continuing the labor steadfastly to the end: “to fight against the Powers of Darkness requires great force” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n8].

See also: Dr Dee

References: IV.1 n8, IV.1 ¶7

Spirit-man

term

In Atwood’s Table Talk, the spiritual man within the natural man, whose work is to move the Ether.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “There is a spirit-man within the natural man” [APP ¶139]; its work is to move the Ether.

References: APP ¶139

Spirit-suggestions

term

In Atwood’s Table Talk, promptings from spirits, which give the spirits footing in the life when uttered.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood warns: “To utter from spirit-suggestions is a fearful thing” [APP ¶127], because doing so gives the spirits footing in the life.

References: APP ¶127

Spiritual agent and spiritual patient

term · spiritual agent, spiritual patient, agent, patient

The work’s two principles, active and receptive: equal Spirits that must both be prepared and allied, each dying in the other so their reunion yields new life.

Atwood names the two principles of the work, active and receptive, as equal Spirits that must both be made ready and brought together: “Both therefore have to be prepared — the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient” [III.1 ¶41]. Each dies in the other, “by death and contrition of the agent in the patient, and vice versa” [III.1 ¶49]. The old life is crucified, and their reunion under another law brings forth the new life.

See also: Agent, Agent and patient, Patient

References: III.1 ¶41, III.1 ¶49

Spiritual fermentation

term

Fermentation performed by multiplying the tinctures, not by using common gold or silver.

Atwood: “The spiritual fermentation is performed by multiplying the tinctures” [IV.3 ¶21], and not with common gold or silver.

See also: Fermentation

References: IV.3 ¶21

Spiritual generation

term

Generation under the law that the parent is bettered in the offspring, up to a fourth or fifth generation.

Atwood states “the Law especial of spiritual generation that the parent is bettered in the offspring” [III.1 ¶30], up to a fourth or fifth generation.

See also: Generation

References: III.1 ¶30

Spiritual guide

term

The one whose constitution and instinct determine how the conditions of the work vary; not further defined.

Atwood says that the work’s conditions are those “which vary with the constitution and instinct of the spiritual guide” [III.4 ¶42]. The text does not define the spiritual guide further here.

References: III.4 ¶42

Spiritual Intellect

term

The intellect which natural reason helps bring into self-knowledge, and which then turns back on the outer life to analyze and transform it.

Atwood describes natural reason as helping to introduce the spiritual intellect into self-knowledge. Once there, “this latter, returning with power upon the life without, proceeds to analyze and revolutionize” [III.1 ¶13] that outer life ‘chemically’. The phrase that follows, ‘this vital perscrutinator’ (the operating agent of the change), apparently refers to this same intellect.

See also: Intellect

References: III.1 ¶13

Spiritual rock

term

In St. Paul’s words as quoted, the rock that followed the Fathers and gave them spiritual drink, identified with Christ.

St. Paul, as quoted, says the Fathers drank spiritual drink: “they drank of that spiritual rock that followed them” and “and that rock was Christ” [III.3 ¶59].

Identified with: Christ [III.3 ¶59]

References: III.3 ¶59

Spiritual union

term

A union that, Atwood says, man can neither cement nor increase by his own power.

Atwood says man can “neither cement the spiritual union or give it increase” [III.4 ¶20].

See also: Union

References: III.4 ¶20

Spoagyric artifice

term

Expression in a passage quoted from Helvetius, whose ‘Abyss’ is disclosed most inwardly, at the centre where the mystery is found.

In a passage Atwood quotes from Helvetius: “There, within most intimately, the Abyss of the Spoagyric artifice is disclosed” [III.1 ¶70]. The text does not explain the expression further.

References: III.1 ¶70

St Augustine

person · St. Augustin

Church Father Atwood cites for a work’s authenticity, for the Church’s adoption of the Mysteries’ language and rites, and for three modes of human vision.

Atwood cites him as mentioning a certain work without doubting its authenticity, although he judged it “instinctu fallacies spiritus” (ours: by prompting of a deceiving spirit); Atwood attributes that judgment probably to the popular notion and thinks he might later have revised it [I.1 ¶11, I.1 n12]. As St. Augustin he mentions an inextinguishable lamp consecrated to Venus [I.1 ¶18]. She names him among the Church Fathers who adopted the language and rites of the Mysteries, and notes that he quotes many lost Neoplatonist books [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9]. He supports her account of three modes of human vision, the third (anagogic) being placed in Elysium [II.4 ¶15].

References: I.1 n12, I.1 ¶11, I.1 ¶18, II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9, II.4 ¶15

St John’s Gospel

treatise

The Gospel, cited by Atwood for those to whom the Word of God came being called gods, and for the True Light perfected in the Saviour.

Atwood cites chapter 10 for the point that those to whom the Word of God came are called gods, set against unbelief: “thou blasphemest, because I said I am the Son of God” [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n37]. She also cites it for the True Light perfected in the Saviour, whose ray cleanses life: “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19, IV.2 n17].

See also: Gospel

References: III.3 n37, III.3 ¶59, IV.2 n17, IV.2 ¶19

St Matthew

person

Cited by Atwood to illustrate baptism by Water set against baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire.

Atwood cites him to illustrate baptism by Water versus baptism by the Holy Ghost and Fire, with the purging of the floor and burning of the chaff: “He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with Fire” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n11].

References: IV.2 n11, IV.2 ¶15

St Paul

person · St. Paul, the great Apostle

Cited often by Atwood, chiefly in the Appendix, for the body as temple, the marriage-union of man and God, regeneration, and the purity of the Art.

In the main text Atwood cites 1 Cor. 10:1-4 on the Fathers baptized in cloud and sea, eating spiritual meat and drinking from the spiritual rock, “and that rock was Christ”, without stating its application [III.3 ¶59, III.3 n40]; the Epistle to the Hebrews, for revelation in the Son surpassing every earlier revelation of the Light: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in times past unto the Fathers by the prophets” [IV.2 ¶17, IV.2 n10, IV.2 n13]; and his saying that the impurity lies in the accuser’s thought, not in the Art: “to him that esteems a thing unclean, as St Paul says, it is unclean” [IV.4 ¶24].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he supports the body as a temple of the Holy Ghost, its members a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶16]; hints at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79]; and his Epistles are said to be better understood in the atmosphere of the higher Mystics than through professed commentators [APP ¶118]. Atwood reads “the letter killeth” as meaning the living letter of the law is too powerful a test for man’s spirit [APP ¶143], and takes “It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption” as the law of regeneration of the anima media, seed of spirit growing to spirit [APP ¶147].

Great Apostle (St Paul). Atwood cites the great Apostle (St Paul), 1 Corinthians 15:37 [III.1 n36], to support the principle that what is sown must die to be quickened and rises in a better form: “thou sowest not that body that shall be” [III.1 ¶30]. She uses the passage approvingly.

References: III.1 n36, III.1 ¶30, III.3 n40, III.3 ¶59, III.4 n25, IV.2 n10, IV.2 n13, IV.2 ¶17, IV.4 ¶24, APP ¶118, APP ¶143, APP ¶147, APP ¶16, APP ¶79

St Victor

person

Author of a commentary that, Atwood says, relates the particulars of St John’s practice of the Occult Art.

Atwood cites a commentary by St Victor as relating the particulars of St John’s practice (healing and making gold, silver and gems for the poor) [I.1 ¶24].

References: I.1 ¶24

St. John

person · St John, St John, the Evangelist Apostle

The Evangelist, cited by Atwood for the Word as Life and Light, for Christ as the Word of Life manifested, and as a practitioner of the Occult Art.

From the first chapter of his Gospel Atwood takes the Word/Light shining in darkness as the same Light: “In Him was Life; and the Life was the Light of men.” [II.3 ¶54, II.3 n60], and also the power to become sons of God [II.3 ¶55]. From the First Epistle she takes Christ as the Word of Life made manifest, the one awaited by prophets and philosophers: “That which was from the Beginning, which they had heard, and seen with their eyes” [IV.2 ¶15, IV.2 n10]. As St John, the Evangelist Apostle, he is cited as practising the Occult Art for the poor, healing and making gold, silver and gems; St Victor’s commentary relates the particulars [I.1 ¶24]. See also St John’s Gospel.

References: I.1 ¶24, II.3 n60, II.3 ¶54, II.3 ¶55, IV.2 n10, IV.2 ¶15

Stanley

person

Cited for reference only.

References: APP ¶96

Starkey

person

Author of Pyrotechny Asserted, cited as testifying that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir and recounting his own wasteful projection.

In a footnote Atwood cites Starkey’s Pyrotechny Asserted as eyewitness testimony (“I saw”) that Philalethes possessed the White and Red elixir, together with Starkey’s account of his own wasteful projection [I.1 ¶73, I.1 n93].

References: I.1 n93, I.1 ¶73

Steel

term

A name Cosmopolite, as reported by Eudoxus, gives to the Mercury, alongside ‘lodestone’.

Eudoxus reports that Cosmopolite calls the Mercury (Our Old Man) by other names, “to which he gives also the name of steel and of the lodestone” [IV.3 ¶10]. Whether the term ‘Chalybes’ is the same name the text does not state.

Identified with: Mercury (Our Old Man) [IV.3 ¶10]

References: IV.3 ¶10

Stoboeus

person

Preserver of an ancient record that Atwood cites for the conformity between death and initiation into the Grand Mysteries.

Atwood cites an ancient record preserved by Stoboeus for the conformity of death and initiation and its stages: “The mind is affected and agitated in death, just as it is in initiation into the Grand Mysteries.” [II.3 ¶37].

References: II.3 ¶37

Stone

term · Philosopher’s Stone, philosophers’ stone, Philosophic Stone, Stone of Philosophers, lapidem philosophorum

The object and perfected product of the Art: for Atwood, the concentrated, fermented Ether or Light of nature, a real entity of spiritual generation, and the soul in its perfection.

Atwood’s account. The Stone is the perfective product of the Art, made in and by the universal spirit; “this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone” [I.2 ¶26, I.2 ¶29]. It is the purified, concentrated Ether perfected by its own Light — “their stone is nothing more or less than the pure Ethereality of nature” — and transmutes by assimilating crude life into its own light; she quotes “Lapis noster, hic est ignis, ex igne creatus” (ours: our stone, this is fire, created from fire) [I.2 ¶44], and calls it “this fermented Spirit or Stone” [I.2 ¶48]; the adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44]. It is “one mineral spirit, exalted by fermentation intrinsically in its proper kind” [I.3 n55]; “By the term Botri is here signified the Philosopher’s Stone” [I.3 n52]. Hidden in the interior of the ‘earth’, it is “the true medicine” [II.3 ¶29]; it comes and is generated with Light, then brings forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30, III.1 ¶49]; its most abstruse principle is the Salt of Saturn (voice unclear) [II.3 ¶41]; the armament contends “for the self-same Stone” [III.1 ¶68], its mother being the secret menstrual (after Eirenaeus) and its Quintessence the soul (after Synesius) [III.1 ¶69]; made in the furnace with ‘our glass’, it is “a new hypostasis, and a new stone”, “that renowned Terra Maga in aethere clarificata”, and “the Stone with the new name written in the Revelation” [II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54]. What the philosophers found is “this miraculous principle of regeneration” [III.1 ¶50]. Only one unclean thing enters its composition; purged after its darkness it becomes a white Elixir [III.1 ¶61]. It is “a pure petrification of the Spirit” [IV.1 ¶29], the concentrated virtue of the Universal Subject, and “the transmutative ferment” = Form of Gold = ray of motive Light [IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶9]; once fermented it coequals itself to all, “the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶28]. The Hermetic method and its end are “the true Christian Philosopher’s Stone” [IV.3 ¶62]; the regenerate soul puts on its crown of light as a new body [IV.4 ¶20].

In the Appendix (later layer) it is “the efflux of such a life, drawn to a focus and made manifest as a concrete Essence of Light” [APP ¶6]; “a real entity produced by spiritual generation”, “a real ens of light” [APP ¶93]; “a metaphysico-chemical birth” [APP ¶108]; life in its petrified first state, to be taken and fermented [APP ¶132]; analogue of the Chief Corner Stone [APP ¶139]; and “The soul in its perfection is the Christian philosopher’s stone.” [APP ¶181].

Quoted voices. Geber and the monk of the Rosary: “The Stone is one”; “our Stone is no other than a foetant spirit and living water” [I.2 ¶11]. Hermes: “the concealed Stone of many colours; which is born in one colour” [I.3 ¶13]; composed from four elements [I.3 ¶26]; “the most precious gold without spots”, the Universal Ferment [I.3 ¶60]. The adepts: “a true mineral petrification” [I.3 n13], with many cover names (the feminine of magnesia, the hen, the white spittle, the volatile milk, the incombustible ash) but one epithet, the Philosopher’s Stone [I.3 ¶11]. Old Alchemists: “this vapour is the Stone known and proven in the Book of Life” [III.2 ¶7]. Khunrath: a glorified King, “a shining carbuncle” [III.3 ¶19]. The adeptest: it is “Ruach Elohim, which moved upon the face of the waters” [III.3 ¶50]. Maier: “et habebis lapidem philosophorum” (ours: and you will have the philosophers’ stone) [III.3 ¶31]. Arnold: dissolve it “in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7]. Norton/Bloomfield: “The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.” [IV.2 ¶36]. Eudoxus: formed “by the conjunction of the spirit with the body”, “the Sea of the Wise”, “an Astral Fire”, and, after Hermes, “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶3, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶16]. Flamel: perfected, it transmutes metals and removes the root of sin from its maker [I.1 ¶57]. The theosophist: “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38].

History. Treatises on it are ascribed to Aristotle, the Alexandrian adepts and Artephius [I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶27]; it was never found when sought “from selfish motives and a blind love of gain” [I.1 ¶39]; Ripley sought it in vain with common substances [I.1 ¶65]; Van Helmont says “I have seen the Stone and handled it” [I.1 ¶76].

Identified with: life as it is [APP ¶132]; foetant spirit and living water [I.2 ¶11]; Permanent water [I.2 ¶29]; pure Ethereality of nature [I.2 ¶44]; fermented Spirit [I.2 ¶48]; Stone of Fire / seed of gold [I.2 ¶44]; feminine of magnesia, hen, white spittle, volatile milk, incombustible ash [I.3 ¶11]; Philosopher’s Stone [I.3 ¶11]; Botri [I.3 n52]; most precious gold without spots [I.3 ¶60]; Universal Ferment [I.3 ¶60]; True medicine [II.3 ¶29]; new hypostasis [II.3 ¶52]; Terra Maga in aethere clarificata [II.3 ¶52]; Stone with the new name in Revelation [II.3 ¶54]; principle of regeneration [III.1 ¶50]; vapour [III.2 ¶7]; our King [III.3 ¶19]; Sea of the wise [IV.3 ¶3]; vine of the Wise [IV.3 ¶5]; Astral fire [IV.3 ¶16]; concrete Essence of Light [APP ¶6]; real ens of light [APP ¶93]; the soul in its perfection [APP ¶181]; Ruach Elohim [III.3 ¶50]; Tincture [IV.3 ¶38]; the Hermetic method and its end (the line returning into a circle) [IV.3 ¶62]; concentrated virtue of the Universal Subject [IV.4 ¶2]; transmutative ferment / Form of Gold / ray of motive Light [IV.4 ¶9]; pure petrification of the Spirit [IV.1 ¶29]

References: I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶20, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶49, I.1 ¶57, I.1 ¶64, I.1 ¶65, I.1 ¶68, I.1 ¶76, I.2 ¶11, I.2 ¶26, I.2 ¶29, I.2 ¶44, I.2 ¶48, I.3 n13, I.3 n52, I.3 n55, I.3 n70, I.3 ¶11, I.3 ¶13, I.3 ¶26, I.3 ¶60, II.2 ¶25, II.3 ¶29, II.3 ¶30, II.3 ¶41, II.3 ¶52, II.3 ¶54, III.1 ¶49, III.1 ¶50, III.1 ¶61, III.1 ¶68, III.1 ¶69, III.2 ¶7, III.3 ¶19, III.3 ¶31, III.3 ¶50, IV.1 ¶12, IV.1 ¶29, IV.1 ¶7, IV.2 ¶34, IV.2 ¶36, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶20, IV.3 ¶27, IV.3 ¶28, IV.3 ¶3, IV.3 ¶38, IV.3 ¶5, IV.3 ¶62, IV.4 ¶2, IV.4 ¶20, IV.4 ¶9, APP ¶108, APP ¶132, APP ¶139, APP ¶181, APP ¶6, APP ¶93

Stone of Fire

collective voice

Heading under which readers filed an unattributed Latin saying attached to the summary that the Art consists in an association of the Spirit.

Elsewhere an adept calls the seed of gold “the Stone of Fire” (see Stone) [I.2 ¶44].

Stone of the wise

term

Atwood’s name for the product of the work: the perfected lowest life, completed in three circulations and analogous to the Head Stone of the Corner.

Atwood says “the Stone of the Wise is the perfected lowest life, its true consummation”, mineral in origin and analogous to Christ the Head Corner Stone [APP ¶46, Appendix layer]. Raised up by the builders while each in turn rejects it, it becomes the Head Stone of the Corner, “as the Stone of the Wise is completed in three successive circulations” [IV.2 ¶33]. See Stone.

Identified with: perfected lowest life [APP ¶46]
