collective voice

A tale Atwood cites to illustrate that wickedness bars approach to the material of the Art.

Strabo

person

Cited by Atwood in support of the view that philosophy was the object of the Eleusinian rites.

Atwood cites Strabo in support of philosophy being the object of the Eleusinian rites [II.2 ¶5].

Subject

term

The material the Art works on, never openly declared by the adepts; something the student must find that reciprocates the design, without which the work stays abortive.

Atwood calls it “even the common Subject of their Art”, which the adepts never openly declare [I.1 ¶82]. One may be “really conversant with the Subject” [III.4 ¶7]. To begin operations the student needs it: “without a Subject to work with and reciprocate the design it remains abortive” [III.4 ¶29]; she discusses it as ‘suitable assistance’. The text does not define it further in these passages.

Subject Identity

term

What unassisted reason fails to grasp, eluding the mind as it pursues it.

Atwood says “the Subject Identity slides evermore behind the retardant mind” — reason alone cannot grasp it [II.1 ¶32].

See also: Identity

References: II.1 ¶32

Subject matter

term · subject-matter

What the work is performed on, constantly concealed by the adepts; also what underlies a species, corruptible and transferable, identified with the metals’ radical moisture.

Atwood notes that even candid texts such as Norton’s Ordinal conceal it: “with the exception of the Subject Matter and certain preliminaries, which are constantly concealed” [I.1 ¶64]. In a second sense it is what underlies a species: not species, “but the Subjects of species rather, since they are corruptible and may be changed”, so it can be freed and transferred to another form [I.2 ¶5]; of the metals she speaks of “the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed” [I.2 ¶4].

Identified with: Radical moisture [I.2 ¶4]

See also: Matter

References: I.1 ¶64, I.2 ¶4, I.2 ¶5

Subject of bodies

term

In a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses: what persists through all change of bodies, receiving and reflecting forms; matter subsists according to it.

In a summary gathered from Plotinus and Porphyry, endorsed by Atwood, it is distinct from bodies and persists through all their changes: “that which receives the forms and reflects them — always remains the same” [III.2 ¶47]. Matter is spoken of “according to the subject which is indefinite, because it is note form” [III.2 ¶49].

Identified with: Matter [III.2 ¶49]

References: III.2 ¶47, III.2 ¶49

term

The soul that suffers when pressed by evil and must be filled by a superior or an inferior power.

Atwood asks: “And what will not the subject soul suffer when pressed by so execrable an evil?” — such a soul must be filled by a superior or an inferior power [III.4 ¶6]. The sense of ‘subject’ here is left open.

term

Sublimation

term

The raising of the Spirit through degrees of concentrated essentiality; an operation that volatilizes and washes it and separates subtle from gross parts.

For Atwood, by grafting and transplanting “a growth and sublimation of the Spirit was effected, even to a third, fourth, and fifth degree of concentrated essentiality” [III.1 ¶9]; “sublimation volatilizes and washes it” [III.2 ¶64]. Vaughan speaks of “a first and second sublimation”, needed for the Matter to be alterable, without explaining them [IV.2 ¶35]. Eudoxus defines it as separating the Elements by “raising up the subtle and pure parts above the thick and terrestrial parts”, and says “Without the sublimation of the Stone, the conversion of the Elements and the extraction of the Principles is impossible” [IV.3 ¶5].

References: III.1 ¶9, III.2 ¶64, IV.2 ¶35, IV.3 ¶5

Substant unity

term

The unity of all that is: fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law, and source of miracles and every natural and supernatural increase.

Atwood calls it “the Substant Unity of all that is; the fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law”, “the source of so many miracles and magical accordances, as of every natural and supernatural increase” [III.3 ¶79].

Identified with: fountain of Universal nature and her Exemplary Law [III.3 ¶79]

References: III.3 ¶79

Subtendent

term

The extracted product, seminally equal to the whole of its parts; identified with the dry splendour and the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine.

Atwood speaks of “that Subtendent which is found seminally equal to the whole of the parts whence it is derived”, and identifies it with the dry splendour: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71].

Identified with: Tincture of the Sapphiric mine [III.3 ¶71]

References: III.3 ¶71

Subtle nature

term

A nature pervading the universe, the All in everything, and alterable by art throughout.

Atwood speaks of “a Subtle Nature pervading the universe, which is the All in every thing and susceptible of artificial alteration through all” [IV.4 ¶12].

References: IV.4 ¶12

Sufficience

term

The fullness Matter and other things reach through desire of the Good, in which they become tranquil, freed from parturitions and natural desire.

In a passage whose voice is unclear, things reach this fullness through desire of the Good: “when things have run up so far as to this Sufficience they become tranquil in it”, freed from parturitions and natural desire [III.4 ¶28].

References: III.4 ¶28

Suidas

person

Cited for dating Hermes before the Pharaohs, for defining Chimia, and for the Emperor’s burning of Egyptian chemical books.

Atwood cites Suidas for placing Hermes before the Pharoahs, about 400 years before Moses, and for his entry on Chemeia: “Chimia est auri et argenti confectio” (ours: Chimia is the making of gold and silver) [I.1 ¶6, I.1 n6, I.1 n8]. He also supports her account of the Emperor burning chemical books because the Egyptians made gold and silver, which she uses to explain antiquity’s silence about the Egyptian Art [I.1 ¶18, I.1 n24].

References: I.1 n24, I.1 n6, I.1 n8, I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶6

Sulphur

term · sulphurs, fixed Sulphur, false sulphurs, impure sulphurs

One of the three principles: the hidden active, luminous ferment or soul of the matter, bound and imprisoned until it is freed, purified and fixed as the seed of gold.

Atwood. Sulphur is one of the three principles, with mercury and salt, into which the ethereal hypostasis separates: “the soul, the spirit, and the body principle; the paternal, maternal, and proceeding substance of life; sulfur, mercury, salt” [III.1 ¶53]. It is “The sulfur, which is the soul and golden ferment” [III.1 ¶53]. In the dissolution the oppressive will dislocates it and it floats on the ethereal waters, and “the blackness” comes “from the sulfur” [III.1 ¶61]. In Sendivogius’s fable Sal mortally wounds Sulfur [III.1 ¶53]. It is the active principle inside the philosophic water, “its own good sulfur, or vital flame”, and tripling it is part of the operator’s weights: “to double mercury and triple sulfur” [I.3 n5]. The adepts give the name to light: “light or sulfur, as they call it, is the true form or seed of gold” [I.3 n40]. In the Mysteries it is “the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts, causing all this manifold scenery in the disruption of life” [II.3 ¶30]. In Sol it is the inner principle, imprisoned until the mercurial Spirit releases it: “his sulphur is imprisoned, so that he is not aware of it, does not feel or know himself” [III.3 ¶30]. ‘Foliated sulphur’ [I.3 ¶34] is not explained.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). “The Sulphur, the pure light of life, is bound down in the inferior mineral region of life” and “Saturn (i.e., Will) has the Key to the prison where Sulphur lies bound” [APP ¶125]; it must be drawn forth and grafted into the medial region to grow. It is “the masculine ferment, the sulphur or divine ferment” [APP ¶182], doubly hidden, to be set free to perfect the passive matter; also “the sulphur (this third, this obscure, this radical life)”, which must return on its matrix [APP ¶183]. “by sulphurs I mean forms” [APP ¶87]; “the impure sulphurs (desires, phantasms)” are the mundane desires in the individual will, to be purified or extirpated [APP ¶94].

Quoted voices. Hermes: “the fatness of our earth is sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]; “this sulphur doth tinge and fix, and is the connection of the tinctures” [I.3 ¶21]; “For the unguents are called sulphurs” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood’s notes gloss this: “The occult luminous principle of vitalization he calls sulfur, auripigment, etc.” [I.3 n24]; “the philosophic sulfur, or Light” [I.3 n25]; of the adepts, “The purified sulfur, fixed and incombustible, is the generating seed of the universal nature” [I.3 n29]. The Benedictine Monk: “the incombustible sulphur that heats or thickens the coldness and crudities of the quicksilver” until they are one body; Boehme places it in the red fire-form, “which is red, and therein the virtue, viz., sulphur is” [III.3 ¶24]. Eudoxus: the First Key opens “the dark prisons in which the Sulphur is shut up” [IV.3 ¶3]; “the Fire and the Sulphur are hidden in the centre of the Earth” [IV.3 ¶7]; “the precious ferment, the sulphur, that balm of Nature, and wonderful unguent” [IV.3 ¶8]; per Geber, “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]; the body must be dissolved, being “the body in which the Sulphur which coagulates the Mercury is enclosed” [IV.3 ¶12]; the true Mercury yields “the fixed Sulphur and the Universal Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16]. The Adept: Argent vive is defiled “being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” but “coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white” [IV.1 ¶10]. Vaughan names “sulphurs simple and compounded” without explanation [IV.2 ¶35].

Identified with: the pure light of life [APP ¶125]; masculine ferment; divine ferment [APP ¶182]; this third, this obscure, this radical life [APP ¶183]; fatness of our earth [I.3 ¶20]; Light [I.3 n25]; unguents [I.3 ¶24]; occult luminous principle of vitalization [I.3 n24]; the virtue (of the red fire-form) [III.3 ¶24]; precious ferment, balm of Nature, wonderful unguent [IV.3 ¶8]; the fixed (per Geber) [IV.3 ¶9]; vital flame [I.3 n5]; Light [I.3 n40]; the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries [II.3 ¶30]; Soul [III.1 ¶53]; golden ferment [III.1 ¶53]; forms [APP ¶87]; desires, phantasms [APP ¶94]

See also: Fixed sulphur

References: I.3 n24, I.3 n25, I.3 n29, I.3 n40, I.3 n5, I.3 ¶20, I.3 ¶21, I.3 ¶24, II.3 ¶30, III.1 ¶53, III.1 ¶61, III.3 ¶24, III.3 ¶30, IV.1 ¶10, IV.2 ¶35, IV.3 ¶12, IV.3 ¶16, IV.3 ¶3, IV.3 ¶7, IV.3 ¶8, IV.3 ¶9, APP ¶125, APP ¶182, APP ¶183, APP ¶87, APP ¶94

Sulphur tingens

term

A notion the quoted adept dismisses as one of the impostors’ fables.

The adept quoted by Atwood rejects it: “those imposters who tell you of a sulphur tingens, and I know not what fables” [I.2 ¶8].

References: I.2 ¶8

Sulphuric spirit

term

The sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher’s Mercury and causes it to putrefy.

Atwood describes the sharp, discriminating spirit of the working leaven, which enters the philosopher’s Mercury and makes it putrefy: “this acute discriminative sulfuric Spirit occasions a putrefaction of the philosopher’s Mercury” [III.1 ¶24].

See also: Spirit

References: III.1 ¶24

Sun and Moon

term · Soon and Moone

In Ripley’s Admonition, the ‘Sun and Moon’ of which our metals are said to be mines; not explained.

Ripley’s Admonition, quoted by Atwood: “our mettalls be nought ells but miners too, Of our Soon and Moone” [II.1 ¶13]. The text does not explain the expression here.

See also: Moon

References: II.1 ¶13

Sun and Moon philosophical

term

Named in a Sendivogius passage as the source of the ‘beams’ whose centres the lodestone’s point answers; not explained.

In a passage of Sendivogius, a parenthetical gloss (speaker unclear) names the beams’ source: “viz. of the sun and moon philosophical” [II.1 ¶10]. Not further explained.

References: II.1 ¶10

Super-essential

term

The higher work, served by the same bodily members as the natural work, in which a hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood: “All members that work here for the natural work, work also for the super-essential.” [APP ¶109] Its hyperphysical exudation supersedes natural secretion.

References: APP ¶109

Superficies

term

Something not to be broken, according to a Pythagoric precept cited as a warning; not explained.

Cited as a warning: “Neither break a superficies, as the Pythagoric precept runs” [IV.3 ¶56]. Its meaning is not explained.

References: IV.3 ¶56

Superinspection

term

In Psellus, the first kind of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, a mere appearance seen by the celebrant and not to be heeded; also a seeing in Hades.

Psellus, quoted by Atwood, names two kinds of apparition in the Chaldaic rites, “the first called superinspection, when he who celebrates the divine rites sees a mere apparition” such as light in some form; it is not to be heeded [II.3 ¶20]. Elsewhere he distinguishes “the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” from the Introspection [II.3 ¶46]; not further explained.

References: II.3 ¶20, II.3 ¶46

Superior stars

term

Glossed as the Ideas of the Divine Mind, from which things generated below are infused as light.

Atwood’s bracketed gloss: “the superior stars [i.e., Ideae Divinae Mentis]” [III.2 ¶19] (ours: Ideas of the Divine Mind). Things generated below are infused from them as light.

Identified with: Ideae Divinae Mentis [III.2 ¶19]

References: III.2 ¶19

Superiors and inferiors

term · superiors, inferiors

In Vaughan, the higher and lower orders: superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate; communion with superiors requires a heavenly life.

Vaughan, quoted by Atwood: “so superiors dissolve and inferiors coagulate” [III.4 ¶44]; without a heavenly life there is “no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

References: III.4 ¶44

Supernal alliance

term

The union in which no faculty of the soul is rejected, all being present under their rightful rule.

Atwood answers an objection: “Neither, we reply, is any faculty of the soul repudiated in that supernal alliance” [IV.4 ¶20]; all faculties are present under their rightful rule.

References: IV.4 ¶20

Supernatural Magnetism

term

The attraction by which the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself.

Atwood: the perfected Spirit draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself “by a supernatural magnetism” [IV.3 ¶29].

References: IV.3 ¶29

Supernatural work

term

In Eirenaeus, a later work whose commencement he sets apart from the literal labour on things as first found.

Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood: “I am not speaking here indeed of the commencement of the Supernatural Work, but of things as we first find them” [IV.1 ¶6].

See also: Works

References: IV.1 ¶6

Superstantial

term

Used of the latent nature of things implied by intellectual necessity, first in thought though later in time, and of the Kabalists’ Law of Light; not defined.

Atwood speaks of “a superstantial nature of things implied which, though now latent and succeeding in order of time, is first in thought absolutely” [II.1 ¶34], and of the Kabalists’ “an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. The word itself is not defined.

References: II.1 ¶34, II.1 ¶40

Superstantial experience

term

The deep experience of things reached by ascending in thought and then descending.

Atwood: by ascending in thought and then descending, one may “hope to penetrate so far as to the superstantial experience of things” [II.1 ¶49].

See also: Experience

References: II.1 ¶49

Superstantial world

term

Named in an objection asking why partaking things do not enjoy its light if true Being is everywhere present; not defined.

Named in an objection Atwood reports: if true Being is everywhere present, why do partaking things not enjoy “the light of the so-called superstantial world” [II.2 ¶20]? Not defined.

References: II.2 ¶20

Supreme mind

term

In Plutarch, the object of the aspirant’s knowledge, which the Goddess urges men to seek, dwelling in Reason as in a temple.

Plutarch, quoted by Atwood: the aim is “the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Mind, whom the Goddess exhorts them to search after” [II.1 ¶50]; it dwells in Reason as in a temple.

See also: Mind

References: II.1 ¶50

Swedenborg

person

Named for comparison: Engelbrecht lived, like him, in the visionary sphere.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood compares Engelbrecht to Swedenborg as living in the visionary sphere [APP ¶105].

References: APP ¶105

Swedenborgians

collective voice

Cited for the idea of “correspondence” between the brain and the spiritual head.

Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): Atwood refers to the Swedenborgians’ “correspondence” to illustrate the relation between brain and spiritual head [APP ¶15].

References: APP ¶15

Sybil

person

The Sybil of Virgil’s Aeneid, cited as drawing inspiration from supernal light and as directing Aeneas to the Golden Bough, which Atwood reads as the alchemical Gold.

Atwood cites the Sybil as drawing inspiration from rivers of supernal light [II.4 ¶13], and as enjoining peculiar rites and sacrifices to Misenus’ remains, compared with those at Patroclus’ pile [III.1 ¶25]. From Aeneid lib. 6 she quotes the Sybil’s instruction on the Golden Bough, “Alte vestiga oculis: et rite repertum” [III.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶16, III.1 n17] (ours: search on high with the eyes, and when duly found…): it is sought by looking upward and yields only to one whom the fates call. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): the Gold Alchemical is the gold Aeneas was told by the Sybil to find and gather [APP ¶20].

References: II.4 ¶13, III.1 n17, III.1 ¶15, III.1 ¶16, III.1 ¶25, APP ¶20

Sybil in Boissard

person

A Sybil figure in Boissard cited for the recreation as a birth of the invisible into the palpable.

Atwood cites the Sybil in Boissard in support of the recreation as the birth of the invisible into the palpable: “Verbum invisible fiet palpabile et germinabit ut Radix.” [III.3 ¶79] (ours: The invisible Word will become palpable and will sprout as a Root).

References: III.3 ¶79

Syllogism

term

In Atwood’s special sense, the true object of philosophy, implicating every science, sought through the categories as a channel for the Divine Intellect’s birth into manifestation.

Atwood uses the word in a special sense: “That was the syllogism so important to be sought after, which also is according to Aristotle the true object of philosophy” [III.2 ¶42]. It implicates every science and is sought through the categories as a channel for the birth of the Divine Intellect into manifestation.

References: III.2 ¶42

Syncellus

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n20

Synesius

person

Bishop-adept and Greek authority whom Atwood cites often and approvingly on the Matter, the phantastic Spirit, the two pairs of eyes, and the practical work.

Atwood names Synesius among authors of extant treatises on the stone (with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Athenagoras, Zosimus, Archelaus) [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34], cites his commentary on Democritus for the work’s standing [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n15], and gives him as a bishop-adept who guarded the mysteries and bound initiation by oath [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n35, I.1 n36]. He is a Church Father adopting the Mysteries’ rites, and among the Neoplatonists whose writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9].

On the phantastic Spirit: “This Etherial Spirit, he says, is situated on the confines of the rational and brutal life” [II.2 ¶10]; he treats desire, will and assent, the purification of the imaginative soul and the trials of Hercules. Atwood endorses this as ‘beautifully suggestive’, an account of ‘the life that is operated upon’ and ‘the artifice’ [II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14, II.2 n11]. From de Somniis: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20, III.1 n19]; demons are progeny of matter at war with the soul [II.3 ¶24, II.3 n26]. He names the defiled soul “Our viscous soul” [II.3 ¶30]. On Providence: efficacy of Divine Works [II.1 ¶52]; the two pairs of eyes, “this is an enigma indicative of contemplation and action” [III.1 ¶45, III.1 n49]; Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “there are two pairs of eyes; those which are beneath are closed, when those which are above are opened” [APP ¶163].

On the Matter: his treatise closes the verbal instructions with “a clear Light, which fills with true virtue every mind that has once perceived it” [I.2 ¶33, I.2 n36]; ‘the Greek saint’ gives the summary, which Atwood calls plain words: “the Quintessence and hidden thing of our Stone is nothing else than our viscous celestial and glorious soul” [III.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶71]; he agrees with others concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. His True Book gives practical instruction on the one Water, which Atwood calls the Experiment of the Fathers: “labour only for that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals” [III.3 ¶60, III.3 n43].

References: I.1 n15, I.1 n34, I.1 n35, I.1 n36, I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶27, I.2 n36, I.2 ¶33, II.1 ¶52, II.2 n11, II.2 ¶10, II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶14, II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶9, II.3 n26, II.3 ¶24, II.3 ¶30, III.1 n19, III.1 n49, III.1 ¶20, III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶70, III.1 ¶71, III.2 ¶60, III.3 n43, III.3 ¶60, APP ¶163

Synthemata

term · Divine Synthemata

In Iamblichus, the theurgic aids and media which act of themselves toward divine union and properly excite the Divine will.

Iamblichus, quoted by Atwood: “the Synthemata, i.e., the Theurgic aids and media themselves” act of themselves toward divine union, “the things which properly excite the Divine will being the Divine Synthemata themselves” [II.4 ¶31].

Identified with: Theurgic aids and media [II.4 ¶31]

References: II.4 ¶31

Tail of the peacock

term

With Iris, the appearance of all colours after the darkness; a token of reconciliation.

Atwood: after the darkness “all the colours of the world will be apparent; also Iris, God’s messenger, and the tail of the peacock” [III.3 ¶13], a token of reconciliation.

References: III.3 ¶13

Tartar

term

In Van helmont, that whose ‘bars and bolts’ a specific virtue looses.

Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, speaks of “a virtue of loosing the bars and bolts of Tartar” [IV.1 ¶39]. Not further explained.

References: IV.1 ¶39

Tartarus

term · Tartarean

The region beyond Hades to which initiates were passed, the immortal abode; also called the death of this life and the Being of the central earth.

Atwood: Tartarus is the region beyond Hades to which the Hierophant passed initiates, “to its immortal abode: for such was Tartarus, the next beyond Hades” [II.3 ¶36]; she speaks of “the physical revealments of these Tartarean realms” [II.3 ¶34], and of the central earth, “but its Being is Tartarus” [II.3 ¶41]. Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Tartarus is the death of this life.” [APP ¶168], passed through by propitiation with the Golden Bough. Olympiodorus, reading Plato’s Phaedo, gives it ethically as the place of the soul’s trial and “physically, in that it is the wholeness of existence” [III.2 ¶9].

Identified with: the death of this life [APP ¶168]

Taylor

person · Thomas Taylor, T. Taylor

Translator and commentator whose works Atwood uses as sources and praises as most erudite, while faulting his reading of the Mysteries as merely immaterial ceremonies.

Atwood relies on Taylor’s translations and notes: his rendering of the Asclepian Dialogue and notes in Plotinus’ Select Works [I.1 n11, I.1 n12]; his Pausanius notes for the Olympiodorus extract and for Porphyry [II.4 n1, II.4 n6]; Proculus on Euclid and a note to Aristotle’s Metaphysics for the Synesius extract and the Anaxagoras passage [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n19]. She praises his Dissertation for setting forth Virgil’s Elysian particulars [II.4 ¶16] and for showing the whole Odyssey to be an allegory of the recondite Wisdom of antiquity [IV.1 ¶22], and calls him the ‘most erudite translator’ who showed Aristotle’s strictures misunderstood [III.2 ¶40, III.2 n36, III.2 n38]. She qualifies his Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries: he examined them philosophically but still treated the rites as immaterial ceremonies representing abstract truths [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n5, II.2 n7].

References: I.1 n11, I.1 n12, I.1 n23, I.1 n27, II.1 n34, II.1 n37, II.1 n44, II.1 n46, II.2 n11, II.2 n14, II.2 n5, II.2 n7, II.2 ¶4, II.4 n1, II.4 n10, II.4 n12, II.4 n18, II.4 n19, II.4 n20, II.4 n23, II.4 n30, II.4 n6, II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶26, III.1 n1, III.1 n19, III.1 n30, III.1 ¶21, III.2 n11, III.2 n14, III.2 n36, III.2 n38, III.2 n41, III.2 ¶40, III.3 n47, IV.1 ¶22

Tears of Isis

term

The blessed Water that nature sheds for the world, contemplated in the vestibule of the first Adytum.

Atwood: in the vestibule of the first Adytum one contemplates “the Tears of Isis, even that blessed Water which nature sheds divinely for the world” [III.3 ¶3].

Identified with: blessed Water [III.3 ¶3]

See also: Isis

References: III.3 ¶3

Telestic

term

An adjective applied to Hercules’ arcane labours and to the accomplishments by which initiates’ souls are perfected; not defined.

Used (speaker unclear) of Hercules: “a part also of the regard of his arcane and telestic labours” [II.4 ¶3]. Atwood uses it of the Initiated, “being made perfect in every telestic accomplishment and virtue” [II.4 ¶39]. The word is not defined.

Telestic art

term

In a passage from Julian, the art whose pre-eminent power is to impart health, understood as symmetry or equilibrium of nature.

Quoted from Julian: “health is a certain symmetry or equilibrium of nature, which it is the pre-eminent power of the Telestic art to impart, ordering all things by the unity within” [IV.3 ¶30]. So the art imparts equilibrium by ordering everything through an inner unity.

References: IV.3 ¶30

Telete

term

The first grade of initiation: being initiated, while ascending, by the perfective gods.

In Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus): “we are initiated (teleioumetha) in ascending by the perfective gods” [II.4 ¶23]. The record treats this as the first grade of the ascent.

References: II.4 ¶23

Temples of Esculapius

collective voice

Cited by Atwood as places where bodily healing was widely practised with minor physico-magical arts.

Atwood cites the temples of Esculapius to show that bodily healing was widely practised there with the minor physico-magical arts [II.2 ¶5].

References: II.2 ¶5

Temporal utility

term

Atwood’s name for the present age’s idol of worldly usefulness, set up by opinion, which even its worshippers feel to be insufficient.

Atwood speaks of “that earth-born goddess of temporal Utility, which opinion has set up” [IV.3 ¶50]: the present age’s idol of worldly usefulness and advantage. She says even its votaries feel it falls short.

References: IV.3 ¶50

Ternary

term · Ternarius

A threefold principle: the thing an offering in the vessel is dedicated to, and the term in the Theosophist’s formula for reduction to the Monad.

An ancient Adeptus (Grasseus, n26) speaks of “a holy oblation or present, dedicated to the Ternary” [III.2 ¶25]. The passage does not explain the term.

The Theosophist gives a formula: “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary” [IV.2 ¶18], that is, reduce it to the Monad by rejecting the Binary. In the same paragraph, at the incarnation the four elements “were united to their eternal Unity and Ternarius” [IV.2 ¶18].

References: III.2 ¶25, IV.2 ¶18

Terra Adamica

term

The red root, which the wise sometimes call Magnesia, and Salt once it has been purified.

Atwood names Terra Adamica as the red root. She says it is “called sometimes Magnesia by the wise, and Salt after the purification” [I.3 n52]. So it = Magnesia, and = Salt after purification.

Identified with: Magnesia [I.3 n52]; Salt (after purification) [I.3 n52]

References: I.3 n52

Terrestreity

term

The gross, earthy part of metals. It binds their central light and must be purged; the Stone removes it from them.

Atwood says metals cannot work “unless they be first purged from their terrestreity” [I.2 ¶49]. Their earthiness overpowers their spirit. In a footnote she says the central light “in metalline bodies is more especially bound on account of their terrestreity” [I.3 n49]. Khunrath, quoted, says the Stone acts on metals by “depriving its terrestreity and foreign oxides” [IV.3 ¶28].

References: I.2 ¶49, I.3 n49, IV.3 ¶28

Terrestrial life

term · Terrestrial

In the Appendix, the sensuous life: it represents the Animal Kingdom and dominates the head in man.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The Terrestrial is the sensuous and represents the Animal Kingdom. In man it is dominating the head.” [APP ¶32]. The reader’s record adds that it typifies the highest life man must not aspire to. This point is not in the quoted words.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶32

Terrification

term

In Eudoxus, turning the Spirit into earth: the only operation of the Fourth Key, done by boiling.

Eudoxus, quoted: “The terrification of the Spirit is the only operation of this work” [IV.3 ¶12]. This is the Fourth Key, and the operation is done by boiling. The same paragraph describes it as the need “to corporify the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12], and as coagulation by the Sulphur. Making the Spirit earthy, giving it a body and coagulating it are apparently one operation.

References: IV.3 ¶12

Terullianus

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n7

Tetractys

term · Divine Tetractys

The fourfold drawn by the Art from three heads. It is identified with the Conjunction and called the source of ever-flowing Nature; such a being was the basis of the philosophic stone.

Atwood calls the Tetractys a fourfold, “drawn from three heads by the obstetric hand of the physico-chemical Art” [III.3 ¶35]. She also calls it “Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root” [III.3 ¶34]. She identifies it with the consummating Conjunction: “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33]. The records also call it indissoluble and the source of wisdom.

She also says “the physical Tetractys springs through the contrite experience into life” [III.3 ¶72]. It springs out of the Calx, with prolific attributes and lasting fruits.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says Pythagorus’s mystic Tetractys was obtained by the theurgic process of APP ¶107. It is “the source, as he called it, of ever-flowing Nature” [APP ¶108], and such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone.

Identified with: the source of ever-flowing Nature [APP ¶108]; Conjunction [III.3 ¶33]

References: III.3 ¶33, III.3 ¶34, III.3 ¶35, III.3 ¶72, APP ¶108

Thales

person

Early Greek philosopher who sought eastern wisdom. Atwood reads his Water as the Matter itself, not common water.

Atwood names Thales, with Pythagoras, among early Greeks who sought eastern wisdom and whose writings are lost [I.1 ¶12]. She says his water, from which all is generated, is not common water [I.2 ¶43]. He “teaches that all beings have their beginning from water” [III.2 ¶33]. He names the principle after its first material appearance, so he differs from the others only in expression [III.2 ¶34–35]. She identifies “the Water of Thales” with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She reads his deed about inscribing the circle as symbolic, not a plain demonstration [III.2 ¶44].

References: I.1 ¶12, I.2 ¶43, III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶34, III.2 ¶35, III.2 ¶44, III.2 ¶60

Theat. Chem. Brit.

treatise

A work Atwood cites to show that blood is the principal matter of each thing.

Atwood cites it for the line “For blood is the principle matter of each thing” [II.1 ¶15, II.1 n14].

References: I.1 n75, I.3 n17, II.1 n14, II.1 ¶15

Theatrum Chemicum

treatise · Theatr. Chem., Theat.Chem.

A collection Atwood calls “an esteemed work.” She cites it for an annotated Sommaire, for Picus’ de Auro, and for the Prosopoiae of the Stone.

Atwood calls the Theatrum Chemicum an esteemed work. It contains a translation of the Sommaire with important annotations, and she also cites it for Picus’ de Auro [I.1 ¶58, I.1 n69]. From vol. 3, p. 763 she takes the Prosopoiae of the Stone, which she calls instructive and elegant. It begins “Terra mihi corpus, vires mihi praestitit ignis” [III.3 ¶8, III.3 n2], which means: Earth gave me my body, fire gave me my powers (our translation).

References: I.1 n22, I.1 n27, I.1 n29, I.1 n39, I.1 n43, I.1 n46, I.1 n51, I.1 n69, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶43, I.1 ¶45, I.1 ¶58, III.3 n2, III.3 ¶8, IV.3 n25

Themistus

person

Cited for the initiate’s perplexity until the conductor opens the vestibule.

Quoted in a footnote: “the initiated is seized at first with solicitude and perplexity” [II.3 n37]. This lasts until the conductor opens the vestibule. Atwood uses the passage to support her account of initiation.

References: II.3 n37

Theocracy

term · theocratic government

In the Appendix, the only true government. Atwood accepts this as a great truth but says it needs a matching surface.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood takes up the claim that theocracy is the only true government (Kirchberger for de St Martin). She endorses it as a great truth, but says it needs a matching surface: “the world’s surface can only be governed by the center from which it is derived — that is, its king” [APP ¶112].

References: APP ¶112

Theoretic science

term

Science that is everywhere condemned. Atwood says none exists today, because the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.

Atwood: “Theoretic science is everywhere condemned; but there is no such thing at this day” [IV.4 ¶28]. Her reason is that the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared.

References: IV.4 ¶28

Theosophic

term · theosophy, theosophically

Atwood’s word for divine, ultimate knowledge grounded in experiment. She says it opens a wider plane than the theological and contrasts it with the merely intellectual.

Atwood calls the subjects of the Poemander and Asclepias “theosophic and ultimate” [I.1 ¶7]: they concern divine capabilities, not physical ground. She hopes to show that “the most famous schools of theosophy have in all ages been based on a similar experimental ground” [I.1 ¶17]. Of Boehme she says the ancient wisdom was “Revealed anew, it will be observed, theosophically, but not intellectually.” [I.1 ¶70]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Theosophic light opens him at a much wider plane of thought than the Theological.” [APP ¶118]. There she uses the word for the light of the higher Mystics, and also for the doctrine of the Neo-Platonists and Behmen.

References: I.1 ¶17, I.1 ¶7, I.1 ¶70, APP ¶118

Theosophist

collective voice

A theosophical authority Atwood quotes and endorses. A footnote at one place names him as Khunrath.

Atwood quotes the theosophist on the hostile reception that the wrathful outer life gives the new light, and on love’s victory over it: “The wrathfulness is mightily exasperated by this appearance of love, says the theosophist” [I.3 n69]. She also uses him, with approval, on Adam and the fall, the two fires, the tincturing of Mercury, the Two Natures, the Mercury as worker and the Artist’s role. On this she quotes “Herein the Philosophers’ Stone or tincture lyeth.” [IV.3 ¶38]. In Amp. Sap. Etern. the Theosophist (footnote: Khunrath) gives the formula “reduce the Ternary by the Quaternary, through the rejection of the Binary, to the simplicity of the Monad” [IV.2 ¶18, IV.2 n14]. Atwood then explains it.

References: I.3 n69, IV.2 n14, IV.2 ¶18, IV.3 ¶38

Thesaurum absconditum

term

In Norton, the “hidden treasure” of the old clerks, identified with the Fourth House or its Lord.

Norton, quoted: “For the Lord of the Fourth House likewise be it done; For that is Thesaurum absconditum of old clerkes” [IV.2 ¶34]. The Latin means “hidden treasure” (our translation). The verse is ambiguous: the treasure may be the Fourth House itself or its Lord.

Identified with: the Lord of the Fourth House / the Fourth House [IV.2 ¶34]

References: IV.2 ¶34

Theurgic art

term

The art of purifying and informing the Mind. Through purification it turns the whole being into inner light and makes the divine Matter manifest in arcane visions.

Atwood says “the Theurgic Art professed a power of purifying and informing the Mind much more beneficial and lasting” than bodily medicine [III.1 ¶11]. By purifying and subduing the passions it turns the whole hypostasis into inner light. Its practitioners consulted the divine intellect only about purification, liberation and the salvation of life [III.1 ¶11].

In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses, the pure divine Matter is shown “by means of the Theurgic Art it is made manifest and imparted through arcane and blessed visions” [III.2 ¶49].

The Alexandrian philosophers practised it, “each professing a genuine knowledge of the Theurgic art, and experimental physics on the Hermetic ground” [I.1 ¶27]. Later, “Theurgic rites, no longer holy, were proscribed” [I.1 ¶30].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says numbers are personally represented in this art, “by which spirit is added to spirit and multiplied as offspring” [APP ¶107].

References: I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶30, III.1 ¶11, III.2 ¶49, APP ¶107

Theurgic rites

term

Ancient rites aimed at the experience of truth, ordered by intellectual canons. Atwood draws on their kinds of invocation to defend prayer.

Iamblicus, quoted: “Theurgic rites conspiring to this end were scientifically disposed and early defined by intellectual canons” [II.2 ¶13]. The end is the experience of truth. Atwood draws on “the different kinds of invocation which were employed by the ancients in their celebration of Theurgic rites” [III.4 ¶23] in defending prayer.

References: II.2 ¶13, III.4 ¶23

Theurgic sacrifice

term

Sacrifice whose end is conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect. It goes together with adoration and prayer.

Atwood: “the end of Theurgic sacrifice is a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She connects it with adoration and prayer.

References: III.4 ¶25

Theurgic union

term

In Iamblichus, the soul’s union with the Divine nature. Ineffable works and symbols bring it about, not intellectual perception.

Iamblichus, quoted: the soul’s union with the Divine nature comes about through “the perfect efficacy of ineffable works” and symbols, not through intellectual perception [II.4 ¶31].

See also: Union

References: II.4 ¶31

Theurgists

term

In Iamblichus, those to whom the gods show a Fire visible to itself.

Iamblichus, quoted: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

Theurgists. Atwood reports Proclus as saying the Theurgists place their chief hopes of salvation in the Elysian fountains [II.4 ¶16].

References: II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶29

Theurgy

term · Theurgic, theurgically, Theurgical

The Greek name for the Hermetic Art. Through it the soul concentrates its vitality, purifies its essence and rises by degrees to knowledge of the First Cause.

Atwood: “Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy” [II.2 ¶3]. So Theurgy = the Hermetic Art. She calls it the practice of the Mysteries. Through it, “through their Theurgic disciplines” [II.2 ¶6], Theurgists shared in the Wisdom of true Being. “The Neoplatonists wrote largely of the Theurgical art” [II.2 ¶9].

Its aim was to concentrate vitality, turn the spiritual eye, purify and analyse the whole essence, and draw out and know the true Efficient: “this was their object and the Art of Theurgy” [II.3 ¶5]. She says this ascent needs those means: “by Theurgic rites, an ascent was made through appropriate media and a gradual assimilation, which without these could not be effected, to the knowledge of the First Cause” [II.4 ¶56]. So whoever seeks the First Principle “must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. That passage does not define the preparation further.

Identified with: Hermetic art [II.2 ¶3]

References: II.2 ¶3, II.2 ¶6, II.2 ¶9, II.3 ¶5, II.4 ¶56, III.3 ¶59

Thin water of life

term

In Jacob Boehme, what proceeds by virtue of the warmth (fire) in the blood.

Jacob Boehme, quoted: “in the virtue of the warmth, the Thin Water of Life proceedeth” [III.3 ¶24]. The warmth is the fire in the blood.

See also: Life

References: III.3 ¶24

The Thing

term

Something mesmerists reach without knowing how to alter and amend it. It is not further defined.

Atwood says mesmerists reach it, but “without the important knowledge how to alter and amend the Thing” [III.1 ¶8]. The capital letters suggest a technical sense, but the passage does not define it.

References: III.1 ¶8

Third life

term · third or lowest life

In Atwood’s Appendix, the lowest of man’s lives, in which fallen man now is; it moves with the creative Essence and is to be raised through the medial life.

Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), calls this the lowest of man’s lives: “Man is fallen; he is in the third or lowest life” [APP ¶35]. It is “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3]. The records also say that the magic of the self-will exploits its release, that it is reached from present life through the clairvoyant life by repeated fermentation, that it is to be raised through the medial life, and that the seeker in it shows the Golden Fleece. By the order of APP ¶32–35 it apparently corresponds to the Infernal (lumbar, voluntary) life, but the text does not state this identity.

See also: Life

References: APP ¶3, APP ¶35

Third principle

term

In Boehme’s language, as Atwood uses it, the sidereal and elementary birth: the medium of perceiving the First, which lies hidden in its mineral life.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood uses Boehme’s term: “the Third Principle, i.e., the sidereal and elementary birth, to use Boehme’s language” [APP ¶27]. It “is the medium of perceiving the First, which is hidden in its mineral life” [APP ¶27], and that life is full of defilement and temptation. Earlier Atwood also speaks of the circulation being carried upward “through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20], instead of the Duad generating directly. The text does not identify it further there, and does not say whether this is the same Third Principle.

Identified with: sidereal and elementary birth [APP ¶27]

See also: Principles

References: IV.2 ¶20, APP ¶27

Third work

term

In Eudoxus’s account, the operation of the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order.

Eudoxus, quoted, connects the Third work with the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order. He declines to describe it: “I will say nothing in particular of the operation of the Third work” [IV.3 ¶14].

See also: Works

References: IV.3 ¶14

Thought

term

In the Zohar passage Atwood quotes, the Principle of all that is: unknown and shut up in itself at first, then developing and emanating Light; God’s creative Thought inverts human thought.

The Rabbi in the Zohar, as Atwood quotes him, says: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78]. It develops into Spirit or Intelligence, as “Thought emanating Light” [III.3 ¶79]. Atwood, apparently agreeing, adds that “the Thought which is of God creative is the inversion of our thought” [III.3 ¶78].

References: III.3 ¶78, III.3 ¶79

Three kinds

term

In Eudoxus’s account, the domains of Nature whose principles and operations the seeker must know.

Eudoxus, quoted, says the seeker must know “the operations of Nature in the Three Kinds” [IV.2 ¶4]. The records note that the ‘three reigns’ of Nature at IV.2 ¶3 may be comparable. The text does not name the Kinds here.

References: IV.2 ¶4

Three kingdoms

term

Three domains of nature, which Atwood does not name in these passages; Hermes reputedly found their quintessential perfectibility in their homogeneal unity, and the torch diffuses life through them.

Atwood reports that Hermes discovered “the quintessential perfectibility of the three kingdoms in their homogeneal unity” [I.1 ¶6]. Later she says the torch diffuses energy, life and joy “in either if the three kingdoms, as we have shown, by its voluntary assimilation” [IV.4 ¶32], pointing back to an earlier proof. Neither passage names the three. The ‘threefold enchantment’ entry gives them as animal, vegetable and mineral [IV.4 ¶4].

References: I.1 ¶6, IV.4 ¶32

Three principles

term

The principles of the work: Life resolves into them in the philosophic fermentation (Van Helmont’s Salt, Sulphur and Mercury), and they are separated and reunited to produce the tincture.

In the passage quoting Boehme, “The same Three Principles gradually assume a new life” [II.1 ¶24]. They act in harmony to produce first whiteness and then the tincture, and Boehme speaks of “the mechanical part of the Three Principles” [II.1 ¶25]. Atwood says Life in the philosophic fermentation is “resolved into these three principles, which Van Helmont also calls Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury” [III.2 ¶28]. The author of The Triumph, quoted, speaks of “the separation and the reunion of the Three Principles” [IV.2 ¶6] without naming them. A separate set of three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation) appears at II.1 ¶18; see that entry. The text does not say whether these are the same.

Identified with: Salt, Sulphur and Mercury [III.2 ¶28]

See also: Principles, Three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)

References: II.1 ¶24, II.1 ¶25, III.2 ¶28, IV.2 ¶6

Three principles

term — attraction, repulsion, circulation · Attraction, Repulsion, Circulation

The three principles of motion: attraction, repulsion as its reaction, and circulation arising from their conflict; equilibrium gives a circle, predominance an ellipse.

Attraction is the occult first principle of motion, and repulsion is its reaction. “Circulation is the third principle, proceeding from the conflict of the former two” [II.1 ¶18], and it mediates between them. When the two are in equilibrium the motion is a circle; when one predominates it is an ellipse. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or a source is speaking. On bringing the three into equilibrium, see ‘threefold secret’ [III.3 ¶9].

See also: Circulation, Principles, Salt, Sulphur and Mercury, Three principles

References: II.1 ¶18

Three worlds

term

The worlds Boehme says he knew and saw in himself; the printed passage names the divine angelical or paradisiacal world and the dark world.

Boehme, quoted: “I knew and saw in myself all the Three Worlds, viz., first, the divine angelical, or paradisiacal; and then the dark world” [III.2 ¶16]. As printed, the passage does not clearly name the third world.

References: III.2 ¶16

Threefold enchantment

term

Atwood’s term for how the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are bound together in man’s natural Identity; only the animal is developed to consciousness.

Atwood says man’s animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are “bound together in the threefold enchantment of his natural Identity” [IV.4 ¶4]. Only the animal is developed to consciousness.

References: IV.4 ¶4

Threefold Law of life

term

The law under which catholic nature necessarily proceeds; its ingress, egress and alternating action make up all the phenomena of the process.

Atwood says that nature “operates her proper progress necessitously under the threefold law of life” [I.3 n35]. The ingress, egress and alternating action of this law make up all the phenomena of the process.

See also: Life

References: I.3 n35

Threefold life

term

In Atwood’s Appendix, our life as threefold (sensuous, medial and divine), whose active, passive and resultant principles must each be evolved separately.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “Our life is threefold.” [APP ¶182]. The three are the sensuous, medial and divine lives, and each has its key and its representative. “Each principle of the life — active, passive, and resultant — must be produced or evolved separately” [APP ¶183].

See also: Life

References: APP ¶182, APP ¶183

Threefold secret

term

The secret of the Art that brings attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond.

Atwood: “great care and diligence is needed at this juncture to apply the threefold secret of the Art” [III.3 ¶9]. In context the secret apparently means bringing attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond. See ‘Three Principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)’.

References: III.3 ¶9

Thrysus

term · thrysus bearers

That in which Prometheus is fabled to have hidden the stolen fire; Atwood uses ‘thrysus bearers’ for those who have and perceive the fire but cannot draw it forth.

Atwood: “For, in the thrysus, Prometheus is fabled to have concealed the fire he stole from heaven” [II.4 ¶54]. The ‘thrysus bearers’ are those who “had the fire indeed, and were able even to perceive it, who were without the power to discover and draw it forth to manifestation” [II.4 ¶54]. She sets them against the ‘Bacchic souls’.

References: II.4 ¶54

Timaeus

person

Cited by Atwood as naming a certain earth as the principle, the most ancient element.

Atwood cites Timaeus as one who “mentions a certain earth as antecedent, and the most ancient element” [III.2 ¶35]. She uses this to illustrate a certain earth taken as the principle.

References: III.2 ¶35

Tincture

term · tinctured, tinctures, tincture of gold, tincture of the philosophers

The colouring, transmuting virtue of the work, or what carries it: the red, living soul drawn from the body, which turns imperfect bodies into gold and serves as the medicine of men and metals.

Transmuting product. Paracelsus, quoted, calls it “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76]: a heavy red powder with an astral fire that turns imperfect metals into gold better than mined gold, and that is also medicinal. He gives “a true sign of the tincture of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶76]. Atwood describes the tinging power that transmutes imperfect bodies as ending as “a most pure and rubicund tincture of the color of flesh and blood” [I.3 n42]: “our tincture is of blood coagulated, which blood is the boundary or satisfaction of hearts” [I.3 n42]. In the Boehme and Basil Valentine passages it is “a brilliant yellow, red, or purpling tincture” [II.1 ¶24], and “this true tincture of Antimony, which is the medicine of men and metals” [II.1 ¶25]. The Christian philosophers Atwood quotes name as their chief treasure “a certain exalted tincture with which the world, if it served God and were worthy of such gifts, might be tinged and turned into most pure gold” [II.3 ¶33].

Soul of the body. In the Hermes material, which Atwood glosses, it is the soul drawn out by the death of the first life: “whence the soul is ediced; which is also the red and living tincture taken from the body” [I.3 n12]. In the end it is “that tincture of many dyes which, being dissolved renews itself, and dying survives itself” [I.3 n18]. Its blackness turns “into the true red” [I.3 ¶43]. The ferment “holds the tincture lest it should fly” [I.3 ¶58], and the quintessence “becomes golden and aurific, communicating its tincture” [I.3 n63].

Boehme’s Tincture. Boehme, quoted, calls it “a Substance like water which yet is no water, but such a spirit or property: but it burns more like a kindred oil, and is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16]. He also writes: “this Tincture is the source of the material world, and gives to all essences virtue to grow” [III.2 ¶16], and “it is the most hidden thing, and also the most manifest” [III.2 ¶16]. It arises in the light: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24], and its thin water-form “is water, which is the desiring tincture” [III.3 ¶24].

Atwood’s own uses. Metals must have “their tincture set free in the subtle Origin of all life” [I.2 ¶49]. The philosopher’s Mercury is “communicative of tincture” [III.3 ¶32]. Spiritual fermentation multiplies tinctures, while common gold and silver “are not tinctures, but gross compacted bodies” [IV.3 ¶21].

Other voices. In Norton’s verse the word first means the colouring of glass [I.1 ¶52]. It is also “the tincture of holi Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10], and “He that would seek Tincture most specious Must needly avoid all things wild and vicious.” [IV.1 ¶49; cf. IV.1 ¶16]. In Eirenaeus’s verse it is a tincture “of silver fine” [III.3 ¶68]. The Master says of the Son-King: “Then is he transformed in his Tincture.” [IV.2 ¶14]; he takes it from the fire and death and becomes ‘of tincture super-excellent’. Eudoxus speaks of “the two mercuries which contain the two tinctures” [IV.3 ¶10] and says the Alcahest increases the metals’ tincture. The theosophist describes the dark Mercury as “tinctured” by light and love, so that death becomes triumphing life [IV.3 ¶38]. For the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine, see that entry.

Identified with: the soul educed by the death of the first life [I.3 n12]; boundary of hearts [I.3 n42]; medicine of men and metals [II.1 ¶25]; a Substance like water which yet is no water [III.2 ¶16]; Water [III.3 ¶24]

References: I.1 ¶52, I.1 ¶76, I.2 ¶49, I.3 n12, I.3 n18, I.3 n42, I.3 n63, I.3 ¶43, I.3 ¶58, II.1 ¶24, II.1 ¶25, II.3 ¶33, III.2 ¶16, III.3 ¶24, III.3 ¶32, III.3 ¶68, III.4 ¶10, IV.1 ¶16, IV.1 ¶49, IV.2 ¶14, IV.3 ¶10, IV.3 ¶21, IV.3 ¶38

Tincture of Sol

term

In Eirenaeus’s account, what the first water partly extracts from the body, taken as a sign.

Eirenaeus, quoted, says that the first water “extracted partly the tincture of Sol” [III.1 ¶14] from the body, and treats this as a sign. The records also note that ‘Tincture’ is elsewhere a name for Reason, and ‘foreign tincture’ what Reason grinds out of the inferior life.

See also: Sol

References: III.1 ¶14

Tincture of the Sapphiric mine

term

Atwood’s name for the cleansed, prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light; elsewhere, the Light from the Archaeus that comes forth as a dry splendour, identified with the Subtendent.

Atwood gives two related identifications. First, it is “the cleansed Augean, the already prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light” [II.4 ¶9]. Second, the Light from the Archaeus “comes forth as a dry splendour, surviving through all. And this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.3 ¶71]. The same passage equates it with the Subtendent: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71]. One passage names a receptacle and the other a light, and the text does not reconcile the two.

Identified with: cleansed Augean [II.4 ¶9]; medial receptacle of the newborn light [II.4 ¶9]; dry splendour (the Light from the Archaeus) [III.3 ¶71]; Subtendent [III.3 ¶71]

References: II.4 ¶9, III.3 ¶71

Toad

term · Toade

Atwood’s name for the putrefying stage of the matter, a stronger poison.

Atwood says the matter, “which putrefying, becomes a stronger poison, and their venomous toad” [I.2 ¶40]. ‘Toad’ thus names the putrefying stage.

References: I.2 ¶40

Tobit

person

The ancient book whose counsel Atwood cites to support the adepts’ practice of keeping the king’s secret close while revealing in part.

Atwood cites the book of Tobit for the adepts’ concealment of ‘the king’: it is “to be honorable to reveal the works of the Lord; but good t keep close the secret of a king” [II.1 ¶7]. She endorses this counsel and says she keeps within ‘the prophet’s advice’ while revealing only in part.

References: II.1 ¶7

Tractatus Aureus

treatise · the Golden Treatise, Tract. Aureus, Tract. Aureus. Text et Scholium, Tract. Aur., Scholium

The Golden Treatise ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, which Atwood cites for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy and repeatedly uses for chapter mottoes and supporting passages.

Atwood cites it as the Hermetis Trismegisti Tractatus Aureus de Lapidis physici secreto, in seven chapters. She uses it for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n10]. She takes chapter mottoes from it: “Opus vobuscum et apud est, quod intus arripens et permanens in terra vel in mare habere potes.” [II.1 ¶2] (our rendering: roughly, the work is with you and among you, and taking hold of it within you can have it). She also uses “Naturam in primisimitabere in arte, magister.” [III.1 ¶1] (our rendering: first imitate Nature in the art, master). On our tentative rendering of the corrupt Latin of this second motto (not the book’s), outer fire only excites, and an inner ethereal agent perfects all. She cites it for the ‘Our Mercury’ passage: “Our Mercury is philosophic, fiery, vital” [II.1 ¶12, II.1 n10]. She cites the Scholium in support of her view that external fire alters while internal fire perfects: “Que l’art imite la nature” [III.1 ¶42, III.1 n46] (our rendering: that art imitates nature). From cap. 4, “Protégé me et protegam te” [III.1 ¶44, III.1 n48] (our rendering: protect me and I will protect you) illustrates the mutual relation of Sun and Moon; the text does not name the speaker. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the author of the Golden Treatise seems to intermix the steps because he describes different repetitions of the fermentative process [APP ¶17].

See also: Author of the Tractatus Aureus (anonymous), Master (author of the Tractatus Aureus)

References: I.1 n10, I.1 ¶7, I.2 n25, II.1 n10, II.1 ¶12, II.1 ¶2, II.3 n40, II.4 n8, III.1 n46, III.1 n48, III.1 ¶1, III.1 ¶42, III.1 ¶44, APP ¶17

Tradition

collective voice — mythological antique devices

Ancient mythological tradition, which Atwood reads as commemorating spectacles of the soul’s liberation that Wisdom instituted and art makes natural.

Atwood treats myths as spectacles of the soul’s liberation that art makes natural. Her examples are the Salamander, Aeneas in Numitius, Pactolus and Midas, Medea and Jason, the Hesperides, Atalanta, Hercules and the Phoenix: “Such are a very few of the games and choice spectacles which tradition commemorates as instituted by Wisdom” [III.1 ¶70].

References: III.1 ¶70

Trance

term

The mesmeric state, which some writers suggest reveals the temple mysteries; Atwood treats it as a key not yet carried beyond therapy.

Atwood reports that some writers “suggest their Trance and its phenomena as a revelation of the temple mysteries” [II.2 ¶6]. She treats the mesmeric trance as a key that has not yet been carried beyond therapeutic use.

References: II.2 ¶6

Translation

term

The final passage for which contemplation of the indwelling Unity is the last preparation; its theurgic rite involves burying the body except the head.

Atwood calls contemplation of the indwelling Unity “the final preparative to translation” [II.4 ¶40]. She speaks of “the theurgic mandates for this translation” [II.4 ¶40], whose rite involves burying the body except the head. Compare ‘translation of the consciousness’ [APP ¶83].

References: II.4 ¶40

Translation of the consciousness

term

Atwood’s later definition of the whole mystery: consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The whole of this mystery is a translation of the consciousness” [APP ¶83]. She explains that consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.

References: APP ¶83

Transmutation

term · transmuting, transmuted, transmutes, transmutare

The conversion of metals into gold or silver; Atwood traces its possibility to a universal subject and reads it as life attracted into the Stone’s light, and the Adept equates it with salvation.

Historical sense. Atwood uses the word in its historical sense: the conversion of a metal into gold or silver. Rhasis practised it publicly (“on account of the practical displays he made of his transmuting skill” [I.1 ¶34]), and she reports that Avicenna did too. Of another practitioner she writes that “there is reason to believe that he practiced transmutation” [I.1 ¶66]. Parliament and papal bulls forbade it, “forbidding transmutation, on pain of death, and the pursuit of alchemy” [I.1 ¶55]. Aquinas, quoted, holds that “Metals can be transmuted one into another, since they are of one and the same matter” [I.1 ¶42]. He adds that it must be done “transmutare metalla scilicet imperfecta secundum veritatem et non sophistice” [I.1 n50] (our rendering: to transmute, that is, imperfect metals, truly and not by trickery).

Atwood’s theory. Atwood sets out to investigate “the theoretic ground and matter on which the physical possibility of transmutation rests” [I.1 ¶86]. She explains how the Stone acts: it “transmutes, i.e., attracts the same away from other forms into intimate coalescence with its own assimilative light” [I.2 ¶48]. The adepts, she says, have shown “the principle of Transmutation” to be “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

Salvation. The Adept, quoted, says: “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18]. Atwood completes the statement herself: a transmutation “of the component principles of life in the circulation” [IV.2 ¶18].

Identified with: Salvation [IV.2 ¶18]

References: I.1 n50, I.1 ¶34, I.1 ¶42, I.1 ¶55, I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶86, I.2 ¶48, IV.2 ¶18, IV.4 ¶2

Transmutative ferment

term

The ray of Light made concrete in life when it is dominant in the circulatory system; Atwood identifies it with the Philosophic Stone.

Atwood says the ray of Light, made concrete in life and dominant in the circulatory system, “is the transmutative ferment — even the Philosophic Stone” [IV.4 ¶9].

Identified with: Stone [IV.4 ¶9]

See also: Ferment

References: IV.4 ¶9

Transverse line

term

In Atwood’s Appendix, the line contrary to the Divine (perpendicular) line; it restores to sense, and the two together form a cross.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the transverse line against the Divine line: it restores to sense: “the transverse line is the contrary; the two united form a cross +” [APP ¶13].

References: APP ¶13

Tree of life

term

The Tree of Life: its attainment is laborious intellectual work (Van Helmont), and for Atwood it lies hidden and hard to find under the oblivion of natural birth.

Van Helmont, as quoted, says that “the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood herself writes that “The tree of life covered over, indeed, with the dark oblivion of this natural outbirth, is latent and difficult to find” [III.1 ¶34]. According to the reader’s record, she adds there that it is revealed only by celestial instinct, and that its bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken.

See also: Life

References: III.1 ¶13, III.1 ¶34

Trevisan

person · Trevisanus, Berhard Trevisan

Trevisan (Trevisanus), cited by Atwood for long, fruitless labour before success and for his image of the fixed watery Form as a marvellous fountain.

Atwood cites Trevisan as an example of one who worked in vain for over half a century until he found the separated Light [III.1 ¶37]. She also names him alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7]. In the footnotes, Trevisanus (spelled there “Berhard Trevisan”) is cited from his Opusculum. Atwood uses him to illustrate the fixed watery Form, his marvellous fountain, “shining like silver and of caerulean clearness” [I.3 n38, I.3 n39].

References: I.3 n38, I.3 n39, III.1 ¶37, IV.3 ¶7

Triad

term

In the quoted Chaldaic oracle, the threefold that shines throughout the world under the Monad’s rule, in which Virtue, Wisdom and Verity appear.

The voice here is the Chaldaic oracle, quoted by Atwood: “For in the whole world shineth the Triad over which the Monad rules.” [IV.2 ¶22]. The oracle goes on: “And there appeared in it (the triad) Virtue, Wisdom, and multscient Verity;” [IV.2 ¶24]. The reader’s record adds that all things serve its three Principles.

References: IV.2 ¶22, IV.2 ¶24

Triple introversion

term

A threefold turning inward which, together with multiplication of the hypostatic unit, makes the magistery manifest.

Atwood says the magistery is “made manifest by a triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit” [IV.2 ¶37]. The text does not explain the expression further. Reading it as a threefold turning inward follows the wording and is not a definition the book gives.

See also: Introversion

References: IV.2 ¶37

Triptolemus

person

Triptolemus appears only in a simile: Hippocrates spread Aesculapius’s remedies as Triptolemus spread the seed of Ceres.

Atwood’s only use of Triptolemus is in a simile. Hippocrates dispersed the succours of Aesculapius as Triptolemus dispersed the seed of Ceres [IV.3 ¶32].

References: IV.3 ¶32

Trituration

term

Grinding, used figuratively for the continual, slow and gentle working of the Philosophic Subject, which dissolves the subject’s innate defects.

Atwood uses the word figuratively, marking it with “as it were”. The aim is “by a continual mechanic trituration, as it were, to dissolve and ultimately obliterate its innate defects” [IV.1 ¶5]. She applies the point “especially to the trituration of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶13]. The record for that passage says this working should be slow, gentle and continuous. The context suggests that the word stands for the continual working of the subject, not for literal grinding.

References: IV.1 ¶13, IV.1 ¶5

Troics

person

Cited for reference only.

References: I.1 n36

True Alchemy

term

In the Appendix, Atwood’s term for Theosophy on its physical side, as opposed to the alchemy the world has sought without finding.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Alchemy (not that which the world has run after without finding) is related to Theosophy on its physical side” [APP ¶78]. According to the reader’s record, she describes it there as a change in the circulatory system of the blood wrought by reiterative contritions.

See also: Alchemy

References: APP ¶78

A True and Faithful Relation of what passed for many years between Dr John Dee and some Spirits

treatise

Cited for reference only.

See also: Spirit

References: I.1 n76, I.1 ¶67

True being

term

The Platonists, as Atwood reports, declared true Being to be white.

Atwood reports a view of the Platonists: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9].

See also: Being

References: III.2 ¶9

True chemistry

term

The genuine art, as distinct from “clouds of sophistry”, whose Light and virtue helped the ancients.

Atwood speaks of “that Light and virtue of true Chemistry, by which the ancients were assisted” [III.1 ¶4]. The reader’s record says she sets this genuine art apart from clouds of sophistry.

See also: Chemistry

References: III.1 ¶4

True fiery water

term

In Aliphili’s words, an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which alone dissolves gold into black earth; called the great and miraculous mystery of the world.

The voice here is Aliphili, as quoted. The reader’s record gives his account: an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which dissolves gold into black earth, and nothing else does this. Aliphili names it “the great and miraculous mystery of the world; that is the true fiery water” [II.1 ¶14]. This gives the identity: true fiery water = the great and miraculous mystery of the world [II.1 ¶14].

Identified with: the great and miraculous mystery of the world [II.1 ¶14]

See also: Water

References: II.1 ¶14

True form of gold

term

The real object of Alchemy’s golden promise; avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it.

Atwood contrasts the true Form of Gold with the dead metal: “neither will be found to be the true Form of Gold” [III.4 ¶11]. According to the reader’s record, she makes it the real object of Alchemy’s golden promise there. Avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it. The text does not define it further here.

See also: Gold

References: III.4 ¶11

True hypostasis

term

Apparently the real being or substance of oneself, which self-contemplation with an unpurified spirit cannot discern.

Atwood warns that if we contemplate ourselves with an unpurified spirit, “we shall not there discern the true hypostasis” [II.2 ¶14]. The reading as the real being or substance of oneself is inferred from this context, not stated.

See also: Hypostasis

References: II.2 ¶14

True Identity of nature

term · identity

The identity in nature that the pseudo-alchemists failed to divine, which would otherwise have to be sought through all creatures by experiment.

Atwood says the pseudo-alchemists worked “without rightly divining the true Identity of nature” [II.1 ¶6]. Without the one subject that contains all, one would have “to search out the identity through all creatures and minerals, by way of experiment” [II.1 ¶9].

See also: Absolute Identity, Identity

References: II.1 ¶6, II.1 ¶9

True intelligible

term

The proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself, which the wise mind holds within itself; the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.

Atwood glosses the term herself: “(since it possesses the true Intelligible); that is to say, the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself” [II.1 ¶37]. This gives the identity: the true Intelligible = the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself [II.1 ¶37]. According to the reader’s record, the wise mind holds it within itself, and the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.

Identified with: the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself [II.1 ¶37]

See also: Intelligible

References: II.1 ¶37

True intention

term · Intention

That on whose discovery the success of the experiment depends; it is present more or less in every mind, though not clearly discernible in all.

Atwood says that success “depends on the discovery of the true Intention” [IV.3 ¶54]. According to the reader’s record, she adds that it is involved more or less in every mind, though it cannot be clearly distinguished in all.

References: IV.3 ¶54

True knowledge

term

In the Appendix, the mind’s experimental contact with mystery, in which the mind consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Knowledge is experimental contact of mind with mystery” [APP ¶75]. According to the reader’s record, the mind there consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle, with an efflux of life.

References: APP ¶75

True light

term

The Light needed before practice; hidden and imprisoned within, it is called the fountain of Universal Nature, and is perfected in the Saviour.

Atwood uses the term in three passages.

  • Needed before practice. Those who failed worked “without the true Light or heeding their injunctions” [I.1 ¶86]. It is not explained there.
  • Hidden within. She speaks of “the true light shut up as in a prison, the fountain of Universal Nature” [II.1 ¶49]. This gives the identity: true light = the fountain of Universal Nature. According to the record, the senses’ outward attraction keeps this light apart from understanding.
  • In the Saviour. She quotes “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19]. According to the record, the Light is perfected in the Saviour, and one ray of it cleanses our life.

The text does not say outright that these three uses are one and the same.

Identified with: the fountain of Universal Nature [II.1 ¶49]

See also: Light

References: I.1 ¶86, II.1 ¶49, IV.2 ¶19

True man

term

In Rabbi Ben Jochai’s words, man as distinct from the man who appears here.

The voice here is Rabbi Ben Jochai, as quoted: “But we must distinguish the true man from him who is here apparent” [II.1 ¶42].

References: II.1 ¶42

True matter

term

The material and proper Subject of the Work, hidden under countless names; finding it is called a great point.

The passage says: “It is a great point to find out the True Matter and proper Subject of this work” [IV.2 ¶6]. This gives the identity: True Matter = proper Subject of this work. According to the reader’s record, it is hidden under countless names and is not named here. The voice is unclear. It may be Atwood, or she may be continuing a cited author, since the next sentence reads “adds our author of The Triumph”.

Identified with: proper Subject of this work [IV.2 ¶6]

See also: Matter

References: IV.2 ¶6

True medicine

term · medicine

In the Paracelsians’ view, a medicine bound in man like milk in a hard nut, which must be freed from impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.

Atwood reports the Paracelsian view: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶10]. According to the reader’s record, it is held there like milk in a hard nut. It must be freed from its impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.

See also: Medicine

References: III.1 ¶10

True rector

term

That which the Art restores to its original rule by hiding the opposing principle; not otherwise defined.

The Art is said to work “to restore the true rector to his original rule” [II.1 ¶21]. According to the reader’s record, it does this by hiding the opposing principle. The voice is unclear, and the text does not define the term further.

References: II.1 ¶21

True science

term

In the Appendix, the identity of knower and known, of subject with object.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Science is the contact identical of the thing knowing with the thing known, subject with object.” [APP ¶171]

References: APP ¶171

True sulphur

term

In Eirenaeus, the means by which the purged Mercury is vivified; not explained further.

The voice here is Eirenaeus, as quoted. Of the purged Mercury he says: “And with true sulfur it can vivify” [III.1 ¶69]. The text does not explain the term further.

See also: Sulphur

References: III.1 ¶69

Truphat

term

In Paracelsus, the matter of the metals, which brings everything into its due form.

The voice here is Paracelsus, as quoted: “The truphat, or matter of the metals” [I.2 ¶25]. This gives the identity: truphat = matter of the metals. According to the reader’s record, it brings everything into its due form.

Identified with: matter of the metals [I.2 ¶25]

References: I.2 ¶25

Truth

term

In the Appendix, Light in its own ether: the Divine Wisdom made visible to itself.

This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “Truth is, as it were, Light in its own ether, the Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous” [APP ¶171]. This gives the identity: Truth = Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous.

Identified with: Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous [APP ¶171]

References: APP ¶171

Truth-telling Oracle

collective voice

Atwood’s name for the Chaldaic oracles (Oracula Chaldaica), which she cites on piety, the fiery mind, and the soul’s way of return.

Atwood cites the truth-telling Oracle from the Oracula Chaldaica in II.3. She uses it in support of these points: piety and the fiery mind preserve the body; the soul’s way of return; the warning against stooping down; and the soul clasping God. One line she quotes is “If thou extend the fiery mind to the work of piety,” [II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶38, II.3 ¶40, II.3 ¶42, II.3 n46, II.3 n47]. She cites it with approval.

See also: Oracles

References: II.3 n46, II.3 n47, II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶38, II.3 ¶40, II.3 ¶42

Turba

treatise · Turba Philosophorum

The Turba, whose maxim that all the wise seek is in Mercury serves as a chapter epigraph and is taken up again in the text.

Atwood quotes the Turba (Ecercit. 1) as the epigraph of chapter I.2: “Est in Mercurio quicquid quaerunt Sapientes” [I.2 ¶1]. In modern English (our translation): whatever the Wise seek is in Mercury. She takes the maxim up again in [I.2 ¶12].

References: I.2 ¶1, I.2 ¶12, III.1 n2

Two natures

term

In the theosophist’s words, a heavenly and an earthly matter, to be reduced to one as they were at the beginning.

The voice here is the theosophist, as quoted: “That Two Natures be reduced to One, as they were at the beginning.” [IV.3 ¶38]. According to the reader’s record, the two are a heavenly and an earthly matter.

References: IV.3 ¶38

Two principles

term

Two principles that stand against each other if the Chaos is split apart too early; not named here.

Atwood warns that if the Chaos is split apart too early, “the two Principles stand up one against the other, before the intended mastery is secure” [IV.1 ¶15]. She does not name the two Principles here.

See also: Principles

References: IV.1 ¶15

Two-fold ignorance

term

In Plato, as quoted, an ignorance that does not know it is ignorant and therefore has no desire to emerge.

The voice here is Plato, as quoted. He describes an ignorance “which being ignorant that it is ignorant has no desire to emerge” [II.2 ¶13].

References: II.2 ¶13

Twofold death

term

Porphyry’s distinction, reported by Atwood, between common death, freeing the body from the soul, and philosophic death, freeing the soul from the body.

Reported from Porphyry: “there is, says he, a twofold death” [II.3 ¶37] — the common death, in which the body is freed from the soul, and the philosophic death, in which the soul is freed from the body. The voice is Porphyry’s as cited by Atwood.

References: II.3 ¶37

Types

term · elementary types

Apostolic ordinances or material signs, such as water, oil, salt and light, which Atwood says signified real efficacies but later became a source of dissension.

Atwood says that in apostolic practice “certain ordinances and elementary types, as of water, oil, salt and light, signified some real and notable efficacies” [I.1 ¶26]. She also calls them material signs, and says that “these very shadows and types of doctrines” became a source of dissension [I.1 ¶26].

References: I.1 ¶26

Typhon

term

In the Osiris fable, the brother who kills and scatters Osiris; applied to the work, the wrathful fire or Efficient of dissolution, and the unclean Instrument that putrefies the gold.

In Atwood’s reading of the fable, Typhon is Osiris’s uterine brother, who kills and scatters him. Applied to the work, he is the wrathful fire or Efficient of the dissolution, and also a name for the unclean Instrument that moves the gold to putrefy. Isis gradually enthrals him [III.1 ¶63].

Asserted identities:

  • The adepts’ names: “Adepts call him the Green Lion, Typhon, Firedrake”. And “or during the mortification, he is their venomous Black Toad” [III.1 ¶56].
  • As the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy: “it is called by them Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities, etc.” [III.1 ¶61].
  • “they gave to Typhon, in this predicament, the name of Seth, Bebo” [III.1 ¶63]. These names import “a certain violent, forcible restraint, contrariety, and subversion” [III.1 ¶63].

Atwood presents these as the adepts’ names, set out in her own exposition.

Identified with: Green Lion, Firedrake [III.1 ¶56]; Black Toad (during the mortification) [III.1 ¶56]; the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy; Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities [III.1 ¶61]; Seth, Bebo [III.1 ¶63]
