Identified with: vital power [APP ¶11]

References: APP ¶11

Wine

term

In Khunrath, the thick, black substance of the first act, called the Blood of the Earth and identified with the Red of Lully.

Khunrath (quoted) describes it in the first act as “thick, dense, and black, blacker than black” [IV.1 ¶36]. It is “the Wine which the Wise have called the Blood of the Earth”, “which likewise is the Red of Lully” [IV.1 ¶36]; it is called Red for its tincture, the color of its virtue.

Identified with: Blood of the Earth [IV.1 ¶36]; Red of Lully [IV.1 ¶36]

References: IV.1 ¶36

Wisdom

term · Sapience, Sapientia, Divine Wisdom, Demiurgic Wisdom, hidden Wisdom, Wisdom of Antiquity, Wisdom-life

The object of Atwood’s inquiry: the ancient internal Wisdom, the true being of Intellect and self-knowledge, identified with Salt, the substance of the Stone, and the Root of Reason.

Mostly Atwood’s own voice. Wisdom is “that Wisdom we are investigating”, identified with Isis and Minerva [III.1 ¶5]; by its Light nature’s universal efficient is revealed [III.1 ¶3]. It is the highest faculty: “The term Intellect, as it is here taken in its highest sense, is synonymous with Wisdom” [II.1 ¶39]; “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37]; it is “not conversant with a certain definite existing thing but simply with all things” [II.1 ¶37]. Ancient science’s theme was “the standard of truth in a rectified intellect”, Wisdom being “an affirmative operative hypostasis, informing, invigorating, and sustaining all things” [II.1 ¶44] and “the offspring of a vital experiment into nature” [II.1 ¶52]. Hermes (as cited) calls it “the good, the fair, and the blessed Eternity” [II.1 ¶43]. It is “not worldly” [II.2 ¶13], intuitive Intellect without imaginative error.

For the method, Atwood ties it to the Stone: Wisdom “was the worthy object of all Hermetic Philosophy, and the miraculous substance of its transmutative Stone”, and “not without weighty cause has Salt been dignified with the name of Wisdom” [III.3 ¶50]; “this same Root of Reason is Wisdom, and that saving Salt” [IV.4 ¶20]. From Ecclesiasticus and Solomon (quoted): “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49]. It is “the vehicle of the Catholic Reason in Identity, the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [III.3 ¶71].

Moral conditions: “No impure leaven (need we repeat it?) can enter into Wisdom” [III.4 ¶7]; the covetous flee “Wisdom’s fiery ordeal” [III.4 ¶11]. “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36]; it is given by God “and send thy Holy Spirit from above” [IV.3 ¶39], the gift of perfecting the work [IV.3 ¶48]. It is “a thing acquired, the reward only of peculiar and arduous discipline” [IV.4 ¶17], “above science, art, and every other kind of faith”, the Well of Heraclitus and the Nothing Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27]; yet “the Wisdom of Antiquity has disappeared from amongst men” [IV.4 ¶28].

Quoted views: Asclepius Trallianus calls it “a certain clearness” [II.4 ¶26]; Reuchlin: “Nothing is in the beginning but Wisdom, or Sapience”, called Ain by the Hebrews [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi says none can tell “in what manner she is contained in non-Being” [III.2 ¶32]. In the Appendix (later layer) it is “a pure exemplar from the first Light or Life, showing man what he ought to be” [APP ¶90], the great Salt Sea or Universal Will [APP ¶94], and the Law of Light’s emanating spirit [APP ¶47].

Further asserted identities: Intellect and Divination [II.1 ¶35]; the intelligible essence [II.1 ¶37]; Pythagoras’s “science of truth which is in all beings” [II.1 ¶39]; “the breath of the power of God” [II.1 ¶44]; “the fear of the Lord” [III.1 ¶8]; Understanding [IV.3 ¶47]; Reuchlin’s Three Persons in Divinity [III.2 ¶10]; the Rabbi’s Principle [III.2 ¶32]. With Sendivogius, God inspires his Wisdom into philosophers [II.4 ¶39]; Atwood also personifies her as a bride the philosophers wooed, bringing a dowry of creative light [IV.4 ¶10].

Identified with: Law of Light; its emanating spirit [APP ¶47]; Universal Will / great Salt Sea [APP ¶94]; Intellect (highest sense) [II.1 ¶39]; Intellect, Divination [II.1 ¶35]; the intelligible essence [II.1 ¶37]; knowing oneself [II.1 ¶37]; the science of truth which is in all beings [II.1 ¶39]; the good, the fair, and the blessed Eternity [II.1 ¶43]; the standard of truth in a rectified intellect [II.1 ¶44]; an affirmative operative hypostasis [II.1 ¶44]; the breath of the power of God [II.1 ¶44]; Intellect diving intuitively without imaginative error [II.2 ¶13]; clearness [II.4 ¶26]; Isis / Minerva [III.1 ¶5]; the fear of the Lord [III.1 ¶8]; Three Persons in Divinity [III.2 ¶10]; Ain [III.2 ¶10]; Principle [III.2 ¶32]; Worker of all things [III.3 ¶49]; substance of the Stone [III.3 ¶50]; Salt [III.3 ¶50]; Understanding [IV.3 ¶47]; Root of reason [IV.4 ¶20]; saving Salt [IV.4 ¶20]; Well of Heraclitus [IV.4 ¶27]; Nothing [IV.4 ¶27]

See also: Faculty of Wisdom, Hidden Wisdom

References: II.1 ¶35, II.1 ¶37, II.1 ¶39, II.1 ¶43, II.1 ¶44, II.1 ¶52, II.2 ¶13, II.4 ¶26, II.4 ¶39, II.4 ¶40, III.1 ¶3, III.1 ¶5, III.1 ¶8, III.2 ¶10, III.2 ¶32, III.3 ¶48, III.3 ¶49, III.3 ¶50, III.3 ¶71, III.4 ¶11, III.4 ¶15, III.4 ¶7, IV.3 ¶36, IV.3 ¶39, IV.3 ¶47, IV.3 ¶48, IV.4 ¶10, IV.4 ¶14, IV.4 ¶17, IV.4 ¶18, IV.4 ¶20, IV.4 ¶26, IV.4 ¶27, IV.4 ¶28, APP ¶47, APP ¶67, APP ¶90, APP ¶94

What, Atwood says, the ancestors sought and experimentally found through subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects.

In Eudoxus, the three closely analogous works of the Art, each repeating dissolution, removal of blackness, whitening and vivifying.

term

In the theosophist’s teaching, one of two principles in everything, predominant in outward nature since the fall and to be subdued as servant to the light.

Xenophanes

person

Reported through Aristotle as first to introduce the doctrine that the One is God, and dismissed there as rustic.

As reported via Aristotle, Xenophanes first introduced the doctrine that “the One is God” and was dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

Z

Zachary

person · Zacharius

Author of an Opusculum whom Atwood cites on long searching for the key, on prayer before the Work, and on one method, matter and vessel.

Atwood cites Zachary’s Opusculum as another example of long searching for the key [III.1 ¶37, III.1 n42]. With approval, she cites him that one should read the philosophers and pray, yet use means: “for no one ever acquired this art by chance, but by prayer rather than by other means” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n17]. Against many furnaces and vessels: “there is indeed but one way of working, in one matter, one linear way throughout” [IV.1 ¶9, IV.1 n12].

Zeno

person

Cited by Atwood for the ether as plastic, generating fire, and, within Vaughan’s lessons, for listening much and speaking little.

Atwood cites Zeno for the ether as an artful generating fire: “Ignem esse artificiosum, ad gignendum progredientem via” [I.2 ¶16] (ours: that fire is artful, proceeding methodically to generate). Within Vaughan’s lessons he is quoted: “Nature gave us one tongue and two ears, that we might hear much and speak little” [III.4 ¶44].

See also: Zeno of Elea (not the Stoic)

Zeno of Elea

person — not the Stoic · Zeno

Cited by Atwood in support of the absolute unit as the ground of Being.

Atwood cites him in support: “if any one should undertake to demonstrate the philosopher’s Unit, he would unfold Being” [III.2 ¶45].

Zohar

treatise · Liber Zohar

A work Atwood cites on the formless Divinity, the Initial Principle as Wisdom manifesting by a point of Light, and the celestial prototype in humanity.

Atwood cites the Zohar in support: Divinity has no form before descent into creation, so no image may represent Him [II.3 ¶48, II.3 n52]; the Initial Principle is Wisdom or the Supreme Crown, the Unknown who manifests — “he begins by producing a point” — with its white appearance [III.2 ¶3, III.2 n3, III.2 n4]. The Liber Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” and shows the covert fire in Holy Writ [II.1 ¶40].

Zoist

treatise

person

His magic is described as the service of the gods [II.1 ¶51]. Atwood identifies with the Stone or Salt “the Prester of Zoroaster which in the Chaldean sense means the Fire Spirit of Life” [II.3 ¶54]. She identifies with the magnetic chain “that ladder of Celsus and of Zoroaster which reaches from Tartarus to the highest Heaven” [III.2 ¶54].

References: II.1 ¶51, II.3 ¶54, III.2 ¶54

treatise

Oracles used as a chapter epigraph exhorting the reader to the Light.

Used as the chapter epigraph: “It behooves thee to hasten to the Light, and to the beams of the Father” [II.4 ¶2].

Zosimus

person

An Egyptian reputed a great practitioner, named among authors of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone.

Named as an Egyptian reputed a great practitioner [I.1 ¶29], and listed with Heliodorus, Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras and Archelaus among authors of extant treatises on the stone [I.1 ¶27, I.1 n34].

References: I.1 n34, I.1 ¶27, I.1 ¶29
